name: A Way Out
detailed_description: PLAY ON STEAM USING THE REMOTE PLAY TOGETHER FEATURE From the creators of Brothers – A Tale of Two Sons comes A Way Out, an exclusively co-op adventure where you play the role of one of two prisoners making their daring escape from prison. What begins as a thrilling breakout quickly turns into an unpredictable, emotional adventure unlike anything seen or played before. A Way Out is an experience that must be played with two players. Each player controls one of the main characters, Leo and Vincent, in a reluctant alliance to break out of prison and gain their freedom. Features CHOOSE YOUR CHARACTER - LEO - A hardened inmate with escape in his sights, Leo isn't the type to make friends. No matter the obstacle, Leo is willing to get his hands dirty and do whatever it takes to get the job done. VINCENT - Even though he’s fresh off the prison bus, Vincent is determined to break out. With quick wits and nothing left to lose, he'll prove that he's not to be underestimated by anyone, inside prison or out. TOGETHER THEY'LL FIND A WAY OUT - Escaping prison with a complete stranger isn't ideal circumstances, but Leo and Vincent have too much riding on it to second-guess themselves now. As freedom gets closer and closer, they'll have to learn to trust each other if they want to make it to the other side. WORK TOGETHER TO BREAK FREE - Use teamwork to solve puzzles and overcome obstacles. EXPERIENCE A VARIETY OF GAMEPLAY - Sneak, fight, run, drive, even go for a little fishing along the way. Note: THIS PRODUCT IS CO-OP ONLY. Play the entire experience with your friends using Steam's Remote Play Together feature.

_childDocuments_.review: is a solid story driven split screen co-op experience that plays more like an interactive movie for a large majority of the game. This however doesn't take away from the brilliant narrative displayed by it's main characters Vincent and Leo or the immense amount of fun to be had within this awesome game.I originally played through  not long after it's initial release on the Origin client (my only actual purchase on EA's Origin service to date) with a close friend and decided upon a recent sale to pick the game up again on the Steam client in order to play through it again with the same friend but this time swapping the characters we played with on the first playthrough.While the entire game is great, I believe this game really does shine for it's mini-games. Spending a large majority of the time played enjoying games such Connect 4, Grenade Brothers, Baseball and a variety of others.Through many plot twists and turns,  truly does stand out among other games for it's incredible story and is well worth looking into if you have a good friend to play it with.If I were to list any downside to the game, it would be it's unskippable cutscenes (even after you've finished the game multiple times), a lack of ability to injure/kill friendlies (not counting letting enemies kill your friend) and perhaps a bit too much in the way of locked combat/animation. Aside from those and the fact that my Steam achievements were instantly unlocked due to it binding with Origin achievements (I already had them all), I don't have many complaints for this game and I would happily play through it again in the near future.

_childDocuments_.review: is a heavily story-driven action-adventure game that tells the story of two convicts,  and . The catch is that the game is playable only in co-op. The game supports both local and online options, and you can use  to stream it to your friend, or you can use  on , where your friend just needs to download the game files, and you will invite him to your lobby. You can also play with random people online, but you cannot play it alone.The whole game feels like a good action film with several interesting plot twists. The story itself starts in a prison where both  and  ended up because of a guy called . As their path crossed during a few incidents, they decided to work together, escape the prison, and find . Both characters are unique in their own way as  is more of a guy who first acts rather than thinks, and  is the exact opposite of him, which leads to several humorous and a bit unpredictable situations. I would say that their personality is interesting and likable, as I was interested in their problems and related side characters, like family members. On the opposite, the villain  is just an uninteresting figure who does not have any depth at all, and the game would prosper from fleshing out his character more. There are also a few situations that do not make sense, and they break my immersion a bit. For example, if a character has another person as a human shield, its weapon’s ammo is unlimited, and he does not reload it at all. However, even with all these problems, I enjoyed the story, as  and  journey was thrilling and emotional. In the end, I will remember some story twists for a while.I highly recommend playing this game with your partner, friend, or another relative, as it adds a lot to the experience rather than with random people. The game lasts about , and I would say that the length is just right. I could probably argue that one more hour could help flesh out some characters, but it would still be quite short. Most of the time, you have to go through small open locations and finish the task to continue to another section. One of the most used gameplay mechanics are quick-timed events, which are surprisingly done right, and there is no tremendous button mashing, so that is a plus. However, do not expect some complex gameplay or mechanics. This game relies on quick-timed events and short different elements. The gameplay is tailored to fit the story, you will not find here difficult puzzles as in  series or more complex combat options as in  series. The game is very forgiving, and the checkpoints are very common.Throughout the chapters, the game changes the environment, tasks, and gameplay activities a lot. The co-operation of both players is very important as you cannot finish the game without it. There are a lot of easy environmental puzzles that fit the narrative and linearity of the game, but I would still wish for at least a few more complex tasks. Sometimes the game lets you deal out with enemies via stealth or shooting. Unfortunately, AI is quite stupid, so you can rush through the area quickly and knock them out. As for shooting, the gunplay is quite good but a bit easy, as well. However, sections, where you drive vehicles, are a bit harder as you mostly fight the camera (this, especially, applies to the bikes). I would welcome some difficulty settings, at least for the enemies. If you are looking for a challenging co-op experience, then you will not find it here.The game also offers various activities and minigames, which are only present in specific chapters. For example, you can throw darts, play videogames, interact with others, and much more. I am not going to name them all, but it varies a lot throughout the chapters, and it keeps the game fresh and interesting. Even if you decide not to do them, you will still receive a fair amount of diverse gameplay.Sometimes the game offers you a choice to continue in certain situations differently. It changes cutscenes and gameplay a bit, so small replay value for at least one more playthrough is here. To put a clear picture, you might decide if you will try to cross the bridge with the police in a car, which is the fastest but more dangerous variant, or if you will go underneath the bridge. Speaking about choices, the game also has two endings, but none of the previous choices matters, as they are more about how do you continue your journey gameplay-wise rather than about longtime story effect. The thing I disliked about this mechanic is that both players have to actually choose the same option. If two players will not choose the same thing then you wait until one of you decides to side with the other player. The game should have implemented an RNG system that would choose in such situations.The second thing I did not like much about the gameplay is how the screen is split in half even in online co-op. I understand this is necessary for local co-op, but it is a bit irritating as your screen is smaller for the whole game. There were few occasions where the game actually let play only one player and the scenes transmitted rather than being cut in half. This option was way more enjoyable and film-like. It would probably also add a bit to the difficulty, as you would not have an option to look to your partner's side.The game looks great graphics-wise. It offers several beautiful sceneries and cutscenes which might be comparable to films. There are several animations for different situations, and they are properly fleshed out. The only minor issue is that you can drive through a few branches during car chases which destroys an immersion a bit, and I would not expect this in this linear short game. As for the sounds, the sound effects themselves are of high quality. As for the soundtrack, there are few compelling compositions, but nothing memorable. The game was tested with an , running at high settings at  frames per second, at  resolution. The game ran without any problems and crashes. However, the connection with  servers caused troubles a few times, as sometimes my partner got kicked, and I could not invite her again, as  did not show her in online status. For a short game like this, it is pretty annoying but, fortunately, the game has many save spots, so you can jump right back to where you ended.Even with the aforementioned shortcomings, I can still easily recommend this game, especially if it is on sale. It is an enjoyable, thrilling, and captivating story-driven experience, and I wish there would be more games like this.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the nuttiest game I have played in my 20 years on the planet. While it may initially appear as just another co-op puzzle game, it actually serves as a unbelievable crossover of every enjoyable game mechanic synthesized so beautifully that it manifests as a gift from God himself. If you want to drift bikes like in Mario Kart, headshot bad guys like you're AWP'ing in CS, and/or absolutely demolish your 'co-op' partner in Connect 4, this game is for you. 10/10 would recommend.

Click on the button named: Environment Variables5. Press the 'New' Button in the System Variables6. Then enter the following name in Variable name: OPENSSL_ia32cap7. Then set the Variable value to the name: ~0x200000008. Find a friend and enjoy the game :)9. Your Welcome

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10!I brought this game only thinking that the story would be about a prison break, well I can tell you now it definitely isn't. Me and my mate played it and we both really enjoyed the story and was very interested in what was going to happen next. The camera design they have gone for is like something I've not seen before considering you can see your friends game and what they are doing, I thought that I would find it quite annoying but honestly after playing it for 30mins it doesn't even bother you and it actually quite a cool little design. Some of the transitions they have put in the game when the camera changes is amazing and very well done. This is also a game where once you have completed it you will want to play again to see the different outcome. I would 100% recommend this game if you have a mate to play with. The only bad thing about this game is it isn't that long and you can complete it in about 5 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Unlike some comments about this game, I'm not here to talk about EA stuff. I want to share my thoughts on the game itself.I played this game with my best friend, and it took us about 5.5 hours to finish, with just a few short breaks. We had a blast with it. The game is great because it offers a lot of different things to do, like mini-games and activities. The art and visuals are lovely, and the voice acting is top-notch, making the whole experience immersive and memorable.One thing to keep in mind is that the story takes a surprising turn, so I'd recommend not watching any videos or spoilers before you play. That way, you can enjoy the game to the max on your own.In a nutshell, I really recommend this game, especially if you have an awesome friend to play it with, like mine.

_childDocuments_.review: A way out is a very innovative multiplayer cooperative game. Before this game, I never thought that a multi-player cooperative game could have such gameplay - as the predecessor and exploration of the It takes two, this one no doubt showed us the possibility of the split screen game.The gameplay of the game is not very innovative, but these gameplays combined with split-screen play can bring players a unique gaming experience. The plot of the game is unexpected and exciting, and I'm not too impressed with the music. The game's picture and graphics quality and rendering level are very good, and you can enjoy a visual feast.Finally, this game is not very suitable for playing with strangers, I think playing with friends is the only way to get the complete game experience. Another shortcoming of the game is that the game duration is relatively short, but this game will not let you down. At the same time, as the developer's first attempt to split-screen games, there are many places in the game that more or less make players feel that this is an experimental game, and perhaps players also need to be tolerant.

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique online co-op story driven game from Hazelight. I haven't played anything like A Way Out before. The game heavily relies on co-operation of two players in order to advance throughout the entire story. Sure the game might feel outdated in terms of mechanics and AI but it was released back in 2018. _childDocuments_.review: A Way Out is exclusively a co-op (local or online) adventure game articulated mostly around cinematics, quick-time events and action / exploration sequences. As mentioned, it requires two players, but only one of the two needs to purchase the game: there is indeed a friend's pass that allows you to share the pleasure with any interested friend.The story revolves around Vincent and Leo, two inmates with distinct personalities, who decide to collaborate in order to escape prison and soon realize how intertwined their destinies is. And two strong personalities mean two different approaches to most situations; up to you and your partner in crime to decide which one suits your playstyle the best.In my humble opinion, one of the finest features of this game is the gameplay diversity. Expect the unexpected: not only you participate in thrilling chases, shooting or 2D brawls, but also more peaceful activities like fishing or playing board games are available. There's also puzzle-solving, such as sneaking a tool into your cell together. All this in a split-screen fashion, which might bring a nostalgia value to some. And if not, don't worry: you'll quickly get used to it!Despite a length of just around six to eight hours to complete the game, the charismatic and endearing characters, the captivating story and plot twists, the entertaining and changing gameplay manage to create a unique atmosphere that keeps you spellbound and magically makes time fly. Let's also not forget to mention the punctual mini games, such as arm wrestling, darts or arcade games; an amusing way to take a break and add some spicy competition between the two players.A Way Out is a masterpiece brought to us by scenarist and director Josef Fares, whose games are, in my book, simply a must-play. If you don't know them already, there is first of all , a lovely game to discover by yourself or with a partner in local co-op only. Then, there is Game of The Year 2021 - another heartwarming split-screen co-op adventure.Do I recommend A Way Out? Absolutely! I can't express enough the surprising and positive impact the game had on me on my first playthrough. Since then, I've replayed this game with two other friends and each time was a wonderful experience for both of us. Do yourself a favor and dive into Josef Fares' universe.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: If you love Telltale games but always thought they'd be way more fun in co-op, then  is for you!This is a co-op only, narrative adventure game in which two prisoners team up to escape prison and extract revenge on a Big Bad Guy. Great fun if you're looking for a movie-esque gaming experience with a buddy and a beer. You can play local or online, but note that this game will require you to install and run the Origin launcher despite being on Steam. The upshot of this is that you only need to buy one copy of this game to play together -- even for online play (the other player can download and run the Origin Friend Pass to access the game without added cost.)There's lots of quick-time events that require that you time your key clicks with your friend and a bit of light stealth is required at points, but otherwise the game is quite linear so there's no room for creativity. You're just along for the story here. As such, the game is short and probably not going to be replayed unless you want to play with a different friend later. Still, really good for a one-off Friday night chill game.

_childDocuments_.review: The best split-screen co-op game so farBefore you consider buying this game, make sure that you have a friend or family member that is willing to play hours of this game with you, because this is a co-op only game.A Way Out is a one of a kind game. Usually, massive story-driven games are only for single player and it's hard to share the kind of experience that these types of games give you. A Way Out, however, allows you to experience a massive story-driven game with a friend. Playing the two characters gives completely different perspectives on the story. The two characters often get separated and do unique things while still kind of connected. Playing a different character after finishing the game gives a completely different version of the game.All the levels are creative and use split-screen co-op's advantages to its best. The cinematic camera angles and changes of screen placements are pleasant and well designed. In the hospital level where the players take turns to controls their characters in full screen, the use of cinematic transitions and long camera shots are amazing. The different choices that the players can vote on could have some influence on how the game plays. These choices don't change anything major, but they make some parts of the levels different.The story of A Way Out is great and the endings are unexpected and emotional. The characters are pretty well made, and their emotions seem real. There are many mini-games scattered around the story for the players to compete with each other. Some of them are not well made, but it's always fun to mess around with a friend and have a little fun.At some later parts of the game, the characters get guns and start shooting people. The aiming is a bit weird, especially if you are playing with a controller. Those parts just feel like a cheaper and more boring version of Uncharted 4 without all the grappling hooks and moving around the environment.There is barely any game out there that targets split-screen co-op as a major selling point except for A Way Out. I highly recommend trying it out with a friend or family member. I hope there are more good co-op story-driven games like this in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest, beforehand, I actually expected something completely different coop-/gameplay-wise from this extremely famous title. But was I disappointed after finishing it with my wife? Nah, can’t really say so. Definitely still a good and recommendable piece of art. I guess you just have to know what you’re getting into. You see, it’s not really a complex game, in most levels it’s mostly about exploration, discovering all the minigames (which are fun to play against each other) or finding different ways to solve a situation. Often the goal is just getting from one place to another, or mastering short skill sequences (which are really easy and casual, actually good when you’re playing with your inexperienced spouse or child). It’s also quite short. But aside from all these aspects, I think where it probably shines the most is in its storytelling, the mechanics and the visuals. Never saw a title before where splitscreen works so tremendously well (normally I dislike this option, because it reduces the view, but not here). And seriously, how the story develops, and how the whole game design works together with the coop concept, still makes A Way Out a milestone in this category that’s absolutely worth playing. After all, it paved the way for the brilliant masterpiece It Takes Two, and is also a worthy successor to Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons (huge recommendation for both of those titles from the same devs as well of course).

_childDocuments_.review: "A Way Out" offers a truly unique gaming experience centered around cooperation. The gameplay mechanics are ingeniously designed to require constant collaboration between two players, making it an immersive co-op journey. From solving puzzles together to executing daring escapes, every moment demands teamwork, fostering a deep sense of camaraderie. The variety of gameplay elements, including stealth, action, and exploration, keeps the experience fresh and engaging throughout.Visually, "A Way Out" delivers a captivating experience. While not striving for hyper-realism, the graphics are stylized to convey the game's gritty atmosphere effectively. Character models are expressive, and environments are richly detailed, enhancing immersion. The use of lighting and dynamic camera angles adds cinematic flair to key moments, making the game visually stunning without sacrificing performance.The atmosphere of "A Way Out" is nothing short of gripping. From the tense prison breaks to the emotional highs and lows of the narrative, the game keeps players on the edge of their seats. The soundtrack complements the action perfectly, heightening the emotional impact of each scene. Whether traversing lush landscapes or navigating treacherous urban environments, the atmosphere remains consistently immersive, drawing players deeper into the story with every twist and turn.At its core, "A Way Out" is a story-driven experience that excels in its narrative execution. The plot follows two unlikely allies, Vincent and Leo, as they embark on a daring escape from prison and navigate the challenges of life on the run. The characters are well-developed, each with their own motivations and conflicts, driving the story forward with compelling momentum. The game's branching narrative ensures that choices matter, offering multiple paths and endings that encourage replayability. Overall, the plot of "A Way Out" is a masterclass in storytelling, keeping players invested from start to finish.1. Unique co-op gameplay mechanics that require constant collaboration between players.2. Stunning visual design with expressive character models and detailed environments.3. Gripping atmosphere that keeps players engaged from start to finish.4. Well-developed plot with compelling characters and branching narrative paths.5. Cinematic presentation with dynamic camera angles and an immersive soundtrack.6. Varied gameplay elements, including stealth, action, and exploration, ensuring a diverse and engaging experience.1. Limited single-player experience as the game is designed exclusively for two players.2. Some players may find the gameplay mechanics overly reliant on cooperation, potentially causing frustration if playing with an incompatible partner.3. Certain sections of the game may feel linear, limiting the sense of freedom in exploration.Occasional technical issues or glitches may disrupt immersion for some players.4. Limited replayability once the main story is completed, as the branching narrative paths may not offer enough significant differences to warrant multiple playthroughs.

He won Game of the Year for his next game after this, It Takes Two.This is a man that speaks to me, as a gamer. And in practically every scene, we were in awe at the presentation.Starting with the small things, like seeing each other's button prompts (he was using a PS4 controller so I saw those on his side, while seeing Xbox on my own side.) to bigger things, like the split screen changing focus whenever an important scene played on one side, as if to say "Hey! Pay attention."At no point did this game hold back or struggle to experiment - The puzzles, the action, the stealth. In no way were these difficult, but they were incredibly effective at feeling rewarding to the player nonetheless. And that's only the gameplay side of it. _childDocuments_.review: A Way Out is a co-op exclusive narrative game where you and another player play as one of the two main prisoners, Leo and Vincent. Just to preface this review, I'll refrain from any sort of revealing details in an attempt not to spoil the game. The story is a troubling affair for me. The interactions, settings, and banter throughout the story were superb. However, the whole overarching story felt fairly standard, and the ending was quite a letdown. If the characters weren't so charming, then I doubt that many people would be raving about the story as they do currently. It certainly isn't a bad story, but it has a decent bit of points that are less than impressive. The gameplay is fairly standard for this sort of game. You have your quick time events, rapid button pressing, basic platforming, and more. There are even sections where you can do more involved gameplay elements, such as driving vehicles or shooting guns. Honestly, it's what you would expect from this sort of game from the trailers and concept behind it, but still. The graphics here look pretty good. They aren't exactly hyperrealistic, but they fit just right with the scenario the game is going for. The sound design is also pretty solid, but nothing that will really stand out to you. Overall, this is a pretty solid co-op game. If you have a good friend or someone else to play with, I recommend trying this game, as it is likely one of the best story-based co-op games out there. It may have its downsides, but that is mostly easy to overlook with how enjoyable the co-op experience is and how expressive the main characters are.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though the game's brilliant mechanics seem bluntly obvious in hindsight, A Way Out was kind of a revelation when I first started playing. Most co-op games I've experienced involved playing  to somebody else, where your respective lines rarely intersected in a significant way except during combat when you both happened to whack the same guy. A Way Out tangles up your lines and throws the two of you into sticky predicaments where you have to  together, and not just fight together. Communication and coordination are very important and you are just as dependent on your companion's poor timing as they are on your shoddy aiming. This results in some genuinely tense collaborative moments and a good amount of laughter (under which some quiet grumbling can be tucked away) when things don't pan out.Fortunately, the game is fairly easy as its main focus is the narrative and the interaction between the two protagonists. The story is the third protagonist by the way, and it provides the perfect premise for your synchronous shenanigans. But it also does so much more, as it is the main driving force behind the whole game, propelling your characters into one scruffy escapade after another. The puzzles and fights you encounter, while very light on gameplay, are woven cleverly into the narrative. Your mutual efforts feel practical as well as natural, and reinforce the two men's cooperation through your own blundering attempts at assisting one another. The sense of striving and failing together seeps from the real world to the game world, smudging your own feelings over your character's in a nebulous blend, and creating an incredibly immersive and convincing co-op experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun interactive co-op adventure. It's like playing through a B tier movie in the best possible way. There are intense action and emotional scenes and times where logic goes out the window, but it's all to make it a fun ride. The ending has a surprise twist that I think made the story better, but my co-op partner didn't appreciate it as much.The gameplay is minimal, it's mostly to drive the story forward with QTEs (some of them synced in co-op), easy controls, some driving and shooting sections. Levels are linear, but exploring them is still fun with the easter eggs and mini games.For achievement hunters:There is a chapter select and all achievements are for doing certain tasks. You can finish all of the achievements 1.5 to 2 hours before finishing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start by saying that this is a fantastic game when it comes to story telling and character development. I enjoyed playing through most of the game with my friend, and we both grew very attached to the characters.The issues that both of us have are that the storytelling and character traits shown throughout the game take a dive out the window for the last 2-3 chapters.Spoilers ahead.Everything makes sense until you get to the twist. It seems like the game was built around the premise of the twist without properly thinking about how to make it fit the story and make sense. The game makes you go through multiple rounds of shooting at each other in various settings hoping that you are so shocked by the reveal that you don't realize neither of these characters have a reason to KILL one another.Vincent get's taken hostage by Leo, they drive off a bridge, then Vincent gets in a Helicopter as Leo boats away. What would you do at this point? The obvious answer shouldn't have been to shoot at the boat to make it explode. Likewise, when the boat DOES explode (you can decide to not shoot it, it will explode of it's own volition) you both take up two sides of a building to shoot each other. This entire scene is just so that you can get to the rooftop for the final chapter, it doesn't matter who does well at shooting their friend as the final choice is decided by a button mash contest. (Turns out that isn't entirely true. Thank you to Misery for informing me that the person who get's hurt more has a harder time mashing.)If you choose Vincent to live you get a scene of him visiting Leo's wife and child for a sob moment, for him to then go to his wife who will take him back in an instant. He hands her his 'resignation letter' and she's finally ready to let him in.If you choose Leo to live, he walks away from the building (guess the police gave up chasing him) and hands a letter, that Vincent had written for his wife, to his wife. (Side note: he had to have re-written the note or else the blood stain would have remained, but it doesn't matter because Vincent DOESN'T GIVE THE LETTER TO HIS WIFE IN HIS OWN ENDING!). Afterwards he drives away with his family (guess the police gave up chasing him).I understand there is weight to the argument 'if it made you angry then it's doing a good job of making you feel' but it's not doing it in the right way.It set up a twist but didn't think about how actual people would react to such a betrayal from someone they grew to trust, both with their secrets and their family.It didn't handle the player versus player scenario well because none of the fighting mattered, and it cheapens the final scene.It's a wonderful game, until the twist is revealed. Play it until that point and then just close the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I got enjoyment out of this game in the same way as I get enjoyment out of watching a bad film with friends. After seeing good reviews everywhere I really thought it would be a good one to play with my partner, but 5 hours later we're both left pretty disappointed. The gameplay was bland, the story cliché, and the 'teamwork' was questionable.The coop was supposed to be the interesting core of the game, but there were only 1 or 2 interesting coop 'minigames' in the entire playthrough. For a game that was designed for 2-players, it still feels like the "coop" is just bolted on.  The vast majority of the "puzzles" were "we need both of us to knock down this door" or "give me a leg up so I can reach", or "help me lift this log that we could totally climb over individually" - basically amounting to "come stand next to me and press a button at the same time as I do". This isn't teamwork that requires 2 person communication, it just means two people have to be present. The interesting ones that actually required a minor degree of skill and cooperation were very early in the game (one person looking out for guard while another is chiselling a wall, for instance). No puzzle required any thinking past "interact with everything that the yellow dots float over". The amount of 'gameplay' here was very minimal, so it played more like a slightly-interactive movie.That would have been fine if it were a good movie, but the story is just "OK". It's somewhat interesting to watch the development of the relationship between the main characters, but it doesn't really seem to go much further than the first half of the game. Transitions to new scenes are done with such little care that the plot just feels like its just bolted together with no real overarching story that makes any sense. Individual scenes can be engaging, and interesting (like the basketball scene), but I didn't feel like it fit together well into a larger story. No player choice actually felt like it made any difference, especially in the long run, and all plot development gets thrown out of the window in what was a thoroughly disappointing, and un-immersive ending. Towards the end of the game we were laughing at scenes that would have been emotional if they had been properly developed.Onto the more technical aspects: the main character voice acting is decent enough, but some of the side characters are bad, lacking emotion. Graphically, the game is pretty good, and the animations are smooth and cinematic for the most part. Some of the set-pieces are quite impressive, if totally ludicrous and unbelievable, like the hospital scene. There are some other cool cinematic scenes that (although forced), are fun. There are a decent number of different locations (for the relatively short playtime of 5-6 hours) that add a nice visual variety. And it was as short as 2/3 films, so I don't feel like I was massively cheated out of my time - we finished the playthrough and it was mediocre, we went through it together, and got that 'multiplayer' sociality that is always a positive. I just can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: A Way Out is a coop story driven game where two players work together to achieve their goal.This is exclusively a coop game, I have nothing against it but I think it should have a solo mode which shouldn't hurt and only would make it to sell better.The game plays in split-screen despite if you're playing local or online. There are some spoiler sensitive scenes I can't speak about where this didn't make any sense.The story is quite good, it comes from the developers of Brothers a Tale of Two Sons. There are two characters – Vincent and Leo. They meet in the prison and decide to break out of it for revenge.From the very beginning you need to learn to work together to bypass various situations and threats. While the game is mainly story driven I wouldn't call it a fully narrative experience. There's quite some gameplay there and it's pretty diverse. Mostly you'll be walking around or sneaking while figuring out how to get to where you need. Which isn't hard by the way, there are no real puzzles. But it has other gameplay mechanics like rowing the boat, driving and shooting. While all of these usually are very poorly executed in similar games, here they work well. Of course don't expect super deep driving physics or shooting mechanics but driving feels smooth, sometimes it feels like a proper racing game. And shooting is also decently done and isn't clunky at all, mostly it works as cover based shooter.Gameplay changes often and there's always something new so the game doesn't become boring or repetitive.You do stuff by pressing or tapping buttons, sometimes in perfect sync with another character, there are no moments when another character has nothing to do. There are sections when one character is more busy than the other but at these moments you still can explore the surroundings, speak with people or play some mini-games. There are mini-games for both players too. Oh and i encourage you to speak with people since that leads to some funny dialogues and little stories. On top of that there are easter eggs which are tied to achievements and roughly half of them are really fun to do because they lead to some short cut-scenes, mostly funny ones.In general gameplay is nearly perfect and has perfect amount of everything, calm moments of silence, talking, action, running and so on. It feels like a really long movie.Graphically the game looks good. Surroundings are beautifully crafted with lots of small details around and things to interact with while character models are good but could be better, it's nowhere near Man of Medan or Quantic Dream games. Although facial animations and expressions are quite good.Performance is perfect, game runs on max settings at 90-100fps easily, played on 5800x, 2070s, 32gb @3440x1440. There's ultrawide support but it's weird. Sometimes when there's a scene of only one character the image is in correct aspect ratio but smaller with black space around it. But there are some moments when the screen space is fully utilized so ultrawide works.Voice acting and sound are good too. Music feels like it's from a movie and plays along nicely with the mood of the scenes. Voice acting sometimes could be ok only but mostly it is good.Overall a very good coop story driven game with diverse gameplay, cool movie-like action scenes and dramatic moments. Definitely worth a buy. Not at full price though since the game is short and has no replayability value. Achievement hunting and another ending could net you an additional hour or so since it has chapter select but that's it.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game with a friend and we both enjoyed it a lot!Definitely too short for the expensive price but if you get it on sale (got it for 9€) then it's really worth it! ~7 hours to finish the story while taking your time and messing around a little. You are two inmates, one who just got incarcerated and another one who has been there for 6 months already. You quickly realise that you both ended up in prison because of a crime boss named Harvey and you decide to escape prison to take revenge on him.The prison is actually just a small part of the game, your adventure will go much farther than those walls! The characters will get to learn about each other and decide on what to do to reach their goal. The story is kinda typical but there are some twists that we personally didn't expect at all. In any case it was very enjoyable and we were completely immersed in it (you feel it when you or your partner is in danger!). The screen is split in two so you can both see what the other is doing and when something important is happening to one character then his screen will extend and cover the other one for a bit. The same thing will happen if there is a shared cutscene, but this time making the two screens fuse. This feels a little weird at the beginning, but you quickly get used to it and it's really nice to see what the other is up to, especially when you split up.The story is divided into scenes/chapters. You go to a place, you do this, then you move on to another scene. You can usually mess around in the scenes and they are big enough to not feel trapped. But it does feel sometimes that you are jumping from one to another a bit hastily.The two characters have very different personalities and will not react the same way to things or dialogues. One is reckless while the other is more cautious. Sometimes when choosing a way to pass an obstacle you'll have to choose which character's plan to follow. But it's also in the little things: when prompted a character will break the locked window while the other will try to find another way. The choices, even the little ones, really help with the immersion.There are several puzzles (ex: how to get this thing out of this room without the guards noticing). From what I have seen, there are always several ways to reach your goal.There are some action scenes too, where you need for example to run away from things. Again, we were really into it and trying hard to succeed. If you fail though (which happens rarely because the emphasis is clearly put on the story/adventure and not on the challenge), you will be brought back to a nearby checkpoint.There are lots of little things scattered through the levels to have fun with your partner. There are often silly things: cut the wood because... why not? Play a board game or darts with your partner and get the highest score. And as silly and useless as it sounds, we would always seek them out to try them, because they were actually fun. Little hidden things throughout the levels; like tell this to that person, play that game, get this score, do this silly thing... Nothing annoying. You can replay a specific level so it was really easy to go back and get them all after our playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: A Way Out is a cooperative adventure story game developed by Hazelight and published by Electronic Arts. It was released in March 2018. Introduced to A Way Out at The Game Awards 2017, Game Director Josef Fares made a comedic appearance in an interview at the show. I suppose its marketing achieved its aim, it showed Fares’ personality and brought attention to, at that point, his upcoming game.A Way Out features a story focussing on Leo and Vincent, two prison inmates that are planning to break out of prison. Purely in co-op, Leo and Vincent are disparate individuals. Leo prefers violence and fighting, contrast to Vincent being diplomatic. This juxtaposition shines in the concept of the story, from their voice acting, such as Leo’s brashness and Vincent’s calm demeanour, to their dialogue and how both prefer to attack the task or react to a situation. Their character development throughout the story was engaging and the climax of the story, emotional.Bringing Leo and Vincent into the narrative, A Way Out’s six-hour story is logical, yet an expected progression, but it results in an immersive and tight story. The context is finely introduced, including how Leo and Vincent went to prison and their motives. Through this character development and foreshadowing, the story builds to an excellent ending that is a fitting end and had a hint of cliffhanger. A Way Out uses cutscenes as its main storytelling tool and it works incredibly well in the co-op context, feeling like an interactive movie.The co-op system is fantastic and integrated incredibly well into the story and gameplay mechanics. The split screen underpinning the co-op allows both players to explore the world. For example, when entering into a cutscene, the screen adjusts to the character in the focus. It is a seamless transition and one optimised very well, only encountering rare stutters in cutscene transitions. The split screen also does not feel cluttered when both characters are doing actions simultaneously, but I think it could have benefitted from players entering into dialogue concurrently.Accessing A Way Out before starting the game however, could have been better explained. It was not overly clear your friend had to download the game through Origin, after several attempts of trying to access it on Steam.A Way Out’s art style and graphics quality is really good. The textures are colourful and clean and the environments are beautifully detailed and eye-popping. The colourfulness and vibrancy of the scenes improve as the game progresses, highlighted in the scenes I conclude by noting A Way Out is an excellent co-op adventure complemented by a seamless co-op system that is integrated very well into the gameplay. Leo and Vincent are superb personalities, backed up by an engaging cast of other characters and an overall straightforward, but thrilling story. For $39.95, I recommend this at full price.9/10• Logical and tight story supported by a positive juxtaposition in Leo and Vincent• Cutscenes and the integration of co-op into the gameplay• Beautiful and detailed environment and colourful textures• Accessing co-op could have been better explained

_childDocuments_.review: A Way Out is a cooperative game in which two players take on the roles of prisoners who decide to work together to escape from prison and get the common enemy. In the gameplay itself, there are quite a few cutscenes, which allow you to get into the role of your character, you get to know their stories in part.The co-op itself often relies on proper synchronization, there aren't too many logical puzzles here, although a few times you have to think about what to do to move on. Overall, the co-op itself performs very well, but it's nothing special or sophisticated. It is worth noting that the co-op takes place on a shared screen. For most of the game it is a vertical division, but towards the end it meets more often horizontal division, which in my opinion performs worse, but it is not too much of a handicap.I personally do not like the linearity in this game. And while the ending of the game I understand and do not have too much objection to it, I did not like the fact that our decisions rarely affected the further fate of the game. What's more, there was often no way to go about something other than the game punishes us. I understand that the game is based mainly on a fairly well-written story, but such linearity was quite noticeable.A Way Out is definitely a good game that I quite enjoyed playing, although it looks to me more like an interactive movie where we can occasionally do something to keep our characters from getting hurt than a game. The linearity hurts a bit, but the story makes up for it, being interesting and engaging.

_childDocuments_.review: A Way Out is a unique action-adventure game that will keep you and your friend entertained for a few hours. Hazelight Studios made its debut with Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons but no one was expecting another offline split screen co-op game back in 2018. It's innovative for the time it came out mostly due to its unexpected ending. However, it is also important to mention that the each section in game feels like tech demo with unique scenarios. It will also keep you on edge almost all the time thanks to its setting. Its gameplay is perfect and serves its purpose as intended. You get to control your characters in split screen, go back and forth between them in well-designed action and combat sequences, and help each other in most cases. You'll bond with each other during the game and feel connected until... Yeah, let's talk about the story a little bit. Both Leo and Vincent end up in prison for several reasons but there is one particular reason that draws them to each other: revenge on the one who made their lives slightly harder than it's supposed to be. They both leave their families behind, their lives behind to get their revenge. With cops on their tails, things won't be in their favor most of the time of course and it is up to you, and your friend to get them out of the tough situations. We had a lot of fun with my friend while playing this. It's a masterpiece and an emotional rollercoaster in my opinion and I'm pretty sure it will leave most of you satisfied as well!

_childDocuments_.review: is a wild ride if you've got a friend who’s down for a co-op experience that's as much about sharing laughs at the game's flaws as it is about escaping from prison. The game’s story is nothing groundbreaking—honestly, it's full of clichés and B-movie dialogue that you can predict a mile away—but it’s that cheesy charm that somehow makes it fun.The game’s forced split-screen co-op can be a blast, especially with the variety of mini-games and the way it creatively uses the screen space. But, be warned, the mechanics are pretty basic, and at times, it feels like you’re just going through the motions. Despite that, the dynamic between the two main characters, Vincent and Leo, keeps things interesting, and the game is at its best when you and your partner are figuring out solutions together. It’s far from perfect, but if you’re willing to overlook its flaws, A Way Out is a memorable experience that’s best enjoyed with a good friend on the couch

_childDocuments_.review: A Way Out is a coop, advanture-action game, where two inmates trying to get out from prison, but they have common goals after that.I played this game with my friend on Steam Remote Play.First thing which surprised me, is the story in general. It's really well made and not that expected. The actions what the characters do and their motives are understandable and almost everyone got a role in the story. I don't want to say anything, but it's really well made, story is not too long or boring at any part, really well played.Another thing which also surprised me is the gameplay. I really thought this game will be a shooter or something, but had lot of different game elements, minigames, secrets to find. Incredibly varied game, and indeed requires to do the teamwork with your partner. The coop works good, however the splitscreen can be a bit annyoing, but this idea wouldn't be possible to do otherwise. There are bugs, like some checkpoints load in buggy, most of the scences are scripted, which in a few places, you can break them, but this is not too bad. Need to mention, that the gameplay is somewhat strict, but in this game I wouldn't mind it. Really fun gameplay!Sound and musicwise also kicking! I really liked the soundtrack, fitted for the action, sound effects were not boring at all. The voice actor did their job perfectly.Controls is pretty easy in this game. You won't need to use lot of buttons. I played the game on Keyboard and Mouse and I can definetly recommend to use it like that, because the game has some shooter sections. My problem with the game, was with the controller controls. In general it's fine, but the shooter sections are horrible. Not too bad, but definetly not like Keyboard + Mouse. I didn't mentioned that, in our case my partner used PS4 controller, but my game showed the XBOX buttons somehow, which was not changeable. Also there is one motorbike section, which had horrible controls, but in general it was fine, except these problems.Last thing is the graphics. In general the game looks really fine, but sometimes it has low textures or things in the distance are not good looking. Sometimes the characters' hair looked weird because of the low "looking" graphics. In general this also fine.A Way Out is a short game with it 5 hours of gameplay, but surprisingly one really fun and joyful experience. Story makes this game lot better and the fun gameplay makes it memorable. If you want to find a coop game for a day, I can definetly recommend to play this. Sadly, after playing it, it will lose it's magic but this is definetly an amazing experience. For 30€, it might be too much. I would play 20, so I suggest you to buy it on sale for an amazing experience!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic co-op game to play with a friend. The game is very scripted, but in a good way. The outcome of actions is pre-determined, but you can choose how you want to get to the outcome, which is a lot of fun.The pacing of the story is great, constantly switching between exploration, puzzle-solving, and action sections. I love the amount of detail in the game. You're ALWAYS rewarded with fun little things by exploring the environment. There are a bunch of little minigames, like throwing darts, playing music, or (best of all) CONNECT 4. This stuff is great, especially because most cutscenes are 2-player, meaning one person is in a cutscene and the other still gets to look around the environment, so neither player gets bored.And don't even get me started on the writing. All of the character interactions with Vincent and Leo are priceless. Leo's writing is especially hilarious, and it reminds me a lot of Valve's script writing.By the end of the game, you'll have a much stronger bond with the person you're playing with.It seems that nowadays, high quality 2-player co-op games are a rarity, but A Way Out gives me hope that the genre can still be successful.

_childDocuments_.review: The technical graphics of the game are acceptable and I have rarely seen any problems in the game. In addition, it should be considered that the game is co-op, and working on the gameplay will be much more economical! But don't worry, considering all the expenses that EA has incurred, we still see beautiful scenery and exciting scenes. Remember what the focus of the game should always be. The textures of the faces and the environment are of good quality and there is nothing to worry about, but anyway, the quality of the secondary characters' faces could have been much better. Of course, apart from the quality, it should also be noted that in some cases, we see very unbalanced physics. It is true that this sometimes caused discouragement and surprise, but considering the history of the director and the overall shape of the game, this problem can be ignored. I would like to point out that yes, many of A Way Out's problems are passable. Because of the productive experience and of course the unique pleasures that are hidden in the game; Of course, if you are not a strict person! But on a more detailed and rigorous review, with all the money that EA spent on Josef Fares and the game development team known as Hazelight, there are some bugs in the game that sometimes really put you off. In addition to all this, the next problem can be found in the lighting of the game! The lighting of A Way Out seems to be something like the early titles of the 8th generation or even a little lower, the general and casual lighting of the environment is very reminiscent of the old games and the lack of work of the previous creators. Anyway, if Josef Fares wanted his game to be accepted by more fans, he should have worked more on technical graphics.Creativity reaches its peak in some stages of the game and may surprise you. The details are cultivated enough to be a means of your enjoyment as much as possible. The environments of the game are also large enough to become the scene of your skirmishes and cinematic sequences. Even the characterizations are at a respectable level and contrary to all the rumors, you experience crazy emotional scenes. Characters who each have their own story, but when they are together, they present you with a wonderful combination of emotion, love and anger.In addition to the beautiful moments you will experience, add beautiful music to be as close to its shell as possible. Usually, the whole process you will go through is summarized in minigames and main stages. The main stages are very, very well structured, not repetitive, and most importantly, designed with a lot of patience. In addition to the main stages, many mini-games are included in the game, each of which looks more attractive than the other.A Way Out is a highly respected and valuable title. Despite the game's physics issues, and some discouraging technical issues, A Way Out is still one of the biggest, and perhaps best, co-op titles of the 8th generation. Because if you want to look at this work optimistically, you have to remove many useless flaws, and look at the wonderful experience you will have with your friends.

_childDocuments_.review: A Way Out presents itself like a prison escape game, which it is not. By the time our anti-heroes meet there is already a plan and means of escape ready to go. You do a couple of simple co-op tasks and you're out. On multiple occasions the co-op tasks didn’t make sense. The game would tell you via prompt or character line, that player 1 has to do something to help player 2, without any base for that action. It would tell player 1 to open some door for player 2 but player 1 never got that information via game-play. Player 1 character just randomly decided, that they have to open this door to help the other guy, with nothing to base that decision on. We never saw, or heard any plea for help. Are those guys clairvoyant?The game then tries to get you hooked by developing several characters and giving them some depth. It mostly works fine and I have no major complains as far as character development goes. However, the plot then takes a sharp left turn and you realize that you have little to no influence on the direction of the main story. That wouldn’t normally be an issue to me but the game has this annoying way of pretending as if you do. To the point where it forces the player to hold a button to aim, and then press another button to shoot an unarmed character, who has their arms up. Execution style. There is no reason to kill that character, you could let them go or capture them. But the game makes you kill them and then has the audacity to blame the player for what it forced them to do. It becomes comical as you can let go of the button mid aim and watch your guy lower and raise the gun repeatedly while the oh so dramatic music plays in the background.There is no depth to co-op. Open the door by pressing the button at the same time. Help your mate up. Catch him when he’s falling etc. Basically it comes down to holding or pressing a button during the same boring action throughout the entire game.Graphics wise A Way Out looks to be about ten to fifteen years old. To the point you have no choice but to remark how butt ugly it is. Some areas look nice but god help the team who made that atrocious store cut-scene right after prison escape. The entire store was just a mess of blurry textures and rectangles. GTA3 style.It took us two sessions to finish the game, 6h total. If you want to play couch co-op, get something else. This was a waste of time and we were left unfulfilled.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, here it is, a game from two years ago that I actually never heard of until (obviously) a friend randomly asked me to play it and here we are.A Way Out is a pretty fascinating, maybe one of a kind game where you need a co-op partner to play the game at all, it's required to have a friend who also owns the game in order to play it. Hope you have friends! So on the face of it that's a pretty interesting little thing, and when designing the game with this in mind the developers had a lot of opportunities to do things that might otherwise simply be a divergence from regular gameplay in another game, but in A Way Out it's all like that. Everything's a co-op challenge.I should probably put somewhere in bold that the guy who wrote/directed this game (and he INSISTS you remember it because his name appears, solo, at the top of the credits first and foremost) Josef Fares, is uh, I don't know if he egotistically likens himself to Tommy Wiseau and embraces his own self-made reputation as a hack fraud of a writer, but part of the 'appeal' of A Way Out is certainly that... the dialogue and the story are extremely dumb, and the interactions between many of the characters and the voice acting for most of them is sub-par. It mostly adds to the charm, fortunately.You (and your buddy) play as two guys. Leo and Vincent. Leo is a dumbass and Vincent is the smart one. There's a fun dynamic between the two and their relationship reasonably realistically develops throughout the game - mostly. As said above the dialogue in this game and the story is poor. The scene to scene events of the game and the way the two main characters interact is really nothing short of stupefying when you think about anything that happens for more than a moment or two, such as the transition from pursuit by the cops to just immediately sitting down and taking their ease so the characters can get to know each other, just weird pacing all around.The framing deserves a special mention perhaps more than anything else. A Way Out uses split-screen throughout the entire game, occasionally interrupting play by splicing in an extra frame to show you something happening somewhere else in the area. Even when you're playing online, the split-screen effect is there so you can see what your buddy is up to, and in some points actually seeing what your friend can see is crucial to progress. Since you can always see two player's perspectives, you can sometimes get twice the amount of information as to guard routes or simply what items are around.So as for the actual gameplay which is the most important part, it's... alright. A fair amount of the game is walking around with your buddy and then interacting with an object and then you both tap a button or hold it or something to open a door so you can progress. Aside from the stealth and action sequences, there's a lot of walking around and interacting with objects, either to progress or simply just for fun - one key feature of the game is that you can play around with a bunch of stuff. This is important usually when one character is busy doing a plot or progress related thing, and the other player can talk to an NPC or throw darts or something to pass the time so you don't get bored. It's clever.A Way Out probably would get boring if all you did was pass button pressing challenges, so the devs made sure to move things along relatively rapidly, and you never really get bogged down with one gameplay mechanic for too long. This game contains a ton of different 'scenes' I suppose where you run away from cops, or sneak around cops, or shoot bad guys or whatever, and they're all pretty fun to play out. None of them really last long enough for you to get bored or frustrated, but by the same token it means that when a section is really working for you and you're enjoying it, you might be disappointed when it ends so fast.I assume that EA was so uncertain of A Way Out succeeding, that they officially entitled it an 'EA Originals' game, I guess like how Netflix has 'Netflix Originals' or whatever? Anyway, it's a very odd distinction for the game, I presume they wanted to distance themselves from it enough so that if the game flopped it wouldn't damage their brand, but they wanted to be able to say here, this is an EA game, this is ours, if it totally did well in revenue.One thing that surprised me is the level of polish. 'Hazelight Studios' is apparently a pretty low employee count development studio? There's not that many people that worked on this, but the graphics are pretty good in general and the game is mostly pretty solid. It's well done. It doesn't quite feel like a triple A title, but it's almost there, it's nice enough that it doesn't feel like an indie game.The plot of the game, in short, is very simple. A couple of guys bust out of jail to go take down a guy that double-crossed both of them. That's about it. The entire game is pretty focused on this, and it feels a lot like a relatively formulaic buddy cop movie, though I suppose your characters are antiheroes going after a much worse bad guy. It has the distinct fingerprints of someone who has watched a lot of movies, and is now trying to make a big budget American action movie, and they're just failing and falling short because they just don't know how to be creative, they're just doing things that they've seen before because those big American action movies have those things. It's funny and satisfying to laugh at, and that is the thing that keeps the game fun and enjoyable up to the end: honesty. Everything in A Way Out is deliberate, rather than sarcastic or ironic. I disliked the ending because unfortunately the writer tried to be too clever, cleverer than he actually is, but it'll just leave you unsatisfied rather than ruin the experience.There's really not that much more to say. The gameplay is the main reason to play it, I think. It's pretty good, I had fun with it, even if I didn't like the ending.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this by saying that I don't think  is as good as most the reviews seem to suggest.That being said, I do think it's a very good game and I do recommend playing it. is  co-op and it shows. The cooperative aspect of the game was fantastic, but everything else felt like it existed only to support the fact that the game is cooperative or just as an afterthought.There are a bunch of mini-games to play through the story where you will either play against your partner or try to score higher than them. Dialogue options with NPCs will also be different for Vincent and Leo.This game is perfect if you want a story-driven game to play with a friend or significant other, where you won't be constantly waiting on the other person. The entirety of the game is synchronous and will put emphasis on one player or the other in original ways. That being said, there are actually not many puzzles that will actually require you to communicate. Most cooperative interactions will simply require both characters to press a button. I suppose the way you feel about this really depends on your expectations of the game. The game does advertise "Use teamwork to solve puzzles and overcome obstacles." as one of its features when in reality this only applies for the first half of the game.While the game was very apparently not developped by a big AAA studio, it does look really good. It's more stylistic than realistic and it works very well. There's a nice contrast between the cold prison and very warm and beautiful exterior sceneries, which made up for the often rough character animations.My main gripe has to do with the story and dialogue. I have seen a lot of people compliment it, but it was in my opinion the weakest part of the game. The overall story is interesting and does expect a few unexpected twists, but is filled with clichés and very simple ideas. Everything screams stereotypical over the top action movie.The two protagonists are textbook antiheros; Two prisoners attempting to break out of jail. They put aside any sense of morality to achieve their goal, killing hundreds of people on their way. This fact alone would be enough to break my immersion; I really dislike casual murders in action movies. But you learn very early on in the game that their main motivation for breaking out of jail is... To murder someone. It's honestly so hard to relate with the characters or anything they stand for.It wouldn't be so bad if it was a typical cat-and-mouse story, where both sides are equally intelligent and competent. But in this case, nearly everyone except for the main characters are seemingly void of personality or any form of intelligence. There is an incredibly large amount of police officers who:So you watch the story unfold, kind of hoping your characters will get caught, but no one seems to be much of a threat. There are interesting twists but none of it feels particularly beliveable.It was certainly not the greatest game I've ever played and similar story-driven games like Quantic Dream's three games are on a completely different level of quality. But I enjoyed my experience nonetheless. Just manage your expectations if you don't want to be disappointed.The game is currently 10$ CAD, 75% off of 40$ and can be finished in about 6 hours. Definitely worth it for that price.

_childDocuments_.review: A Way Out is a cooperate two player adventure that has you working together as partners.  You start the story as two people in jail who become friends and who concoct an escape plan.  The plan is to escape and to find and kill the mutual enemy that you both have.This game offers an absolutely amazing gaming experience.  The gameplay itself is not phenomenal, but the interactions between the characters, the character development, and the overall storyline are what truly makes this game shine. Add to that outstanding voice acting, great cinematic direction, mixed with beautiful graphics (at least for its time, but still good today), and you get a heck of an experience that everyone should have.You cannot play cooperatively online, it is only couch co-op, but if you use the SteamPlay option you can invite your friends over the internet to connect with you on your game.  I played this in person rather than online, and the experience was phenomenal.  The game takes a direction most would not expect and the ending after having played together is an emotional rollercoaster.I can't speak highly enough about the story and the dialogue written for the characters.  It makes it very believable and authentic rather than just words on paper.  It draws you in and you are absolutely immersed in these two character's story.  Vincent is an older man that aims more for intelligent solutions to solving your obstacles while Leo is the younger man who aims to use strength and violence to solve problems and you get to choose how you overcome obstacles.  While this doesn't necessarily change the outcome of the game it does provide a certain amount of replay value to see how different ways of solving problems would end up.During the entire game you will find random things you can do with two players like play darts, baseball, basketball, connect 4, and more.  It provides respite from the storyline itself and gives you a bigger meaning for being two players in the same game.  I also feel it's a sneaky way to show a relationship is being built between the characters.  They start to care for each other.The director and story is written by the same individual who made Brothers: Tale of Two Sons as well as the most recent It takes Two.  Josef Fares is a great storyteller, understands how to get players immersed in the world he creates to the point that you have an emotional attachment in ways that other games have not replicated in my personal experience.This is not a long game, and it deserves to be on your wishlist.  There aren't too many games like it.

_childDocuments_.review: A friend and I play games together in regular weekly session. This one had been on the list for a little while and it did not disappoint.Story is pretty punchy, and generally maintains a good momentum. Main characters are well defined and engaging. And the surrounding cast works as well. This is pretty important, because, realistically, gameplay is mostly a walking sim. Which isn't surprising, if you're purchasing this title, it's for the story, and not frenetic gameplay. That's not to say it's all walking though, there are a few stealth sections, a few chase scenes, and a handful of 3rd person shooter segments, all of which are nicely spaced out. At least until the end of the game, where a few areas started being a filler-y. What makes A Way Out really stand out, though, is the way co-op is implemented. You are always playing in split screen, which can dynamically shift the focus between characters depending on the action. This works great and can setup some pretty awesome set pieces.The games is visually lovely, and spans various diverse locals, ex: . All feel alive in Unreal Engine.Music is adequate, and the voice acting is good.A note on length, this is on the short side. We played the game in 2 sessions, with the first being ~4hrs and the second ~1.5. This was a leisurely pace.Final Rating 5/7 - Worth picking up for a short, story-focused action game. Perhaps not worth the full $40 though. The friend pass system is dope, only needing to buy once for 2 players is nice so you could also split the price.Note: EA App inviting is wonky and very inconsistent. Worked without flaws the first time, and took us about 30 minutes to connect the second time.

_childDocuments_.review: A Way Out is a story about revenge, love, hate, and brotherhood. Those thinking this is a run of the mill prison escape are in for a real treat. Gameplay seems to be what can only be described as an interactive movie, which could have been the next evolution in how storytelling is told by developers like Telltale Games. The camera brings back fond memories and basically has you both play split-screen which in my opinion really emphasises the fact that the people who are playing are "brothers" or at the very least linked to each other. I couldn't stress this enough but play it with one of your closest relationships, whether that be a brother, sister, boyfriend, girlfriend, best friend you name it. The person you play it with will most definitely determine how you feel about the game. Treat this game as a movie and just enjoy the masterly crafted story telling with a person you would watch your favourite movie with. I jumped the gun on this game expecting a fast pace, prison escape between two prisoners. I didn't expect the level of storytelling this game provided. The gameplay becomes secondary pretty quickly as you are sucked into the story of these two characters. It really emphasises teamwork at the highest level. Almost every sequence of events depends on the other person watching your back. In this case, two inmates become a brotherhood. This leads to interesting plot developments even after the great escape. I do feel the game should have had another ending though but in the grand scheme of things if that ending was an option the game wouldn't have impacted me nearly as much. So I understand why they decided not to include that option.Gameplay can become slightly tedious at times. A lot of the time I thought of ways to do certain tasks or get through areas on my own. However, the game really limits you to how they want you to play it, only allowing certain actions or outcomes regardless of your approach. Which is why again I'll say to treat this as an interactive movie. Some sections are slow and take a bit of time. I feel they just added filler to make the game a bit longer and worth the price. It ran well on my computer with no graphical or gameplay issues to speak of allowing you to dedicate your full attention to the story with it's finest moments coming from cutscenes, not gameplay.Would I recommend this game to a friend?: YesShould I buy it for the full price?: No, I'd recommend getting it on sale. How long is the game?: Most people finish between 5-7 hours.Is this co-op only?:Yes, you need at least 1 friend.Replay ability?:Not really, unless it's a few years later.If you are a person that loves singleplayer storytelling and wishes you could play it with a friend this is the game for you. The game does have it flaws. Very short for a game of that price, the gameplay is very restrictive and a lot of interactions are not needed. However, the amazing music and the masterfully crafted story make up for these in waves, and although you will come out of the game frustrated for not having other options you will soon realise that it needed to happen that way. Leaving you with one of the most memorable endings in gaming and one of the most unique co-op experiences you will ever have.

_childDocuments_.review: It is no surprise to see Josef Fares deliver a AAA title for the indie scene. A Way Out plays like a blockbuster mastodon but with the subtleness and creativity of sophomore cinephiles. It surprises, it captivates and it goes all the way in every single possible way. This is how Spielberg would have directed a video game and this is how your summer matinee guilty pleasure would have been brought to life in an interactive experience, all the while leaving very little to scrutinize and hark down upon. A Way Out is a love letter to cinema and a flirtatious invite for us monkey brains to be able to adventure in the shoes of our big screen hero. A POV dream come true.That is basically the gist of the success I address this game, as it more often than not plays itself with easy mechanics and button holding skill checks. It is an immersive marvel that elevates a movie script into being larger than life through the eyes and fingers of the players. The game comes alive, much to the credit of its tight writing and editing. Camera shots that would impress you normally is elevated even further in the context of you playing the scene out. A Way Out is absolute cinema on the PC, but what about the game?It plays out as a co-op split screen where you pilot a supposed main character each. You more often than not are assigned your own goal and free roam with npc chatting and minigames at your disposal, while coming together now and then for high stake quick time events or chases. The gameplay ranges from stealth, vehicle riding and gunplay, with adventure game feel in between. It is all pleasantly amusing and carefully balanced in the narrative, with slower moments surprising you with effectual progressions. You simply do not want it to end. The good thing is that you can take your time with before-mentioned dialogues and carefully sprinkled minigames. Maybe you just want to compete in Connect Four, pitch some ball or play some music together while gallivanting through the scenarios. A Way Out is not a gameplay masterclass but it can truly entertain you and give that well needed escape from reality.The story is at points hammy but goes through enough change in scenery and objective that you wholeheartedly keep being excited for what lies beyond the next story beat. The unlikely pair of protagonists in the abrasive Leo and methodical Vincent keeps an equilibrium of humor and heart; while you escape prison and set out to right the wrongdoings that has befallen you.Some passing negatives on my  would be that the acting is not always up to snuff even though Josef's brother Fares Fares (that is his name) puts in a stellar showing as Leo. Graphics look great but will not age particularly well and the whole easy co-op spiel will definitely be a turn off for some. In a way it was for my duo who found it at times uneventful and void of gameplay, but did in the end still enjoy the time we put into it. That is after all the biggest crux of A Way Out. If you do not have someone that shares your interests, a playthrough might result in a monumental waste of time and money, as you are supposed to relish in it together. I am for one happy I had the privilege to do so.

_childDocuments_.review: The story of A Way Out begins in prison with two separate inmates, Leo and Vincent, who don’t know each other. While their individual stories progress, players have to build a relationship based on trust as they break both men out of prison into the world beyond. This co-op only experience is meant to be played together with a friend on a couch or online. A Way Out is a game uniquely tailored for two players to work together no matter the situation. Through a compelling narrative, Leo and Vincent will embark on an emotional adventure, where they live some memorable action moments that they face together including car chases, stealth passages, melee fights, shootouts and many more. [Electronic Arts]
