_childDocuments_.review: is a photography-simulator-game by , i.e. Naphtali Faulkner, a lone Maori game developer.The game's premise is easily explained: You're an amateur photographer and courier in Tauranga. You have a checklist of motives you have to photograph, but as long as you don't run out of film, you can also photograph whatever you want and still earn some money.Despite the fact that no game I've heard of before has dealt with the concept of photography so intensively, the fact that it's a decent photography-sim isn't even the coolest thing about the game, because it has a really impressive artstyle, reminiscent of Jet Set Radio, so you actually want to take photographs, and it has subtle but effective storytelling too! As the levels progress, you'll inevitably notice that Tauranga is facing several crises, but by the time you really start questioning what's going on, it's already too late. But I won't spoil anything here, most of the social commentary is something a person in 2021 should be able to pick up on, with some - and SciFi-vibes sprinkled on top. However, this is all conveyed via environmental storytelling, so don't expect a blockbuster here.The game is fairly short at some ~4 hours of playtime. I'm cool about the price tag though, the game has some replayability since you keep unlocking new lenses and ways to edit your photos. Actually, I'm fairly convinced you have to play the game twice to unlock all the tools anyway, but as of writing this review I just finished the game the first time around. Also, the game actually saves all of your photos on your PC, which is really cool but can add up to quite a bit of storage space, so keep an eye out and maybe clean up your gallery folder after each playthrough. There's also DLC for the game, but I can't say anything about it yet since I haven't played it.All in all, this is a pretty stylish, conscious indie-game that I can recommend to anyone that's into artsy stuff and wants to have a fun evening!8/10 - Cops are dirty!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This unique game is set in futuristic New Zealand. I thought it was an odd setting for a game when my mum first told me about it. I soon realised how well this idea works for a game like this. The aim of the game is to take photos of different objects, angles, and people that are shown on your bounty list. You traverse through different scenes and settings that vary drastically between levels, looking for specific things to take pictures of, all while taking in the amazing views, and getting an up-close insight into all the little details of each level. The levels aren't all innocent and pretty either, so you get to explore the nightlife, subways and other aspects that would usually be excluded when creating a game. It portrays some problems that New Zealand is facing at the moment, as well as some crazy futuristic catastrophes. Not to mention the amazing sound track that the game uses. Some very alternate, interesting music that made the levels feel more real and immersive.I enjoyed this game a lot more than I thought I would and it is definitely an experience that you wouldn't get from many other games.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: There's something relaxing about photography modes in video games. "Photo mode" is still a relatively new concept in games, but when done right it can absolutely shine, offering the player an opportunity to take a break from the game's larger world to focus squarely upon a small portion of it. I've spent hours in different games just taking photos, listening to the ambiance of the world and music around me as I tweaked the lighting and angling to get it just how I wanted it, before going off to find another spot to take a picture of.Umurangi Generation might not be the pinnacle of photo modes in video games, but it hits almost all the right notes to put it in contention. The camera feels both approachable and capable even for those unfamiliar with photography, taking all time and scoring pressure off and giving the player room to experiment as they see fit. Aiding this is environmental design which maintains a great balance between intrigue and cohesion, finding new ways to keep each level fresh and engaging while maintaining a clear identity. As well, specific points of interest big and small are spread out incredibly well, never leading spaces to feel overburdened or artificial. The specific photography objectives in each level don't fare quite as well, unfortunately, seemingly existing for the purpose of guiding the player but often becoming obstacles themselves. When a level's objectives work well, they form an interesting mix between photography and navigation puzzle, but later levels can make them so demanding as to make an interesting or even simply clean shot impossible.But what Umurangi Generation excels at by far is tone, atmosphere, and narrative, all while rarely spelling out direct plot points. The world of Umurangi has a constant subdued bleakness to it that's hard to compare to any other game. It's a world that can best be described as defeated, the final throes of life being upon it and no options afforded to the player besides that of simply being present. This relationship between the player and the game-world leads to a special connection, with the dire state of the world and the hopeless lives of its inhabitants feeling much more tangible when the player is forced to be among them rather than saving them.Ultimately, I can recognize that Umurangi Generation is a game that might be hard to pitch to people, considering it's a quiet, dour photography game. That's totally fine. But, it is a game with such a finely crafted world and atmosphere that I would be lying if I said I didn't want everyone to at least give it a shot, and it is certainly one of the best games of the past few years.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Lets get the few stupid complaints out of the way. Sometimes getting temporarily stuck on geometry(never actually cared). Last complaint is no dlc for more levels cause that's going to be cheaper than the new camera and photoshop i now want to buy.This game is by far one of the best I've played in a while. For me it just feels good to play. The camera feels like a film camera. The music is 10/10. And the world and themes are inspired by all the right things. This game threw me back to my high-school photography classes that i took and then put me in an incredible world with incredible friends(idk how they have so much character as silent people and a pengu, but they do).Each level feels unique and lived in beyond what most AAA games do. The world and story left me honestly struck by the end. I don't want to spoil anything about the world/story/themes of this game cause it's worth learning by playing, but it is surprisingly lovely and dark in perfectly balanced measure. with a honestly very moving ending at least for me.I've already replayed a couple levels trying to get all the extra objectives done, to get more film gear(need a canister location guide for a couple levels) and even though i was racing the clock i would still be like 'wait is that a shot, can i hop over here and crouch and yeah that's IT!' wasting a full 30 seconds just trying to get the right angle. This game isn't for everybody, but  if you actually enjoy taking photo's with your phone or u always wanted to try photography, please try this game. It's beautiful the whole way through, completely unique and absolutely fun with a jaw dropping world to boot.This review was on the game the day released btw
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I like the style and the gameplay... but why is it timed? Photography is about framing a shot, and looking at details. This is the opposite of that: complete the objectives given the scene as you run around and also try to collect things that the devs hide. I feel like the game was made for us taking our time but got changed for the worse at one point, or at least it feels like it. Too bad.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Stage 1: Yo, this is chill. I love the lo-fi Y2K aesthetics.Stage 2: The clever usage of positioning yourself to get the objectives in shot has caught me by surprise and efectively merges both free-roaming chill creative photography and subtle positioning puzzle elements resulting in... wait, am I in a war zone?Stage 3: Getting all the upgrades and film canisters makes the player pay attention to its surroundings in ways I couldn't have imagined. I'm kinda blown away with how the game makes me fall in love with its stage and environmental design while being almost minimalistic.Stage 5: WAIT, WHAT IS HAPPENINGStage 6: DAMNStage 8: HOLY MOTHER OFFinal Stage: TUMBLING DOWN TUMBLING DOWN TUMBLING DOWN-------------------------This is my review. I won't say anything else because I don't want to spoil the game for you. Umurangi Generation is a landmark title in the photography videogame genre and one of the best experiences I had this year. If you see the trailer and think to yourself "yea, I would vibe with this" then get this ASAP.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: The fact that there are people on this earth that haven't played Umurangi Generation is a crime. This is a phenomenal achievement in terms of storytelling and gameplay. It's an extremely relevant and powerful story told with not a single line of dialogue, all you have is your buddies and a camera. Experiencing the game is in it's own right the story, you see the story you want to see which is a direction that I love in games, no overblown cutscenes or expository audio logs even though you can tell a good story with those. The game gives a list of objects to take photos of and you can be as creative as possible and it's perfect for anyone who likes photography or just art in general. There a few glitches that I experienced that hindered my enjoyment slightly; the detection on some of the objectives was really janky sometimes I would take a photo miles away from the objective and it would mark that off the checklist and sometimes I'd be right in front of it and it wouldn't count at all, sometimes I would walk into an object and get sent flying 100 metres in the air which was cool occasionally but most of the time would send me off the map and respawn me at the beginning with a 2 second time penalty, which was less cool. I'm going to get into minor spoilers for the game even though there isn't really much to spoil so if you don't want to read the rest that's fine, please play this game it is incredible and also get the Macro DLC which adds so much to the themes and sandbox. The red sky generation is what the title translates to and essentially the game is about the denial of accountability of older generations and what people would do when they know the world is going to end and the answer is party. None of the citizens can really do anything about the war the UN has started with the alien race trying to invade and you as the protagonist can't report on anything that's actually going on so your only option is to take pretty pictures as creatively as you can but don't take photos of blue bottles. The government takes the neo-liberalist approach of never addressing the real issue and making you pay for a temporary solution. The Macro DLC adds to this while being a much more depressing story. It pretty much uses the iconography of Neon Genesis Evangelion to explore issues in the present, it's also set in New Zealand. The culture of New Zealand is very integral to the themes and aesthetic of the game, it feels very spiritual and in-tune with it's indigenous culture while incorporating a future aesthetic, rebelling the colonialist mindset of westernisation = better and the erasure of national identity. It also uses retro technology to add to this rebellion, you use a film camera throughout the game and the music constantly uses samples from the PS1 and PS2 era (the music is incredible btw). The music seems very much inspired by Jet Set Radio which is a game all about rebellion. This is then juxtaposed with the divide between the wealthy and the poor (called surface dwellers). The wealthy are shown to have a very different style that completely ignores the cultural heritage while at the same time advertising and commodifying the style of those surface dwellers. The DLC extends it's roots in our current events by having a level where you are taking photos of a protest against the UN occupation, the game becomes truly ominous and it shows how fast the government uses it's own weapons against the people they're supposed to protect. This is even scarier when only 2 levels before you have to take photos around the weapons they were creating to be used against you. "Painting is not done to decorate apartments. It is an instrument of war." - PicassoThis quote perfectly sets up how this game tells it's story, it's a game about making art to preserve the lives of the umurangi generation and rebel against the modernisation of the video game medium. It's a lovingly crafted artwork that takes advantage of it's medium to let the player express themselves while also making them witness the oppression of culture and the manipulation by our governments not to protect us but to suppress us. This game deserves to be spoken in the same breath as classics like Silent Hill 2, LISA the Painful, Fallout New Vegas and Shadow of the Colossus. 10/10 play it now. Right now. DO IT.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: good tunes, cool visuals, neat gameplay. would be excellent if it werent for the incredibly picky object detection in photos and the utterly atrocious collision detection and platforming physics that make manoeuvring around the levels an ungodly pain in the ass. i cant personally recommend it purely because of how unfun it is to play despite everything else being pretty good.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is dripping with aesthetic, style, and heart. It celebrates street culture and doesn't shy away from making a statement.You play as a photo journalist(?) who documents different angles of a very turbulent time. You're scored based on your photographs, but honestly, you can ignore the scoring aspect.The base game feels significantly kneecapped by the slow moving speed - the Macro DLC fixes this by giving you roller blades, a can of spray paint, and more in-depth settings to tweak your photos. The DLC improves the game so much I can honestly say I wouldn't recommend the game without it.I 100%'d this game in less than five hours with fairly heavy use of guides, for the sake of expediency and my own patience.YMMV but I recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Bought the game after the interview with the developer on the Dads and Sons podcast. It's not bad, but it feels very raw. And I don't mean "raw" in an artistic sense... Or rather maybe not only in that sense.It feels like a playable proof of concept, not a finished game. Proof of a neat context, but still. UX (settings menu for example is clunky), onboarding (tutorial is very limited and text-only) and the gameplay loop (no real incentive to take cool pictures instead of just rushing through the objectives) all feel like they could use some work. The internal logic of the world is also a bit unclear - like, from what I've seen, you live in a totalitarian dystopia but yet you can walk anywhere you want and photograph anything you want with the only penalty being getting smaller paycheck.I don't regret paying for the game, supporting a cool developer who clearly cares and hopefully will make better games in the future, but I can't really recommend it as a product. Maybe wait for a discount or something if you want something quirky but feeling a bit amateurish.On an upside, the art direction is very consistent, music is good, some of the locations are really pretty (some are also dull and lifeless though) and I like the story as a concept.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: In this game, explore a stylish, edgy world where you slowly realize that everything has gone wrong. Your only goal is to take photos of certain things like "7 birds" or "a shotgun, a pistol, and a rifle". Fill the list, and you can move on to the next level. While hunting for the correct angles to grab these photos, you take in more and more of the messed-up world and gradually figure out what's really going on. In one level, a discarded newspaper reports that the prime minister is on vacation while alien invaders are at the nation's doorstep. The wall next to it is plastered with army recruitment posters, advertisements, and propaganda informing you that yes, we're winning the war. That's not to say that this is a downer of a game. For all the cynicism and despair evident in the world, there runs a theme of youthful rebellion and even hope and a call to action, because sometimes in the end all you get is one shot. Let your camera be your lens.Simply put, a collectathon should not have lore this good. Make sure to get the DLC as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: What little there is is not polished enough to be worth the price of admission. For the devs I have so many questions:Moving around is one of two things you do in game and it feels like complete ass. It's excruciatingly slow, sometimes you clip through stuff that looks walkable, sometimes you clip through stuff upwards. Sometimes you can't jump even though it seems like you're standing on something. Sometimes you'll slide off stuff, other times you'll stick to it. Apparently if you buy the DLC there's some kind of sprint. Again. w h y ?This isn't a problem on the small levels but trying to find that one last thing you're missing on the larger levels feels like a choreSometimes it's near where you started, other it's just somewhere arbitrary. This wouldn't be a problem if you could see it while playing the level, but it only shows up once all the primary objectives are complete.Looking for tiny black cylinders hidden in a large level ON A TIME LIMIT isn't fun. On the note of film canisters why do they never increase the amount of film you have beyond 24? This isn't just annoying, it's counter-intuitive to anyone that actually knows how a film camera works. This is a Unity game. Unity has prefabs for all sorts of UI elements but rather than choosing my resolution through a dropdown I HAVE TO KEEP CLICKING IT UNTIL IT BECOMES THE ONE I WANT. THERE ISN'T EVEN A SEPARATE CHECKBOX FOR WINDOWED MODE. IT'S JUST THROWN IN WITH RESOLUTION. Why can't I use my scroll wheel for the level select? Why can't the game remember what language I speak? Why am I told what I unlocked for completing a level if I already finished the level and unlocked that item? Why am I booted back to the start screen if I want to choose a level after completing another? Why can I not restart a level instantly? Why do I have to press a key on my keyboard and not use my mouse to go through the start screen? Why can't I bind actions to my mouse? Why do I rebind keys my click+hold+release and not just click? I wouldn't waste my virtual breath on this if it were just a few things but it get so much so horribly, horribly wrong.I don't mean stylistically. It's like there's some kind of post-processing effect that makes anything rendered further away than about 2 metres look like it's being rendered at a much lower resolution than it really is, and then upscaled. Or it might just be really aggressive lowering of texture resolution at distance. It's extremely similar to looking through a first gen VR headset. This goes away when looking through the viewfinder of your camera, which makes me think it's some kind of artistic decision about how we see pictures as being more real than reality. But I hate it. Just playing the game makes me feel like I need glasses. In the era of post-launch support many of these issues should have been smoothed over months ago.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A brief and buggy experience with half-finished mechanics and yet it's also one of the best games of its year.Eight small-ish sandboxes with hidden objects to find and snap stylish (or not-so stylish) photos of. It's not the most riveting setup, but then, there's also a war going on, and victims and soldiers increasingly fill each area as the game progresses.If you're trying out Umurangi Generation, chances are you'll lose yourself in its world.Oh, and the soundtrack is worth picking up, too.And the DLC -- which is even better.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I like everything about the idea of Umurangi Generation, but I think they failed in the execution. I love the stylized PS1 graphics, but the game runs poorly despite how simple its visuals are. I love the idea of being incentivized to really explore a level and take pictures of the objectives, but exploring the world isn't fun when getting around feels so awkward, when the objectives are unclear, and when the bonus objectives you clear don't seem to even count towards anything. The soundtrack is great, but every time a song finishes, there's a massive stutter to load in the next song. It's clear the developers had a great vision, but just don't have enough experience making games. I'd love to play a polished version of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: The concept and visuals are really cool, but the actual gameplay experience is frustrating. The character moves painfully slow and the jumping also feels clunky. Instructions are often unclear leaving you to wander around aimlessly at slow speeds. It's the kind of game that you want to enjoy but the feel of it just leaves you frustrated.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice walking simulator with a little photography game attached. The photography is fun, you get little challenges to find certain shots, and you can mess with the ISO, f/stop, aperture, and whatever else you'd want.The game really shines with it's universe. It's a cool Maori cyberpunk kaiju vibe that's got a political message in the way most games are too timid to attempt. It's not perfect but this is the kind of art video games needs more of.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umarangi Generation is a very cool, unique experience but one that will only appeal to a select group of people.  If you are not a "make-your-own-fun" kind of person or you are not a creative person who enjoys exploring things through being creative, this is not going to be for you probably. If either of those things DO describe you, you might like what you find in this game. I'm a professional illustrator and an amateur photographer and I loved the entire concept of this game - exploring these small stages and finding shots that interest me was a real delight.THE GOOD STUFF:THE NOT SO GOOD STUFF:TLDR - This is a super unique photography based game focused on creative play and the player finding their own fun through discovery and creativityIf you liked my review and want to see more from me, check out my Curator page over at
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: It may be pretentious, but ignore the time limit, get absorbed, and focus in on what speaks to you in the game. Umurangi Generation is the story you tell through your photographs. The game really enables the player to become a photographer at every level that matters, so develop your own style and make some kickass art. I wound up making a quick photo book based on my experience, and it was one of my most thoughtful experiences I've had in gaming. I think the meta narrative of my interpretation of the developer's world through that book is such a neat concept too. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A very mild recommendation, as this game mostly left me wanting more done with it, but I can't bring myself to give it a thumbs down.My expectation of this "photo game in a failing society" was that the photo element was going to lean more towards photojournalism. That would be an extremely compelling way to do photo-taking in a setting like this, but that's not what's in here. The objectives instead largely ignore what's happening around you, and while that was no doubt an intentional choice, the objectives are left feeling disconnected from the game world, almost like randomly-generated quests.People can argue that the 10 minute timer objective can be ignored, and while that's true, the presence of a countdown clock in the UI is always going to be seen by many players as a force compelling them to move quickly. Would have much preferred this element be left out of the main playthrough and kept in an alternate mode.The music and "vibes" are fantastic, and the rage underlying the chill presentation is palpable. It's a world that's compelling to be in, but one that ultimately demands more exploration and examination than this game is able to provide.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game knowing nothing more about it other than you can take photographs and that I loved the art direction it has. Umurangi Generation portrays a bleak dystopian sci-fi future through the lens of a young courier working for the Tauranga Express. You’re given a list of things to photograph each level but you’re free to take as many pictures as you like and as someone who has a casual interest in photography I really enjoy this part of the game! There is a time limit set for each level to deliver your package however you can ignore this as it’s only for a bonus. I definitely don’t recommend rushing through things on your first playthrough. The environmental storytelling in this game is expertly crafted and is worth experiencing for yourself firsthand. I’d also recommend buying this along with its Macro DLC as that provides extra levels that expand on the game’s themes. A refreshingly angry and passionate game with heavy social commentary. It’s worth sticking around until the final shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I like the idea of this game, but sometimes it just doesn't accept your photos for no particularly obvious reason, and that's incredibly frustrating given that the game has a tight time limit and doesn't offer any kind of feedback. It also sometimes decides it's a platformer, but controls aren't nearly precise enough for it and it always feels like half of any platforming section is down to luck of the geometry not getting in your way.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Video game photography has seen huge growth in recent times. You'd be hard pressed not to find a photo mode in most of your favorite AAA titles of the past few years, but those modes are complimentary side content at best. Despite their inclusion, there aren't a lot of games that allow you to actually be a photographer in the truest sense of the word.Believe it or not, photography is much more than just taking a picture. The picture is the result of scouting out a great shot, getting uncomfortably close or uncomfortably high up, fiddling with an ultra-precise tool to get just the angle you want, and tweaking minutia in post. Photography isn't just a skill; it's a process.It's certainly possible to take some great photos using in-game photo modes, but floating around as a ghostly camera just doesn't have the same challenges as being a corporeal photographer. Umurangi Generation fits that niche perfectly. It's a first person shooter, but you won't be shooting bullets; you'll be shooting landscapes, portraits, and close-ups.Set in a post-apocalyptic New Zealand facing a Kaiju invasion and UN occupation, Umurangi Generation puts you in the shoes of a photo courier with an old-school camera. Umurangi Generation sports neon cyberpunk city streets, vast skylines, and dingy UN checkpoints coated in graffiti. This makes for a ton of good source material to have fun photographing.The game will present you with objectives like "get a close up of the word Squid" or "get a wide shot of 2 coffee cups" and it's up to you to figure out how to put the shot together with various lenses and post-processing sliders. For lack of a better word, the "hit detection" for when you are doing picture objectives can be a bit shoddy. It works about 7 times out of 10, which is far too low for a game that tasks you with taking pictures.On top of this, some of the objectives are outright sadistic. I spent 20 minutes looking for the letters "RTD" which ended up being on the side of a random car. One objective I got stuck on involved taking a longshot photograph of 5 american flags. It left me flabbergasted for a while, and I couldn't even take the picture when I found the angle because I had gone over the photo limit. The photo limit is a crucial misstep in my opinion, one that punishes players who just want to take cool photos (which is kinda the whole game).The game's biggest flaw is that it has tons of untapped potential. Being a photographer can often be uncomfortable, awkward, and even dangerous. The environments are very static, and people never react to anything you do. I think a crucial part of photography is the interaction the photographer has with the subject; that potential is squandered here.The player is also given money per photo based on color, content, and composition. This encourages the player to follow the fundamentals of photography, but this whole system seems contradictory to the game's ideals. In the tutorial, it is stated that photography is subjective, yet they've implemented an objective scoring system of sorts. It might be there to push players into learning the fundamentals. If that's the case, it's nowhere near consistent; my favorite photos were frequently worthless.And that just might be the point.It's hard not to see how Umurangi Generation holds a mirror (or rather a camera) up to our own world. Your favorite photos might not be worth anything to your payroll. Walls defiled by graffiti and propaganda posters also advertise post apocalyptic sci-fi movies and gaming bars. People dance to the beat of bizarre indie music not 50 feet away from the wreckage of a giant robot. While it's not subtle in its discussion of occupation, existentialism, and escapism, Umurangi Generation conveys its message through mostly wordless storytelling.Is Umurangi Generation the most amazingly fantastic indie hit I've ever played? No, but it taps into something I didn't know I wanted: fully realized videogame photography in an interesting world. It makes for great photography practice, and even stores the photos on your PC.Umurangi Generation is weird, flawed, and great. If you haven't given videogame photography a try, then you probably should. If that's something you already enjoy, Umurangi Generation is a bite-sized cyberpunk photo trip that's absolutely worth its price tag.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I can forgive jank as long as it doesn't get in the way. You know what I mean? I really like the ideas here. As a photographer irl, a photography game should be an easy recommendation! But I quickly discovered that walls are merely a suggestion in this game. You can easily clip through any wall and most geometry by walking against with with no effort. Which by itself wouldn't bother me, like I said, I'm willing to forgive some jank as long as the idea behind the game is solid (which it, I like the environmental storytelling on display). The problem is ramps and stairs are also a suggestion. I regularly clipped through the ground whenever I tried going up a ramp or stairs (of which there's a lot, at least in the 1st few levels ). It would happening over and over again. And in a game that is timed, it's really frustrating to clip through the ground and lose time like that.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Evangelion but from the point of view of a photographer and with the aesthetics and game design of a PS1 game. Jet set radio and pokemon snap had this as its child. i struggle to think of anything eles that's even similar. You take photos, you have list of things to take pictures of, a list of bonus tasks to complete and a timer for said bonus tasks, that whilst does not stop progress i did think it took away from the experience first time round as i felt rushed trying to find the tasks in places i don't know and sometimes times wasn't fully sure what it was wanting.  Now the timer dose fit its ps1 style aesthetic, but still dint enjoy that part.  Each level is relatively bite sized, yet dense enough in design and style. Really great soundtrack. Fairly short overall but some replay due to timers and various tasks for unlocks.  Really cool story telling with its levels.I would wonder what someone who hasn't seen (or enjoyed) EVA takes away from it thou, but as a fan of that and similar shows that have stuff straight lifted from for this, i thought it was really cool. The DLC feels like it looking in a different direction too look at story-wise, that i'm not fully sure is as strong as the base game but still enjoyed.Really cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Photography is good on the whole, but the gamification around it is frustrating at best and downright awful at worst. Main deliverables that are listed are a mix of interesting problem solving, say you need to frame a series of signs just right to spell out a word or series of numbers, and just a list of 'three chickens and a milk bottle'. Not perfect but tolerable most of the time, if stifling for being really creative in a lot of cases.Then you get to bonuses. Pixel hunt tiny film canisters tossed carelessly around the level. Rack up a hundred dollars worth of points by just shooting film into the sky until enough money has been earnt. Run the level three times to figure out how to take the photos, where the film canisters all are, and then getting all that done inside 10 minutes. NEVER were these bonus objectives fun to do. I get the argument that you can skip them, but bonus objectives are meant to be a fun extra tough challenge not just outright annoying and a constant chore to complete. Putting extra unlocks behind them also makes it 'incomplete' to finish without doing these bonuses, pushing you to beat your face against it to really beat a level.The world is very interesting, and the set-up is too. But then everything is just left to hang in the wind and atrophy. Who are you? You have mates, who are they? Why, through asking them to pose which is the only way you can interact with them, do they seem to ricochet widely between the huge swings the story and level progression take? I can understand you four, being average people, have no ideas of the bigger things in play. That all is mysterious too, but stands out far less than the fact you are friends with a penguin and that seems normal. Is the penguin magic? An alien? Just a penguin? Did you steal a penguin?Only so much is shown through the levels themselves, the narrative wordlessly transitioning from place to place and progressing the main story of the world, and through newspapers and such decorating various levels. You cannot interact with anything at all. if not for the hands you can see holding the camera you could very well have just been a floating ghost camera taking photos without any change in the game at all.With just a bit more work to make the world feel actually alive and not like a clockwork diorama, with the gameplay refined to be fun and meaningful, this could have been a real solid game. But lacking that, progression is an awful trial and the story does not give you enough to be worth the effort you need to put in. And since you need to go through all that to unlock everything and just have a cyberpunk free roam camera game? Not worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Killer soundtrack, tasty visuals, inspiring worldbuilding and straight-up impressive environmental storytelling.However, the gameplay didn't click for me. On one hand it wants you to pay attention to every nook and cranny, absorb the environment, and understand it. On the other hand, it wants you to do it as fast as possible. Obviously, the solution is to pass through every level twice - the first time to do reconnaissance, and the second time to 360 noscope everything. I get it. But why!? I fail to see how this contributes to what the game is trying to say. It feels to me like the developer heard some feedback that the game was "too boring" and then decided to add this time limit to spice things up. In the end, I think it only serves to pollute what is at its core an already marvelous game.All things considered... this is a good, although confused, game.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This is singlehandedly one of the best games I've ever played. I first found out about this game from NitroRad on Youtube. I didn't end up picking up the game until a few months later and I wish I would've picked up this game sooner. As soon as I started I couldn't stop. I ended up playing this game in one sitting, in one evening. I give this game nothing but my full support.P.S. This game started me on my course to watch the entire Evangelion franchise, another thing I can't thank this game enough for as it's become one of my favorites series.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Such a sweet experience.It's the kind of game that gets better the more time you invest into it. First you'll stumble through all the objectives, until you decide to revisit each area and start to absorb all of its' weird and unique beauty. If you have any interest in photography, this might just spark that bit of curiosity needed to try some other lenses or perspectives as well!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Great soundtrack, great vibes, well-executed environmental storytelling, cool photo mechanic. The Marco DLC is good and I'd say an essential part of the experience. My biggest problem is the game puts a 10min timer in the corner right at the start, adding pressure and rushing the gameplay. When, in fact, timer is an optional objective, and there's nothing stopping me from taking the time and exploring all the corners of the level, which is the most fun part of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is a game about taking photos during the apocalypse. and tells the story of a world entirely through asking you to take photos. This game mechanic is a pretty genius move, as you are hyper-aware of your surroundings at all times and understand the story that is being told without any dialogue or exposition. Taking photos is a lot of fun and editing them afterwards and using different lenses gives you some pretty cool effects. There is a lot of the fun to be had in the game is with the vibe, the general premise of the game, the music, and the world, which I can't spoil too much, but based on these factors I can really recommend playing it. The game took me 3 hours to complete so you don't really tire of the gameplay in that time, and the objectives for each level were generally fresh and interesting.There is some general jank to the game, certain things are a bit buggy, but it doesn't take much away from the experience, as it fits the vibe and general punk-ness of the game almost better than a really polished game would. Which doesn't mean that it's always nice, but it's not that bothersome.There are however a few things that actually annoyed me: one thing were the additional objectives during a mission, (such as finishing the level in a certain time, collecting items, etc.) I found none of these to be very enjoyable. I only really started having fun with the game when I started ignoring the timer and the collection aspect of the game. The other side-objectives were fine but I feel like I would have enjoyed the missions more without any extra objectives. Similarly, once you complete all the main objectives, you have to leave the level by finding a physical point in the level to exit from, which was exhausting, not that much fun and could have easily been solved by a "Finish Level" UI button. Finishing all objectives and side objectives during your first try at a mission is borderline impossible and replaying the level just to get it done in time wasn't really something I was interested in, but was something the game encouraged. Some of the levels were just slightly too big to be enjoyable to explore and my favorite levels usually were the really compact ones. Additionally, some lenses were a bit hard to use and the game sometimes explains objectives and basic controls in a way that isn't clearly understandable. Umurangi Generation generally feels like a good game with a great idea and cool mechanics, that could really have been improved by getting some playtesters to play it before release.I genuinely wouldn't recommend this game to everyone. If you want a hardcore photography game, or a very polished gameplay experience, you might not have a lot of fun with this. I personally really liked the game, though. The game has a great sense of humor and style and some pretty memorable moments, and is really making you feel seen for worrying about the future of the planet in modern times.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wondered what it would feel like to be a background character in Evangelion? Well this is basically that game. You take photographs and chill with your friends in a world that you learn of through purely visual storytelling the more you play. It's beautiful, relaxing, and  haunting to play. Also the soundtrack is amazing and I've been listening to it on repeat since I started and finished playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I came to Umurangi Generation via the rave reviews in the gaming press... most of which gave the impression that it's a thoughtful (and politically charged) narrative, hidden behind a chill photography composition game.What they didn't mention is the time limit on each level - which completely destroys any "chill" feels from the game, and prevents you from feeling like you can actually truly play with each setting - and the floaty, imprecise controls for traversal (which wouldn't be as much of a problem, if it wasn't for... yes, that time limit).So, I can't recommend this game with these two massive caveats on its core gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is greater than the sum of its parts, and some of those parts are NOT great by any means.  The sounds aren't cohesive, the movement is frustrating, the controls unintuitive and messy. The Tony Hawks mission structure clashes with the multitude of photography mechanics, to a baffling degree - you are encouraged to gamer-goblin every objective in every map as fast as possible, so you unlock more interesting options for your creative photography endeavors. This would be fine, its often fun even, but forcing you to collect tiny collectibles in huge levels AND forcing you to do every single photo goal instead of letting you choose one or two to neglect is a huge oversight. You WILL get stuck searching for one tiny film box or that one motif, often hidden in graffitis that melt together with the blast of colors in every corner of every level.  I could go into detail on a lot more stuff ( events never happening after level 1, broken achievement, grading ), but you get the idea. There is hardly anything not flawed about this game.But the overall experience is so damn interesting. The world is both depressing and exciting, the atmosphere is thick and oppressive while the vibe you get is strangely liberating. The game never alternates between pessimism and optimism, it radiates both simultaneously. The levels aren't all well designed, but they are all a delight to look at and explore. And once you actually get to ignore the missions and just relax to snap pics for the intrinsic value alone, Umurangi Generation really shines.Special shout-out to the OST by Adolf Nomura / ThorHighHeels. 60% of the songs are phenomenal, 20% are weird and 20% are ear-grating; I think every player will put different songs into those percents, but it's hard to imagine the soundtrack could be lost on anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. Sure, you could treat it like Tony Hawk and get the specific pictures in a specific amount of time in the most efficient way... or you can explore the world built in the level's vignettes and encapsulate moods and emotions even the developer didn't know were present.You take pictures of cool stuff, use the lens you want and edit it to your liking before sharing to Twitter. That's it.I guess there's some excellent social commentary on the current quarantine and dope music too. If you like music.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I'm on the fence for this one, but I'm leaning in the positive. It's got a nice aesthetic, and to see the story unfolding in the background as you're going about your job is a neat touch. However, some of the photo missions are more difficult to complete than expected, and the controls can be a bit unresponsive, not to mention that collision detection in this game will hinder much of your movement if you're really trying to explore the levels.These issues hampered my enjoyment of the game, but I want to see more from the developers, especially if they improve in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is the most innovative shooter I've played in years. Your photos don't matter. They're for you and who you show them to. The sky might be red, but you have the HSV controls.With excellent and constantly surprising visuals, a killer OST with over a hundred tracks (including Macro, which IMO is an integral part of the experience), and unbridled creativity, this is a game everyone should own. Period.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: As a game by itself, this isn't anything crazy. Basic environmental exploration through the goal of taking pictures. The movement is kinda janky, I've clipped through a impressive amount of walls and floors just by brushing up against them, randomly being launched like 20 ft in the air eventually just became a movement method, the deliverables could use some greater elaboration at times, and I cry a little inside anytime I see I need to use the telegraph lens.  And yet, I think I completely adore this game. The use of environmental storytelling is incredible. Despite the low-poly graphics, the environments are interesting and impactful and a pleasure to explore. The additional of all the different lens and the different edits you can add onto your pictures are cute details encouraging the player to have fun, take cool pictures, and fully take in the environment outside of just the obligatory items. But of course, I have to mention the emotional impact of the story, as I'd argue that is the main selling point of this game. This game is raw with frustration and rage and fear and grief, and it makes it incredibly clear. Both the big and little moments still buzz around in my mind sometimes. So many times I'd stop right in my tracks to absorb a scene. In my opinion, the storytelling alone makes up for all the gameplay jank. I'd also like to mention that the story line is so much better with the DLC, so if you're interested in fully experiencing the game, I highly recommend just getting the DLC and playing them back to back. The DLC also seemed to have less glitches, in my experience. Also OST goes hard.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: UG has been a bit of a gamble for me. I’m not really into photography games and I’m not knowledgeable about the subject in real life either. Many games allow you to take pictures on the side, I tend to mostly ignore this function because it feels pointless without any objectives. The negative reviews focusing on the tight timer, unclear objectives, janky gameplay and bad controls also had me spooked. And yet I feel very happy for getting the game against all odds. It seems as if the game is misunderstood with some of the claims.The game has 8 stages and 4 DLC stages. Each stage has a couple of main objectives that you have to do to complete a stage. The main objectives are taking pictures of something unique related to each stage. There are also optional objectives that are always the same regardless of the stage. You can think of earn x money with your pictures, find x amount of film canisters etc. Each stage has at least two camera tools to unlock. One is for completing the stage and the other is for completing everything, including the optional objectives, in one go. This means getting it done within 10 minutes. I usually HATE timers in games but it’s really not bad here. You can perfectly ignore the timer and take as long as you need. You can even turn it off from showing in the options menu. You can attempt it after exploring a stage thoroughly. It’s easier than it sounds because the stages are not big at all. It’s easy to get everything done quickly once you know where everything is. In fact, I’ve had instances where I’ve (almost) done everything on my first try once I understood how the game accepts the pictures taken. It’s also better to unlock some lenses early before attempting the timers because they will make things FAR easier.This makes UG feel like an arcade game. None of the objectives you did before are remembered, so you’ll always have to do them again. But it works because you’ll always have the lenses and other tools you unlocked plus remembering what you did before. It also does an excellent job of giving you an idea of how actual photography works. This along with making the gameplay and progression system fun, while informative, impresses me a lot. Some people mentioned how the objectives can be unclear or how some screenshots are not being accepted while they should. This has not been my experience for the most part. Some of those pictures are required to be taken with certain lenses, you’re shown the icons in the objectives menu and it was mentioned in the tutorial. It makes it feel like those people missed these important aspects. The controls are also fine with mouse and keyboard. It’s similar to an FPS with some minor differences for the most part. The complaints were mostly about the controller, so do keep that in mind. The game looks and sounds like a Dreamcast game a bit. I’m slightly reminded of my time playing Jet Set Radio. The achievements are enjoyable to get too. There are some creative ones that might get annoying to figure out but the game has tons of guides to help out with that.The criticisms regarding janky gameplay and a few bugs are valid. Sometimes you jump really high when you go up the stairs. Jumping can also not work when you’re too close to objects. These are the kind of janky gameplay problems that can be dealt with and avoided once you know how they trigger. The UI is not the best. It feels clunky but it can get the job done. In terms of bugs, the speedrun achievement does not work. Right now you can either go back to an older version (it’s introduced with the last update), use SAM or pray the devs will patch it at some point. It doesn’t seem like the latter will happen since the last patch we got was in 2022. The game also has weird performance issues but it’s not something I’ve seen others mention. So it might be my set-up in combination with the changes I’ve made in the options menu. The game has a kind of annoying and pretty constant stuttering. It’s worse in certain stages and can disappear after a while. None of this is solved by forcing 60fps through Nvidia. UG is a required taste. Not everyone is going to put up with the lack of polish. But what it does is unique and it does it really well. I paid €1,85 for the game and DLC when it was on sale. It’s definitely worth it. The normal price for both is too high but they’re worth considering when they’re cheaper.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Buy it!A ton of fun, can finish it in 1 play session, but would also be worth to come back afterwards just to enjoy the scenery and take more pictures! Also the soundtrack is worth listening to on its own.The time limit can help you come up with really creative angles and compositions on the fly. The editing was a lot of fun as well. Just wish navigation was a little easier sometimes.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Had my eye on it for a while, as the photographing mechanic seemed novel, and the artstyle unique.Well, big disappointment, I'm afraid.The biggest problem I have with the game is with how crude it is. I sometimes like low-fi aesthetics, but in this case it goes directly against core of the game - text becomes insanely aliased when it is very important for the political message, the platforming is very buggy (with the character getting stuck whenever it collides with something, the double jump being finicky and momentum based, some things look like platforming but turn out to have no collider, etc.) and even the photo mechanic, when it's about capturing specific objects is too permissive and you can easily take a picture of a special objective by mistake - sometimes while the object is obscured by something else.The platforming is the biggest frustration, because the levels seem built with a lot of verticality and I could imagine myself have fun *exploring* them - but they have nothing to explore and are very basic. Whatever platforming seems interesting and free - as when you try to climb high - turns out disappointing when there are misleading platforms without colliders or simply no reason for you to get to the tricky spots in the first place.And it's just floaty and unpolished in general.Other than this, the game is just a series of levels with objectives and just about nothing else. The bonus objectives are always the same (go quickly, make money, find X of this tiny irrelevant item spread throughout). It tries to give you more mechanics with different lenses and so on, but they don't have much of a purpose. As a game, it goes through the motions without getting anywhere.The political message, finally, mostly goes over my head. Basically, "UN is bad". I'm sure there is more to it in the way the levels are arranged, in sequence, the characters and themes portrayed, and so on. But the core of the game is so unsatisfying to me that I can't be bothered. I'll admit this particular complaint may be more on me than on the game.Finally, the aesthetic is cool. The music, especially - reminds me of Lethal League, in a very good way. But not enough to save it.Perhaps I'm simply in the wrong mindspace for the game, but it really failed to capture me, and instead the crudeness of the most basic game elements marked the majority of the experience. I've played 4 levels, and I think I've had enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: It is a short and sweet game, oozing with a unique kinda style.Your job is to complete certain shots in each stage, how you accomplish that is completely up to you. The further you progress the more lenses and filter options you unlock, giving you another good reason to go back to earlier stages and see what you can do now.Also gives you another chance to discover more about the world and soak in more of the aesthetic while some great beats penetrate your eardrums. It is a bite-sized experience that just gets better and better with every run.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A masterclass in environmental storytelling. The camera is one of the best-realized cameras in videogames. I don't like that you have to search for these small collectibles on a time limit to upgrade the camera, but honestly my enjoyment of exploring the world and taking pictures of all its nooks and krannys completly overshadowed its faults.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A photography focused game that tasks you with taking pictures of various things around the different locations in the city. There's plenty of other things to see in each location however and you're free to take as many pictures as your film will allow. You'll also get more ways to play around with the photography as you progress if you're into that sort of thing. The game has basically no dialogue or exposition, so looking around the different areas is how you'll find out about what's going on. You'll also get to appreciate the game's brand of somewhat dark humour. The simplistic artstyle is pretty endearing and you get to listen to a nice, chill soundtrack while you take your photoes. Overall I recommend it to anyone who wants to take it easy and take in the sights.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: The game has potential but it's too picky when it comes to qualifiers. I spent more than an hour trying to photograph ten solar panels from God only knows how many vantage points. There were ten solar panels in the photograph on numerous occasions but none of them counted because I didn't have the EXACT angle the developers were looking for. I watched a walk-through and the host had a hard time too but finally got it. But in the photo, two of the solar panels were barely showing...it's like, how could that possibly count?? Lol. I will say the soundtrack is good and the controls seem to work fine. It's a good idea, overall, and I could see how people would like this. But I can tell already, I'm not going to have the patience required in order to play this. If you take a chance on this, be prepared to consult how-to guides, etc. It might be up your alley but it requires a lot of fiddling around.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: The way this game gets the player into the story is really neat. You're given  enough guidance and information to start each level, but the bounties for the level force you to pay such close attention to the environment that you start to pick up on details you're not even required to take a picture of. It's simple, but highly effective.I can't say I'd recommend this game to everyone... but if I thought everyone would get what makes this game so good, then I would.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a huge disappointment. I really want to love this game, but it does everything it can to prevent me from it. To me, the game's identity is vibing with friends trying to take pretty pictures while piecing together environmental narration about authoritarian governments and the apocalypse. This would be a proposition where *taking the time* is crucial, in order to appreciate all of this. And I am absolutely on board with that. However, The game gives you gamey-ass objectives that go against this entire philosophy. In each level you have to find specific items in the area, take pictures of specific things. Which means you're only looking for those rather than appreciating the place for yourself. But worse, you have to do all this ON A TIMER. And the timer isn't gentle either. Plus the games asks you to do some parkour-y stuff, to go explore hard to reach places, and do it fast, but the controller is absolutely not suited for it. The impression I get is that of developers that went "oh yeah we are making a video game, let's put video game stuff in it", without thinking any further than that, without taking a minute to consider the actual impact it had on the experience, without stopping to check if it was coherent with what the game was. I really would have preferred something way more open-ended, with less objectives, less challenges, less constraints. Less attempts at gamifying something that wasn't meant for it. It's okay for games to pursue something else than the traditional idea of "fun". But when you do it, do it for real.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: As a hobbyist photographer, this game is a lot of fun. Taking photos in surreal environments is great. You learn about the world and the events unfolding around you as a passive observer, while still being very much part of the world. The levels can feel a bit static at times, but this gives you plenty of time to explore.Fun game for anyone interested in Photography.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Either a fresh, laidback, visual experience or an engaging, arcadey, bumpin game; Umurangi Generation is one of those games where the pleasure is found with your view on gaming in general.To a common player, it may just look like a straightforward "Find objective, complete objective" game. Of which, let's not lie to ourselves, it is and that can be pretty dull for some people. But, I found myself playing each level twice: Once to intake my surroundings, keeping mental notes, understanding the worldbuilding and crackin' lil gags with the NPCs around the stage because I enjoyed putting myself in the character's (invisible) shoes. The second time, with the information I had gathered, to go with a more arcade "speed clear" approach since trying to map out an effective path to knock out every objective in under 10 minutes was a fun little challenge. Now, I didn't go HAM on it to try and get the best darn time there is but more like a little trial of "Okay let's see what I can do..."I enjoyed the approach to every level and how it followed a narrative. A narrative that at first would probably make you go "?????" but then you remembered details you had seen in previous levels that then make you go "Ahhhh yeah yeah!!!". It ain't anything SUPER mindblowing that will raise you're* IQ by 200 but its still pretty cool.The game was definitely longer than what I had in mind. To a point where I even thought "What to heck where is it going to take me next after the previous level? Isn't this enough???". Near the end of the game, I felt a bit engulfed by the objectives and started paying a bit less attention to the details in the stages (I blame the film capsule collectibles making me look at the floor). The game didn't overstay its welcome though. I was really into it from start to finish and even checked back some earlier levels to put some pieces of the puzzle together.Overall, it's a fun, chill game to boot up and just get yourself lost in. Cure a migraine or two yeah? Its really enjoyable to jump around and try to get some cool vantage points for shots (AND break out of bounds because the collision is a bit buggy at times (I phased through a wall in almost every level)). I feel like some levels's cash bonus objective could be tweaked because I found myself "farming my friends" for quick cash pictures which broke a bit of the immersion.I'd say its a nice grab for ~$10 but its aint too much of a rush to grab it NOW and play it. Find that special moment in your life where this game will be some sort of meditation for ye. The music is dope too.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A good, short but sweet game. The music is amazing and I listen to it all the time now just cause its such a good vibe. Paired with the unique visuals in game and its such a relaxing experience. Obviously if you are into photography this game is for you, as this is the main focus of the game and it does it well. But overall if you are looking for a nice calm, almost zen like experience to help unwind, this game is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking at your games library and making raspberry noises with your lips, please try this for something different.  It's a photo-take-athon and the adjustments you can make to your photos are pretty cool, although I'm not into social media so I bet the options pale in comparison to image filters on whatever social media platform you're desperately trying to get noticed on.  However, for ignorant sods like me, if you feel like you have a vague creative streak but haven't really had the time to go down that path, I recommend this to dip your toes into some crazy photo taking opportunities.  Choose the lens, tilt the camera, choose some egregious or muted colour settings, the game saves them for you in a folder and then, like me, set them as your desktop background if you can navigate Windows 10 settings better than I...Umurangi Generation has a very interesting setting, and the anti-UN sentiment, as a failing to a fictional world catastrophe, or as a statement from the game producers, is pretty cool.  Oh yeah, NATO can suck deez cashew nuts too.  That one's from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This really is like Pokemon Snap meets Jet Set Radio in post-apocalyptic Aotearoa / New Zealand setting... very fresh. I think my only complaint is the first person controller here, which doesn't seem to detect grounded states very well -- so sometimes it won't let you jump even though you feel like it should. You can secretly DOUBLE JUMP but the game doesn't tutorialize this... except in the input options menu? Last pro-tip: make sure you look at the tutorial screen for a minute or two, so you understand what the photo scoring system is about.But other than those nitpicks, this is a great and expressive photo hunt game, in a very fresh setting, so well done Veselekov!!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This game felt like it was half-done.The game made my insides shiver with excitement as I'd first read its description and saw the abstract-"color-blocked" pixel-y environment it had- I really liked solving photography related puzzles and taking pictures in Life is Strange, so the idea of a game being based solely on photography sparked a very high interest in me. Unofrtunately it did not last long, after playing for about 50 minutes I decided to return this game and its DLC, here's why:-Controls. The main reason why I returned the game basically. I almost choked on my hot chocolate when I crouched for the first time ever. Like they say- in Russia you don't drink Vodka, Vodka drinks you. Same goes for this situation, it's not you who crouches but the surrounding environment that does. It feels as if the ground just lifts up closer to you and goes further when you undo the "crouch". Jumps are no different-in short, navigating with such controls remindes you that you're just a gliding camera rather than a photographer trying to catch some cool frames. Pretty sad for a game where exploration has quite of an emphesis. -I know the low res and non-aliased edges are part of the aesthetic, and it's usually a style I adore in games- but not when it's painful to look at! Bounties such as finding scattered film rolls were a pain in the #*^. This also made the "exploration" part feel like a chore, which should have been one of the most enjoyable things to do in this game.-The tutorial. I could perfectly get the information given in tutorial via a controls tab in settings. It was not interactive, a lot of information was given at once without letting the player to digest and engage with.-In the menu I experienced multiple visual glitches while switching between let's say settings and tutorial, it was as if an additional flashing frame was added in-between, I don't think this was done delibiretly if the devs did not intend to trigger a seizure in epileptic players... A miniscule problem I know, but this makes the game look "messy".-Lack of a story made maps feel as lifeless shells stuffed with objects. I couldn't care any less about NPC's as they were no different than a bucket filled with paint. -Tasks were non-creative, addition of clunky controls and eye-hurting graphics did not help it either.Only thing I liked about the game was the map layouts, and that's pretty much it. I did not find soundtracks anything of revolutionary unlike many people in here. I do not recommend this game, you can spend your coin on much better games. 3/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation deserves to have far more people talking about it. I'm planning to revisit and replay this game again soon but, in a nutshell:Atmosphere is top tier - the art style is cool and evocativeThe camera gameplay rocks. As a hobbyist photographer its fun to see camera work modeled so nicely in a lil indie game.The story just needs to be experienced and felt, the vibe setting is excellentBless up to indie, indigenous devs making cool art and telling stories in a unique way we don't get to experience often.Well worth your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I had a phenomenal time with this game and the dlc I also listen to the soundtrack regularly. I think about my time playing it from time to time with fondness and know its something I need to replay soon, I just love the art style, music, and atmosphere in this world it inspires creativity and made me want to really explore what I could do with the camera and explore for secrets within and out of the boundaries of the maps. The game also has a good sense of progression as you unlock different lenses and such through out the game. This one is a 10/10 for me highly recommend the dlc as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: "Don't huff paint and kill fascists at the same time, kids!"I was introduced to Umurangi Generation by the Youtube channel Super Bunnyhop, and I really, REALLY liked the concept! I've always thought that the first person shooter style of play could be used for something else, and target-based photography with scoring is an excellent idea, and so I got the game and sat down to play.Precisely two hours later the end credits rolled for me, and I was a little underwhelmed.So what is the game about? Truth be told, I don't reall know the answer to that. The game has absolutely no dialogue, and while it does some interesting worldbuilding with how it sets up its scenes and levels, there isn't much of a story arc to follow here. We find ourselves in a city preparing for chaos, an alien invasion of some kind. I feel inspirations have been drawn from Godzilla and Neon Genesis Evangelion. There seems to be a ban on photographing some critters that appear in the game, so maybe there is a secretive coverup plot?Hard to say, though, as nothing is ever explained. Instead the player ends up getting tasked with photographing spray paint cans and cats and graffiti and other random objects in a way that gave me no idea what the role of our character really is, and then to 'make a delivery', which I guess is delivering the photos we took to a place, such as the back of a van. Why? Again: the game does not say.What about the photography itself? Is it crisp and fun and challenging? Well, not really. I ended up completing several objectives by accident due to the wonky target detection, and some of the objectives are very poorly explained, which can cause some frustration. Take a photo of 4 things, when there are only 3 of those things in the scene? Hmmm...The visuals leave a lot to be desired as well. While the game goes for an highly stylized art style, far removed from photo realism and well suited for a small team and limited budget, it felt a little too crude at times. The movement around the levels is janky, it's easy to clip around to places you're not supposed to be, and there is no risks, challenges or even fall damage to worry about. There is a time limit of sorts, but that only seems to relate to a bonus challenge, not the core game itself.The only part of the game that stood out to me, really, was the music. While it doesn't seem to really relate to the scene or location in the game, many of the tracks were absolutely great and I found myself jamming to them quite happily.Still, a good soundtrack can't really save a poor execution, and sadly I find myself unable to recommend this game. As much as I love the idea, I feel like the game doesn't do nearly enough with it, or construct an engaging narrative in which the player could feel involved. I can see the developers wanted the player to feel like just a passenger in the sidelines, witnessing something greater than themselves, beyond control, but the ride is too short and lacks an engaging destination.Playtime: 2+ hours (A single playthrough)Ratings (1-10)Visual: 7Audio: 9Story: 7Gameplay: 5Overall: 6
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is a declaration of dismay against the government and corporations that have failed to save the world. Consequently, it burns brightly and there's nothing we can do but watch. This is the central premise of Umurangi Generation, one of the few games that spoke loudest to the COVID Generation. Umurangi Generation is a first person photography game. You play the role of a photographer, who documents the chaotic end of New Zealand. Beautiful landscapes are replaced with dystopian cities, ruins, and a red sky. These are the subjects of your photos, a world gone to hell because of government failure. Anger and frustration flow through many of the game's levels.I feel that Umurangi and I share the same anger against government incompetence. In 2020, the world shut down as COVID ruined everything. I saw neighbors die, businesses shut down, and the corrupt thrive. The country suffered as we watched our geriatric government leadership conduct the most useless nightly “talk shows”. All talk, no game. Millions infected, and thousands dead in the nation. It was the most powerless I have ever felt and I wasn't alone. Perhaps you feel the same, reader? It's okay, the world can't kill us yet. However, I can't say the same for Umurangi’s end times.It's very easy to see that Origame Digital experienced the same revolting feelings we all did. All the revulsion and anger against the status quo that keeps us down. Besides, the game was released in the middle of the chaos in 2020. What resulted is a generational piece of art that expresses the same powerlessness we felt then and now. Umurangi speaks to the times.The game evokes this punk-rock aesthetic in this near future setting. There’s a fury seeping through its tone, but there’s also a chill hangout vibe that flows against it. Yes, the end of the world is here and we can’t do anything but take pictures and hangout with the crew. These are the last days of a chaotic world. However, I will not speak of what ails the setting of Umurangi Generation, doing so would only ruin half the fun. What is obvious from the beginning is there’s something that dooms the world and there is nothing you can do but watch. As the game continues, the player slowly takes the role of a historian of sorts, documenting a crisis in progress. In light of this, Umurangi tasks you with taking photos of… Cats, birds, candles, graffiti, and much more. The subjects of your photos feel normal, which adds to the initially chill vibes. However, this ordinary set up eventually contributes to an entirely different tone, a feeling of desperation to hold onto normalcy. It’s a relatable feeling because we did that during the pandemic and even today. The gameplay is very good and simple to pick up. As mentioned earlier, the game tasks you with capturing photos of several things such as cats or cars. There’s a ten minute timer, but it feels inconsequential. There is nothing stopping you from taking your time, exploring the level, and getting the best shots possible. Umurangi Generation doesn’t make use of cutscenes or dialogue to tell a story. Instead, it uses environmental storytelling to great effect. The game invites the player to assemble its story, creating an engaging narrative experience that forces its players to seek out pieces of story. Throughout the levels, you’ll come across newspapers, graffiti, television sets, and posters that each detail the maddening situation that afflicts the world. As a result, the narrative never feels disruptive and the player is always in the middle of things. It's an immersive way to tell this story and the most fitting way to do so.The OST by the magnificent ThorHighHeels should be praised. Not only does this man make banger video essays, but he’s also creating banger music as well. The music of Umurangi Generation is nothing short of fantastic, always expressing this “Sophistifuture” tone (as he would say) that really adds to the atmosphere. The music always feels nostalgic, relaxing, and also disruptive in some tracks due to the presence of robotic sounding voices. It all fits perfectly with the game.The game also shows a unique Maori perspective that I would love to see more in video games. Diversity is the spice of life after all. While I can’t speak much to its Maori identity as I’m not one myself, I can definitely say its expression of identity and culture adds so much humanity and creativity to the game. Umurangi Generation is a protest in the guise of a video game. It’s never shy about its disruptive and frustrated attitude. There's a lot of righteous anger that the story directs straight at its in-game governments as they continue to fumble important work. Thanks to its solid gameplay loop, great environmental storytelling, and a fantastic soundtrack, Umurangi Generation is able to lift a mirror that lets us see the madness. 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A personal story of friendship documented through an aperture lens - photography at the end of the world. Umurangi Generation fills in the gaps of mecha shows like Neon Genesis Evangelion with the average Joe's experience using evocative and expressive photography scored by the dankest sounds of punk DJs crafting tracks in bathroom stalls - grimey, bodily fluids and all.A fast-paced story but one that, by it's nature, is individually crafted. I can't highly recommend it enough.
