_childDocuments_.review: I never really considered myself a photography person. The underlying complexity of making photos anything but functional sounded like an arcane art, and one that needed a significant commitment to make it look good.Umurangi Generation made me feel good, perhaps even competent, at photography. The freedom to approach the stage from any angle, with a variety of tools, and then to apply various filter effects through multiple sliders is joyful to say the least. Starting from just upping the exposure on a photo that's good, but a bit dark, and moving on to balancing multiple effects to get something that you wouldn't think can look this good is extremely satisfying.The game definitely is an experience that is best unspoiled - not as much because of the twists and turns, but because of how it relies entirely on environmental storytelling. The playable stages are all a part of a consistent narrative, told exclusively by the way you, as a player, perceive it. It is much less about what kind of a hidden, objective lore you can glean from it, and much more about personal affect. What will catch your eye? Which detail will you focus your lens on, trying to make sense of the lousy future you've found yourself in? That is entirely up to you. Well, mostly.If you can grab Macro DLC, you definitely should. If you're not sure, just get the basic game, and it should convince you enough to get it. It more than did for me.

_childDocuments_.review: is pretty much the ultimate "lo-fi beats to relax/study to" game. There's not really a whole lot to playing it. You just walk around taking pictures of things in environments that are totally static except for characters going through animation cycles. And yet its culmination of lo-fi graphics and music is still absorbing enough that I played through each level multiple times and got 100 percent completion.It's one of those games with low-poly, low-resolution graphics designed to look like it was made in the late 90's (other examples like  or  deliberately evoke the original PlayStation but  is more like the Dreamcast). But instead of being a horror game its vibe is somewhere between  and  -- colorful urban landscapes, anime-inspired characters, rap music, impending kaiju doom. It works so well that during my first run I kept playing just to see where each new level would take me. These levels aren't just attractive in a sort of retro, cozy way, they're also packed with small details, just begging you to photograph every inch of them. The chillhop music fits all this perfectly. I bought the soundtrack and still listen to it.What really shocked me is how  strings its levels together to subtly tell its story. The first few levels look like typical urban and cyberpunk stuff with shades of militarism creeping in the background. Eventually it becomes clear the player and a handful of other characters who appear in all the levels are moving through a world beset by kaijus as giant robots try to fight them. You don't really see the fighting itself, but rather its impact on the regular human population, like those sparse scenes throughout  that show normal people trying to survive on streets and in shelters, escaping the battles. Laced throughout those landscapes are various bits of social and political commentary, mostly around the theme of government incompetence (developer Naphtali “Veselekov” Faulkner tells me this was a response to how the Australian government handled the recent bush fires and climate change in general), as well as indigenous symbolism owing to the developer's Maori heritage.The actual "game", the photography, might simply be an excuse to give players something to "do" while just vibing in the late 90's anime atmosphere  so expertly sets up. Even if it is, the game pays close attention to the snapping of pictures with the player character's DSLR camera. It kind of operates like a gun in a first person shooter -- the click of the camera's shutter being akin to reloading a shotgun, selecting each style of lens (standard, wide-angle, etc.) as if they were weapons, finding additional reels strewn throughout each level to replenish your ammo.All you really have to do is essentially a scavenger hunt -- photograph certain objects or concepts in each level to unlock the next one. Some of these turned out to be fairly challenging "puzzles", but what really drew me in were the extra objectives and the additional lenses you get for doing everything in each level under a time limit. Those extra lenses and other tools, which I won't spoil, significantly alter the game. The later ones are basically cheats.Looking back a month-plus after finishing , I'm shocked at how much it stands out in my mind from the rest of what's come out in 2020 so far -- AAA games included. It's one of the most aesthetically pleasing games I've played in recent memory, period.

_childDocuments_.review: Umarangi Generation is a game that feels like it has loads of potential in 2 different ways, but manages to lose all of it by aiming down the middle. While I'm glad I played it, I can't say that I enjoyed it at any point. On the positive side, it looks absolutely fantastic and stylish. The world is relatively interesting to explore and the levels generally get more interesting as you go along. But the game tries to walk the line between "art-with-a-message" and "video game" and I'd say it failed me miserably on both sides. From a technical standpoint, it barely functions. I walked through walls, got launched 15 feet into the air by walking up stairs. got stuck on things and fell through the world once or twice. I'd carefully line up a camera shot and wouldn't get credit, or I'd randomly snap a shot of emptiness and get an achievement marked off. And don't worry about focus because you get full credit no matter how blurry the shot is.Here's the thing though, none of this would have been a meaningful problem if this was an artsy-free-roam-walking sim. Snapping photos is extremely satisfying, reading the notes on the walls, trying to piece together the lore... this is all good.But this is where they introduce "Game Mechanics" You are now on a 10 minute time limit for each mission, searching for hidden film and searching for ultra-specific combinations of set pieces that can only be snapped from one specific point, angle and film. Many shots are even puzzles like telling you to find something, only to have it solved by finding the word or a certain angle that forms into the target. The end result for me was that instead of a chill, casual scavenger hunt with a hidden lore and message... it was a stressful series of being launched off the side of a building because I dared walk on the stairs. I can't read the lore because time limits and the objectives are hidden and puzzle-y.Instead of a light and fun photography arcade game that has me expressing myself and finding pieces as im exploring the world... I find myself searching for ultra-specific spots to stand. Instead of exploring the site of a massive Kaiju battle... I'm stuck trying to find the right angle to fit both skateboards into the frame.There's alot of really cool things here, and I am glad I played it. But ultimately... I can't think of a single type of person I'd recommend it to.

_childDocuments_.review: There are so few games that give you the strangely dirty feeling of having inhabited a place. It's oddly got nothing to do with fidelity, complexity, features, physics, RTX enabled godrays tickling the hairs in your player character's nostrils, none of that. If I had to tie it to something tangible, it's about how well a game makes you feel that the space has existed before and after you got there. Was something going on here? Is there evidence of that? What else goes on when I'm not Doing The Game Stuff? This kind of design makes the game's world balloon in your mind as you fill in so many blanks left there by the developer. Umurangi Generation is an entirely extra life I've lived in a marvelously ♥♥♥♥♥♥ future where my friends and I are just trying to make the best of what feels like the end of the world. Taking photos, unlocking extras, and moving through the story is so much fun, and if you enjoyed Pokemon Snap or actual real world photography at all, there's so much here for you.Cyberpunk games like this do not come along often at all. Seize this moment and play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually gorgeous, and the photography tools are really powerful and fun to play with. The spaces your navigate and document give you plenty to do. It's also wonderful that there is so much going on beneath the beautiful surface, in terms of it being a meditation on the feeling of being young and powerless while the world collapses around you. There are a few bugs and some jankiness here or there, and I'm not wild about the stress the timer mechanic gives me (you can just ignore it, esp. your first time through). But overall, I found it a really interesting experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing! Often fiction is about the big players. For example, Evangelion main cast are the "most important" people in their respective worlds. Or the PC in each Fallout game (or almost any RPG, for that matter), whose decisions change theirs respective universes geopolitical configuration in an scale which is almost unthinkable for an every day person. All those fictions, in a sense, subscribe to the (very colonialist and eurocentrical) "Great Man Theory" of history by giving their protagonist choices world changing consequences.But what about the common people living in the shadows of these (metaphorical, but sometimes literal) gigants? What about people like you, or me?Umurangi Generation is the answer to that question. We learn, without any dialogue, the experience of the opressed and ignored. The game shows us how would be the life fo the people outside hegemonical narratives in the face of a world changing event of which they are not the protagonist, but just some folks trying to keep alive in the face of adversity.Also, the soundtrack is SO GOOD!!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most unique videogames that have come out in recent years. A game whose core gameplay is about photography and tasks you have to do based on the tools your camera has. Many people compare this game to Pokemon Snap, but there's a significant difference to that game: Umurangi Generation, for one, isn't on rails and the levels have lots of verticality. Plus, as mentioned before, you can take pictures and use different filters, effects etc. The other part of this game which is very well thought out, is the environmental storytelling. There are so many things going on as you proceed and the game encourages you to explore the curiosity the levels may cause you. It will make you have questions like  You see, this is a dystopian game and I would argue that it's one of the best in this category. In fact, I would go as far as to say that, as a sci-fi dystopian game taking place in the real world, Umurangi Generation is the best game of that kind since Deus Ex. Don't let the Jet Set Radio inspired aesthetics fool you, the game is actually very bleak. Yet even with all its bleakness going on, it serves as a sign of hope in modern gaming. Many people argue nowadays that games don't try enough to be unique or engaging, and that the developers are not as passionate as they used to be. Well, I use this gem right here as my disagreement to such statements. Especially since the developer behind this is still supporting his work 2 years after its release. Did I also mention that Umurangi Generation is DRM free? Yeah, you can buy it here on Steam, but Steam isn't required to get the game running.With all that said. my final verdict is:

_childDocuments_.review: If we’re to watch the world burn, better we do it through the lens of Umurangi Generation, a window into an artistic and vibrant culture standing out against a dispiriting reality around it. It’s not some altogether hopeful and optimistic lens, but it’s a gripping one, no doubt. Umurangi Generation feels like nothing short of a miracle, a photography game which truly elevates itself through its worldbuilding, its atmosphere, and its triumph in capturing photography’s varied joys.	First, it must be said that this game positively oozes delectable vibes. From its low fi beats to its use of moody color and the general impression of each level as this singular, outstretched moment, the game’s aesthetic and presentation are incredibly chill, although the scenes certainly grow more dire over the course of the game. The art design is wonderful, with numerous styles which should be more disparate than they are. These range from sketchy wall graffiti, to the simple and charming models, to the various posters and billboards, many of which even employ real-life photos. These all blend shockingly seamlessly, and produce a world soaked in its own cultural and advertising landscapes.	Umurangi Generation’s worldbuilding is exceptional, as it conveys so much culture, counter-culture, and context simply through the scenes, environments, and progression of its areas. And while the player character is never explored in the game, the presence of your friends in every scene grounds you in that diegesis. At first the game seems content merely to tease a bigger picture informing the world of your photo-ops. But soon you’ll find yourself a witness to a momentous event for this world. It eventually becomes clear these photo shoots are not wholly discrete and arbitrary occasions, but a timeline of scenes throughout that greater event. These inject new context and tension into the situation. At first I was casually chilling with my friends on a rooftop photo op. But then I was thrust into an escalating crisis, one which proved positively absorbing. The ending at first seemed sudden and underwhelming. But it soon sunk its teeth into me and became a harrowing sendoff to my time with this world.	The game is unapologetically political, too, allowing a richer, more relatable landscape. Art and politics aren’t treated as disparate entities, for the game or for its world. Rather, they coexist and interact meaningfully. Graffiti and other art in the game are often thinly veiled – or even blatant – in their critique of the failures of government and authority in the wake of disaster. Newspaper headlines and movie posters will reflect this, and you get a solid sense of how things got this bad. These even provide a chance to gleam hints of the terrors imposed on this world, before they’re directly presented to you. And despite the sci-fi edge to Umurangi’s world, many of its problems are all-too-real and strikingly current.	At its core, Umurangi is a mostly straightforward photography game. To progress, you simply need to snap the photos described in your objectives list. Find your subjects, nail the angle, and employ the right lens if necessary. In practice, many shots are quite demanding, working as their own miniature puzzles, asking you to really the scene at its macro and micro levels to work that perfect angle. The fish-eye lens does admittedly break several objectives once you unlock it, as its sweeping reach can capture numerous targets at once, assuming they’re not coupled with specific lens requirements.	Photography is further baked into the game thematically. Each stage feels itself like a snapshot of this world, a moment caught in suspended animation for you to roam and purvey. Every area is a window into this world’s people, culture, context, and history, even its  history happening right in front of you. But there’s never some sweeping score or choreographed cinematography to superficially dazzle you. Rather, discovery is wholly naturalistic and thus more humanistic.  get to develop the world through exploration, and by seeking to capture key scenes and details. You dictate your own experiential relationship with the environment, and the game challenges you to both recognize and produce meaning from the scene. There’s a true and unrivaled wonder to it all.	The controls are quite intuitive and simple, although the double jump can be a bit unwieldy at times. When you whip out that camera, though, everything works like a dream. The plethora of options before and after snapping the picture ensure there’s ample room for customization and creativity thanks to a surprising number of lenses, camera add-ons, and editing tools. I’m certainly excited to jump back in and see what I can produce. Fortunately, the game fully embraces its own social potential by directly connecting you with all your photos to share and save as you please. Umurangi Generation really feels like a platform for expression, both for the game’s own developer, but also for the players. It’s a brilliant realization of how real-life photography and other media presence can inform our understanding and perspective on a work or event. I also appreciate how the developer left all these extra little alcoves and pathways. Some require light platforming to access, but these are seldom required of the player to access for the main objectives. Rather, they’re simply additional spaces allowing new perspectives and unconventional angles for the creatively inclined.	Every core objective – save for one – is wisely rooted in the same focal action: taking a photo. This keeps the focus finely honed in on Umurangi’s gameplay and thematic conceit. Perhaps a bit contrary to this is the scavenger hunt for film canisters. These are scattered through each area, and occasionally, there will be one which proves quite tricky to track down. Reaching the payment amount, conversely, is rather simple to the point of being trivial. Most of the value of your shot seems to be determined by its content, in which you can simply snag a few fish-eye shots with plenty of  on-screen for a considerable payout. But these extra objectives are only needed if you want to seek out the additional modifications for your camera. While I understand the risk of overtuning a system assigning a monetary value to subjective imagery, the current system doesn’t encourage any creativity or experimentation, especially as it downplays the other two Cs the game champions, color and composition.	The game is conducive to both players looking for a lax photography simulator and those craving a more “gamey” experience. Those in the latter camp can pursue those optional objectives in a scramble to achieve them all within the ten-minute time frame. The time limit is far from strict, as once you memorize the photo and film canister locations, you can probably clear most stages in about half the allotted time, easily.	Umurangi Generation has a few ever-so-minor hitches which could perhaps be ironed out. But as with any truly masterful work of art, these faults pale in comparison to a package of otherwise outstanding achievement. As a photography game, Umurangi comes alive as a venue for inspired and motivated creativity and expression. As a narrative experience, it provides a shockingly heavy and political story, which manages to be more impactful in silence than most games could ever hope to manage with heaps of text or spoken dialogue. Those looking to get to the credits and get out might find it a bit fleeting. But I found myself enraptured from beginning to end. Umurangi Generation attracted me with its uniquely humanistic and grounded photography simulation, but I stayed for a world so alive, so expressive, so yearning, so , that I just had to be there alongside it for the end.

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun and interesting game!While the movement is a bit clunky, it's not so bad once you get the hang of it (double jump early into your first jump to get maximum height). The amount of evocative detail in each of the levels is fantastic and goes a long way in telling the game's story.Umurangi Generation tells the story of its setting via the incidental details in each level. The story it tells is broad and thematic, but also deeply specific, clearly in conversation with a lot of cyberpunk and apocalyptic ideas.To encourage close scrutiny of the spaces, the photography mechanic sets up a number of bounties, collections of items that need to be photographed together (sometimes with specific lenses, or specific proximity). I found these to be fun puzzles in their own right, but also vectors through which I noticed other interesting details about the levels.Gradually introducing new lenses and effect sliders was a great way to gradually introduce photography concepts, though I wish I'd gotten more time to explore some of the later options.All told, this game makes me more certain than ever that we need more games that use photography as the primary mechanic. It's such a natural way to guide exploration through densely detailed spaces.

_childDocuments_.review: this game manages to do the hideo kojima thing, where logical inconsistencies, weirdly implemented, half-baked but innovative game mechanics, and semi-coherent, preachy philosophies end up transcending the experience and becoming the object of love instead of derision, like a shot to the arm of purely, obviously inspired passion. it creates rabbit holes of feelings that reflect backwards onto you, like having a conversation with someone who spills their entire being onto you at a 7/11 before never meeting them again.everyone should play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Really cool game, think about a mix between a collectathon and photography, you're launched into a level with two checklists of stuff to "collect" (one mandatory and one optional), except that most of it consists in specific subjects of photography to find. When you've taken all the mandatory shots you can go to the next level, but if you manage to complete both lists under 10 minutes you can unlock an additional tool to add to your camera in order to take better / different types of pictures or increase your ability to edit them and make them more beautiful. The further you progress, the more lenses you get and the more specific the requests will become. Umurangi Generation is able to use this core concept to make you pay attention to little details everywhere in the world, and to gradually and gracefully unveil its themes in order to let you understand what's going on and to tell a story with its scenery alone and no dialogue. Said themes are very relevant today, and give the game a sort of melancholic beauty through the life and little details still mattering despite an obvious sense of impending doom. It's a gorgeous game from an aesthetic standpoint (considering you're ok with low poly), the color palette and the layouts of the environment are tasteful and provide a good amount of opportunities to make very beautiful pictures, giving an insentive to complete the optional challenges to get more photography tools. The OST is also a massive banger and plays a big role in cementing the vibe of the game. The game also highlights bits of the maori culture which is rarely seen in media, and it's refreshing.In itself, it's rather short (8 levels, add a few - very good ones - more with the dlc), but I can see enthusiastic photographers spending some more time with the sole objective to take some pretty shots, and if that's your cup of tea there's a speedrun mode and a few specific items to unlock in the dlc that might recontextualize the game for this purpose and give it a longer life span. Even for a few hours only it is very much worth it, though. Truly a great experience. My only complaint would be that a bug prevents me from getting all achievements as I'm unable to get the speedrunner trophy even though it should be impossible to get a bunch of other trophies that I do have without getting this one... Hope this is going to be patched as it's a bit frustrating.

When I was getting into it I was hoping for something akin to sludge life, a free roam open world tagger type of game with its story through conversations, but I was wrong and still love it. It's take on the idea of what I like to describe as a photography collectathon as you are given different things to take pictures of in different areas in each level with some bonus things on the side. The way how it is done is good but there is one thing I'd like to see if possible. Some type of hint system. Instead of like a pop up every minute make it through the people in the levels so you aren't stuck on a level for an hour trying to find a film reel, but it doesn't have to be like "look under the desk at this location," make it like "hey you looking for one of those weird cases, I think I saw one like under some desk a bit back," like not too obvious or heck even hide something in conversation like in KatiKati you go to the guys near Pengi and one dude says hey have you seen that butterfly graffiti in that back alley? It's pretty nice if you haven't seen it." Then again I guess the way how collectathons work is figuring out by looking everywhere, but it does get tedious now and again. Overall a 9.9/10 in my book. That's not even mentioning the music of the game by Adolf Nomura with all the songs vaguely sounding like songs you would hear in other game. The tone always hits in this good way from up beat to slow with the idea of something ominous for how the day and age is in the story. That plus lens requirements really make bounties a chore more than anything. And lastly the one gripe with this is the controls Even being used to them control the photographer is challenging. You get stuck on a lot of things and jump like a 1cm off the ground. _childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation serves not only as a really cute photo-sim game, but also a really subtle political commentary on New Zealand/Australian Politics. As an Australian, it makes me feel heard in a way no other game has with its direct criticisms of our Prime Minister. It's art style is between Jet Set Radio and a Playstation 1 Game, which fits it's tone perfectly alongside the quirky lofi/breakbeat soundtrack, capped off with a really intriguing cyberpunk aesthetic that rejects some of its core tenants for Maori folklore, which is incredibly fresh and welcoming. The base game I found incredibly enjoyable, if brief, akin to something on Itch.io. The soundtrack is excellent, funny in some places. My only reservation is again the length, and how unless you've been paying attention, it's over-arching narrative comes at you incredibly fast, confusing to some degree. Despite, I wholeheartedly recommend it!! Mad props to the sole dev behind this. Tends to be one of those "you either love it or you don't" games, but I think it could be a lot of people's 'thing'.The DLC is really where the potential of the game comes out. It's also short, slightly shorter than the main-game. However, it retains its subtle storytelling in a way that comes together a lot better, feeling a lot of Neon Genesis Evangelion, which the Dev has stated is an inspiration. Highly recommend the DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoys photography irl, I had a great time with umurangi generation. It's a charming game with a great OST, especially in the DLC. Is it janky? Yes. Did that detract from the experience? Not at all. I personally think you'll get the most out of it if you like exploring, and also just taking photos. The goals itself won't keep you entertained for long, but if you actually take your time to take some photos, I think you'll get a lot more out of this game. Also, all the unlockables are great later on and give you lots of gear to frame your shots.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I think it's the best game of 2020. I think it's an all timer.Umurangi Generation is beautiful. It wields style. Its levels are generously decorated and palpably full of stories.Umurangi Generation is the loudest, angriest game that never speaks a single word of dialogue. It yells about the world, how it treats people, how people treat it. It yells about how the repercussions of decisions made by those who don't care affect the lives of those who become forced to care.Umurangi Generation made me want to be a photographer. I learned a few tricks through playing, which gave me the head start I needed to learn to proficiency with a real DSLR. The skills I learned translated back to the game. The pictures I take now are better than the pictures I took before. I want to get my own DSLR. Umurangi Generation taught me to love the medium of photography.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly pleasant and relaxed game in which you're tasked with taking photos during the apocalypse.It's such a game (you could spend ten minutes in a single level or spend an hour plus if you really get into photoing stuff) that it eschews cinematic or literary storytelling and delivers everything you need to know (with a fair emotional punch) through the environments you explore.It is so wonderfully evocative and it's hard to describe the sense of world as you wander around and let the story flow through you.

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation's world and environments do indeed have a lot of charm and love put into them. It feels like a showcase of multiple artists and that is always great. The soundtrack is a great addition, and the apocaliptic storytelling is shown in the lenses (no pun intended) of those living casual lives. Partying at the end of the world is a concept I adore, but I wish I had more context about it.This game features no dialogue. All of the in-game storytelling is told by the environment and sometimes by radios heard in the ambience (I was able to hear this only once in the 7th stage, because I usually kept the background music slider to the MAX because the soundtrack is so ♥♥♥ great, hence why I'm sure I missed a lot of the audible storytelling).I don't have an issue with environment storytelling, but I do feel like I needed a base. This base is given to the player in the store's description in less than a paragraph. Cool! But I wish I had this ingame too. Am I an idiot? Yes, therefore why I am stating this here so others don't commit the same mistakes as I.I experienced the game fully blind. I wasn't able to appreciate the "♥♥♥♥♥♥ world" setting because I.. kind of took it as normal. I thought it was just the culture of a fictional world. I didn't quite fully "get it" until I finished the game which isn't necessary a shame, but it did make me go like "huh? oh.. ok" when it ended.I don't think the presentation of the story was bad at all, don't get me wrong, I was just hella clueless and too focused on the game aspect of it. Why? Because .When I first started playing, I thought it was an exploration game, but it's more of a "photograph speedrun". I have a lot of issues with timed stuff, specially on exploration games. Sure, it's not a game-over per sé, but if you fail to finish the level in under 10 minutes, you'll fail this side objective, forcing you to repeat the level and the movement is quite clunky and it takes a few levels to get used to the collisions (side note to this: after you finish the game you unlock hover boots. If you jump too quickly, you can get a super jump or three jumps, making the navigation way more fun. I don't understand why they didn't give you this as a default accesory thing, aside of the obvious progression system after each level).This game features 7 main objectives and 5 side objectives.The main objectives are quite easy to do. Some of them required me to google some words because they were very specific and/or I lacked cultural context (which is okay! but something that needs to be noted). These main objectives are really fun to do because they incite you to explore the map and have a "photographer's eye/mindset". It's great!The side objectives have 2 of them that are fun. Somehow find a way to do a photo group with all your friends in frame and recreate a photo. I love how these (just like the main objectives) makes you play with perspective.The rest of the objectives are quite lacking. There's one for finding all collectables in a level (small, dark rolls of films that get easily camuflaged with the environment), one for getting X amount of money (score) in a level and (here's where the timer comes) finishing the level under 10 minutes.These side objectives by themselves are ok, but because of the timer, you end up speedrunning stuff rather than stopping to appreciate things. I personally used a guide for all the collectibles and speedran them. Once I got them all, that's when I first started actually playing the level and that was quite an unfun playstyle but my neurodivergent [self]  to get all objectives in a single run, otherwise the dopamine wouldn't be there. Another side objective is getting X amount of score which on paper sounds cool because it's the game incentivating you to take cool shots, but because of the timed objective, I ended up playing normally and finishing everything else to then find a place that got me a lot of score and farm there until I got that objective. I'm glad the developers didn't make it so you couldn't farm, otherwise I would be an anxious mess because I have less than a minute left on the timer and I still need to get 40 bucks and I have only 4 shots left on my film and I still don't know where the extraction point is.The game also has a mechanic that penalizes you for taking pics of "blue bottles". I had to ask a friend while I was near the end of the game what the ♥♥♥♥ these blue bottles are and apparently they meant the  "Portuguese man o' war" AKA a blue jellyfish. Why are they called blue bottles? I don't quite understand but they look like small pints of blue pain, scattered in the ground or walls. I never understood why you're penalized for taking pictures of them aside of a vague hypothesis. I feel like this mechanic turned out as something annoying rather than interesting because sure, it means that you have to align your shots way better, but the detection is quite generous and sometimes you can get flagged and you don't even know what you're doing wrong because you don't see them so you try different angles and it "suddenly" works now.I really like the experience that this game gives you, but it's hard to ignore these flaws, hence why I just accepted them as part of the game and the faster you do, the more you're gonna enjoy it. It wasn't until the last 2 levels that I was enjoying  and moving in the world. Thankfully, the DLC adds more levels and no achievements so I will fully explore them at my own exploring pace to try and play it without a completionist mindset (which is honestly what I recommend to fully enjoy this game).EDIT: There's quite a few bugs with achievements and graphics. Apparently the game is locked in low graphics regardless. I have the game in ultra and I was like woa that's cool but then I saw people with different screenshots and idk if it's a me problem or what but for some reason, it's always in low.

_childDocuments_.review: Photography games tend to be either very simple or very complex.  For most games nowadays, they're a cute feature to show off the graphics and intricacies an entire team of animators and programmers spent months or years slaving over and want you to enjoy all the viscera.  But it's rare to find a photography game that stands out so unique, so strongly in its own identity that it marks itself above the crowd.Umarangi Generation is a mid-apocalypse punk-Maori game with a dinghy-good soundtrack and a satirical tale where the vibes dip deep into dire town and become strangely terrifying.  Despite not being especially long and being extremely visual with no narration or story dialogue, its fresh cel-shaded style and cultural identity make it a unique little game for those needing a fresh new snap-em-up.PROS:- Gorgeous cel-shaded visuals- Lots of photo options, all of which are saved to your PC for sharing!- Strange punky soundtrack that hits the atmos right.CONS:- Scoring system is rather simplistic compared to other photography games- Level geometry is a bit clunky sometimes

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation rules. It's a chill-paced photography game set in a crumbling future society. Each space offers a set of objectives, and it's your task to photograph said objectives. The game offers no outside dialogue aside from the music, but the atmosphere and environment builds it's own story as you explore this world. There is certainly a narration in the game, but as the player it's up to you to fill in the blanks. I will absolutely return to finish all the side objectives and achievements, if only to explore this world a little while longer.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not normally comfortable with paying $20AUD on odd-looking games, but this was worth it.  SuperBunnyHops' video review of it intrigued me.A massive improvement & evolution of the "collectathon" concept.  There is a mild amount of vanilla collect-a-thon (film canisters), but the majority of the game is a better "photo-a-thon" instead.  You have to work out good angles & lenses to get certain collections of items in shot (with varying rules), which is surprisingly fun.  I spent a lot of my time parkour-ing and glitching myself up walls to get interesting angles for otherwise simple tasks.  I'm sure some big game studio is going to see this game and completely misunderstand why its "photo-a-thon" implementation is fun.  They will release a game that tells you to stand at position X, face Y, zoom a camera and press a key.  Don't be this game studio.Physical motion in the game is a bit frustrating, you often get stuck on the side of objects and then have to give up by dropping to the floor of each map.  Gravity keeps increasing your fall velocity even when you're "pinned" against walls, so as soon as you find yourself rubbing against a wall you know it's time to give up.  About halfway through the game I got more used to it and learn how to move a bit better, but it's still a PITA.  Faster move speed would be handy at times for when trying to climb back up to where you fell, but it would probably be better to avoid the problem in the first place.I don't want to put spoilers in here, so I'll just say the worldbuilding and story are great.  Little bits of detail, some subtle and some in-your-face-with-guns-firing.  Lots of variety in ways of telling the story, about every trick in the book (_other_ than characters reading to you the plot) is used.The levels have a lot to explore.  Upon replaying some earlier levels I discovered entire areas above street level that I didn't know you could get to.  I'm somewhat miffed by the edges of some of the maps.  Invisible walls are my enemy and even the few small places they are used really annoy me.  They feel like a rushed/lazy measure inside levels that are otherwise really detailed and interesting.  Lots of billboard meshes are non-solid and you fall through them, this ruined a few good photo opportunities for me.  Albeit not all players will try to play like I do (explore the edges first).The last level felt detached from the rest of the game.  I'm left feeling that I didn't quite understand some of the subtext (probably, knowing thick-old-me!).Stylised.  Love the characters.  Use of 2D (graffiti, signs) and 3D (people, world) done really well; especially in a world where many games seem to only bother with good 2D work for the HUD and nothing else. + FOV adjustable + No crashes during normal play, very reliable. + Runs on Linux (I believe via proton) - Pixelisation visual effect.  Wasn't too bad and definitely added to the atmosphere, but was a little irritating at times.   - Soft-locks with a black screen if I tab out to another Window.  Possibly a Linux, Wine/proton and  3-monitor bug specific to my setup. - FPS not brilliant in large scenes when looking at lots of objects (but luckily this isn't too much of an action game, so I'm able to tolerate it without getting sick)A really good example of how quantity of assets (or even quality of individual assets) doesn't make a game; they could have defaced half the art and it would still be great.   This game's power is in its unique way of letting you enjoying the in-game worlds AND how it ties that mechanic to the story/world.  I now wish I could get a similar camera mechanic & goalset in many other game worlds.(To any aspiring game-devs reading this: think of how much fun this game is without having to put lots of effort into AI, animation, complex physics or voice lines.  Use these lessons to improve your bang-for-buck and reduce your time spent doing boring stuff!  Also take note that I somehow ended up liking my 'friend' NPCs in the game, despite how they never talk and never move from the one spot.  A tiny amount of interactivity can make a world of difference if done in a unique way.)All of this is, of course, counter-acted by the fact the game devs are Kiwis and therefore this game sucks.  10/10, would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Not just the best snapshot (ha, get it, it's a camera game) of 2020, but of our current moment at large. Umurangi Generation on its face is a game about taking photos to check off a list to progress to the next level. There's no dialogue, very few named characters, a plot told entirely through time and place. But it's one of the most effective I've encountered this year, drawing on real-world environmental and political upheaval with more than a little anime influence to frame what life looks like at the end of the world. Its levels reward close inspection above and beyond what its objectives ask, either with your own eyes or through the robust tools given to the player to take just about any variety of photos. The ending - for both the main game and the DLC, which I highly recommend to complete the package - will stick with me for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate taking pictures. Written words have always suited me better.When the approximately four hour Umurangi Generation released in the midst of the reverberating COVID-19 pandemic and Black Lives Matter protests of 2020, I felt extremely ill-equipped to talk about its place in these contexts. A photography game set amidst the collapse and hubris of institutions in the face of existential catastrophe was so unintentionally and yet perfectly timely that I was stopped in my tracks. The words never came.But in the months and years since, the pictures that I tried to take there haunt me still.In that “pointless” pursuit of capturing something just out of reach; in doing enough to get to the next day; in framing those moments of peace, of levity, of kindness, of hope; while still confined in an environment that felt inescapable.In the countless cynical and hopeless moments that have existed between then and now, I needed this practice as a kindling reminder:To persist.Part of a collection of short game diary entries from

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried liking this game. But simply put, it's not a good game.If I approach this just as an art, it's cool. The urban punk style really grasp what a "♥♥♥♥♥♥ future" can look like, the way the developer wrap the theme of a big disaster is honestly very cool. The implementation of Te Reo language while scarce, is a nice and smart way of making people interested of that language (myself included). That being said, I would've enjoyed it better if this is just an artbook or something.The gameplay is sadly the worst part of this game. You play as a photographer working for a company to takes photos. Every photo has value that's represented by "dollars", the better the game thinks your photo is, the higher the price. The game also supplement a lot of way to personalize your result either with a lot of choice of lenses (which needs to be unlocked by progression) or post-processing edit to change your photo brightness, color, and mood. I think a real photographer will appreciate a lot of these choices.So with that said, what is the GOAL of this game? Being a photographer, is it to capture the most amazing photo (at least as defined by the game)? Or being a courier, is it to take photos of what your clients want? Well actually, the point of the game is just you find random things to take picture at. I'm not kidding, this game is just "Where's Waldo" with extra steps. What's worse is that most of the things you'll need to find is hidden or require a specific angle that the game arbitrarily choose whether it's correct or not. It makes a frustating experience. And, except the lenses, all the options that is provided actually doesn't have any effect in the gameplay, which is kinda baffling for a game centered on photography. There's also the issue that the game assets area arguably looks bad, and the photography aspect make of the game makes it very obvious.We haven't even talked even talked about the movement, which just feels bad. _childDocuments_.review: There's plenty of ways I could praise Umurangi Generation: I could talk about its lovely dreamcast-esque artstyle, ThorHighHeels' spotless soundtrack, its genuine educational properties as a photgraphy simulator or its undeniably *intelligent* worldbuilding. Those are all true. Instead though, I'm just gonna say that this game literally changed me as a person - more specifically, as a writer.Umurangi Generation handles themes that are otherwise considered "delicate" due to their polarizing nature with all the grace of a roided-out silverback in a glassware emporium. It has exactly zero ♥♥♥♥♥ to give about the snotty video essayists that could misinterpret its extremely *blunt* messaging or criticize its "lack of nuance" and has no problem pointing at things and going "these things suck, period". This is especially true in the Macro DLC, a 4-stage map set that will likely get realer every year since its release. All of this is done through a masterful reinterpretation of familiar themes, tropes and aesthetics for which the director's love and appreciation is apparent. So much so that a way i like to introduce this game to people is "Evangelion from the eyes of Kensuke Aida", especially in reference to a particular stage in the Macro DLC (which also winks at the Tanker chapter from the start of Metal Gear Solid 2). So basically, Umurangi Generation is a game that should remind us that "caring about things" and "making an enjoyable game" are not opposite ends of a spectrum - something which we, as an audience, have spent *years* being subconsciously conditioned into thinking following spectacular failures in the triple A industry and the milking thereof by disingenuous content creators. You know who you are, and you know what you've done."Punk" may be a term whose meaning has been diluted to death in the past 40 years, but every now and then something comes along and it definitely fits the bill. Umurangi Generation is that "something", and I wish I had the utter titanium balls to write something as insightful, thoughtful and ultimately, utterly "punk".

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but it is plagued with technical issues from the get go.  There is no slider for mouse sensitivity, only four presets; you can clip through walls and into objects just walking and looking around normally; and you frequently bounce off of objects to find yourself launched up into the air far above the level, which is especially bad for the required platforming.Beyond these technical issues, I have more subjective complaints.  The art direction is terrible once you are in the game.  The screenshots and trailer make the game look like it has a cohesive, 3D comic-book look, like  from Black Pants Studio, but the actual in-game art looks more like placeholder art.  The film canisters that you have to find to earn upgrades blend in to the environment far too easily, looking more like black amorphous blobs than cylinders with a cap, and the aforementioned physics issues (randomly bouncing) make searching around the maps rather unpleasant.  But I think worst of all, given the game's unique photography mechanic, is the starting lens you are given: some kind of telephoto lens with a narrow depth of field, in a  cramped map with all but one of the subjects of interest nearby, making taking the photos feel awkward and making it difficult to get everything you want in frame.It saddens me to give this a thumbs down, because the concept is delightful, but this game needed more polish before release.  As it stands, it feels like playing a beta for something grander that never was and likely never will be.

_childDocuments_.review: Uncovered spoilers follow. To put it in simple terms for anyone looking to purchase the game or doesn't want to read an essay, Umurangi Generation is a game about being a photographer in an extraordinary situation they have no control to alter the course of, and it feels like the perfect game to represent 2020. It is highly recommended, but it is not perfect.------------------------------My favorite film of all time is Pacific Rim, a film in which the world is set upon by monsters from the sea hellbent on the destruction of humanity and everything it's built. In response, humanity built giant robots to be piloted in defense of itself, to meet the monsters as the approach and beat them down to prevent the extinction of humanity. As time goes on, these fighters, these Jaegers, are brought down by a threat that only gets more and more dangerous, and humanity finds itself wanting to instead hide behind walls instead of fielding more. It is only by virtue of a few remaining pilots that a large enough force is able to gather and defend against an ever-increasing threat, to win for good. It is the story of humanity triumphing in the face of adversity, where those in charge are at least willing to let them try.Perhaps the biggest blow to my own personal ability to believe in this narrative was 2020, in which many governments of the world failed to contain major disasters in the name of egos, money, division, and skepticism. Within the US alone, my country, 500,000 people are dead because of a virus we failed to contain, and the entire western coast of the country burned in some measure, with aid initially denied at various points due to attempts to twist the fires as being political. And this was just within my own country. And many other places in the world experienced similar feet-dragging and refusal. We have seen, in no uncertain terms, that the governments of our world are susceptible to refusing to deal with the problems at hand.And, ultimately, the story of Umurangi Generation is very much an expression of this feeling of distrust in my mind; even if we were to field such fighting robots to defend against the invasion of kaiju, the people we'd trust to be in charge of that would mismanage it by insisting that the pilots make public statements and posture for the people rather than making them better defenders. They would focus on tiny issues, trying to keep some measure of control to make themselves feel better, and send them to break up protests. And when push came to shove, they would refuse to be more prepared for when it gets worse. And more and more people would die because they refused to handle it correctly.In this way, Umurangi Generation is the game that most captures 2020, and the sense of despair, helplessness, fury, and fear that the year instilled in basically everyone. Perhaps, in a good world, the events of Pacific Rim would be our response to such a threat, but the world we have is one where the response depicted in Umurangi Generation is what we would face. And you, as the player, are in no position to change this. You're not one of the people on the front line trying to push the tide of an ever-increasing threat back, because most people wouldn't be. You're a normal person, to a degree, performing a job in the hope that the people in charge won't mess everything up, and in turn the story of the game is a chronicle of the end of the world because the people in charge  mess everything up. On an artistic, story-focused level, the game delivers beautifully, because this story is evident in every level and environment as time goes on.However, I do feel like the game has a few problems that undermine it all a little bit, and missed opportunities. I feel like finding film canisters is a neat idea, but I feel like it's a missed opportunity for you to instead be searching for small things in the environment that expand on the story. It would have been cool to collect newspaper clippings or other objects that tell the story of the world by their appearance. A damaged UN helmet, a note from someone in the middle of a kaiju attack, a broken toy, or other things to that effect. It also seems like it would have just been better if there wasn't a limit on film; it feels pointless, as canisters refill your film, so you're never at risk of not being able to take a shot if you don't grab them all, but it feels unnecessary in that case.Probably the biggest thing undermining it all is the 10 minute time trial challenge on every level, which I feel just serves to rush the players into completing bounties and leaving as soon as possible. While it is optional, the presence of the timer in the upper left and the fact that bonus equipment is hidden behind this objective makes it feel more mandatory than it should be. There's a constant pressure and it feels like you can't just enjoy exploring the level, and it reduces engagement with the story on the first time through because of it. Between this and the prior issue it makes it feel like taking non-bounty shots for your own personal enjoyment is discouraged, and it feels like trying to understand the story more from looking at the environment will just cost you equipment.These are my only real issues with the game, and neither really feel like they're insurmountable issues for myself. But they are frustrating, because it does feel like the story could have stuck even better if at the very least the timer wasn't present. Overall, I really do love the game, and is my favorite game from 2020.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly dull and artsy fartsy walking simulator with no real substance or engaging gameplay loop. Now I'm not a photographer of any kind, but I do enjoy taking random pictures every now and again so I thought this would be an interesting experience... Except the game doesn't really give you much freedom or incentive to take pictures aside from a very specific and often obtuse laundry list on top of a timer in tiny block-like levels, so it feels more like a puzzle game without the puzzles, if that makes any sense. The performance isn't great, even though everything is low poly and low res, on top of an awful forced graphics shader that lowers your internal resolution to god-knows-what making everything incredibly jaggy and consequentially seeing anything beyond a few meters is a nightmare, so good luck finding those collectible film rolls without crawling on the floor like you're looking for your lenses! Last but not least, the controls are slow and janky, half the time the double jump doesn't register for some reason making exploration not that fun, not that there's really anything all that interesting to find in the levels I've played. Other than that, it does have a very cool, stylized art direction and funky soundtrack reminiscent of Jet Set Radio which is always a positive in my eyes... But that's about it for the positives really.So if you're really, really hardcore into photography and you've already exhausted any other photography games, maybe get this in a deep discount... _childDocuments_.review: They say beauty is in the eye of the beholder, and having a snappy camera can't hurt in portraying that beauty.  Photography at its core is the practice of seeing one's point of view, encased in a still frame.  These point of views can come from all emotions: fear, love, admiration.  These emotions can form from any location: a concert, a political event, or in such cases, the impending end of the world.As a courier for the Tauranga Express, your camera is your job.  You and a group of friends are dispatched through various territories in an alternate-future Tauranga Aotearoa (actually known worldly for its diverse culture in religion and arts), tasked with showcasing the city's vibrant and booming culture whilst an impending world-dooming, intergalactic war shadows in the distance.  Each location is given a set of objectives to supply your parcel, how you supply that parcel is entirely up to the shooter. will immediately catch vibes of  mixed with a little , as objectives are tasked to small details like 'Union Jack', '3 Targets', or 'The word XCF'.  At first glance these won't make a whole lot of sense, but a few laps around each area should eventually find what you're looking for, even if some are deceptively hard to attain, and may need a google search to recognize its terminology.  Photo Mode, which is activated by default, will allow on-the-spot color correction and lighting with each photo.  You can tinker with color hues, bloom, focus, and exposure to perfect the acquired taste.  Additional parts for your camera will unlock with each completed parcel, and objectives will later ask for specific lenses and distance, requesting a keen eye and a good brain-racking to find that perfect shot.  Finding that perfect shot could not be more enjoyable with the radical areas that are ripe for the snapping.  Taking homogeneous references from the likes of  and  and coating it with a stylized graphic palette that would find home on a PlayStation 1,  mixes together a beautiful cocktail that's just as enjoyable to look at than to indulge in.  Sunset-kissed rooftops sheltered in a rainbow of spray paint and markers, neon-smeared streets submerged with loud music and dancing citizens barricaded under UN protection, hazy back-alleys immersed with candles and memories of those fallen.  It's such a treat to not only provide your own photos of the world around you, but to absorb that world's past and current issues through completing the parcel.As the atmosphere of each area is brought together with its visual achievements, the cherry on top is the fantastic selection of tunes chosen to bring even more life into Tauranga Aotearoa.  Boom-bastic beats riding shotgun with lo-fi vibes and smooth b-side instrumentals compliment each area, though I did notice a slight pause in play a majority of the time the tracks switch, but nothing to really deter from the gameplay.Once the initial tour of  is completed, special optional objectives are around to continue your stay.  These optional objectives are available immediately when playing, but it's best to keep these on repeated attempts as to not deter from the initial gazing of each stage.  Optional objectives aim for a set amount of money earned (fancier shots earn bigger payouts in your parcel), recreating the postcard supplied on each stage, finding all the extra film hidden (which also resupplies your camera's 24 picture count) and getting a sweet shot of all of your buddies, all while completing the main objectives in a set time.  Finishing these objectives will grant more equipment to tinker around with and further expand your palette.For budding amateur photographers and lovers of the vibe-y, low stakes genre of video games,  is a no-brainer.  Spending a couple hours bumping tunes, snapping pics, and watching the world slowly burn has never looked so good and been so fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is a rare case of a game that clearly has something to say, but isn't so self-conscious to blurt it out. Things are obtuse and opaque, but by leaving elements open to the player to interpret, it allows the very specific (and strange) story to hit home about so many elements of today's real world.Mechanically, it's undeniably rough around the edge. I had to quit out of the game because the focus stopped working, I got a movement glitch roughly every 5 minutes that gave me a super high jump, and my first play session gave me quiet a lot of motion sickness.If you can, it's absolutely worth trying to see through those mechanical shortcomings to explore what Umurangi Generation has to say.

_childDocuments_.review: Great little game! Loved the world design, and the level of detail with the photography mechanics. _childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is a relatively short and beautiful aesthetic photography game. The environments are all aesthetically interesting and a lot of fun to explore. The music and soundtrack are really great and tie in well to its aesthetic direction.Each level is fairly small and vertical, which makes exploration focus more on detail and camera work. The small level size also works to its benefit during the (optional) timed challenges, which are not challenging after playing through one time and getting your bearings. The tightness of the level design can make the platforming elements imprecise and frustrating at times, but the problems aren't pervasive. The story and world building is told through the environment and natural progression through the levels, which is pretty interesting, but leaves it all fairly thin. I think it works pretty well, especially given the detail and photography focus, but I do wish there was a bit more, because the world building is interesting.I would recommend Umurangi Generation to anyone interested in exploration and photography.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty cool game with a pretty cool concept. You're essentially a photographer that's given a task to take photos of specific items. _childDocuments_.review: There's some pretty glaring bugs:- It is very easy to fall through the map, to the point where I accidentally did it in normal gameplay maybe 20 or so times in my playthrough. I honestly just found it funny every time.- One achievement, "Speed runner", doesn't work on the current version of the game. This is a minor annoyance, unless you want to 100%.- Many translucent objects (glasses, windows, certain creatures) are completely invisible, even though the object is there and you can bump into it. This is a moderate annoyance, considering taking photos of your surroundings is the entire gameplay loop here.The last two can be fixed with an easy guide that walks you through downgrading the game's version, and I'd recommend new players immediately do that.However, with that preface out of the way: I was blown away by this game. Umurangi Generation's narrative is something that needs to be played to fully experienced, it's poignant, thought-provoking, and always at least simmering in the background. The photography is fun, and pretty involved once you start unlocking new tools. I took some legitimately good shots! Having photography bounties is a brilliant way to force the player to explore the map in ways they probably wouldn't otherwise, all to the game's benefit. Please, play this if you can. Especially if those annoying little bugs get fixed and you don't have to mess around with files beforehand.

_childDocuments_.review: It's incredible how heavily the narrative of "for a game about observation the timer is really polluting the entire experience" as if the timer isn't only a necessity in the pursuit of a perfect file and as if the levels aren't designed with the intention of replayability. You are only as limited by the timer as you feel the need to be, and I think that speaks volumes more about the individual than the game's arbitrary score attack elements.That said Umurangi Generation isn't a perfect game by any means, namely dragged down by jank controls and sometimes awkward placement of objectives that feel as if they intrinsically limit creativity behind the player's approach. Yet overall the game's stellar visuals, themes, and especially the soundtrack are indisputably all bangers. There's a clear Evangelion influence present that took me by surprise, but wholly welcomed, and I believe it's perfectly encapsulated by the set pieces in a way that generates an extremely eerie atmosphere that is wholly unique to itself. It provides the player with the inescapable sensation of being a spectator to something much greater, and Macro further expands upon that with some of the best levels of the entire game in my opinion.It's a short, tight experience that I don't regret at all.

_childDocuments_.review: What YOU Need To Know:In the start the game seemed kinda confusing.But I actually ended up enjoying this game a lot more than I thought in the start.The gameplay loop actually get's pretty easy and cool to understand.It seems to me we are a journalist in this futuristic city were there's happening a conflict. A civil war, maybe a godzilla attack, maybe both. But were stuck in the middle of it. And throughout the game you travel across the city exploring this conflict, each area has you complete a set of task or photographies. So you travel around these small contained very dense filled with detail areas and try to spot these objects your looking for and capture them on your camera. I thought each location was pretty unique and cool, and the soundtrack jeez, just made it a blast walking around snapping pictures. You also get different camera lenses that makes some challenges harder or some funnier, and more choices for editing in post-processing in these pictures. It's all very cool. Only problem I have with this game is the jank. Luckily no gamebreaking bugs, they've made easy fixes for falling out of the map, but still the fact that happens is a bit wack. Walking and jumping/crouching sometimes feel weird. And the backdrop for some of these levels are so rough made, that sometimes it takes you out of the very well made level you're standing in. Other than that I thought it was pretty fun piecing together the story of this city, cuz you get no help. You just figure out a long like a journalist.I'd recommend :)6/10 - Good

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a really neat concept and the execution is great. In a sci-fi dystopia, you are tasked with taking photographs of a range of different subjects. It gives photographers and casual snappers plenty of simple steps without turning away pros either. The way that different lens types are handled is very nice and there's plenty of options that satisfy all tastes. Little collectables help flesh out the world and picking up film canisters gives you the opportunity to take bonus shots.It has great vibrant 3D environments with puzzles and some subjectivity in terms of how you take the photo. For the most part it doesn't penalise you for thinking outside of the box or getting a unique angle. Do you leave out the messy paint can and graffiti or do you keep them in the frame? You may have to take a photo of 10 solar panels for example, which means getting into the right position. There's some basic parkour which gives you access to some of the best angles and this is a key part of getting around the maps. There's enough under the hood to keep people engaged and there's a world ready to be discovered and unearthed. I'm super excited for the future of photography videogames.

_childDocuments_.review: As you take every photo for each objective, Umurangi Generation reminds us of every facet of life that is doomed to devastation without proper action. Even as the movement occasionally becomes clunky, or the models fail to get enough clarity, the game guides us through the vast scale of lives that are both so fleeting and prominent, emphasizing every picture. And it also shows just how much we don't want to let that go. Taking pictures, even at the end of the world, still in some way is an attempt to remind ourselves of the absolute state of things. That it could've been prevented. That things were actively being led to failure. That we don't want to take this lying down. That we're angry at the world, and rightfully so, for how it's treats and discards us. But also that we're still living, existing, and taking photos up until the end of the world.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I can't say I'm the kind of person who would enjoy this game the most. It's a game about photography, and I'm really not good at it... and yet, as I said, I love this game a lot! It's still very enjoyable, even for photography inepts like me!I think one of the things that make this game so fun for everyone, is the requirements you have to meet in the levels. Obviously, optional tasks such as "Finding all the Film Canisters in a level" or "Finishing the level under a certain period of time" will be fun to some. But I'm referring to the actual mandatory ones: take a picture of X and Y thing(s) with Z lens. It makes you look for said items, find the right position, use the needed lens, and maybe do some awkward repositioning. They make the mandatory objectives look great (most of the times at least...) and force you to get creative! And, in the process, something may catch your attention as well, and you may decide to take a pic of that too! That's how I enjoyed it the most at least...Presentation-wise,  is phenomenal! It has this low-poly, cell-shaded anime artstyle that is just... so good! It gives some nice Jet Set Radio vibes, but thanks to the much dimmer lighting and depressive atmosphere, it still stands out by itself. The soundtrack is mostly composed of some unique chill music, that I've found myself listening to quite a few times since I played it. Not something I listen to very often, but I love to have it in the background and hum to it every once in a while.And the story... well I'm going to be completely honest, I'm really bad at catching any media's plot, even when it's spit on my face, so I may not have got it all. That being said... the story is really cool! It starts with you and your friend chilling, visiting different locations and such, but it quickly becomes obvious that things are really not okay: Prepared military camps, and memorials and candles to remember the deceased at first; and not much later, gunfights against gigantic incomprehensible beings and desperate people  to evacuate the area. There really aren't many negatives I can point out. The movement is a little wonky, and the collisions can be pretty clunky (going upstairs is fun sometimes, some others it's frustrating). It's also a pretty short game, but like, so what? Just enjoy the scenes, take some cool photos, listen to those beats, and witness the end of the world...

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is one of the most interesting games I have ever played. I came across this game during my research on in-game photography. More specifically, I was looking at video games where photography is a major part of the gameplay. As a photographer, I can say that the parameters used to rate the photographs taken by the player are quite absurd. However, I was expecting this and it doesn't decrease the pleasure of being creative with all the functions that the game provides, and there are a lot of them! The visual style is based on a cyberpunk world and its presentation is inspired by old video games. I think the decision to go with the retro look is very attractive, as there is no actual try to illustrate a photorealistic world here, which makes the photography in this virtual space seem even more abstract and artistic. What fascinates me the most about Umurangi Generation is the world it portrays and the story it tells. It's absolutely brilliant that the story isn't told via cutscenes, scripts or text, but exclusively via the different levels and the objects and characters they contain. The story reveals itself to a good observer and a photographer is in the end nothing else. It also runs very well on the Steam Deck.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A game about hanging out and taking photos at the end of the world. Lets you be endlessly creative with its scenes and photo settings as you unlock more equipment. Only nitpicks are very awkward movement and I wish there was no map time limit to unlock everything. Continues the trend of indie games just always having the best soundtracks.

_childDocuments_.review: The quintessential scifi disaster photography game. You thought you were solving fundamental visual puzzles, but you were actually investigating the failures of your society. One of the few dystopian stories to encourage you to savor the present.Shoutouts to the soundtrack to being one of my most played music for the past year and getting me in the mood for DJ Tariq.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: From a gameplay angle, it can be very janky at times. From a political angle, especially in the Macro DLC, it is very blunt. If you're someone who demands polish from your games and doesn't want to have "politics shoved down your throat" you're not gonna have a good time here. Luckily for me that wasn't the case. The gameplay mechanics are actually a bit more interesting than your average photography game - sometimes you actually really have to think about how exactly to get the shot it's asking you to get, and that can be quite difficult at times - whether it's searching for the specific thing the bounty is asking you to get (for example, it might feature somewhere you don't expect, like on a poster or a computer screen), or lining up the shot itself with the lense it asks you to use. It's almost like a puzzle game in that respect. Visually and thematically, what you get here is very much inspired by both Evangelion and very recent protest movements globally. The main game tells a story that is laregelly about the apocalypse. The DLC is much more interested in how our current world order is ran by powerful but simple-minded hedonists who do not care if their actions result in the death of their subordinates, ordinary citizens, or even the earth itself. If you do enjoy the main game from a thematic standpoint, I do very much recommend the DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I would get a simple and relaxing photography game, instead I got  a top notch environmental storytelling in a tight little package.The game revolves around taking photos that meet a certain criteria, using different filters and processing methods to really give flair to your image, but you’ll soon come to realize that it isn’t a pastime of the main character, and through the lens of their camera you can really have a feel of the world around you.Why are there barricades around large bodies of water, why your employer penalize you from taking photos of █████ ████ “blue bottles”, are all questions you can answer yourself looking at posters, papers, people’s tattoos.As I said, the most unique aspect of the game, other than the premise of being put in a little sandbox to take photos and edit them on the spot, is it’s very clever to communicate the feel and story of the world through cleverly constructed environments and details.The game can look and feel rough around the edges, but the worst aspect is that in every stage you’ll be tasked to take a photo of specific things, some of them hidden so much in the background or in places you normally wouldn’t look that it’s not uncommon to wander around for half an hour in an otherwise ten minute level.It's not very long but it’s rather unique, with it’s own sense of style and with a different kind of approach to storytelling, that’s a recommended from me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the ultimate masterclass example of "Show don't tell", the game and soundtrack has a great story, world building, and atmosphere, without practically saying a single word the entire game. Gameplay boils down to essentially a first person "I Spy" game where you have to take a photo containing the complete request like "Take a photo with a zoom lens that has 5 birds in it" This is a lot of fun as you scour the level not just for the items in question, but a good place to take the photo so you can get just the right angle.The clever bit is that asking you to take time to look at everything to find the items forces you to look at things that aren't the item you're looking for, but identifying the environment around you gives you a ton of insight into the world, the people, and what's happening.The game is super fun, and all the unlockable lenses and upgrades are fun to take back into previous levels to get more creative photos and find new secrets. It's worth picking up and experiencing it for yourself, at least the base game, though if you like the base game, I'd recommend the DLC as it adds new lens options for really interesting photos.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a phenomenal game, and a testament to the capacity of video games to operate as directly political media. For the most part, the game is simply a heap of fun. The photography mechanics work great, the levels are vibrant, and the music slaps. Political commentary is peppered throughout out this on colonialism, the nature of international institutions like the UN, and the environmental crisis. As this is all achieved through environmental storytelling, none of it comes off as heavy-handed, and the player is left with a lot of room to think about things without being forced to. This gives the game's final moments some frankly *incredible* tension and political commentary, as the final levels of both the main game and the DLC are the only times it works in more direct political messaging. The impact of this combo is breathtaking.I love Umurangi Generation. It has advanced the medium of video games as a whole.
