_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever watched Neon Genesis Evangelion, or any other Kaiju-fighting show, and wondered what happens to the citizens of the cities that are destroyed by the collateral damage? When the giant mech shoots it's 1400 mm calibre rounds at the monster, the cartidges have got to land somewhere right? Wouldn't they destroy buildings and cars? Have you ever thought about what it would be like to actually live in a worn-torn cyberpunk city, like Tokyo-3? Do you really think that if an alien invasion ever happened, for real, or any other apocalypse for that matter, that our governments would handle the situation appropriately? If the sea turned to blood, how would you survive, let alone the economy? Umurangi Generation explores those questions, and more, through the medium of photography, exploration, and quiet contemplation.You play as a young photographer, vibing with your friends and making art, in the last days of earth's existence. Because what else are you gunna do? What else *can* you do?This game was made initially after the 2019 fires in Australia destroyed so much life, after the direct results of climate change were laid bare for all to see, and no-one seemed to care. Since then, we've seen a similarly tepid response to the Covid pandemic, and I think the DLC (Macro) explores those aspects of generational frustration more than the original game did.If you're worried about there being 'lame social commentary', or if you think the game might be 'too preachy', then I'd say you can lay those fears to rest -- mostly. The game doesn't have any explicit message, it's objectives simply ask you to look at the environment, and to see the implicit damage for yourself. There's no dialogue even, just diagetic storytelling, through the art direction, clothing, graffiti, music, billboards, and stray newspapers. Ultimately, this is a game about finding meaning in the end times. Something I'm struggling with a lot at the moment. If you are too, then this is an easy recommendation. The 'red sky generation' are the last people who'll ever live. I'm not sure if *we* are that generation, you and I, that is, but it sure feels like it sometimes...I also think it's neat that the game saves every photo you take to your harddrive and opens that folder for you when you quit the game. It means that you can literally take something away from the game, as well as metaphorically. In some ways it's also an educational game about photography, and may be a gateway to making art by yourself.It's art. In every sense of the word.Oh, and the soundtrack kicks ass too!

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game that doesn't quite work for me. A game about photography feels like it should be slow-paced and allow you to explore at your leisure but all the tasks - find 10 of these, get this very specific photo, do it all within ten minutes - makes it feel rushed and stressful. The telephoto tasks are a particular headache as you run around each level trying to find one awkward spot where you can get the right items in frame. It's as if they felt they had to gamify what is essentially a walking simulator and the two approaches grate against each other badly. I'd still say it's worth getting, but with the benefit of hindsight I would have enjoyed it far more if I'd just ignored all the secondary tasks and spent more time with each level, just poking about and entertaining myself first and foremost, and I'd suggest anyone buying it play it that way first too.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi is the kind of game where you get out of it what you put in.As an objective based game, it tends to be somewhat lackluster. How interesting someone finds this is entirely dependant on their interest in treating the world as a canvas. The main content of the 'story mode' is a list of levels with photo objectives. Capture a few birds in one shot, do a close up on a skateboard, that sort of thing. The joy is in capturing the details of the world through photography. Stylistically, Umurangi shines with art direction, music, and environmental design that I can only describe as powerfully bold and authoritatively subversive. The whole game feels like a rejection to authority and abuses of power. I feel the game is at its best when you immerse yourself in the atmosphere it creates, as Umurangi is not carried by the depth of gameplay, rather the mood and story that is conveyed by your own capturing of said atmosphere. You keep the pictures you take too, which is really cool.I can say with absolute certainty that this game will not appeal to those solely seeking extrinsic motivation. For those who want a game for style and atmosphere, Umurangi will more than provide if you are willing to look.

_childDocuments_.review: many thoughts, most of which have been better articulated by other people. but ig i will say that, being the perhaps Undue optimist that i am, i appreciate some of the little things which convey some kind of Meaning, or at least a gleeful embrace of its own nihilism, beyond the absolutely crushing content of the world around you. mostly i appreciate that your friend group stays together , they never say a single word but their presence, and taking the bonus group photo, is always a weird source of comfort. this very easily could have been a lonely story, but ig its not called Umurangi One Single Dude. we are all in this together
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance Umurangi Generation is a chill photography game with artstyle similiar to Jet Set Radio, but once you look closely there is much more depth here. Its environmental story telling is top notch, providing social commentary through its setting of "♥♥♥♥♥♥ futute" that doesn't seem that far off from our own crappy reality. I highly recommend you watch Errant Signal and Super Bunnyhop essays about this game on youtube, they are amazing.Gameplay wise its very simple. You are equipped with a camera and have to complete photo bounties in each mission by taking photos of specific objects, sometimes with extra requirements, such as using fish eye lense. There are eight levels, each being a small sandbox for you to express yourself creatively. You start with your basic camera and unlock more specialized lenses, filters and settings for it as you progress through the game and complete extra challenges. I recommend you ingore the time limit and collectibles on your first playthrough and just immerse yourself in this world and try to piece together what's going on. There are many ways to accomplish each bounty and express yourself. Just go wild and experiment with perspective and your equipment!Music and overall soundscape of Umurangi Generation is one of its strongest points. Its a very unique mix of electronic and hip hop music, which suits the setting perfectly. There are no voices in here, but this game's graffiti and propaganda posters speak volumes.I have only a few small gripes with Umurangi Generation. Biggest of them being the controls. Movement feels stiff and unresponsive, I also gut stuck on geometry a few times. However, considering that you can't really fail in this game and it doesn't require fast movement its not a big deal. I also found it a bit annoying that you have to manually scroll through your entire selection of lenses and can't just pick it using for example a radial menu. Its a bit tedious, but again, no biggie.I highly recommend Umurangi Generation if you like photography and enjoy slow paced, chill games with extra depth. For me it was such a nice change of pace from what I usually play. It succeds in almost everything it sets out to do and you owe it to yourself to give it a go. Big kudos to this game's creator Origame Digital!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty cool game!I really liked how the mechanics all made the biggest strength of it: the environmental narrative. They make you search for words like "xcf" or "cop" and use a very specific lens and make you scour about every face, every word, every thing with full intention of finding something. And that makes you start picking up some of the pieces for a nice and strong message that doesn't seem to get old. We truly are the generation seeing the end of the world. Loved it even if I didn't understand everything.You do get to make a lot of cool looking photos. Try tilting the camera a lot! This game proves you can make a game entirely about photography and it would be fine.I would like a more sophisticated movement system, and that the game woudn't be so upfront with a timer. If you see the timer, just don't care about it. Take your photos, find the stuff, make beautiful pieces.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a difficult game to review, partly cause Steam does not offer an Undecided/Middle of the Road/Sideways Hand option, but also due to the nature of the game's narrative. These are just my feelings, so take it with a grain of salt where applicable.Let's start with the gameplay. Someone originally pitched it to me as an avant-garde Pokemon Snap, albeit with more freedom, and I can certainly see the parallels. You roam around in artistic 3D environments taking pictures, unlocking new camera features as you go. While you  snap photos of whatever, there's a limited amount of film and objectives to complete in order to finish a given level. Unlike the Nintendo game, however, Umurangi has somewhat unorthodox methods for judging your photos. I still do not have a firm grasp on what constitutes a "great" scoring photo as the game's tutorial explicitly states such things are subjective. This sounds great on paper, but as an actual mechanic it could certainly stand to be better defined since score is tied to a stage's bonus objectives.The stages themselves range from cramped, difficult to navigate mazes to open (in a limited way) areas that, nonetheless, still manage to be difficult to navigate for different reasons. You can jump twice, but the second is not terribly effective, and you can crouch. I assume the latter is just for taking variations on a given shot cause I never found it useful in the game itself. I did, on the other hand, get caught on the level geometry repeatedly throughout the game! Sometimes a jump would leave me on an undefined edge where I could slide along but not jump the last few pixels to the spot I was hoping to reach. Other times, I had to shake my character loose from a pipe or other obstruction I'd somehow gotten caught on.I said you had limited film, and this is true, but it's also ! Every level has a number of tiny, frequently hard to see film canisters hidden throughout, and picking one up will refresh your photo count. Very handy in the few levels with an absurdly high bonus score objective, not that the game informs you of this. Collecting all the film in a level counts as one of the bonus conditions towards unlocking a second camera ability if you do them all in one go. Unfortunately, this means  from the necessary photos to optional ones and picking up all the hidden film capsules, to boot. They're devilishly easy to overlook. Good luck finding them without a guide!I'm not trying to be hard on the game, I just personally found it to be as aggravating as it was fun to play. That's ultimately part of my problem with there being a 10-minute time limit being present as part of the bonus conditions. On the surface, it appears to be a game about taking your time, soaking up the atmosphere, and doing your own thing. Yet at the same time it has photo limits, a timer, and a score count.It also has a neat "recreate the postcard" bonus objective! It's a nice idea. It's also somewhat frustrating. I can take 10 nearly identical photos that don't count but apparently another one will count. Was I slightly to the side? Was my zoom a little different? I have no idea. It's possible to select the pause menu's postcard and get a larger view, but the sometimes dark look of the photo means it's not much help.This is, unfortunately, another of the game's problems for me; the user interface isn't terribly helpful. The tutorial has a yellow text with no bordering that makes it very difficult to read. The menu options are black text on a white rectangle, like something out of MS Paint; it stands out as odd in an otherwise artistic looking game. There is also the fact that exiting a level takes you back to the title screen instead of the level selection screen. If you're struggling to do everything in 10 minutes, this will become very tedious.I want to stress that , it's just that there is plenty which could have done with some more polishing. Gameplay quirks or hang-ups that, while sometimes minor, nonetheless got in the way of my  enjoyment. If you just wanna run around the environments, taking pictures, and making your way through the unspoken narrative, you will probably enjoy this game.My other problem with Umurangi, however, has to do with the DLC. This is a lot more subjective than the rest of my review because the additional levels are a lot more aggressive from a narrative standpoint. I don't want to get into it for risk of spoiler, but I certainly found them to be less enjoyable, especially the last two levels. They are all fairly large compared to the main game's level design, and if I understand it right the developer was in an angrier frame of mind when they made them. It uh.. shows. They're visually impressive, as is most of the game, but there is a very distinct mood change from the regular portion of the game.The last thing I'll comment on is the music. As I played the first few levels I kept thinking, "Gee, all it's missing is some Jet Set Radio-esque music!" because it was just sorta inoffensive, generic background music. Then I heard TARIQ talk during one level and immediately longed for that boring, lifeless music from the earlier stages. I think TARIQ is meant to be memes, or social commentary, I don't know. I just know , Dolphins are neat, though, I appreciated the idea.I'm bad at summarization, this is far longer than I'd like it to be, and it doesn't feature a handy bullet-point list like some folks use. If you read all of this, I thank you. These are just my thoughts on Umurangi, not a professional review. It's a very  game with a unique premise and gameplay we don't see often. I got it on sale; I don't know if I think it's worth the full price. I'd love to see another game that plays similar to it, though!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Admittedly I don't believe this game is for everyone; if you lack of patience then this game isn't for you. It is more of a game that you go about finding spots to take pictures of, simple task yes? well to be frank it is simple but also not that simple. The game is very easy to understand that it plays out like 'Hide-N-Seek'; you gotta find place's to take pictures that are easy to find; while some more challenging to find (It does make the game more fun due to this). If you get lost for a bit by being overwhelmed by the limited time you have; my suggestion on the first run of the game is to not worried about the timer-! There is no game over. You will not get punished even if you stayed in for a hour or so like I have. After your first run, you shouldn't be lost at all if you want to 100% run the game; even with a 10 minute run in each level that it really isn't that hard to get below the 10 minute mark to beat each level. Just do not do it in your first run since the new areas gets you more lost rather than just confused. Only problem I had about playing the game is finding Film Canisters that are spread across the game; but other than that I had no real issues trying to get each level done. If you are into Interactive Visual Storytelling while playing a genre of video games that plays out more niche from other games. Then this game is for you. It is a beautiful game with a wonderful soundtrack! Is it worth every penny? Of course, every bit of it that it comes with multiple modes after beating it; with many other things you can do with your camera. It even has creative mode that allows you to do whatever you please. I won't speak to much on the story, because it is a visual experience; but I will say that it was a beautiful one.

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is a game I didn't have any expectations for when booting it up for the first time. Not high expectations, not low expectations, just a complete blank slate. I ended up being blown away by the experience, which is probably why I felt compelled enough to write a Steam review.The core gameplay loop is satisfying; sure, you can boil it down to "just taking pictures", but given the variety of tools at your disposal even from the start (that expand as you complete sets of photo bounties) you start to consider the actual compositions of your shots. It never feels like a game where you're expected to know how to actually do photography -- I sure as hell don't -- but it rewards you for experimenting. Being able to save the photos you take into a folder after playing is a nice touch, too.The entire vibe of this game is probably the strongest selling point, though. Despite there being a time limit to "do well" on your photo deliveries, if you ended up exceeding that time limit it doesn't automatically boot you from the stage. This allows you to actually examine your environment, pick up on the details of what's going on in this world, getting a sense of the injustices that the people you are alongside throughout the entire game are going through. All the while, a varied soundtrack that embraces so many varieties of influences (from microtonal jazz to rough analogue house and many more) matches and enhances the vibe. The stylish low-poly graphics add to this charm, and even help bring the experiences that much more down to earth during its shift in its final act.Despite the fact that there's no dialogue in the game, you really get a strong sense of what's going on through its environmental storytelling. In fact, taking on the role of a photographer encourages this fact, having you consider your surroundings both from a gameplay perspective and from a human perspective.TL;DR: Umurangi Generation is a great game, balancing appreciation of photography with a story about indigenous resistance against their oppressors. ♥♥♥♥ yeah. More games by indigenous developers need to be celebrated, this one included.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I totally adore this game so much, the OST is spot on awesome, as someone who loves to take pictures in videos and IRL this fills my love for photography and it makes me so happy!  The level of control you have and the almost endless amount of different types and levels of photos you can take is truly great, I love it so and i would recommend it 100%. Im gonna be taking lots of pictures and i wont ever stop here!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This won't be for everyone, but this was totally for me. It's kinda short, it's kinda buggy in places (but not in a game-breaking way), it's kinda rough around the edges, and all these things, and more, made it really compelling.At a basic level it's what it says: a game about photography. Wander around 8 different levels and take photos, either trying to hit all the achievements or not. But there's also a story here, one that, for me anyway, was told in a perfect way. It's not spoon-fed, it leaves a lot of wiggle room for your own take on it, yet there's a pretty clear message as well.The soundtrack really worked for me too.Do I recommend it? Yup, no question. Will you, the reader, like it? I have no clue; but you might thank yourself for trying it.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Giving this a thumbs down but will say there is a lot that i like about it. The general idea, the gameplay and the art are all really good. Unfortunately, the objectives are usually extremely nebulous, requiring shots that are extremely specific, even when there appears to be alternate ways of getting the same shot (see 15 Candles and Cat & Bird objective on the 4th level). It's a bummer that a game that ostensibly encourages experimentation can't recognize when the player experiments. The ten minute time limit on every level doesn't matter at all except for completionists, but still gives me anxiety seeing it tick away, feeling like I'm not fast enough or smart enough. Maybe the sequel will be better. If you want a better, much chiller photography adventure experience I recommend Toem, and Alba: A Wildlife Adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: one of the best games to come out in the past couple years for sure! followed the development since it was announced, interacted with the team (super nice people!) and played the entirety of it in one go. then came the switch release and that was wonderful as well. such a joy to replay the engaging story and challenges alongside friends who were new to the game. wonderful and dynamic soundtrack, addictive visual design, as well as a story and culture that grabbed my interest from the get go. grab this game during the holidays and get a copy for your friends as well! kia ora!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: wonderful wonderful game where you take photographs with a relatively authentic photo-taking and editing experience. you enter a small, digestible stage and are tasked with taking a variety of shots with specific parameters like "Five seagulls" or "A Union Jack". there's a handful of common bonus objectives as well. the photo editing lets you use common sliders found in most photo editing applications. the different lenses also take different kinds of shots just like in real life.the style and atmosphere is top notch. covid meant I couldn't go outside to shoot (and couldn't see people to shoot either) and this game is a wonderful alternative. the world and 'lore' is super cool too. it is a bit "environmental storytelling through graffiti" but it actually makes sense with the world's punk and dystopic setting.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good!The story, while minimal, hits a bit hard with the conclusion - and the photography choices the player can make throughout the game are great.The challenges the game gives you have a perfect balance of difficulty and freedom - only denoting something that should be in the shot without intruding anywhere else. As well, the designs for each character are great - and the many references to different cultures are played well.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: As long as you go into this knowing it's about taking photos of a cool world and not much else, I would recommend it. Personally I found the bounty aspect of the game rather tedious, and the timer even more so. I feel these aspects were shoehorned in after someone on the team mentioned that taking just photos wasn't "game-like" enough, to the detriment of the game. That said, the world is cool and interesting, and taking photos of it is satisfying. Don't think it's worth full price, but a good pickup if on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty much a summary of what went wrong with the world in 2021 all neatly packaged into a photography game. If you are wealthy and affluent enough to go into space like Jeff Bezos or Elon Musk, the door is open for you. If not, which you are in this game because you are doing a gig photography job. You're stuck on earth in a permanent state of disrepair, wasting away the time partying to forget the malaise, all while surrounded by giant bluebottles. The game doesn't explicitly tell you this, but you'll know when you see it.This game doesn't need cutting edge graphics to be entertaining, but there are some imperfections that makes playing a bit irritating. Sometimes you end up getting catapulted into the sky if you walk up a surface, other times you can't even walk up a single step. Keep that in mind.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: The movement is clunky and occasionally glitches out (things like having gravity affect you while still having 0 y movement, causing the moment you get to move downwards to make the character shoot down with far too much y velocity).That's the only downside I can think of at the time of playing. It's a game that, at first, was made with concern over the world. The Macro DLC is downright angry. And it works. The cyberpunk aesthetic works for the vibe the game is going for, the "no photographing the blue bottles" tells all the story it needs to without having 100 hour long cutscenes. It works.And I am ashamed at the society that it suggests we are.Also you have a penguin friend. Yes please.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this up because I like the idea of a photography game and I really like the art style. I was very surprised to have played this and found that it was telling quite a story through the photography. There are a bunch of levels to the game and each one you get to explore and take photos. You have a specific list of things to take pictures of, but you can run around and explore and do what you want. As you progress through the levels, you start to learn more about the world and learn why things are the way they are. I didn't expect to have such a deep story revealed through taking pictures like this, but I'm happy I was able to experience it. The levels are small, but very detailed leaving you plenty to photograph. You eventually unlock filtered to edit your photos and different lens types, like the fish eye lens. As a photographer myself, I find the photography mechanics to be fairly realistic. It's a game and some corners are cut, but having some control over depth of field, lens type, and photo editing was pleasant to experience in a game. My only complaint is that it's a bit short. I completed the story in about 6 hours. It does look like there is a dlc with a lot more content, so I hope to check that out eventually. Anyways, if you like creative and relaxing games, definitely give this a try and test out your photography skills.Runs perfectly on Linux with Proton Experimental.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation claims to be set in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ future, but it quickly becomes clear we're already there. It represents the world in a stylized setting with some exaggeration but the general thematic elements and some of the locations feel straight out of real life. The photography is very immersive and the objectives are well done, being challenging while rarely getting frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: What a great game, the art-style is very pleasant and minimalist, but accomplishes a lot. Picture taking is fun and being rewarded each level with a new way to experiment with photos is great. While the game is about photography, it doesn't lazily throw you into a generic urban environment to take pictures in, small details of ongoing crises and the gloomy future, making it interesting to explore each level to learn small titbits about the fictional world that you are photographing.Other than jumping being a bit iffy sometimes (which is such a small issue anyways) and objectives not wanting to be completed (can be a little annoying sometimes), this is a great game for people that enjoy taking pictures of things or are interested in the idea. Please buy the game and give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: We should never have built a world where this game was made, but we did. Even still I'm thankful this work is out there to capture the humanity and beauty and emptiness and love and disillusionment and all-out, screaming, impotent anger that builds up behind the scenes for those outside of power. My only complaint is that the DLC is a separate, optional buy -- It should be mandatory for anyone who enjoys the base game. Obviously recommended. I rate this The Game I Will Stan To All Of My Friends Knowing None Of Them Will Ever Play It /  10.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't know what to expect before playing Umurangi Generation, but it suprised me with its sense of character, open level design, and storytelling through lore and structure. I loved the deep photo mechanics, with the ability to swap lenses and change various elements of the shot including bloom, exposure, and tint. But you don't NEED to like taking photos to enjoy this game, in fact I think you may have more fun if you don't. Objectives push you to find a checklist of items and you can scavenge the levels finding whatever you'd like, taking random pictures in between. The non-linearity contained within each level allows the player to see what they want from each level and learn about the world at their own pace. There is a story in this game, and although there is no dialogue, there is an astounding amount of emotion running through the game's levels, as well as its music and art style. Quite an interesting experience, and one I recommend strongly, especially to aspiring....or uninspired photographers.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is a fantastic few hours. You will not be challenged with intense gameplay, or balancing lots of systems. You will be sent into a dying world with nothing more than your camera and your friends. You have objectives, but your photos are not graded on a quality scale. The game itself in its tutorial insists that it's unfair to grade art objectively. Your photos are your own expression, with each objective having usually one or two places you can complete it on a map. It's not a long game, but the little time it holds you for is a great time. It's chill and beautiful, all backed up with a fantastic score by ThorHighHeels (who has a great YouTube channel if you like obscure Japanese video games btw). This isn't a game for someone who wants a very active, demanding experience. It's a game whose value is what you find in it. If you've ever just wanted to get lost exploring a game world, snapping photos to remember it by, this might be the game for you. And even if you're on the fence, if you catch it on a good sale, I think you should give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely one of my favorite games of 2020. Take the anti-establishment teenagers of Jet Set Radio and set them mid-apocalypse documenting Kaiju attacks, environmental and economic collapse, and a UN occupation and do it in the style of Pokemon Snap. Bleak, heartbreaking, colorful, irreverent, wonderfully cynical. This game perfectly captured the absurdity of the world around me as I played it during the peak of the pandemic and civil unrest of the summer of 2020. Add in an incredible soundtrack and some of the best environmental storytelling I've ever seen and it's an easy recommend from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Generation is THE photo mode that you actually want to play with. Okay, maybe I'm overselling it, hear me out.It's a good on-its-way-to-be-great photography game with a few mechanical flaws. I kept asking myself what does this game wanted to be. If it's meant to simulate the adventurous photographer experience, then it has done its job pretty well. I'm just gonna list down the flaws real quick:- the movement system can be a bit stiff sometimes- the camera would detect faraway targets that're outside of the visible frame- the targets of the objectives can be a bit finicky for the frame to detect- the depth of field effect radius probably needs more refinement- that's it I guessFrom this point on, my comment on the game will be heavily subjective with mild spoilers.I kinda love this game. I got all the achievements and I kept on playing because the game is just that fun of a space to run around, especially after I unlocked all the late game upgrades. What keeps me coming back are the aesthetics for sure, the Jet Set Radio charm (including its jankiness) is definitely here. The game's vibes, man. Enhanced by beautiful colors, fun soundtracks, and all this cultural bonfire surrounded by these quite bleak worrying subject matters.The environmental storytelling showcased the idea of helplessness for being a mere citizen, witnessing large conflicts and catastrophes that no one has control over. As a citizen of a Commonwealth country, I think I can kinda sympathize with the Maori presented here. All these wars and geopolitical talking points are just too much for one person to bear, and for this game's case all the player can do is take nice pictures and say "I was there when it happened." Yeah it's a bit depressing, but that's that. I'm too stupid to talk more about this.The photo shooting mechanic is great. All the clickety-clack sound effects are just as satisfying as an M1 Garand ping. Climbing around these levels reminded me of my own college photographic experience, my mates and I went to places that we shouldn't. We tinkered with the ISO, aperture, shutter speed just to make dumb pictures that nobody will see. This game gets it.Recommendation-wise, if you're a photography fan, get it whenever you can.If you're looking for a game to chill and just wander around, this game would be a nice detour.Niche as hell. You have been warned.Sequel wishlist:- extensive camera angle manipulation- hotkeys for the lens- include any form of optical illusions or gestalt imagery- functional halfpipes?- more camera types? (a TLR camera maybe? no? okay...)
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A fantasic game that encourages artistic self expression and exploration. You slip into the role of a photographer, who is tasked with photographing specific objects or words, like "1 Cat & 2 Birds" or "The word Squid". Some objectives are even a bit open to interpretation. After taking a photo the game will quickly rate it and give you some money which basically represents your score. You will do this in a variety of cool looking cyberpunk levels with a PS1 aesthetic. Each level is like a little open world and the objectives can be tackled in any order and in multiple ways. The challenge mostly comes from certain restraints, like having to use a specific lense that is only effective at certain distances or has trouble capturing multiple objects. Another challenge you can impose on yourself are the optional objectives, which are however always the same in every level.You will also have a wide variety of tools avaible, with which you can play with however you like. As mentioned before, you will unlock different lenses like a telescopic lense, which allows for photos with a lot of depth of field and makes it easier to capture far away objects, but has a narrow field of vision. On the other extreme is the fish eye lense, which makes it easy to capture multiple objects at close range and warps the picture in stylish ways, but has no depth of field and is useless when the object is far away. Besides the lenses you can also unlock some filters, with which you can edit your photo immediately after shooting it but has no effect on the rating.The game isn't just a neat street-photography simulator however, it actually has a plot which carries through each level. There aren't cutscenes or any dialogue, instead it's all visual storytelling. Lets just say that all of the levels have some stuff going on in them, placards you can read and recurring motives, that imply what's going on in the world outside the small levels.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A unique take on treasure hunting games, with a definite kiwi sensibility and understated but interesting worldbuilding. You may find the traversal a bit off-putting if you come from other first person games with a double jump (e.g. Destiny 2), but don't let it put you off - people should play this game, especially if they are interested in photography.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, lots of fun, with a fantastic soundtrack. Wonderful method of storytelling and world building without actually feeding the player anything directly.  Kind of encompasses what it's like to work during a global crisis without making me feel bad. One of the better games I've played during the pandemic for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I love photo modes in games. I'll drain hours taking pictures and tweaking settings to get something that's remotely passable as "artistic".I especially like it when a photo mode gives me full motion control of the camera, allowing me to shoot photos from whatever position I want to get the perfect angle. Unbound from the player character, I can frame any scene in such a way that tells a self-contained story.Bonus points if a photo mode can make me instantly change poses and facial expressions, and even hide characters altogether. Throw in the ability to change the time of day to adjust the in-world lighting, impose cinematic black borders, and slap on logos of the studio and the game itself, and you've got the transformative power to make your own little narratives out of these digital worlds.Umurangi Generation is a game that's ostensibly for those who like photo modes in video games yet denies the decontextualization that such modes enable.You cannot photograph that dance party in the VR-cade block, bursting with youthful energy, without the massive UN "EMERGENCY LOCKDOWN PROTECTIVE BARRICADE" looming in the background.You cannot photograph the subway crowded with face-masked citizens corralled by automatic rifle-toting soldiers without the neon billboards advertising escapism via end-of-the-world movies and military enlistment propaganda.You cannot photograph beautiful candle arrangements without memorials to loved ones who died in a catastrophic, reality-shaking event.You cannot photograph your cool friends without seeing cyber-streetpunk fashion mixed with Maori stylings and New Zealand iconography.You cannot photograph the word "COPS" without the following words "ARE DIRTY" or "COME HERE TO KILL US".You have to painstakingly position your character within the world, never once being able to detach yourself from your body, and manually shuffle through the different lenses and their varying levels of zoom and depth of field to get your job of delivering particular pictures done for dollars you don't get to spend.And you cannot stop that timer from ticking, constantly reminding you of all the pressures it represents like blowing deadlines and opportunities, well past the point of no return.So why not take the moment to listen to the best soundtrack of 2020 and be present in the time and space Umurangi Generation demands you to inhabit, examine, and reflect on, as we ourselves live through the slow-motion apocalypse of neoliberal decay?
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: i absolutely love everything about this game except for the heinous level design and poopy diaper controls. agree with all the praise, it's unique and a lot to love but damn...it just feels like total garbage to wander around. in a game about wandering around, i feel like that kind of matters.dope soundtrack though, i want to love this game but the jank won't let me (and this is from someone who can get down with pretty high levels of jank).
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: really enjoyed this overall, the photography mechanics are super fun and feel good and it sort of indirectly tells a really interesting plot. the art style is also absolutely killer, so that's always a good plus. i did feel like it ended a bit faster than i wanted, though, when it was over i still really wanted to see more of the world!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Amazingly atmospheric world set up with so little fanfare. No dialogue, no action, and still somehow one of my favorite video game experiences of the last 5 years. Incredible soundtrack by ThorHighHeels sets a mood I've been happy to be stuck in ever since I finished this game. All of that aside, just a really fun time to take pictures in these cool environments and sus out what led to this '♥♥♥♥♥♥ future'.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Oh my god this game is amazing. The world the game is set in just sucks you in, it just feels so alive with all these little stories going on in the background, people hanging out with friends, protests, memorials, and the actual story is absolutely insane, but really cool. What's more is that none of it is directly told to you, its all in the background, left for you to figure out. And the gameplay? It's absolutely superb, allowing you a ton of control without it being too complex for beginners. The game is absolutely gorgeous too, giving off a more chill JSR vibe, which makes it a joy to photograph. The music gives off that same chill JSR vibe, heavy use of samples and it's an absolute jam, man. Also, hot tip: get the DLC. It features some really good upgrades like the ability to sprint and get really close to the ground (which really helps you get some really good shots) and some fantastic levels to boot. In summary: get this game, and the DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Tells a story all by using the world around you. The world is falling apart and all you can do is watch and take photos.You go around the map and take photos. To complete a level you have to find all the bounties. To get an extra unlockable you do the same but you have to find film, reach a money quota, take a photo of all your friends, yes the penguin too, recreate a post card, and drop off the package in 10 minutes.This game is very experimental and I love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the short length of the game fool you. This game is 100% perfect when you just need to chill. From the locations, to the gameplay, to the music. Everything about this game is created solely to help the players unwind.Now if only this game had multiplayer. A bunch of people all taking pictures together? Shoot, count me in.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: If this game did not have a timer running on every stage, it might have been my game of the year. As it is, the experience was slightly ruined by what is an optional goal to complete the objectives within a time limit. Even though I knew it was optional, I still had a hard time ignoring the timer and found myself rushing through the levels instead of soaking in the atmosphere and the story.  And that is too bad, because the atmosphere and the story in Umurangi Generation is absolutely amazing. I love the way that this game tells its story through what are essentially 3D tableaus. This is environmental story telling done right and it utilizes the medium of video games in a beautiful way. It also has an amazing soundtrack and an incredible ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: i heard about this game at the very tail end of 2020, and immediately got attached to it, being a fan of punk and photography already individually.i played the entire game start to credits yesterday, and the dlc this morning, and, im happy to say that not only did i enjoy it, but its probably one of my favourite games full stop!unfortunately, some of the levels made me sort of anxious, after i realised you could run out of film, and the timer always being visible on screen (while also not showing up on the level complete sreen and still coutning on fadeout!), in addition to getting overwhelmed by all the bounties. i think maybe it would've be more enjoyable had you been able to sort of find bounties as you progress in the level, in order to make it less daunting, since i genuinely felt like i was put into option paralysis at the beginning of some of the levels.something that would also help is have a hotkey to display the bounties on screen all at once, quality of life stuff like thatfilm is less significant since, i understand it is a part of the game design, but it would be nice if at some point the game just gave you unlimitted film at least (haven't 100% it yet, so maybe it is and i dont know!). though, at the same time i kinda wish there were in game hints to help guide the player since some things are really tough and, more importantly, frusterating to find i also kinda wish there were sliders for things like iso and apeture, as is i never want to play with the options because of how long it takes to cycle options and experiment, in addition to the develop menu being more complete, like, being able to back out without consuming film, letting sliders youre click holding be adjusted when the menu is invisible, making the menu a lot more user friendly on controlelrs, stuff like thaton controllers !! would love if you could use both a controller and mouse/keyboard at the same time, since it would really help for speedrunners who have preferences for different actions, and make the game much more accesbile to people with unique physical situtations, like myself, who cant hold a key down comfortably for long periods but nudging a stick feels fine.anyways, the game!! thigns i likedi loved the games completely silent and almost entirely static storytelling, it pulls it off incredibly well and i dont think ive ever felt so attached to a group of silent protagonists like this beforethe aesthetic and setting is awesome. theres a train level, i like that :).a ton of options for taking pictures and i always want to go back and find new shots and execute ideas, especially not being able to go out and take my pictures under lockdown.i want to, try and provide as many issues i had so the game has the oppurintity to be the best it can, so i gonna add things as i go,- stairs are really obnoxious to take photos with since they are really buggy- no way to begin hovering prior to a triple jump, and no way to drop from a hover and begin hovering again, which makes readjusting shots on the hover boots really painful- no way to lock your ground speed makes it so its really easy to slide of small terrain and forces you to continually jerk back up- roller blades leave a trail even when u enter camera view, and, on the flip side, it disapears which makes taking pictures of the trails really stressful or maybe impossible
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute banger of a game. Lots of fun exploring the often oppressive urban cyberpunk environments just making art. Yet to touch the DLC but in the base game alone you're given a wealth of creative options for taking pictures. Outside of that creative aspect the objectives in each level are fun to go for too, it's tons of fun trying to run through a level as fast as possible and try to complete all the objectives in under 10 minutes. Best cyberpunk game of 2020.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic game. Bounced off it the first time I tried to play because the time limits in each level spooked me, but I'm SO glad I came back and tried again. Now I can't stop playing it. It should be noted that the time limits are only an extra layer of challenge, and you don't need to follow them to progress (though if you beat them it does unlock certain equipment upgrades).Looks great, the soundtrack is banging (also very funny at times), and the story is one that keeps revealing more layers the longer you play. It's sad and angry and beautiful and life-affirming and terrifying and one of the best games I've played in a long while. A game for our f**ked up times.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished the game yet but the level of detail and creativity here is astounding. Don't be fooled by a slightly simple aesthetic, there is a ton of polish, charm, and intention put into almost every corner. The presentation also consistently draws you in to this world, leaving you feeling like you can play "just one more level". Even if somehow the last couple levels I have left completely drop the ball (I doubt it) this will be well worth the purchase and I don't think I'd change my tone about this review. Highly recommend, especially if you're interested in making games or games criticism
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: 2020 mood: The GameI like that I can purchase a GOTY contender, its DLC and an absolutely banging OST for less than the cost of a dozen rounds with my waifu. Get angry at this world. Get this game and OST. Get creative with your photography. And Ves, get this game onto all the consoles this year, please.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely amazing to play. I highly recommend trying it out, and look through the environmental storytelling. If you have about 5 hours to kill, you can get through this game in one sitting. The angles and ability to play with the photo settings, and the subtle hints to big dramatic stories it ends up telling about how people would react to a world ending event is amazing. Get this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I don't suffer from motion sickness but this game somehow made me motion sick. You feel like a slow moving tennis ball on a stick with wheels duct taped on the bottom rather than a character. So I had to refund. My ideal movement for a game like this would be something like Titanfall, quickly zipping from location to location to take shots with my camera. This isn't what I was looking for.Also, not a huge fan of the Playstation 1 style graphics. I don't feel motivated to take photos of any of the NPCs as they just stand idling staring into the distance. It's not dynamic, unpredictable or fun to capture static models.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: The amount of care and detail put into this game's levels and worldbuilding is incredible! I strongly recommend this to anyone looking for a short game that understands what it means to be cyberpunk and fills its environments to the brim with personality. Controls are a little slow but, given this is a game you want to take your time with and soak in, it's probably for the best.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is a chill game with a memorable style, environment, and soundscape. The immerse and detailed photography simulation creates engaging gameplay. Each level's unique settings and soundtrack have me wanting to return to them just to re-experience their vibe. Thor High Heels music for the game is something I could have playing in the background on repeat. It sets an unforgettable mood. (Also, I highly recommend checking out his YouTube channel). Everyone clealry put their all into this game and it shows. It is a brief but exciting experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I seriously didn't know what to expect going into the game, but it ended up being an amazing time. You can play around and try to make really good looking, creative photos or you can rush around trying to get all of the required photos as quickly as possible and both play styles feel really rewarding.One of my favorite parts of the game though is the worldbuilding. Just by playing in the game for a few hours you get a vivid feeling of what it's like to live in this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ future. Genuinely an amazing time, I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is likely going to be my favourite game from this year. I don't think I've been "into" a game faster than the first 90 seconds I spent inside this one. The music is amazing, each environment is brimming with creative ways to capture it, and the overall narrative that plays out is worth seeing through your own lens.I also love photography/mechanics. The ways you can quickly edit photos is really satisfying. After being in a bit of a slump creatively, I feel renewed to try some different lenses and ideas IRL because of Umarangi Generation, and that's pretty cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: In high school, I had to take classes in photography. I hated it. For years after, I occasionally took photos, but had classified photography as something that was "not for me". I heard about Umurangi Generation from a review on youtube, and decided to check it out, as maybe I had passed judgement on an entire medium of art unfairly. It turns out I had done that. Through interesting levels with great worldbuilding and incrementally giving the players new toys to play with, this game made me see that much more can be done with a camera than what I was shown in class. I love this game, and it is absolutely my game of the year for 2020.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Light spoilers follow:I wasn't sure what to expect when I bought this game, but I was really surprised. Umarangi Generation is a really minimal game that tells a huge story simply by making you an observer of the people and environments within a war-torn sci-fi world. You play as a point-and-shoot street photographer / photojournalist, of sorts, tasked with taking photos of an assortment of subjects, gradually unlocking new lenses and photo-editing tools as you go along. There's very little dialogue outside of the tutorial and you're free to explore and compose your shots as you wish (the game is more or less agnostic about the artistic quality of your photos). There are big nods to sci-fi touchstones like Jet Set Radio and Evangelion along with an excellent electronic soundtrack.But while the photography scavenger hunt mechanics and lo-fi cyberpunk aesthetics are what initially drew me in, but the real hook for me was getting to explore the world and unlocking the next level to see another puzzle piece of the story. It's a world that's at times both gritty and colorful and the developers really seem to focus in on all the tonal juxtapositions of life in wartime as well as how young adults (and penguins) find ways to thrive in the midst of violence and authoritarianism. It's a game that invites big questions. I found myself thinking a lot about how a big, unwieldy experience like war is both clarified and obscured through the lens of a camera. Really a one-of-a-kind experience. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love it.The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard all year, also taking on a narrative role.The visuals are just perfect for what the game tries to achieve. Very refreshing take on storytelling, taking the current photomode trend and building a full game around it.Only the "bonus unlock" mechanic doesn't really fit in my opinion and seems to be mostly here for video game reasons. Would have much more enjoyed getting the extra stuff as a result of finding hidden stuff, instead of rushing through it with a guide.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I'd heard Umurangi Generation really highly recommended for its environmental storytelling and soundtrack and style, but I wasn't sure if I'd enjoy the actual gameplay of taking photographs. In real life when I try to take photos in real life I often impatient trying to figure out how to capture something as interesting as the view I can see through my eyes with the limited perspective of my phone camera.Taking interesting photos is easier in a designed space like this: levels are very dense with interesting details and people and contrasts, and you can often clamber up high to get a new perspective on things - I've found it fun trying to piece together interesting shots, and the game introduces new filters and tools slowly enough that even more fairly-photo-illiterate self can keep up and feel like each new option adds things.The thematic/scifi/setting stuff going on is great as lots of people have said, but it does also do a great job of making "take cool photos!" fun and accessible IMO.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is just what I needed. While it's movement may be janky and it's optimization poor, the Dreamcast-esque visuals, thumping soundtrack and wonderfully in-depth photography system makes up for it. Almost every level is a banger with complimentary design and wonderful variety in visuals. The only major flaws I've found is that some targets are way to specific, often "hampering my style" and making some levels infuriating when they'd otherwise be consistently fun. If you love the idea of a sandbox photography game with a visually unique world to explore, give Umurangi a chance!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this up last night and meant to just play it for a bit before bed, but Umurangi Generation is so engrossing I had to see the story all the way through before I could put it down. It's an awesome ride that will keep surprising you all the way to the end. Its soundtrack and visual style will immerse you in a world with a rich history with many layers to peel back as you work through your scavenger hunt list in each area on the road trip.The photography system is robust and accessible, making it a fun toy for amateurs to play with and a very powerful tool suite for people with more of an interest in photography. While setting up your shots, figuring out where to get the right angle or something, and noodling with your photos, you're left with a lot of time to think about what's going on in this world and what you haven't seen yet, which makes sure every time you get the answers to those questions it packs a punch like a freight train.It's an awesome story told in a unique way in a complete, compact package with plenty of bonus challenges and extra unlockables to keep you going if you want more.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible. The style is spot on with games like Va-11 Hall-a or Jet set radio, the soundtrack is an absolute banger and straight from the 90's from how it sounds. And the story is the star of this game. I'm not discrediting the photography in this game cause it's staggering the amount of detail that went into how much it goes into taking photos. The story though, is why you play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: The "vibe" of this game is fantastic - the lofi/vaporwave aesthetic is executed beautifully here through the visuals and the soundtrack.However, what truly makes Umurangi Generation shine is the visual storytelling and the themes it touches upon, very much inspired by real world events (2020 in general tbh).Soak in the world, take some photos, and hang out with your virtual friends.Also get the DLC, it's a fantastic expansion to the base game
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: This game does everything it can to make an enjoyable experience out of taking photographs in a "♥♥♥♥♥♥ Future." Everything from lenses to color settings, to trying to find a good angle to get the perfect shot is so amazing. I only have a few complaints about this game and the only one that is worth bringing up is that the base game only has 2 stances for taking photos (crouching and standing up, as well as laying down added as an unlockable in the DLC). But this isn't that big of an issue because even with this shortcoming the game more than makes up for it with all of the other unlockables and things it allows you to do with your pictures, and if you want to do editing to your pictures that the game doesn't have, all you have to do is go to the games gallery folder where it outputs your pictures. This is a game where artistry meets fun and it really got me interested in photography. There is a laundry list of objectives in each level that challenge you to meet them, but if you're anything like me that's not what will keep drawing you back in, what will keep drawing you back in is the freedom this game gives you to just take pictures and have fun doing it.If I had to describe my feelings about this game in one sentence it would be this: I want MORE!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Probably my favourite game released this year. It's wonderful to have a creative outlet in these trying times. I had always wanted to get into photography, but a decent DSLR, not even taking into consideration a tripod and different lenses, is like a million pesos, so a game where I can go into the indepth parts of photography is wonderful. Also the soundtrack slaps.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Played both the base game and the DLC. Honestly one of the best experiences I've had even with my sub-par laptop graphics card. Idk, as somebody growing up in the *current word* the Umurangi generation really speaks to me, the game seems to have it's finger on the proverbial heart beat of the current zeitgeist, too use a horribly pretentious word. This is doubly true in the new DLC which is more focused on more recent events. Also the soundtrack is a total bop and you should check out the composer's youtube channel ThorHighHeels.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Aggressively good game with an incredible soundtrack and great themes. It manages to portray the bleakness of a dark future with surprising hope, as one day there will be a last generation. _childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is the best game of 2020 no contest. great mechanics, storytelling, level design, visuals. some of the stuff in this game legit made my jaw drop and nothing else has done that this year. kicking myself for not having played it earlier. best advice is to ignore the timer for the bonus you get for package delivery on your first playthrough. you can always replay the earlier levels if you want.  and you will.

_childDocuments_.review: very fun and interesting little game!! it's got kind of a hidden object game sorta feel, giving you a list of increasingly specific things you have to photographand the photography angle of the gameplay gives it a really fun twist, with each photo being saved to your hard drive and built-in image editing
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful, moody and atmospheric game in an older, PS1 style. The game is a first person "shooter", in the more old fashioned sense. You explore through several densely packed areas armed with a camera and a bounty list of what needs to be photographed. The adventure starts off very point and click, but as you progress, and the story opens up, more options for your camera are unlocked as well. From different lenses, to colour, contrast, and lighting options, you can revisit old stages and see them in ways you couldn't before. This beautiful apocalyptic photography sim is easy to get lost in, and I hope that you do.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Photography is very fun for me, so this game is right up my alley. Most of the musical tracks are great and the way you can manipulate, frame, and change your lens to create different shots are awesome. The story for the game is told in the details and has a retro kinda vibe to it. My only gripe was that some of the places were a bit hard to do, so you have to really think out of the box for some of these. Do try and check it out when you can!
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Take photos during the end of the world. Umurangi Generation is a dedicated photography game with a hint of speed-running. You can either snap photos just to score points or really dig into the different camera lens unlocks and filters.It's set in a future New Zealand with an emphasis on Maori culture, disillusionment, graffiti, and a great big dash of Neon Genesis Evangelion.There's a larger world and story at play that you can pick up from the environment, but as a photographer you're just a witness to these final set-pieces of future.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I'm no photographer but this game sure makes you feel like a very artsy and sophisticated one.It's experimental artstyle coupled with the atmosphere of depair and useless struggle in the face of a nearing end creates a chilly experience.But I guess everyone can see something unique or familiar in this, depending on your perspective.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I suck at writing reviews but I just can't put this one off.Umurangi Generation is one of those games that will stick with me for a long time.The soundtrack and world building are stupendous. The photography aspect is well and good, and its why I initially purchased the game. But once I started really getting into it I noticed I was way more enamored just exploring the environments and reading all the signs/advertisements to piece together this world i'm in. There is no dialogue, yet I grew attached to my buddies throughout the game. I'm not sure what this visual style is called (i would really love to know if it has a name) but i get strong Quadrilateral Cowboy vibes from it. The models remind me of the early 00's/Playstation 1 era games. It fits so well though, i'd like to see this style used more often. This game is worth full price all day to most people. And I feel like if you are immediately digging the game just by the pictures on the store page you wouldn't have any regrets making the purchase. If you are on the fence, there's a demo that does a perfect job at giving you an idea of what the game is. At least try that!Oh, and ignore the countdown timer. I didn't pay it any mind during my entire playthrough. Please don't rush the experience just for the time bonus. It's not worth it. Relax and explore.I really hope Origame Digital does well with this title so they can make more experiences like this. They are right up there on my stalking list next to Sukeban Games for the foreseeable future.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: I've put a ridiculous amount of time into this inspired photography sandbox.Umurangi Generation's low-poly cyberpunk dystopia is a joy to explore with ThorHighHeels' incredible soundtrack. The game goes beyond 'wow cool future' cyberpunk, with a world that takes today's problems to their natural sci-fi conclusions and expresses those ideas through amazing environmental storytelling.It's also a wonderful game to relax in, revisiting levels and taking even more photos in ways you hadn't before.A HUGE recommend, whether you're a photography pro or if the only photography you've done is on your 3DS' front facing camera.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Spoiler Free Review: This game is for people who are into art of all kinds, who prefer to use art to express themselves more, and maybe people who feel anxious in the current pandemic. I strongly recommend you go into the experience totally blind, like I did. There's tons of awesome environmental storytelling that's enjoyed best with fresh eyes. I can't describe how much this game has meant to me, especially now in mid 2020. The cyberpunk art style is cool and might callback early y2k aesthetic, but its really product of -this- time and I hope more game enthusiasts will take a look at it when they reflect on this year. The low poly graphics and unsteady controls gave me motion sickness. I had to take a lot of breaks, but I played it all the way to the end. I would argue that it's the best photography game ever made. There's so many games that try to tell me what to think with their gameplay, but Umurangi Generation was the first I've played that honestly asked me what I thought. I loved it and I hope it finds more people who will love it, too.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: A first person photography game that uses Māori symbolism and Jet Set Radio as influences to show how the generation with no future deals with the end. Take pictures of your friends, the environment, and people at the end of the world caused by environmental issues and a kaiju attack from the sea. Each of the levels range from you and your friends in towns full of memorials and film and recruitment posters, street dance parties before the world's end, bloody combat zones, train rides of survivors, etc. Unlock new lenses, camera options, editing options by finishing levels and completing objectives. Gives you a lot of options to take pictures how you want once you unlock everything and are no longer trying to finish under time constraints.Jumping can be awkward with double jumps not always working or falling through things you would think you could stand on. Unlocking the hover boots pretty much removes the issue in addition to opening up some nice photo opportunities.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: I really really want to do this game justice, but I feel like no words will - this is a game you need to xperience, because talking about it or even just wathcing someone else paly is just not it. _childDocuments_.review: While it is a short game, the mechanics are solid. _childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is one those unique games that stands tallest, even amidst industry giants - at once perfectly accessible, heartfelt and engaging, this is a title that should be on everyone's list of games to try.It is refreshing to have a game that asks you to care and observe your surroundings, taking in the sights, framing the shot, and absorbing the story - with this title having released within the context of Covid-19, rampant inequality, despotic and apathetic governments, and the ever looming climate crisis, Umurangi Generation feels like an emotional outlet.The game does a superb job of handing over total creative expression to the player, drip-feeding tools and techniques as they progress - one level might see you getting to grips with a standard kit lens, before handing you another lens or editing function in the next. It feels perfectly paced and in harmony with the confidence and ability of the player.Although one might be able to beat the game within a few hours, it feels as if it could be endlessly replayable, especially with the new tools the player unlocks throughout - as the credits rolled, I felt ready to jump back in, to capture new sights and imagery, and to let more story details wash over me. In these times, I feel this game should be an essential pick - creative expression within a safe space, a sense of camaraderie, and a critique of those who have collectively failed us. This game serves not only as an outlet for its creators, but potentially for all of us.
_childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: In 2020 Umurangi Generation is an extremely important game. It shows that you have to look at the world to truly understand it, form your own idea of it, document it. The visuals are unique and allows the player to build their own vision of the world. The music is amazing, it adds so much depth to the locations you explore and the themes that surround them. Umurangi Generation is an incredible game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Went in expecting a sandbox game, came out the other end a war photojournalist.Have you ever wanted to combine a skating-game-like freeform scoring system with professional photography in a run-down country torn apart by controversy and crisis? You want some Evangelion references with that? I laughed, at first, when I saw the plugsuit-wearing UN pilot, bloodied, sitting on a bench next to a peacekeeper standing guard with a rifle. I wondered if they knew the peacekeepers I had photographed earlier, sitting around and bumming smokes off each other, writing graffiti on the roof of a skyscraper as they waited for the rain to pass.Then the attack happened, and I saw my friends clutching rifles, desperately holding out against an impossible enemy while the soldiers tied their bandages and writhed in pain. I took pictures. I recorded every moment I could--pictures of the blood-soaked survivors gathered 'round over some American Style Fast Food, under an advertisement that advised them to "Unleash your inner child!".I saw civilians who wanted the UN to go home. I saw desperate loners dancing in the street next to a "VR GAMER PARTY VAN". I saw memorials to the dead and messages from the dying.Ten out of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ten, this is a game I never knew I wanted.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a photographer at all, but this game has me considering taking it up...The levels seem lovingly crafted not only to tell a story, but to provide endless visual opportunities to explore and capture the world. Once you take a picture, you can edit with a bunch of different settings, starting off nice and simple for a novice like me with just a few settings. But even this was surprisingly enjoyable and addicting. More exciting things are unlocked and you get more of a grasp of how all these might interact to really bring out a unique picture.As others have mentioned, there is a timer on each level strictly for an optional objective, as explained in-game. It helps you unlock more things, but it’s something you should just ignore and come back to. _childDocuments_.name: Umurangi Generation

_childDocuments_.review: Umurangi Generation is a fun, if short, game about photography in a neon dystopia. The gameplay is very simple, but the flexibility it offers combined with the open-ended mission objectives gives the game high replay value. Overall, I like Umurangi Generation a lot. The art style, level design, and music are drenched in aesthetic, and the environmental story telling is rich and realized. The game is a little short (only lasting 8 levels), but I don't mind a game being a little on the short side as long as it's deep in its gameplay. In each level, you're given a set of 7 "bounties" which ask you to take pictures of certain things, sometimes with specifications on distance or lens type. It's not quite as open-ended as a game like Pokemon Snap; honestly, it feels a little bit more like a Tony Hawk game in terms of level structure. Additionally, you have 5 bonus objectives which are the same in every level: recreate a postcard, take a group photo of your friends, set a high score, find all the hidden film canisters, and complete the level in less than 10 minutes. My main critiques come from the lack of incentives to perform these bonus objectives. The game lacks achievements, upgrades, or secret levels to reward you for your hard work. In a way, I appreciate this simplicity, but I want some sort of feedback for my performance. The game doesn't even save your highest score, which I figure is the bare minimum for a game with an arcade-style loop.If you're looking for a lengthy, complex campaign, then this game isn't it. However, if you're looking for a fun, bite-sized experience, with great music and visuals, Umurangi Generation is a sure hit.

_childDocuments_.review: What i would describe as a "chill" game, it is all about being there and taking in the atmosphere, the objective of taking pictures just being there as a reason to soak it all in. Although the game is relaxing, it isn't without challenge. It does require some problem solving to figure out how you're going to get some things in the same shot with a specific lens. The game has a narrative, but it isn't forced down your throat. It takes place in the various environments of the game where you carry out your objectives.I thoroughly enjoyed the experience, the music and visuals were a perfect blend, the game is oozing style. The gameplay itself is simple, yet brings a real sense of catharsis when you get that perfect shot. It also comes with pretty limitless creative expression. _childDocuments_.review: The movement takes a little getting used to, so until you get used to jump strafing you'll feel like you're not moving as quickly as you want. But that's a good thing because it makes you take in the environment. The whole point of this game, at its core, is environmental story telling. The challenge hints can be frustrating at times, but in the quest to answer just what they want you'll end up soaking in the extra details. Ignore the timer your first time through a level and you'll have a great time. Great replay value since as you unlock more lenses and processing options you can get new perspectives on earlier levels. I wasn't sure what this game was going to be going into it, but by the end I felt like they really pulled off what their goal. Minor tweaks (clearer hints on a couple of challenges) and maybe just a slightly increased base movement speed would make this game perfect. Or maybe it would ruin it. Maybe the point is to go slow.
