_childDocuments_.review: i want to start out that this looks like a very fun game, and if you're looking for a real review, please look at other replies. i am very excited to get into this game. however, i have a brand new, windows 11 high end PC i got a couple months ago and i had a MAJOR issue trying to launch this game for the first time. if you are in a similar boat as i was, i have found several fixes that might help. i urge to not give up on this game if you cannot launch it first try. i can help, please contact me if none of what i listed has helped.below is what i commented on a few videos:hello! to anyone who is having issues launching this game with a dll error even though you've watched millions of videos and articles, this is for you.i was trying to install unravel 1 and didnt realize it was an EA game when i bought it through steam. and for whatever reason, it would not launch. sometimes i would get an error about the dll file, sometimes i didnt. after i reinstalled both EA and unravel about 20 times (no joke) i was still at a loss. here is what i did:-reinstalled clean copies of dll for 32 and 64 bit and placed into the System32 and SysWOW64 folder-uninstalled and reinstalled Microsoft Visual C++ 2015-2019 Redistributable-turned off G-Sync on the Nvidia Control Panel for Unravel-banged my head over what the possible issue is because i have the correct files in the correct place-changed the properties in the game files in steam to open as administrator, and then undo that-returned the game on steam and then rebought it again in hopes its perhaps just a steam error (it was not)-cleared windows cachewhat ended up working was i went into control panel and then uninstall programs. for every** Microsoft Visual C++ Version, I repaired it (you can do this by going to uninstall and it will give you an option to repair the file)i then uninstalled Microsoft Visual C++ 2010 version and reinstalled it (it does not give you an option to repair it) and THAT is what worked for me. here is the linkif the link does not work anymore, just look up Microsoft Visual C++ 2010 and its the first microsoft link.if this helps one person, i'll be happy. i wish everyone good luck on fixing this unbelievably annoying issue

_childDocuments_.review: I have pretty mixed feelings about this game.First of all: ♥♥♥♥ EA for forcing the use of Origin, especially for a game that doesn't even have multiplayer features (and for good reasons at that).The aesthetics are great, the soundtrack is wonderful, and I like the execution of the narrative, even if the narrative itself is not one to get me hooked. It also tends to provide a feeling of freedom, it doesn't tend to feel like it's forcing you to do anything. But, quite unfortunately, I still can't really enjoy the game. Before I even finished half of it, it turned into a game I just tried to finish for the sake of having it finished.Though I tend to be at least decent at logic puzzles, I still tend to be bad at puzzle games. Important here is that there are games that don't leave me feel stupid. Sadly, Unravel doesn't fall into this category. Unfortunately, though, I can't tell exactly why that is and it may be very subjective. However, it certainly doesn't help that the game didn't try to assist me whenever I got stuck in trying to traverse the actual primary path (not just the optional secrets). There were few hints or indicators for anything at all, while it is frequently not even clear where the player is supposed to go in the first place. I ended up seeing myself forced to look up a guide if I wanted to continue. Trying to do anything to save yarn - a limited resource, after all - also was never really rewarded.In short, I absolutely can not speak for the gameplay. Though with puzzle games not being my main genre by any means, I can't really tell why. The story didn't get me hooked at all, but that is most likely quite subjective. The soundtrack is certainly amazing, though.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but I didn't. There were some moments that were enjoyable enough for me finish it. There were not enough for me recommend it. Unravel seems to insist upon itself for being "beautiful" but that's largely without merit in my view. The game is linear to a tee, which means it lacks any real sense of exploration and adventure. You're always tethered too, needing more yarn at each checkpoint. You feel... trapped? You certainly don't feel free. In an adventure game, this is such a major issue. So much could have been done with this concept. Instead, the puzzles become repetitive and tiresome. Often, you have to repeat sections by design because the only way to find how to move forward is to die. But my greatest criticism is with the outright stupidity of the game's mechanics. The physics often defy reality. And the logic... as a ball of twine, you can drown while your head is above water. You can tie yourself to an anchor and get blown away because it's not the anchor you're meant to use. You can fall to your death but only if you hit the ground; if you grab your tether a second before impact, you're magically okay. And all as a freaking ball of spun cotton. Cotton is not going to die from falling or drowning or because you missed a game mechanic. Your enemies should be cats, the elements, and things to become tangled in. Thistles. It even looks stupid. At one point, you push a cylindrical float on its long edge up along the top a wabbly string. And it's perfectly stable. Your strength and weight appear to vary greatly depending on the contrived scenario. It's stupid, frustrating, and so linear that it's boring. Play something else.

_childDocuments_.review: Unravel follows the adventures of a small character named Yarny, created from a red ball of yarn, as he explores various natural environments.The graphics in Unravel are absolutely stunning. The environments are detailed and realistic, with great attention to textures and lighting. The colors are warm and vibrant, creating a welcoming and cozy atmosphere. The animations are also very fluid and realistic, bringing Yarny to life convincingly.The soundtrack in Unravel is also excellent. The music is soft and soothing, creating an atmosphere of contemplation and serenity. The sound effects are also very well done, with realistic sounds for Yarny's footsteps in the snow or the rustling of leaves under his feet.The atmosphere of the game is particularly well-done. The world of Unravel is peaceful and enchanting, inviting the player to get lost in its idyllic landscapes. However, there is also a certain melancholy in the game, reflecting the memories and emotions that permeate each level. This atmosphere is reinforced by the poignant cutscenes that punctuate the game.Finally, the immersion in Unravel is total. The player is transported to Yarny's world from the first minutes of the game, thanks to the enchanting atmosphere and intuitive gameplay mechanics. The gameplay is simple but challenging, with clever puzzles and well-balanced platforming challenges. Overall, Unravel is a captivating game that is appealing for its graphics, soundtrack, atmosphere, and immersion.

_childDocuments_.review: Unravel is a beautiful game – from the outright gorgeous graphics, to the fantastically animated and impossibly cute main character, and the brilliantly subtle story it tells via small clues and metaphorical imagery that tugs at the heartstrings. Unravel’s greatest strength is in how it plays on your own nostalgia, not by invoking old school gaming tendencies, but by building its core experience around your fondest memories. It resonated with me on an emotional level by simply playing on my own memories and experiences. As a game it’s a fun and highly inventive puzzle platformer, with some genuinely creative gameplay mechanics at work, although it’s let down by some floaty controls and some annoying sections. It’s a great game, made with obvious love by a passionate team, and is most definitely worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything I could say about this game has already been said: stunning visuals, gorgeous graphics, and a heartwarming story. Yet, it’s a game without words; instead, the music speaks volumes, capturing the traditional folksy essence of Swedish culture and enriching the breathtaking environments that unfold throughout the journey.While many games transport players to fantastical realms, Unravel immerses you in the beauty of the ordinary what's right outside your door. It invites you to experience the extraordinary nature of everyday life, capturing what it feels like to wander through a moody, cozy forest. Every detail, down to the last leaf, appears as if it were delicately handmade with care. The love and effort poured into this game are evident in every frame, because it’s their home the creators of this gorgeous game. The plot beautifully weaves together themes of love, loss, and the act of connecting broken bonds, inviting players to reflect on their own experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: Steer clear of this game.First of all, even though the download for this game is 3GB in size and includes the full game, you are still required to install origin and make an account with EA to play the game, that is already on your computer. You cannot play the game that you legally purchased on steam, on steam. Why even sell it on steam? Strong-arming people into using your client is neither a good business model nor a good way to convince them to use their client. I bought the damn game on Steam because I want to play my games on Steam, and because I purchased it through Steam, there is a certain expectation that 3rd party DRM won't be so intrusive that it will get in the way of playing it. This is strike one.Okay, so I begrudgingly set up the origin client + account, which takes up 15 minutes of my time (15 minutes that I could have spent playing the game if EA knew how to run a business properly), and then I attempt to start up the game, but wait! I get a black screen! Why? Ostensibly because my monitor is 240hz capable but is running on an HDMI connection that only supports 120Hz max, and the game must be attempting to run at that refresh rate, which won't work because, again, this is an HDMI connection. On top of that, the game has no settings, internal or external, that allow one to change it to run windowed or, I dunno, change the framerate to something I can actually use. Strike two.Finally, after nearly an hour of struggling with the game, starting and closing it repeatedly like an insane person, somehow I actually got a picture. Couldn't figure out how to get out of the house and lost interest before I did. I probably lost interest because the process of even getting the game to be in a playable state was so much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that I was tilted before I even began. I'm not really feeling that this game is worth $20 + an hour of troubleshooting. I make $12 in an hour at my day job, so you could say the real cost is $32. Anyways, there is no strike three. I can't recommend this game. Not on steam. If you want to play it in a sane fashion, get yourself a 60hz monitor and buy it through EA's storefront, since they want you to use it so desperately. There is literally no point in buying it on Steam. You'll just have to bury yourself in dozens of clients and go insane trying to keep track of which game you have on which storefront so you don't accidentally buy a game twice.I'll try playing the game again some time later when I'm not pissed off, but my recommendation won't change.

_childDocuments_.review: The game's cute and all. I have some gripes with it but I wouldn't give it a negative review if it wasn't for Origin. It is so annoying. Not only is it an extra hoop you have to jump through, it doesn't let you start the game if Origin is not up to date or if you are offline. It adds nothing to the experience, it only takes away from it.There are some questionable design choices. Like not letting you set up the game before you start. In this day and age, where everything gets streamed all the time, this is completely unacceptable. Imagine sitting through the entire opening cutscene before you are allowed to adjust your volume and graphical settings, only to play it all again for the viewer.Further on, it is hard to tell what keeps you from progressing. There are hidden conditions you have to meet, that the game doesn't tell you. In the first stage there is a lot of handholding where you are flat out told what to do. So if your style allows that in this otherwise silent game, then why not tell the player what they should do next to avoid frustration? Not everyone plays this in one go.Speaking of which... I just hate it to repeat things I have already done for no good reason. You make a difficult jump over an instant death trap but instead of letting the player start at the ledge to try again, you make him redo puzzles up to this point. Same with these GOTCHA moments. "Oh, you didn't know you were gonna die if you tried that? Well, joke's on you! Go back and retry, dummy!" I would have liked this game a whole lot more if the puzzles were exclusively asking your wit and not so much your reflexes. Because what is satisfying about solving puzzles is the A-Ha moment and not the way you got to the end. Gotta admit, the main mechanic with the yarn trail is surprisingly well thought out. Problem is, the game doesn't help you overcome your natural instinct to be as efficient as possible. Often times the level design makes you waste your yarn and other times you get replenished very frequently. It feels arbitrary and not earned. Just counter-intuitive in terms of ressource management.Although the graphics are beautiful, I get the feeling the developers try to manipulate the player into accepting everything by pulling their heart strings. The majority of players is indeed very gullible and uncritical. For me it is just eye rolling to see all that sentimental stuff with the photos. I'm not a family guy nor overly nostalgic so all that has no meaning to me. I don't want to sacrifice good and coherent game design for that.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to start by saying: Thank you EA for funding this amazing game (Screw you for being greedy still, but thanks lol). Unto the review, Unravel will break your heart and nurse it back to its original healthy state. It is quite the experience that uses Physics to the extreme. It's not your typical "easy" platformer, however, as it's plagued with difficulty spikes and puzzles that made no sense (before I figured them out by doing random stuff until I got the doors to unlock lol). You wake up in the first floor of a farmhouse as Yarny, a piece of yarn, left by the previous owners of the farmhouse.  As you explore the base floor, jumping through crates of the new people who've just moved, you discover some picture frames left by the previous owners! Each picture frame represents a level, a memory... and a loss. Once the level completes, you find a piece of yarn that unlocks a diary entry in a photo album. At first, this will look like your standard platformer, but as you continue unlocking these memories, you'll find out that not everyhing is sunshine and rainbows. The game starts with you finding out about this old woman who'd written this diary; her hobbies (mainly gardening) and how nice she was to animals and people alike. This quickly turns for the worst four or so levels in as these diary entries will become extremely dark, telling you (the player) how multiple tragedies came down upon this old woman who NEVER lost hope; she's lost her family to a hurricane (as you can see in the Hurricane level), her dog to a snowstorm (as you can see in the Storm level) and her husband to what I assumed to be cancer. You finally understand what Yarny is by the end; a piece of yarn that represents the grandmother's love for knitting... and her only friend after the passing of everyone she's ever loved. It is a very sad tale that had me balling by the end but it also made me happy to see that this old woman, despite everything, have never given up hope for a brighter tomorrow... It is also alluded to the fact that she's still alive, happily caring for her grandchildren and they are the ones moving in with her in the farmhouse, the ending is open to interpretation.  The gameplay is quite fluid, with a very balanced used of Physics and Puzzles. The only problematic thing were the difficulty spikes and how you can get stuck trying to solve a puzzle and have to restart the whole level... It was never annoying, however, as the game's visuals and amazing Celtic soundtrack had me enjoy every single moment of this fantastic tale. I'd recommend this game to almost ANYBODY, regardless of their tastes in videogame genres! This is one of those games that will leave you wanting more long after you've finished it. Hopefully the sequel has brought much more to the table and I'll definitely be playing that sometime soon. 10/10 game, I highly advise platforming fans to try their hands at it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's difficult to give this game a thumbs down - it's visually endearing, has a great soundtrack and an adorable main character. There are many memorable moments that will pull on your heartstrings. However it's difficult to enjoy the heartfelt warmness of the game due to frustrating game mechanics. There are moments when it's not clear what part of the scenery you're exactly able to walk on, there are moments where you will die because you don't know about some specific hazard in advance (and why can you die as a creature made out of yarn anyway?), and there will be moments you will get stuck on a puzzle because it's not clear what's expected of you or what exactly you can interact with.If you're a patient person not easily disturbed by annoying game mechanics, then do give this game a go. If not, well, you decide.

_childDocuments_.review: Unravel is the first installment of the series made by the Swedish company Coldwood. It’s a  cute platformer about a yarn toy collecting memories of an old granny. Full of themes tackling the subject of growing up, passing time, growing old, and loneliness but also about family, heritage, and love. A short beautiful story in the most picturesque Swedish landscapes. You can just feel the emotions beaming out of the photo album full of memories both the sad and the happy ones cuz that’s what life is all about. I finished this one after playing Unravel Two with my significant other. I thought that I might not fully enjoy playing it by myself but I was pleasantly surprised that I was very wrong about that. I’m even inclined to say the first one was way better. It just felt more personal, more… real? authentic? Don’t get me wrong, the second one is still awesome. I just kinda FEEL the first one stronger. I’m glad I came around and played it. Wish you have great fun too. ;)100% Achievements! YAAAS! xDD

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely beautiful reminisce, its main issue is the ethereal meditative "narrative" that it contains. These are the memories of a... grandmother? family? It isn't clear: we're restoring a photo album, but which contains photos of a dumpsite cleanup (who puts those in a family album?) and of a funeral (apparently not of the grandmother who puts this together). It has the incidents that help us to get to know a family, but it lacks the connective tissue that helps us to care. The poetically-penned lines before each group of photographs are lovely but say really nothing more than platitudes - kind of like those "thoughts" that Hobby Lobby sells for middle-class white women to put on their walls: that kind of "home is where a family lives" stuff. But perhaps that isn't such an issue. The game is a meditation on family at best, with fuzzy memories of generally uplifting familial moments. And our "narrator" is Yarny, who is appropriately adorable, well-animated, and generally very appealing. He walks through gorgeously-realized landscapes: seascapes, forests, dumpsites, snowscapes, and for whatever reason, junkyards. The background reveals incredible glimpses of the wildlife behind Yarny going about business as usual: the foreground is a toybox of things for Yarny to interact with, including crabs and will-o-the-wisps. Don't pay too much attention to the physics of the game. Why Yarny needs to go _through_ a car crusher is beyond me (much easier to GO AROUND IT, KID).  Building a "bridge" out of yarn that allows a steel wheel to roll up it is a bit of a stretch. But oh well. The yarn-mechanic (Yarny's always tethered to the past, see) is a clever doubled-edged sword: his running-out of yarn is a clever way to introduce checkpoints (thank you, Yarn-Fairy, for leaving random knots of yarn around the world) (and the animation is cutely harrowing) and also a nice way to provide a way back over obstacles. As a narrative, the game is less than it should be. As a meditation, it works very well. And its chief attraction is how beautiful it is. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Unravel is a conceptually fine game, but the execution in every single aspect, besides the music, is flawed in some way or another.Visually, the game looks alright, there weren't many moments that blew my mind, the lighting is fine, and the textures are good enough, I especially like how the snow, for example, looks in the later levels. It all seems very cozy, but there is one big flaw: Gameplay relevant or not, it blends in with the environment.There were many moments during which I had no idea where to go, objects that look like they're part of the foreground are in the background, and ones that look like they're part of the background are in the foreground. Some ledges look like they're unreachable until the Yarny somehow manages to get up there. It's not intuitive to make a puzzle-platformer a guessing game for what you can actually use or not.The gameplay has even bigger issues. Fundamentally, it's a neat little idea, interact with the physics, try to use the fiber that sticks off of your Yarny to solve puzzles by tying small bridges, or simply use it as a trampoline, swing around, pull objects, but watch out that you don't use too much of your yarn, since it's limited, and you might not be able to reach the checkpoint, because there are one or too many knots.What we ended up getting instead is a very simple puzzle-platformer with rudimentary riddles that break quite often. The main issue is the physics engine. Most things do not make sense, you can solve a riddle, die, do it all over again, however it somehow doesn't work, because the physics engine doesn't function, so you look up a walkthrough, and you find out you've been doing it right all along, but the game is being unreliable. The developers probably knew that, which is why most riddles are very simple and lack depth. The core difficulty is knowing what to use, because everything in the environment blends in. Platforming isn't challenging either, but sometimes the Yarny won't push something, or even grab a point to swing over a gap, resulting in cheap deaths.It's the inconsistency that makes this supposed cozy game frustrating to play. Not only that, but the limited yarn is inconsistent too. There is no clear indicator for how much rope you get per checkpoint, sometimes you walk for a mile with no checkpoint or issues in sight, other times the game denies you crossing a 1-meter wide river, so you have to go back and untie a few knots to actually reach your destination. If you want the player to be mindful of their limited walkability, then it should be made clearer with how much yarn you're working with.The last issue is the general level design. Most of your time will be spent simply walking, not even interesting walking, but plain old going from level section A to B to solve another riddle that might or might not work. Undoubtedly, the most infuriating issues come from the gimmicks that try to make the simple walking sections interesting. Be it water, bugs, or a blurry stealth section, they all aren't enjoyable.Water slows you down tremendously to the point that when you fall in the puddle you'll never get out, eventually you die very slowly. The bugs are just padding, they limit your movement, to free yourself you have to mash a button, although it might not help you, since they can cling onto you immediately after shaking them off. The worst might be the tiny stealth section, dozens of birds try to catch you, and they announce their attack by flying towards you. The reason why it's infuriating is that the birds are so incredibly blurry that you can barely even see if they're about to attack you.Additionally, the game adds some element of surprise by, for example, making the ground you're standing on collapse, or a small rock avalanche occurs, these almost always result in unfair deaths, due to you not knowing what to do. Sometimes you gotta flee, sometimes you gotta dodge them all, and sometimes you gotta do both and then jump on one to save your life. To add insult to injury, the visuals still don't help you in making these split second decisions, since you don't know what's part of the playable field. Each death felt completely unjustified, as if you're supposed to know what happens in your first playthrough.If I had played this game before Unravel 2, I definitely wouldn't have picked up the gem that is the sequel. Unravel 1 has its ideas, but they aren't polished. 5/10

UNRAVEL is a platform game based on puzzles and the laws of physics, which tells the story of life and the accompanying passing.The main storyline, which consists of Yarny's emotional adventures, is related to the recovery of the hero's memories and the search for traces of his lost family. The plot is given through symbols and photos constituting the background, echoes of distant memories. The very figure of a nice red creature symbolizes the bonds that bind relations - "love creates bonds like threads of yarn". The yarn is not only an allegory, but also a great idea for gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: - 2/10. Wholesome. Cute. Average. 2D simple platformer with some puzzles. Okay. - I was softlocked three times in three different places and I didn't even finish the game.- I keep hearing a second set of footsteps in the left side of the screen even though nothing's there.- If the music changes it's volume throughout the game on it's own what's the point in the volume slider.ᶠʳᵒᵐ ᵐʸ ᶠᶦʳˢᵗ ᵖˡᵃʸᵗʰʳᵒᵘᵍʰI didn't finish the game and I don't think I will. The game has a cute character and a wholesome story so far, but the level design with the art style, in addition to the flawed puzzles just make the game a pain to play. Every object you're supposed to interact with, as in moveable objects, blends with the level design so much you often don't see them. There was a part where you had to take a wheel which had half of it hidden behind a texture, so naturally I didn't see it, and shortly after you had to use this wheel to balance a plank so that you could climb to the other side. Did they not try to just run forward and jump across in testing? Because that's what I did and it worked, and then following that you had to pull on a locking mechanism that dropped a ballast on the plank which was supposed to launch the wheel to the other side. But guess what, I had no damn wheel so I had to break my head for a few minutes trying to clear the next part and I couldn't, so I had to reset to accidentally move the wheel when I was climbing back up.Next, some of the puzzles you simply cannot solve on first try. There's absolutely no indication. A good example would be when I was climbing a mountain and rocks were rolling down on me so I had to hide behind ledges so they roll above me. Then at the top, there's a massive rock that's rolling on me and no spot to hide so I ran back to the last ledge I hid in, and bam, the stone rolls above me and I live. I go up the mountain and I can't climb further because apparently I had to bend some branch on the floor so that the stone would hit it and hold it in place so I can climb on it and then jump up. Again, softlocked. I had to restart as I couldn't progress. Many similar instances throughout the game (even though I've completed 5 chapters).Another example of poor design is there was a part where hamsters try to get you. You're on some small hill above them and your only way forward is by jumping down. So I did. The hamster killed me. So I tried coming from the back, but there's another hamster there so I couldn't get in. So I climb back up, go to the front, and try going down with the rope only for the hamster to kill me again even though I wasn't that close to it. Throughout the game if you fell from a big height you'd die, so you suppose there is fall damage, and so you don't try jumping from this hill forward as you expect yourself to die. BUT, apparently, infront of the hamster are tiny plants which look like rocks that emit gas if it/you step on them, so the hamster cannot even go forward. I saw them but there was again no indication that these are NOT rocks. I had to yolo it.I did not feel like I was playing a game. In the beginning it was cute, but going forward it just kept getting worse. I kept feeling that instead of wanting to know what's next, I wanted to get it over with. The softlocking and awful puzzle designs really killed it in the end. Whenever you finish a level, instead of progressing to the next you have to go and find the picture of the next level. It became annoying, especially when the camera takes it time to align itself so you can actually see platform you can grab onto at the edges of the screen. Also, you have to install the EA launcher to play the game.TLDR;Cute characters, wholesome story, but the gameplay is really bad. I do not recommend this game at all.

_childDocuments_.review: I came for puzzles. What I got was the same puzzle again and again. It was less of a puzzle game and more of a *beautifully crafted blah blah blah nominations and awards blah blah blah art game*. Yes, the game looks really nice. The story behind the game is probably nice too, I didn't really understand what was going on. The music was boring and I turned it off halfway through the game because it made me sleepy and without the music I could cope with the game a lot better. As an *art project* this might be a good thing, but it is not a *game*.Everything in this game is very slow paced. The music is slow, the character is slow, the cutscenes are slow. The progression is slow, the puzzles are quickly solved on paper but take time to get through (because you have to tie a knot at 6 obvious places to make the 20th bridge of that kind, that lets you push an object to a desired place to do something), the level selection takes time because you have to walk through the house to the new level every time you beat the last one. If you want to play some kind of walking simulator with very obvious puzzles in it, then this game might be for you, but I came for puzzles and platforming and this game does neither well.

_childDocuments_.review: The idea for this game is cute and likeable: You play as a little red wool figure called Yarny who has to use its skills to make its way through several platformer levels. Apart from jumping, Yarny can extend a lasso to reach higher places and swing from it to gain momentum, push and pull objects and build bridges. Gameplay thus includes some puzzle elements where you have to figure out how to get from A to B by combining the skills and using the objects around you. A further limitation while making your way forward is that Yarny unravels while he moves forward. Sometimes, he's literally at the end of his rope, so you cannot continue until you find a new spool of yarn to add new material to his body.Graphics look really good: The player character is adorably cute and well animated and the environments are very detailed, colourful and realistic.Why then the thumb down, with all these good features? Gameplay can be frustrating at times. Why, for example, can a yarn figure (no bones, no lungs) die if it falls from a certain height or drown in seconds? Both of which can happen quickly if you misstep.Also, there are segments where the character rushes through a section of a level and you either are able to quickly spot and execute all the moves you need to make, or your character dies and you repeat the sequence until you finally make it. Which happens quite a lot in other regards, too. Sometimes, it's not quite clear what you have to do, so you have to try things, which may then kill the character. Not a fun experience. Or you have an idea what to do, but if you make a wrong move, you are back to square oneAnd with one level taking maybe 20 minutes, I also found it annoying that if I left before finishing it, the next time, I'd be back to the start.Lastly, while not really being a downside, there is a backstory to the game, but it feels disconnected from the player. You see someone's memories here and there, but they are not "yours" and you don't get to really interact with them, so it doesn't serve to make you feel invested in them.I got to play the sequel in coop mode with a friend, and pretty much all the gameplay issues have been addressed in a way better manner there.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: This game forces you to install Origin, which crashes immediately when launching, making me unable to even start the game. Origin managed to just barely not crash long enough for me to start the game once, and it was mediocre.Technical issues:This game forces you to install Origin. This is questionable in and of itself, but I don't really care if I get to play the game. Which is exactly the problem. I didn't. Origin crashes immediately after launching it. I spent 3 hours with EA customer service who simply regurgitated "solutions" from google search results that I had already tried. But here comes the kicker: Through sheer luck one time Origin managed to just barely not crash long enough for me to start the game. It crashed one second after the game launched, but the game kept working. This means Origin isn't even needed for this game to work. Yet you still need Origin to launch the game, which it doesn't let me.The gameplay:I managed to play this game for just over an hour somehow. The gameplay was unique, but it was never used to its full potential. There are tons of instant death traps in the levels which force you to completely redo the last 5 minutes of the level you just did, even though deaths wouldn't even be necessary. The game essentially has a rewind feature by letting you climb back up your yarn, but they still decided to make you waste your time by putting death traps everywhere. I played the first two levels and had to look up solutions 3 different times, each time it was because the solution was to interact with an object that didn't look interactable. Everything has the same art style, so all the objects easily look like they're a part of the background.

_childDocuments_.review: I first tried Unravel some time back and thought something along the lines of "looks great and it clearly wants to send some message about going down the memory lane". I had a chance to play a bit more of it and... Well, it got the looks and atmosphere, all right, it is pleasing to watch, indeed. But as a game... Generally, as a platformer it's ok, but its physics seem a bit inconsistent, which makes some even obvious puzzles fail because of it. And there are places where the level or puzzle design is simply... Lacking. I am not talking of places, where you need to think a bit more to solve a puzzle. The best early example is an episode with kite: it's easy to get to it, but when you do, how are you to figure out, that you can actually control how it flies and that control is not dependent on your swinging?So, my personally opinion - watch a walkthrough. It will please your eyes, you may like the message the "story" tries to deliver, but playing it.. Better try Trine series or something.

_childDocuments_.review: Setting/World - 8/10Story - 6.5/10Music - 8.5/10Voice Acting - Not ApplicableGame play - 6.5/10Aesthetics - 7.5/10Others(Animation, Sound effects etc.) - 8/10Overall Review - 7.5/10(Unravel the beautiful world, not story)PlotYarny, the red yarn that serves as our protagonist, has been accidentally dropped by the owner in the house; Yarny, then starts wandering  the house, interacting with various house objects, until she finds the pictures of the family members. The game begins when Yarny starts going into the world shown in the picture, to collect mementos made from red yarn, like her.ReviewStory and WorldI really liked the game, just did not love it. When you first start going into picture world, the world amazes you, you start appreciating the aesthetics, the music, the game play and the overall world itself, but then you start wondering: Why am I here? What is the purpose of this? The story was the biggest let down of the game because there was none, at least not a coherent one. The game would have been much better if there was one overarching story, instead of smaller ones, which you could not care less about.MusicThe best thing about the game was it's music. I loved it!  Also cannot go without saying every level had a different music, which is just amazing.Game playI really liked the mechanics of the Yarny, and the excellent detail like Yarny starts losing her yarn, making her bare bone, so to speak if she does not get more yarn. The overall mechanics of the game is very good and on par. I just wish their were more to do in the world, instead of just traversing, and doing basic platforming. The puzzles were good, not great; It takes not more than 5 min(maximum) to solve the the most complex puzzle in the game, expected more complex puzzles.P.S Don't play this game for the story or puzzles, but play it for the world in the game; The game is short too, 6-8 hours maximum.

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are awesome, no doubt. The music could have been a little more...ambient. The violins are sometimes piercing my brain. As for the gameplay - this is Unravel biggest weakness. If I was a 10 year old child, I probably would have liked it. But the pacing of the game is too repetitive. I'm almost at the end, and I've used nothing but the same mechanics from the first level over and over and over again. Most of the puzzles and platforming are super easy. It was not until the level with the poachers, when I finally met some challenge, but it seemed so out of place. The whole game just feels like a walking simulator. Almost all of the events are scripted and the obstacles seem fake. I do not recommend wasting time for this game. There are so many platformers out there. Better replay the Ori series instead of wasting time on this.

The swinging is neat when it either is too slow or too fast.I mean, I wouldn't call it a bad game, but it was certainly a rather dull and irritating experience for me. I looked at the game's achievements and only half of the player finished the first level and only quarter finished the second which, I believe, proves my points.

_childDocuments_.review: This game requires the EA Origin game launcher to run. I wouldn't have bought it for that reason alone if I had known that before I made the purchase. Unfortunately for me, I waited too long to play the game for the first time so that I can't even return it.Now that I am stuck with it, I am trying to power through it. It's definitely not a difficult game. While it is visually impressive and the character animation is quite good, I find it to be incredibly boring and not fun. The music is so incredibly repetitive, monotonous, and sappy that I can't roll my eyes hard enough. The game is trying to be sweet, touching, sentimental, and meaningful. I suppose it succeeds at doing those things, but that does not make a good game for me. I intend to finish it, but I really don't want to play it anymore. I regret buying this (along with its sequel). My recommendation comes from being sorely disappointed by a game that I was very much looking forward to playing.Update:  I did finish Unravel and Unravel Two. I think Unravel 1 is the better game because if feels more complete and cohesive. However, Unravel Two is more fun to play and much more challenging. I still didn't really like either game.

_childDocuments_.review: This review includes both Unraveled and Unraveled 2.  I played them back to back, but played #2 first, solely for the Couch Coop with my wife.  Wow, both of these games are insanely immersive.  The graphics, and the music is top notch beautiful.  The biggest difference between the two is the Coop of #2.  The levels are not terribly hard but are just hard enough.  Unraveled 2 also had+ Better and More Consistent Movement+ More Carefree Swinging+ Carry your teammate+ Bonus Challenge Levels.  (Hard)After finishing #2,  I went back and played the first one.  Almost immediately, I noticed two things.  The puzzles were harder, and you died a lot.  In fact, I know we died here and there in #2, but I didn't notice it like I did in #1.  About half way through the second chapter, it dawned on me what this game really was.  It's basically Limbo with beautiful imagery, music, and a lasso.  If you enjoyed Limbo, or Little Nightmares, this is an easy recommend.  I got both games on sale for  a little less than $10 and got about 25 hours between the two games.  So that seemed like a good deal.  I enjoyed both of them, but if you don't have a coop partner, the better game is the first one.  The first one has better puzzles and there are more of them.Only ConRequires Origin to play.  It's a minor ding, but that crap shouldn't be necessary for games bought on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really rough to go for the thumbs-down on this one, but I personally just didn't enjoy it very much and can't recommend it. It's not really bad, and if I could I'd rather have a neutral rating for titles like this – I'm sure there's people out there for who this is the right game.My biggest issue are the controls and how the movement feels. It's clunky, it feels like wading through pudding. It should be fluid and fun and joyful. I constantly felt like fighting against the game instead of working with the game, and it was super frustrating because the game actually isn't very hard to figure out, but the controls make it harder than it should be to make the game do what you already know you need to do.The story didn't do much for me either, but that wouldn't be an issue if the gameplay itself was more enjoyable. This is one of the many EA titles I played in 2022 after doing their "1 year for 5 bucks" offer on the EA Play membership via Steam. For many of those games even that felt like a waste of money, but for this one I'd say give it a try – you might enjoy it more than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: this one actually pains me to write a bit, because i've been looking forward to playing unravel ever since it was announced and we saw yarny for the very first time.for the record, the game isn't actually "bad" - yarny is an adorable protagonist, the visuals are stunning, and the story is vague enough to be universal.the problem lies in the fact it's not very accessible. quite often spotting the red loops you can hang from is very different, due to them being obscured by various environmental effects (like fog), or straight up blending in with the environment. additionally, yarny can be a bit unresponsive, which can make reflex-oriented segments super frustrating. he's not broken, and a certain stiffness of his movements is understandable, considering he's just a tiny doll - but my god, does it get frustrating. especially when you're trying to get out of the water. also the soundtrack, while generally good, can get annoying after a while, since the tracks seem to (at least partially) reset whenever you respawn.all that being said, it is a fairly enjoyable game. it simply poses an unreasonable challenge to people with poor vision (like me, miss "OH LOOK A DO-oh, it's just a suitcase :(").

_childDocuments_.review: This is EXCRUCIATING.  I know these types of games are supposed to be challenging, but this is ridiculous.  There are very few save points, so you have to make it through nearly impossible jump after nearly impossible jump all in one sitting in order for any of your progress in that section to be saved.  You can't just play for 5 to 10 minutes casually, because when you come back, you'll have to repeat all of that.  I also have the same complaint about this game that I have about other similar games, and that is the endless requirement to redo maneuvers that you've already successfully completed.  You can manage to complete jumps 1, 2, and 3, but if you miss jump 4, you now have to start all over and redo jumps 1-3.  I don't know anyone who enjoys that kind of repetition.  The music is also really repetitious and just adds to my frustration rather than creating an atmosphere.  I've also yet to discover any kind of story. At all. Period.  I feel like I'm jumping around for absolutely no reason other than to raise my blood pressure due to frustration.  This game just really needs a lot of work.  The character is cute, and the graphics are really pretty, but the game play could be so much better.  Will I continue to play it?  Probably, because I'm stubborn and I want to at least beat the level I'm on.  But no, I don't really recommend this game.  I've heard that the sequel is better, so maybe I'll give it a try, but if it turns out to be anything like this, I'm going to give it a hard pass!

_childDocuments_.review: Unravel, the game that made me realize the therapeutic power of yarn and the hazards of overthinking puzzles. It's like a cozy evening with grandma, but with less knitting and more existential pondering.The graphics are so charming they make me want to knit a sweater for my PC. It's like the developers dipped the entire game in warm hues and sprinkled it with the magic of childhood nostalgia.The gameplay is a gentle stroll through a world where yarn physics is both your greatest asset and occasional nemesis. It's like trying to solve puzzles with a string theory degree while occasionally getting tangled in your own brilliance.The story is a heartfelt yarn (pun intended) about a little creature made of yarn, trying to stitch together the memories of a family. It's like the world's most adorable therapy session, complete with emotional tugs and the occasional "Aww" moment.In conclusion, Unravel is not just a game; it's a soul-soothing experience, a reminder that sometimes the answers are hidden in the most tangled places. So, grab your yarn and get ready for a journey that's as heartwarming as a handmade blanket on a winter night.

Yarny's journey is filled with reminiscences and emotional memories.Platform and Puzzle Mechanics: The game combines platforming elements with puzzles. Players can swing, climb and overcome obstacles using threads.Nature and Environment: The game world includes natural beauty and diverse environments. Each level represents a different environment and theme.Sound Design and Music: The game's sound design and music enhance the atmosphere. Emotional moments and environmental sounds enrich the players' experience.Community and Reviews: "Unravel" has received positive reviews among players and critics. While the game's emotional storyline, creative puzzles and visual design are appreciated, some players have criticised the game's difficulty level or controls.Development and Publisher: Coldwood Interactive is the developer and Electronic Arts (EA) is the publisher.Conclusion: "Unravel" offers an emotional and creative platforming and puzzle experience filled with an endearing character. The game's graphics, story and atmosphere create a world that draws players in. If you are attracted to visually impressive, emotional story and creative puzzles, "Unravel" may be an enjoyable experience for you. By checking out the game's community and reviews, you can evaluate whether the game is right for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally Unravel wasn't available via Steam, so I had to purchase it via EA Origin store, I completed the game and all the various challenges/achievements with that version, hence why my play hours on Steam is quite low.Unravel is a very simple game, just a side scroller in many ways and each map is really just a series of puzzles and challenges that the player solves using the yarn, pulling on objects, or using the yarn to swing around. It's a very relaxing experience as you assess and solve each puzzle.The visuals are excellent, and each of the maps is beautiful to look at, including the home where you start each chapter of the story, with lots of small details with critters, leaves, etc making the world seem alive. The music is also excellent and fits perfectly with the relaxing atmosphere of the game.I wouldn't say any of the puzzles/challenges/achievements are difficult to complete, but I feel that is part of what makes the game fun. Unravel isn't pushing you hard to solve complex puzzles and allows you to relax and work through each map at your own pace, enjoying the visuals, story, and music. Most of the time I love games that push me, challenge me, and make me work hard to "win", but sometimes it's nice to fire up a game like Unravel and just relax.I would highly recommend Unravel to anyone looking for a relaxed/chill game experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel sorry for the developers.  I don't know what you do after making a game like this.  It just feels like a masterpiece.This game was released over seven years ago and I am just now finding it, but it is absolutely timeless.  The production value is as good as it gets.  Every single frame is a work of art with endless attention to detail.  Even if the game was unplayable, it would be beautiful just to look at.The game play is smooth, flawless, and well-considered - a real joy to play.  So, even if the artwork was entirely lacking, it would still be a fun game to play.And, the concept and feel are fresh, interesting, and full of surprises.So, this checks all the boxes and then some.  It is just so well put-together, marrying the concept, smooth and fun game play, and absolutely beautify artwork, and doing so seamlessly.But what about the soundtrack?  Well, the soundtrack is solid.  It adds to the overall aesthetic, and is good by any measure - just not as strong as all other elements.  I find myself unfairly judging the soundtrack because the rest of the game is just so exceptional.  I honestly don't know what you could have done better.OK, so that ends the rant portion of the review.  Let it suffice to say that I think this game is pretty close to perfection - a playable work of art.  So, what is the game like to play?Well, at the end of the day, I guess you would call it a side-scroller.  That seems to put it in a class that doesn't match the experience, but technically I think that's what you'd call it.  You play a quirky little character made of yarn and navigate a world of pitfalls and challenges using your yarn skills.  Sounds boring, but if it helps, the action feels a lot like you might expect a Spiderman game to play like.  It has some similarities to other games, but I don't want to make those comparisons because I don't think it helps understand what is unique about this game.The overall feel is fairly laid back and melancholy, with a heavy emphasis on navigating the natural world.  Each scene is really well-observed and provides novel experiences.  At no time does the game leave you feeling like you've done this before.  You learn some skills and build an understanding of how to interact with some objects in the environment, but it never gets tired or repetitious.The challenge level is ... I would say low-medium.  This isn't a nail-biter or something that's going to cause you to bang your head on the wall.  It challenges you just enough to keep the game flowing along nicely, but still making you work for it a bit.  I feel like it hits that delicate sweet spot where you really get to engage with the environment, but never feel like you are being punished by it.This is helped by the fact that there is rarely only one solution to a challenge.  In fact, I would say that that is usually at least two equally viable ways to get past most challenges, plus a few more "creative" options.  That means that there are things in the environment that you can interact with, but you don't need to.  I like this because it doesn't spoon-feed the solution by showing you the elements you must use to solve a particular challenge exactly the way the developers want you to.  Instead, they make the challenge solvable, and put things in the world that you can use for various ways you might go about it.There is a plot.  I have to admit, it isn't crystal clear to me what it is.  Ostensibly, the plot is no more complicated than a funny little character exploring a series of mini-worlds to try to find prizes - a fairly familiar mechanic.  But, there is a strong backdrop that is, apparently, trying to tell a rather sentimental story.  They use a sort of photo album / scrapbook device to tell that story and help set the tone.  And, the device is used quite effectively in terms of hooking your attention and inviting you to engage in the story, beyond the surface game play.But, unfortunately the story was lost on me.  I was able to piece together some general feelings and moods, along with some vicarious personal memory experiences.  It made be really WANT to follow the story.  It was just never clear to me.  It may click better for others.  But, even if it only serves to set the mood, it does so effectively.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember this was my childhood game which I didn't have the will to continue after chapter 2. That was for one unrighteous reason: I criminally underappreciated Unravel. And I'm not even referring right now to the gorgeous, realistic scenery or the expressive instrumentals because those were the things I did acknowledge back then. But the story? The way it slowly unravels itself within the strings of an old woman's memories? That was the part I should have looked deeper into.You see, Yarny is just an inconspicuous fella made of a red thread. But in his tiny filamentous hands lies the power to relive the memories of one family and mend a broken bond. He will traverse forests, seasides, mires, snowy lands and so on by means of his strand that is constantly unrolling and trailing behind him and which he will use as a lasso, a trampoline or a whip.Every in-game chapter is a different chapter in life. We get to experience the innocence of childhood, the first teenage infatuation, the pitfalls in the adult world and the fragility of elderly years. Yarny collects all these moments and, after each chapter completion, compiles them in an album which then reveals new heartening photographs and reflections linked to them. And, like in real life, memories can be positive or, well, less positive, the tone of which is mirrored in the scenery of respective levels. Cheerful moments will have colourful and vibrant landscapes, while gloomy ones will bring a dark, distressing atmosphere and havoc. Honestly impressive how much information can be drawn from a bare environment. And when there are those glints of the past added, it gets pretty emotional at times. Really makes you reflect on your own life and be grateful for what you’ve already experienced.Looking at it from the angle of my past mistake, I am content I have given the game a second chance. In some way, Yarny has also unravelled my own memories and reminded me of the importance of cherishing the moments left behind. Maybe he shall now aid

_childDocuments_.review: Unravel is a beautiful and engaging puzzle-platformer game developed by Coldwood Interactive and published by Electronic Arts. The game follows the story of Yarny, a small creature made of yarn who must traverse through various environments to collect memories of a family's life. The game's beautiful graphics, relaxing music, and heartwarming story make it a truly unique and unforgettable experience.One of the most striking aspects of Unravel is its beautiful visuals. The game's art style is absolutely stunning, with vibrant colors and stunning landscapes that truly immerse the player in the world of the game. The level designs are also incredible, with each level featuring its own unique puzzles and challenges that require the player to think creatively and use Yarny's abilities in new and interesting ways.The gameplay itself is a joy to experience. As Yarny, the player must navigate through each level, using his yarn to solve puzzles, swing from platforms, and create new pathways through the environment. The puzzles are challenging but never frustrating, and the game's controls are tight and responsive, making it easy to move Yarny exactly where you want him to go.Perhaps the most impressive aspect of Unravel is its emotional impact. The game's story is simple but deeply moving, as Yarny collects memories of a family's life and explores the beautiful natural landscapes around their home. The music in the game is also a standout feature, with a gorgeous orchestral score that perfectly captures the game's themes of love, loss, and the beauty of nature.Overall, Unravel is a truly exceptional game that offers a unique and unforgettable experience for players. Its beautiful visuals, engaging gameplay, and emotional story make it a must-play for anyone who loves puzzle-platformer games or is looking for a game that will touch their heart. I highly recommend Unravel to anyone who wants to experience a truly beautiful and memorable game.

_childDocuments_.review: Completely different aesthetic, but gameplay-wise this reminds me SO MUCH of Abe's Oddysee. It's also a side-scroller and it has that same kind of feeling where you go through each level section by section, figuring out how to overcome obstacles. Sometimes you have to use your brain, sometimes you need to time your moves or angle your jumps just right. You move at your own pace, you get time to think things through before trying something and if you fail you just try again until you get it. Sometimes a hazard will surprise you or make you jump a little. Sometimes you need to take a leap of faith and see what happens.I'm super impressed by how much can be done with some very simple concepts. Even the most insignificant twigs on the floor become important. Everything is on an extremely small scale (You are tiny. Puddles on the floor look like gigantic lakes. When you meet a lemming it looks the size of a hippo in relation to you.) but despite that the environments feel big and involved.For a game that cost less than £2 in the sale this exceeded my expectations. It's challenging but not overly difficult or stressful, it's charming and fun but not boring. I wouldn't say its the best game I ever played, but it's certainly enjoyable and well worth a try if you're looking for something you can dip in and out of.

The narrative about pollution, activism and a family being torn apart is really cliché and I feel like I've seen it in hundreds of games, but the story was well done, I believe the fact there's no dialogue and it's all shown through pictures helped. I really like games like Dark Souls where most of the story is in the background and you have to pay attention to get it. Too many games shove the story in your face. _childDocuments_.review: - Looks outstanding in 4K. Barely any framerate issues in that resolution- The environments look quite pretty and are fairly varied- Not much in the way of character design, but Yarny is cute enough- The music is quite good and plays a large role in setting the tone of the game- Throughout the course of the game, you complete levels, pick up secrets, and try to fill out a magical photo album that cryptically reveals the story of the family who presumably made Yarny- The vibe, in general, is moody and contemplative- The game controls quite well. Even though the majority of the puzzles are physics based, I didn't run into any wonky behavior from the set pieces- The controls are well-tutorialized, so you'll have an easy time figuring out to do after the first level- The puzzle design is actually quite creative. Some of the secrets are fairly deviously hidden- Although I didn't run into any trouble with Origin, it does have to connect. If you've had issues with Origin in the past, keep that in mind. EA unfortunately loves their bloatware- The game performed admirably on my system (i9 10980HK/RTX 2080 SMQ/48GB RAM) in 4K resolution with hardly any issues. There was some minor shadow flicker in one cutscene, but it seemed fine otherwise- No bugs, framiness, or audio issues. A well-made and well-optimized game- . Definitely give this one a try if you like chill, easygoing puzzle platformers. Keep in mind that the game is only 6-8 hours long when setting your price point.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings for this game. For the atmosphere, the creativity and some of the puzzles I absolutely love it. From gameplay perspective I have a few problems. They are not that big of the issue, but prevents Unravel from being a masterpiece.The one thing you should know before you play it: it doesn't really worth to be a completionist in this one. For that you need to do each level without dying, gather every secret collectible (5 per map) and do some other (fun) tasks. That sounds good, and is good, but some of the collectibles are pretty illogical to find, and there are a few levels which requires at least a few retries to do without dying. You don't need to do everytjing in a single run, but really, redoing levels kills the main selling point of the game, the atmosphere. If you like challenges like me you'll find enjoyment in that to, but I regret I chased the achievements.So about the real issues in gameplay:- When you create a game (especially without text tutorials) you need to introduce the new elements to the player wisely. It was done relatively well in Unravel, but there were quite a few really annoyingpoints in the game where objects surprisingly acted differently. For example the branches you've learned to use as rafts suddenly sinks under you. You try it two more times and realise you did nothing wrong, but in this section of the map there is a point where the water sinks it down and you need to jump beforehand to an object you thought was part of the foreground before. There a quite few of map design elements like this, and since the game uses physics sometimes it even randomize, making the learning harder.- The idea of you having a fixed rope length, and need to "retangle" time to time is awesome, especially that you visually see the character getting thinner. The problem is that this isn't defined by the mechanics, only the map design: you need to visit each point in a certain order, otherwise you'll run out just before you reach the next. Sometimes it is literally on the other side of the screen, sometimes it is 6 screens away. Few times it bugs out, and you think you've done something wrong, but repeating everything its enough. It doesn't seem like a big thing, but it broke immersion a quite a few times for me.- The map select intermediate menu follows the same concept as in several other platform games: it is a mini level where you need to go to certain access points to start a level. Thats not a problem on its own, but it was done HORRIBLY here. Each time you finish a level, you'll teleport back to the start and have to wait for the animation, then go back. Jumping around this minilevel is no fun, and you might even have trouble finding the next level easily (yes, I'm looking for you Mountain Trek, I've found literally every other frame before you).- Combination of the second and the third point: if you intend us to replay levels if we want to 100% the game, then 1) add an option to skip cutscenes when replay 2) don't teleport us back to the house when we finish a level 3) don't kill us out of nowhere when one such objective is don't die. There are a lot of places on the maps when you need to instantly knew the new controls for a mechanic or die (like the kite on level 2), do a leap of faith to reach a hook you can't see, something just falls on you out of nowhere, or you introduce a deadly new element camouflaged as background objects.TLDR: it is absolutely worth playing if you like the genre, and the reward for the collectibles (photo album) is absolutely lovely. Don't approach it with completionist mindset unless you don't mind frustration from flaws for exchange a little challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: Unravel is a simple but charming platformer. At around 7-8h it's not very short, giving you time to get immersed, used to the physics and have some fun, but also not long enough to get tedious.The game's main theme seems to be nostalgia, broadly related to growing up and ageing, and the passing of time and people. Unfortunately, it didn't get to me emotionally at all, even though I tend to be a very nostalgic person - I think it lacks something more tangible that people could connect to emotionally.However, the gameplay was fun enough that I quite enjoyed the experience. The puzzle- or agility-based fragments were mostly fun to play and balanced in terms of difficulty, but what impressed me the most was the creativity of the yarn concept and its implementation. Yarny looks suspiciously realistic, as do the environments he traverses. Everything is beautifully designed, and the way Yarny uses >himself< to move around is both amusing and entertaining.Overall the experience of playing Unravel was very pleasant, enough that I'll definitely play the sequel, but it lacks the emotional appeal that could make it truly memorable.

_childDocuments_.review: If the seminal  was a bit more forgiving, a bit cuter, and a bit more physics oriented, then it would feel a lot of like . The WOW-factor here isn't a new gimmick or cutting-edge tech, but just a dozen well designed levels centered around a very polished core gameplay experience.This game definitely a surprise hit as it was hardly on my radar when I picked it up during a sale.  is not a particularly long game, clocking in at a little under 9 hours for a 100% completion run, but don't mistake that for a lack of content! A dozen extremely well-crafted levels, supported by some fantastic visuals and sound design, shows a ton of care of went into the creation of the game. As for the difficulty, it's certainly not the most brutally challenging game, but in no way is it a "hold right simulator" either.The central mechanics are dummy simple: you can throw your yarn to catch hooks to swing from, and you can grab onto your yarn trail to "reel yourself in", sort of like a belay line. Each level then takes those mechanics and adds interesting puzzles and physics challenges to keep the gameplay fresh from level to level. In particular, I was quite pleased with how the game organically rewards players who like to go above-and-beyond. Players are not punished for "speedrunning" through the game, you'll get the same ending and get to experience 90% of the same gameplay. However, collectible Buttons are ever-present to reward those who enjoy exploring and a bonus achievement awaits those who want an added challenge of perfecting each level.: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Unravel.So... Unravel is... Well it's  something. Something special. Something very special. I cannot full describe every single emotion I felt whilst playing this game, but I will surely try my very best.First of, Yarny, our red, stringy protagonist. Is absolutely adorable. I don't think I ever felt so attached to a single character as I have with Yarny. His animations are so well crafted, and so much care has been put into his design. Yarny is probably my favorite character in any game I've played thus far.Secondly, I must mention the environments. They breathtaking, awe-inspiring, beautiful and so wonderfully placed. Every single level feels  immersive, and Yarny just fits perfectly in them. The puzzles placed in the environments are also very clever and fun, and the element of yarn is one of the best ideas I have seen in any game. The whole scene, with all the elements and love put into them, perfectly creates a wonderful experience.The story line is very intriguing and well-written, with some moments almost guaranteed to make anyone tear up. I never thought that the environment and story could so wonderfully combine and create... Well this.However, what makes this game so truly magical is the soundtrack. It is definitely my favorite from any game.  Frida Johansson, Henrik Oja and everyone else working on it absolutely  here. I have thus far learned three of the songs of this wonderful soundtrack on the piano, and I always feel refreshed after playing or listening to one of their songs.So... I may have been a little too positive, but this game deserves all the praise I gave it in my opinion. I have no complaints.

_childDocuments_.review: I knew about this game ever since they showed it for the first time on E3 2015, but due to various reasons, I held off playing this until now. If you love platformers, you will love this game. The best part about this game is the story-telling that's done with the help of level design. You play as yarny, as he travels back to retrieve the memories of a granny. Every level you complete, you unlock pictures for the picture-book of thegranny.What starts as some light hearted levels, surely picks up pace in the middle levels where the themes are much more mature. It is pretty stunning how the devs have been able to display that amount of emotion just by the environment and yarny. You feel immersed in the game.As of the platformer mechanics, the remain the same throughout the playthrough. However the puzzles on every level are quite different compared to each other and some are quite challenging aswell. Along, with which you also have collectibles which you collect for the completionists. The last level however will melt your heart in a way. The puzzle and platforming mechanics feel pretty tight, and if you want a game that does not take like forever to complete you can jump on this and have fun. Cant wait to play Unravel 2, unfortunately dont have friends for that :(

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the cutesy design of the main character fool you, in the overload of games that employ artificial cuteness just for the sake of being 'adorable' this is a genuinely whimsical & enchanting game. The graphics are gorgeous and the unspoken story is heartfelt. Fortunately, the story does not get in the way of gameplay, and there is plenty to be happy about in terms of the gameplay. The yarn gimmick is well used in a vast array of physics-based puzzles and never really overstays its welcome. There are many well-directed set pieces and the game remains interesting throughout by the sheer variety involved in nearly all its elements. It is rather easy, and there is no violence, so it is well suited for kids (mind you, there are some mild scares such as a bird suddenly swooping over Yarny etc.). All in all, I loved Unravel all the way through.
_childDocuments_.name: Unravel

_childDocuments_.review: The yarn mechanic is very interesting, you have to complete the obstacles and puzzles in a certain way to stop your yarn from tangling or running out which adds a new element to your typical problem solving.Everything in this game screams game of the year, the attention to detail in every environmentis stunning and the visuals are breathtaking enough to make every screenshot a potential wallpaper..Going through each environment/season and exploring every nook and cranny is exciting, exploration is rewarded as and finding every secret is just as fun which i've managed to complete without a guide (except for some..)The music and sound department is top notch and is the only thing that narrates the story since the whole game is silence, the storytelling involves taking  you through a life journal of a person, some feels might be had.A nice little hidden gem of mine, saw it on sale and brought it without knowing much about it, will definitely be in my G.O.A.T. collection.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot describe how incredible visuals are. I know that practically every game now has to have oversaturated, unnatural or even "realistic" look - but in this game, graphics, shading is very well combined. Of course, it's a game from 2016 and graphics got "better" so this game would probably use better graphics - nonetheless it would probably work well.Graphics aside, I have to tell you that around 4th level, I've started to feel that game developers are running low on ideas at some moments. Some levels are pretty pleasant to play, new "mechanics" even - fun - but some moments that unnecessarily extend gameplay or some places that you want to/could (but you can't) go, or lack of logic at times. The saddest in the whole experience - I guess - is probably that there's probably no chance to walk this game through without a death at the first try. The worst thing is that alleged "restart from the last checkpoint" button doesn't set movable objects (and some other things) to the original position/state.Why do I consider this game as worth to buy? It quite looks like a poem. Story is not entirely clear, words depicting the world... and of course, music that is absent in poems. Game has some flaws, but you can tell that this game was in the forefront of developers' minds.Unfortunately, music is not available in game folder (in .mp3, etc.).A little note: no "Options" button in main menu, so at the beginning, game may be loud. Options are after you start the New Game.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most beautiful games I have ever played! The environments look and feel icredible, and the attention to detail is just simply astounding. This is a good example of what you could call "eye candy". Also, as a Finn, the Swedish landscapes felt very similar to what I have gotten used to here in Finland, which was a nice addition.The gameplay is just ok: The puzzles are not very challenging but they are usually cleverly designed, and will keep you interested for the short duration of the game (5-7 hours). The storyline is fine but nothing special.Maybe the biggest downside is that the game is sometimes not consistent with its own mechanics. Sometimes you are able to traverse long journeys without your yarn running out, while at other times you travel much shorter stretches and your yarn is constantly running out and you have to design your path carefully. As if the game occasionally remembers that "oh yeah, we also had this 'yarn running out' mechanic, let's use it again".

_childDocuments_.review: Unravel is a beautiful, charming puzzle platformer. You play as Yarny, a tiny being made out of yarn. This opens up potential for many unique gameplay options: rappelling up and down your yarn, making trampolines, and some epic Tarzan-style swinging action. The yarn also limits you; you need to constantly rebind yourself with spools found around the level. The scenery of this game is beautiful. The story (so far) hits halfway; I prefer to focus on just the gameplay and not worry much about the story. Fair warning: I'm not the best at puzzles, so take this with a grain of salt, but you're going to need walkthroughs. If you're stuck, give it a go, but don't be scared of using walkthroughs. Some of these puzzles are hard, and you're going to feel stupid when you finally figure them out. This game is only twenty bucks, which is low in gaming standards, I think. I personally waited for the Yarny Bundle to go on sale to buy the game. Sometimes Unravel and Unravel Two in the bundle can be down to seven dollars on sale for both games, which is a fantastic deal, but I would still reccomend this game at full price. If you're wondering about specs, I have a potato of a laptop, and I can run this game fine (albeit at a lower res than I'd like) with only a few lag spikes. Overall, I'd recommend this game to anyone, especially more casual gamers, who's looking for a relaxing yet challenging & satisfying puzzle/platformer. If you've got a friend and like co-op, Unravel Two might be the better option, since they made the gameplay smoother, and it's overall more satisfying playing with a good friend. Good luck, Yarnies!

_childDocuments_.review: I received this game as part of the EA Play Pass for $5 USD monthly. This game surpasses that value. I feel that the devs truly poured a lot of their souls into this project. They were clearly very passionate about the idea and the details. This puzzle game isn't that hard, but there are some puzzles that may take a few different reapproaches. I think the game does two things exceptionally well. One, the atmosphere they create with the scale and details of the environment you play through is surreal. You are only meant to be maybe 6 inches tall and it's cool to see that be a distinct part of level design. The devs really got creative with this. I also think an important factor to that atmosphere was the auditory side. There isn't any real dialog in this game, and the story unfolds through music ques and body language, which translated really well for an inanimate object. It's strange how they were able to capture emotion in just some red yarn. The other thing I think this game does really well is the mechanics. It's really interesting to have yourself anchored to your pact decisions and each path you take has a cost at how much yarn you unravel, and if you use too much, you may not be able to reach the next checkpoint or solve the puzzle. I think this is really unique for the genre and allows for a lot of freedom in gameplay. With the many approaches you can take, even though many of them may not be fruitful, it's still fun to explore them. I think this game did a really good job with secret/hidden areas and collectibles. Many are hidden in areas that reward you for your curiosity, exploration, and outside-the-box thinking. I definitely think this game is worth playing. I recommend picking it up on the EA Play Pass, as that is probably the cheapest way you will experience it. I got all the achievements and did everything the game had to offer in around 20 hours, so that may play a factor in whether you decide to buy individually or through the pass. Fun game.
