_childDocuments_.review: I finished Sea of Solitude a few days ago and it's been on my mind since, despite it being a very mediocre experience. The visuals looked great and reminded me of a dark version of Submerged, a game I loved with a very similar setting, but this ended up falling a bit flat for me. Maybe I was expecting something different based on the trailer and description, but it's not as dark as I thought it would be.While the game touches on very real problems, the message tends to get lost within the cringey voice acting and frustrating combat. To be quite honest, it would've been more impactful if they had left those things out and focused more on the storytelling and gameplay. I would say that maybe only two of the characters actually did a good job voice acting, but Kay (the protagonist) was not one of them and she does the most talking....it just ruins the immersion. However, the visuals were stunning and fit the overall theme very well. I just felt like there was a very noticeable gap between how the game looked and the message it was trying to convey.As for collectibles, there are two types: messages in a bottle and shooing away seagulls. The messages make sense and would've been a great way to improve the storytelling aspect of the game, but I still don't understand why the protagonist felt the need to shoo away seagulls, as it had no real purpose. I did appreciate that I could return to a chapter if I missed any collectibles, but it would've been nice to know which ones I was actually missing. Since the game doesn't tell you, I had to use a guide and my own memory (which, I'll admit, isn't as sharp as it used to be) to determine which ones I needed. This definitely could've been improved.To be clear, I don't  to give this game a negative review, but considering there are only two options and the cons outweigh the pros, I feel that's the most reasonable choice. If I had to give a rating, I'd say 6/10 . It's just a shame because I can see the potential and passion behind it, the execution just could've been better.

_childDocuments_.review: I love arty games, and I love games that are a labor of love, but even despite those positive biases I was really disappointed by this game.The art style was genuinely great, but the voice acting was regrettable, and the writing/metaphors were way, way too on-the-nose. Again, I'm a sucker for allegorical games that let you explore fantastical worlds, but this one just felt half-baked. The upside is that it's not too long - these are the kinds of games you should be able to sit down and finish in one sitting. But even at $10 I felt like this was overpriced. $5, maybe.I seriously appreciate how much the developers loved this game, and the obvious time and effort that they put into it, but it's really hard for me to recommend this game when RiME already did everything this game does better, cleaner, and two years earlier.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to love this, I really did, but there were just some things that I couldn't overlook during my play that made the experience... really unfun. I don't mean to write this to get the game down, because the game - and therein the studio - has so much potential! So I'll give a quick overview of what bothered me to the point of not being able to even play anymore and even feeling the need to refund it, so in the future those things might be avoided :)! The first thing that struck me, two minutes in, was the voice acting. It was so bad that I instantly turned the voice volume to zero, and that might have solved the problem, BUT! The character noises and voices of the little enemies like kids and the blue ice things still had the voice lines in the world volume, and hearing "This is fUn" and "summertime's the bEst" several hundred times in the most unconvincing acting made me eventually quit the game... so please, if someone insists on having voices, let the player disable all! of them in the voice volume, also the little character grunts or gasps. The second reason I quit was the gameplay, and I wanna underline that the boat sections were amazing! But there were so very few. Driving around on the boat was unique, fun and beautiful, but it lasted for a good three minutes until I was to run around with clunky controls for an hour or more, using trial and error to get around the monsters - especially in the gym level. It was probably the least fun I've had in a game, and doing some research I heard that the gameplay loop stays the same until the very end. There are a few more little gripes I had, that made it unenjoyable but I guess those rely more on personal taste or low budget, for example the on the nose symbolism (subtlety is key), the lack of polish which lead to a break in immersion (if you have a big scary water fish, don't let his beard and movements be stiffer than a bulls neck) or bugs that made me have to restart the level which - considering the gameplay - was a big nuisance for me. Still, I want to leave this on a positive note and say the artstyle, the character art - especially Kay's - and the general atmosphere is absolutely beautiful! With a little more effort, a little more subtlety and a little more experience in writing this studio will create the most wonderful of games!

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet.A quick warning: for those not in the right headspace, this game has references to self-harm and self-termination. It deals with struggles in life and if you're not in the right place to deal with this there are other games out there. The extent that this game covers those subjects isn't extreme, but it's there. So let's get one thing out of the way right off.. This isn't a 'platformer' in the sense that Inside or Limbo or Stela, Gris etc are. When I watched the previews, that's the vibe I got - Little Nightmares, Inside, blah blah. I was expecting wild chase scenes, getting mauled over and over by monsters until I got the action sequence down just right, solving complicated puzzles, and the like. This game is a lot more like a very interactive movie - although there are things you 'do' in this game, it's far less involved than others in the genre. Not to say it's one of those types where every now and then you click a button and that's it... No, again, it's quite interactive, just not as much so as some others in the genre.That being said, it's not one of those 'die a million times before making it to the next scene' games. There is danger, and you can die, but it's not unforgiving. There also aren't really any in-depth 'puzzles.' There are a few light 'make your way over here to further the story, and you'll have to search a little for the way' bits here and there, but nothing that will cause any real stress. This game is far, far more about the story, the scenery, the symbolism than the gameplay. That might be a 'pro' or a 'con' for you depending on what style of gameplay you're in the mood for.. just making it very clear what you can expect from this title!Personally I liked it. I very much enjoy the harder platformers, yes, but games like this are very nice to just 'escape' into every once and a while... sometimes it's nice to beat a game without jumping out of a third story window every couple hours.I beat this game after about 3.5 hours. I did not get all achievements, and I likely won't go back to get them all, but I don't imagine it would take a lifetime to do so.I'll give a brief synopsis while avoiding as many spoilers as possible. Our protagonist Kay wakes up in a strange, dark world filled with monsters. She, herself, is also a monster. This dark world is filled with corruption - painful memories and painful truths. Kay has to confront these memories and truths to banish the darkness and defeat the monsters - and find a way to find a way back from being a monster herself. With help from some friends, can she learn to deal with the pain in her life, right the wrongs, and bring light back to the world?Most of it is walking around and occasionally jumping a little, or zipping around in your motorboat. Finding your way isn't terribly difficult - you have 'flares' you can cast into the sky which will almost always point the way, so if you're stuck, it's easy to get back on track. You do little tasks, avoid being eaten by monsters, and work your way through the story.I wasn't particularly emotionally 'moved' by this one. There were sad parts and happy parts, creepy parts and cool parts, but I never really found myself deeply and powerfully moved. This is not to say it's a bad story, and I could see some folks being quite touched by it, indeed. Maybe it's just something I don't connect with. I don't know. Again - not a bad story at all. I really enjoyed it. Just putting it out there that if you're looking for something that's going to emotionally shake you to your core, this may not... or maybe will... be it. Hard for me to say.The graphics were very nice and pleasing to watch. The controls did not feel clunky or glitchy, except for some parts where I felt a little frustrated with the jumping mechanics. The music was very beautiful and the sounds natural-sounding. The voice acting was occasionally a little cheesy but not to the point of being a real distraction or moment-breaker (at least for me). Overall, a very, very pleasing play-through experience, and I'm glad I had the chance to play.The final question I always ask in my reviews is: worth full price? Well, I don't know - for 3.5 hours to play through, $20 is a bit of a steep price tag unless the game is just 'that' amazing. While I really did have a great time playing it, I don't know if I would have felt fully satisfied had I actually paid $20 for it. Again, I wouldn't discourage anyone from giving it a try... but what I would encourage others to do is wishlist it and wait for it to go on sale. I've seen this one pop up on sale from time to time for a while now, and just decided this time to pull the trigger on it. I think I paid somewhere from $5-$7 for it, and that's a fine (and possibly ideal) price. If you can catch it in that price range, it's a very good bang for the buck.Overall, very short, very nice, and TOTALLY worth it if you can catch it under that $20 cap!

_childDocuments_.review: > When humans get too lonely, they turn into monsters…Sea of Solitude takes you on a personal journey of a young woman’s loneliness. I went into this game expecting a story about how the protagonist, Kay, experienced personal demons (directly personified as the monsters in-game) spawned from her own feelings of isolation, abandonment, and/or general loneliness, and how she learned to cope with them in a way that would show growth as a human being.Sadly, I was disappointed both by what the game ended up portraying, and how it was presented. As others have noted, the story of this game is not subtle, though I believe part of this may come from translation or an otherwise insufficient understanding of nuance in English/American writing and cultural norms. I say that because some of the lines feel like they have a clear intent and purpose, but the word choice and structure of dialogue does not feel natural (to an American) throughout most of the narrative. The voice performances also often fell short in terms of delivery with pacing and inflection, which made it all the more difficult to feel engaged with the characters as emotions often felt forced or generally lacking. (One exception I think is the wolf monster, who feels much more natural and heartfelt in his delivery).The story itself is told almost entirely through vague anecdotes of past, without ever showing those events as they happened. Each section focuses on a different "monster" and very bluntly talks about an issue they experienced, from which Kay "learns a lesson" that she tries to apply in the next section. The first of these is very blunt, almost over-the-top, but they do get slightly better as the game progresses. Again, I think the wolf monster is presented the best and shows the most depth of the three main sections, but still leaves much to be desired.Two parts of the story structure feel particularly limiting in the game's ability to communicate the narrative. The first is how Kay responds to each situation. While the intent seems to be that she needs to learn how to cope with each situation, I felt each part started with Kay saying "there's no problem here, what's wrong? I'm helping" and ended with a resolution of "...and then things were okay, because I've made this not a problem anymore."The second is how surface-level the actual representation of each issue seems to be. Kay's responses are part of this, but the pacing of the narrative with the gameplay, the focus on vague anecdotes to the past instead of real experiences, and the overly-direct writing style make any real attempt at portraying nuance beyond "this is good" and "this is bad" rare if not entirely invisible. The second and third sections do handle this better than the first, but not enough to feel like any issue was really understood beyond what gets said aloud in any of these situations.The game shows some of the effects of bullying, depression, anxiety, and difficulties with relationships, but largely ignores the causes and depth of these issues. Combined with resolutions that effectively dismiss the very real long-term effects of these issues on people's lives and personalities, the result seems to imply that everything will be fine and happy as long as you learn "the right thing to do." In many ways I think the attempt to portray these issues may be more harmful than helpful in how the protagonist is "successful" in the end without having fully addressed any of the situations or showing real growth as a person.Outside of the story, the world of the game is quite beautiful and I would enjoy spending more time in it. The mechanics mostly feel good, apart from some weird forced cameras and very cumbersome slide-your-mouse-100-feet sections. The experience seems fairly polished, and I never really felt like the game itself was holding anything back from the experience.Overall, the game was somewhat enjoyable to physically play through, but very simple and somewhat repetitive. The story was hard to engage with for many reasons and didn't really provide any commentary beyond very literal statements that I struggle to say are helpful for most people. The game tried to address very serious and impactful topics while avoiding any amount of nuance or depth to their presentation.I wish I could recommend this game as it is wonderfully rendered and touches on topics that are quite personal for me. But while the ideas around this game are worth talking about, you will undoubtedly have a more meaningful conversation by talking about what the game didn't do than from playing the game itself.

_childDocuments_.review: Spend 3-4 hours as a black-furred monster girl, learning Very Important Lessons about mental health issues as you explore a dreamy sunken city and interact with various manifestations of depression, self doubt, family strife and other fun stuff.  Given the short length of the game, the lessons are a bit heavy-handed and forced but it does do a decent job of expressing that there's no single solution to these things.  The graphics and design are well done, the Depression Kaiju are impressive, it all fit together nicely and there's enough game play to keep you moving but it's definitely in service to the story.  I thought it was a fine enough way to spend four hours but I'd have a hard time telling someone else to spend that time on some dark stuff versus "Shooting alien zombies for four hours is good fun".  If you're willing to play for the experience, you'll likely find it worth the time.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been struggling with chronic anxiety and OCD for a while now. I've engaged in serious self-isolation and found that video games were a coping mechanism and a distraction from overwhelming thoughts, but this game really touched my soul. It made me really think about all the monsters I live with within myself, but it also helped me come to terms that I need to make some peace with myself and my monsters.This game is beautiful. The story, the music, the voice acting, the monsters, everything about it is hypnotic. I played it all in one sitting and wept when it was over, but it also led me to have a heart to heart with myself and maybe I'll finally start to move on with my own life. I hope so. It'll be a fight all my life, but I have to keep fighting. This game taught me that. If I stagnate in isolation and loneliness, I'll never be happy.That said, this game deals with some really heavy emotional stuff. If you're in a delicate state, it's really going to impact you. I ignored the warning and went in anyway and it still shook me more than I expected.It's a great game, but be warned, it's a hard and heavy one. Just know that the ending, the peace and closure you receive at the end...how I loved the ending. It was all worth the journey. And it was beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review: This is somewhat of a serious review so beware of spoilers if you intend on playing this game. So if you can read this,  I suggest you don't read my review as I am goofus. Also a pro gamer tip: continuing jumping into the direction you want to go to go fasterAside from trying to avoid being eaten by a whale as I am not open to recreating the Book of Jonah. The Sea of Solitude is an emotional roller coaster of a game that evoked my feelings on many levels but primarily the feeling of Melancholy. I can say already this game will be emotional for some who can relate to some scenarios or won't affect anything at all. I'm no therapist but this can really hit deep in your soul if you had some traumatic experiences so play with caution. I however am not afraid to go evoke these feelings of melancholy and depression. I can only relate to bullying with one person: myself. I was definitely good at bullying myself down to my lowest point cause of self-deprecation. But some scenarios definitely hit hard. Life may give you the hardest challenge of coping with loneliness, loss, anxiety, bullying, and depression. And you better believe it that this game will also teach you not only to feel it but to listen, it will yank your attention otherwise and listening is a good skill but however not used very well for some scenarios aside from the bullying. We all have 2 ears and 1 mouth for a reason. To start off, you are alone on a baoott in this vast open sea alone and that can be telling you something right away: You are alone for some reason, weathering the storm by yourself because something happened. Out in this dark stormy open sea filled with desperation and hopelessness. For anyone who is familiar with fighting anxiety and depression, this is how we are introduced to Kay, a teenage girl who looks like a demon but is afraid, tired, and sad. Kay is not who we should be scared of as she is our character to follow along the story and progress but there are two monsters who are downright horrifying and they speak to you in every worst way possible, one of them screaming what feels like self-loathing dialogues that absolutely sting and feels like you are being stabbed in the heart and the other that just tries to push you in the wrong direction. It's not people she knows but spoiler alert, as how I see it, these two monsters are your inner demons, your own dark thoughts, and voices that will emotionally manipulate you slowly to the brink of killing off everything you love about yourselves and worst-case scenario, the thoughts of disappearing and ending it all. I forget to mention that these are very good metaphors and there is a lot of them in this game. The manifestations of your inner demons which voice negative thoughts, and temptation that will try to bring you down. Just like real lifeThese feelings of loneliness, anxiety, and pain is what the game captures and just like how Kay faces them, she struggles to stay afloat literally and figuratively. Trying to not drown in her own thoughts in the deepest darkest blue ocean that not only would it kill her but surrounded her in eternal darkness. After all, these feelings of emotions is a good sign to tell you that you are alive and human but of course, it ain't a nice road trip to go through. But in a way, it tells you that you are not alone in life.During your journey, you will come across some bright aspects of the game and like a moth, I was attracted to the light as one could describe; light full of warmth. Casting away the dark storm and monsters which presents to you calm after the storm but only for a brief moment. Yes, the darkness and monsters come back and can definitely say it's another nice metaphor. Fighting to survive but your inner demons keep coming back to ♥♥♥♥ with you. It's a real story in itself, go through the darkest times, fight your inner demons, embrace the warmth, go back in the past to understand what happened, dark ♥♥♥♥ again, warmth, rinse and repeat. It's a wild ride that won't be pleasant but that's the natural way of things.Then you come across the bullying part and this was played out very well with Kay and her younger sibling, Sunny. A great way to describe that sometimes people struggle to reach out because sometimes the others just don't listen and Kay just surrounded by her own happiness with Jack, failed to notice that Sunny was struggling with bullying which he had such thoughts and I quote "Maybe it would be better... if I just disappeared."oh boi was this a great example of listening to someone in their dire moments but Kay failed to do so until she found out way too late. Sunny was fighting alone where he needed someone he could tell his troubles to the most and that being Kay, feeling neglected and felt like nothing in the world is what led to the quote I just mentioned. So while she at first was distant from Sunny's life and was more focused on her boyfriend, Jack. Kay does prove that she really loves her brother by telling him that she is always going to be there for him.Then emotional disconnection between the Vivienne and Adam displaying miscommunication and only for it to get worse was difficult and upsetting to go through. That one line.. "I always loved you. All of you. I still do. That's why sometimes you have to let go. I don't know. So you're able to move forward and heal." How can you love someone and still let them go? It has never hit hard like a bullet train going at 200 mph. As Vivienne was willing to let go but also mentally wanted to fix everything as she knew she was the problem but Adam was miserable, losing control of his emotions, and placing blame and hatred towards the other. Unfortunately, it seemed like they eventually separated.Things can't be changed but the present and future matter and it's what happened with Kay being present in between them.If there was something thing I hoped it was implied in the game as well. Love when you are ready, not when you are alone.Jack's relationship with Kay. Whilst it was sweet and seemed perfect. Jack distanced himself from her because he didn't want to hurt her any further and for any reason, preferred to be alone. Nothing could be understood here but eventually, Kay had to let go and that's when it all went to ♥♥♥♥. The one she loved and even though was being extremely caring and worried, just upright left her and many of those can understand that feeling of being separated from the one you love. Thrown down into the deepest pit of despair and you better believe that the monsters return except that it's a bit different. The monster in the shell, even though was hostile towards Kay at first, you start to notice that she cares about Kay and wants her to understand that. I already mentioned that the monster was her inner demon but it gets better when you realize that she is Kay's feelings of self-loathing. It's pretty clear, the embodiment of her anger and hatred towards herself that gets significantly stronger and almost to the point that she is trying to destroy herself was a great metaphor for the monsters in this game.Overall, this game was a journey for Kay who was on her way to self-recovery and the ending with the beautiful island full of colors and absolute solitude with the calmness of the sea. What better way to describe it, than walking along the sandy beach on the island alone as the sea can be very beautiful at times. Would I recommend this game to everyone? Not really but it is a choice and an option!

_childDocuments_.review: A Bit EmbarrassingIt's a well made game that plays smoothly and intuitively with wonderful character and environmental design. But the dialogue feels like the director literally handed their college therapy journal to the development team, who I imagine asking "Oh, so you want us to rewrite this to fit your monster aesthetic?" "No, don't rewrite a thing. Just copy and paste all the dialogue." It's like an English major who hasn't fully grasped the concept of metaphor. 'Re-skinning' the drama from your past doesn't make it allegorical, it just makes the experience a bit embarrassing for your audience. I was all in for a game that would take me on a personal, maybe even emotionally painful, journey. What I got was a look at the director's unlocked messenger app. I honestly enjoyed playing this game, and I'm glad that I did, but I also wouldn't recommend it.UPDATE: EA still sucks.

_childDocuments_.review: Sea of Solitude is a game that feels authentic in what it's trying to express. You aren't some hero off slaying monsters or saving the day. Sometimes the best we can do is try to heal and save ourselves from our own monsters, that feeling the pain is part of being human. _childDocuments_.review: This is a mixed bag for me, I'd give a "neutral" recommendation if there was such an option. The gameplay is pretty cool, the soundtrack is nice, the art is great... but the acting and the story oscillate between high highs and low lows. The voice of the protagonist in particular is a sore point. The scenario also feels a bit hammy, full of metaphors that felt, to me, mostly too obvious and shallow for their own sake. I would've liked to see some more... complexity, depth, obfuscation (?) added to the plot elements. They didn't draw me in, in part due to their simplicity, and in part due to their presentation (protagonist VA).There have been far more interesting games using the themes of mental health, self-worth, family issues etc. as central themes, and in comparison, Sea of Solitude stumbles too hard there for me to give it a thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: Your enjoyment of Sea of Solitude is going to be based entirely on whether or not you can engage yourself with the story. The gameplay mechanics are quite shallow; it's practically a walking simulator. The game consists of pressing Q to figure out which direction to walk. Occasionally there will be a ladder to climb or some obstacle to wait for, but any puzzle the game offers is quite simple. There are two types of collectibles in the game, in the form of seagulls and bottles. The seagulls can be shooed away, causing them to fly off and giving you a view of the area. The intention is that the camera follows them and shows off the environment, but the view is so limited and barely helpful that they are mostly inconvenient. The bottles offer insight into the main character's thoughts, but can easily be missed. For a game that wants you to engage with the character's thoughts and story, it seems odd that they would also hide some of the story in missable locations. That being said, most of the bottle's contents are inconsequential and could be gleaned from the actual dialogue. There is also no way to track the aforementioned collectibles, meaning you basically just have to use a guide and play through the game again if you are unsure of which ones you've missed. I did encounter a glitch where I could not get rid of the bottle message until I found a new one. For a game that claims to be about loneliness, it never really leaves you alone to explore that topic for more than a few minutes. The section about bullying is so poorly written I almost quit three chapters in. If you can make it past this section however, the story gets much better. The game is very overt in its meaning, leaving little nuance or allowing the player to consider the scenarios for themself. This isn't necessarily a bad thing; not every game needs to be Pathologic levels of story.  I do have to mention the voice acting for the main character, as it is hard to listen to at times. I do wish they had recast that as the accent can ruin the immersion.The art style and character design is quite good, including some idle animations. The game is quite short, only amounting to a few hours of playtime. The change in tone between the bright daytime sections and the dark night time is quite powerful, giving a sense of danger and anticipation. From a 100% achievement perspective, the game is not too difficult to finish, though it will require some grinding and a guide for the collectibles. In summary, if you receive the game for free or have access to it through EA Play it may be worth it, but I would advise playing something else.

_childDocuments_.review: Sea of Solitude has a very deep and dark subject matter which explores mental illness well. It also addresses the horrible effects of bullying on young people in a realistic manner. The art style and graphics for this game are lovely, the lightning is great and the colours throughout the game were fantastic. The gameplay wasn't anything unique or special, though it did have some good moments. the story wasn't anything special either, although I can really appreciate the purpose behind the games narrative. The voice acting could be much better, and the emotions behind a lot of the characters/voices seemed very straightforward without too much depth. The game is also a little short, 2-4 hours for an average playthrough. The designs for the game, specifically the monsters, are amazing and there were a lot of moments where i felt really intimidated getting into dangerous situations with them. I feel there's not really anything too amazing that stands out about this game to make it innovative or unique, except it's subject matter and how it handles it, but i do feel that it's still a good indie game and should be experienced!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good. I related to the things that Sunny was going through to a certain degree, so not as extreme. But I also related to both Jack and Kay. The loneliness and wanting to put everyone before myself, times when I feel like giving up, and Jack pushing those that he love away when he needs them most because he's afraid of causing more harm than good. There are some things that I haven't told anyone about myself till this day because I never know when it's the right time to, or if I even should. I feel like this game captured really well what it's like when facing your 'inner demons', and facing those who have 'inner demons.' This game got me in my feels, but that's because it did a good job at what it was meant to do.

_childDocuments_.review: A very narrative focused game with light platforming and exploration to fill the game out.  The game is all about exploring the issues in the main characters life, especially the people in her life, which are represented by obstacles in the game that must be overcome.  The gameplay itself, is very straightforward with exploring small areas, avoiding monsters, collecting some items, etc.The game has a cool look, with very nice water effects.  The story is the star of the show though, and if you follow it all the way through it can get a bit emotional.As a game though, it leaves a lot to be desired, at least with mouse and keyboard.  Turning is just not tuned right.  You can adjust it but it just never felt right, either moving too much or too little.  And the menus have no mouse support at all.  Also has an EA launcher with a required login for a single player game, completely out of place and seemingly unnecessary.  The rest of the gameplay was fine, but you will find much better examples of that style all over.  One note though, the focus mechanic is not explained at all and had me stumped with needing online help to understand (you need to move the mouse in the right direction until it lines up with some target).  Was probably worsened by the bad mouse support.End result, is a minor recommend, but only for those looking for a casual experience and who are especially interested in the story / journey and don't care much for engaging gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: This game makes me cry. I feel the pain and emotion in the story and the art of the world and the way you interact with the monsters / characters. It's like my life. I spend many nights sitting at my desk alone. I am not really alone, I have a wife, a child, a dog and a cat. I have a father 30 minutes away from me and friends I can call and visit. Yet, I still feel alone. I do things for others all the time to help and be useful, but I still always feel like I was just used instead of being appreciated that I helped. I lost my brother when I was young, I have held that on my shoulders for years and still do that it was my responsibility for his death because I was his bigger brother and I failed keeping him safe. It has tortured me and still does, and it eats at me silently in the back of my head. When my wife and I get into arguments, and we sit in different rooms, All I can do is hear voices telling me the good the bad and the ugly, all together confusing and jumbled. I think shes lying, I ask for the truth, I get the truth, I deny the truth. I search for the truth even though I have it. It hurts me. It really does.I should have my wife play this game to understand what it's like to feel alone. Perhaps she will maybe understand the kind of pain that I have been in and how mentally ill and discombobulated I really am, even tho i try so hard to be a good Father/Husband. I am a huge fan of this game already and while I am still only on chapter 3 (I stopped to write this review) I know that by the end of tonight or tomorrow I will have finished it. Cried a few more times and possibly put this game as one of my highest of all time for its pure emotion that it can drag out of you. Maybe I'm broken and have many monsters, but that doesn't mean I am not searching for the light that is me.

_childDocuments_.review: The concept is truly remarkable, and the graphics shine brilliantly. It's a world that could be described as dark, gloomy, and often teetering on the edge of the eerie and the frightening. Yet, when you eventually reach the light, it's akin to a radiant beam of sunshine that breaches the depths of your soul, dispelling the isolation and fear that have held you captive. This game is woven with numerous hidden messages, offering profound lessons about moving forward and the art of letting go, among others.However, I must confess that my only complaint lies in occasional frustrations stemming from the controllers. There are moments when it becomes necessary to step away, as the game's somber atmosphere can, paradoxically, sap your energy.Drawing from personal experience, it's perfectly acceptable to stand alone and abstain from relationships if that feels right for you. No one should ever make you feel lesser or inadequate in the realm of relationships. It's vital to distance yourself from anything that dampens your spirit or drags you down.

_childDocuments_.review: Sea of Solitude is a gripping, story-driven adventure game. Players journey with Kay on a boat around the submerged city in an effort to discover the reason behind her transformation and the story around her. The developer delivers a wonderful experience. A beautiful ride accompanied with an emotional journey is the great combination that gets me fascinated from the beginning to the end, let along the lessons to be learnt from our protagonist. Layer by layer, a family member at a time, the game gradually tells you what it is to be human, what it takes to change, and what it is to accept. I may not have the same experience in real life, but the compelling story and the fitting metaphors make me truly feel the struggle the characters have.Even if you may not be touched by the story, the game still offers a beautiful trip on boat. Sailing around the submerged city, bathing in the warm sunlight, and gazing through the crystal-clear ocean around you are already great experiences. The reassuring calmness makes you feel truly at peace. The feelings are more valuable after the character suffers from emotional downfall. When the light casts away the dark, gloomy rain, the ocean becomes calm again. You sit on the buoy, indulging in the warmth with two feet in the water. The distinct yet seamless transition between two weather not only amplifies Kay`s emotion but also makes the boat trip significant during the journey.In my opinion, a good metaphor can make a story effective. The story in this game is no exception. I mostly adore how the game characterizes Kay`s family and her boyfriend. Sunny, Kay`s little brother, is a huge crow hiding away from the bullies in school. It is believed that a crow symbolizes a new phase in one's life.  This fact not only means that Sunny needs to push away the fear he holds, but also hints Kay how she can do to make it through the trial. Meanwhile, the others focus more on their personalities. Kay`s father is a chameleon, representing his wish to get away with everything and to find his inner peace; Kay`s mother, on the other hand, is an octopus, representing her desperate needs to do anything to hold her family from falling apart. Kay`s boyfriend Jack, is a wolf, representing his lack of trust in anyone besides himself about important matters. Even Kay herself has three metaphorical beings: the Girl is her positive yet twisted self, the Shelled-Monster is her instinct to forget and run away from everything bad in her life, and finally the Sea Monster, always swimming in the dark water around, always talks in a tender seducing tone, is her idea of plunging deep into darkness in a self-destructing way. With these good metaphors, Sea of Solitude conveys a strong, effective story.With everything crafted and mixed together beautifully in the story, the game wishes to tell two simple things in life: to listen, and to leave behind. Often time an argument happens, whether between couples or family, because both parties forget to stop and listen to each other. To listen, to achieve mutual understanding and support; To leave behind, to give each other time and space to calm down. Kay fails to hear her brother's problem and Kay`s parent fail to give each other a room to breathe are the prime examples for the ideas. The whole game wraps these two life tips together, seasoning them in a touching, potent stories about a teenage girl and her family.Not much to complain. This game has a good story, simple platforming, and simple "combat". The only discomfort I have is that on some ledge, if the wave rises, it would trigger the Sea Monster`s chase sequence. This is a bit confusing in some places for me to discern which ledges are safe shores. Otherwise, for a story-driven game, Sea of Solitude manages to deliver a quite rounded experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is visually striking and deals with mental health, loss, bullying, and how a variety of relationships in our lives impact us. NOTE: this game handles some heavy mental health issues, so you should take that into account if you want to play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes you on a journey with Kay, who's all alone in a flooded city, surrounded by monsters and loneliness. It's like she's treading water in an endless ocean of emotions, and she's trying to find her way through it all.At first, Kay only has her wooden rowboat, which becomes her safe haven. The city she explores is underwater, a mix of pastel colors and dark blue-green tones, reflecting her emotional turmoil. As she travels by boat, on foot, and even swims, she confronts her inner demons represented by monstrous versions of important people in her life.Each monster reflects a traumatic experience she's had, like her parents' divorce or her brother's bullying. The game uses metaphor to tell her story, and it's not subtle about the power of loneliness and self-hate. Kay's internal dialogue is loud and sharp, leaving little room for interpretation, but that's perhaps the point—it shows how negative thoughts can consume you.However, the most impactful moments are the subtle ones. Messages from her past self hidden in bottles show that she's been in this dark place before. The game isn't about winners or losers; it's about finding equilibrium in life.Kay's journey is about learning to approach challenges, knowing when to face them and when to let go. And that's how she keeps going, even when knocked down—she never gives up.Overall, "Sea of Solitude" takes you on an emotional ride, exploring the depths of loneliness and the strength to endure. It's not perfect, but it's a meaningful and personal experience that will leave a lasting impression.

My therapist would like this game I think.Good game but only gave me 4 hours of gameplay. The price for this game is $19.99. If I spent $20 and only got 4 hours of gameplay I would be pretty bummed. _childDocuments_.review: Since I have more criticism for this game, lets start with the compliments. - Sea Of Solitude is visually mesmerising and when accompanied with a great soundtrack, well layered puzzles and mechanics- all enticed me to play the game start to finish. The base concept of the story is alluring and realistic, with similar tropes in games such as Beyond:Two Souls, and Fe. But at the end of the game, I felt disappointed for a number of reasons. For starters, even though the core concept of telling the story of a disturbed family through artistic and non-human imagery is absolutely fantastic, the dialogues and the characters are very derivative to that of something like Neon Genesis Evangelion. To put it in perspective, playing this game instead of watching Evangelion for the story/psychoanalysis, is like eating fish droppings while convincing yourself it's caviar. The dialogues and story telling were very basic and too literal for something trying to be abstract. This was definitely a huge let down as I wished for a more compelling story telling style and dialogue for such a beautiful and comically-eerie animation. And then the characters: the protagonist is 24 and names a mysterious ball of glowing light that paves the way to the next checkpoint as "glowy", like, lol seriously? And she even refers to the magical fairy girl as "girl" (ugh). Every character in this game expresses a dulling sense of naiveity that made me eye-roll a bunch of times. There is definitely some soul behind this project, but there are better art mediums that outclass Sea of Solitude by miles. But, I can see why people would really love this game, I get the appeal. 5/10

Between the music and the constant change in lighting it does catch the eye.- Tells a predictable but intriguing story concerning mental health.- The boat feels good to control.Meh:  - Voice acting starts weak, gets better.- Predictable- Lacks much in the way of "gameplay".Negative:- The camera is a bit of an ass.- Immersion breaking graphical glitches ABOUND!  Too many times something touching was supposed to be happening and a goofy texture would pop out of nowhere or "hair" would phase through the ground.  That sort of thing.  It sounds nit-picky but when immersion in the narrative is all you have, it really hurts the game.- Full Price is too expensive.  It can be beaten in three hours easily.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game for one evening. I would say just beware that if you are paying more for this than you do for a movie ticket you are not really getting your money's worth because it won't last longer than that! I got at 75% off on sale, so it was certainly worth it.Can't say I understand the whole premise of this game having "heavy themes about emotional trauma" and the disclaimer is pretentious in my opinion. The theme of the storyline is about not fixating on yourself and accepting everyone's (including yours) problems. Basically the protagonist learns to be empathetic to other people and herself. In other words - a relatively common premise. It's well-made, great voice acting and environment design. There are some timing challenges in the game but it's really casual otherwise.I have to say that this EA Originals programme might be the one good thing to come out of EA in the last decade. If they continue using the FIFA money to fund these little gems, maybe they could get in our good graces again some day. Maybe.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. Played it as part of EA Play. And seeing as the full price is €20 I'd say wait for a sale. As usual I try to write my reviews once I'm completely done with the game (to give you guys a good estimate for the hours played).The amount of hours your see here is the story combined with all the achievements. (Give or take with some idling)- The art style combined with the theme about being alone and facing your monsters and darkness makes for an amazing game with a great story. The transitions between "happy" and "darkness" are amazing, one moment you are casually jumping across rooftops or in your boat enjoying the view and the next you are swimming for your life with a racing heart.- For the people who care about achievements it's all very do-able. There is a chapter select and you can come back for any achievement so none of them are missable. - Graphics, this kind of style never gets old for me. It runs flawlessly it looks 'realistic' enough where it gets real scary and spooky at times. And it just overal is an amazing setting with great visuals.- The controls. I would like to mention this one specifically as well since I saw a couple of reviews saying the controls are god-awful. I must say I played this one with a controller and it was all super intuitive and had no glitches or struggles at all.- Short. For a game being €20, 7 hours seems rather short. If you would just complete the story and ignore the achievements you could cut it down by another 1-2 hours.- Voice-acting. This one stood out for me right away. It is kinda bad, I have nothing really more to add to this one, after a couple chapters you will get used to it and don't pay as much attention to it anymore.TLDR; Defintely a must-play. Wait for discount though, it's a tad short.

Player is forced to slightly change tactic at least once (the change itself is consistent with the plot).It's hard to describe what's cool there without getting into spoilers. Like "No message" thing player can find. So I'll just say the game is brilliant. Obviously tastes vary. In cons I'd put the length of the game. _childDocuments_.review: Sea of Solitude is "platformer/puzzle" game about life, bullying, mental illnesses and some other bad stuff that can happen to anyone.You'll travel areas by foot or by boat and exploring a strange world to uncover the story of the main character, and the people around her.I discovered this game 2 years ago during an E3 conference, and was interested in the tone and look of the game.So here I am, finally playing it!First of all, the game forces the installation of Origin in your computer.. I think I don't have much to add on that point.But more about the "game" part of the.. you know.. game! Well, it feels "gamy".. like you have collectibles in the world (and kind of a lot..), every time you get one a little counter increases, letting you know how much you have left. It's.. not really the type of game I wanted collectibles, it kind of killed the "serious" and more narrative type of the game. Buuut, I'll say they kind of reward the player for exploring. (side note: I quickly checked, but I can't find a counter during the chapter selection, which could annoy someone wanting to find everything)Speaking of exploration, the structure are sometimes weird. You can pretty much parkour everywhere, which is fun in itself, though it feels weird at times because you don't know where to go, even with the flare hint, it was minor, but it happened. My biggest problem with the "parkour" is clearly the movement.. it is very wanky. I often got weird animations, fall for no reason, got through a wood platform in the water, and the worst: got really stuck in a weird position for 15-20s, my character couldn't move, had zero animation, and I honestly don't know how I got out.I also got a situation where I fell during a "wind-up" animation (on an object, I won't spoil anything), the object froze, wasn't completed, and I couldn't start it back, I had to reload.This game being narrative centered, you'll often be in cinematics (or an automatic scene, not especially a "movie", you got the idea), aaaand I have to say, I don't understand all the camera angles, some turn for no reason, some forces the angle when you clearly understood the situation; It was minor but it was here.The volume mixing is not really good, I had to constently change the volume to reduce some really loud voices and do the opposite for low voices, I never found the perfect volume.The subtitle boxes are appearing weirdly too (I may be on an overdose of the "weird" word at the moment), and not always exactly matching the voices. Some quotes repeat themself way too often too.THE POINT OF ALL OF THAT IS: on a technical level, the game is clunky.BUT, other than that:Puzzles are ok and don't cross the line of being too repetitive.Voices do the job, some better than others (it sure talks a lot at times, but it's the theme)I love the  designIt's not , but some scenes are gorgeous and colorful.Musics are really good too.And finally, the story, the themes, the symbolism, -while not perfect, and leave some subjects to interpretation for the players- are definitely here.

_childDocuments_.review: "Maybe" would be better.  I love the story and where everything was going but there are some important bugs that made the game unplayable until I worked around it, or got used to the inconvenience.  tldr; I'm still glad I played it because it was a good story but the game play itself was marred with some unfortunate technical issues.  If they fix those in future updates, this will be a very good game. My review will focus on the buggy stuff.* Pretty* Appropriate atmosphere* A story that many will be able to connect with (not super new, but that's not important. We have a lot of shared pain that we need to explore whether it's new or not)* :  Despite the game appearing as if it is really made for controller, I did find that every couple seconds, the game would start spinning around and around. I thought they were being obnoxiously 'cinematic' or artsy for a bit until I unplugged the controller (which works fine in every other game I play) and just used the keyboard. The problem stopped when I used the keyboard.:  Despite allowing the changing of keyboard bindings, it would NOT allow me to change the jump from the space bar to the left control key, so I had to jump with my baby finger through the entire game. I get used to it because a lot of games force me to play in this awkward way, but they usually aren't the games that actually HAVE the ability to change your keyboard bindings, so that was weird.  So once I accepted that the controls just aren't going to be very good for me, I was able to continue playing the game and finally just get into the story. I wish I could have just been focusing on the story from the start though. I feel like the technical issues really broke the immersion for too long given how short a game this is. * I know it's part of the drama/cinematic effect, but the camera slowly choosing different angles for me was not a nice way to play this game. I like to see where I'm going. In a first person game it is quite disorienting to suddenly be looking at yourself side-on as you run, with no idea where you are running anymore because the environment is too closed in to pull out to a wide-view for this angle to still be playable.   Also, when shooting the beam of light thingy you lose the ability to control where you are looking at all, resulting in at least one scene where you are shooting blindly until you hit something because the camera decides to just point down at you while are trying to aim.  This mechanic really didn't work well purely because of the camera issues.If there was an option to turn off cinematic camera so the camera is exclusively controller by the player, I would have found this much easier to play.It's a lovely game, not very hard, quite short (about 5 hours - making it more than I usually spend per hour of game play but it will be more worth it when the sales get a bit deeper on it).  If they tidy up the controls and wandering camera this game will be really wonderful.I admit the decision to pay more than I usually would for a game this short was 100% due to the music in the trailer but in the end, if it ever occurred in the game, I never noticed it so.... maybe don't fall for that like I did.

_childDocuments_.review: first of all, the art is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gorgeous. this game gets full marks on illustration and animation. the sight of the human head piranha chasing me and chomping me up get my heart pumping and scared. the water rises and subsides beautifully. i love the little details on different buildings. butsome of the dialogues and characterizations weren't very realistic and felt more like what the writer thought the characters would think, instead of the character thinking it. i wished that the devs had done more research, read stories about the people their characters are based on or even interviewed someone in that role. somehow, the characters in this game seemed half-baked to me, like their only purpose of existence is to be depressed so that they can be a cog of this game, instead of me as a player taking a glimpse into their lives, and it shows. i hoped to see "fuller" characters who are also depressed, not depression defining them completely as a person to the point that they are nothing else. but of course, some people are like that. it is just my wishful thinking to want to know more about the person behind the depressed soul or their attempts to fight it, positively or negatively and how that worked out, or how they go through their days during depressive periods. depression is multi-faceted, and this game showed a very limited view of it.the example of the odd dialogue is in the school of pain, where a character is being bullied, there is a lot of "we'll kill you." screams when the protagonist was being haunted by the "mobs/people who caused the pain". i find that very ineffective. it's like telling someone point blank that you are making them cry, without doing the actual action. there are allusion to certain events that made the bullied character depressed, but there was never much elaboration on how it hurts or digs deep into his heart.additionally, the gameplay is interesting at first but you have to deal with repetitiveness and wonky camera. crossing the waters while a human-head piranha is after you dominated the first 50% of the game, while a hoard of zombie-like mobs will chase you all the time throughout in different places at during the middle to end arc of the game. it feels like the devs just designed activities that they reuse again and again while trying to make that less boring by padding them with the "story". that being said, i quite enjoy the skyscraper part of the game.usually, people play games for the story or the gameplay, or both. but both are quite lacking for me. buy this if you love the art style or want to support games about mental health so that there would be more future games made to bring awareness.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a must play in my opinion.The graphics, while not realistic like some other games out there, are still pretty beautiful and amazing. The water physics can get a bit annoying in some places when dealing with waves, but overall were fine. The world as a whole was beautiful and fun for me to just run/ride around in and look at and enjoy.the collectibles/side items in the game are more or less put in your path as you follow the story, with maybe 5-10 of them strewn about the over-world as a whole. So its not overly difficult to find and collect every one. I'm only missing a few of the two different types, and that's because I wasn't overly concerned with hunting for them. And the game does a good job of letting you know when they're nearby (Kay reacts by looking at them or saying "huh", and the bottles you collect have a ring/hum to them while the seagulls squawk/call out to you when you're near). I'm confident that if i'd been diligent in looking for them at all times when playing i would have collected them all with little effort.The story overall is amazing. The way they represented and handled the difficult topics of sensitive nature in reminded me very much of Disney's Inside Out. You learn about the story at the same time as the PC does and so you're carried along her journey in a natural and realistic manner. I honestly believe that everyone should play this game all the way through at least once with a fully opened mind. If you don't go in expecting it to be an action game or to have a lot of fighting or violence in it, then I'm certain you'll love it.Everyone's lives are complicated and everyone is going through or HAS gone through something that is represented in this game. And as such be prepared for new and old scars to be itched at as the game seems to actively help you heal those wounds.Personally i was hit by several of the aspects represented within the game, which has caused me to reevaluate my life a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: The game really resonated with me. I've been in the same place as the protagonist so I also understand that this game's metaphors are kinda specific so not everyone will identify with them, but in it's core is a simple life lesson, "The only one who can take care of you, is yourself". Gameplay is really simple, visuals and music are nice, characters are solid and they serve a unique purpose in telling you what this is all about. Maybe the only sin of this work is it being a 4-5 hour game of something that can be summarized in a sentence, but I also think that maybe understanding the message and really internalizing it are two different things, the latter being the real challenge, in that sense play as a medium to reach the audience feels like a fair choice.I recommend it, buy it or play it as part of EA play as I did, either is fine.

_childDocuments_.review: It's during World War 2. The German war machine is conquering Europe, and either killing certain occupants or sending them off to camps. A group hides out for many months in the sewers to escape them. One of them is a woman hiding her pregnancy, for fear of the babies cries attracting the Germans when it is born, and the group ousting her for their own preservation. Eventually the child comes into the world, and does what babies do. It cries. A lot. In desperation the mother tries to shush the infant. She goes too far, and the child is smothered. A terrible tragedy, and one that raises many moral questions in the face of adversity. Does the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few? How was this woman treated after she accidentally killed her own child, when she did so (albeit inadvertently) to protect the others? Did the others judge her badly, even though it was done for their benefit? How did she deal with it afterwards? I bring this up here, because it is an example of humanity trying to get by under the worst conditions, and also because that may not be how events actually went. Some people in the sewers with this woman claim she was distant when the child was born, and may have had what we now know as post partum depression. Her emotional bond was not there, and not in her right mind, the accidental smothering was not so accidental. She wanted to do it, and circumstances gave her a reason where she wouldn't be blamed (if she actually considered anything beyond the bleakness that she was feeling there and then)A sordid time in history, and what seems like a clear cut case for compassion, but in the cold light of day another side is revealed, that asks more questions about the human condition.So why am I bringing it up here? This game has nothing to do with that specific event. Its about a girl called Kay who inwardly struggles with self-loathing, due to her being so self-absorbed that she completely ignores various ugly calamaties befalling her family. And she's not distracted by particularly worthwhile things either, but vacuous and shallow stuff like cute dog pictures, and relationship troubles.The kind of thing that as an adult you learn are meaningless, or at least, there is far worse ♥♥♥♥ out there to concern yourself with. Maybe now you understand why I led with that true story up above, as it's the kind of thing that has some intellectual "meat" to "chew on" (for want of better terms) and puts in perspective the sheer gulf between the two dilemmas.  I'm an adult. This game is about a teenage girl, and her teenage girl concerns. I'm not one, and never have been. And as I'm not a woman in a mans body either, I don't expect to ever understand the concerns of a female from the intimate perspective of, you know, being one. In either sex the troubles of the teenage individual are not ones I would belittle (well...mostly. stuff like bullying, which this deals with, is horrendous, but the rest I'm sneery of. blubbering about someone leaving you when there's billions of people in the world you've never even met to be able to make any comparison to, and you've hardly even lived any of your life yet? pathetic!), but they're far from compelling for me, since I went through them myself, and whaddayaknow, the world doesn't end because of a teenage crush turning to crap.Long story short: I really, really, really, don't think I'm the audience for this. Well..I know 100% that this game wasn't made for the likes of me i.e Old and male. Despite my perhaps obnoxious dismissal of it (note I didn't put "game", as it does actually have some game-play, and it is fairly strong, so no need for the quotation marks to emphasize it being a pissy walking simulator or similarly vapid experience as a "game") it doesn't have much to say beyond getting in a young girls mind as she mentally beats herself up for having her head stuck up her own arse.If you're a teenager, and a girl, you could connect with this. Unlike Gris, where it was a wordless narrative about being a depressed girl and the emotional connection (apparently - I didn't get anything from that game either) was from how its style pulled you in, and made you feel, this has spoken dialogue. So it is unavoidable (for me anyway) that you are expected to identify with their sex, as you can hear their thinking and attitude all throughout. I can't do that.I don't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about anyone who spends any time looking at cute dog pictures, as that activity has no value to me. Giving her words, and making her femininity so explicit when compared to the wordless, essentially unisex, "story" of Gris, gives me a disconnection as a male.To me it's only value was in how well it visually / sonically / artistically tried to put you in her mental space, and whilst it's good at that...uh....I've seen it done much better, and with more subtly, and / or with deeper content. Partly this is the case because I've lived longer, and have experienced this in various formats over the years. Whereas someone younger won't have done, and might find its symbolism to be more rewarding. Personally I got bored with it, as it's pretty darn obvious. Oh! Kay is being attacked by a shadow monster, wonder if that's her own rage? It is? Gosh! It took all of about 5 seconds to figure that out, since it's far from being inspired. The game-play is fine, albeit pretty easy, and so far the main action is totally cribbed mechanicaly, and in its setting, from a set-piece in Evil Within. Kays mental world is a town submerged under water, and her dark self constantly hunts her when she's in the water, so you'll be "frantically" *coughs* swimming to whatever safety presents itself (buoys - which leads to a cringeworthy joke about...boys, or floating debris, or various buildings) This is meant to be intense, and scary, but there's no challenge to it, so it fails on both counts. At its best it's a mildly reasonable diversion, though again - maybe the youth, or genre newbies,  will find it better without my jaded familiarity. The other aspect of it's gameplay is a bit of a puzzle / platforming section, though this isn't exactly super-amazeballs either. It's decent enough, as is its other main chunk, but with the story, and her perspective, and the-seen-it-all-before-but-worse-than-that-I-don't-care-for-it realisation of her mind, it just doesn't do much for me. Were it just a review for me, I'd give it a negative. Its not bad, but I don't much care for it. Based on its quality, and my own self-knowledge of me being a grumpy, cynical, contrary old geezer, however: it gets a positive. But you should note that after two hours I'm fairly happy to not bother playing it anymore, and the obligation as a "professional" (ha! ha!) reviewer to properly experience it up to the end can ♥♥♥♥ right off. Its not that interesting as an experience, or as a game, that I personally feel the need for a definitive opinion. Especially since I can imagine there being an audience for this, and I'm clearly not it.

_childDocuments_.review: brief overview:     2/5 I would recommend as a great visual and story of mental illness, unfortunately it does not provide an unbiased view of mental illness. So, I would only recommend if you have the perspective to see through the biased and to not be influenced by the skewed opinions.  Review proper;     The game has a stunning visual style and great pacing with the story and characters. It is a great allegory for mental illness and the problems associated with it.   The story for the first 7 parts is great and unbiased, starting in chapter 8, where the father is introduced, there is a change in tone. The father is shown in the later chapters as a liar, manipulator, and workaholic. While the mother is shown as a reactional figure to the father's actions. The mother is shown to have her own issues, but all her issues are shown to be from the father’s actions. The mother strictly plays the role of the victim within the story while the father plays the aggressor.   The boyfriend also plays a part later in the story, he is shown to have symptoms of depression and possibly an isolationist disorder. The boyfriend is shown to be hurt by gestures that were meant to help and comfort them. The pain and wounds acquired from this is shown in the game to be the result of the main character interacting with them, but the underlying themes show the wound could have been opened by anyone, it was simply the main character's interaction which caused the altercation. The game also mentions the boyfriend getting “randomly mad for no reason.”  All the female characters were hurt and scarred by one or more of the male characters within the story, the mother was reactional and got the majority of her issues from the father. The main character and the mother were given justification for how and why they feel the way they do. The male characters were never shown as people and were not explained past why they hurt the females in the story. The only exclusion to this is the younger brother presented in the early chapters, but this character was provided as a reason for the issues later developed by the main character, the pain was a part of the main character's story and not the brother’s.   The older males in this story are painted to be the cause of mental illness without ever giving a solid explanation of their feelings or reasons to feel that way. All the females, in contrast, were given reasons to feel the way they do and were given validation that it is ok to feel that way. The males were never given such reasons or validation.   It paints men as villains in the story and is not a true, non-biased look at mental illness rather, one extremely specific example from a storywriter who wrote men as the villains within this world.  I would not recommend for use on young teens without the proper perspective to look past the biased.

_childDocuments_.review: A great indie game with a powerful and emotional theme (for me anyways). It resonates with me because there are people in my life who I love to death that are experiencing some of the stuff in the story. I myself even ride this dark sea of solitude, struggling to not be a prisoner of my own mind. The graphic style is great, the use of color and the implementation of weather really emphasizes its intended mood. From the sunshine of happy memories to the choppy waters of an individual's own personal darkness. I also like the symbolism that is inserted into this game, I didn't notice it at first but even the small details have a big meaning in this game. In terms of gameplay, there's not really much. It's really straight forward and simple: Go to the objective, do a b c and d to progress, and move on. Also collect these things for lore and stuff. The voice acting is decent, not golden globe worthy but that's alright. This game is more of a "just sit back and experience it" kind of work and by god, is it an experience. It's only a few hours long but its definitely worth the $10.

_childDocuments_.review: While much shorter than I imagined, the aptly named Sea of Solitude is definitely worth the $10 spent. It is a much needed wake-up call for more interest and understanding in the area of mental health. I initially happened across this game from Cornelia Geppert's TEDTalk, where she described in detail the representations embedded in the story and was eager for it to come out. Our protagonist, Kay, is swept up into a sea to face her burgeoning loneliness and demons of her own making, each demon representing a different emotion, thought, or person in her life. One of the most telling is Kay's relationship with her boyfriend, who wears a beautiful white mask to cover up the deep, dark depression he suffers from. This resonated deeply with me because I also experience the depression symptoms described and portrayed in the game. I found it very interesting to confront the same thoughts and emotions that I think and feel come through the game. It was a constructive experience for me to take part in playing Sea of Solitude coming from a similar place Kay is. Some of it was difficult to hear/watch, but I think I'm better for having played Sea of Solitude. Lastly, while some of the plot seemed a little thin at times, the art and soundtrack more than made up for it. I definitely need to get the OST for the game and have a large amount of screenshots to go through! I highly recommend this game to play. It is short (~4hrs), but packs a punch. I would recommend purchasing at $10 or less just because of its short length. If you are interested, here is the link to Cornelia's TEDTalk:

_childDocuments_.review: One of the game's most significant failures lies in its writing. Instead of providing a deep, thoughtful exploration of mental health issues, "Sea of Solitude" opts for a superficial approach. The game attempts to cover multiple themes but only skims the surface, reducing complex emotions to simplistic moral messages like "this is good" and "this is bad." This lack of depth makes it difficult to connect with the story or its characters, leading to an experience that feels more hollow than heartfelt.Kay, the game's protagonist, is another weak point. Throughout her journey, there is no significant character growth or development. Kay’s behavior remains largely unchanged, which undermines any potential for a meaningful character arc. The game presents her perspective as the correct one without allowing room for nuanced understanding or change. Apologizing in the game feels empty, as it fails to acknowledge or address the gravity of previous actions, making the narrative feel disjointed and unconvincing.The game’s attempt to evoke emotional responses is equally disappointing. "Sea of Solitude" relies on floating "audio log" orbs to deliver key story moments, a method that feels more like an audiobook than an interactive experience. This approach falls flat in a medium that has the potential to immerse players through gameplay and visual storytelling. Unlike games like Titanfall 2, which successfully build emotional bonds between characters through shared experiences, "Sea of Solitude" simply tells you how to feel, rather than making you experience those emotions naturally. The first few minutes of the game show a glimpse of what could have been, but this potential is never realized.To make matters worse, the voice acting—especially that of Kay—is abysmal. Kay’s voice actor delivers lines with such a lack of emotion that it borders on robotic. In a game that revolves around emotional depth, this lifeless delivery is a critical flaw. It’s hard to feel invested in a story when the protagonist’s voice lacks the necessary passion and nuance to convey her supposed turmoil.The gameplay itself is equally lackluster. Most of your time is spent traversing an empty world, solving repetitive puzzles, and engaging in brief, unremarkable platforming sections. The game offers little incentive to explore, as there’s nothing of interest hidden off the beaten path—just useless collectibles that add nothing to the story. While the platforming controls are responsive, the sections are few and far between, leaving you wishing for more variety. The rare moments of boat travel or encounters with enemies like the mermaid and ghosts are too sparse to break up the monotony.The game’s visual design is one of its few redeeming qualities. The monsters, particularly the mermaid, are well-designed and visually striking. However, even the most impressive visuals can’t compensate for the game’s lack of substance. The soundtrack is serviceable but forgettable, doing little to elevate the overall experience."Sea of Solitude" is a prime example of how eye-catching visuals and ambitious themes cannot carry a game that fails in its core design. With shallow storytelling, poor character development, uninspired gameplay, and lackluster voice acting, the game misses the mark on nearly every front. It’s a disappointing journey that promises much but delivers little, leaving players adrift in a sea of missed potential.

_childDocuments_.review: 18 minutes and I think I've seen enough. My review is based on those 18 minutes of play.Let's go over the good first: The game's city is modeled after Berlin, and it sure feels like it. The controls are fluid and tight, for the most part... and I really like the usage of non-native English voice actors. This should be far more widespread than it is, considering that most English speakers are non-native (). And of course it looks quite nice, if a little dry.As you start, the plot hits you in the face right away, but fails to grab you (at least it failed to grab me). The writing and the quality of voice acting both were quite bad, and considering this is a story-driven game, this is a huge hit against it. The gameplay was there. Quite average swimming, platforming, getting away from monsters. Not bad, but not good either. And finally, I'm a little sick of the "depression as an aesthetic" thing. The illness is incredibly widespread, and everyone's suffering from it in a different way; and I believe we finally have societal awareness that it exists and it's treatable, thanks to the artists and people who raised that awareness. That said, I think we've reached a point where depression is being romanticised - and that, in turn, will lead to the overuse of the term and eventual return to "oh, just get over it" kind of reaction from the society. And that can be incredibly harmful.That's all there is to say. It just failed to grab me, that's all.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought a lot about what to say about this game. So, I guess I'm just gonna break it down by section. Spoilers. 1. Sonny. There's nothing realistic about the way Kay and Sonny interact. The scene when he proclaims she's not listening is cringeworthy. Kay blames herself for Sonny's misery, but it's never brought up on where the parents are in this scenario, and why Kay--a mere child--needs to know how to approach her brother's big emotions as he's being sexually harassed at school. Kay blames herself, and no one takes the time to tell her that her "solving" that situation wasn't her place to begin with. 2. Vivienne and Adam. Adam doesn't love Vivienne. I hate that the game implies that at the end, and the line "How could you love someone and still let them go" makes me uncomfortable and upset. Vivienne loves Adam, and she has to let him go because she loves him. Adam doesn't love Vivienne. If he did love Vivienne, then these intense levels of marital struggle wouldn't be insurmountable. Though Vivienne's reactions to Adam we know that Adam is an emotionally abusive husband, because Vivienne is in a "I can fix him" sort of state. She's been convinced that she is the problem, and she knows the solution. Adam even considers cheating on his wife because that's how miserable he is. 2 ( Continued). Something I did appreciate about this section is the complex emotion of being the marraige-fix-it baby and cope with the fact that despite being the innocent party, Kay is technically the reason why her parents are miserable. It's an incredibly complex emotion and difficult to understand, but that's what therapy is for, and it's clear this family is in desperate need of it. 3. Jack. I don't like that Kay is punished for caring. While Kay might not be equipped to help Jack herself, she is right in the sense that Jack isolating himself is not going to improve his situation. Beccause it's not just Jack breaking up with Kay--that's not the isolation I'm talking about--but the fact that he's physically isolating from everyone. But I suppose that's what we see at the ending is Jack in his own sea of solitude. 3. (Continue) I was frustrated at the "I learned to listen!" motif, because it's just not that simple. Healing isn't linear, and Kay needing to learn a lesson implies that she's a part of a problem. Again, the way she and Sonny interact isn't realistic, and it's not Kay's job to handle Sonny's problems. She can be there for Sonny, but she's the sibling, not the parent, It's unfair to put Sonny's misery on her shoulders. The same way this sort of punishing behavior towards trying to help Jack makes me incredibly uncomfortable. 4. Kay. The problem with Kay is clearly that she helps everyone else before she helps herself. She is convinced that if everyone else is happy, that then will make her happy as well. Her second issue is that she feels ignored. That she's alone, and that nobody loves her. I'm not sure how I feel about her monsters trying to help her in the end, because it conflicts with what we saw about the other monsters. I suppose my biggest complaint is that Kay needs to learn a lesson. Kay needs therapy.
