_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Shadow Tactics, ATOM RPG, XCOM, then you will probably love this game. It will make you think strategically and will make you plan ahead for your encounters (otherwise you will most likely lose). The missions at the beginning give you a good sense of the game but later as you unlock more characters you see that there is more complexity to it.I was never really such a big history fan but i got into the story and it does remind you about the harsh times people had to go though. Dialogue is never boring to me, almost always explains why exactly you are there or tells you something worthy of note. If you are used to tons of dialogue (like in Dragon Age for example) then this part will probably not suite your fancy. There are of course some bugs but nothing game breaking (at least i haven't found anything that bad). Fights are usually pretty quick but can also be very painful for your team if you don't position well. I just have to say one more thing, the character you first get to play as is a total champ. I literally passed missions using only this guy(mostly because he has a silent ranged 1-hit ability). The other characters are OK too but some of them are very very situational. The thing i would kind of criticize is the looting...to much stuff not enough space in your backpack but that's just a minor gripe. Certainly worth a buy.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved it. Initially you will miss the mechanics of Desperados/Shadow Tactics, but once you get the hang of it the gameplay is excellent here as well (it's really just about it being different, rather than worse). The story is really well made, I liked the fact that you can improve your weapons and your camp, I also really enjoyed the missions although I have to admit the previously mentioned games require more variety in your approach to killing the enemies (I ended up choosing 2 characters that could handel all missions, I would bring a third along just to switch it up a bit). With that said, it has great things that increase the difficulty such as guard dogs and the high difficulty level. Gun battles are actually a lot of fun and it becomes an RTS when you have to quickly react to surround the enemy, move your men behind cover or away from grenades. I understand why people might have been initially dissapointed because they were comparing it to Desperados/Shadow Tactics but as you get on in the game it really does get better and I think in some ways it's more "realistic" (yes I know it's just a game) than the other 2 games I mentioned. _childDocuments_.review: I really want to give this game a thumbs up (can we get a neutral thumb?) but I just cannot, I enjoy the game but it gets just as equally frustrating after a certain point even on normal difficulty; the game has great voice acting, a compelling narrative, nice graphics, memorable characters, and even fun stealth missions but without saying too much I feel like the game loses something of a grip on what the focus is in later missions and can't decide if it's a Stealth Game, something more in the vein of Commandos, or an Isometric combat game (which it does not do well frankly there are better titles for that kind of combat).You gain a lot of combat oriented skills but its an incredibly tedious time when trying to use them as they will basically all lead to an instant alert status, individual guards looking for you, versus a platoon knowing, versus the base knowing is very poorly distinguished  and lead me to reloading often when playing simply because I'd have a single guard look for me and out of nowhere killing them lead to the entire level going on alertearly game there are places to place guards corpses which you (the player) are expected to remember; it's very rewarding to use these places, these are more or less replaced with bushes but it leads to another gripe in which enemies that are in a caution like state will randomly start walking through these bushes and sometimes they will really wander into a bush that could be at the literal corner of the map leading to an alert status that ends your game mind you this could happen while you're doing an objective nowhere near said corner, the enemy could be on alert for storyline reasons, it destroys the stealth by late game and gives the impression you are supposed to fight more but....Well the combat is very ambush oriented, rather, it will really benefit you to ambush every last Wehrmacht, SS, Polizei, and Axis Power Solider you encounter if you don't want to suffer from injuries or have to risk the dreaded revival task whilst still fighting seeing as the death of even one partisan will lead to a game over. This is actually something that is impossible to criticize on it's own merits because it is logical seeing as you are leading a squad of Partisans and not a Red Army Battalion with regular logistics, fire support, or reinforcements and it's outright enjoyable to execute said ambushes against enemies especially if you take out, say, an entire platoon of enemy soldiershowever this is not Men Of War where you can take direct control and instead can only rely on setups; it is impossible to execute ambushes against unending reinforcements with an utterly tiny window to retreat and end the mission where you will be seen while trying to run to it, it is impossible to run in such a scenario, someone in squad who doesn't have the ability to be hard to hit WILL GET INCAPACITATED and you can't end the mission,  it's like what are you supposed to do in such a situation? it feels like an intense spike in difficulty that defies all the logic that came before such moments and they do appear in this game because of that I can't suggest this game to friends but I will pour endless hours into it and suggest to anyone interested in buying this game to give it a shot for sure but be warned the later levels can become excruciatingly difficult

_childDocuments_.review: Game does not support Windows 7. _childDocuments_.review: First - fly in the ointment.1. Bugs. A lot of them. Only me discovered the following: the hovering of the body thrown on the shoulder in the air; hanging of a body in the air when you put it into cover (however, this does not affect its detectability by enemies); sometimes Fetisov's skill when he shoots a cone from a submachine gun does not work (and I don't even know what it is connected with), though this is his most important ability. The number of bugs is completely unsurprising and completely forgivable given the size of the development team. They will gradually fix the bugs, but the game will remain.2. The number of people on missions. The logic of sending three people to the last, most difficult, tasks is incomprehensible. I was sure that four could be sent on the last assignment, but no! Well, come on, does it religion that won't allow you? Or is three is some special lucky number? I understand that this is explained by the need not to attract attention, but I am not asking a whole squad. At least four! Moreover, on some assignments we have four people - but not on the last! No, of course, in fact, the tasks are quite comfortable with three, but still ... In general, here I rather grumble and the voice of a swag lover speaks in me)3. Level-up. Even Zorin himself cannot be leveled up to the end - not to say about other characters. And this despite the fact that almost all killings I committed secretly (the game generally directly pushes on a secret path, but this is its plus, which I will talk about later). And I also don't quite understand why the developers decided that. Is it for partisans don't turn into uber killing machines? They will not, even with full skills. In general, this is also more my grumbling than a sensible remark.Now is ointment, because, as comrade Isaev teaches us, it is the last words that remembered.1. I never imagined that I would play my favorite Commandos in a genetically familiar environment. For this alone, the game can already put an unconditional A.2. The characters of the heroes. They are really different, so the heroes differ not only in their abilities. The authors somehow managed to create real, living characters that you empathize with with a few lines of biography and voice acting, and together with Fetisov you shout "Eat the lead!" and together with Morozov you whistle falsely "Buy bagels, hot bagels") The commissar is absolutely wonderful, a man of iron will and iron hand. "I myself will not give up and I will not allow others" - that is how it should be.3. Much has been written about this already, but it is a true reflection of reality. The Soviet people are not represented as bloodthirsty madmen who kill for the sake of murder, and at the same time are at war only because there is a "zagradotryad" (c) behind them. Moreover, for an attentive player, the game provides an opportunity to feel those conditions. If you have no food, what will you do? It is not good to take food away from local residents, who were already robbed by the Germans, but you are taking away, in essence, not in order to eat and be in comfort, but in order to continue the struggle. The commissar blew up the train and thus caused a punitive operation against local residents. Yes, he did it on purpose. But had he rather to sit in the headquarters and do nothing? It isn't him who started this war, it isn't him who harm civilians.4. Excellent display of battle. First of all, guerrillas shouldn't get involved in combat at all. If the battle has begun, then the partisan was mistaken. Combat is the task of the regular units. The partisan's tasks is sabotage and stealthy murders; he will lose in a direct battle. Therefore, the game is pushing with all its might to covert passage, and rightly so. Skirmishes are well displayed. Leaned out - fired, didn't really aim - hid. Repeat until you hit or be hitted. One, or, if you are STRONGLY lucky, two hits on you - and you're gone.Me, like all people, rarely go through the game to the end, and do it only when the game is something special. So this is the very case. For fans of Commandos - a must-have, for the rest of the players - they may also like it and be introduced into the world of tactical games.

_childDocuments_.review: Me vs. Russian games! Round ! Heaven or Hell!  Don't get me wrong, though. I kinda miss , when Russians finally started to make games in a proper way. , , , ... Those games were freakin' bad for your mental health. You tried to beat ? You were a different person ever since. And if you actually managed to do that, there's a big chance that at this point you already dyed your hair green and went out hunting bats. And yet, I was always curious about them. Russian games, I mean, not bats. Just because, thanks to being late to the party and not knowing the “rules”, Russian developers were often able to offer something different, something that you won't see anywhere else. From mind-blowing story in  to open world  in . I mean, seriously. An open world... ... back in ...  Mind blown. There was always something. And even though actually playing those games felt terrible (to say the least)... like I said, I was always curious. Me and those games are like  and his . I always want more, and yet, every time it's like “”. Every... single... time. But OK, the past is the past. Maybe,  the times changed and it's finally a time for us to get something seriously good from Mother Russia? Spoiler alert – no, it isn't.Let's start with the good stuff, though. First of all – I seriously like the way this game looks. I mean, it does look like a cheap indie game and optimization is kind of horrible (I've experience some serious  drops on the machine that can easily run the third  on max settings), but still, there's something about it that gives you an authentic feeling. Playing this game is like having fun with those plastic miniatures from . You know, that certain manufacturer of scale models and historical miniatures. Some sort of Russian . ? It does look like one of those great historical dioramas. Talking about historical part, though. That's the tricky part here. See, this game? It's far from being historically accurate. The funniest thing about it is the fact that it feels  like Soviet schoolbook. That's  how Soviet kids used to learn their history. Every single character here is superhero, saint and a poet. All at the same exact time. Fighting in the name of ,  and other butch... I mean, God (wait, mentioning God was against the law in Soviet Russia, my mistake). Even the criminals here are saints. Because those are  criminals. And, as we all know, those  dudes were without sin or fear. . Like I said, though, that's the tricky part about this game. And you know what? I actually liked all that. And since the game claims to be a fiction from its very first screen... Like I said, I kinda enjoyed that “very Soviet” approach.Finally, like many other Russian games out there, this one comes with some really nice ideas. Technically, there's nothing groundbreaking here. Don't expect this game to show you anything you haven't seen before. And yet,  (not to be confused with , creators of  trilogy) created a pretty interesting blend. What we have here is a mix between  ( series spin-off) and  with some base building elements. Sounds great, right? I mean, seriously. Controlling a group of Soviet partisans during the , getting the new members on the way, building the base, playing through non-linear missions full of stealth and action? It's gotta be great, right? Well, unfortunately, it's time for me to put my  face on and say “”. Because this game? It's anything  great. First of all – it's terribly,  made. “Fog of war” mechanics is so screwed up that very often you'll die just because enemies will appear from nowhere (the game will assume that enemies are still covered by fog of war, while it totally won't look like it to you). Stealth is mess and lacks the most basic indicators. You played ? ? Yeah, well, this game is nothing like those. Ages old  was more advanced than this bull. Heck, even the very first  was more advanced than this. You want an example? Here's an example: in this game you can whistle to get enemies' attention. But there's no way to tell who'll hear you. Like... seriously, ?  And it's not only that.  is also one of those games, where half of the time you'll get “game over” screen just for being seen or heard by the enemy. One mission even comes with a timer. Because everybody likes having stealth, instant deaths  timer at the same exact time, right? Playing this game is like driving the Russian car. Long story short – you won't want that.Naturally, quite a lot of bugs is included too. Because it looks like in Russia, you can't have even that. Even though you will have some tactical freedom during the missions, there are only  of them, the maps are very small, level design is really boring and uninspired, etc, etc, etc. No optional missions available, of course, and even the base building turned out to be a huge disappointment. Long story short – you just send your troops to get some loot (alternatively, you can collect it during the missions by yourself) and then you build some structures, in which you'll be able to make food (hunger is a thing here, but most of the time you won't even think about it) or upgrade weapons. _childDocuments_.review: I was really craving a game like this for a very long time and it has definitelly scratched that itch. It really reminded mo a lot of the old Commandos games. I've been ingame for 32 hours, but I would say it took me about ~28 to complete the story. If you can afford is, the game is totally worth the buy, I really enjoyed it, but that said I would like to go into details about some (not all) of the games mechanics and give my feedback about what I enjoyed and disliked. Please feel free to comment with anything and especially with updates if something has been resolved. Sooo this is my first proper review on steam, and I didnt know there was a word limit. I was actually 5650 words over the limit in my original review which you can find here and nelow is a very, very reduced version of the original.This current system is great if you can pick 3-4 favorites that you will use through out the game. But if you would like to keep things interesting by changing up your squad composition each mission it is not really worth it because of level differences between all your partisans.It would be much better if all XP gained would be added to all your partisans equally. That way they would all be the same level and it would not feel like putting your self in a disadvantage just for trying to enjoy the game by playing all the possible characters. If not as a update to the default way this game plays, it would be nice to see it added at least as a playthrough modifier that you could turn on at the start of a new playthrough and could not disable it later on.For most missions you get to pick who gets to come, but there are few where the game forces 1 or even all three (very rare). I would change this up for all the later missions where the player can only pick 1 partisans so that they can always pick two at least. If we fail to pick a combination that works, we can always restart the mission, that should be up to us. Maybe the game could just say "you should probably bring X and Z for this mission", but leave the choice to the player, because taking this choice away from the player when he had it previously is just no fun.A lot of times I was thinking how cool it would be if I could bring all my Partisans to a mission, especially past the first half of the game when you already have quite a large group. I understand that with how leveling works in the game now it would not be really balanced, because you would soon have a small army of really strong (high level) partisans. Just as with my suggestion for the different leveling system, I think being able to bring as many partisans as we have would make for another really cool playtrhough modifier which we could only enable at the start of a playthrough and not disable it later on. The way I would go about balancing it would be to lower all XP gains...I played on normal difficulty, but would have really loved to played on hard. The only reason I did not pick hard was because in this  game on hard there is no saving the game! I would add the "no saving" as a playthrough modifier that can only be enabled at the start of playthrough and not disabled later on. This way players who actually have the time can still play like that, and the players who do not have the time can also experience the hard difficulty mode.Out of the 15 missions the game has, I really enjoyed 13 of them, the other two, not so much and they both shared one same mission objective - defend against waves of enemies. I was playing on normal difficulty and these two game segments were impossible to overcome using the same tactics I was using everywhere else. The only way I was able to beat this was to restart the mission, bring all the explosives I had stashed, and abuse the system in the game where you know roughly where the next wave will come and I would just put a mine there or throw a grenade there just as the enemies were spawning. This was the least fun I had in the whole game because I knew I am exploiting the system and was just save scumming to make sure my mines are in the right place.... I would change these two missions so there is only maximum of three waves.I did experience some bugs. One was annoying but I managed to work around it. Another was game breaking but restarting the game fixed it. Another was a character skill did not work after unlocking it so I hope that gets fixed soon because I had to reload a previous save and pick another skill.------------If I had a chance to erase my memory of this game and play it again I totally would do that! Even in its current state. But because I can not do that I will be hoping that the devs add one of the modifiers I was suggesting in the future because I would definitelly love to try all of those (hard difficulty with saving / take all partisans to mission / all partisans gaining xp) and if note at least I hope there will be another game like this or a DLC :)

_childDocuments_.review: What a lot of fun!  Several nights I was up till 3am playing this.  Some important safety tips:- The enemy runs from grenades. _childDocuments_.review: I love this game! Yes, it has bugs, and yes, there's some minor things that could've been done better. However, there's lots of hidden tactics in this sweet little game, you just need to play it longer than 10 hours. It's one of the best games I've played in recent years.I read reviews of people complaining about the lack of depth, and general problems with stealth. I did most of my missions in stealth, that's how I prefer to play, and thought it wonderfully enjoyable and tactically challenging. I'd take my time, save occasionally, and normally spend an average of 2-3 hours in a mission. I'd try different Partisans, my favorite combo being the female medic, Valya, and Morozov, the knife-wielding thief. He'd whistle and then Valya would quickly and silently chloroform the soldier when he came to investigate, and since Commander Zorin was always along he could chuck the knife if I needed some distance, and Belozarova with her trusty speed and knife-fighting.I challenged myself to not be found, and not use grenades or guns, but instead, knives, mines, traps, and silence. On occasion you had to use your guns according to the mission parameters, so I always made sure my insurgents had guns and ammo. I've over 60 hours of game play trying various Partisans and different ways to go about tackling the missions.For the visuals, I think they're fantastic, colorful and yet have that touch of war to it, so it's not too drab and strikes a healthy balance with its color pallet. As for the characters and the story, I think it gives a solid but basic outline, if not one-dimensional, and derivative, at times. There's a strong sense of propaganda in the game that fits well with the era. It's a video game first, and many of us know that not all Partisans were like this group, some were the bad guys, too, and that the Soviet Union wasn't all peaches and cream, to put it mildly. Moreover, it's refreshing to me, to say the least, to play a game where it isn't Americans winning the war single-handedly, or another D-Day battle, or the Western Allies taking all the spotlight with their propaganda. And on top of that, to actually have it spoken in Russian (instead of being another game exclusively voice-acted in American English) granted me another level of immersion and respect for the game.Lastly, I always prefer a game where I can play both sides, it's enjoyable to play as the Axis, as well. I wish they had this in the game, but I understand why they don't. And it's, again, unfortunate that certain WWII games (Partisans '41, too) aren't allowed to stop censoring historical symbols because of the laws of the country that the game is made or will be potentially purchased in, or a personal, or group, desire to censor historical symbols they find offensive, while at the same moment being hypocritically supportive of other symbols that might be offensive to others. The censorship of historical symbols is an impotent, and insidious, form of education.In any case, I'd highly suggest this game, on sale or at its normal price, but to be on the safe side, wait for a sale, there's plenty of reviewers that'll disagree with my personal assessment of the game. An easy thumbs up for a fun and challenging game.

_childDocuments_.review: Really good game! This game blends the strategic gameplay style of Commandos with a small shot of real time strategy combat. It reminds me a little of the old school game: Soldiers at War. The difficulty is pretty forgiving when you are stealthing and the combat in the beginning is pretty easy. The difficulty scales fairly dramatically for the final levels, especially in the last mission where no mistakes can be made. You are given a small team of Soviet partisans during Nazi occupation. The atmosphere is great and there is enough grit and grim to make you feel at war. Sound is outstanding, the visuals remind me of an oil painting, and the story is fairly linear (I think its a good thing). Each team member has a fairly unique skillset and they gain experince and new abilities as you fight your campaign. There is some base management, though I believe it really does not add anything to the game . You could beat this game in roughly 20 hours, maybe faster if you are more about the gunplay than stealth. Only downside is some may feel the story is too bare bones. This isn't bad and does allow you a different play through for next. Overall, this is a great game. I recommend this to anyone who is a fan of Commandos and Desperados.

Even if concealed or far away. 2. Save scumming. Could not play without frequent saving and loading. Sadly, this game is very unforgiving.3. Voice acting was not great. _childDocuments_.review: A great game overall. To make it short, I really enjoyed playing it, and it is a refreshing change from the typical WW2 settings. You play as the local resistance on the Eastern Front, not the typical US/British soldier, paratrooper, marine etc.PROs:+ Challenging; you need patience and you have to use your environment and character abilities to advance+ Nice story; underdogs against the strong enemy, and the addition of traitors or collaborators makes it more realistic+ Easy micro management; there is a lot, yet never overwhelming.+ Great voice overs and text; In-game characters speak Russian, German (and English), both in audio and speech bubbles+ Each character has different special abilities; Choosing who will join is important+ Nice music and ambient soundCONs:- Some weird glitches; they happen during combat and also during the camp menu/scene- Few crashes when loading/leaving mission; not sure if unique to my Laptop and settings, but I thought I mention it.- Short story, and it ends with after final mission; there is no open end to continueAnd lastly some "neutral" points I like to make:- Ammunition and guns are very rare; I know it makes the game more challenging, but I find it weird that even the enemy soldiers who visibly carry weapons somehow drop little or no ammo and rarely weapons. Weirdly enough, many of them carry random crafting material.- There are some "game logic" situations which I understand are always present in games, but the fact that no enemy ever questions why their friend who was on guard duty is suddenly gone...is weird.- There are some in-game characters I rarely used, especially near the end. The reason is that some of them are only useful when in direct combat, but during stealth missions (or when low on ammo), only the stealth-based characters are useful.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Commandos, except you play as the good guys this time.+ You can go loud, and it works. RTS-style combat feels good enough for a stealth game that it feels like an actual option. And ambush tactics actually work. - The interface is perhaps worst-in-genre, and this is a genre with pretty bad interfaces. Still, it's good enough despite some frustration and bugs.- The meta-game is cool in concept but terrible in execution: Build a base, run missions, upgrade stuff. But a few issues ruin this entirely: 1.) There are only 2-3 weapons per category, and only 2-3 possible upgrades per weapon. Pretty quickly you end up with top-tier gear and nothing to spend your supplies on. 2.) The base activities are strangely balanced. At the beginning, you can assign a partisan to gather 20 food. All the later food activities have a *worse* return, the next one being 11 food per partisan. This might have posed an interesting tension if food were at all scarce. 3.) Consumables are too plentiful. My stockpiles are nearly limitless, and every map includes enough extras for you to get by even without bringing any.+ Gameplay itself is basically what you'd expect from the genre. There are zero innovations to the stealth side, but that generally doesn't stop these games from being satisfying for a while.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been looking forward to giving Partisans a try ever since finishing Shadow Tactics, which I found fantastic. Sadly, Partisans is only a pale shadow of that tactical masterpiece. I thought a similarly styled game set in Soviet WW2 would be fantastic, but unfortunately it just hasn't grabbed me and is overall a letdown. While Shadow Tactics is a clean, highly polished, smooth experience, Partisans is workable, but overall clunky and at times challenging to manage. Like many games set in WW2, the colours used are a drab mix of dirty browns, and dusty greens. While not unexpected, it is somewhat disappointing that this hasn't been taken into consideration when designing the game. Brush and undergrowth meant to hide your team is not always apparent, and occasionally you may think you are hidden but one character is not quite inside the bushes.Speaking of not quite hidden, the stealth in this game could use a lot of work. Most notably, in an early mission I set up an ambush with two characters taking cover behind a fallen tree on one side of the road, and a third character hidden in the tall grass on the opposite side. Using the tactical mode, I ordered my two men taking cover to open fire, and instructed the third to remain hidden. I planned to wait until the enemy patrol was fully engaged then strike at their exposed flank. Not exactly tactical brilliance, but a nice first effort right? Wrong.As soon as I opened fire, one member of the enemy patrol immediately turned and began firing at my man hiding in the brush. With no cover he very quickly died. No worries, I must have made a mistake and he wasn't properly hidden or I accidentally had him attacking. I quick loaded and tried again. The same thing happened. I tried several more times, convinced there must be something amiss but no, once battle had begun all enemies seemed to immediately know exactly where all my characters were. So much for strategic options.While Shadow Tactics featured a cast of colourful (literally) characters with clearly defines roles and interesting unique abilities, Partisans has, well, drab brown man with rifle, drab brown man with pistol, and drab grey boy with shotgun. Characters each have an inventory and can equip different items. There are a variety of guns that come in different qualities, and you will need to make sure you have appropriate ammo for each of them. Although each character has their own set of perks they can gain as they level up, many of these are boring, generic, and overlap multiple characters. They are also rather vague. One chain of upgrades is "Improve rifle accuracy > improve rifle accuracy a lot > improve rifle accuracy a huge amount!" Another is "Increase effectiveness of cover." Yawn.Unlike Shadow Tactics, the unique abilities each character unlock only play a minor part of getting through each level. In fact, these unique abilities are entirely optional. If you don't want to invest any perk points into them, you don't have to, and then your band of green and brown soldiers will be indistinguishable from one another.In addition to your missions, Partisans introduces a base for you to micromanage. You'll get to send your units out on missions where RNG will determine whether you return victorious with loot or in failure with injuries. You will need to make sure you are also sending your people out to scavenge food, or else you will starve and moral will drop. That's right, you have a moral level to manage as well. You can make a unit spend a day inspiring the others to improve moral, which comes with some general bonuses. If you steal from innocents or fail in missions, your moral will drop.  None of these camp mechanics really add anything to the game, and for the most part are just a frustratingly tedious way of passing time between actual missions.Now, I suspect the game gets a bit better as you get further into it, but the first couple hours are just so average that I felt no desire to continue playing. I'll compare this game once more to Shadow Tactics in mentioning that each time I sat down to play it I ended up playing for far longer than I'd intended to. I may come back to Partisans at some point to give it another shot, but it's much more likely I'll just wait for the new Shadow Tactics game on its way.
_childDocuments_.name: Partisans 1941

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic concept that is frequently stepped on by janky and non-intuitive controls. On the tin, this very nearly delivers what you would want in a game like this: interesting character mechanics, thoughtful voice acting, and solid variety of missions in the progression. However, even with the whole slow-time focus mechanic, it's really agony trying to control your partisans in any situation requiring precise maneuvering. Some objects have to be clicked directly, while others you have to frantically click around to find the hitbox of a weird and imprecise feeling pop-out menu. Extremely inconsistent, which makes it annoying to master.On the battle maps, the inflexibility of the camera makes it challenging to comfortably maneuver. You have the benefit of full 360 degree rotation, but no tilt control hardly any zoom. It's such a small margin of zoom that it nearly makes it pointless to include. But I feel like the main issue is that there is no intelligent cutaway system (a la Sims), and any object that disrupts the camera/cursor will likewise block your clicked selection. Especially frustrating when trying to make small, tactical adjustments when things start getting bonkers.This general jank continues through the characters, levels, as well as in the over-world camp system. I loved the idea of getting stuff during missions that would carry over to camp supply, and those supplies can be buttressed by doing asynchronous, over-world missions. But again, the whole thing is diminished by the inconvenient means of exchanging gear between characters (handled chiefly through another bizarre pop out menu when click and drag is not available). On the first several missions, I missed the opportunity to send various squadmembers on the async missions, thinking I had selected them for tasks, but when viewing another task for a different partisan, it deselected the original (unless "applied" via a second button click).The inventory menu system is pretty wacky as well, and besides the aforementioned item exchange difficulty, good decisions were made into weird results. For instance, they had the good sense to put 'store all' and 'auto sort' buttons on the party members. Makes it easy to  dump stuff post mission, since clicking things is a nightmare here. But even with the forethought of the clickable categories, the filtering system doesn't behave like you'd expect; items get grouped separately from other like items. Ammunition of the same type ends up on different rows. There are reasons for some of it (eg. item quality for guns), but for most others it doesn't feel intuitive at all.I really wanted to focus this review on specific, control-based aspects, but I also feel like because of the above concerns, it makes some gameplay quality fumbles feel less excusable. At the end of the day, it's a weak stealth mechanic. Most patrols on static, pre-defined routes. Same old stealth rpg tropes of an arrow sticking out of a guy's face, but as long as your timer elapses: "huh, must've been the wind" before going back to the same spot.This part specifically deals with the English version of the game: lack of a large enough pool of contextual dialogue, and just generally lazy writing that diminishes the seriousness of the occupation motif. I'm sure there is a lot lost in translation here, some breakdown between Daedalic, Alter, and the subbed version we ended up with. Because the ambient npc dialogue, constant "my eyes hurt from crying" from every NPC, and even the sort of superficial overworld campfire conversations, all sort of felt like big Mass Effect: Andromeda, "my face is tired" level of banality.I took this many characters of your bandwidth here because I ultimately like the game. It's entertaining, but immensely frustrating because of these oversights and limitations. In some good ways, it feels like playing a tiny Company of Heroes on the Foxhole engine. In nearly every bad way, it feels like playing a tiny Company of Heroes on the Foxhole engine.

_childDocuments_.review: War is always a terrible thing. However, the fight between the German Reich and the Soviet Union in World War II was one of the most brutal conflicts imaginable. Both sides fought with extreme brutality and without mercy. This was not a war, this was a fight of annihilation. And it is precisely in this scenario that the real-time tactical game Partisans 1941 is set.Partisans 1941 consists on the one hand primarily of a real-time tactics part, in which you move your partisans around the landscape with the click of a mouse and in real time, but also of the turn-based administration of the partisan camp in the forest, in which you distribute your meager resources and assign tasks to your partisans.The plot is presented exclusively from a Russian perspective. The main character is a young Russian with peasant roots, who made a career in the Red Army during the Russo-Finnish Winter War and now serves as a captain. He is captured immediately after the German invasion of Russia in the summer of 1941 and, after attempting to escape, is to be shot informally. Only a jammed gun saved his life and allowed him to flee into the woods, pursued by the Germans as well as by local collaborators.At first sight the realtime tactics part is a Commandos clone, which is not that bad, because Commandos (Pyro Studios, 1998) was an excellent game. However, if you play Partisans 1941 a little bit, you'll soon see clear differences. For example, you don't play elite soldiers, who carry out spectacular missions at war-crucial points, but you play dirty, half-starved partisans without ammunition, who hide in the forest from the German occupation forces. Slowly the surroundings are scouted out, more comrades-in-arms and weapons are found, the own camp is expanded and finally more and more important (and better defended) targets of the Germans and their allies are attacked. One part of the game consists of turn-based management of the partisan camp, the other part consists of key missions, which are played in (pausable) real time - similar to Commandos.Before a mission, you assemble your unit from the available people and assign equipment to them. Inventory management is much more detailed than with Commandos. Weapons, ammunition... all this can be taken out of the camp and assigned to individual partisans before a mission starts, whereby different members of the partisan group have different abilities. Of course you can also give your grandmother a heavy machine gun, but it doesn't make sense.During the missions you control a group of three men in real time, but unlike Commandos they automatically open fire on the enemy. Gone are the days when your own elite soldier is lying defenseless on the ground and gets beaten to death by German recruits, just because you as a panicked player don't click on the right icon fast enough. Also, units start sneaking automatically when enemy units are detected and have not seen you yet. This makes the game much easier to play and is also quite realistic. Which soldier not tired of life would continue openly when he sees an enemy patrol marching directly towards him?During the missions, you repeatedly encounter civilians talking to the partisans. Apart from the collaborators, who have been equipped with old weapons by the Germans and in return support them in the suppression of the population (and often fill their own pockets), the civilian population supports the partisans with information, material and sometimes also with active assistance, but in any case does not betray them to the German invaders. It is possible to eavesdrop on opponents and civilians during their (self-) conversations. Usually only a few sentences, but often it is not recurring comments, but conversations adapted to the situation. Really well done. Buildings can be entered, you will find needed resources like food, ammunition or spare parts. Stealing from the population is not recommended because it lowers the morale of your troops. But it's not too big a problem, most things belong to the Germans anyway.During the missions you can find hotspots that can be manipulated. So sometimes small "accidents" can be caused without using up ammunition and thus enemy units can be decimated... Oops, the handbrake was not on. Or oh, no idea who lowered the lift so suddenly.When a battle ensues, you will hopefully have your people behind good cover and you will also have made sure that enemy units are caught in crossfire or in open field. Planning the firefights is extremely important, otherwise your comrades will die faster than flies when fighting against well-trained and armed enemy soldiers. The own units have different special abilities, which make the battles much easier - if you use them correctly. My favorite is the ability of Sanek, a 14-year-old boy who has joined the partisans. He can put away his shotgun, walk around with a stupid whistle, and walk among enemy units like a villager, completely unnoticed. Most of the time anyway, in some places he does stand out.It is possible to put his soldiers into a defensive mode so that they don't automatically open fire when an enemy comes into range. This is very useful for executing ambushes effectively and attacking enemies only when they are in an unfavorable position for them, i.e. somewhere without cover. The game runs in real time, but - except in the highest difficulty level - can be paused (or slowed down considerably) at any time by pressing a key. Own soldiers usually do not die immediately. If they are hit and have no life energy left, they faint and can only be resuscitated by one of their comrades. A game over only occurs if all three fighters become unconscious during a mission. Killed enemies can be plundered, sometimes they have useful things (ammunition, bandages, weapons) with them. As in Commandos, you can also pick up corpses and let them disappear somewhere to avoid attracting the attention of patrolling enemy units. When enemies see dead comrades, they sound the alarm and start to scan the surroundings briefly (for a few seconds...)... before falling back into their usual routine, even if after a while a dozen of your comrades are lying dead in the area.You can zoom, rotate or scroll the visible image section at any time to either get a better overview of what is going on or to position your troops precisely. Enemy (and neutral) units disappear in the fog of war if there is no direct visual contact. Pressing the M key opens a tactical map where you can view the entire level. A click on an enemy unit and you can see its cone of sight. Not quite realistic, but very helpful for positioning your own troops well or sneaking past enemy units.Luring enemy troops into ambushes, laying mines, blowing up infrastructure, distributing propaganda leaflets, cutting telephone lines, intercepting supply convoys, poisoning enemy supplies, eliminating targets... the field of activity of partisans is quite extensive. However, one must not starve to death, must not face the German troops in direct combat, must be content with a very primitive field hospital for his wounded, always has too few soldiers, weapons and ammunition, hardly any information about the rest of the war, no home leave... it is not easy to be a partisan.Partisans 1941 does a good job of offering an entertaining, challenging game on the one hand and telling a little bit about the Russian partisan war in World War II on the other hand. All in all a clear recommendation for fans of historical real-time tactical games.

_childDocuments_.review: The game scratches an itch, in a way that I've been giving the game a lot of tries in hope the good outweights the bad. The basics, though pretty simple, are a lot of fun. You gain characters over time, spend skill points to make them better in certain areas, gather resources (guns, ammo, explosives, food and.. resources) and kill nazis through stealth or tactical shootouts. In between missions you can gather more resources, gain XP or create equipment, kinda like the Robinson Crusoe boardgame (where you assign character tokens to tasks).  The story brings enough variety in terms of missions and they allow for multiple plans of attack. Executing a flawless ambush through tactical excellence is very rewarding, as well as going through a mission without ever being spotted. With the relatively low price of the game these things alone would make it a good deal and recommendable...BUT.. I can't recommend it for the massive unpolished state the game is in. It's not uncommon having to reload a quick save 20 or 30 times per mission due to a fault of the game. Here's a list of things (in random order) that really ruin the mood and break the flow of the game: You want to go through that door? No you can not. O wait you're walking away? Here I'm open for you now :). HAH FOOLED YOU, I'M CLOSED AGAIN. Now you're dead.... Doors and the playable characters don't get along. Probably nazi collaborators. Enemies can see and hear through (multiple sets of) walls and doors. Crouched characters behind cover will still be seen by enemies through 3 sets of windows (even if they just walk by). Enemies can go from chill to instant aimbot blitzkrieg in the blink of an eye. You want to do a double back stab takedown with two characters? Nope, there's 0.5 second between stab 1 and 2 so BLITZKRIEG ENGAGED. Hell, sometimes a nazi with a knife in his throat will go blitzkrieg, turn around and instantly kill his assaulant. The instant alertness becomes even more irritating when it happens in combination with the earlier mentioned x-ray..When cutting a throat, there will always be a few seconds where the character is unresponsive and the body of the victim is dropped to the floor. This prevents quick takedowns and relocating of the body.. and regularly is a reason for being spotted. If only the characters were trained in keeping hold of their victims.... (or at least through the use of a skill point). Cover only allows for 2 or 4 sides to be used depending on how big the cover is. If an enemy is diagonally placed relatively to your cover, you will have no cover at all from any of the sides. .Your characters will get stuck behind the smallest of obstacles and sometimes even take a detour instead of a straight line. This can result in moving into enemy vision (instead of the saver straight line) where they will blitzkrieg your ass in a heartbeat.. Left mouse button triggers movement, (theoretically) opens door, interacts with hiding places, takes cover, loots supplies, picks up enemies, loots enemies, picks up thrown weapons, interacts with gun emplacements, interacts with objectives, interacts with light/alarm switches and attacks enemies. This goes wrong more than once.. and always at the wrong time. I would like to see key + mouse click combinations to seperate these actions.. While doing a mission full stealth, it doesn't help if your characters randomly decides to attack an enemy rambo style. There's also one character that can go incognito and walk around. But if you've clicked too close to an item (wall or crate), he will suddenly take cover and open fire. If you've clicked on a bush with a body in it, he will grab his big ass shotgun and of course trigger the enemy to go instant blitzkrieg. . You can select your characters through keys 1 - 9 as you would expect.. BUT, characters are placed in order that the game wants. This would be fine, if not for the fact that each mission you can have other characters and they are always placed on the first few keys. You will have to remember what character is placed on which number by the system each time you start a new mission. Sometimes these placements are even changed after loading a quick save. It would've been better to allow users to assign their characters to certain keys, or simply have a dedicated key per character (which should be possible as long as there are max 10).. You found great cover and flanking positions? Too bad. These nazis got nothing to lose. They will swarm your position without taking cover themselves, or even throw a grenade at their own feet if they can take you down with them.. You can use foliage for cover. But with the angle of the camera it's not always clear what's considered hideable foliage or foliage simply functioning as a wall. If you do find foliage where you can hide, it's not always clear where it ends. The character is marked as hidden or not through a barely noticable striped overlay.. so maybe it would help if the bushes themselves could have some sort of highlight on mouse over or when a character is in it.

_childDocuments_.review: Good story, WWII historical game from the perspective of Soviet soldiers and citizen-soldiers fighting a guerilla war on their German-occupied home turf.  Interesting cast of characters, including a 14 year old boy armed with a slingshot, a hunting knife, and a grudge against the Nazis.  On most missions you can choose to go in guns blazing and grenades flying, but usually I preferred the stealth approach.I found the gameplay to be kind of like XCom, but it real time.  There is a tactical feature that lets you just about pause the game (time still advances, but really slow) so you can issue your keyboard/mouse commands without getting blown to pieces while you're fumbling with the controls.Graphics are as good as they need to be.  View is from above at an angle, but you can control the camera to spin any direction you want and there's an amount of zoom in-out to be used too.  Controls seemed a little wonky at first, but I got used to them.  Voice acting is there, it's all in German and Russian, but you get subtitles (mine were in English, I don't remember if there was an option for others).  The game crashed on me one time, but I didn't really get the feeling that it was buggy.  I saved frequently so it wasn't a big loss.Maybe skip this one if you don't like stealth, or lack patience trying to figure out how to progress.  If you have the patience to solve these puzzles and play the stealth game I highly recommend.  It took me just under 35 hours to complete the story on "easy" level (which I found plenty challenging).

_childDocuments_.review: Partisans 1941 is exactly what it looks like - Russian Commandos. You crawl around, knife Nazis, and hide their bodies in the bushes. You have grenades that are medicore and mines that are strong. You have a basic base like in Robin Hood. You gain XP and earn perks. There are 8 partisans and 15 missions of medium size, some during the night. You get to pick partisans for missions. The enemies are dumb and have annoying dogs.What the game adds to the genre is a decent and kinetic shootouts system with covers and scarce ammo. Though stealth goes a long way, occasionally you resort to annihilating enemy squads from carefully concocted ambushes.The game lacks the cinematic quality and grand scale of Commandos 2 or the character and mission variety of Desperados 1-3. Music and graphics are mediocre but do the job. Loading times are fast.Overall, Partisans 1941 is a satisfactory entry to the genre that genre fans will enjoy. I thought Desperados 3 was a notch better; but Partisans 1941 is still worth playing. 7.5/10

I have some small nitpicks here and there, and so far stealth feels pretty repetitive. _childDocuments_.review: What a delightful piece of eurojank.Ok, techincally, russ-jank. But the point remains. It's a flawed little gem in the vein of S.T.A.L.K.E.R or the first Witcher. If that seems like high praise, it is. It's a lot of fun once you start to wrap your head around the lack of polish. Simple inventory commands we think of as standard are hidden in sub-menus, sometimes the HUD is a law unto itself and guards get stuck on alert, partisans get stuck in skills and you'll catch yourself asking "bug or feature" over several unexplained design choices, but despite all of this, I really loved it. I'm getting towards the end of the campaign now and the story isn't complex, but it's engaging and serves to drive some interesting missions, the characters are solid and come with a good range of skills, however there are some that are infinitely more useful than others. "Whistle" for example is borderline game breaking and will let you happily lure guards, one by one, to their deaths all day. The stealth aspects are solid, if somewhat 'cheese-able' as mentioned before. I feel that the game could have used a little more polish in that aspect, for example, A stationed guard who sees you for a second will either ignore you or go straight to combat, there is no jump to the 'search' state  (as triggered by finding a body or an explosion etc.) for a partial detection. A guard will return on his loop to talk to a room full of guys who have all mysteriously vanished and won't notice. However at it's core, despite my nitpicks, it's a solid system and it works very well for the core gameplay. The gameplay loop relies on this solid foundation. Each area of the map is a fun little puzzle to be solved and the variety of skills available give you plenty of room to be creative. Here stealth and combat intertwine. You can choose to pick off the guards one at a time, ghosting them one by one as you misdirect and lure them from their buddies. You can set up a devastating ambush to lure them into a minefield. Take out a few key pieces of their defence and set up  a  characters special ability to clean house. Combat and stealth follow the same DNA, for open combat to be successful it must be planned and prepared. Several reviews point to the combat being a bit ♥♥♥♥, I disagree. While your partisans can't hit the broadside of a barn in the first mission or two, they gain proficiency quickly. Simply opening up into a pitched battle with a german platoon with your 3 guys doesn't work and it if it did, that would make 99% of the game redundant. Funnel that platoon through a chokepoint into your crossfire and drop a grenade on them or trap them where your skills can work. The maps are varied and interesting, sometimes very challenging, sometimes blown wide open by the inclusion of a certain skill in your roster. The graphics are functional and I had no performance issues on a mid range PC. The base building/management is easy enough and just serves as an way to top up resources, heal fighters and upgrade weapons. The resource management doesn't add anything, or take away from the game. I guess what I'm getting at is that to me, it's that pure eurojank vibe, like S.T.A.L.K.E.R you can have a lot of fun with the game, but you'll get out what you put in.  Don't expect a polished perfect game, but a fun little sandbox to kill fascists in.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good entry level squad-based puzzle game where you need to sneak around and take out enemies one by one. What sets is apart from the Commandos series or War Mongrels is the equipment personalization for different characters (most of them have two weapons specializations) and the possibility of creating ambushes to take out some of the enemies with guns blazing. The latter is really refreshing, because you can have a more aggressive playthrough (although the odds of winning unexpected firefights are quite low). While its great because it doesn't punish the player for not following an intended sequence of eliminating enemies, it can make the puzzle solving bit undeveloped. Also, once you unlock a partisan who can whistle to attract enemies, the game became very, very easy. The graphics are charming, the sound is nice, the setting is great but the story is mediocre at best. It is unfortunate because the setting asked for a very serious take on guerilla warfare but somewhere along the way it turned into a very generic set of expectable missions (taking out a bridge, prison break, etc.).It's fun but I think it will appeal mostly to players who never played similar games. They will appreciate the flexible gameplay rather than a very constrained gameplay of Commandos or War Mongrels.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm somewhat hesitating about YES or NO here. If there was a 10-score system, I think I'd give this game a 6.As a big fan of Action Puzzle games, as I call them (Commandos, Desperados, etc.), I was quite excited about Partisans 1941. It seemed like the devs wanted to try a different approach to the genre, but after 100% the game I'm not sure that any of the core changes worked out well.TL;DR. The game is really unpolished with dozens of small issues of all kinds popping up here and there. Also, the game provides no real challenge (I’d say no challenge at all) or incentive to combine the skill of partisans to achieve the mission goals. Instead of several distinguishable characters with distinguishable abilities, we have 8 semi-Jacks of all Trades, only three of which can be taken on a single mission at once. I can still recommend the game, but only if you haven’t played other similar games (especially the modern ones like Shadow Tactics or Desperados III). Otherwise you will most likely find the Partisans 1941 experience subpar.The game is thematically very close to Commandos series — same theme (war vs Nazis), similar objectives (kill leaders, destroy a huge artillery gun, etc.), no complex storyline (just go kill this or destroy this), etc. The game tried to move away from a time-proven formula by introducing new mechanics, but I personally think that none of them worked out great.- Looter shooter system. There are guns of different types and different qualities. Ammo, throwables, mines, medkits — everything is an inventory item now and must be looted instead of being usable skills. Therefore, each character has a limited amount of space. To my mind it added nothing of value to the genre other than a need to sort the inventory mess after sorting another mess while trying to pick items using an awkward and sometimes glitching UI. You can’t actually go permanent gunz blazing, so all that system seems to be applicable only under specific circumstances that are somewhat rare.- Intermission camp. Instead of playing one mission after another, we now have a camp where all partisans sit around the bonfire and attempt Global Map tasks. There are Food and Materials resources which can be gathered during missions by looting dead enemies or various objects and then spending time sorting the inventory mess. Food is spent to feed your party. Materials can be used to construct various buildings that provide access to makeshift consumables, weapon upgrades, healing as well as additional sources of Food income. Again, I’m not sure what value this adds to the game – I’ve completed the campaign on Normal difficulty and I never ever had a situation when I needed any of the buildings except for the Food ones. And I only needed those, because out of eight people you can only take three on the main missions while others are just sitting there eating the food reserves and participating in secondary tasks that grant experience points.- Skill Trees. Instead of a predetermined set of usable skills each character has a predetermined Skill Tree which can not be reset! As you gain experience (there is a certain incentive to kill every enemy on every map) you can move down the Skill Tree to unlock 1-2 usable skills and some passive ones (running speed, body carrying speed, melee / grenades / weapons proficiency, more inventory space, etc). And again, I don’t see any benefits here — passive skills are often duplicated between characters and even usable skills are somewhat similar (AOE damage in a circle or AOE damage in a cone, pacify with a slingshot or pacify with chloroform, etc). So instead of a shorter roster of distinctive specialists with distinctive skills and personalities, we have almost a dozen similar 3D models with different voices.As far as other aspects of the game are concerned, they remained pretty much the same. But, man, this game is EXTREMELY unpolished. Small issues of all kinds are literally everywhere! Review limitations won't allow to mention everything that I encountered, but here are some:Sometimes the partisans won’t complete an action, especially if you order them to place a mine — they simply stand still with the mine outline being visible.The cones of enemy sight are really unprecise at times and they might detect you outside the visual color zone. On top of that, some of the in-game objects seem to be blocking the cones, but the enemies can still see and even walk through them (especially noticeable with truck cabins). By the way, a very useful mechanic of placing a mark on the ground to detect enemies that can see the mark is not available in the game at all.There were multiple UI issues throughout the game: more than dozen of times I wasn’t able to loot dead enemies until I rotated the camera under a very specific angle. Inventory sometimes vanished and I needed to close the inventory window and open it again. Some of the Global Map secondary tasks always showed twice in the completion window although clearly only one was completed. There is a tooltip missing for the amount of Materials you will get from a Global Map task.Several mission-related examples: there is a brief cutscene introducing the prison guy, where he uses a  whistle to lure an enemy into the bushes and then perform a knife kill in the face with the special skill. Well, guess what? You can’t do this sequence in the actual game! Because every such attempt will result in an immediate red exclamation mark and alarm — you can only use a knife in the face skill from behind which is pretty much useless in most cases. At the same mission Zorin explains that blowing up AA Guns is a loud undertaking, so we need to destroy the Comm Center first. This is clearly not the case, because I’ve blown up the guns before going to the Comm Center and nothing happened — nobody sounded an alarm or anything.Or take the AOE skills of any of the four partisans who have them (the sports guy, the tough lady, the grandpa and the one-eyed commissar) — their efficiency is very questionable, because partisans can be easily wounded or killed while using these skills! It does add to the realism of the situation, but this realism takes away any practical uses (in other similar games all AOE targets die at once).Inventory auto-sort function is awkward to say the least. It can’t automatically sort items of different shapes (you have 4 empty spaces in a straight line, but found an item with 4 spaces as a square? Sorry, please sort the inventory manually). It also can’t sort identical items close to each other, which is a real pain in arse at the Intermission camp warehouse.Another thing that I didn’t like personally — the game provides no challenge. As I’ve mentioned a bit earlier, 80% of my playtime was controlling Zorin, the very first playable character available in the game, to eliminate everything and everyone with a knife. There is no incentive to use your characters skills in combination in order to overcome a difficult situation, because there are no difficult situations to begin with (I was playing on Partisan difficulty). Back to Battle DLC introduced those one-time missions and with all modifiers turned on, the maps became quite challenging, but unnecessary annoying because of how enemy reinforcements work.Why do I still recommend the game in the end? Two main reasons:1. There are only a handful of games of this Action Puzzle (ok, ok, Real Time Stealth Tactics) genre available (both from 2000s and the modern ones).2. At the very core, Partisans 1941 is an OK game. It’s highly unpolished and has some questionable mechanics, but the game can be safely played and finished. So if you haven’t tried any of the similar games yet, Alter Games creation could be a decent acquaintance. But if you played and enjoyed titles from Mimimi Games, chances are that you will find Partisans 1941 too different and of subpar quality.

_childDocuments_.review: Partisans 1941 is a mix of the old Commandos games and the Russian-made real time strategy/tactics series Men of War, with a dash of the XCOM style metalayer in there too. As the title suggests, you control a band of Soviet partisans during the Nazi invasion of the USSR in 1941, and the game consists of a series of missions (semi-scripted and hand-crafted, not procedurally generated and random – worth clarifying I think) with the opportunity to manage your partisan hideout between them, and send your guerrillas off on tasks that will resolve off-screen, such as supply raids or ambushes.Proper missions consist of a mix of stealth and combat, often switching from one to the other – you can sneak around to set up the perfect ambush, then Go Loud with grenades and gunfire before returning to sneaking around – as long as your brief firefight didn’t result in any alarms being set off or reinforcements called in. This means you want to target things like German radiomen, or maybe set up traps near alarm systems that enemies might run to activate, while also trying to get it all over and done with as quickly as possible and with as little meaningful return fire as you can manage. Your partisans are capable, but they’re always heavily outnumbered and even on the lowest difficulty (which the devs recommend you pick for a first playthrough) they’re vulnerable to gunfire if not in cover.This all combines to make for a very satisfying gameplay loop – reminiscent of XCOM 2’s ambush phase out of combat, or even the feeling that you get from clearing a room quickly in an action game like Hotline Miami. The stealth itself is robust enough (although it can get a bit fiddly indoors – more on that later) and you have some fun abilities to get you through the few enforced stealth segments in the game. For the most part, missions are generous in letting you raise the alarm and still continue, but a handful of missions are either entirely or partly dependent on a failstate if you alert the enemy. These missions are also the more linear ones – most of the others present you with a location and let you pick how to approach it, but the forced-stealth missions are more reminiscent of the ‘one optimal path from end to end’ design seen in games like Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. This isn’t necessarily a negative.The partisans themselves are also fixed characters, unlike most other similar games where they’d be randomly generated to some extent and based around archetypes or classes. Each character can use every weapon and item but they have their own skill tree that boosts their effectiveness with, say, rifles or shotguns or pistols, as well as some unique abilities for each one. Red Army captain Zorin can throw knives, for instance, and ex-sergeant Fetisov can fire long bursts from SMGs that kill everyone in a cone in front of him. As another example, Sanek the 14-year-old who’s definitely lining up some heavy-duty PTSD for later in life can exploit his youth and saunter around in the open without attracting attention because the Germans just think he’s a kid. This variety is cool and gives each partisan their own particular niche, but since they can make use of every normal weapon and item anyway the game gives you a lot of flexibility in how you approach situations.The characters themselves don’t have particularly deep characterisation or development as the story progresses, but it gives a nice sweep of the different kinds of people who would potentially get involved in a partisan unit – soldiers, aggrieved locals, ex-criminals, and so on. It’s also nice to see the representation of women in the unit, since female partisans were not at all uncommon historically. The story is also fairly straightforward and doesn’t really have a particular arc, but it does a good job of presenting different scenarios for each mission – rescuing a hunter in the woods, ambushing a supply convoy, saving townsfolk from SS deathsquads, staging a prison break, etc.The plot is also pleasingly willing to confront the brutality of the Nazi invasion of the USSR – reprisals by the Germans against civilians are a constant theme, and the threat of torture and murder and casual cruelty from collaborators is always looming. The atmosphere is compelling and convincingly realistic, even though your unit of defined partisans has an unbelievably good success rate – I suppose if the developers wanted to convey the high rate of deaths among WW2 partisans then they’d have had to come up with another couple hundred characters to rotate in and out of your unit, which is a bit of a tall order, I guess. Even so, the portrayal of the Eastern Front is head and shoulders above that of the whitewashing of games like Company of Heroes 2. I also appreciated being able to switch the spoken audio to Russian while keeping the subtitles in English – I don’t speak Russian but I do enjoy that kind of linguistic immersion, and I liked that the Nazis still spoke in German throughout too.The user interface is generally good but could use some tightening up. The way cover positions are calculated and displayed is a bit fiddly, especially indoors (it’s impossible to take cover around open doorways, for instance), and doors themselves are a pain in the backside to deal with at the moment as they’re prone to swinging open and shut repeatedly when you activate them, although I understand the developers are looking to fix that. While the inventory management is mostly fine you’ll definitely get bogged down in swapping the appropriate ammunition between people who need it (and it took me quite some time to be able to distinguish the different types of rifle and pistol ammo based on the icon rather than having to meticulously hover the cursor over them each time). It made me miss the feature in Men of War where looting bodies or containers with a group selected would ‘smartly’ assign ammo to everyone who had the relevant weapons in their inventory. It can also be annoying that view cones – showing where exactly enemies are looking at any time – are the same overlay colour on the ground as markers for using abilities, which can make it tricky to set up ability usage while also keeping an eye on who can see what.The last thing I have to say about Partisans is that when it ended, I really wanted more. The story, as mentioned, doesn’t really have much of a climax, and while I guessed that the final mission was in fact the finale based on its title, it doesn’t feel like an appropriately large event to close a narrative campaign. I held out some hope that it would in fact just be an End Of Act 1 situation, especially as the last shot in the game before credits is of your partisan camp now snow-covered and wintry – I was really hoping for a winter segment to the campaign, particularly with the mentions in-game of ‘fishing before the lake freezes’ and so on. This is both a compliment and a criticism, I guess – it felt like the game was a bit too short, but also I was having so much fun with it that I wanted to keep going. I hope the developers are able to make more of this game, either in the form of DLC or an expansion or sequel.All in all I highly recommend this game to anyone who’s interested in the setting or genre. It’s got a few rough edges but a great core game shines through and I’m impressed with what the developers have accomplished here. Za rodinu, and all that.

As a lot of people have mentioned the English voice actors all have British accents but instead of finding it jarring it gave me some nostalgia for Soviet novels I've read about this time period that were translated by Brits.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a heavily Russian/Former Soviet Union narrative driven. Although the story settings could be of interest to the Westerners, a straightforward good soviet guys/bad Germans looks a bit sassy. Do not take me wrong, my own family has suffered during the WW2 in Russia/Belarus. The game misses so much in terms actually developing deep characters or explaining how and why different characters ended up being  partisans. Everyone had own motive and circumstances leading there. If there would be at least some hint of grey moral/some moral depth to the stories of those who lived under occupation the whole game would be a completely different experience. At the moments it looks like, it sounds like and it is Soviet Pioneer patriotic propaganda. Sadly, over the last 30 years creative media in Russia made a huge U-turn going back to Soviet motives. Still, if you are not after a deep story or character development - it is a nice game to sink in several hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Partisans 1941

_childDocuments_.review: Not my typical genre of game but after watching CohhCarnage play it, I decided to give it a shot. Most games that I play I tend to try a tactical, stealthy route and this game definitely enables you to take that course of action. Eliminating patrols and hiding the bodies feels great and the coordinated assaults is smooth and easy to learn. The overall art style of this game is wonderful and the music was really well done!There are only two issues I am experiencing with this game, both of which could be chalked up to my lack of knowledge and experience with this genre: First of all, the controls are pretty tricky when trying to be quick and I occasionally do the completely wrong action. Sometimes I try to loot a body but end up picking up a different one or shutting a door. A loot button would be nice here (although the mass-looting is really nice - definitely glad I don't have to do it one body at a time). This also effects cover; I sometimes go to run to cover and my guy will run laps around it trying to figure out where I meant to put him. Maybe this will become more natural with experience. Second, there are a million tutorials for every little thing but the more confusing aspects of the game are left for you to figure out. I was uncertain which bar was stamina and which bar was health. I also did not realize there were positive/negative buffs - this also pertains to no idea how to handle them. In the first "real" mission my guy was concussed so I tried to fix it with health kits. This only replenished my health but did not fix the concussion. I then thought that maybe it would go away with time - nope. Syringe? Nope. Eventually I figured out on my own that I needed to assign my character to the health tent at camp to make this go away. Less basic tutorial and more complex ones like this would be great.Other than those two minor things, great game that I am excited to continue with! For the gentleman that left a review saying "Bad story" after 0.3 hours - dude, that's not cool. This game's story is already pretty cool and better than I'd thought and I am only a few hours in. Great work, devs! You should definitely be proud of this one!
_childDocuments_.name: Partisans 1941

_childDocuments_.review: I had such a good time playing this game, a fitting successor to 'Commandos'. Even on easy, this is a hard game that teaches you to cruelly cut your opponents apart without giving them the remotest chance. If you're sloppy then the Nazis will gun you down. There's a great and evil thrill to scanning a new map, then deconstructing the patrols, cover and sequencing. You sneak up to them, knife them and hide their bodies in a huge pile. Sooo many Nazis, soo much blood! But when you make a mistake this newer generation of the isometric-murder-savescum-er gives you cover and small unit skirmishing, and some base building as well. I felt immersed in the setting and loved hearing Russian and German spoken - it gave me chills. So buy this game! Encourage the devs to make sequels, more sequels! and then MOAR sequels! Death to Fascists!

_childDocuments_.review: Taking the role of a small, under-equipped squad is a novel angle for a real time strategy game like this. Strategy games are in a dearth right now, so this is not a bad game in the slightest if there is a need to play something new, but it simply does not stack up against some of the heavy weights of the genre.
