_childDocuments_.review: For the first 4 hours, I loved this game. The mobility and gunplay in this game is very fun and the campaign is rather short. An average gamer can beat the story within 1-2 hours. For my casual gamer, I would recommend picking this game up. For my achievement hunting completionist, please reconsider. The gameplay loop gets awfully and horrendously repetitive. The story isn't all that compelling and the grind in this game is absolutely ridiculous. Once you beat the campaign, you have access to 2 other modes: Fire Fight and Rogue Steel. As a completionist who unlocked all 52 achievements this game has to offer within the next 30 hours, I got extremely sick of this game quite fast. Fire Fight is relatively simple, as you eliminate enemies while completing certain challenges, such as 'Kill 2 enemies during a flip" or "Kill 3 enemies in 1 dive." Most of these challenges are easy with slow motion. The bad thing about this game mode is that you accumulate points whenever you finish a Fire Fight stage. Stages require certain points to unlock, thus forcing you to grind previous stages repetitively in order to finish this mode. On top of that, some of the later stages have relatively large maps and over 100+ enemies. Enemies are not revealed to you until you have killed all but 5-10 people, so whenever you play on a large map, tracking them down and finding each one can be a pain. Rogue Steel is the roguelike gamemode of this game. This is the grindiest, most mind-numbing component of the game. Your run puts you into 10 random stages from the campaign and, upon completion of each stages, you received a perk that could make your run easier or harder. Selecting the perk that makes your run harder allows you to gain more points. Rogue Steel is the only gamemode that allows you to unlock modifiers that you can activate during Fire Fight and New Game Plus, jacket cosmetics, and arm cannon cosmetics. As an achievement, you must unlock all jacket cosmetics and arm cannon cosmetics. To unlock all cosmetics, you must play at least 25 runs and accumulate a total of 32,500,000 points (you get roughly 500,000 - 1,000,000 per run if you picked all perks that makes your runs harder). If you want to play a game just to feel badass, go for it and pick this game up. Play casually and kill some enemies once in a while. However, if you are a completionist and achievement hunting, you are going to have an awful time. The first 4 hours of this game will be great. You will hate it by the next 30.

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel will make you feel stupidly cool. Unlocking the mouse mid-air and giving you the repelling kick will allow you to make the craziest kinds of stunts in slow-mo. The Soundtrack is also great, so many jams one after another and they are atmospheric too.The whole map is essentially destructible and after a firefight, it seems like you've done just that. So giving you a gun that deliberately lets you destroy whole chunks of the environment to traverse through these new gaps is amazing and you can shortcut like crazy. The fights are intense, stand around for 2 seconds and you are most likely already dead. I think there could have been a bit more enemy variety and maybe some guns that aren't pure high-speed projectile weapons but there is enough to keep you going.Although most things look like assets they are highly stylized and the same is true for the entire game.If you are into movement shooters then this is highly likely something you will enjoy, even if it is a bit janky.

_childDocuments_.review: An unfortunately short but action packed & beautiful game. The closest game to come to Warframe's parkour movement & flow system I've experienced. Mix that with FEAR & Superhot and you've got the general vibe of the game. Severed Steel is truly a beautifully designed and composed game that really needs to flesh out the content as the game is dramatically short at 4 hours to beat for me on the 4th difficulty. The destruction engine is also quite a thing of marvel once you've beaten the level and can actually stop moving and observe the chaos. The soundtrack also that strong 90's-00's feel and is overall punchy and really keeps the energy & momentum going. I would watch this game developer company and what they do with this game, as the foundations set by this game are extremely strong.

_childDocuments_.review: so glad i finally got around to playing this amazing gamethe combat loop is tight and very refined with super fast, exhilarating shootouts that feel both intense and cathartic, seemingly drawing inspiration from john woo movies and the matrix (and of course you have bullet time). the movement system is likewise very fun, fluid and unique taking clear cues from titanfall while simultaneously being its own thing with acrobatic stunts and a unique aiming system unlike anything ive ever seen before in an fpsthe main driving point of the combat is the fact you only have one arm meaning you cant reload and have to throw your weapon when youre out. this pushes you to zip around the map finding weapons or picking up your dead enemies' weapons which works really well to keep the game's excellent flow going. there are also some upgrades you unlock later on but ill leave discovering them to youthe level design likewise complements both the combat and movement systems extremely well, it all comes together so flawlessly, great game designobviously sound design is amazing and every gun feels great to shoot but thats a given i honestly loved it. very worth the $25 and i say this based off of just the campaign which while short, was definitely sweettheres also a level editor complete with steam workshop support, unlockable modifiers, ng+ and two modes i havent even touched yet, one of em being a rougelite?? honestly great value, if youre seeing this and are debating picking the game up, do yourself a favor and pick it up at least on sale

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel was definitely an enjoyable experience for me, most people's experiences will vary. Still, if you are a fan of the max payne series, superhot, and even a bit of metroid prime. Severed Steel should be your go to game to get that fix. What I absolutely Love is that Severed Steel gets right into the action. Yes, there is a story but it's prolonged by repetitive cutscenes that go on forever. You're really into the action, as fast possible. There were some moments in some of the cutscenes were Steel (The main character) Looks really creepy, and her 3D model doesn't look all that detailed.But, you don't really notice how basic some parts of the game is. You're constantly running through crazy velocity speed toeliminate and take out all the enemies in sight. Your character Steel can slow down her momentum and focus on aiming precise shots on enemies. You can take out several enemies, and you can also take out 2 enemies with one single shot. The game provides multiple methods on how you eliminate your opponents. That slowdown gameplay mechanic that you do in the game is so captivating and addicting at the same time. There's something about slowing down time to shoot enemies in games that just never gets old. I guess that's why I really love the max payne series so much.To be honest, The story wasn't really clear to me. I kinda just skimmed through it. But all you need to know honestly is that steel got screwed over but this organization. She lost her arm in the process, she replaces it with a laser cannon. Now go fight all the bad guys. That's all really need to know, and I kinda respect Severed Steel for putting more emphasis on the gameplay first. That definitely is why I can't recommend this game enough. I just want to get to the game faster.Unfortunately, if you only just play the campaign. You'll get maybe possibly 2 hours max from the game. But, if you play New game plus. Play through the other modes like rogue steel, firefight runs, and complete all the achievements. You are definitely going to get more out your money from this game. I found rouge steel to be the more interesting mode out of the bunch. Basically in that mode, you have a selected amount of cards and each individual cards gives you an ability or takes away an ability. If you choose and ability that is a downgrade, your multiplier will go up. You want your multiplier to go up to earn more points. When you have more points, that will allow you to earn new levels, and cosmetics for Steel, The enemies also get their own set of abilities each run. It's randomized, so some runs will be in your favor and others won't Sometimes Enemies will get Golden Shields which will make it harder for you to take it out. Sometimes enemies will die on contact from an exploding door. Each run is not the same, but that makes the game so damn replayable. The other firefight mode basically just tally up points for you to unlock new levels. It also suggest for you to do the objectives within the level. Most of them are not hard. For example the objective would be like. You need to get 8 headshots, or you have to eliminate an enemy slide kicking into them. I think the hardest objective for me was to get a certain amount of enemies to die by using the perk that makes door explode. That one was tricky because the enemy can be dumb at times. It's still manageable though! This game also have a level editor, but I haven't used it. Hoping more players do make levels for the game. There are a good amount of levels you can download through steam workshop. Plus, there are bonus levels that you can play after you finish the game for you to enjoy. These set of levels were developed by the team for the community to enjoy.Now, if you want to go the extra mile with this game. You can always do a no death run. I tried it for myself, and it brutal. Especially when they are some enemies that shoot nonstop at you. It's interesting, but it will definitely frustrate you.This is why I love Severed steel, the replayability is strong with this one. If you love max payne, Goldeneye, perfect dark, superhot. You're gonna really enjoy yourself playing Severed steel. I never go for 100% or trophy achievements, but severed steel earned my time and patience with the game. I just had to get every moment in with this game, because honestly this is one of the best games I have played in the last few years.

_childDocuments_.review: Given the opportunity, players will optimize the fun out of a game.Memember mirrors edge and half-arsed movement mechanist in some other FPS games? Imagine that, but with a heavy focus on combat and art-style that looks like rayonism painting, that looks entirely flat, killing all your depth perception. Even with raytracing there're no reflections of you. You have no idea if you are moving forward, or if you are hugging an indistinct wall and are shuffling in place. Because these walls don't look that different from corridors. Especially on black+neon maps with no conventional lighting.Now add the extra short time to kill on the second difficulty. Thinking that you are cooler than anyone is what makes you die instantly. Especially with this weird gunplay. I never saw anyone who can outrun a bullet. These are not projectile enemies, almost all of them are using hitscan weapons. While you memember Yamakasi and show them your sickest breakdance moves they just shot you. With guns.You can't reload the guns and always run out of ammo, you are supposed to just pick up another one. So you are often find yourself in situations when you are unarmed and need to chpok an enemy in melee to steal their gun. But enemies just clip through you and shoot you in the back. The melee combat is the worst part of this game with how it has no physicality, while it is mandatory and results in most of your deaths.So in reality this is just a Call of Duty on a higher difficulty, with entirely optional movement system, and with a free wallhack. You camp in place and slowly hunt wallhacked enemies or you die. In my imagination Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare plays something like this.To put another nail in the coffin of acrobatics — the kinaesthetics suck. Everything is floaty and there's barely any feedback to your actions. Whatever you press you don't know if it worked or what. You can't feel the status of your body.I just wanted to support a game without disgusting pixels, without lazy roguelite campaign, without low poly.When you are stuck in corridors against the enemies with hit-scan weapons this is not fun. Especially when the dudes with magic shields, and elite enemies show up. On the semi-open maps where you can easily break the line of sight this feels more like a proper movement game — Mothergunship or Immortal Redneck. There's wall humping. So you can just climb walls. There's solid feedback on kill. You can kick wallhacked enemies through the walls and ceilings — since the game allows clipping.There's a real campaign mode which you can finish. It has terrible disgusting uncutscenes, which are worse than nothing. The mid-game boss  CEO is just box. It stands right there in the room with its nuts wide open. You just stand in one place and kick it in the nads, it does nothing and dies. There are also a stupid angbadang grindathon treadmill with unlocks where you can play with yourself; a roguelite mode which i didn't touch with a 12.0396 metres pole; a new game plus; some fan campaigns or something. SO people whol love to do the same thing over and over can probably amuse themselves.In the first couple of levels the music is nice — it's some not-boring dnb. But then it's replaced with generic erotic sounds of butthurt.All in all it is a mediocre FPS, with sometimes decent movement, and slight destructibility — explosives are rare. At its best it is a 2000s wacky FPS, but on bad maps it's a bad CoD.

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel is a fast-paced first-person shooter that offers a thrilling and satisfying gameplay experience. While the campaign may be short, there are other modes to keep players engaged and challenged. Despite the lack of significant rewards in the other modes, players can still enjoy pushing themselves to their limits.This game is perfect for players who have limited time to spare, as it only takes a few hours to complete the main campaign. However, the game is designed so that you can come back to it and enjoy the other modes whenever you have time to spare. The mechanics never get old, and if you come back to finish the campaign after stopping halfway for a while, you won't feel like you've missed anything.As someone who isn't experienced with fast-paced FPS games, Severed Steel was one of the first shooters of its kind that I played and enjoyed. It allows players to take on each level at their own pace, even on medium difficulty, without feeling overwhelmed.Each kill in the game is incredibly satisfying, whether players are performing advanced parkour or simply taking out enemies without sliding around. It always feels amazing to slow-mo kick an enemy, steal their pistol, shoot them in the face, and throw their weapon at another while planning your next kill.While the game's soundtrack may not reach the levels of Carpenter Brut, the music still helps set the mood and enhance the gameplay experience.Overall, Severed Steel is a fun and addictive shooter that's easy to pick up and play. Its short campaign, engaging mechanics, and satisfying kills make it a game worth trying out for gamers of all skill levels.

_childDocuments_.review: Movement focused FPS game that merges ideas from several titles I've liked, Mirror's Edge & Titanfall for movement, but with the combat elements of the original F.E.A.R. games. The level design and music also feels inspired by Mirror's Edge, but an ultra-violent version where combat is the central focus. The core loop is simple: You take no damage from enemy fire as long as you aren't moving normally, so you chain together wall running, slides, and dives in order to maintain invulnerability. As long as you're doing this, you can use the time-slowing reflex ability with no drain on its otherwise limited gauge. This lets you accurately shoot a whole bunch of different enemies at a time. Fragging opponents restores your reflex gauge (and health, on the lower difficulties) at the cost of your ammo, which you can't reload or replenish. So you steal fresh enemy weapons instead. Finally you have a cannon that can blast through most objects or surfaces in the environment to make dynamic entry to areas that'd otherwise be inaccessible. Many weapons can also damage the environment, so if you drag out a fight you'll quickly find less cover and runnable surfaces to use.The campaign was short but had a generally great level design throughout (save for a few "get to the exit" ones that seem to go by really quick). I beat it in one ~3ish hour sitting on the standard difficulty, but there is a ton more content including several challenge modes, a New Game+, and bunch of different difficulty settings and modifiers. There isn't much of a story, nor is one really needed, but given the amount of stuff on offer it surprises me collectible lore tidbits aren't among the things you can unlock. Maybe I just overlooked it, but if absent that feels like a missed opportunity. That's my only real nitpick though, otherwise Severed Steel is a real gem of an offering. Would absolutely recommend it to anyone, on the caveat they like shooters and don't have motion sickness problems.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick summary: The best way to describe this game is as a messy but fun high octane shooter. Overall, it's got a lot of personality, but is almost devoid of the polish that a game like this needs to really flourish. Movement is clunky and often unresponsive, and the controls just seem strange. The combat flow is very fun when things work, but intense situations really highlight the lack of control that you really have over your character. This is certainly worth 20$, though 25$ is kind of pushing it considering the extremely limited content. Replay value is all this game really has going for it since the "Campaign" is barely an hour long. Going into a bit more detail, the game's controls are just strange. Most modern games with a slide mechanic allow you to slide via the crouch key, but that's not an option here (At least, not that I saw. There are a lot of smaller customization options, some great, others strange. I looked, but couldn't see it.) Considering how crouching is almost useless, it's easy enough to rebind it and forget about it. It's still a pretty strange oversight, though. Adding to this, the melee key is also the use key, something that is exceptionally annoying. You hardly use the use key, but it just feels a bit off regardless. These are primarily minor flaws in the game, but they do show either a lack of understanding for how a game should feel, or perhaps a lack of knowledge on how to properly code some things. Either way, it's a nuisance, but not much more. The biggest issue is the awkward movement within the game. At first, you might not notice it all too much, but once you start trying to really push the game to its limits, that's when things start pushing back. I'll briefly run through things, then elaborate more. Wall running is about what you'd expect from an indie game -Basic, but functional-, but ends up lacking in functionality once you try to chain stunts together. Sliding is pretty fun, but also lacks a lot of real functionality due to the kick function. Kicking is near useless, and ends up being more of a burden than a blessing. Diving is the most useful tool in your kit, being the most versatile ability you have to get around. The wallrunning is functional, but not much else. It's very finicky when you're actively diving and sliding around maps, as it seems to only sometimes activate when you're being heavily mobile. Considering that your survival demands you to use these abilities, an inconsistent and unreliable wallrun is a big problem. It doesn't lead to many issues, but it adds to the pile. Sliding is fun, but usually isn't as helpful as diving. It's a lot of fun thanks to how it allows you to freely look around while on the move, and of course, allows you to avoid being shot. The time it takes for you to be able to get back up, however, is kind of an issue. I understand that it would be a bit broken if you could slide, then immediately jump into a wall run, but it's...it's not very fun when you can't. This actually makes your modes of movement pretty linear, but I'll get into that after going over diving. Diving is the most versatile movement tool at your disposal, vastly blowing sliding out of the water since you can go through windows, fling yourself over enemies, and avoid the bumps on floors that sometimes snag you. It is, however, a bit iffy on the height that you can go to. Sometimes, you'll just kind of slap the floor instantly instead of going anywhere, despite looking straight forward. Other times, you'll go WAY higher than usual, and I have no idea what makes these things happen. I've tested it while holding still, and it's entirely random how high I actually go. It's not often that the variation happens, but when in combat, that little bit really takes you out of the flow. Adding to this, I'm not actually sure if I am allowed to dive into a wallrun. Sometimes I can, sometimes I can't. It seems, again, random if it works or not. The issue with all these issues combined is that combat is dreadfully linear once you realize the constraints. Finely tuned control over your character is one of the most important things that a game like this can have, and sadly, Severed Steel is found lacking. The inconsistencies really hinder fully enjoyment of the game. The typical flow, no matter the map, tends to go the same thanks to the lack of overall functionality. Instead of being able to chain a variety of moves, you'll most often find yourself sliding into a dive, then jumping into an air slide or another dive. Wall running is kind of a game of chance, so maybe you'll mix one or two in every now and again. The issue there is with the map size, so you rarely actually gain anything from wall running. Furthermore, you sometimes just magnetize towards walls at bad moments thanks to the inconsistent ability to do so while diving, meaning your character often does something you just don't want. Lastly, the kicking. Kicking blows. Not only is it inconsistent with actually colliding with your targets, but it is somehow the most disorienting feature in a game where you can literally flip upside down. I found the flipping feature fantastic and not at all disorienting, yet kicking usually left me unsure where I was for a second or two. Why is this? Well, it magnetizes to enemies, and instead of just adjusting your character by a small bit, it just yoinks you straight away from whatever you're looking at. Are you speeding by like a bullet? Not anymore, that kick just made you do a 180 and now you have no speed. Getting shot at, but try to kick someone? Guess what, now you're vulnerable. Kicking is actually the worst thing you can usually do since it opens you up to damage and doesn't even knock enemies down. It just briefly stuns them while everyone else can mow you down. It is singlehandedly the worst feature in this game. I almost never used it because it just rips you from the combat to an almost literal degree. This game is a lot of fun, but it's just way too short for how unpolished it is. I'm definitely going to sink more hours into it, but after 1.5 hours, the game really doesn't match up to most competitors in terms of gameflow. The gunplay feels really, really nice though, and shooting is very satisfying. At first, bullets from smgs felt really underwhelming, but they forced me to get a bit creative with my attacks. ARs and shotguns are just pure satisfaction, so I ended up enjoying both. Heavy pistols are just...they're perfect. I'm more than happy to have bought this game, but the lack of polish for what I would consider the game's biggest mechanic is just disappointing. The game's campaign is more of a gimmick than an actual feature, being barely an hour and entirely devoid of actual story. It's really just the "Firefight" maps strung together with mild coherence. All in all, a fun game, but one that comes up short when compared to others. It has a few unique features that help it stand out somewhat, but never nails any single thing well enough to be praised for its flare or attention to quality. 20$ is definitely a fair price thanks to replayablity, but 25$, as petty as it may sound, just seems a bit strange considering how genuinely lacking in content the game is. Relying entirely on replayability is a gamble when the game is as underbaked as it currently is, but even at 25$, it's still worth picking up if you're as into these fast as hell shooters. Give it a try, shoot some bad guys, and see if it's your type of thing.

_childDocuments_.review: Love this one. It takes a really interesting approach to encouraging stylistic gameplay. You have a slow mo ability that burns unless you are doing stunts and doing stunts is basically the only way to avoid damage. All weapons only have one mag so you have to constantly be switching. This may sound tedious, but it is not as all of the weapons are pretty good at quickly dispatching your enemies. another this that sets this game apart is the ability to customize your experience. There are so many options that can make the game more tailored to your taste. Way more then I have seen in almost any other game. Music is great. It is EDM that really fits in with the flow of combat. Then there is the excessive amount of content in this game. There is a campaign that is pretty short, only about 5-6 hours. Which sounds like a negative, but I see it as a positive. That campaign is alone worth the price of admission. However, ontop of that there is a Firefight mode with over 50 levels, a rogue like mode, and bonus campaigns. Each of these you could easily sink more hours into then twice what the campaign takes to complete.Pros:Fluid gameplaySkill based combatMakes you feel powerfulGreat soundtrackCons:Not much of a story, if you care about that.Wall running can be temperamental.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game that knows exactly what it wants to be with the story serving more like a 3 hour long tutorial and introduction to the mechanics rather than an actual story. There's a big arsenal of weapons you can unlock, a decent amount of enemies and an endless amount of modes and stages both from the main game but also from the workshop. The game offers you tons of freedom on how to move around, wall running, kicking off walls even doing flips and dives. It's refreshing albeit kind of floaty with weapons serving mostly as single use (clip) items. Make no mistake, you are playing this for the score attack and the arcadiness rather than any meaningful story experience. With leaderboards, a daily mission and even a roguelite mode mixed in for good measure and if you get bored with all that, there's tons of modifiers to try for each. The soundtrack is also absolutely excellent and it enhances the experience a lot and I say this as a metalhead first. Grab this wether you want to have some fun or even just show off. _childDocuments_.review: This game's awesome! It feels genuinely hyper unique in that it's like you have almost no friction and little weight, which feels kind of off sometimes if I'm being honest -- but I really want to emphasize how it feels like nothing else because of that and it does start to feel natural and intuitive. If you run at a wall and you've played Titanfall before, it feels about the same, just more free form in that you basically have a triple jump and can reverse momentum completely on a whim.It's a really cool game though and I can't recommend it enough as something that just clicks well with me. It's a little short, but the firefight mode is a challenge-based run through with a leveling system that I've been enjoying. I do wish there was an option to make your luck (health kinda) more visible. On the harder difficulties slipping up for a microsecond kills you and it can be tough to tell if you're in a dive or just have your luck up in general. Also hope there's updates or a sequel that refines it a bit more weight-wise. Where something like Titanfall really sells your momentum using the heft of everything, this kinda feels a little too light sometimes with how little momentum factors in. Slowmo as a resource also feels a bit strange where I found myself not using it as much because it felt like I should always use it and there wasn't a reason not to. The mutator for limiting slowmo is great and I think I'd actually like to see an even more restrictive version of that because when the game is at full speed it feels incredible, but realistically I should just hold down RMB at all times.Oh also the last level was rad. That's the short version of my thoughts. Game's great, love it, will play it from here on as a habitual lunch time game.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/14/23 edit: Game has been updated so you can save progress in Rogue Steel and grind has been reduced. Still leaving my review as-is though because I don't think that's enough to flip my opinion to a thumbs up.I knew going into this that the campaign was short but I was hoping to get my money's worth out of the extra game modes. Unfortunately, they're just not fun to play and have way different pacing and tone than the campaign. If you're looking at this just for the campaign, be aware that $24.99 for 2½ hours of gameplay is definitely not worth it. While the campaign is very good, the two extra game modes (Firefight and the newer Rogue Steel) aren't. Firefight has a meta leveling system where you unlock new starting weapons, arm cannons, and difficulty mutators (which include positives, negatives, and cheat codes). However, it's very grindy with an exponential exp curve that feels like something out of an online game battle pass system. You'll be forced to grind certain levels over and over, stacking difficulty mutators and re-achieving challenges, just to continue to unlock new maps. It's great that there's 42 levels in this game mode, but I was really feeling the grind on only map 11 unlocked.Rogue Steel has a card system rogue-lite element where you pick difficulty modifier cards before each new map. As you work your way through new levels, your score is tallied, modified, and the difficulty continues to ramp up. The announcement for this mode sounded cool on paper, but it's terrible to play. There's no checkpoints mid-level and some of the levels have high enemy counts. Most maps in other modes have 20-25 enemies and the map I stopped my run on had 55 enemies; death means starting the whole map over with nothing to show for it. The worst part is there's no save system between maps; this means you have to run all 10 maps in a row, without exiting the game, in order to receive a score and rewards.I commend the devs for using so many color harmonies other than the stereotypical modern cyberpunk take of blue and purple, but it's sometimes so colorful and saturated that it's hard to look at. There's also a really ugly low quality rust palette used on certain maps (that looks more like a staticky scab) that stands out for the wrong reasons. The levels feel like they were painted from a collection of materials from different authors because you'll get realistic wooden floors next to cartoony metals and sometimes the aforementioned rust added in too. Then there's the complaint about the "cyberpunk" themes... I could write a 10 page essay about how garbage modern cyberpunk has become but for this game it just distills down to a visual theme. The character models look fine, but they look like they're pulled from any generic cyberpunk character pack on a 3D model website.Sure, the campaign is a frenetic, wild ride through a wide variety of colorful levels. The soundtrack is fitting but nothing amazing. Enemies have callouts and swear at you, but it's all the same voice actor. Parts of this game feel like a ton of effort went into it (like player movement and gun play), while some parts feel like bare minimum. I picked this up for $7.49 on a sale and even then I feel a bit let down by the experience. This game is way overpriced for what you get. If the store page piques your interest, wait for a deep, deep sale. Otherwise, I wouldn't recommend this for the average person.

The level design is pretty good and one can see that the devs put thought and effort for players who might think outside the box. _childDocuments_.review: All show, no substance - a game made only for being looked at, not for actually playing.The game has one major flaw that completely breaks it - whatever you do, if you're not completely standing still or running in a straight line, you're completely invulnerable.Yup, that's right. The player is constantly invincible if they as much as jump in place. Or if they wall-run, or dive, or slide - which means if you're doing any of the given means of traversal you can not die. You can also not fail any mission (except a single one early on that has a time limit) while moving. And since you can wall-run forever, even on as much as a lamp-post, and you're double jump refreshes as soon as you touch a wall, you can literally just beat any level by sticking to a wall and being completely invincible.And if that weren't enough to completely take any and all challenge out of the game, while you're constantly invincible you also get unlimited slow-motion as well... Very interesting.Oh, and the cool shots you see whizzing by you during slomo are also fake btw. You can't actually dodge bullets in this game (not that it would matter since god-mode is constantly on anyways) - all weapons are hitscanning, both yours as well as the enemies'. The tracers you see are purely for visual effect. The only projectile weapons are the grenade launchers and your arm cannon - but again, these pose a threat only to your enemies, since you're constantly invincible.Even the flamethrower is a hitscan weapon for some reason, hitting enemies long before the visual flame is even half way to it's destination.

This gameplay formula is a core of linear campaign and additional, single-player (with competitive elements limited to online leaderboards) gameplay modes. While there is a healthy amount of nuance and customizability to it, available from the start and partially locked behind progressions mechanics, this intensive gameplay loop of linear strain of arena shootouts, spiced a handful of parkour philosophy and some rogue-lite elements, is the cause, road, and destination in Severed Steel, with pretty much everything else like a variety of (completely destructible, voxel-based) environments, vide selection or armaments, gameplay and difficulty modifiers, mission objectives or optional challenges, acting as a support structure for it.   his is a very compact and condensed, mechanical experience with other components like story and narrative or even stealth gameplay appearing more as gestures that are being politely winked and waved at, than anything worth talking about besides mentioning it. Not a case of neglect, simply omission and lack of focus- mostly by design, certainly to some extent because of the limited development resources. And to be honest, when looking at the end result- allocated in a very considerably smart way.Whether that's an issue or not, will eventually fall on the player's expectations and the amount of enthusiasm that can be mustered for an experience of this type. And because of that, I'd say it's  advised to try the demo version before purchasing SS, as even for fans of high skill/mobility elements listed here (and present in titles like Trepang2, Turbo Overkill, Ghostrunner, SuperHOT, Ultrakill, F.E.A.R, even Max Payne or modern DOOM games to some extent) this formula might not be fulfilling and satisfying enough to carry the whole experience, especially when buying without any sale discount.   f expectations are set on a level that can be met by Severed Steel- this is a highly recommended purchase. From the first, introductory campaign level to the last 'Rogue Steel' run you might go for, this game will maintain its quality and fun factor on an even level- from start to finish it is a finely designed, well-crafted blend of high-octane shooting and frantic movement mechanics, coated in simplistic but totally serviceable and nonetheless pleasant, clean, cohesive visuals that occasionally (when environmental design, textures, shadows and lighting come together) generate really impressive scenes. _childDocuments_.review: Having first heard of  through the gospel of that 8-foot-tall cybernetic kangaroo hybrid from the mythical kingdom of Australia Gmanlives, my interest was immediately peaked. Then not long after having played the downloadable demo I was fully invested and convinced of the game's potential. Now, having fully played and experienced everything that the game currently has to offer I can safely make the verdict that  is truly wonderful.This game offers some of the most air-tight, satisfying and intuitive movement and shooting controls that I've ever experienced, and though the game is admittedly short it's foundation is rock-solid and it's gameplay loop is as addictive as crack. Providing a challenging experience that avoids being frustrating due to bite-sized level segments that are fun to play over-and-over again. The basic premise (according to the art book) is that the player takes on the role of Steel, a physically-enhanced clone manufactured to perform gruelling tasks in an inhospitable environment who is discarded as soon as her usefulness comes to an end, and if that premise doesn't give you  vibes then I've got to ask what you've been doing with your life. With that in mind the game gives the player a quick rundown of the basic movement controls that you'll be needing to make full use of before dropping you right into the action. What can be said about the game is that it is highly respectful of the player's time and doesn't waste a second of it on unnecessary exposition or distractions, dropping them right into an expertly crafted starting level that is open in layout but with some enclosed spaces, giving the player free reign on how they want to initiate combat in a similar method to . You'll need to wall run, double-jump, dip, dodge, duck, dive and dodge in order to survive since while performing these inhuman feats of athletics the enemies in the area cannot damage you, and it provides your primary mode of defence. The combat loop of  is the definitive highlight and is entirely what the game focuses all of it's energy on. In order to promote this method of play the game does not allow the player to reload their weapons, which makes sense in the game's setting since Steel wouldn't want to weigh herself down with extra magazines when she needs to be as lithe and agile as possible. Instead you'll need to make your shots count, keep moving around the arena and constantly pick up fallen weapons or even swipe a sidearm out of an enemy soldier's holster. The enemy AI in this game is hyper aggressive, as if they've been injected with pure epinephrine prior to combat. Enemies can often be witnessed communicating with each other and converging to the player's last known position, and they can lose sight of you if you escape their line of sight, in which case they'll fan out and begin sweeping the area. The dynamic AI demonstrated by the enemies provides the game with it's high replay value, as you'll rarely have the same encounter twice. What I'd have liked to see with the combat however is a bit more enemy variety. Not to say that there aren't a lot of different enemy types, a lot of them wield different weapons and there is a respectable array of heavy units, but for the most part they don't shake up the combat and promote different strategies. What I'd have liked to see is more of the flamethrower type enemy, who is covered head-to-toe in nigh-impenetrable armor who can only be reliably taken down either by stealing his flamethrower (which is laughably overpowered in the player's hands) or shooting his exposed gas tank on his back. Throwing in more units like this would spice up the combat encounters and make it more dynamic than just jumping around and shooting heads. Another instance of this was the boss fight which I won't spoil too hard, as it really kicked up the thrill factors another notch and it was unfortunate that there was only one boss fight in the entire game, and it wasn't even at the end. Map layout is mostly spot-on, with several alternate routes and designs that encourage the game's strengths, offering a tasteful variety of wide-open arenas, high verticality and narrow corridors that each test the player's abilities. Some certain maps however aren't up to snuff, with one level taking place in this indoor golf course that is way too open, while the apartment level is very constricted and bottlenecked which makes it less replayable on the Firefight game mode. But in contrast to this the train level is absolutely thrilling to play, hopping between two speeding, multi-layered train cars racing side-by-side. Mission objectives in the campaign are also wisely implemented in a way that doesn't detract from the gameplay loop, and are there mostly as a prod for the player to progress and to shake things up a little so that it's not all just "bop all the nerds".At the time of this writing, I've logged in just over five hours of playtime, during which I've beaten the campaign and have unlocked most of the weapons, maps and mutators for the Firefight mode (which is basically just objective-free versions of the campaign maps). Still after that I can easily see myself logging twice or even three times that much before my interest begins to wane, and that's just with the base content, not counting what the community-made levels available on the Steam Workshop can offer, made from the built-in level editor.  has got a great set of bones in it's body that allow it to stand strong and unique in the sea of it's competitors. High weapon variety, lots of replayability and a very bright and flashy design accompanied by a decent soundtrack (it's a little too dub-steppy in places for my tastes, but it's still some pretty good stuff). Definitely recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is actually the third time I've reviewed Severed Steel. I'll try to keep things brief this time. After playing over the course of a whole year since it launched, I absolutely love this game. Obviously, I'm really biased here, so if you're a newcomer that has never seen this game before, watch a few minutes of some gameplay footage before you make a purchase. The simple combat loop you'll see is basically the whole game. The campaign will probably only take 2-3 hours on the default difficulty. If you like fast-paced shooters with high mobility, it's a great time once you adjust to the controls, but you probably won't get to double digit playtime hours if you aren't the type of person that enjoys the spectacle of a simple but solid combat sandbox. If the reason "because it's just fun to me" isn't good enough to keep you coming back, then you probably won't feel like investing a lot of your time here.Between firefight mode and the recently added "rouge steel" update (which I don't recommend you just jump into until you've at least beaten the campaign and also spent a bit of time with firefight mode), you have a bunch of options for short-term pickup sessions after finishing the main campaign. Experiment with the controls, mechanics, and all the options, because you might find a combination of settings that click with you if the default settings aren't to your liking.After 50 hours in, I don't feel like there's a "right" way to play this game. Sure, you can easily cheese most encounters by spamming dives, kick-slides, and wall runs. Yes, some weapons drastically outperform others. None of that matters to me personally. I feel that the game's biggest strength is how easy it is to just zone out and have fun playing it once you understand how it works.Always remember, in most cases, you don't NEED to aim for the head. Body shots will kill too.

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously I didn't play for long, I was pretty excited about this game, but for me, I can't really say I enjoyed it because of simply how.. weird this game feels to play.It's clearly inspired by movement shooters and things like the matrix, and it's pretty cool, but when it comes to playing it, it doesn't feel nearly as cool as the trailers.The game is almost requires you to play in slow motion to be accurate which isn't always fun, I think the best way to play a game like this is to have slow mo in times where you need it, but when you need it all the time because there's always 5 dudes shooting at you and you need to constantly be moving to not die, (and I couldn't really find a reliable way to tell if I was even close to dying, could just be my fault) it falls apart a bit.The movement also just doesn't feel good to me. Sliding and diving feel more restrictive than they feel liberating and I feel like in this game that's about movement and wall running the weird restrictions on them makes the game feel very clunky.You can be good at this game and you CAN enjoy it, I just simply didn't. _childDocuments_.review: Technically this is an early access review, as I was in the beta. but if ANYTHING, this shows how the beta and the developers took all the feedback, suggestions, and tips that came via the beta and not only fixed, but even enhanced on or made better.But let me get to the meat and potatoes of what Severed Steel is as a wholeAt it's heart Severed Steel is a cluster♥♥♥♥ of the following games: Mirror's Edge-This is via the parkour and gunplay Hotline Miami-Tons of enemies and you die in very few hits, and it pays to try new strategies and approaches as you attempt a level. It also takes Hotline's elements of interactive/destructible envrionments and amps that up to 11 given that you can make alternate routes by destryoing wallsSuperhot- The environments take that kind of art style appraoch but make it feel more sci-fi dystopian/futrusitic as well as time manipulation Lastly, Severed Steel takes  a tad of the Matrix (You have to slide and wall run to dodge and avoid bullets from enemey soldiers, and you better learn fast if you want to make progress and surviveNow all of this wouldn't matter if the game was garbage, but thankfully it is executed BEAUTIFULLYOne moment you'll be bolting under tables while slowing down time to gun down enemies from across the room blazing at the bad guys with an uzi, the next you'll slow down time after kicking a door down before using a computer console to make yourself a new route by blowing it up, Not to mention you get upgrades as you get further into the game, akin to a modern shooter like Doom or maybe The Metroid Prime games as examplesWhile Severed Steel hasn't necessarily done anything new at face value, the mishmash it creates with all these different elements is executed to create a very energizing, fast paced, and immersive experience that always gets your eyes glued to the screen and your blood pumpingTop this off with the "icing on the cake" of this game being a very energetic and fitting technopop/dubstep soundtrack with some light rock elements, comic book style cutscenes that tell the story of a bionic woman experimental android, (Comics style reminds me of like you take Shank's cut-scenes and give them a more gritty feel with a cold futuristic vibe akin to something out of Dark Horse Comics) and the PLETHORA of user made content, and this is UNDOUBTEDLY a game I can HIGHLY RECCOMENDFaith Connors, Jacket, and Mr Anderson would be VERY proud

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel is a great game. It's fast a paced first person shooter with a lot of different guns, brilliantly modelled levels with lots of lighting and reflections making good use of ray tracing and DLSS. You can get around the levels with great freedom of movement, diving, sliding, jumping and wall running to avoid the sometimes hoards of enemies blasting away at you. The bullet time/slow motion mechanic works really well too, as well as any game that has ever made use of it before. It's a mid priced game so the game play doesn't last as long as a higher priced game but that is to be expected. As well as the campaign mode, in which there are four difficulty settings to challenge you, there is a firefight mode that you can have plenty of fun finishing off. The soundtrack is also a great addition to this game with the style of music matching the visual style of the game really well. Would recommend this to anyone who likes first person shooters with a futuristic visual style.

The destructible environments are also pretty cool to mess around with too. It's great fun, strongly recommend it to fans of shooters and fast-paced, intense action.

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid movement-focused FPS. The main focus of Severed Steel is definitely the action. You don't get a ton of tools to play with, but when combined with the focus on movement and the fact that the game forces you to switch weapons on the fly, the combat feels very satisfying. Even if you aren't a twitch shooter veteran, the generous slowdown mechanic helps quite a bit to keep the fast pace of the game from being overwhelming. Most of the guns are serviceable, with a few standouts that I always try to snag. None of them are particularly unique, but the variety keeps things interesting.I appreciate that the game gives you plenty of difficulty modifiers to choose from, including a modifier that improves your character's mobility at no detriment to your score modifier. There's a fair bit to choose from if you find the game too challenging / not challenging enough beyond the standard difficulty levels the game offers.The game is quite short if you only play through once, I beat the main story and the side levels in just a few hours, though this is typical of many FPSs. The aforementioned difficulty modifiers lend to the game's replayability. EDIT: Since writing this, I've gone back to the game a few times to try out the roguelite and free-play style modes, which add some nice varied content once the main story is completed.Soundtrack is solid and it feels appropriate. Graphics are serviceable, they keep things simple.The only sticking point I had with the game was gravity. A few levels have glass floors or large open spaces to fall into, which sent me back to my last checkpoint more times than I care to admit. Maybe I just ought to be more careful, but it did frustrate me regardless. Overall, if you want a fast-paced parkour FPS, I can recommend giving Severed Steel a shot. It should be pretty clear within the first 2 hours of gameplay whether you'll enjoy the rest of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I am thoroughly addicted to this combination of leaping, diving, shooting enemies, and pounding synthwave music. On paper it doesn't seem like 3D voxel destruction lends much to the proceedings, but it's the final "secret sauce" ingredient that ties the whole experience together. The dynamic impacts, holes, and outright destruction created by your gunfire (and that of the enemies' weaponry) is what gives emphasis to the destruction wrought by both parties and the creative element to getting your first-person avatar from start to finish in a creatively satisfying way. In every moment, you're asking yourself if you should dive through the window, kick open the door, blast through the wall, or dive under the table, all moves immediately accessible at the press of a button. You don't have to play this one for the challenge of doing it all completely unscathed at full speed; you're dynamically chaining stuff together on the fly. It's a combination of satisfying "question and answer" gameplay with your own custom level of difficulty. The "Question" is: "How are you going to [Get from point A to point B], [Kill your Target(s)], and/or [survive the next 2-3 minutes of high-enemy-density combat encounters]?", and your answer as the player is always "[A super-cool combination of kicks, slides, dives, wall-runs, double-jumps, weapons-thefts, and LOTS of shooting and explosions]!"The campaign is probably 4-6 hours long depending on how well you play the game and how many times over you play it. But that's only doing it once! Every level begs to be played multiple times on higher difficulties, with modifiers, or even just faster and smoother than last time!Post-campaign, there's also a "Firefight" mode where I've spent additional hours unlocking levels, mutators, starting weapons, and more! If you felt like any of the levels were over too quickly, or could use more randomized enemies, then this is where you can get your fix of upside-down flamethrower swan dives! I've got 9 hours in this game at the time of writing, and I still haven't worked through all the default maps yet. There's a playlist function and map-specific challenges that are tons of fun to chase after, keeping me coming back for quick hits of action between other games. When I'm sick of those, or want to chase more new stuff, there's Workshop support to add in fan-created levels and content for even more variety! This is a game that sat too long on my wishlist. If it's on yours, I recommend you pick it up too!

_childDocuments_.review: A true movement shooter, the likes of ULTRAKILL and Titanfall 2, with more of an emphasis on style, with free range of camera motion and stunts. Being able to kick off of a guard then shooting them in the face THEN diving through a window THEN turning upside down to shoot another guard in the back of the head makes my brain secrete dopamine like nothing else. The frantic elements of having to pick up enemy guns and varying levels of destructible terrain lend very well to the movement and combat styles that'll have you diving past enemies to grab their guns to then fight with. (also the voices of the guards are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hilarious and whoever voiced them needs a bigger cut)There are a lot of things wrong with the game though, but none of these things are enough to have turned down my purchase.Firstly, . I played the free demo of it a while ago, which went up until chapter 1, and it feels largely the same, movement and combat wise. It seems that all that extra time went into the cutscenes, level editor, and more levels. And even though there are a lot of levels, the game is WAY too short, like an hour and a half campaign at medium difficulty. There are also elements introduced which seem like they're going to be used more but then just... aren't. There is 1 boss in the entire game that signifies the end of chapter 5 and took me 2 attempts and 3 guns to kill. A portal element is introduced that pairs  with the movement mechanics but is only in 3 levels total, and one of them is the final level. The overcharged hand cannon is only used in the final level as well. The portals and lack of bosses is especially heartbreaking because those parts where easily the most fun, and would have been amazing to play with more. I get that you're supposed to use all of these elements in the level editor to then play with yourself, but still, the game is way too short.Secondly, the movement system takes a bit of getting used to. Every system is pretty clunky to use, which lends to the feeling of the game feeling unfinished, but at the same time feels extremely floaty. It doesn't feel like you have any weight, which may be a turn off for some people, the wallrunning feels more like gliding across the wall than anything, you fall slowly, your slides go on as if you're on ice, things like that, it never bothered me but I can see if it bothers others. The double jump is finicky at times, for instance if you dive, even if you started on the ground, you cannot double jump, dives and slides are very hard, impossible sometimes, to cancel out of, kicking doesn't work in dives, kicking off of a wall makes it hard to actually go in the direction you want, wallrunning is tied to where you're looking and not where you're moving, and this is really nitpicky but explosions don't have any knockback. All of these can be subverted to an extent with practice, but I would still like to see more controllable movement.These two sound pretty bad, and they kind of are, but honestly in game you would never notice. The gameplay is still amazing, the movement is still fairly fluid, the music is great, and there are a lot of side things besides the main campaign to toy with.

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel is a good FPS game with only a few bugs, mostly due to portal interactions. The game has a solid foundation of mechanics for the slow but fast paced gameplay that the on-demand bullet time gives you. The main campaign is short at only about two and a half hours, but that's not really something to worry about as the alternative modes of Fire Fight and Rogue Steel are where the meat of the game is, with Fire Fight being a Score Attack style mode and Rogue Steel being exactly that, a short rogue like type mode.With the majority of the game being in those two modes, and the campaign being as short as it is, and the gameplay as fast as it is, you're going to be playing the same maps *a lot* and very quickly, so if replaying the same maps again and again isn't your cup of tea, maybe give the game a pass.The Rogue Steel mode I feel could do with a few more mutator cards and the frequency of the maps made for it being raised somewhat, so that they actually show up in the map pool instead of it being 95% campaign maps, but those campaign maps still work quite well, as having the level objective being more than "kill everything" gives the mode some variety.In the end, game good, solid mechanics, go play if it interests you.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot stress enough how much fun I have playing this game...I've been playing video games since the early 90's and it's been a long long time since I've had such a fluid, hectic and fun experience. Below I've booped some of the games that have fantastic mechanics that Severed Steel has taken inspiration from and perfectly and cohesively tied together for a worthwhile and wonderful experience. (RED FACTION)It reminds me so much of the original Red Faction, in the sense of it's incredibly destructive environments that I often see advertised in other game titles *Cough* Levolution *Cough* that always seems to be very lacklustre a straight out disappointing. In Severed Steel it's absolutely great. (HOTLINE MIAMI)Then a sprinkle of Hotline Miami (The soundtrack in this game is extremely good and compliments the speed and intensity of the gameplay itself perfectly) and of course the running out of ammo flinging your gun at the enemy to knock them out mechanic is wonderfully implemented too(TITANFALL)I personally think the movement and wall running is better than Titanfall which it seems to be compared to quite a lot for fair reason, but I personally enjoy the much more fast paced hectic version of Severed Steel movement, the ability to leap over an enemy with a bulletproof riot shield, then turn yourself upside down in slow motion mid air and one tap him in the back of the skull...what other game lets you do that?...because I honestly can't think of a single one that lets you kill and move so stylishly with ease and no clunky camera angles or issues, you feel like an absolute bad ass playing it. (MAX PAYNE)Not just for the obvious slow motion mechanic here, but for the simple addition of adding in a dedicated dive button mechanic, which...my god...it is extremely good funTo add and finish up here, a couple other pluses before the negative nitpicks-LEVEL EDITORI personally have not tried it out yet, but I am excited to, I think it adds a serious level of longevity to the game with it having such solid and fun mechanics.-PERFORMANCEFor Me it runs well, I play 3440x1440 resolution with a 3080/32GB Ram/i7-8700k I had V-Sync on playing it so it was usually in the 144fps mark, I also have OBS Replay Buffer too going, so that usually takes away some FPS. I only ever seen it drop down to 100fps during a train mission with a huge explosion, bar that it ran very well. -NITPICKS/CONSI personally would prefer a dot reticle option and an option to turn off the "Double kill" type colourful high score stuff floating over the enemies when you kill them, I tend to try to have games as immersive as possible, then a audio character slider for the volume of the characters, having the music up quite loud would be recommended in all honesty, otherwise you are going to here a lot of "HEH HUH HEH HUH!!!" From the main character jumping, which you tend to do a lot. Another thing is the enemies shouting "TARGET SIGHTED!!!" and kind of spamming it. I've spoken to the Developer on Discord about this and he has said he might look into adding a volume sliders for the characters, so if that's a major turn off for anyone, it might be remedied in the near future. Beyond that, I highly highly recommend this game and buying it.Thanks to the Dev for making this, I may not have a lot of playtime as of this review being written, but I literally replayed the games Demo about 3-5 times, I had so much fun, glad it's finally out and excited for the future of the game and the Dev's future titles too.
_childDocuments_.name: Severed Steel

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel is an adrenaline-pumping, momentum-driven experience that excels at delivering smooth gameplay and nonstop action. The game prioritizes fluidity, ensuring that objectives are clearly highlighted, allowing players to stay immersed in the action without worrying about getting lost. This streamlines the experience, enabling you to focus on the core of the game: pure, unrelenting movement and combat.One of the game’s most exciting mechanics is the player's invulnerability to enemy fire while performing acrobatic moves like jumping, sliding, dodging, and wall-running. This keeps you constantly on the move, forcing dynamic interaction with the environment. The tactical depth is further enhanced by the ability to slow down time, a mechanic that recharges with every enemy kill. This gives you the chance to scan rooms, assess threats, and strategize how to take out enemies efficiently.Adding to the chaos is the arm cannon, a destructible force that allows you to blast through walls, creating new paths or vantage points to ambush enemies. It’s a great tool for breaking up firefights and completing objectives creatively. The lack of a reload system makes the gunplay incredibly fast, with weapons constantly being swapped as you defeat enemies. This keeps the pacing quick and fresh, avoiding the lull that comes with reloading mechanics.Visually, Severed Steel is excellent. The neon-on-black aesthetic offers a stark, high-contrast look that’s easy to read and strikingly effective, especially in the middle of fast-paced action. The electronic soundtrack perfectly complements the high-energy gameplay, fueling the experience and keeping you in the zone.Overall, Severed Steel is an addictive, kinetic rush where every moment pushes you forward, and the blend of tactical decision-making with fast reflexes makes it a standout in its genre.

_childDocuments_.review: My 30 minutes experience, in the second-to-last difficulty, consisted mostly of me changing things in the gameplay options menu to try and make the experience enjoyable. Unfortunately, not enough flaws were remedied by the options. To me, at this time, Severed Steel is a movement shooter where neither the moving or the shooting are fun.Running, jumping and sliding around the maps made it feel like my character was covered in oil and the levels were covered in vaselin. After changing some options in the gameplay menu and trying things out, I managed to achieve the best possible result at this time, which, unfortunately, was not enough to improve the movement for me.I naturally expected for the sliding to turn into running after I let go of the CTRL key, but instead it just kept going, and for too long. The diving feature and the double jump conflict with eachother... I'd say to either have the player do a dive when holding down jump or have the jump, as well as the mid-air jump, behave like diving does. As it stands, rather than the movement feeling grounded and pleasant to pull off, it feels confusing, bloated and quite sloppy.In order for going fast to feel good, going slow needs to exist, both as a thing to be avoided and a thing to give weight to the movement. I believe this is a key issue with the movement in Severed Steel: There is no slow, only fast and faster. I'll use the combat systems of Dark Souls 1 and the latest Lords of the Fallen as an example: One is slow and methodical, giving a pleasant sense of weight and impact to each attack. The other is everlastingly fast, with every weapon being fast no matter its size or weight. Its attacks can also be cancelled and switched into a roll at any given time, completely lacking most senses of weight, impact or meaning to attacks. Severed Steel feels like Lords of the Fallen, with movement in place of combat.As you run, jump and slide around, the crosshairs often move slightly, but without returning to their original place, which served as a wrench tossed into the cogs of my precision. I don't know why this was implemented and, while I can think of reasons why, I don't believe any of them will change the fact that this is ultimately detrimental to the fun of running and gunning.A unexisting feature that I personally missed, and that would have improved my enjoyment by a lot, was aiming. Not even iron-sight aiming, mind you, just a very quick zoom-in tied to my right mouse button. I like slow and powerful weapons, like a Desert Eagle. I like one tapping enemies, specially in the head, but I couldn't do it in here because of the problems mentioned.I believe Greylock Studio members should play some of the most popular movement shooters and seek to understand what is it that makes their moving and shooting enjoyable, because as it stands, Severed Steel suffers much by an (alleged) amateurism from Greylock Studio. There were also problems with audio, UI, and levels.Unfortunately, I don't believe the developers will care about this criticism, if they even read it, as the game seems to be doing just fine with Overwhelmingly Positive and Very Positive reviews, but if Greylock Studio sees any worth in this, I hope they can take it forwards in the Echo Point Nova.I'll be very happy with reforming this review at a later date, should the points made in it this critique change for the better. In the meanwhile, I shall keep the game on my wishlist once more to try out again in a near or distant future, if it receives an updated to improve the running and gunning.

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel is a game that is absolutely beautiful in it's simplicity: a collection of relatively straightforward ideas that come together to form a cohesive whole that results in a greatly enjoyable gameplay loop. If I were to break it down to those elements:-Diving, Sliding and Wall-Running are movement option that also make you much harder to hit by gunfire.-Generous slow-motion meter that refills after kills letting you pick your targets-Weapons are picked up from enemies (and rarely off the arena) and no reloading means you need to watch your ammo count.-The environment is almost 100% destructible.Those "ingredients" are combined with fast-paced gunplay that rewards skill and failure is rarely frustrating because how quickly you can get back into the game. While a little on the short side when it comes to the campaign, it offers a lot of replayability via different difficulty settings and the Firefight mode that lets you play each level with various modifiers and an unlock progression system. Just like in character-action games, it could be considered the "true" game after the campaign.I heartily recommend this title. Music is banging too.

_childDocuments_.review: Here is what the game should plaster on every piece of advertising because it would make me buy in instantly: enemies can't hit you as long as you are doing stunts! Wall runs, dives, and slides all turn you into an invincible killing machine. You regain health and slow mo power with kills. In this game you don't die because you pushed too far, you die because you stopped. It's all about going forward-forward-forward! Have I mentioned that everything is made of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ voxels and you can just blast through walls with a handcannon to get to more enemies? The solution to a fight is almost never to hide or retreat. I love this! The guns feel fun and satisfying and there are definitely some standouts you will be excited every time you get. The campaign is short and the enemy variety isn't huge, but there are plenty of levels past the campaign and other things that help spice up the gameplay. The story isn't the focus here. If you want an FPS that rewards you for keeping your foot on the gas 100% of the time, this is it.
_childDocuments_.name: Severed Steel

_childDocuments_.review: Any game that can mirror Mirror's Edge and its parkour is fun in my book, but this game focuses more on the action side than the parkour side. Gameplay revolves around using parkour moves for i-frames, slow motion, and grabbing guns from dead enemies. There is also a plasma cannon that you acquire after the first chapter that basically lets you bust through walls, and it can be used as an area of effect "grenade" in a pinch.Though the gunplay is satisfying (headshots are awarded with a "ping" sound and a pink burst on heads), the gunplay itself has issues. Some of the guns do not sound great, while some have weighty feel to them when you fire and hear the resounding boom. The visual design for them are also nothing too impressive, but they are at least recognizable, and in a game like this, that is definitely an important concession to make. Also, I would rather have guns that look decent and don't require me to stare at it to figure out what I'm holding, than a great looking gun with tons of detail that doesn't fit the art style.Speaking of which, the visuals are pretty good! The game has its own style which works well, and the tracers and bright lights bring out the action and make things feel like you are moving even faster than you are. The music is not bad, though it's not to my taste, and it's also not what I would have expected to be in a game that is focused on action. The tunes are mostly pretty relaxed, even if there is a very, very repetitive and fast bass line going through most of them, which is what provides a sense of urgency.The story is not the reason why you are thinking of buying this I bet, however it's a serviceable one. Without spoilers yes, there is a beginning and end to the story, though it is simple. If the story was present in just about any other genre of game it would probably be too simple, in fact.Level design is mostly pretty good, with a mix of thematic, structured levels (like a train level, an office level, etc.) as well as more abstract levels that are built out of large cubes, stairs, walls, etc. The latter levels are still grounded in the world of the game, but feel more like a video game level than any "real life" room or building.Finally, the game's campaign is very short. I beat the game on severed steel difficulty in about 2.5 hours or so, which is rather short. However, I fully intend to continue playing the firefight mode, which has you go back into the levels of the campaign and shoot for high scores. You can unlock a few things as well, like "mutations" which change how the game works, as well as what guns you start with, for example. That and the announcement of a level designer coming next year means that even if the short campaign is a deal breaker, there is content on the way, and I am quite hopeful about the prospect of a level editor, as what the game really needs is more content.
