_childDocuments_.review: such a good game, I highly recommend this game to anyone that likes boomer shooters, anything close to doom or dusk, ♥♥♥♥ like that. the destruction in this game is so simple but so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ advanced at the same time. I love to have a huge fight and then walk around the arena and see all of the destruction, all the walls have holes in them, the glass is broken, there are fragments of terrain everywhere.if you like backflips, explosions, and slomo  paired with some pretty good movement and gunplay. you get a super fun shooter that is fun for hours imo.
_childDocuments_.name: Severed Steel

_childDocuments_.review: * Don't let the small time played sway you, I put a LOT of time into the demo, and the full game is even better. *   As a kid growing up in the late 90's / early 2000's, The Matrix and movies inspired by it have given me a serious appreciation for bullet-time and games that feature it.   This game has as much or as little of it as you want. Combine this with solid gunplay, a decent amount of weapon, enemy, and level variation, and a movement system wonderfully similar to Titanfall 2, with a touch of Max Payne for good measure, and you get Severed Steel.    Is there much of a story? No. Do I care? Not even a little. The graphics are pretty, the soundtrack is bangin', and the gameplay is satisfying.   Thanks for making the best non-Matrix Matrix game I've ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: Severed Steel

_childDocuments_.review: The campaign is short but you can tell there's a ton of replay value there, and the extra wave mode and level-editor are welcome additions to squeeze out more play time. The gameplay itself is so fun you'll be looking for reasons to keep going, and the AI is dynamic and fun to fight against, so it feels like replaying missions of FEAR over and over like back in the day.Overall, I definitely recommend this, even to people tiring of the old-school shooter trend, as there's enough fresh here to satisfy anyone that enjoys blowing things up.
_childDocuments_.name: Severed Steel

_childDocuments_.review: The mechanics are top notch for rewarding more stylish parkour-y playstyle rather than being a simple case of breach and clear doing headshots while in slowmo.Fully understanding how some moves work like how diving is your last movement option as you can't chain it into any other parkour move that gives i-frames, made the game click for me. Sticking to walls via wall running, slide kick in the air to get i-frames, diving towards places with cover. Its ALL SO GREAT.
_childDocuments_.name: Severed Steel

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little movement shooter with some unique ideas and a solid gameplay loop, but I have a couple gripes.1. The dive is entirely too restrictive. Being unable to cancel out of the dive feels... janky, at best. Obviously I assume this is to prevent you from chaining invulnerability states forever, but it just feels weird when you dive at a wall and are completely unable to cancel into a wall jump or wall run or anything like that. I'm sure this part of the game gets less awkward as you play more of it, as movement shooters tend to be, but every gamer instinct I have is screaming at me that this just feels wrong, and I can't quite get over it at the moment.2. Some enemies are wayyyy too bullet spongey. I don't necessarily mind this, but when the bulk of weapons you get are low damage rapid fire weapons like an SMG, it's frustrating to enter a room and have to unload several guns worth of bullets into a specific guy. 3. The level destruction mechanic is super cool and by far the best thing about this game, in my opinion, but it feels like it only really exists to make getting from one room to the next easier. You can use it in a combat setting, but I haven't found it particularly useful given how fast paced this game is. It just feels easier to shoot everything instead of trying to make creative usage of the arm cannon. I also wish that regular guns damaged the environment more, anything short of the flamethrower barely leaves a dent in anything. I think if the game felt more like R6 Siege on several layers of crack, that would be really cool, but again, it is what it is, and the mechanic is really cool regardless. Despite the fact that I wrote 3 paragraphs of complaints, I do really like this game, and hope that more movement based shooters continue to come out. If you're looking for a stylish and fun entry in the genre, then you can't go wrong here. Great game, but if I'm being honest it just makes me more excited for a future game from these devs.

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel is a short and sweet high octane FPS with players taking on the role of a one-armed protagonist named Steel as she fights her way through the EdenSys facility.It is worth mentioning right away that though this game  have some semblance of a story if you squint hard enough, it doesn’t make all that much sense, taking a major backseat so that the gameplay can take centre stage. This game does have cutscenes interspersed at certain points in the campaign which are monochromatic stills with only light animations accompanied with sound effects and music. To give some perspective, all the cutscenes in this game have a total length of about three and a half minutes, and honestly, any attempt to give this game a fully fleshed out story would probably just detract from the overall experiencePlayers will go from level to level, running and gunning in order to complete specific conditions to progress. These objectives are varied and help to keep the gameplay feel fresh on each level (e.g. kill all enemies, reach the end of the level, collect an item and escape). Guns can be found at certain points in levels or taken from enemies, both by picking up their main weapon when you kill them or by taking their sidearm from their hip. Killing enemies will fill the player’s slow motion metre which can be activated at any time by holding the right mouse button. Beyond this, Steel is capable of performing what the game refers to as ‘stunts’. These consist of (double) jumping, diving, sliding, and wall-running. Performing any of these actions will make Steel invulnerable to any and all forms of damage, and since most of these stunts can be chained together, with a little bit of practice, a player can be in a constant state of invincibility. This is an incredibly fast game that will not wait for you. Stand still or stop doing stunts for even a brief moment and chances are you will die.Eventually in the campaign Steel’s severed arm will have a cannon installed to it. This opens up new gameplay opportunities as weak enemies will be vaporised by its blast, tougher enemies will be knocked back by the shockwave which also causes them to drop their weapons, and it can be used to blast holes in walls to help create shortcuts to objectives.One thing about Severed Steel that stuck out to me is how customisable the game is. Remember, as long as you are doing stunts you are invincible and as long as you are killing enemies you can activate slow motion. This can make the game quite easy once you can keep pace with it. Increasing the difficulty can help make the game a bit more challenging, but the game includes a bunch of modifiers that you can freely enable to make the game tougher. There’s one that makes you take damage whenever you touch the floor, another that makes all weapons have only one single bullet, and one that prevents you from using weapons altogether. Using modifiers like these will give you bonus score multipliers. There are modifiers that can make the game easier also, but naturally these will give you negative score multipliers.There are other game modes available that can give the game a bit more replayability. For starters there are bonus campaigns from the devs and the community that were added post-release. There is a game mode called ‘Firefight’ which is something akin to an arcade mode in that you pick a level, choose your difficulty, starting weapon, canon, and modifiers. You then play the level aiming for the highest score you can achieve. Your score will then be converted to exp which will level you up and allows you to unlock more weapons and modifiers which you can then use in subsequent playthroughs of the main campaign and in Firefight itself to help you create your own new challenges if that’s what you are after. The other game mode, called ‘Rogue Steel’, is a roguelike mode that sees you playing through a campaign of ten randomly selected levels. Completing a level allows you to select a perk card which can make the run easier or harder. An interesting mechanic in this mode is that at certain points the enemies can choose a perk card for themselves to give them a buff to counter you. All of the interconnected systems add more depth and options to the core gameplay which the player can freely choose whether or not to use. This helps Severed Steel stay fresh no matter how many times you play it, assuming you can look past the fact that the campaign can be beaten in less than two hours.

_childDocuments_.review: this entire review will have spoilers, so if you don't want the game to be ruined for you I'd suggest playing it. I have finished the main campaign within an hour and 30 minutes, on the Severed Steel difficulty.  I usually don't leave long-winded reviews over a game, but this one is such a middle ground for me. On one hand, the game has good mechanics and a very strong premise.  but at the same time, I believe it doesn't truly know how to get everything wrapped up and presentable for the player. I would like to also state the game was gifted to me so I'm not going to make the points of "people pay money for this?" as I have no right to do so. However, I can see the problem some people find in having with it. This isn't a terrible game, but it's not the grandest.  Now usually for games you can look at it and go "this level is drastically different from the previous one I just left," while in this game I questioned if I died or even progressed further into the game. Halfway through I do see a drastic difference, but I believe that the devs got scared to try something different while developing the game and wanted to keep the same aspects to it "corners have lights" "floors have lights." The levels that go against this are so minuscule in comparison to all the similar-looking levels. The game entirely feels like it has 12 different enemy types, which in most games is enough. Go look at the doom 2016, or eternal where the enemies more-over are copied and pasted with some extra ones thrown in. The problem with this game, however, is that it throws many of them all at once and never tries to stray from the set path for how they're placed. Particularly during the middle section of the game, it feels like the enemies were just spam clicked through the level with little to no thought about it. For a game like doom, it has where a new enemy is shown it  by making you acknowledge that enemy is there and you have to go out of your way to find a new way to take it on. In SS, I genuinely flew by new enemies and didn't realize they were there until I took a second to even notice them. (especially the flying ones that go high enough to leave the player's natural viewport.)I don't know if this is a mechanic, a bug, or an oversight. However, many times when my gun had full ammo it just decided to not shoot, I even questioned if I just couldn't count the amount of ammo I had left in the magazine. It most likely is a bug, but it has been such a problem while playing it genuinely killed me multiple times during the play-through where I feel like I just got cheated out of progressing faster by the number of times the gun just didn't want to fire. Very early on, in the first two-three levels, the game teaches you its very simple mechanics, you can slide, jump, jump off walls, and many other movement mechanics. Well, many times I found jumping on walls once you hit a higher speed it will just throttle you. Now I know what many of you might be thinking "well yeah, it doesn't want you to laser past everything," but in my eyes, the game focuses heavily on the movement tech. So why would it want to throttle one of its biggest selling points? If a player wants to rocket across the map, let them. It may just be a bug where it just won't jump off the wall as it's not read, but it really feels weird when the entire time you build up speed the game just drops off. Like many other people mentioned in their reviews, the game sometimes just insanely lags. Many of this can be chalked up to UE4 being a horrible engine in many retrospects, as many games that are made in it seem to always have this problem; but I feel like how simplistic the level design feels, and the lack of very high-end models, this game shouldn't suffer as many lag spikes as it should. When I say lack of reason, I feel like there isn't a reason to finish the campaign. The story entirely is just bland at best, the only boss (as I'm not counting the final level where you burn through doors as a 'boss') is buggy at best and can easily be blown through within 2-3 minutes with ease. I just feel like there isn't enough there during the campaign to really warrant wanting to actually achieve any goals in it outside of the fact to finish a game you paid money for, as previously stated I was gifted this and this is the only time I will be mentioning money.  Additionally, the final level just feels like they ran out of ideas for level design and just decided "let's make the last level 1/3rd of the gameplay." Why couldn't there be a boss that has the same abilities as you? Why wouldn't there be a bigger design, the game has portals that teleport you right? why not use those portals to warp you around killing different bosses, I know the premise is "breaking out," but why couldn't it be developed better than "laser blast through 3 doors."I know the game is new and the workshop is just starting, but I feel like the game is REALLY hooking on the workshop taking off. The campaign itself is so short, and in my opinion lackluster; however, I just feel like the devs are REALLY hoping the workshop does better than the game itself could. I have been following the game since the workshop beta came out, and many of the workshop maps are higher-in-detail and more thought-out than what I feel the devs came up with. I know this game is simplistic at best, but when 99% of the time you can basically just ignore the actual level and just skip to the end, it defeats the purpose of even exploring. There isn't even an incentive to explore the entire level, but many workshop maps during the beta really thought about exploration and even encouraged it to make the map easier and more enjoyable. The game is definitely not bad in comparison to many other indie games, but I just don't think it's really good either. It's in such a middle ground of the mechanics are just good enough to be cool, but are oversimplified to not really warrant using them. (it basically makes you spam slowmo or be a movement god, no in-between.) So I would recommend this game to people who like high-movement-based shooters, but if you're thinking this is a story-driven, high-quality campaign-based game; please spend your time and effort elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm on chapter 3 and really enjoying the game so far. Pacing, feel, visuals and music are incredibly enjoyable. However, I think there are some clunky mechanics that could have been executed better. The dive mechanic cannot be cancelled mid-air (or at least I don't know how as of yet). Sometimes you get stuck diving for a really long time when jumping from up high, and you can't double jump or kick walls to cancel it. This creates awkward situations where you're diving into enemies and want to kick them mid-air but just can't, and often end up passing by them and have to aim backwards. Sliding can also be somewhat clunky in a similar way. There is a lot of non-controlled camera movement which gets in the way of aiming and shooting. I do well at FPS games in general but in this game I feel like I'm depending on the slow-mo to actually be able to aim, which is in my opinion a bad thing, since this is supposed to be a cool fast-paced game.TLDR; I recomend this game for the aesthetics and innovative gameplay, but would love to see some mechanical improvements regarding player movement agency when diving, sliding and trying to aim shots.

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel is good game but it's far from being a classic though.While not perfect the game still deliver some of the most satisfying bullet time combat we've had the chance to witness in the recent years.It's fast paced, the weapons feels great to use and there are many at your disposal to cause some impressive mayhem and chaos.Unfortunately the physics are still a bit clunky, movements are kinda floaty and for me it feels like the character is walking on ice all the time.Nothing too bad but this is the main reason why it prevent this game from being a must have.Severed Steel main character only have one arm and as result she cannot reload weapons, that means you will be constantly changing weapons once they are empty.It's a nice concept and it's actually well done and in my opinion it makes the gameplay more dynamic.The developers recently added a new mechanic to the game with the arm canon and it's pretty fun to use.Levels are pretty short, most of them are well designed but some looks very uninspired and doesn't really fit the fast paced action going on.The graphics are decent, nothing jaw dropping but the unique art style makes up for it.Colors are very bright and it sets a very distinct atmosphere for the game.The story mode is very short, I finished it in around two hours and it's just a succession of random levels without any real connection between them.It was pretty easy except for the burn the estate level with the flamethrowers which was downright terrible.At least there is more after completing the story with the firefight mode and community custom levels that comes with the level editor.I've been playing Severed Steel since the first betas and been following this project since it was still called Impact.The game is good but it's far from being one of the best indie fps like many people claim.Games like Maximum Action or Get To the orange door are better IMHO.Severed Steel is fun to play and that's what really matters in the end, it does get repetitive after long sessions but it's the perfect kind of game to play if you just wanna blow things up and feel like an unstoppable killing machine.Buying it on sale is probably the best option if you are unsure about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I knew going into this that the campaign was short but I was hoping to get my money's worth out of the extra game modes. Unfortunately, they're just not fun to play and have way different pacing and tone than the campaign. If you're looking at this just for the campaign, be aware that $24.99 for 2½ hours of gameplay is definitely not worth it.While the campaign is very good, the two extra game modes (Firefight and the newer Rogue Steel) aren't. Firefight has a meta leveling system where you unlock new starting weapons, arm cannons, and difficulty mutators (which include positives, negatives, and cheat codes). However, it's very grindy with an exponential exp curve that feels like something out of an online game battle pass system. You'll be forced to grind certain levels over and over, stacking difficulty mutators and re-achieving challenges, just to continue to unlock new maps. It's great that there's 42 levels in this game mode, but I was really feeling the grind on only map 11 unlocked.Rogue Steel has a card system rogue-lite element where you pick difficulty modifier cards before each new map. As you work your way through new levels, your score is tallied, modified, and the difficulty continues to ramp up. The announcement for this mode sounded cool on paper, but it's terrible to play. There's no checkpoints mid-level and some of the levels have high enemy counts. Most maps in other modes have 20-25 enemies and the map I stopped my run on had 55 enemies; death means starting the whole map over with nothing to show for it. The worst part is there's no save system between maps; this means you have to run all 10 maps in a row, without exiting the game, in order to receive a score and rewards.I commend the devs for using so many color harmonies other than the stereotypical modern cyberpunk take of blue and purple, but it's sometimes so colorful and saturated that it's hard to look at. There's also a really ugly low quality rust palette used on certain maps (that looks more like a staticky scab) that stands out for the wrong reasons. The levels feel like they were painted from a collection of materials from different authors because you'll get realistic wooden floors next to cartoony metals and sometimes the aforementioned rust added in too. Then there's the complaint about the "cyberpunk" themes... I could write a 10 page essay about how garbage modern cyberpunk has become but for this game it just distills down to a visual theme. The character models look fine, but they look like they're pulled from any generic cyberpunk character pack on a 3D model website.Sure, the campaign is a frenetic, wild ride through a wide variety of colorful levels. The soundtrack is fitting but nothing amazing. Enemies have callouts and swear at you, but it's all the same voice actor. Parts of this game feel like a ton of effort went into it (like player movement and gun play), while some parts feel like bare minimum. I picked this up for $4.99 on a sale and even then I feel a bit let down by the experience. This game is way overpriced for what you get. If the store page piques your interest, wait for a deep, deep sale. Otherwise, I wouldn't recommend this for the average person.

_childDocuments_.review: Severed Steel is a single-player FPS featuring a fluid stunt system, destructible voxel environments, loads of bullet time, and a unique one-armed protagonist. It's you, your trigger finger, and a steel-toed boot against a superstructure full of bad guys. Chain together wall runs, dives, flips, and slides to take every last enemy down. name: Taur
detailed_description: Taur is an action-strategy sci-fi game. Inspired by a multitude of games in classic genres such as tower defense, shooter, real-time strategy and more, creating a unique type of gameplay. Created by one-person indie studio Echo Entertainment. Gameplay Prime Cannon : Control the powerful Prime Cannon, equipped with a primary and a secondary weapon that can be fired simultaneously. Weapons : Unlock and upgrade different weapons, and bring them to bear at any time on the battlefield. Abilities : Unlock multiple, powerful abilities and use them to turn the tide of battle. Build : Use the resources gained from secured war zones to expand your Taur defenses by building a variety of auto-turrets, droids, aircraft and more. Destruction : Every unit, structure, tree and plant is fully destructible, leading to tactical advantages or disadvantages over the course of a battle as the environment is destroyed. Attacks : Plan your defenses for different types of attacks such as full-scale invasions, air raids, tank sieges and infantry skyfall attacks. Imperion : Defeat the increasingly massive armies of the warmongering galactic droid empire known as the Imperion. Campaign Control : Prevent the planet of Taurea, home of the Tauron droids, from falling into Imperion hands. Control of the planet will either be gained or lost over time, depending on your success on the battlefield. Should the Imperion gain full control of Taurea, the campaign will be lost. War Zones : The Taur can only be deployed to one war zone per day, forcing you to abandon the remaining ones. Abandoned war zones may incur loss of control, and their resources are lost, so choose carefully. Resources : Obtain resources by successfully securing war zones. Use them to build new structures, reforge weapons and research new tech. Forge : Use the Forge to reshape the quality and damage of your Prime Cannon weapons. Research : Unlock new tech to be used in battle. Overlord : In order to win the war and end the campaign, you must find a way to defeat the extremely powerful Imperion Overlord in battle.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is half of my dream tower defense.The scale of the combat and the intense firefights that I can help out with is there. I love sniping away at the enemies while I watch my turrets and minions do the work. The fact I get to have so many units can be so fun.The thing this tower defense game is missing is that it has very little feeling of getting stronger and building a base. your turrets are paper and die extremely fast, you have no way to alter the terrain at all, and you also earn no resources until battles are over. That means in battles where you are barely hanging on, getting strings of lucky hits and taking down half the enemy units, you're still just alone, with nothign to do in between each wave.Overall this game feels really polished graphics and mechanics wise, but it just feels like it misses out completely on half of the stuff tower defense games do, while delivering really well on the parts it does have.The other issue is that even an hour or 2 in, your still fighting like 10 enemies at a time. So you are basically sniping a few enemies at a time, with no turrets which is really not that fun. I wish the game would move forward WAY faster. I was hoping to be able to jump in and immediately see the giant battles the game shows us in the store, but it seems you will have to play a LONG time to get there, and even if you do, you might lose it all in one bad mission.TL:DR: I hope they make creating a big setup with lots of turrets quicker, because that is where this game shines, and also make losing turrets a little less devestating. I think most people would be fine with making missions last longer and be harder if they could actually gain more resources during the mission and enjoy the extreme firefights this game was meant to be. (units also being a 1 time thing each mission is a pretty big bore tbh, would definately prefer longer missions with checkpoints for unit respawns)LOTS TO IMPROVE ON, but when the game is in it's zone, it is probably the best tower defense out there bar none. Just let me experience that earlier and more often.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a recommendation, but with some major caveats. I'll break it down into good and bad here. I'll also go in depth on a major complaint I have with the game.The Good:- A fun and relaxing tower defense game- A nice balance between the impact of your towers and the impact of your own manual fire control of the Taur Prime cannon- Very sleek aesthetic, the game and models looks good in a classy indie way. The guardian robots look especially cool with a Greek Hoplite style spear and shield armament- Very nice explosions, satisfying visual feedback and spectacle- Switching taur prime weapons on the fly is cool- Rewarding tech tree and upgrade system- Campaign system with some freedom of choice and some leniency towards occasionally losing missionsThe Bad:- Lack of content. The main campaign can be finished in about 5-7 hours depending on whether you succeed in the first attempt at fighting the end boss. And by that time the gameplay will have gotten quite repetitive, and you will have virtually exhausted the tech tree- Somewhat poor weapon balancing. Certain weapons feel very useless while others are clearly superior like the Ballistic Missile. - Lack of variation between missions. While the different maps are nice, your base layout is always the same. What's more, except for towers that were destroyed on the last mission, the game automatically starts you off with the same layout you finished the last mission with. I'll go deeper into this below, but basically you end up building a jack-of-all trades base and then play every battle with the same layout with very little freedom to adjust and change your base.- Inability to specialize for given map and enemy type. I mentioned this above, but this deserves its own point. Ahead of each mission, you will know what type of enemy force you will face, be it infantry, tanks or aircraft. But since you are forced to carry over your towers from last mission, you will have at least some of your base be completely pointless against the enemy, like SAM sites against infantry or melee guardian droids against enemy tanks or aircraft. And destroying a useless tower to build something else will only refund you the cost at the end of the battle. Why there is no menu to view and make changes to your current base layout in between missions is beyond me.- Lack of unique missions. The main campaign has you hold out for 50 days against randomized enemy attacks until you fight the end boss for the first time. But in all that time there are no other special missions to spice things up. Like they could have made a mission for each time a new advanced enemy type was introduced, like the various tanks or the stealth bombers, just as an example.- Weirdly disconnected campaign system. In the game you're defending planet Taurea from invasion, and each day you're presented with up to three random defensive missions to choose from, these then give you various rewards. But this feels very different from what defending a planet would be like when you would actually fortify and hold specific locations. Also there are never any urban or industrial sectors to defend, always just wilderness.All in all I really like a lot about this game, I just wish more had been done to encourage variation between missions and some more investment into holding on to this planet. All it is right now is a bunch of random wilderness areas for you to arbitrarily fight on, where it could have been so much more. It's also sad that the game is so limiting relative to other Tower Defense games, where each map has a different layout and will need a new defensive plan to beat. I was very engaged from the start until a few hours in when the game started to drag and I really started to miss more variation. I'm not sure the game is worth its asking price right now, but if you really like tower defense games you can give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: is a tower defense, shooter and strategy game hybrid with a sci-fi setting. The technologically advanced but peaceful world of Taurea refuses to share its knowledge with the militaristic Empire: this situation becomes a casus belli to warrant a full-scale invasion of the planet. Entrusted with complete control over the Prime Cannon, an experimental Tauri battle fortress, players will have to face increasingly difficult battles, manage resources, plan technology research and ultimately defeat the Overlord in command of the invading army.🔵 🔴 Let's start with the good points. First of all, I really want to commend how Taur manages to blend mechanics from three different genres without making any of them too predominant, instead striking a very accurate balance between them that ultimately works and brings variety in the various gameplay stages between one battle and the other. There is a good variety of things to research, upgrade and experiment with: finding the optimal combination between offense, defense and utility skills is all about trying out new things until you get a hang of everything.The battles in this game start off slow, but eventually become epic sieges where you'll command a fortress bristling with guns against entire armies - paired up with quality effects, physics blowing enemies away left and right, and destruction effects, engagements become something glorious to see. The visuals are simple as far as geometry goes but make up for that with effects, lighting and other technical eye candy that contribute majorly in making the game look good. Last but not least, the pacing is one of the best i've seen lately, and as long as you don't screw up too bad, the progression always proposes challenging but never unfair levels.Now onto the bad side. The most annoying factor in Taur would be the RNG-based primary weapon upgrade system, which relies on an ARPG-like rarity system rolled at every upgrade tier. One moment you can have a Legendary Tier 4 gun, and then a moment later find yourself with an Awful Tier 5 primary, much worse than a normal Tier 1 one! Needless to say, it can become frustrating and extremely expensive in terms of resources, to keep trying your luck.The variety of enemies could use a boost, as 3 infantry units, 3 tank and 3 aircraft types get stale pretty soon, also there are no real "late-game" enemies to match your superior firepower by then - only quantities of them. Certain weapons, towers and abilities are worthless investing in, because others are just better at doing a specific role without downsides.🎮 The gameplay of Taur is divided into Battle Preparation, Research and Combat.Is done in an overview menu showing the planet and up to three available encounters of various types, each rewarding a different amount of Energy, your prime resource, and a variable amount of Crystals, used for both research and building defenses. A gauge at the top shows your control rate opposed to the Imperial one, and if the Empire gains 100% control of Taurea, as a result of several losses on your side in battle, the campaign will end and everything will have to be done from scratch. Choosing carefully the next engagement based on what resources you need and what your defenses are at the moment is fundamental to not get overwhelmed, striking the enemy where it hurts.Is twofold. Most of it is done in the tech tree, featuring various branches leading to better technology, upgrades, abilities and tower types. Each stage has a cost in Crystals and Energy, increasing the further it goes. Passive upgrades such as better unit health, armor, or ammo capacity for prime weapons have multiple stages of progress each more costly. Be wise in what you choose as there is no respec function. The other part of research is done in the weapons terminal, used to increase primary weapon power with the aforementioned RNG based system - which can make or break your most powerful defense. Is wave-based as in tower defenses, but without any counter. Enemies often come from all sides and not on pre-determined paths. Tower building can be done in a small area around your Prime Weapon and slots have to be unlocked for a price. Each tower has health and can be destroyed, in which case nothing can be built in that slot until the next battle - 100% of the tower cost is refunded. In case of total destruction, you can start the next level as new, all materials refunded.Having a balanced defense composed by units, diverse tower types and using abilities at the right moments are all essential factors to winning the fights, often against overwhelming odds. Units cannot be commanded but instead act on their own, and quite well. Wielding the prime cannon, and being able to swap between 4 primary and 4 secondary weapons, you will be an integral part of the defense, supporting your units from the fortress. 🔩 There are no bugs, stability issues or other technical problems to report. Optimization, given the somewhat simple graphics, is not the best as GPU consumption was around 90-100% in 1440p, 144hz - however it goes to a much more acceptable 60% if the frame rate is limited to 85fps. At high refresh rates the game is not well optimized. Even if the graphics are not very complex, the high number of on screen enemies and excellent effect quality can become heavy especially later on when battles become huge. At least a mid-tier machine is recommended in my opinion to run the game smoothly. Taur is an original, well executed tower defense with several unique twists to the formula. It has some dents but overall is a fun and engaging game that TD and strategy fans will enjoy for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: After a while, I now have to admit that I'm eating my words and change my review. TAUR got off to a rocky start, but it's safe to say that the developer seems to be committed to improving upon it, especially seeing how they've been determined enough to rise from the grave and update it several more times since I published my initial review. I will admit some of the original issues still stand, listed below:#1: There is no autonomous weapon reloading, in order to reload a weapon you have to swap to it, hit the reload key, then sit there and do nothing for the 5-10 seconds the reload takes, this is time where you are likely being attacked and taking damage where you can't fight back because if you swap to another weapon all reload progress is lost and you have to do it again.#2: Enemy scaling at the endgame gets a little crazy, while I haven't encountered a single Air Raid mission since playing the new update, which was my grand pet peeve beforehand as they were almost always a guaranteed loss if you didn't have an absurd amount of aircraft control centers or designated AA to counter them. I do remember they were the silver bullet to kill a run, but new tools at your disposal like the special super-units seem like they're designed to be a hard counter to that.#3: Difficulties don't feel accurately portrayed, an endgame 'light' resistance mission will still drop swarm after swarm of aircraft, infantry, and vehicles on you, the only difference between that and an 'extreme' seems to be that extreme drops them all at once and in much shorter gaps.Now, onto the pros of this new update:#1: A persistent endgame content option in the form of the newfound resistance/rebels, which are basically three squads full of super-units you can create and deploy on your own. They can be upgraded through their own separate tech tree and they also have ranks, which they go through and get even more dangerous as they survive battles and level up. This basically lets you tweak and make three entire teams of very strong super-infantry that you can deploy to a battle in order to help even the odds. As you'll always be replacing, rearranging, and improving these guys...There's now a new thing to do during the final loop.#2: The added 'super' units, which come in the form of a large experimental hovertank and a gigantic space-battleship that orbits the map, are a massive endgame resource sink but also a really powerful utility to help you clear hurdles you otherwise couldn't manage. They don't level up like the rebels do, but they are persistent and each upgrade makes them more and more dangerous. Take my advice, once either of them are maxed out you basically have a deployable boss you can send to any mission you want which heals itself over time when it's not in combat. Give them a reprieve between missions if they take too much damage and they should be ready to fight again after a day or two.#3: General rebalance and tweaks to gameplay do offer more options and try to get you out of a sandwich. For example, the new trade system means that overabundances of a resource you might have can be traded out for one you need instead of having to hope and pray you get it from an RNG mission reward. If you've got a surplus of energy and not enough tower cores or crystals, the merchants will probably be able to hook you up.Considering how they still haven't abandoned the title and are very much still keen on providing new content even if it nearly takes half a year between releases? I can no longer knock them, as they have fixed some of the issues I've had with the game and are trying to improve it, even if certain choices (Such as the specialist heavy units that the enemies got an update or two ago) might make it harder.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a kind of game I always wanted. Visually it is nice to look at, upgrade tree and resource management is an engaging task.There are 3 reasons I can't recommend Taur in it's current state:1) While I was engaged in a loop to see how the strategy will evolve once I have more tools at my disposal and enemies grow in numbers, I had to do a lot of manual shooting with that cannon, and, no offence to designers of the game, but that was a terrible idea. Some auto-aiming could have gone a long way. Shooting enemies in this kind of fashion actually looks cool and makes you fell like a part of the action but prevents from observing the battle and analyzing it. By the end I realized that I should have switched it up with a less frustrating gun, but it was too late: hours of frustrating aiming were wasted. Developers should ditch that gun, I felt like I have forgotten how to use a mouse.2) Sudden spike in difficulty. One moment I'm easily overcoming a mission of any difficulty, 2 missions later enemies come in some inadequate hordes. It felt like something is off the first time it happened. Maybe something worked not as intended. I think it was around day 50, don't remember, stopped looking. 3) And the biggest problem is with the format itself. Because I was too busy shooting enemies, I couldn't really learn much about my structures' and units' effectiveness. I was hoping that I'm making some good strategic decisions when researching, upgrading and building the base, but I'm just not sure. Maybe I lost because it was not an optimal build, but I just didn't learn much from my failure. The wave was just too big. While the first two problems can be fixed with making player agency more comfortable and re-balancing the game. The third one probably lies in a fact that the arsenal of the player (guns, abilities and structures) are more like toys in a looter game: pick your style, play it the way you like it. But at the same time game wants you to be strategic: there is a fail state, you can't just grind forever. While there are planty of good ideas there are some design choices that are wrong IMHO.

_childDocuments_.review: I only got a chance to play this game after the dev had released the first balance update, so I can't throw down many of the reviews that claimed the game was too hard or un-intuitive  at the very beginning. I can however say that the fact that the SOLO developer listened to all those complaints and posted and update within a day of the game being released should speak volumes about the amount of effort they are willing to put into this game. On that note, I am currently on day 107, and am yet to encounter a single bug which to me is bewildering.I managed to defeat the campaign on my first attempt (although I lost against the overlord on the first two encounters), and I enjoyed every second of it, but it was definitely not a cake walk, the game never became a mindless click to kill grind machine, but instead keeps you engaged the whole time. The game didn't force you to go through an extended and boring tutorial, but instead guides you through the first few levels with very handy and unobtrusive tip boxes (such as pressing left shift key to switch between ground and air aim which a lot of people seem to have missed, or are just rather poor at leading targets). The tech progression system and pace is quite arguably the greatest and most enjoyable that I have encountered in any game that I can remember, although I thought it was slow at first, once you get past around day 40, it gets much easier to see where the game is going.For the most part, I neglected any and all abilities aside the shield charger, but as the game progressed past day ~60-70, you really need to start utilising your abilities, which I believe any well balanced game should do, and this makes the game that much more enjoyable.All of the explosion effects and weapon systems just felt super polished, and I really liked the feel of the initial railgun, so I kept that as my main weapon and upgraded it, which got me all the way through the game (using the beam exclusively for the overlord shield) which has a pleasant resemblance to Warframe, where you chose a weapon you like, and upgrade it, rather than being forced to use some lame gun because all others seem like pea shooters compared to it. Some of the maps have terrain between enemy spawn zones and your tower, which some seemed to complain about, but all you have to do is use indirect weapons rather than wait for the enemy to get right in front of you. Don't have any indirect weapons upgraded? Don't choose that battle! The small touch of being able to choose which battle to partake in to get the resources you want for your next big upgrade changes the game so dramatically, and I don't think I could imagine a better way it could have been done.

_childDocuments_.review: Puny game. It is fun though!This is a "Wave defender" turret game. It's less a "tower defense" because the tower building element is not particularly large. There is no path or pathbuilding, you aren't building tower combos and you aren't interacting all that much with the towers midgame. Except to cuss if they get blown up. In reality, this is a turret defender game, aim a gun to skillshot the baddies, rapidly swap weapons for maximized firepower and apply cooldown abilities to control the field and boost your defenses.As you progress through a campaign your towers grow in number and power, which is good because the enemies will quickly outgrow what you can deal with with just your turret and human reflexes, a line of friendly grunts will take and hold the frontline while a small variety of support weapons and air units starts suppressing incoming threats while you focus on applying crowd control or direct damage where needed. The towers you choose to use are largely just a matter of what your stage in the game requires, initially a small group of friendly grunts can hold the line fine, but eventually if there is even a small gap in your defense line your base will come under attack immediately, similarly you need to build Anti-air, Anti-crowd and anti-tank in a balanced manner, or else you're wide open. The game operates in a roguelike manner, survive a certain amount of scenarios and beat the boss to beat the game, a small variety of scenarios keeps things interesting and a mission / resource picker system lets you / forces you to pick your upgrades carefully. The time this takes to finish is by no means enough for you to even get close to fully upgrading all the things, so you do need to make some style choices for your tower setup, turret weapons and unit spawners. This is actually pretty cool, and frankly this is the most replayable element of this game, can you beat the boss? And how will you do it? Past the boss there is an infinity mode, which is where you can start filling in the checkmarks to get a 100% upgraded base which is pretty cool. But at this point you've experienced the whole game. It took me two evenings to reach the stage where I had essentially finished all the content and there is nothing left but experiencing the random challenges in new random configurations, the upgrade system doesn't have the kind of depth to make the grind perpetually satisfying. I guess if the game can be improved, it'd be more enemy types, more tower types, and more varied spawn systems for enemies. For one I'dd like it if the scenario types got mixed up with some randomized event spawns, for example a tunnel that opens up and starts spewing a horde of infantry, or a sudden rain of tank drop pods. I.E, instead of scenarios being a single element and following that recipe, it'd be fun if stuff was a little more mixed up and randomized, for the sake of variety.At this point you might assume that the game is'nt  worth the buy, but let me sell you on this game a bit. Every step of the game actually manages to be engaging. Initially you have no upgrades and very few towers, so all the little enemy minions feel very close and personal, soon enough your upgrades will be managing the little minions so your job becomes sniping the slightly bigger brutes and specialists, who in turn you have to leave to your automated defenses as even bigger stuff starts showing up, in ever greater numbers.The game does a good job at generating a screen full of enemeis and gridlock circumstances where all your stuff is firing on every cylinder with enemies right at your gates (something you only really experience in the very best defense games, Kingdom rush for example). At it's best, this game is FUN. This game is also pretty, and it sounds good, the simple.... vector based(?) light diffused low-poly shapes work together to make it look like an admirably designed strategy game, it reminds me of Supreme commander and Homeworld. I expect I'll be beating the final boss a couple more times before I shelve this game, the first run was a victory on hard, so i's time to try the brutal mode, at which point I'll probably have spent 3-4 evening on it, which is quite alright for a 25$ game investment.

_childDocuments_.review: Need stats! Game play is repetitive, but that's ok for game you just want to jump into a quick session or two of wanting to blow stuff up after a long day at work type thing. But there are no stats for your towers. And no way to replay a level. So there is no really good way to tell if your offense/defense config is optimized or which towers are doing what. The upgrade panel shows limited properties. "Upgrade to +10% damage"..... 10% of what? No way to tell until you go into the build menu in-game. And then only if your building a new tower. Adding in a post game stat page would do wonders for replay value. After beating the main 'boss', there really feels like little to no replay value in continuing at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Unusual tower defense.Two races of drones are fighting each other. One of them decided to entrust its protection to us.The gameplay features an unusual tower defense.The goal is always to protect the main building. There is a tower on it, which we control manually. She can make simple shots or launch a rocket (becomes stronger after pumping).There is a global campaign. Every battle is a day of enemy invasion. It's kind of like stages. For their passage we get resources and make progression to our defense. Every day the attacks are getting stronger, but our power is growing.In addition to the main tower, we can place our assistants on the battlefield - the rebels, they fight on our side.Enemies are quite diverse, from small drones to large powerful mechanisms.Consider the pros and cons of the game, sum up.+ Nice graphics.+ Excellent music and sound design.+ Good progression of our city.+ Many support units that fight for us.+ Many kinds of enemies.+ Great battles.+ - Sometimes it is very difficult to see specific targets. You have to strain your eyes. Some will like it, some won't.+ - In my opinion - there is some protracted process. Long walk to epic battles.- Enemy air units are very hard to hit.At first, the fights are simple, but over time they turn into battles of epic proportions. Fans of unusual tower defenses may like it.

_childDocuments_.review: A tower defense game that tries to break the mold by throwing the player into the hot seat as the Prime Cannon.  Unfortunately this game just about whiffs on everything that is fun about a tower defense game.  The Prime Cannon is utterly impotent, and the AI controlling your towers is fairly impotent as well.  Resources are really limited which makes the game more of a chore and a nuisance than a challenge.  Good AoE options are scarce, most of them scatter large groups of enemies dealing 33% of their hp, making having lots of AoE options counter-intuitive.While the idea of having powers is nice, they too are fairly "meh".  Having the ability to slow time for 6 seconds isn't that impressive when most of your guns take 8 seconds to reload.  Thus it becomes a boring chore to participate in the fights since your main purpose is to kill high priority targets with extremely weak weapons (good luck getting legendary level X weapons like I lucked into) that spend 90% more time not shooting than they are capable of actually of firing downrange.  While the artstyle is passable, the amount of clutter and crap aiming against small targets makes your Prime Cannon feel even more impotent since even if you're a god you'll miss ~50% of your shots against regular enemies.  While having all the weapons is neat, there's really only 2 weapons that are efficient against swarms of enemies or high priority targets.All in all, you're missing out on about 1 hours worth of content with 5 hours of grinding.

_childDocuments_.review: Not even remotely fun until a complete balance overhaul.While the elements of a pretty nice game are all here - nice graphics, quite innovative approach to TD, engaging basic gameplay loop - it simply doesn't work together as it is.First of all, and most glaring is the "defeat loop": the game only gets harder with each passing day, but your defensive buildings won't persist between battles: if one battle wipes some of your towers - you are likely to fall into spiral of defeat: buildings are costly, and it's entirely possible that rewards for winning a battle are less than the cost of towers you lost; and all the next missions  And that's only for winning with some losses. If you outright lose a battle - it's very likely that you will lose majority of your towers in the process, and it's simply impossible to recover from that.Secondly, just the raw units' stats seem to be off: e.g. enemy tanks' wave can quite literally oneshot your tower if you happen to have no shield - they don't attack anything else but your tower, and every shot deals a very substantial damage, so even if you got a few HP upgrades, your tower might still go down before you kill them - it's a simple DPS check of you vs them. And if you lose - well, it's a defeat spiral even if you lose no other towers (because you won't be getting victory spoils).Basically, the game eschews all the traditional TD values - there's no room to experiment, to retry, to find out working strategies; you're not allowed any mistakes in the entire campaign run (see "defeat loop"), you have to win every single battle, and you have to pursue a very narrow "optimal strategy" (e.g. gettings shields is a huge priority for instance) in order to be able to work through campaign.To top it more - even your tower weapons seem to be given absolutely no balancing, as they only start decent, but fall off the power curve extremely quickly. Your basic cannon & mortar are fine on day 1-5, but on day 20 they do very little  if you do a lot of upgrading (without any upgrades you're likely lost already to tanks, see above).It doesn't seem like devs ever tried to let any other people play their game. It's entirely possible that if you know enough about how exactly the game works and plays - winning the campaign wouldn't be terribly hard. However, it's also very evident that if you don't have any prior knowledge - then gaining such knowledge isn't fun at all, as you're required to spend hours beating early campaign battles only to fail something on, say, day 15 or 20, lose one battle, and with it - lose all hopes of winning without restarting from scratch.

_childDocuments_.review: The games fun enough and looks nice, but its too expensive for what youre getting, and the balance is pretty heavily off.The games not complex, some basic pro/con balance should have been set in stone when designing the enemies and players weapons and defenses, and there should have been more weapons, abilities, maps and one or two more invasion types/game modes.The game doesnt have mini bosses or complex enemies, it just ramps up by throwing more trash at you, but youre not equipped to deal with huge numbers of trash, you have only 1 decent personal weapon with splash that you can fire every 15 seconds or so (great disappointment to people like me who like explosions) and your bases defenses, which while chimeras (which are HE cannons) are great at dealing with large numbers of ground enemies as they have splash, damage, range and knock down, you have no flak to deal with large numbers of aircraft, just guns that miss 90% of the time, SAMs that dont have anywhere near the volume of fire you need or little lasers without the range to stop bombers actually getting to you.Without getting too into it, youre left with 4 of the 8 personal weapons being actually useful (miniguns, laser, big rocket and auto AA missiles), another 4 basic defenses (guardians, rangers, chimeras and interceptors) plus the talos missile defense, a shield and some large weapons that you cant field in numbers high enough to really appreciate, so whats it matter what you pick for those out of the remaining 2 choices each they have.Even though you have a really drawn out upgrade tree thats much smaller than it looks, the game really needs tiered upgrades to flesh it out, so that instead of unlocking the useful defenses and then forever gambling with the forge to upgrade your personal weapons, a defense can upgrade and sidegrade, for example the Talos could have you choose between upgrading it to redirect the missiles it intercepts or be able to intercept many more to save space. Theres plenty of room for those kinds of mechanics in the game.The game just doesnt have enough in it, and the balance cuts that number down by making things useless.Also, if youre going to make the levels only a minute or two long, make more maps or make them more interesting to look at.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid TD. Day one I've had zero bugs, load issues, stutters, ect. Great release. Pros:-Game play is fun and exciting.-Music is nice and relaxing.-Graphics are very nice indeed. -You can "ESC" smash through stat screens when you are in a hurry to get to the next mission.-Resource management is very important. You can't just favor one side of the tech tree and expect to survive.-Game ramps up slow with easy to understand, unintrusive game help tips.-Decently sized tech tree with ample amount of units/abilities/support structures. In between:-Missions are short. Even for a TD game. Could be that I'm still just early on in the game (@ day 37 currently). Great if you don't have a lot of time for long game mods, but very lacking if you are expecting more. (Edit: Post day/mission 50 the difficulty and time spent per map go up).-Only one game difficulty that ramps up over time. You either keep up, or die and leave a negative review.  -Rocks exist.Cons:-No co-op. I know it's a tower defense game, but something just screams it would work here with a few tweaks.-There is only the campaign mode currently. No endless or survival maps. (Edit: False. Post final boss kill, the game opens up unto an endless mode that allows you to finish filling out the tech tree, upgrading weapons, and changing out turrets/units as you see fit.)-No built in map editor for community content. Replayability could suffer because of this.-The price point after the release sale seems a bit much for what the game is. If more content is delivered over time, then it seems spot on. (Edit: After finishing the game, I no longer agree with this opinion. It was worth what I paid for the stupid amounts of fun I had today).

_childDocuments_.review: Taur is a tower defense game located in a faraway planet, which is under attack by a foreign robot race. The goal of Taur is to build a bastion composed of multiple turrets and fight the enemy in different points of the planet each day, while also developing the structures at our disposal and researching new technologies. The enemies, unlike other tower defense games, do not follow paths in the map but rather spawn around the tower and attack it.In Taur, we control a single tower with two fire modes and (eventually) different abilities, both of which can be exchanged later in the game in favour of newly researched weapons and skills. The very first levels will see us, the players, manually shooting the enemies as the only possible way to win, since the game uses requires resources to research and build new turrets and structures, resources that hardly are available at the start of the game. This is my first gripe with Taur: every new game start sloooooowly: it's just you, shooting enemies that spawn is small waves and slowly make their way to you. There's no difficulty, it's just an initial phase that you have to get through.After the initial phase, the situation gets quite... strange. There are a few levels of the right difficulty, but after those the curve just spikes: the first time the game spawned a new unit against me, it spawned three of them. These units were tanks with missile launchers that literally one-shot me because I had no missile defense, which was useless before that point in time. Then, the level after that spawned a mass of small enemies three to four times larger than anything I've ever seen before: another lost round. After losing three rounds in a row, the game just spawns three normal tanks against me, which did little to no damage, and the round is an easy win. The difficulty is, in fact, very inconsistent and it's easy to find an incredibly hard level between easy ones, or a very easy level between incredibly difficult ones.Progress in Taur is measured by the current level and in the number of resources at our disposal: energy and power cores. These last two elements are collected at the end of each level, even if we fail at defending the place. Energy is used for literally everything: research, buy new construction slots and towers, while power cores are used only for the construction slots and towers. The problem here lies in the slowness for which power cores are obtained: in order to build a turret you have to first unlock its construction slot (energy + corresponding power core) and the purchase the tower itself (again, energy + one or more power cores).For each level, you tend to get just from one advanced power core to a handful of basic ones, not depending on the difficulty of the level, but on some seemingly random parameters (thus, difficult scenarios can give fewer rewards than easy ones). The worst situation you can find yourself in is when you need basic power cores, but none of the levels will give you one, sometimes for two-three consecutive days. This makes you stuck with your current composition and unable to change or upgrade it, since all advanced structures also require basic cores.It is undeniable: Taur looks very nice in its coloured graphics and light effects and when the screen gets filled with explosions, enemies and aircrafts drifting around the game gives the feeling of a very great battle going on. Even here, though, there are aspects that could use some improvements: models look blurry when the zoom-in function of the game is used and the game just can't run a 60fps, for some reason, and instead ranges to 48 to 56 fps at all graphical settings and situations (small or large battles): the strangest thing is that sometimes very large battles get higher frames than small ones, for seemingly no reason.While Taur needs some proper balancing in both difficulty and progress speed, the game is quite fun and can boast massive battles with tons of units on the screen, giving that epic feeling in some of its levels. The game can also be played in small sessions, which can be handy for those players that just can't play for hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game on sale and yet I STILL don't recommend it.TLDR - It's fun for a little while, but it gets boring pretty quick. There is no real end game, so once you beat it you're unlikely to ever want to play it again. Zero replay-ability in my opinionI'll start with the good stuff, the gameplay loop is fun at first, defend and upgrade your stuff between rounds. The core gameplay loop is honestly fun in the beginning. Having a little control over the primary gun and everything else being automated was a good balance of interaction and automation.However I feel the Cons definitely outweigh the Pros for this title...The gameplay loop while being fun at first gets really old after a couple hours. The only reason I played beyond about 2-3 hours was because I wanted to max out all the research for the turrets that I enjoyed using. Unfortunately that made very little difference as you get late game. (Seemed about the same with or without upgrades to me)The final boss of the game just gets thrown at you over and over until you're able to defeat him, which is super annoying. It basically forces a loss on you which requires you to rebuild your base and your rebels morale takes a hit which you have no control over.Also every time you lose a level you'll need to rebuild your base which is also super annoying. They do have a button for quickly rebuilding what you had previously. However you're constantly trying to improve and change things up to see what works better. I found that how you organize your towers doesn't seem to honestly matter much either.I just got so bored with the same 5-10 levels that look and play the same, no real variation in play style required. For a $25 title, I expected a lot more variety. (I got the game for about $19 on sale and still felt it wasn't worth it in the end.)I also was not impressed with how inaccurate the manual aim stuff tends to be, you get this little green laser to see where you will hit. A lot of the time 50% or more of my shots would miss despite being aimed directly at what I intend to hit.I wish we could manage the organization and setup of our base between rounds, but you can only change things mid match while you're fighting stuff. Poor design, could have been easily fixed by having a logistics window to switch up your design between fights.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR review: Its not bad. Its not good. Taur is just ok. There is fun that will last until Taur gets too repetitive and stale for you. Also, to me, Taur feels like Unity was used to make a tech demo showing off physics, destructive/fragmentary effects, and some crude AI which would explain why it feels a bit shallow as a game.-----------------------------------everything else------------------------------------Taur is slightly unique as far as tower defense games go given that its a bit of a hybrid between turret defense and a primitive point-and-click on things until they die game. In fact, the genre changes from a point-and-click to a tower defense as the player progresses. The player must research towers and accumulate resources to place them, so winning battles early game is up to the player's ability to point and click on enemies since they won't have many towers to place if at all. It can get very hard to keep up once you experience that first major bump in difficulty and don't have enough firepower or automated defenses. Honestly, I really hated Taur because of this.But by being stubborn and persisting, and the direction new updates took the game (the rebel forces help), Taur does get better as it slides further into turret defense. It can also become quite satisfying as the screen becomes filled with crap attacking you and it all explodes into cubes and scraps that fly everywhere.There's also a strategic meta game when it comes to research where making the right choices on upgrades can have a tremendous effect on the ease of a battle as the game gets harder.There is one major dumb thing in Taur that really bothers me. Its how the game handles upgrading player point-and-click weapons. Upgrading weapons in the forge, Taur shows the player a min-max range the player weapon is capable of, but its not handled as 'weapon inflicts between min-to-max damage on hit'. Instead, the forge randomly picks a number in this min-max range which I presume is the actual, fixed damage the weapon does. Upgrading a weapon increases its min-max value no matter what, but the damage it deals can go down from where it was. By a lot. Its really lame!Another stupid thing is its REALLY EASY to lose track of the cross hair as more and more enemies fill up the screen and you can't tell where you're shooting unless you RMB to zoom in.Anyway, Taur can be fun and is kind of short. Its lacking a bit of variety and could stand to do some more with itself if it had more enemies, event battles, and bosses. Unfortunately, there's only 1 boss. It appears at day 50 and every 25 days afterwards and it will absolutely crush you until you've progressed enough to defeat it. And as you work your way up to defeating that boss, Taur is recycling the same handful of maps, battle types, and enemies. When the boss is defeated, you're rewarded with a lame text ending. You have the option to continue the same save cleaning up the tech tree and absolutely crushing giant waves of enemies. This actually is kind of fun until that feeling of stale repetitiveness creeps in and it all just feels boring. Honestly, Taur is very shallow as a game. This shallowness lends itself to making Taur feel more like a tech demo showing off physics and graphic fragmentation.Taur is ok but a little short. It is yet another game where if steam had a 'maybe' choice in between yes and no I'd pick that. $25 is a bit pricey. It goes on sale for $20 on Steam from time to time which is still a little pricey, but more fair. The good news is the developer is continuing to support and add things to the game. No matter what, the game isn't bad. But its not a must buy either.Can't wait for their sequel Re-Taur'ded. I hear its special!

_childDocuments_.review: A unique and refreshing take on the tower defense genre. There's something immensely satisfying about seeing 25 B52 bombers raining down payloads upon (ignorant savages) tiny robots. Enemy variety is excellent, the recent additions of rebels and superweapons have made adapting to different missions much easier, since beforehand you'd usually build around automatically losing one or two scenarior. With this they've also remedied the complaints about resource starvation with the trade system, and fixed running out of one specific resource before everything else. Highly recommended, although it does get tedious waiting for the overlord to spawn after you've got everything fully upgraded.

_childDocuments_.review: I generally enjoyed the game for a single play-through. Wouldn't buy unless on sale.I only give a low ranking because two supposedly key mechanics, the rebels and the sentinels, don't seem to have any actual representation in the combat part of the game, and I've found that annoying enough to write a review and give a thumbs down. To explain, those two "units" previously touted as new features or game "expansions" are just background elements like an additional skill tree that improves on "units" that are not visible in play. So, there is no way to connect the investments in those "units" to any aspect of the play or outcome of battles.  It just ruins a key part of the game which is the strategy around investing your resources to get and upgrade units that have an obvious function in the game play.   I would also add that in the same way, the trade aspect is very simple and is just a small expansion on resource management with the so-called "factions" uninfluenced by player action and therefore irrelevant - its just there for the game's sale pitch but doesn't really do anything for game play.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, the visuals of this game are very well done and satisfying to watch, and while the gameplay seems very in depth at first, you quickly realize how shallow it is.The first few levels feel fun and satisfying, especially seeing the visuals of everything for the first time and unlocking new tech and trying it out.The game quickly goes downhill from there, mainly because of these issues:- Very small and for the most part uninteresting tech tree. I found myself consistently unlocking new techs and being disappointed by them because everything is too well balanced (the highest tier artillery turret did next to nothing) . The only thing you can upgrade for the majority of structures is how much health they have. - An extremely unsatisfying endless resource grind, especially for unimpressive end game tech.- Lack of diversity of enemies ( few variants of infantry, tanks, and planes, but nothing really unique aside from the end game boss which I didn't make it to in my 2 hours). - The sound effects could use some work (explosions sound like a distorted crash symbol, which I personally found out of place and pretty annoying).The game does do some things (very) right:- Visuals are fantastic, especially particle effects and lighting. The low-poly matte styling is easy and fun to look at.- Everything is super polished. You can tell everything from the AI behavior to the building system had a ton of time put into them, and work great.- The difficulty is at a good level. I found myself challenged and occasionally losing levels, but able to address my tower's weaknesses and recover without being completely crippled. By the end of my 2 hours of gameplay, I had most of the tech tree unlocked, I was at stage ~30, I had about half of my towers module slots filled, and the game was just not feeling very fun anymore. The game definitely has some potential (what features are in the game currently work well, and are highly polished), but is 100% not worth $25 right now given the lack of content (explored most of it in 2 hours).
_childDocuments_.name: Taur

_childDocuments_.review: Not well tuned/playtested. Unfriendly difficulty curve. No sense of progression between campaigns. After two failures, one on easy mode, I don't have any reason to go back; it takes too long to try out a new strategy in a completely new campaign.I think part of the problem is that there are too many upgrade paths available from campaign 1, so there can be too many variables to figure out what works and what doesn't. This is also structured more like x-com (albeit with shorter campaigns) than, say, a traditional RTS where you can replay a failed mission. This is fine if you're clear that you're buying an x-com-like, but most of the marketing seems to sell it as a more traditional RTS. (And most roguelikes are not targeting 2hr+ failed attempts, either.)The x-com-like component means an individual mission failure compounds, which again is made worse for new players by the too-broad upgrade options. Plenty of other games have solved these problems well, so there's little excuse for this one to neglect that element to the extent that it does.(and yeah the weird mouse acceleration thing bugged me too.)

_childDocuments_.review: The concept of the game is great, the implementation is done by an absolute sadist and is terrible.The UI is decent but leaves some things to be desired, but it's mostly the gameplay itself. "light waves expected" ending up with more enemies than an "extreme" map.Every platoon or building you have will be destroyed in short order by a map going from manageable enemy numbers at wave 1 to 5x more than what you could ever handle regardless of ingame progress at wave 2. And that is on normal difficulty. Said buildings need to be purchased with resources, but if you lose the building you also lose the resources, and getting back those resources to be able to rebuild would take multiple victories, which means a single defeat can and will spiral you into a campaign end. In addition, you get to choose between 2-3 maps to play on at a time, but even if you win that one, the others you didn't choose add a 'abandoned' penalty, so gaining back points takes a ton of victories. Not to mention with some maps having higher penalties than rewards forcing you to choose that map. Aiming is also ♥♥♥♥♥♥, with projectile weapons not hitting anywhere close to where you're aiming making it all even harder. And the laser requires such precision with small units that it's nigh unusable against anything but tanks.I love the concept, but the implementation is just terrible.
