_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER: I think this game is well worth the $10 price tag.  Seeing all the insanely positive reviews, however, I feel a need to manifest a sort of balance in the universe in pointing out a lot of the gaping flaws in this title.I'll preface my critiques with this; the rhythm-combat of this game is exceptional.  This mechanic is what makes this game an easy sell.However...Nearly everything else is pretty lackluster.  Here's what I mean;-The game tries way too hard to be an Undertale in its design outside of combat.  Seriously, the entire UI and character design is virtually the exact same excepting the inventory screen.-The game's story tries so hard to convince the player that it's a woke abstract existential masterpiece and that, as the narrative and "absolute truths" are revealed to you, you're supposed to be absolutely blown away at how profound and philosophical the bit in question is.  Spoiler alert; the so-called absolute truths are absolutely laughable and easily contradictable even in the moment that they're presented to you, and the actual story behind the game tries to convey the message that "life without death is meaningless" when it actually comes across as "murder is fine because you're releasing your victims from their mortal coil lmao."-Speaking of the game's abstract thematic, some of the art often feels lackluster.  Don't get me wrong; a lot of the art is very well-done with talented artists behind it, no doubt.  However, in most areas in the game, the level design is laughably simple, from a bar with two colors making up the entire interior's color palette, to a monotone pathway in a completely black void.  Now, the obvious explanation for this is "bro, the art so basic because the game is supposed to be abstract."  And that's sort of my point here; it feels like the abstract nature of the game is presented as a reason for the level design being bare-bones, which presents to me as dishonest.  Now, don't misunderstand, I completely get that the game was developed by two people, and that it would take an absurd amount of time to create really nice art for all the areas.  I just personally dislike the lack of detail in many areas being attributed to the game's purported minimalism rather than the fact that this game had extreme development constraints.-Speaking of the graphics, there's also a few elements that serve to completely break the theme of the art style, which comes across to me as extremely jarring.  The main example I have of this is the rather arbitrary occasional use of 3D models.-This one's more nit-picky, but it still felt cheap so I thought it worth mentioning.  At some point in the game, there's a so-called "endless hallway", which DOES have an end, and I've gotten to it, but it took LITERALLY AS LONG AS THE ENTIRE REST OF THE GAME (~6 hours.)  Sounds like the devs watched a bit too many 2b2t videos on YouTube and just couldn't hold back on putting the nether highways into their indy game.  Oh, and if you are ready to send me a message saying "lol just use a macro bro," I did.  I set up an AutoHotkey script to hold D for 4 hours.  Around 2/3 of the way (I think) through the corridor, the developers decided to put random rocks in your way so you have to actually path around them.  Now THAT'S what I call gameplay.-(Addendum 3/14/21) I knew I'd forget something, and that thing was the shallowness of the characters.  Seriously, the game wants you to care about its characters, but most of them are based around a single gimmick that gets old after the second time (see: Noseferachu) and have incredibly little dialogue (we're talking like, 4 lines, for some characters.).  Seriously, character deaths in Undertale were so impactful because of how slowly and thoroughly the characters were presented to the player; that's why that game actually succeeded in making the player care about their actions.  And as a nail in the coffin, Everhood straight up doesn't give you a choice with regards to yeeting a character or not, so how are you supposed to feel bad when the game forces your hand?No hate to the devs, I think they did a fabulous job with two people; I just thought it necessary to point out that which very few others have, and that's that while this game has definitely made some interesting contributions to the genre, it is certainly no flawless masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: While I enjoyed my time with Everhood and I don't regret playing it... I walk away feeling that this was a love letter to Undertale that tried too hard to *be* Undertale... while also not understanding why it worked. This is definitely more of a "thumbs middle" rather than thumbs up or down kinda game, but I feel like I have to give it a thumbs down purely to offset the overwhelming praises from everyone else.The gameplay is the standout star of the game. It's fun, different, visually gorgeous and challenging. Nothing but good things to say here. At the same time, I feel like it shows it's hand way too early when showing off it's visual showcases of special effects, because by the time the game reaches it's ending, you've really got nowhere to go but where you've already been.The music ranges from decent to fantastic. There are absolutely quite a few songs here I'll throw in my Spotify playlist for sure.The story is purposefully ambiguous and I was beginning to wonder if maybe I was missing something, when even one of the characters mentions that they have no idea what's going on. I decided to hold my judgement and wait for the grand reveal of what's actually going on before forming an opinion. The reveal itself is fine, and the twist to obtain it's ending definitely takes your expectations as an Undertale fan and subverts them, so I'll certainly give them their due for that. The ending tries to be even more epic and grand in scale than the game it was inspired by, but it doesn't earn it's hotdogging and grandstanding the way that Undertale does. There are multiple points where it could have said "Okay, here are the credits, thank you for playing" but then it comes back and says "HERE'S ONE MORE VICTORY LAP FOR THE HELL OF IT!" which got old pretty fast.Clearly, a lot of hard work and love went into this... but the story, the characters and the meta-narrative just fell flat to me. I'll pretty much forget everything I experienced here within a few months... and none of the characters will stick with me. I know that I should be reviewing this game for it's own merits, but when it's merits all come from the inspiration of another, it's kind of impossible not to compare it. Especially when they throw in character designs that are remarkably similar to an Undertale character as well as very *wink wink nudge nudge* mentions of "determination". All in all, I'd say this is a solid 8 out of 10. Again, it's *not* a bad game. There's fun to be had here. but you'll also feel like you've already been down this road before if you've played Undertale. If you wanna scratch that itch again, go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is not Undertale. Undertale is a comedy with tragic undertones and notes of horror along the way, driven by quirky and lovable characters you have the chance to murder if you don't understand what's going on. Everhood is a philosophical challenge sneakily disguised as an Undertale clone with a rhythm-based combat system. If Everhood is one thing, it is difficult. Not to beat, no. It can be challenging, but not overly so. No, it is a challenging game to experience. In Undertale, there is no question that the right thing to do is the right thing to do. It's so obvious, isn't it? I won't say anything more on that topic except this: Everhood will make you question a lot of things, and in my case, maybe even re-examine the way you think about life. _childDocuments_.review: One of the not-so-many games that take advantage of their medium, taking you on a surreal adventure through a strange world.Main gameplay is dodging rhythm-fueled attacks with plenty of twists to it. It's a simple concept, but combined with the unique pieces of music for each battle, it works exceedingly well. On top of that the story is two cups of silly, a fork of existential thoughts with a sprinkle of meta-commentary on top - a truly wonderful mixture.One thing I can complain about is that the game isn't long, as it took me less than 6 hours to finish, despite fair amounts of meandering about. However, it was a very pleasant 6 hours and I will most definitely still come back to discover more secrets and complete things I have not managed to complete on my first go. I may yet regret this decision.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I liked this game, for it's price I think it's worth it if you like to play games with good music and an interesting battle system. I understand a lot of the complaints people have, and agree to a degree. The game does suffer from its short run time as well as trying to have a deeper emotional connection than it builds between you and its characters. I also think some of the environments could have been a bit more polished. I did like all but one song that I encountered throughout the game, and I did like the characters as shallow as they may be to some. I also enjoyed the story the devs made I think it is an interesting point of view and a decent dive into the concept of death and mortality. It's hard for me to write a list of straight pros and cons, because I think a lot of the elements people feel strongly about are objective. However, I had fun the whole time I was playing. To me I enjoyed it, and it was more an experience than a story or lesson. I do look forward to the next game the devs produce, and hope it will be similar to Everhood but be more of a full length game so the devs have time to produce the deep and meaningful story they are more than likely are capable of.

Despite the story not being too satisfying for my taste, the gameplay and music carry the game  and made it worth playing multiple times.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a sucker for story-based RPGs and I've liked pretty much every one I've played, but I don't understand the overwhelmingly positive feedback for Everhood. Music and gameplay is awesome. The cursor battle was probably my favourite part of the game. Narrative is okay and I even agree with it pretty strongly. But the game falls completely flat past that.The characters are so non-dimensional it brings down the game completely. The meta-narrative was pointless. The game tried so hard to force-feed me a huge second-hand acid trip that I just couldn't care for. There's just not much to it on a story level and it leaves so much to be desired. I was excited halfway through waiting for some juicy exposition however the more I played the more I was let down. To put it simply, the latter half of the game felt empty. It felt like it wanted Undertale's attention but I can't tell if there was heart put into it or if it was just a cop-out for Ninja's Fortnite Pewdiepie reaction bait. It's like Everhood uses acid filters as a surrogate for dialogue. Also I don't understand why there was so much bloom on the carnival level. I was enjoying it and wanted to further but it soon ran out at the end.I'm open to people trying to justify the game. What did I miss? Is every copy supposed to be personalized?? In the end I can't tell if it was a cop-out or if it just didn't budget it's resources well. As a story game, it feels unfinished. Everhood could have been done a lot better in my opinion, and I wish it was.

_childDocuments_.review: ///SPOILER FREE REVIEW///Everhood is an interesting Indie Game with a seemingly simple premise. You must get your arm back, and to do so you must engage in 'battles' which are essentially a cross between a rhythm game and bullet hell. What I like most about Everhood's gameplay is that the gameplay doesn't get old as most fights introduce new elements that are unique to them specifically to give each encounter a unique feeling. This is only emphasized by Everhood's strongest element; it's music.A bunch of talented musical artists contributed to the OST for this game and it shows. The visuals and gameplay compliment the music extremely well and create a heart-pounding experience. In addition, the game has multiple endings so it has definite replay value.I definitely recommend this game. It has inspiration from many classics and it shows, yet it manages to carve out a unique identity with a thought-provoking story and gameplay unlike what you can find elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: This is boss rush: the game. If you don't want that, avoid this game at all costs. It is fine on the normal difficulty setting if you don't mind making numerous mistakes. It regenerates your health faster after a mistake, Hard difficulty is probably the intended difficulty, especially since that was the default setting. It lacks panache. It's more akin to a solo senior project in college than a game. The introduction of mechanics of different obstacles during the rhythm sections are too quick, leaving under developed potential opportunities for other game mechanics. The story was threadbare between fights and lacked much wit. The music during a fight is a suggestion, and a bad one at that. When trying to navigate the incorrectly sized musical battle field, you don't have confident auditory guidance. The extra line and space in the field vs a current score's setup are obviously for gameplay concerns, and I get that. However, I think it perverts the entire concept... at least make music on that new scale. That would be refreshing. I don't understand why this is so highly praised. The writing is freshman tier, the coding is mostly decent enough, and the aesthetic clash is like a rough draft. The advice the game gives you is that it's about the journey, not the destination or some bs to make you think you're not struggling through a concept of a game that was given 10 percent of the work it deserves. The Undertale reference to Gaster is terribly out of place. This game oozes a lack of that extra push that it needed. I would be interested in a refined version, but since many reviewers are too busy pretending this is a good game, I doubt the devs will get the critical feedback they need to actually capture lightning in a bottle. I would drink dirty water during a drought, but I wouldn't call it good water. At any rate, I feel these devs got more attention than they bargained for and I hope they sort it out to make this game into an actual gem. The potential is there, but it isn't here.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you want to know what it feels like to feel? Everhood is an absolutely fantastic meld of two genres that have been mimicked yet not perfected in their recreations: Undertale's (to an extent, Earthbound's) zany world filled with peculiarly lovable NPC's and sharp humour, and Guitar Hero's side to side music based note playing. That sound weird to you? It should. This game nails it! I picked up the game because I thought the trailer music seemed pretty great, and the visuals looked nice, but lo and behold I was in for an emotional, tear jerking story through a 10-11 hour experience. You play D&D, run through a 2.5 hour hallway (if you want,) and dance with some trippy gnomes. No real explanation can do this game justice, it's something I wish I could experience blind again. Just like in Undertale, the characters you meet will all leave an impact on you, and the bittersweet finale will take you for a sad spin. You'll meet frogs who play guitar, angry ATM's, and listen to some funky music. So far Everhood is easily my GOTY 2021.Rock on Everhood.

_childDocuments_.review: To get this out of the way at the start: lots of comparisons get made of this game to Undertale, and that may well be because both want to pay homage to Earthbound/Mother, they likely share influences. I think this game captures that spirit much better than Undertale, full-stop: I'll come back to that though.Everhood's gameplay is a joy, and blows out of the water any Earthbound-like I've seen: it's as if Guitar Hero was a boss fight game. It comes packing the amazing OST needed to back that gameplay direction up, and has a wide range of music genres/styles that keep things interesting. The game often leverages what type of song accompanies what foe, moment, or location as an opportunity to catch you off-guard, betraying your expectations, and making for genuinely funny moments.Let's get back to talk of its inspirations, though. I think one big thing it has over a lot of the other games made by Earthbound fans is that Everhood takes itself less seriously (most of the time), and when it is serious, is mainly prompting introspection which is neat. The more common approach however, is being heavy on narrative/character drama, as Toby Fox's games mostly are, the Lisa series is, etc. All those games are good in their own rights, but if they're all trying to recapture the spirit of Earthbound, I think they're not as close as this game feels, to me at least.Everhood much like Earthbound is a wacky, bizarre journey that you never know what will happen next in, and all these games inspired by Earthbound seem to want to "get real" occasionally. What I liked is the way Everhood achieves this, less off narrative occurrences, character deaths, heart-string tugs. Its serious moments are often building up to, or foreshadowing, questions about different versions of the concept of an afterlife, and which you believe are better or worse. It's this that makes Everhood's narrative approach feel like it stands on its own ground more than many other games in the always-growing, somewhat tired "Earthbound inspired indie RPG" family.All-in-all this is up there for one of the finest 2D RPGs I've played, and I highly recommend it. I also recommend playing it on one of the two hardest difficulties for a real test of skill, that satisfying feeling of mastery or finesse in overcoming its tougher fights.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is a love letter to Undertale. It's a love letter to creative minds and to boldness. How many times during my gameplay I whispered " What the hell, this is insane ", while jamming to the bangers the BGM had to offer and trying to dodge a wave of insane and trippy patterns. It's very hard to describe what you'll experience by playing this, but one thing for sure is that you will remember it. The storytelling is fast, and that's something I personally really like in a game. You're hooked, and just wants to know what's next. The fighting system is smooth, innovative, while still using familiar gameplay basics. Everhood will also give you a lot of challenges, and the game itself is quite hard if you're aiming for all the different endings. But the developpers thought of everyone and added a "story mode" to enjoy yourself without having to tryhard, as well as a colorblind mode and a photosensitive mode ( because ouh boi, during some fights, if my eyes could cry for help, they totally would have lol ).   I think I'm probably gonna try to do all the achievements if my hands and brain can make it lol ヾ(`ヘ´)ﾉﾞ Already did the corridor thingy, I just need to get all the "No Hits" achievements and the "Surviving the Incinerator" one !! 	It's a very unconventional indie experience, I laughed a bunch and really enjoyed myself. Couldn't play something else until I finished it. Fully recommended,Bravo ♡

_childDocuments_.review: At the end of the game  there’s a message that asks the player “How did this game make you feel?” And my only answer is… content. I didn’t need this game’s message about the nature of death or anything like that. Nor did it change my life. It just made me feel really content. Which is something I really appreciate. And it also has a really fun combat system. The combat of Everhood was truly one of a kind, it’s simple in its idea, but its execution is very complex. It leads to very interesting battles that I was always invested in. In short if the combat looks fun to you. You’ll like it… probably.The only objective problem I had with the game was the amount of flashing lights which almost made me refund the game. Thankfully there are ways to mitigate this, there are settings to adjust to make this less of an issue. A more subjective problem is that the replay value that this game offers isn’t necessarily something I enjoy. Lots of “Do this fight but without getting hit” and stuff. Those sorts of things don’t personally interest me.Everhood is a delightful game that made me feel content with its story and the role that I played in it and… Maybe it made me feel a little content with myself too. It’s worth your time. I promise you. 4.5/5

_childDocuments_.review: *This review contains spoilers.*If I were to summarize my thoughts on Everhood in one sentence it would be "not quite there".Story: 4/10This is the weakest aspect of the game by far and it frustrated me because I see a lot of potential in its ideas that just aren't fully realized. Part of this is due to the English being spotty, which make certain segments that delve into more complex subjects a lot harder to parse through. I frequently found myself confused at the events taking place and only after thinking on what had happened did I begin to get a small grasp on what the game was trying to say.I read a negative review saying that the game is promoting some kind of "killing is good" message, and while that is far from what I took from the game, I can't deny that I can imagine someone coming to that conclusion because the game's messaging feels confused. I read the game's story from a meta-context, that every character is essentially a video game npc trapped within the boundaries of the game for eons and eons. If I'm on the money, I feel like you could explore a lot in that department. Sadly, however, I feel this aspect of the game is frankly undercooked.Gameplay: 7/10Everhood's gameplay is incredibly unique, not quite a rhythm game but having the trappings of one. Everhood's gameplay, especially with the harder encounters, is very fun to power through. While I was mostly satisfied with the early encounters, the moment the arm is introduced, earlier encounters suddenly gain a new level of difficulty while new encounters with the deflect mechanic in mind become veritable gauntlets, both running against the clock and the enemy's health bar. The mechanics are well explored.I do, however, have problems.First of all, difficulty in the game changes two factors. One, it changes your health bar and the speed of its regeneration. This is fine. However, it ALSO changes the enemy's health bar, causing fights on insane mode requiring you to kill the enemy to become slogfests where you spent up to ten minutes trying to whittle down an enemy's titanic health bar. If there is one piece of advice I'd give to the devs, it would be to change how difficulty is scaled, because fights such as these are less difficult and more tedious.Second of all, the game has a number of what I would call "filler encounters". Everyone has a unique track, everyone has a unique fight, but I can't help but find encounters such as the troll and zob to be incredibly boring compared to the battles against the gnomes. And it's not even a matter of trippy visuals, the rematch with green mage and the battle against the pointer were both really fun. If I were to give one piece of advice here, it would be to go even farther with the style of the game.Music: 8/10Everhood's soundtrack slaps, and it's not too often I come across a battle theme I dislike (with some exceptions) and throughout the game I was bobbing my head. Though I will admit that those exception tracks (like the troll, again) did weigh down the experience a bit. The highlight tracks were definitely those used by the secret bosses and the most difficult story encounters. My only wish is that rematches had some kind of revamped song to go with them. Not all of them have to be like green mage, but having a remixed zigg song for his rematch would've been great.Visuals: 7/10While I do think the game could stand to have its visual style be showcased more often in combat sections, I think that overall the visual style, while reminiscent of Undertale, is able to stand on its own using a creative combination of pixel art, tweening, particle effects and rudimentary 3D models. The only thing that bogs me down is that much of the amazing visuals are relegated very early on to the gnomes encounter and are oft seen until the endgame/secret bosses. I think having more cinematic encounters throughout would've helped the style of the game quite a bit.Overall: 7/10There's a lot of potential with this concept, and I really wish I could've called up the devs and asked to help edit their script, because there's a lot going on here that I would love to see pushed further. The story has potential but it ultimately doesnt land at all, the gameplay is good but needs fine-tuning, the music is great but some tracks just filled space, and the visuals are great but the best visuals are rarely ever seen.All in all, while I give this game an ultimately positive review, I feel like there are too many issues with the game for me to give it the glowing review that I would love to give it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is supposedly a rhythm game, but Everhood is actually a bullet hell "dodger" with music. Button timing has very little to do with the music timing/rhythm, especially considering I just finished playing and have played quite a lot of other rhythm games like Guitar Hero, FNF, OSU/EBA and DDR.The story is trite and played out, and only like 10% of the music is catchy, considering most tracks aren't very long.This game has an extremely pretentious ending that is a waste of time to unlock. Anyone who tells you that it's worth playing because "The ending will blow your mind" is too easily amused by vague writing and abstract wording.Everhood is an "Undertale clone". You can dismiss this claim, but it's very clear what game this Everhood drew inspiration from in terms of its presentation. You listen to music and dodge projectiles on a track. The bullet patterns have very little to do with where and when you need to dodge.If you've ever played AVICII Invector or Audiosurf, This game has very little in common other than the field layout.Not lazily done and looks very good. It feels like a mix of 16 bit and 8 bit with simple colors, the sprite animations are good too.If you like "hot beats that actually slap tho" then I guess some of the music is ok. Other than a few issues with sudden volume increases, I don't hate the music.Not every battle can be won this way, but for most of them you can stand in either the left or the right and not think about those "CRAZY" patterns too hard. Not all, but most.For some of the tracks, one minute the music is at the perfect volume, the next its very loud and distorted. I don't want to play with my volume while I'm dodging gaudy projectiles. And yes I checked my sound drivers. Other games and applications work fine.I'm happy you played Metal Gear Solid 3; it's a good game, but your game isn't deep enough to need a "ladder sequence" that goes on for way to long. If you've never played MGS3 and don't know what I'm talking about, there is a sequence in this game were you walk forward for 30+ seconds in dead silence, similar to the ladder climbing sequence in MGS3 where you climb for like 30 seconds.If it's not an homage to MGS3, it's incompetence instead, which is worse.Games can be expressive, especially when talented artists make stunning visuals. Warping the screen like one of those old windows media player visualizations isn't what I would call "artistic" as makes the game harder to look at. I need to be able to see your game in order to play it. They don't call them "visual games" for nothing. Think about the physical health of the player who is playing your game when want to convey an acid trip.The term "Juice" is used in video game development culture to mean "making the graphics and sounds do CRAAAAAZY STUFF" and most of the battle VFX fit this obnoxious category of pervasive thought. On the battlefield  glows, and the background objects "whack out" to get that "WOAH DUDE WOAAAAHHHH" reaction from e-celebs playing the game so they can market it to children.I don't really have a problem with the unity engine, but I don't understand how this game can suddenly start chugging in the home world with the all the doors, that Green and Purple world with the clock, and the alligator with the guitar's second fight among others. Unity has a bad reputation because of stuff like this.I'd honestly be surprised if a simple looking game like this could run on the same hardware Metal Slug 2 was made on, and that game looks and preforms way better than Everhood.If you are looking for something similar to Undertale, this is not your game. There are quirky characters, and a very small amount of the dialog is genuinely funny, but the rest of the game is a pretentious slog that's trying to hurt me physical, and not emotionally like Undertale. In Undertale, you aren't just rubbing your head on every single thing to find out where the next boss fight is like you do in Everhood. It feels very shallow when a good chunk of the game is picking up items and doing a minigame because "Hey, here is more gameplay!".This is very much an "Art Game" and there is enough style over substance to match. It's a shame the sprite art is so good. Because of the art, I tried very hard to overlook the rest of the game's flaws. Overall this was a very tedious experience, especially if you want to get all the endings (it's not worth; don't bother). The battles feel like a waste of time, the music is sometimes too loud, and the VFX are trying to make Everhood the last video game I am able to play. You're better off staring at a Windows Media Player 7 Visualization for a few hours. You'll get a pretty a much more relaxing experience, and the music will probably be better and more to your taste. Save your eyes and avoid this travesty.

_childDocuments_.review: I normally dont write reviews but this game heccin deserves it, the combat is an interesting and unique concept, the battles are challenging, but not frustrating on a dark souls level, though some particular fights might get on your nerves (yes im looking at you purple mage), the ost of the game is truly amazing, i rarely buy a games soundtrack but i love it, barge, feisty flowers, wrath of god, Ballistic, Revenge, they all sound sooooo good! And dont even get me started on the story and characters, the characters all have unique personalities, each being enjoyable, even the villains, and the story is the crown jewel of the game, its nothing i have experienced so far, not even closely in comparison, no, this is honestly one of the best and most interesting stories ive witnessed so far... you wake up in an unknown world, travel on search for certain items, and only late discover the ulterior motive, the purpose... in this game...there is no "good path" or "bad path", there is only two paths, and your decision which you deem correct, though you need to be aware, that whichever path you take, there will always be a side unhappy with your choices, no matter which path you take, some will still see you as the villain....honestly, 10/10, its an amazing game and deserves to be played by more people, its unique in so many aspects, and enjoyable in even more, simply amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is an amazing game with a ton of love and care put into it. The game is a rhythm bullet hell. An "anti-guitar hero" if you will. Each enemy is a song and will throw attacks at you based on that song. You can respond and dodge them reactively or rhythmically. These songs are great and fit their characters well, they quite literally dance to them (as much as you can for some entities). By themselves they are quite catchy and you'll potentially learn to love songs you may have once hated earlier in the game. You get full freedom to replay any song/battle.Battles never get visually boring. In fact, the game is visually overwhelming at times. This is intentional, its part of the experience and I think it's neat, its never overdone for the effect it's trying to achieve. But there is a photo-sensitivity option available. Battles are each very unique and interesting to actually play as well. They also get pretty difficult. Easy and up have the same song patterns, just different health's and regen. And has zero bearing on any achievement.And the story is great. And the story hurts. I can't force you to care for these characters, but if you suspend your reality for a moment and let yourself, the game won't disappoint you.It's time to come home.
_childDocuments_.name: Everhood

_childDocuments_.review: The combat and accompanying music is fantastic, and it's probably worth playing the game for that alone. However everything else beyond that is quite lacking.The game clearly has inspiration from Undertale, which is completely fine. The problem is, it fails to understand what made Undertale a phenomena, and its attempted deviations fall completely flat. The kill vs spare mechanic lacks any of the necessary subtlety for its subject matter (especially considering the intended path). The characters lack complexity and the memorability needed to make weight of the decision have substance.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is a very quirky and fun time for anyone looking for a good "rhythm" game to play. Enjoyed every second of it, the beautiful pixel art (mixed in with 3d sometimes) and psychedelic nature, plus the great story and soundtrack makes for an unforgettable experience. The setting itself is wonderful and unlike most other things I've seen, and alongside great humour is intrigue and mystery that keeps you wanting to grind through the entire game. It's priced fairly as well, my first playthrough lasted around 5-6 hours total, but if you're going for secret bosses or NG+ I can see it easily lasting longer. And once you get tired of the base game you can always turn to the many fan made tracks/bosses, or make one yourself!Overall, highly highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get how this gameplay is any fun.Which is a shame, because the graphics are baffling, the music is absolutely stellar, and the demo videos show a surprising amount of variation. Just too bad that this is basically just one of those old 80's handheld games with the car in the 4 lanes avoiding obstacles.The battle gameplay is boring, frustrating and repetitive, and distracts from the beautiful music, which it really has nothing to do with. You keep expecting to discover some way to use the music to time your moves... But no.So, you die a lot and keep having to start over again. Which wouldn't be such a bad thing, if the dying/retrying loop was *immediate retry* instead of "slow, unskippable death animation + a menu choice".The pauses in the extremely slow NPC animations are equally annoying - just let me skip ahead already, I want to be able to consume your story in a speed I like.The long, boring walks over the empty, boring worlds just take too long, even when running (which you can only do in the cardinal directions), which keeps you hitting invisible walls and slowing down.In short, this game yanks you back and forth between "way too frantic to appreciate the beauty" and way too "Myst pace (but with old-timey retro inspired graphics)".Having read through the other reviews, I would love to experience the story and the beautiful artwork further, but this gameplay and this pacing just isn't worth it.There is ONE amazing part of this game though - the sound track. Man, it's one of the most amazing sound tracks ever. Simply baffling. Just buy the sound track and play it in your car - it's STELLAR.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a stereotypical Earthbound-inspired JRPG. The only part of this game that I could say is inspired from Earthbound would be some trippy backgrounds that plays when the game talks to the player. And of course, it's not a JRPG.Everhood is not a rhythm game either, as you are dodging the music's notes rather than aiming for them--thus, the game does not expect precision from you.Instead, Everhood is a game where you avoid projectiles, just as you avoid problems in the game. That is, until you reach a point where avoiding things is no longer possible...This game is a masterpiece. It is more focused on narrative and characters than on gameplay, if it wasn't obvious enough from the trailers.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to be putting spoilers in this to try and make a point. First off, the music and game play is incredible. The characters are pretty interesting, entertaining even. The only problem I have with the game is the story. The game is heavily influenced by Undertale, which is fine with me if you can make a good game. At first, as you're progressing through the game, you get to a certain part and think, "Oh, if it's like Undertale, then not killing everyone gets me the good ending." Wrong. Doing that is the equivalent of the genocide route of Undertale. The game want's you to kill everyone to get the intended ending, which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up if you think about it, because there are quite a few characters who don't want to die, but there are also some that do want to die. Taking someone's life away when they don't want it is ♥♥♥♥♥♥, but if they do want it, then you have that ability to grant it to them. I know some people might say, "But it's explained later in the game," which is one of the problems. It explains it to you later and not when you get your arm back. Yes, I know there's also the literal image of Buddha and how that implies reincarnation, while also giving the message of, "A lot of people fear death. But this is something that is inescapable and eventually will happen. Enjoy life and get the most out of it. Hang out with friends or family." Still, the thing that bothers me is having to kill people that either don't want to die or are rather content with their immortal lives.

_childDocuments_.review: You ever played Frogger? How about playing Frogger while on LSD? No? Alright...Well now you don't have to anymore! Everhood is exactly like the drug! Uh... I mean, and Frogger, too.This game is insane, it starts off as weird and ends up even weirder, but in a good way! there is only one thing I disliked about this game, and that's the fact that it "forces" you to do things you don't want, which... ended up being good in the end? So then my complaint was over, but I was still "mad" at first I guess, but in order to get the proper ending of this game, you should follow what the game tells you, as much as it would pain you to do it, honest! "What's next, the sewer level before the tower?" In this game you will get to demonstrate your reaction times and even show to your buddies your hard earned diploma of handling very long planks, if you have the skills to do so, btw, DO NOT HARM THE AUTOMATIC TERROR MACHINE.Every time I was talking to a new character I could feel their emotions through the screen, and there is nothing more satisfying than giving you a good fight just for the sake of... protecting themselves? no that can't be right... FUN! they do it for fun! These characters you meet throughout the game want to style on you with their moves, and they're not amateurs! One time I had to pause the game just so I could laugh when a knight shows up to fight you, raises his sword, throws it on the ground and starts styling on you like he's the king of the 80's disco.Also, Green Mage, my beloved. The silliest and most fun character to interact with in this game.And no, I will not be talking about the gnomes... I... I still need to recover...

_childDocuments_.review: First off, the game is very intriguing and unique, especially with its battle system. It's actually one of the main reasons I stuck around: I LOVED the battle system ever since I first saw it, and I'm not disappointed in the slightest! (Except in my skills. I died A LOT, even on Easy mode. RIP my non-existent Gamer card). This game did NOT play with the trippiness, and it was both cool and slightly disorienting. But fun nonetheless! Especially with that sweet, sweet music~ (Though, I would look into adding a function that lessons the amount of effects on screen. Even with the current accessibility options, one of my friends was getting nauseous, and even experienced dissociation because of all the effects on some of the battles. They got through the game despite it, but may others be warned!) I also really enjoyed most of the characters in the game. The interactions with them were enjoyable at least, and made me enjoy talking with them even more. Especially the biggest support characters. And their battle interactions! Oh, absolutely nice. Definitely liked most of the supports after going through their interactions. Though I found it almost odd how they just... were conveniently at the same places you were, every time. Like they just teleported there. It's probably not a big deal, but I almost found it odd. Wish that was explored. Which brings me to my next topic: The story. I'll say two things right off the bat: I LOVED the story, and I know that some things are meant to be up for interpretation (or some info is being held captive by the Devs on purpose). I love the overall message that the story, and it brings happiness to my heart. But thanks to a few discussions with one of my friends (who has currently played Everhood 4(?) times), I feel that game should have expanded more on the past events prior to the game, or at least have more interactions with the environment or other characters that would have explained why certain things had to happen. While I understood why things turned out the way they did in the end, I feel there were some justifications that were missing. Like, (Spoilers ahead!) I only just finished my first playthrough of the game earlier today, so I know that maybe there's more things for me to learn in my second playthrough. Again, while I did enjoy the story, there are some plot holes that a friend and I examined that leave us wondering. But, nonetheless, I enjoyed this game, and definitely recommend this to anyone!!! Thank you, Devs, for this wonderful game.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is a frustrating experience as it has a lot of problems, but I enjoyed it enough that I'll try out the sequel in the hopes that at least some of the issues will be fixed and provide the experience that this should have been.You play as a puppet who's had his arm stolen and you're on a quest to get it back. You walk around, talk to people, and occasionally get in a battle. The battles have music in them and notes come at you in one of 5 lanes which you need to dodge until the song ends. This isn't a rhythm game. The notes aren't coming at you in patterns to the music or anything like that. Occasionally the game provides a brief minigame instead of a normal song battle.This has a lot of problems. Enemies stand really close to your character in battles. I'm not sure what the exact timing is, but once a note comes out, you have somewhere around a second or less to react to it. You're not setting up or planning any kind of strategic moves here, you're simply reacting as quickly as you can to not get hit by whatever is currently flying at you. This inability to be able to see future notes can lead to the problem that depending on the direction you choose to go, you may accidentally pen yourself in and get hit. It's not a huge deal, but it is an issue and will lead to you failing on occasion. There will also be some battles where you're mostly going to be hanging out in the same 2-3 lanes all battle long.A minor issue related to the above is that the enemies show up at the top of the battle screen with various animations that play throughout the fight. Since you have to be so focused on dodging notes, you rarely get a chance to actually look at these to enjoy them. They're almost a complete waste. It's as though they were made for the enjoyment of watching someone play this rather than for the person playing the game.The difficulty is all over the place. I played on hard, but I guess the game is entirely the same as normal with hard making it so you only take 3 hits instead of 5 to die and you regen health slower. Once you get used to the quick reaction style gameplay, it gets pretty easy for a long while. There was a long period after the first 3-4 battles where I don't think I failed again until after I'd gotten my arm back and some of the more difficult battles start occurring, though there are a sprinkling of easy battles in the late game as well. Probably the biggest issue with the difficulty is they run out of ways to make the normal battles non-repetitively tougher and decided to resort to using artificial difficulty as a crutch. Expect occasional battles where words are covering up portions of the grid and hiding notes, or bright flashing lights prevent you from seeing, times the screen rotates, or stretching/making the screen wavy/etc so you can't tell where you are in proportion to notes, etc.Also in regards to the difficulty is that winning some of the more difficult battles never really came down to me getting better, but simply that certain sides are far more difficult during certain portions of songs. There was one song where I must've failed 15 times while on the right side. Then I thought to myself, maybe I'll try this on the left side when it gets here. Went to the other side during the portion I was having issues with and succeeded on the first try. Winning a battle you've been losing can be as simple as switching which side you're standing on during the portion you're having trouble with, which doesn't feel satisfying. Leaves you going "oh, I should've tried that earlier instead of trying to persevere."The biggest weakness in this is the most obvious one just by looking it. It desperately, desperately, desperately wants to be Undertale, and fails in pretty much every way in trying to replicate it. You're not going to care about the story here. The dialogue is mostly bland and the humor is hit and miss, typically more on the miss side. Probably the biggest failure are the characters which lack any real standouts or development. In Undertale, through either the story or boss battles, you got to know the main cast of characters, which resulted in your decisions having an impact. Here, well... there's Jerk Guy who's just kind of a jerk. There's Greedy Pig who's greedy. There's Sneezing Nosferatu who sneezes every time you talk to him and likes a certain video game. You have Blue Thief palling around with you all game long and I don't know that I can even begin to describe his character because I'm not sure he actually has one.Considering this is trying to be Undertale, you should already have a good idea of what the game is going to have you make a choice about doing later on once you get your arm back. The almost entirely bland cast of characters and lack of story stakes means you don't care much about the decision you have to make.Another minor issue is portions of the game are moving along very sterile black backgrounds with some sort of dotted pathway that you have to follow. If you move slightly off this pathway you'll be constantly crashing into invisible walls. Not sure if this was an intentional choice or whether they just weren't creative enough to come up with something to fill in these backgrounds, but it is noticeably distracting and hurts the game.This is a rough one. Everhood is mostly pleasant, somewhat enjoyable, and has occasional well crafted set pieces. It should be more than what it is though and mostly fumbles the story, characters, and dialogue that should make this stand out. It's like playing volleyball, having someone set you up for a spike, but as you jump up, the ref blows the whistle to signal that play is dead so he can go take a bathroom break and the ball just plops down in the sand.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're reading this before playing the game then please do me a favor and pretend that Undertale does not exist. You will feel compelled to compare Everhood to it and you will be doing the devs of this game a HUGE disservice for the amount of creativity and thought that went into this game.Everhood is an adventure-based rhythm game that has you going across vaguely connected areas and getting into music battles with weird people. The strange characters, unclear location, and distractingly good music often makes this game feel oddly dream-like. Nothing really makes sense and the game just has you go with it. Make no mistake though, both the themes of this game and the difficulty of the battles are real and intense at times.This is not a game that just wants to be silly all the time. This game wants to... well honestly I'm not entirely sure. The themes and story of this game are clear, but sometimes honestly Everhood also just feels like a canvas for the devs to throw out all their strange ideas. That's not a criticism, but more the most vague way I can explain to you what Everhood will be like if you decide to play it.I do have to say that the gameplay got kinda old for me and I found myself far more interested in the story and weirdness of it all. The songs in Everhood are really good, but I would get frustrated if a battle took me too long since I just wanted to see what happened next. Maybe if you're into rhythm games you'll disagree, but I found it exhausting at times.Still, Everhood is cheap and pretty short; well worth it all in order to join the game on this absolutely bizarre journey. Also, I said this a few times but the soundtrack is really good and you should buy that too.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game on a recommendation from a friend, with "if you like Undertale, you'll probably like this game" being the selling point. Naturally, I loved Undertale so I decided to give the world of Everhood a try. And after beating it, I can say with full certainty: the love that the devs (gnomes?) put into this game is consistently apparent. Visually, the game's simple pixel art style with very minimalist backgrounds may not seem like much at first glance, but in battles, all that minimalism gets thrown out the window as your eyes are subject to some of the most gorgeous visual flourishes I've ever seen in a pixel game. Every battle is unique, colorful, and dynamic, and generally a treat for the eyes. I say generally because every so often, the games visuals can go a little overboard. This game does come with a photosensitivity warning, and it is well warranted because those visuals can be overwhelming at times, with constant flashing colors, harsh lighting, spinning perspectives, and blurring effects. While these do create a gorgeous visual, I'd be lying if I didn't say they gave me a headache at times, and could even be so overwhelming that they distracted from the battles. That said, this wasn't the case for every battle, and it wasn't enough to take away my overall enjoyment. On the note of the battles, they are unique in execution, being primarily a rhythm game with an emphasis on evasion. The controls are simple, with only moving and jumping to start, but behind its simplicity lies some of the most challenging battles I've ever faced. You only have about a second to process what's going on and react accordingly, and that's just for a single instance in battles that go on for 2-4 minutes each. If you crave a challenge, Everhood's No Hit Achievements for literally every battle are among the hardest things I've ever tried. Fortunately, the game does have accessibility in mind, so it has difficulty options to make things easier or harder to your preference. I will say though that at the highest difficulty the battles can be a little tedious with some major damage sponges, but even then that encourages controlled aggression to finish the non-looping fights quickly. While challenging, though, the battles are immensely satisfying as you're literally moving to the music of each encounter in battle. And I'd be remiss if I didn't mention that Everhood has one of the most FANTASTIC soundtracks I've ever heard in a video game. Each battle has a unique theme, and I can't really say there's any song that's bad... Even "Really Bad Song" which is intentionally designed that way with purpose! While music is subjective and not something I can readily describe. All I can say is your ears will not be disappointed. The story is a bit on the short side, being fully beatable in about 5-6 hours. This isn't necessarily a bad thing in and of itself, as the story's writing is well written and very succinct. The only thing I can fault the length of the story for, without spoiling too much, is that the game's moral dilemmas that it asks you to consider would certainly have more impact if more time was spent with certain characters. That said, with the time they did spend, the character writing is fantastic; it's got the right mix of witty, deep, and sometimes even downright silly. The story has heart, and it definitely left me with emotions at its conclusions. Plus, to its credit, the game does have multiple endings so the short length gives you the opportunity to readily access them all. I may have played Everhood due to it being compared to Undertale, but the game is very much its own thing with a unique and well defined identity. While the visuals could sometimes be overwhelming and the story left me wishing it had a little more meat to it, I thoroughly enjoyed the game from start to finish, and would recommend it to anyone who's not photosensitive. Seriously, I cannot overstate that photosensitivity warning. But if that's not a problem for you, give Everhood a try. You won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Deserves a spot up there with the indie "RPG Maker greats" (Undertale, LISA, OFF, Yume Nikki, etc.).  This one was made in Unity, but you know, same vibe and all.The key difference is that, unlike those mentioned above, Everhood actually has fun gameplay: you dodge Guitar Hero charts, in a nutshell, and that's a lot more interesting than it sounds.  There's also (mild spoiler)  introduced a few hours in, adding to the depth.  Difficulty is always adjustable, and there are also no-hit challenges for the ~gamers~ (AKA masochists, like me).The music is phenomenal, the visuals are pure eye candy, and it's all such a feast for the senses.  It's difficult to see this in the midst of the action but take a look at playthroughs on Youtube and you'll notice nuanced details put into the characters' animations during battles.I think the weak point is the story but honestly the characters are still cute and charming, even those with limited screentime (and take the rose-tinted glasses off - Undertale had a bunch of characters with barely any lines, and plenty of people went wild for them).I'm one of those lazy people who never reviews things, but this game is truly special, and I hope that it blows up in popularity.  The devs have put a ton of love into this game, and it shows.

_childDocuments_.review: What Everhood has going for it is a unique art style, great character design/pixel art, a memorable world, catchy music, and a unique conceit as far as the plot goes.For better or worse, Everhood wears its inspirations on it sleeve. Undertale is the most immediate and heavy (more on that in a sec), with a main character who resembles Geno from Super Mario RPG, a psychedelic world that recalls both Yume Nikki (and its successor, Omori), and a darkened pixel world that reminds one of OneShot. All combined with the relatively unique angle of being a rhythm game.The downside is... sometimes it feels like it's leaning *too* heavy on Undertale's concepts. You're immediately faced with a white, monospaced, Undertale-esque font that is used in the entire game... one of the first bosses is an evil ATM with a Flowey-like face who wants your soul, and there are nods to genocide/pacifist routes (that don't especially feel like they're being adapted to break new grounds).It's unfortunate too, because Everhood DOES have its own style and vision separate from Undertale. It's an incredibly fun game, with some interesting characters (I loved the Green Mage). The concept behind the main plot (which I won't spoil) is really rich, although ultimately some of the lore and characters who appear at the periphery through the game (a rabbit, gnomes, a certain cat...) aren't as deep or as interesting as you would have hoped.Criticism aside, Everhood is a good game. It's fun to play. The musical battles have great tunes and are enjoyable. The world is psychedelic and trippy and entertaining. The characters are satisfying (although sometimes I wish I felt for them and adored them a little more). Yes, Everhood leans on its predecessors a little TOO much at times, but ultimately it IS its own game and should not be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is everything that an indie game can and should be.  It feels like indie games have been saturated by melancholy and an overindulgence in trying to be "deep".  Everhood, however, proves to be quite a refreshing journey that manages to keep the thoughtful elements one expects from the genre, but brings a whole new level of exciting atmosphere.  Every step into the game is truly a blast: from the interactive battles highlighted by amazing music, to the interacting with wacky characters.  In all, I loved my experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Upon first glance you'll probably think this game has more than a few similarities to Undertale/Deltarune and while you wouldn't be wrong Everhood does more than enough to forge its own identity.The main hook to Everhood is its combat sections, the key here being that all the bullet patterns you face are entirely connected by the beats and notes of the songs each battle literally throws at you in a guitar hero-like grid that you must dodge. The songs by the way are absolute bangers, so you'll definitely have more than a few favorites as you play through the game. It should be noted that while there isn't a setting to make the songs battles themselves easier there is a setting to control how much damage you can take before a game over and how long invincibility frames last after taking a hit. Your health regenerates as long as you don't take any hits for a period of time so ultimately its a pretty forgiving system, but don't be surprised if you run into a song or two that requires a few retries.When not engaging in battle you'll be traveling an overworld that while lonelier than say Undertale's Underground is populated with plenty of memorable characters, there to either help or hinder you on your journey (Or simply just vibe, not everyone has to have an agenda you know). The story itself starts out quite confusing but overtime those blanks will be filled in a slow-burn that takes you across several different landscapes, the graphics may not be anything groundbreaking but ultimately they're enough to get the emotion and scope of the adventure across.One word of caution, this game has more than a few twists both in plot and in gameplay (again, not unlike Undertale/Deltarune) and as such I would strongly recommend getting into this game fresh and reading as little about it as possible for the full experience, this review not withstanding lol.Add the fact that you're paying no more than 10 bucks and you've got a real gem of a video game to enjoy.In conclusion: Welcome to Everhood :-)

_childDocuments_.review: Instant dislike. FIRST battle makes it apparent this isn't what I want in a rhythm game.A well done rhythm game has musical feedback. In regards to rhythm, you can tell what beat to move on based on the proximity, and when you execute an action it makes a sound that fits with the music. In those that also use pitch, there is some indication as to what range the pitch is in (higher or lower at a minimum), if not precise notes.In battle one, this game has neither. There's no musical feedback upon executing a move. There is no way to tell which beat to jump on. Also, the pitch of the music doesn't give hints as to where the attacks will emerge from.This is not an issue of difficulty; I was doing this on Story Mode, and I have extensive experience with music. I honestly don't care about the story or anything else; those are secondary concerns. I wanted a good rhythm game where I felt like part of the music. This is not it.

_childDocuments_.review: There's something to really be said about the perspective of Everhood. While compared to other games, I feel that it is much more "real". There are several themes explored here; the culpability of murder from the perspective and situation of Red and the subsequent exploration of the guilt and grief felt; the control given by looking in on Red as yourself in comparison to games like Undertale; the power you as either yourself or as Red over the other characters in Everhood. The one grievance I have is the fact that the ending is.. odd. Many of the themes I previously mentioned are left open in exchange for a happy ending. Red is exchanged for Pink in a trade that is both unsatisfying and confusing. The devs don't seem to be certain whether they want Pink to love murder or to hate it. Your power is there, but the reason given for your power existing is contrived and so unbelievably confusing that it might as well not even be there. I would desperately recommend this game to anyone, and yet at the same time I feel like it could have resolved itself so much better than it actually did!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastically fun and often creative game, but I personally cannot recommend it.All the positive reviews are not lying to you: it's original, it's witty, it's enrapturing to the point that you really care about what the characters do as well as the impact you have on them.So why am I not recommending it?I have two main gripes with this game, which are free to be debated. The first has MAJOR spoilers, so proceed with caution. The second is spoiler-free.Secondly, the gameplay.At first, learning the game is fun and rewarding, and it lasts for a while. You're allowed to tone down the difficulty at any time if it ever becomes too challenging.And it does. I stuck through the whole game, start to finish, on hard difficulty, because I am no stranger to challenging games and do, in fact, enjoy a fair amount of difficulty.I've beat all of Hollow Knight. I beat Rain World and stuck with it, despite its brutality, which beat me down into the ground over and over again. I even beat all of Celeste and modded it for additional difficulty too.This game's most challenging parts are most certainly not harder than some of the above things that I've completed.But the time required to become fast enough, skilled enough, or precise enough to learn and become used to the patternless bullet hell it often throws at you, is not something I decided to invest in.This is not a rhythm game, despite it sometimes feeling that way. You dodge the notes of songs; you do not play the game to the beat of the songs. This is a bullet hell game, and you will constantly be reminded of that.I want to enjoy the struggle of these harder challenges. I really do. But when the game expects you to learn the more difficult bosses of the game not from experience and adapting, but from blind trial by error, I get too frustrated too easily.This kind of learning and skill development is not fun to me, especially not after spending ten hours only to realize that everything I have already learned is close to worthless due to the ensuing bullet hell in which every moment is practically indistinguishable from the next, thus stunting my ability to develop my skills further.I will admit, the gameplay is, for the most part pre-endgame, quite enjoyable. The music is fantastic, and it sometimes even gets stuck in my head because it's so damn good. The dialogue is cleverly written, and it has absolutely made me laugh on a number of occasions.If this is all you care about in a game, then you are for sure in for a good time.But if you're expecting  and challenging gameplay that rewards you for utilizing what you have learned while also teaching you new things, this is not the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: It's complicated to talk about Everhood because there's a twist about halfway in that turns the entire game on its head. It isn't for everyone, I know I struggled a bit after finding out on my own, and that's why I really can't recommend this game for everyone. It's an experience, and if you can handle the pain along the way, it's a pretty good look at life.I feel like Everhood's strongest asset is that it looks at the world in a way that a lot of games don't. It's an artsy experience, and likely controversial. Past that, the music and gameplay are incredibly solid. The game almost literally reinvents itself at the halfway point by expanding on its core loop in an interesting fashion. The varied techno-driven soundtrack is also spectacular the whole way through - aided by some pretty grandiose art. Plus it's understanding which helps. The game doesn't mock you for your choices (though it tries its best to help you understand) which gives hesitant players more time to think about what they're about to get into. This was the biggest reason I was able to finish this game, so thank you devs for that. Everhood is strong, stable, and solid from beginning to end. And very strange.HOWEVER, Everhood definitely has its flaws - and whether they get tweaked is yet to be seen, and frankly unlikely. The first is with the writing, as it's very much an "almost got it". The devs have a great concept they're chasing, but at some points I got this distinct feeling they were trying to have it multiple ways. As someone who writes a lot, I know the pain all too well of writing and realizing that the point is sorta going everywhere. Like someone trying to describe a beautiful natural event to someone else but stumbling over the beauty. It WORKS, but I feel it could be refined and improved at different moments. Given this game is narratively focused, I do feel that knocks off a few extra points in places. Thankfully the game doesn't over complicate or over explain. To it's favor certainly. The other I know can't be fixed easily and that's with the core gameplay loop. For the first half of the game, it works fine, but when you get to the second half - without spoiling too much - you're often fighting with the game's charting. Getting hit resets things so you're encouraged to throw whenever, but it only lasts a couple hits before disappearing - or a single hit if it's larger.  And some of the fights are on a time limit, so it sucks to dodge well and then have something that should have worked be countered by a random attack. Sure it's all planned out and all so you can expect it, but really, you expect me to memorize the whole damn chart? It only really matters for the time limit fights, otherwise the devs are considerate enough to give you lots of loops to work through.So yeah, final verdict, Everhood is good. Very good. I can't gush over it like I would - say - Undertale because, again, it really ISN'T for everyone. It handles an adult subject with a varied (and likable) cast of characters and I do feel like it could be refined more but I'm not smart enough to really know how. Plus there's a lot of visual effects that may not go well with those vulnerable to flashing lights or dizzying effects (though there are options to toggle them). You take the good and the bad with this game as that sour sweetness makes the experience all the better. If you are going to give this game a spin, definitely do so at full price - and grab the soundtrack while you're at it. They do a good job of not revealing who the battle tracks are for each character in the soundtrack so you can literally listen to it at any time. Oh, and Hard mode is indeed a good starting spot but there's no shame in lowering the difficulty if you can't handle it. Especially when you get closer to the end.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute masterpiece. (Personal Game of The Year)Going through the list of games that came out in 2021, I realized that I wasn't exploring the Indie scene enough. Shuffling through bigger releases, constantly playing mediocre games that don't do much for me, I decided I should just look at my wishlist and get the first thing that looked even remotely interesting for me. Specifically, an Indie game.I stumbled upon Everhood, and while I did have the expectations of having a fun, fast-paced experience, I didn't realize just what a great decision I made. It's a rarity nowadays to play a video game that keeps surprising me and puts a huge grin on my face the whole time I'm playing it. The gameplay loop is addicting. Essentially, imagine if you were playing Guitar Hero, but you had to DODGE the notes, rather than hit them? That's what the game is, it's a concept where you're a character trapped in multiple Guitar Hero levels, and the flying instrumental notes are out there to kill you. It's so simple yet done so well. What helps this a ton is that there is not a single poorly made track in the OST. Every single song in this game is amazing. From funk, to house, to straight up techno, it has it all. For a fan of dance music, it's a rarity nowadays to find games that have soundtracks like this. I would often find myself trying to extend specific boss fights just so I could listen to the songs more.The world is charming, the characters are weird and quirky, but also very likeable and original. The world is uncanny, filled with medieval castles, and acid trip fueled funky towns, where members of the cast go to play D&D. Everything in the overall design department is done in such an off the wall way, but it also never becomes weird to a point where it doesn't make any sense. Besides being an already amazing game from the gameplay loop perspective, Everhood tackles themes such as humanity, morality, and existentialism. It raises philosophical questions that you could ponder on for hours. It always seems like when your character is faced with these questions, the developers actually intend them for you, the player, to think about.It's always a treat to play special games like these, where you can just see how much care and love the developers put into the project, and it translates so well. I'm really glad I went on this journey with them, and just like they kept thanking me for playing the game while I was there, I have immense gratitude for them as well. You guys really made something special with this, and I have no idea what you will have to make to top this, but I'll be sure to stick along.Thank you.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Long before time had a name, the First Spinjitzu Master arrived on our world. A mere child, to find a world engulfed in chaos. This chaos was caused by Wojira. _childDocuments_.review: There are many Absolute Truths, but one of them is: You should give this game your credit card information.(TLDR of this review: The story is good, the gameplay is supreme and it even supports custom battles. My only complaint is that actually making custom battles is really annoying because you have to use a ton of external tools. Hopefully they fix that in the sequel, because yes there is a sequel in the works.)In all seriousness, this game is incredible. The story is really good with a bit of extra lore you can find through some digging, but it's not the backbone of the story like FNAF and you don't need to know it to have the story click with you. Don't believe me? I got this game for free on my birthday while having the entire game spoiled ahead of time, and I still teared up when I reached the end. If you're not much of a story person either, this is also just a really good rhythm game on it's own. It's got a ton of gimmicks and trippy effects to make you play worse, and it definitely makes sense why they collabed with Rhythm Doctor because that game screws with you a lot as well. Granted if your goal is simply to beat the song, you can generally just use 2 of the 5 lanes and just spam jump and sometimes move, which is a bit lame, but the Replay Battle feature adds a scoring system that encourages risk and reward by giving more points for grazing difficulties and a multiplier depending on the difficulty. On top of ALL of this, the game supports custom battles, so there is even more content to enjoy. The best place to get songs is the Everhood Discord because the game doesn't support Steam Workshop. Heck, it doesn't even have a built in battle maker, you have to download Unity and use a ton of external tools to make your chart, and good luck doing more advanced things like the game does. That is one of my biggest complaints, but the custom battles people have made are still incredible. It's a shame that this doesn't have the popularity of other rhythm games, I'm kind of hoping that someone makes an FNF mod just to bring more attention to the game, even with the toxicity that might follow.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Everhood is really great until you reach the difficulty spike. Very unique rhythm-based game with quirky characters and deep themes. Achievements Level: Virtually Impossible.When it comes to Rhythm games, I'm pretty ♥♥♥♥. Everhood, however, is very unique in that it makes me feel like I'm not so bad. Until it does. At the price of $10, this game is an absolute steal. The characters are wonderful, the story is compelling, the themes are deep and intriguing. The soundtrack is phenomenal, it has some absolutely incredibly songs that go hand in hand with the insane visuals. Overall it's very trippy and cool with a bunch of twists and I HIGHLY recommend giving it a try!There are, of course, some drawbacks in the game. For the most part, boss fights can be beaten with some determination and skill, with none of them feeling unfair. The issue is that that isn't really true once you beat the game the first time. A lot of the post game fights are so fast and require such precision and muscle memory that they feel unbeatable even on the lowest difficulty. Salt is rubbed in the wound when they also have minute-long unskippable cutscenes before the fight even begins, which really hurts morale. On top of this, there are a lot of sections in the game where you just walk in silence for a while.As for achievements, I do not recommend hunting it. I personally did not 100% it, and it's such a daunting task I don't think I ever will. The game requires you to beat every boss hitless, walk down a silent hallway for multiple hours, and grind an unreasonable amount of a gameplay mechanic that could never be achieved organically in order to get every achievement. I did the hallway one while I watched a show, but the boss achievements are just too difficult for me to even imagine. As for the grind aspect, after ~25 hours of actually playing the game I got less than 5% of the required moves for the achievement. Usually I try to get every achievement before I review a game, but I just couldn't do it with this one. It is fun to go in and try to get some of the other bosses, at least!

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely good game, the gameplay is enjoyable, the OST is fantastic, and the story manages to be surprisingly good as well.The gameplay is pretty simple, the exploration part is basically every RPG Maker-like game ever made, interact with items, walk, sprint, etc. etc. and the combat consists of walking sideways and jumping to avoid enemy attacks. While being simple it manages to be extremely fun! Tough I'd recommend you to go with the higher difficulties, I played on normal and I didn't encounter any major struggles, it wasn't a walk in the park, but I feel like it could've been a little more challenging.The OST is fantastic, the combat themes especially are amazing, they give you that motivation and energy you need to go through the fast-paced combat segments in which the enemies attack you in rhythm with the absolute banger you're hearing.I went into this game completely because of the gameplay, so I had no idea what the plot was about, boy was I in for a ride. I don't know how to explain it without spoiling it, so let's just say it's about immortality and what it entails. Hell, I almost cried at one part of the game, getting emotional consuming media is extremely rare for me, and of all things this game was the last place I was expecting to almost cry.So yeah, amazing game, the price is pretty fair so if you're interested you should just get this, regardless of it being on sale or not, it will be well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a stylish game with good music, but most other things in the game kind of fell flat for me.The game tries to connect with you emotionally with a story that it paints as something epic (literally bringing about the end of an immortal world), but it does nothing to nurture those emotions. I didn't care about any of the characters, since you don't interact with a single one for any significant amount of time. I understood how the game *wanted* me to feel, but it didn't put in the work, so it ended up as something that looked nice but felt empty.The battles were also more frustrating than fun. Tests of endurance, memory, and reaction speed. It's a bullet hell style game where you have very little time to react to the bullets. This is made even more frustrating when you gain the ability to shoot bullets back. Bullets you shoot back can get blocked by enemy bullets, which means often you shoot a bullet and then an enemy bullet unpredictably appears and blocks it after you've already shot it. It wouldn't be so bad if shooting your own bullets was easy, but shooting back is a whole process of first absorbing one of their bullets, absorbing a second bullet of the same color without getting hit (but you can't absorb a second bullet too quickly), and then finally you're allowed to shoot back one bullet. Feels great when it takes 5 seconds to shoot a single bullet, but then when you finally shoot it the enemy spawns a bullet which blocks it right before it reaches them. It feels like the game is purposefully frustrating in this regard, urging you to push past the frustration to beat it. It didn't work for me.The choice of having invisible walls nearly everywhere in the overworld with only some floor tiles visible to hint where you can walk is yet another place where style is prioritized over functionality. Looks nice, plays poorly. Frequently ran into the corners of invisible walls, and you can't dash diagonally or change directions while dashing. So even something as simple as moving around in the world adds to the frustration.
