_childDocuments_.review: So I pulled the game out of my back log and wanted to finally continue playing it or rather start over because I only had about 70 minutes. I remembered that the setting was really cool and trippy in the first hour and I stupidly had the idea to make a stupid "haha kids don't take drugs" joke as a review. Yeah, no, I can't do that. The story of this game doesn't allow me to make that stupid joke. When I started playing the game again, I didn't expect to shed a few little tears at the end. All the characters are memorable and just greatly written. The story of this game is one of a difficult decision. This story is also about immortality and I'll leave it at that. Gameplay wise the game is really good but it is not a rhythm game in the real sense. The game consists mainly of exploration and fighting, with gameplay similar to the Megaman Battle Network games, or One Step from Eden. The special thing is that the enemy attacks are based on the rhythm of the music. On the subject of music, good God, it's just fantastic. Together with the battle backgrounds, every single battle is unique and memorable. I am so happy that I own the vinyl. On a side note, I played the game on hard, the 2nd hardest difficulty, and it was pleasantly challenging.This game is hands down my game of the year for 2022, and I can honestly say I didn't expect it to be. So please do yourself a favor and buy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game unfairly gets compared to Undertale a lot, but I can't describe the feeling this game gives me as anything other than how it felt to play games like Undertale and Oneshot for the first time. The same sense of wonder and wanting to become completely immersed in this world, wanting to figure out all of its secrets and finding every single little piece of lore or dialogue there is to be found. And of course, being confronted with a moral dilemma as the protagonist, that when resolved, impacts me in real life just as strongly. I've played this game near nonstop for four days and I've just about seen everything there is to see in it. Even then, I know I'm going to replay this many times in the future- not just for the gameplay, not just for the story, perhaps only to feel like I belong in the world of Everhood for just a little bit longer. This game is so much bang for your buck I felt I should be paying *more* than the $10 asking price for it. I can't recommend it enough. Do yourself a favor and experience Everhood.

_childDocuments_.review: For as much as I was excited to get to this game, I must unfortunately say that it was a disappointment. I think it would've been fine if the whole premise revolved around the combat/musical gameplay mechanics and was more built around them, but instead Everhood tries to insist that it is a narratively rich video game while not really presenting any deeper points or engaging the player. It likes to pretend that there is a bond being built between you and the characters, but it never attempts to make you care about them. The pacing is all over the place and everything happens so fast that it's almost impossible to focus on any event or conversation. The best thing I can say is that it's a game with lots of potential, which sadly goes untouched. It doesn't know what it wants to be and therefore any identity it has leaks from it. In short, it doesn't give anyone a reason to care about what it wants to say.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood has been living in my head rent free ever since I played it, so it's about time I give it a fair review, at least, about what it is.And what it is, is a wonderful ride into nothingness. For those of us that that struggle and dance with existentialism like an estranged lover, sharing moments of meaning and spewing poison and toxicity at each other, Everhood is the bittersweet song playing in the background. It's catchy, it's mystifying, it's unfathomable. It's a rhythm game, except that it is not. It's a deeply intimate journey into nihilism, an experiment on futility, an observation of eternity, and it swings its story like a hammer at whoever is mad enough to pay heed, like some clinically insane half-naked rambler on the street, that for all purposes and intents, may as well be a god trying to tell you the meaning of this life, and the next. I love Everhood, I love its songs, I love its characters, its characters that I love to fight and I hate to kill, and I love to see what the game demands of me, and what happens when you refuse to play by its rules, and to contemplate that the option to refuse to play by its rules is contemplated by the very existence of itself. It goes beyond the yume nikki-eske vibes of simply asking questions and making you consider interpretations, it gives you a simulation, a real, tragical situation spawned from the byproducts of immortality, and it asks you to do something undesirable, something unreasonable. It asks so much of you, and I wouldn't have it any other way. I love Everhood, for all that it is, and all that it isn't. And what it is, is great.

_childDocuments_.review: Context: I beat this game on hard mode a single time, and have not played through New Game+. NG+ doesn't seem to change much, however, so I think my review is valid regardless. This is a game where I really wish steam just had the ability to give number score because I don't wholeheartedly recommend it, but I also don't want to dissuade anyone from buying it. Overall, I'd give it a 3/5. The story is fine. The characters can be charming, and the game is clearly dripping with undertale inspiration. Unfortunately, by being so comparable in tone and style to undertale, it ends up acting as a foil for how good Undertale is at storytelling. It really just throws characters at you constantly, which makes you feel more like an observer rather than somebody who's interacting with and impacting the world. The pacing is so fast that you never get to form any sort of bond with the characters, and are only left with that initial charm, since (BIG SPOILERS). The pacing also makes the world feel incoherent, as you barely get to adjust to the existence of one area's whackiness before it puts you into another whacky area (a lot of time having some overlap that doesn't feel cohesive). It can feel as if the devs just came up with a bunch of different areas separately and then mashed them together.The game's story also suffers from what I call "Firewatch Syndrome", which is when (also spoilers bc I don't want to change any expectations)  . Pretty much what happens is that at the end of the game The music is good, nothing insanely good but it's a bit better than most games that don't have any emphasis on music. If most indie games are B or C tier when it comes to music, and undertale is a high A tier, this game is probably a high B. The gameplay is novel, and certainly an interesting idea, but I found it getting stale at some point. There's only 3 real ways that it puts a twist on the core gameplay outside of minigames, and 2 of those don't come into play until you're in the latter half of the game. I also feel like the game overestimated how good it's battle system was, because at the end it just keeps throwing more and more and more and more battles at you, and I found myself wishing that the game would just end already so I could have the satisfaction of beating it. Also, minor critique, but I wish there was the option to change the deadzones on controller sticks in the settings. I played this using an old xbox 360 controller, and found myself getting snapback inputs where I'd flick the control stick in on direction and it'd immediately input an input in the opposite direction afterward (ex. flick the stick to the right to dodge an attack, only to then have the stick snap back and have my character move to the left instantly afterwards so I get hit by the attack). Overall, the gameplay is fun for a good bit, and maybe I wouldn't've been as annoyed by the constant end battles if I wasn't finishing the game in one session late at night. I've criticized the game a lot, but it's still enjoyable enough. Most of my criticisms are with the nuances and not the foundation, which is fairly solid. The characters are still fun, the gameplay still is pretty good, and overall it's still a pretty cute and charming time. I'd say for $10 it's up to you and how much that money means to you, but on sale it's definitely worth trying out.

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets a lot of complaints about it being like an Undertale spoof, or a bad rhythm game, but I couldn't disagree more. Ever since Undertale, why is it that every pixel game with sick beats has to be compared to Undertale? The gameplay and combat mechanics remind me nothing of Undertale; It looks and feels more Guitar Hero-ish, but instead of reacting ON the beat of the music, you're playing around and reacting TO the music. I personally love this change of gameplay. There are tons of games, or rhythm games that can have you reacting and playing by being ON the beat, but changing it up and making the player have to react TO the music, if you're open to the idea and change, it's actually really fun. This game does a wonderful job of presenting captivating visuals, and music from all kinds of genres to mix it up all throughout the entire experience of the game, and I would recommend this to anyone who wants a free enlightening acid trip to some tunes.

_childDocuments_.review: What I liked about Everhood: The Soundtrack. It's pretty good, has some jamming tunes, very enjoyable.The problem is that everything about Everhood that isn't the soundtrack just begs the question of who it's for. Is there a community of people out there who wishes they could play Undertale but worse? Undertale without the charm? Undertale with controls that somehow feel sticky and unresponsive? Undertale with weird pauses at the end and start of every interaction that makes the game feel almost laggy? Undertale with repeated hints and dialogue bites you don't need like every item picked up reminding you that you can open your inventory?The battle system is a nice idea, but even the *tutorial fight* felt like it dragged on for twice as long as it should have.You might think that the comparisons to Undertale are a bit uncharitable, but lmao, it verges on plagiarism and should at the very least be labelled an Undertale fangame, considering that even some sprites, expressions and presentations are yoinked 99% from Undertale.Anyway, at this point someone's going to go "nerrrr but you didn't play the game long enough!!!!" and a more schoolarly and wise individual might wonder, gee, what made the reviewer drop the game so early?It was a puzzle which might be elementary to some people, but... imagine that you hear a vague piece of music. And then, entirely from hearing it, you have to replay it from scratch on what amounts to a fiddly keyboard with what I calculate to be about 2000 different combinations(but please don't hang me up on that math, it's been a long day), so it isn't even trivially brute forced, nor does it require any intellect, and it has weird and annoying things like your position on the screen affecting how a given tone sounds.Naw, don't play this.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, comparing this to undertale is unavoidable. There's clear inspiration here.  Uses the same font, very similar artstyle and environments, but it's not what you expect. What Undertale did to JRPGs?  You know, the whole going against player expectations of the genre and flipping everything you know around? This does that, but for undertale fans. It's not at all what I expected going into it, and I went into it thinking it would be like Pacifist, normal, and genocide runs with different endings.What I got was one of the most charming and funny games I've ever played in the first half, and existential dread, the torment of immortality, and the refusal to accept death and the terror of the uncertainty of the end in the second. The whole game is nonsensical until you get to the end where things sort of start to make sense.  The characters aren't as memorable as undertale, and it's not gonna give you those *feelings* that you might be looking for.  But the game is constantly funny in the first half. Tons of memorable moments that are worth the price of admission alone. Had me audibly laughing at multiple times.  Once you get to a certain point, mood wiplash hits HARD.  If you liked undertale, you'll like this.  If you like psudo-rhythm games, you'll like this. If you like charming characters and hilarious writing, you'll like this.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was one of the most disgusting experiences I have ever had in a game. I had to put down this game for a while and not play it just because I felt so creeped out. Even towards the end, I never felt like I had a place or control over anything going on.And you know what I loved it because of that. In the end I still managed to feel a kind of peace,  a lot of things still weren't really explained to me, but I still felt like where I ended up was the right place somehow. It had an actual impact on me in real life and made me come more to peace with all my own problems.All of that being said, the actual game part does leave some things to be desired. _childDocuments_.review: I love the music and the visuals, it's a very creative game. Probably my favourite fight was with Zigg, I had the silliest look on my face when he pulled out the laser eyes, and it was very satisfying dodging his beams. The characters are funny and silly; this game did make me laugh a fair few times. I had a hard time with the controls but I still want to recommend this to someone who doesn't mind a game that requires very precise movements and key presses. I reckon this game would be really satisfying to someone who's actually good at it. For me personally, due to the fact you can still beat most battles on normal/hard despite making a tonne of mistakes (because of the health regen system), I felt as though I'd come 1st in the race despite tripping over all the hurdles.The controls made me put this game down once I got to the battle with mecha Flan. This game requires you to move diagonally a lot of the time, or carry out actions in very quick succession - the animations of which don't seem to be able to overlap with each other.The timing on the jump/roll is insanely precise for a game that constantly has you zig zagging side to side and over obstacles. When I picked up the sword during the DnD level I noticed how hard it is to move THEN deflect -- you seem to have to wait for Red to completely finish shifting into the next lane before he can either jump or deflect, so you'll get moments where you move to get in front of a red attack, and you think you've tapped down/S before it hits you, but your character is still completing his dodge animation.  The 4 directional movement in the overworld gets old fast, especially on the obstacle course (for some reason Red just refused to run consistently no matter how much I double tapped the directional keys). I was sort of hoping, when I first met the frog character at the start, that I simply could move with the beat of the song, so I could relax and enjoy the beautiful animations at the top of the screen. But I quickly found that you had to dodge/jump over the obstacles a few beats after the notes were played, which felt less satisfying. I had to treat the game like a bullet hell and just sort of stare vaguely into the middle of the screen so I could see everything that was going on - really wears out your eyes after just a few minutes. So A+ for charm and creativity. But a personal C for the controls.--- Edit. The controls are definitely a lot better when using a gamepad.I think this game could still benefit from giving you the option to extend the view range for the oncoming notes, so you have more than half a second to react.

_childDocuments_.review: I was drawn to this game because of its art style, the music that I heard in trailers, and the Guitar Hero-style gameplay.  I stayed invested in the game after purchasing it because of its tongue-in-cheek dark humor and the acid-washed philosophy that was being delivered through the vehicle of Everhood, the titular pocket of space-time where you are welcome to groove for the enduring expanses of eternity.    You may guess by watching a little footage of Everhood that its gameplay would become a little repetitive--explore the world, meet an obstacle, then slide left and right to complete the songs--but the devs play with the formula in a very inventive and challenging way.  I’m also a sucker for games in which you can unlock new areas and items by doing favors for characters.  You know, unlocking door X by getting the key from dude Y by finding a rare Z for him.     The game has a satisfying increase in difficulty that led to me cruisin’ and groovin’ through many of the more rudimentary encounters, while the “boss” encounters killed me a number of times.  This is to be expected, and the challenge was fair overall.  At  times you do get burnt out of replaying the same segments, but those are usually signs to take a break anyway.     Nearly as important as the fast and lively gameplay is the aesthetic and artistic direction found in Everhood.  The devs clearly did a lot of mushrooms, and they want you to know that.  The pixelated landscapes have bright neon objects, plants, and buildings which contrast with the blankets of void that stretch between areas of interest.  The backgrounds to many fights have patterns of light and fractating images that are honestly a fairly accurate representation of drug-induced psychedelic visuals.  So I’ve heard, anyway.    This aesthetic and some of the philosophies that are found among hippies--oneness, reincarnation, and self-discovery--are characteristic themes that you should sit back and enjoy as you progress throughout the game.    Another selling point of the game is its versatile and energetic soundtrack.  When I first started playing Everhood, I was a little disappointed by the heterogeneity of the music.  There’s little cohesion between the tracks, with most of them adopting their own style.  As I continued playing the game, I realized that this is intentional.  Each character you encounter has a distinct, unique personality, and the music choice for their “battles” are diverse and distinct for the purpose of fulfilling some characterization.  Some tracks are very light and upbeat when the stakes aren’t that high.  Others are intense, gripping, and require great focus.  This threw me off at first, but I grew to really appreciate these design choices as I progressed through the game.     The story in the game is one that is inventive and will keep you invested in progressing through the game.  The role the red mage plays in the groovy purgatory that is Everhood is one that is pivotal to the themes of reincarnation and spiritual journeys that the game really wants you to explore.  There are some branching points in the story that result in different endings, though some players wished for more alternative endings to fit their opinions about reincarnation and Everhood, rather than forcing you to conform to the developers’ opinion of what makes a “good ending.”I understand where those players are coming from, but I think it’s understandable that the ending is played out as seen in-game.  The developers want you to live through their philosophy by playing their game, and to stray from that would be to diminish the impact of the themes that they worked so hard to develop.  It’s important to understand that this isn’t exactly an RPG--it’s a cool and introspective rhythm game that has meaningful choices interspersed throughout.In conclusion, I was very obsessed with this game for a while and I went about recommending it to all of my friends.  I encourage you to give the game a shot if you’re into indie titles with unique soundtracks and aesthetics paired with inventive, fast-paced gameplay.  The game is well worth the meager price tag that it wears.

The game itself is fine (I've gotten to the turning point in the story so far), but I decided to go back for one of the most notorious achievements in gaming right now: , an RNG nightmare. It is by far the single most egregious slap in the face to completionists I have ever seen, not even to mention the fact that there is an achievement for doing 150k jump rolls, which they threw in for the "lolz" (actually one of the developer's words). It doesn't matter if it's optional—you KNOW there are people who enjoy fully exploring games and taking on the challenges developers set out for them, and the idea of punishing people for wanting to fully complete games is gross. The rest of the game could be a masterpiece for all I care—a vast majority of my play time will consist of trying to achieve , so that's what I'll grade the game for. I'm still going to complete everything because the  gameplay outside of this part is good, but for anyone who cares about 100%'ing games, stay far away. _childDocuments_.review: Was stoked for an overwhelmingly positive reviewed rhythm game, but this feels more like an underwhelming bullet hell living inside the shell of a concept for what could have become a rhythm game. You would expect the movement and dodging your character does to correspond to the music somehow, but it's more that the enemies do things to a beat and you can choose to respond to them however you wish, outside of the meter of the music, and the music doesn't seem to have any impact on the gameplay outside of vaguely telegraphing when attacks are likely to come.  The gameplay isn't satisfying to me at all - I just feel like I'm jumping around in clunky ways to avoid clunky attacks -- there's no snappiness to anything, leaving the experience just.. disappointing and frustrating.Perhaps I didn't play long enough, but the 30 minutes I did play featured 4 different fights, all of which had the same lackluster mechanics and the videos I watched mostly seem to feature just harder versions of this same gameplay, so certainly not for me.If you're a fan of rhythm games, I do not recommend this for that feeling at all - it does not feel like  rhythm game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're going to ape Undertale this hard, you need to understand why it works. TLDR: I don't think Everhood earned the payoff it goes for, which killed much of my enjoyment of the game. The gameplay is fun enough if you like bullet-hell Guitar Hero, but don't expect anything like Undertale's writing. If you pick up the game after seeing all the positive reviews disagreeing with mine, I hope you like it more than I did, but don't say you weren't warned.If you've ever wondered why games like Undertale are so effective at getting you invested in their characters, it's because you spend time with them. Not just 2 blurbs of text spouting some absurd philosophical viewpoint, but learning what makes them tick, their shortcomings, their hopes, their history, even if it's simple. More time with them is better for getting players interested, but if you drag too little personality across too much game time, it becomes irritating instead. So it's a balance.Everhood does this balance poorly, or at least it did for me. Characters rarely have more than 3 lines of dialogue per interaction, and about 2 character quirks so you can remember them. It's not the worst, but it wasn't enough to really get me invested. Points for Green Mage though, he was cool.This isn't the nail in the coffin, though- that's the ending.For a game about accepting the end, Everhood spends literally half its runtime ending. After the 3rd "goodbye" it really stops meaning anything. Minor spoilers: When you copy something everyone loves, sure, you'll see some level of success. But if you don't know how to write a compelling narrative, it's ok to make it silly instead. Instead, Everhood seems to be under the impression it's saying something truly profound, which I think falls on its face.

_childDocuments_.review: A Pixel LSD trip that is 100% worth experiencing!The story revolves around Red and their journey through Everhood to try and retrieve their arm from Gold Pig. The characters in this game don't have any voice acting but the writing that went into the texts that the characters speak to you in was really smart and very witty making each encounter that you experience that much more enjoyable. The story itself is simple enough to follow, but the themes that the game deals with are truly well developed and left a really great impression on me as the player. Have to say that i was satisfied from start to finish. The setting of Everhood is really stunning to look at and cleverly layed out as a good chunk of the game has the player walk around black areas with a pixel art path with hints of life here and there which adds to the mystery of the place. Each area that you walk through really has its own personal identity and makes the experience really immersive. Visually, the game is really well layed out. Technically, there weren't any issues and as  i had a constant frame rate and did not experiences any bugs or issues with the game. The Art Direction is brilliant. While some can compare the look of this game to Undertale, I think that it does enough with its design that it stands out as its own thing and has some really memorable visuals whether that's environments, characters or even the arenas you fight the bosses in. Sound and Audio are fantastic with the soundtrack full of Bangers and always having me bopping my head each time i went into a fight. The Audio also matches the game really well and adds to the overall experience. In terms of gameplay, it's truly one of the best and most challenging rhythm games out there. The movement of Red feels great both traversing through the world and in combat. The way combat plays out is really well done with enemies attacking somewhat to the beat while the player has to play off beat and dodge or parry their attacks which i think the way that the devs executed this was really well done.Overall, Everhood is an exceptional Indie title that deserves more credit than its got and is one of the best games that i have played this year.

_childDocuments_.review: The biggest problem with the game is it tries too hard to be Undertale (I mean look at the Everhood picture on steam, the ATM literally has Flowey's face). Like how there's too many games that try to copy Dark Souls, this one tries to copy Undertale but without the soul and writing that made that game so popular. The combat shows promise, but never enough to be truly satisfying or challenging (the game is very low difficulty, even on the harder modes). I heard a lot about the music, but the music never truly got my attention since most songs sound like random notes are thrown in just to be objects to attack you and not to listen to. The characters didn't stand out to me and weren't fleshed out, and in a game where choices matter like Undertale, having characters that you don't sympathize with or care about ruins the premise entirely. f you haven't played Undertale, then go ahead and put your money into that game and not this one. If you HAVE played Undertale, then you already know what happens in this game. It's one of the most dissapointing kinds of games where there's so much potential in it, but it just falls flat in too many places to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is a good game that feels like an acid trip with a story to boot and wonderful music, but is destroyed by its gameplay. The main sellers of this game are the music (which is great)  and the art, except you can’t see the art 90% of the time because you need 100% focus on the bland boring board. You miss so much in this game that's right in front of you because you have to choose between seeing what you want to see or not repeating the last five minutes of gameplay. After you die from the pig you get into a fight that I lost twice and both times were from trying to look at the sprite work that I would have no other chance to see except for during the fight. Which is sad because the sprite work is the best part of the game but it actively tries to prevent you from seeing any of it!The gameplay itself is rather boring and repetitive and when it's not it's trying to show off that the devs could do something technically but they didn’t think of whether they should, which sucks because it's the only gameplay you have. Let's take a game that everhood clearly took a lot of influence on: undertale. Where if you don’t like one gameplay gimmick another one will be there shortly.As for some nitpicks I hate the fact that the game difficulty screen has a hard mode as the default but has a mode titled “Normal” so… which one do i go with? I went with hard during my time and I think it was the intended difficulty.Also another nitpick is that the text volume keeps changing. Like the sound of grey door and midnight town door are the same but grey door is quiet and midnight town door is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loud.Honestly the game is better watched then played and that is a sad thing to say with how much passion i can tell went into it. Best of luck to the developers of course and I hope they do well in their future projects.I heard the game was about six hours long but I don't want to play anymore and will be watching a let's play instead.

_childDocuments_.review: In case anyone else somehow landed on the same assumptions I did, Everhood is NOT a rhythm game, in the same way that playing an air guitar is not the same as playing a real guitar. While the attacks come in time with the music, the position is completely detached from the notes, meaning that the music aspect is a red herring; it won't help you dodge attacks, and the game boils down to rote memorization of the set pattern of attacks as they come.  This might just be me misreading the game, but I had it pegged as an Undertale-clone rhythm game from the reviews I read and the trailers I watched. While the Undertale clone part was solid, this game is almost the exact opposite of a rhythm game; listening and moving with the music actively kneecaps your ability to properly dodge attacks, as the notes come in un-telegraphed patterns along with the notes in the song, giving one an extremely short window in which to dodge if one is relying on the music to signal incoming attacks.Granted, my experience of this game lasted less than 15 minutes, with me having a viscerally bad reaction to the first real fight I ran into. I got to that point, and abruptly died several times, before force quitting the game and refunding. Me dying a few times was essentially guaranteed; I was treating this game like a rhythm game, not like a bullet-hell rpg dressed up like a rhythm game.I really wanted to like this game; The artstyle and aesthetic are fun, if more than a little derivative, the music is great as long as you treat it as a part of the scenery, and the overall presentation is well done, if a little light on the explanation. I just went in expecting one thing, and got another, and was pretty pissed about that.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: I'm going to save spoilers for the second half of this review.STORY: The overarching plot is thin and shallow. It's intentionally vague and ominous to induce intrigue in the player, but it mostly fails at that & after the big surprise was revealed to me, it really wasn't worth it. In place of an engaging story, the game throws a villain at you, and character driven micro tasks.CHARACTERS: It's Undertale with another coat of paint. The characters have some charm, but some of them feel like "oh, they're wacky alright! it's wacky!" and "why are they even in the game?" The game mostly fails to make the characters interesting or actually do anything with them. The charm is surface level.GAMEPLAY: Everhood provides a unique gameplay experience, I think? But, with the previous two problems listed, this is actually the kiss of death: the gameplay fails to be engaging. As much as it requires of you, pressing left and right and up and down, that's really all it is. Timing. As challenging as avoiding projectiles might be, there's simply not enough player input or decision making to make it fun to redo any fights.MUSIC: The music's great, for the most part. The way it plays into fights is enjoyable. I would say music is the highlight of this game, but you might as well just get the OST. Projectiles are timed to the music, but avoiding them has nothing to do with it.VISUAL DESIGN: Heavily reminiscent of Undertale. Enjoyable enough. A little too simplistic and empty, but that was the intent. Visual design isn't a problem and the game fails on other merits.SUMMARY: The game lacks "engagement" in gameplay, story, and character writing. It's deceptive. It teases charm but doesn't *do anything* with any of it. That's my ultimate critique of Everhood. It throws a bunch of vague charm & intrigue at you and then doesn't do anything, up to the climax and near to the end of the game, it hasn't *done* anything to make me want to finish it. It hits similar "story beats" to Undertale without earning it. Besides that, it has good music.SPOILERS: The story did nothing with Gold Pig. He's "the bad guy" and thoroughly isn't interesting outside of aesthetic. The story has done basically nothing with the most important characters in the game. By the time I was killing Rasta Beast, I felt nothing. What was he supposed to be?? Why was he in the game?? The game makes several minor attempts at getting you to care about side characters by giving them dialogue and having you spend time with them, but they're shallow, they're surface level, they do nothing and say nothing. They're accessories.I know the game has additional endings, but the one it pushes you towards is killing everyone. Killing all of the NPCs. I felt nothing, killing any of them, but it sure was dark and gloomy. Some of them want to die, some of them don't, some of them beg you not to *after* the game asks if you want to kill them, and then you can't change your mind. It's silly. It's really silly. This aspect of the game is such an Undertale copycat without earning it.I'm frustrated with it because I was intent on finishing it, but it was boring me to death and I had to redo a fight a couple times and just didn't have the motivation anymore. The challenge of it isn't a problem, it's that I know I'm getting *nothing* for overcoming a challenge. I'll get some mildly charming character dialogue & then Green Mage dies. Yippee. Another number towards finishing the game. Do something with the characters, *please.* Having you interact with them and then having you kill them off is not "doing something."

_childDocuments_.review: It's quite a good experience. But it does have some notable flaws. None that break the experience, but just makes it feel a bit unpolished. I think this game suffers most if you want to play it on expert and enjoy precision challenge games.First of all, the controls are bafflingly not remapable. This is a ridiculous oversight, as my down key on the keyboard is kinda sticky so it's not reliable on precision charts. Also I wanted to use a custom rhythm game controller, but could not remap the controls to get it to work.Secondly, as far as I can tell there's no input buffer, so if you press the same key twice in too quick succession you will just drop an input entirely. On some expert charts this is a real issue because you have to be practically optimal to win the battle before the song is over.There's also no audio video sync option, something of a standard for rhythm games. Luckily not a big deal because of the nature of the gameplay, but still would've been a nice inclusion to make things feel just a bit tighter.I've also noticed the occasional visual hiccup in the game, where I see a wrong loading frame after walking through a door or something. It's a little distracting.So yeah, I really like this game, but I really want these tweaks to make my experience just a little bit less frustrating (when it isn't supposed to be).

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. It mixes Undertale's aesthetics with flashy rhythm game segments, which should be perfect for me. The early game has that idiosyncratic Undertale humor mixed with fun characters, which I enjoyed, but it's what comes after that led me to making this review. First off, the plot is just awful - it's all over the place and feels like it needs to throw in unexpected plot twists every couple of hours to keep the game fresh. More egregious is that It doesn't understand the ideas its pulling from and ends up telling a ineffective story at best to a morally bankrupt one at worst. Spoilers for entire game below:Ultimately, feels like a game made by a couple guys who barely understand Buddhism and read Nietzsche once and thought he was an unparalleled genius. Just a disappointment - at least a lot of the fights were fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my second review after some consideration. The biggest flaw with this game is splitting itself between a fun psuedo-rhythm game and something that's trying to be grander, existential and more story driven. The first half of Everhood should have been extended and been the entirety of the game with more investment into the world building and character development. The game explains next to nothing about the origin of the world and who the characters even are. There is so little dialogue for each character it's kinda sad.  Now compare this to the first 45 minutes of Undertale, the difference is night and day tbh. And then it tries to be super deep and forces you on a genocide run for what? The game doesn't develop the characters enough for me to care about them. Even Goldpig, the main antagonist only appears like 4 or 5 times in the whole story. I don't know who he is, why he wants my arm and the game doesn't do much to help. The sudden switch from the friendly characters to all of them suddenly hating me is weird as well. Surely they know that I'm searching for my arm from the beginning otherwise they would not have immediately hidden away when acquiring it.Basically, the devs should have either cut out the first half or cut out the second half and instead made that the main story and focusing more on lore building. The soundtrack is outstanding though. So credit to the artists. Overall though, for 9.99 this game will never be as big as Undertale. It's stretches itself too thinly trying to juggle light hearted and fun gameplay with deep themes that don't hit nearly as hard as they should have. What a shame, could have been so, so much more.

_childDocuments_.review: For a game that's supposedly only about 5-6 hours long, it feels like forever.The characters are one dimensional and do nothing but tell jokes, every room you enter's just a black background with steps showing you where to go.Why does everything have to be quirky? When they're all having mood swings at the speed of light how am I supposed to simply understand how they feel? Someone can be all hyped up to battle you, then give up before anything even starts.I guess my main issue is that nothing has any meaning in this game. There's a lot of these spaced-out 'deep' segments where you're told about morals, or death or some ♥♥♥♥, but what's the point? You'll just be playing D&D with your "friends" in the next scene anyway.The gameplay's... something. The battles are flashy, and occasionally quite pretty, but the beat-focused music loses purpose when your actual movements don't match at all. Speaking of, it's decent but samey, and most of the top-down parts don't have any music at all. It's pleasant enough when it's actually there though.And screw all y'all trying to 100%, there's multiple joke achievements you can only get by wasting hours doing practically nothing.I only kept coming back to this game because I always thought it was better than I remembered, however along with all the content in the game I truly remembered nothing about it at all.

_childDocuments_.review: A rhythm game where the bosses attack to the beat of music and you try your best to dodge it all (you can try dodging to the beat if you wish but this won't be a terribly good idea in later fights). There are difficulty options and there's even one for those that just wish to experience the story without having a rough time with the fights. Also, there's a very legitimate photo-sensitivity warning here and the game does have an option to tweak these effects. Still be warned if you suffer from epilepsy. Also, if you suffer from motion sickness very easily then don't grab this game right now. There are times where the screen will move, spin, and completely turn upside down. There's no option to turn this off.Should be noted, because there will be people that will make this comparison, there is some Undertale influences. Namely in the quirky nature of many of the game's characters. Also, the graphic style is fairly similar (NES/SNES styled but with black backdrop use to make things seem more empty or lonely).That's about it and I will note that you can look up a demo that was posted outside of Steam. So, if you aren't sure then you can check that out.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. The people who compare it to Undertale aren't wrong, but are wrong at the same time. The graphic style, the dry humor, the overall weirdness of the game, and many of the environments are reminiscent of Undertale in a lot of ways, but remain unique by each of their own merits. Everhood is a game about the unknown, and truly plays with the player's mind throughout, always making them wonder what exactly they are looking at, and never quite giving them the answer. It plays at the idea of life itself, alongside immortality and the deficits of both. The "absolute truths" it gives you are all very insightful, and provoke a lot of pondering with each one. Because of that, this game is truly special, and appeals to a lot of the things I love to see in any form of literature or media. Through all of its weirdness and seemingly happy portrayal of most characters, it still manages to make something just feel...off in a lot of areas, with soundtracks (or the lack thereof), offputting environments, or dialogue that upon further thought seemed a bit sinister. Everhood seems a bit cliche the first hour or so, but is pleasant for the gameplay aspect of it. I thought that was all there might be. But this game does not disappoint. For every turning point in the story, it introduces a new kind of feeling, whether that may be a sense of euphoric nostalgia of something you never experienced, maybe a feeling of unease, or simply fear of your own consciousness, this game is truly a work of art.A quick summary:Gameplay and Mechanics: 8.75/10Soundtrack: 9.5/10Story (Thus far): 9/10Environment: 10/10 (Simple, but amazingly effective)Characters (Thus far): 8/10*Bonus for thought provoking and existential dread: 10/10Overall: 9.25/10

It has no subtlety whatsoever about whatever fourth-wall break crap that it wants to push on you, and almost feels arrogant about the information it knows about that it refuses to give you.  Which is a shame because occasionally it is kind of creative.* While I really liked the soundtracks, your actions in this game do not match up to the music.  The music is in sync with how the enemies fire their projectiles, not when you need to dodge them, so you're actively encouraged to ignore the rhythm to properly jump and dodge projectiles.  This is the complete antithesis of what a music game is supposed to do.  In Crypt of the Necrodancer, you move to the beat.  In Guitar Hero, you play the notes in sync with the music.  In Rez, you fire projectiles that accompany the main theme.  In this game, you just kind of listen to the music as you dodge projectiles, so it's not even really a music game at that point.* The story is boring and uninteresting, leaving you in the dark, until you get your arm back, and even then, it basically has one hook to reel you back in.  From there, it's just more boss battles and figuring out which path you're going to go.  Certain parts of it remind me of Transistor, and that told a story that was way more nuanced.* The difficulty curve is not great, and unfun-ness of the gameplay made me not want to try in the first place.  I just kept decreasing the difficulty, until I finally set it to Story Mode in the last Frog battle.  Even then, it still took time to get past that battle.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an experience. 10/10 for sure. This game seems to be inspired by Undertale in some aspects, however, this is no Undertale clone. It has its own ideas with its own essence and it pulls them off flawlessly (at least to me). This is a game where the less you know about it the better, but just know it's gonna have twists and turns and a whole bunch of wonderful things in it that will leave your jaw dropped open in surprise and amazement. The maps that you traverse play like Undertale, where there's not much to look at or do within them (there are some really cool mini games though), however the battles are where the game really comes alive (just like Undertale).  Basically the battles are like a reverse guitar hero bullet hell. The notes come at you (you don't control them) and you must evade the notes and get to the end of the song. The game starts off with blue crescent notes and wall notes. The crescent notes you can jump over no problem, but the wall notes, you must evade. I'm sure you can only imagine how crazy this all gets at the very end, but your imagination can't quite paint the true idea you're gonna experience if you play this.Just like Undertale, I felt "feelings" at the end of the game. Again, I want to remind you that this is not an Undertale clone, it's just inspired by it, just like how Undertale was inspired by Mother. They all have their own flair. This game is so creative and amazing, I can't recommend it enough. Every time I succeeded, it felt rewarding. The mystery of the game was intriguing, especially because the game doesn't really care if you know what's going on or not. In fact, it recommends that you don't know. With my 16 hours of game play, I know I still haven't seen everything yet, even though I beat it. This game has so much for you to discover. If you like Undertale, if you like Bullet Hells, if you like dope Music, buy this game. I 100% stand behind this.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood may take lots of inspiration from Undertale, but there is no shortage of creativity and uniqueness here. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, as much as this is a love letter to and inspired by Undertale, it tries to imitate too much and the whole product suffers for it. This isn't an abysmal product. The music is absolutely stellar and was the main driving force for me to finish the game. The soundtrack is worth the purchase. The gameplay is also fun if you approach it as more of a twitch action game than a rhythm game. That's about it for the positives. I realize there is more going on, but I think I've had my fill already. As for the negatives:- Characters are weird for the sake of being weird. There is no more depth beyond their 1-2 tropes.- The environments, no matter how detailed they start out, all devolve into a nearly black screen with speckled sprites giving you a path to follow.- The story (through playthrough 1) is a breakneck pace, to the game's detriment. The themes and emotional moments the game wants you to have are left by the wayside due to the pacing.- Ironically, the ending of playthrough 1 drags on. I believe I was told a version of "let's finish this" at least 4 times before the credits rolled.If you purchase the soundtrack and nothing else, you will have made a good purchase. The game itself leaves a lot to be desired and ultimately tries too much to be another Undertale instead of breaking away and forging it's own identity.

_childDocuments_.review: Very unique. The game is something like a cross between Undertale and a Rhythm Game. I found the positivity of the theme refreshing. I would say the price point is fair for the amount of content and the high quality of the soundtrack. The downsides are that, unlike Undertale, most of the characters aren't very interesting. I had a soft spot for the blue thief, but even he was fairly one note over the course of the game. As a result, the more emotional moments tend to fall fairly flat. That's not to say I felt nothing, I did enjoy the story, but just that I think it could've been better in this regard. The gameplay was quite easy throughout the game, and there were only a couple battles where I even died more than once on hard difficulty mode. Lastly, the plot was only semi-comprehensible. Towards the latter half of the game, I understood what I was doing, but only half of the reasons why. Certain plot twists in particular felt fairly random, and while I'm sure there's a wiki that lays it all out plain, I generally find it to be a poor storytelling when I have to go looking for explanations outside of the story itself when I have to look up "who is the person and what the heck are they talking about?"Overall it was a solid game worth the price of admission.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is an experience which takes inspiration from Undertale in how it develops its characters but presents a core difference in the way you interact with those characters. Every single NPC you interact with is overflowing with personality, and while certain characters can feel expendable, the feeling that you can have running through this world and spending time with everybody really is something amazing,The combat is absolutely enthralling, and will no doubt keep you engaged throughout the experience if the characters and plot don't by themselves. Without spoiling anything, the combat is also used as a worldbuilding tool for the player to interact with directly in the later stages of the game, and allows players of all skill levels to interact with the story on a meaningful level. Without going into spoilers, the method of combat is incredibly engaging and presents varying difficulty levels within optional content, allowing both experienced and less so players to engage strongly with the combat and how it links directly with the game's ideas. I really want to talk about why this exactly worked for me and how this game puts a fundamental twist on the otherwise similar setting to Undertale, so from here on will be spoilers. No doubt this game is best experienced blind (as is everything), so I HIGHLY RECOMMEND playing it through once as you will not regret it at all.~~~~~~ SPOILERS ~~~~~~~

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is a 2D Rhythm game, most commonly compared to Undertale. While yes it is a rhythm game, it's not anything like OSU or Taiko. It’s hard to explain until you see or play it. The game is like an “entry level” rhythm game focusing more simple dodging than exact time inputs.As for the Undertale comparison, yes they on the surface have similar world building and an overall feel, however it isn’t a shameless rip off or anything like that. You will get 2 very different experiences playing these games.I personally loved the gameplay, it just felt nice. It offered a good amount of challenge, especially end-game bosses. If you wish to be a pathetic coward, you can put it on Story Mode, making everything unbelievably easy. Some people in early reviews said performance could tank during some fights but I never noticed that, I run an Acer Swift 3 too, so nothing fancy.Overall gameplay is smooth and satisfying while also offering a nice amount of challenge.OH YEAH BABY. IT'S A BOP.Maybe it’s not for everybody, however I loved this game's soundtrack. Not every song was great, but most were and man was it awesome to hear a great song while beating some of these fights.The graphics when in the overworld or walking around are pretty simple. (Think Undertale). However in the fights they love to twist and warp your expectations. A lot of these fights not only sound amazing and feel outstanding to play but on top of that they look so cool. That being said, it’s nothing absolutely groundbreaking, just really solid.This is a more philosophical and “I wonder what I would do in that situation” type of story. I think the characters were hit or miss though. All of them I liked in some way, whether it be the dialogue, design, or backstory. That being said, some characters were just sorta...there? I wish we could get a prequel to explain who these characters are. The game isn’t super rich in narrative and most things are left for your interpretationIt does have multiple endings, however realistically speaking one of the endings is the most polished, the easiest to obtain, and just feels right.It’s technically replayable, however I didn’t super enjoy going back and doing stuff over again. Everhood is one of those games that is so much better the first time you play.GO. IN. BLIND. Just do it.The game is about 6-10 hours depending on difficulty, completion % and how much you lose at the fights.This game is absolutely great, it's such an outstanding and memorable experience. It also pretty commonly goes on sale, however 10 dollars is still a great price for this game. You don’t have to like rhythm games to play this or games like Undertale. It’s a game that can stand on its own two feet and be a unique and captifying adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: Everhood

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely love this game. The story really cuts deep and you don't even realize that it's doing it until it's done. The pixel art is beautiful and the 3D models don't feel out of place stylistically. The devs created an anti-rhythm rhythm game style of combat where you can't let yourself get caught up in the beat of the absolute bangers that they created - and every fight has a unique song and beatmap. The devs really took liberties with the typical tropes of what a "fight" consists of and turned them into something absolutely beautiful - I got chills from certain fights where the visual effects just hit right. I'm currently working on a no-hit run of the game and I'm not even close to irritated that I lose fights - it just means I hit the "Restart the Banger" button. Do yourself a favor. Don't go get coffee from Starbucks for two days and buy this game instead. It's $10 well spent.

_childDocuments_.review: Everhood is what the store page says it is and that is a trip. Playing this game was like getting in a bumper car that was about to take you through a very bumpy race track and filled with racers that want to do nothing but bump into you. The story of this game is pretty simple at the start and I for one love simple beginnings, they make build up to the more drastic or twists in a game feel a tad bit more impactful and emotional. and if you want to know what I mean by this then I would recommend highly, that you play this game.The difficulty in Everhood can range from a slap to the face or a walk in the park, with battles and encounters changing every so often. The range changes can go from simply dogging, to needing to play a simple game of tennis on a sega genesis, or a kart racing mini game. During (what feels like) actual boss fight however the game can really thrash you around, making you have a need to learn what needs to be done or what pattern should you look for which is also helped by the bumpin soundtrack that plays in the background. My only complaint (which they might have patched by now) is the visuals, which could even the most strongest of eyes wince or close just to keep you from going blind or having a seizure. Thankfully this game dose give you a very big warning about that on launch.The music in Everhood can be summarized as having no strait theme, but a vast and colorful batch of songs that almost anyone would find a favorite in the ost guaranteed. Music in this game will almost always take you into the perspective of where you are or who you are facing with environmental changes happening on drops, reverb moments and other musical opportunities. on a final note I loved the message of this game and would recommend this gamethank you for reading and I hope this helps you with your choice.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good production quality of the utilized assets that unfortunately fail to make up a good or anyhow interesting game due to complete lack of creative vision. From start to finish, Everhood feels like a 100% commercial product desperately trying to replicate the formula of a game that succeded solely from the lack of thereof.You can go play that garfield fight minigame on Newgrounds and have more fun in 5 minutes than after playing Everhood for hours. Ngl Everhood is how I imagine AI generated games are gonna look and feel like in the future. Fever dream with no substance.

_childDocuments_.review: I completely forgot to review  after beating it when it was fresher in my mind, which is an absolute shame because it's one of the most creative games I've played in a long time.  draws the  comparison for some clear reasons; the wacky characters and writing, unique combat system, and multiple endings. That being said,  is an extremely unique game; it's quite psychedelic and existential in ways I've never before experienced in gaming. The combat is absolutely genius, it plays on that tried and true music game formula in such a cool way - jumping over and rolling away from the notes flying at you. It's thrilling to play, and the music is absolutely killer.  is a really special game and one I look forward to diving deeper into once my backlog has been conquered. I did find the game to be quite difficult, but it has a good range of difficulties available. I highly recommend  to fans of music games, unique RPGs, and anyone who enjoys innovative boundary-pushing titles clearly created by passionate developers. Beat it so you're ready for the sequel!

name: Company of Crime
detailed_description: Company of Crime is a criminal empire-builder featuring tactical turn-based missions. It takes place in 1960s London, the cultural capital of the world and home to a plethora of subcultures and businesses. Your task is to build a company that will own the criminal underworld, or if you play as the chief inspector of Scotland Yard’s famous Flying Squad, tear it down piece by piece. In the process you will go to pubs, clubs, vets, tailors, harbors and many other locations as you expand your influence over the city. Your team consists of either gang members possessing the different skills required to pull off criminal tasks, or detectives that have mastered the art of investigation. The big question is ultimately this: who will take London? Features: Tactical turn-based melee combat With a focus on melee combat and tight spaces, Company of Crime sets itself apart from other tactical turn-based strategy games. Units have a zone of control that makes them tied to the choices you make. Block enemy movements, build superiority in numbers, and gain flanking bonuses by attacking from behind. You can even kick enemies where the sun doesn’t shine to create safe passageways to units that would otherwise get free attacks. If someone grabs a gun, either find cover or go after them to wrestle it away before the bodies start piling up. Heat mechanics When doing your dirty business, you’d be wise to silently extort your way through the underworld. Loud gunfire or shooting enemies will only attract more opposition, and a criminal empire that blows its cover won’t go far. Fighting the outcome of too much heat is always more difficult than avoiding it, and if things get too tough, you better have some leverage to get the cops off your back. Level progression This is more than just cops and robbers. Whatever the mission is, there is level progression beyond just hit points and stamina. Beating up the owner of a pub is one thing, but you can’t just bail before the police arrive. You’ll have to first assemble any evidence that will prove it was you at the crime scene before jetting. Building legit business with criminal means Building a criminal empire requires a legitimate cover. Progression of the game takes place as you… ahem… “convince” people to sell their businesses and homes to you at a bargain price, or at least turn a blind eye to what you do in their back room. Owning more locations will unlock more items, features, and elements, but will also potentially expose you to a surprise attack from the police or a rival criminal family. Not just your own story While your task is to create an empire of crime or to tear it down, this is not just your story. This is a story of 1960s London with beatniks, mods, lemonheads, rockers and every other cultural identity of the time. It’s also a story of a falling empire. The Cold War UK is shining in the cultural world, but is facing ever-increasing pressure from inside and out. There is a mysterious order trying to tear down the British Empire from the shadows, and who better to fight it than experts of the underworld and the famous Flying Squad. Reactive Police Shady business takes place in obscurity, so police gameplay is more reactive. You get the call only when violence takes place, but that’s not the best way to find evidence against the criminal families. Assign sergeants to discover shady places, speak with informants, and apply for search warrants to raid questionable locales. Make sure they don’t burn the evidence before you manage to arrest them, or they’ll walk free as quickly as they were taken in.

Will you build an influential criminal empire, or head up an elite Scotland Yard task force and crack down on the rising tide of corruption? Case out targets, then dive into the melee with your hand-picked team of gangsters or detectives.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I played now for 3 hours straight and I think the game is okay... Worth the price, no. Let me explain why:1. The mechanics of how the heat works is not the best, even if you don't use violence the heat goes up way to fast and laying low in reality doesn't help much.2. After all the objectives are done in a mission as simple as extortion you can't leave if the cops don't show because you are going to get an objective to pick evidence only UNTIL the cops show up so you can be already in the escape zone and still have to come back. 3. The game only goes tactical on the specific assignment. You can't wander around the map.4. The logic implemented on the combat is sometimes confusing.5. You do feel after a couple of hours that the game starts to get boring, even with the concept that is incredible the game falls to trap you into it.There can be a list of issues I think the developers could fix but at the end this is not the space to do it. I'll be happy to share this with the devs. So to finish my "Review" sorry if is not enough information, the game concept is great and I was really excited for it but at this point I can't recommend this for this price. NOT WORTH IT.P.S: After playing for almost 8 hours now I kinda change my opinion on the heat system but the police coming in when the brawl hits the first line in situations like the Bethnal Green's residential is chaos. Is impossible to get that mission completed because there is only one door to the building and it has two floors so to find the enemy and knock them out takes too long and by the time you finish with the main objectives you already have at least 7 cops on the door, so again... bad level design. Another thing that could be better is the raids almost 6 cops for two henchmen. Is basically a lost cause.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; an okey xcom-like game where you lead a small gang in 1960's UK, that falls short in gameplayPros:+ Pretty original, not much games like these out (combining crime mechanics + empire building + combat)+ The combat is OK+ Managing your own small-crime imperium seems like a really cool idea!+ The style game is going for is fun, not too serious and not too jokey. Think about a dark comedy, with brawling but not too much violenceCons:- The gameplay loop seems to get a bit tedious and boring after a while (not enought things to do and cannot really do any micro managing for the crime empire)- The UI has some problems. Not the most intuitive, took a while to figure out where everything is.- The combat is just "ok"- Too much repetation in the missions. Different kinds of missions don't really feel any different.- No real story (There is a small story that plays behind the scenes - doesn't really catch attention)My overall feeling while playing this is that I'm almost having good fun, but not quite. Just falls short for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Company of Crime has a couple of really fun elements that you've not seen in any other games. These things give it something fresh and novel that sets it apart from games such as Omerta or Gangsters: Organised Crime that follow a similar theme.The focus on melee combat is quite fun, especially when your crew levels up and gets their diverse skills. The first time you see a character bash someone's head onto a surface, or kick someone in the nuts, you go "Oooohhh. ouch! *shudder*". These moves give it a lot of flavour, as does the overal presentation. What the game lacks in visual fidelity, it makes up in spades by sheer character.The campaign and its map feel decidedly boardgame and help drive you forward as you go from mission to mission. You generally return to locations a few times but where I feared that might make the maps go stale, I actually found it helped me strategize. Never once did I feel I visited a place too often. As you gain various levels of control, bonuses and new mission types unlock, adding to your arsenal of things that help you take over London's crime scene.There are a few small bugs but none that break the game or the immersion. There were a few moments where I wasn't sure what the game was requiring me to do. Fortunately the devs have been present in the forums today answering questions. Overall, a fresh take on a fun genre in a setting that has been under-served recently.

Level progression and difficulty is non-existent. (basically nothing in the game ties in together)- Extremely repetitive.I really gave myself a chance to like this game, but it's really not very fun :( . How do you call this fun???Not worth my money at all. I wish I can refund this.

_childDocuments_.review: The latest patches have improved so many aspects of the game that many of the reviews here touch upon.The setting and atmosphere in this game is spot on. I am almost done with the criminal campaign and I have definitely enjoyed the game. The focus on melee combat can seem a bit dull at first, but the idea kind of grows on you after a while and it gets more diverse when leveling up the different characters and facing new enemies. There will be different locations, surprise events and story missions that keep the game interesting. Dealing with civilians does get easy and safe/boring, but it's a nice change between the more dangerous assignments. Managing the heat is the real enemy at the start of the game. I once lost to a heat emergency situation, but loading up the game I was able to just save myself in the given timeframe.  I personally like to take my time in these kinds of games and not worry about a forced time constraints or catastrophic events etc. (XCOM, Mechanicus for example). Once I've got the hang of the heat system I was able to take my time with taking control of one district at a time, and especially later in the game even take risks and be a bit more reckless if I wanted to.After reading most reviews after launch I was not sure what to expect, but the game really grasped me. It's not perfect, but the developers have clearly improved some key areas based on player feedback. If you are interested in at least the setting, turn-based combat or both I would definitely recommend giving it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Company of Crime

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes at the end of the day, when you need to talk about a game you'd recommend to someone, there are situations where you won't say it's a "good" game, or that it's a particular pleasure to play, but you recommend the game because, for all its flaws and shortcomings, it has a spark. It has something that among the rest, makes it unique and enjoyable. Such is the case for Company of Crime.A game set in London of the 60s, with a focus of gang wars and a strong influence from modern X-COMs, and to some extend Phantom Doctrine, has something to seduce. And indeed, the ambiance is there. The music, the clothes, the environnement. It's all there. Yet, the game is, well, it's janky. There is no hiding it, there are a bunch of bugs, some of with I had the dubious honor of helping to fix, but when you consider only 2 persons did all the QA, and the game was made by a very small team, you need to understand where you're going. It is very much a game to get in the 15 euros or less, as that's overall the value of such a game. It's not  big budget game, and what it delivers, I'm afraid to say, can't possibly compete with a juggernaut like Firaxis backed by the greedy bastards at 2K("2K, you love it, we ruin it!"). The core loop is repetitive fast, the enemies not varied, and while the heavy melee focused combat feels fresh and in some aspect reminds a bit of Into the Breach by some aspect(positioning and use of your skills to control the battlefield are key, and can lead to nice combos), at the end of the day, it won't be something able to keep you hooked for too long, which is a bit of a shame.Yet there is fun to be found, the simple pleasure of throwing opponents over tables, hitting them with bottles and ashtrays, holding them while an other of your character goes to town on their head with a hammer while a Shaft-like music is playing... In that I feel like the experience is pretty unique for a turn by turn game.I want to give a special mention to the developers behind the game too. Since release, they were very present. Asking all people leaving negative reviews to tell them where they failed, and how to make the game better. Answering to question and bug reports, fixing said bugs. A year after release, they are still there, and they are pretty approachable. I appreciate that a lot, the courage to face people being very harsh with their game, and the will to constantly improve, and the effort to give themselves time to really stay in contact with the players via the Steam forums, while others companies will either ignore you, or try the predatory system to force you to come to their forum/discord server/website, in the hope to control their "communities" for future profits, and to also control their voices and opinionsI'm recommending this game the same way I recommended The Bureau, despite the fact they have shortcomings, they are games with soul, which contain the embers of greatness and what could have been.

_childDocuments_.review: Company of Crime is a turn-based strategy game. This is very true. Aside from that, it wants to be so much more but doesn't deliver to be considered a good game.The setting is very interesting and very much unused in the genre. The problem is: There is so much potential and they can't use it. The story isn't really good. Its narrative could be so much more if they didn't try to give the player freedom. I said try because it doesn't feel like you have much freedom at all. It looks like you can do whatever you want, approach the game how you want, but you can't really. There are a few missions you need to work off one after another. There is no diplomacy system or something similar in place. The missions are boring. Most of the time you are not allowed to kill someone. While that is realistic to some degree, it spoils much the game could offer. The question is, how realistic should it be while still being fun? There is almost no need to take weapons with you because most have a chance to kill someone and if you do, the mission is failed. Also, most locations look the same. Enemies don't vary that much and there are just 4 classes to choose from. Every mission is the same. Go in there, maybe steal something, knock off the boss, the police arrive and you need to leave. Leaving means going to a marked location and click on "leave". This works even if the police or enemies are standing right beside you. It's unlogical (at least place a car next to the marked location to make it somewhat realistic if you're going for the realistic approach in this game?) and plain boring. If someone of your crew gets knocked off, enemies won't kill him most of the time and if you leave with the rest of the crew all are save (just need to rest/heal or spend some time in jail). This is also unrealistic if they are not going to jail. Why should another gang leave him to go? The music is atmospheric. Well, at least in the menus because in battles there literally is no music and it seems off. Let's talk about the battles. They work like in most other TBS games. 2 action points you can spend however you want. Some abilities you won't ever use because there is no need to. The game is not tactical most of the time. You can approach each mission differently. Go through the back door/front door/etc. and place your crew members accordingly before the mission starts but it doesn't matter. You don't even know where enemies are. If one of your members goes through the front door by himself and enemies attack them, the rest of your crew loses time to help out. The best way is to go through the same door with all of your members and just attack enemies. Yeah, there are a few abilities that are nice to use and help you out but overall this has nothing to do with a tactical turn-based strategy game. It's very casual and a joke compared to games like XCOM. It also has the tag RPG. There are no RPG elements besides leveling up your members and choosing one of two abilities at each level. Company of Crime had so much potential but it's just not good enough to be considered a good game. 30USD/€ are way too much to ask for. Even 15USD/€ on a sale is too much IMO. Skip this game or, if you really want it, buy it for 5-10USD/€. It probably can be fun for casual players who rarely play Turn-based strategy games.

_childDocuments_.review: There are currently around a million hex-based tactics games created by independent studios. Fortunately,  is the rare tactical game of distinction, proving that there are still new ideas in this crowded genre. In  you play as a couple of British lowlives in the mid 60s. The music is groovy. The atmosphere is filthy. You send your gangsters out on missions across a map of London and watch the timer tick, while managing resources like money and respect. But then a mission begins and you zoom in on the  tactical map.What your characters can actually do in a tactical combat game is pretty tricky. Even though XCOM is the game that defines this genre today, you actually have a pretty wide range of things you can do in combat. Depending on the character, you might be able to wrestle, throw, subdue, or emotionally manipulate your targets. Not only can you change the positioning of the enemy, but yours is also very important. Because depending on where you are, you may also have access to improvised weapons like chairs, bottles or even walls. Unfortunately, the strategic layer leaves quite a bit to be desired. It's functional, but less inspired than combat. You assign your guys to different places on the London map, then you… wait. It would be nice if there were some exciting strategic decisions.We should also be talking about the other feature in the game, which is that you play not only as thieves, but also as police. It didn't drastically change the gameplay, but functionally looks like a second campaign. Overall, this is an original twist on the XCOM-style of strategy that lets you experience both sides of the 60’s London crime scene.- Groovy 60s style- Great tactical fights- Melee-focused combat is fun- Different classes- Tedious strategic gameplay- Graphics are a bit blurry- Combat is too repetitiveDISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY |  | GREAT | AMAZING | MASTERPIECE

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is not bad, but it's always the same thing, over and over.5 hours later, 1 area controlled, 10 more to go!And you still have to go back to previously conquered areas because other gangs will try to take back places from you.It feels like you're never making a step ahead and have to fight on the same maps every time.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is exceedingly dull. Like, incredibly dull. Typical gameplay loop: "Case" an area, if it doesn't auto succeed you go in and beat up some guys/shoot some guys. That's pretty much it. Oh there's a strategy layer, but it boils down to "make money so you dont go negative" or buy stuff from the black market. Once you've played the first 2 or 3 missions you understand the entirety of the game. It lacks all depth.It has some good things going for it, like a unique visual style, decent animations and a genuinely expansive combat system (think xcom's skill picking), but at the end of the day it just wasn't very fun. Everything feels incredibly slow, the missions are tedious, the 'plot' is blasé, and the writing is extraordinarily generic. The game feels like a mobile game ported to pc with a greedy price tag slapped on.Truthfully, I only tried it because I'm still waiting on Empire of Sin. I would have to give this one hard pass unless the game goes to 9.99 USD.

_childDocuments_.review: Criminals playthrough... and all I can say is... this game is annoying.EDIT: ^ This has been pointed out as intended. See @platypus developer response.Also, they way the police are implemented as the criminals is frustrating. There is no end to police once they start rushing your encounter and more spawn practically every other turn.In theory that means you have to finish your task and escape while the cops are chasing you.... in practice it means if you don't complete the mission in 4 turns you're screwed. Not fun.I also don't like how opportunity attacks are 'per adjacent square' instead of once per player. This means if you have a character walk through the 'Fog of War' and there was an enemy an another side of a door... it has 3 chances to hit you with opportunity attacks.It's also not self-evident which actions are free actions and which actions cost 2 action points. Until you learn which is which, you may find yourself wasting opportunities or wondering why your turn is over.My short summary thoughts:The concept is good but it feels very rough around the edges.

Towards the end of the Police campaign, I was relieved to see the last two story missions happened back to back, so I did not have to raid another place ever again. Not recommending the game due to the repetitive aspect of the game.Overall, Company of Crime is okay in terms of turn-based tactics.
