_childDocuments_.review: For those who like turn-based strategy games, the game is appealing BUT, it has more negative aspects than positive. In general terms, the first flaw (but which can even be ignored) is the fact that the thieves' campaign is too long and repetitive. Long games are interesting, when there is content that justifies it (not the case). But the game's biggest problem is the police campaign, which is all buggy. I got to the point where I couldn't play anymore: whenever I try to do any mission, my policemen disappear and I can only play with Grahm (a chief policeman, who enters the story), and the mission is always the same: to arrest 2 very weak bosses, who don't even belong to any gang. Then the game becomes practically unplayable and you can't complete the story. I could be describing other smaller bugs, but in a game with bugs so big that it doesn't allow to finish the story, I don't think it's even worth continuing to give more details... It's a shame that the game is in this state...Score of 4/10 due to the number of bugs.

_childDocuments_.review: The game had a ton of potential but seems to have been abandoned by the devs and left to be a buggy mess.The Police campaign especially has way too many times where it gets glitched out randomly and forces you to start the whole campaign from the beginning, unless you happened to make multiple saves that you could return to and hope that you don't get locked out from being able to get further in the story.I hope this game is gonna get some updates and bug fixes, but until then I cannot recommend for anyone to buy it

_childDocuments_.review: I've played four hours so far and enjoyed them. The graphics are great, music is cool and I love the theme and idea of the game. I've only unlocked the second area in the game so far and therefore have not progressed a huge amount. The game works fine as far as I can tell although there are is an annoying feature/bug/thing that needs to be altered or removed in my opinion. For example, I perfectly completed a mission and all my units were going towards the exit zone with no more objectives to complete. Guaranteed 100% perfect success. Suddenly a "we have left something behind" objective appeared and now we had to collect it. Well I am sorry but...we didn't actually leave anything behind, and now every single copper in the UK is somehow outside the building. Meaning we now have to slog all the way through it, up a flight of stairs and into a cupboard for this..."thing" we left behind without being arrested which is literally impossible because every single cop in the world is now surrounding us. So all your guys get arrested and it's game over basically for no reason...The other thing I hate is how ALL employees of businesses behave. You work at the dry cleaners with your boss and 2 other people...suddenly 4 men armed with guns and hammers charge in and demand your boss pays them protection money each week. What do you do? Say yes and they'll leave immediately OR valiantly charge into battle for your boss with your fists against people with guns and die? Other than that and the odd other personally irritating thing it's a fun game. Would be even more awesome with a few more features like a sandbox mode or character customization, even if it is just the ability to change characters nicknames etc.

_childDocuments_.review: Pick this game up on sale, 66%off just few month after release; I guess there is probably a reason... or few.1) UI: Can't find inventory manual; no idea what weapons and items my gang have, no idea who has what until mission crew selection (even that, you can only see them one by one, instead of a list of crew and their equipment, stats, etc.)2) AI&Strategy: For a strategy game, there is no strategy to your play; no need to pick which door to bust through, just go together, rush toward the nearest enemy, then move on the next. AI enemy will just rush at you straight forward, no strategy whatsoever. Started a game on the hardest setting, almost own two towns (owning businesses, not just extorted them), haven't lost a fight once. Also, see comment (5).3) Bugs: For examples, Police raid my place. The policeman in the front is just fine, but then... two floating head rushed out from kitchen to attack me. Floating Heads! Sometime in mission crew selection page, your crews' hair & eyeglasses will be behind their heads. I'm not sure to laugh or feel sad that this is a released "complete" game.4) Extremely Repetitive, absolutely no variation: Every mission is the same, go there, beat up everyone, then leave; Every one of them. _childDocuments_.review: ‘Ere, me old china, can I get a quick word in your shell-like? There’s this new game in town: Company of Crime. I’ve given it a bit of a butcher’s, so let’s get out yer drum and head dahn the cruiser, and I’ll fill you in.Right, that’s enough of that. I was going to write this entire thing in both dialect and Cockney rhyming slang, but looking out of the corners of my minces, I can already see the copy editors sharpening their knives. Company of Crime has given me enough virtual brutality that I don’t need to experience any in the real world. At least this time I have an excuse to use proper British spellings, although I’m sure they’ll edit those out too. Pillocks.So let’s quickly move onto the game itself. Company of Crime is a turn-based tactical combat-’em-up set in the swinging London of the 1960s. Guy Ritchie’s anachronistic XCOM, if you like, where instead of soldiers, cities, and aliens, we have gangsters, nightclubs, and coppers. It’s up to you whether you want to take the reins of a rising criminal empire or stamp out crime as an officer assigned to the Flying Squad.Wild thingBarring the style, which definitely deserves a lot of words, the most interesting part is the way it handles tactical combat. See, while this resembles XCOM in so many ways – the perspective, the interface, the fact that each unit has two action points per turn that you can use to move or attack – it differs from it hugely in one major respect. Gun combat isn’t a good idea.Which makes an awful lot of sense. If you’re playing as the rozzers, you want to arrest people so you can get evidence and information about other criminal hangouts. And if you’re a gangster, then using guns is a really good way to very quickly attract a very heavy and very angry police presence. Guns are, barring a few missions and events, a last resort. So melee combat is the order of the day.And to Company of Crime‘s credit, it handles this pretty well both in terms of aesthetics and mechanics. You don’t just “punch” people. You can grapple them, kick them in the bollocks, or poke them in the eyes. You can fling beer bottles at them, smash a chair over their head, or hurl them over a table. You can even hurl insults or threats to inflict different status effects. Units have a zone of control; enemies entering or leaving that trigger an attack of opportunity. But position matters a lot, so deciding whether to risk getting clobbered just to flank a foe is theoretically an interesting tactical decision.In the company of crimeAll of this culminates in some truly beautiful chaos. There’s a real sense of a ridiculous bar fight in most of these brawls, with bottles sailing through the air and people being flung left and right. Just, uh, in what’s almost stop-motion, considering the turn-based nature of the thing.This delightful visual spectacle extends even as far as the world map. Company of Crime has a strategy layer, too, where you pore over a map of London and plot out robberies, extortions, and takeover bids. One of my favourite little things about the game is the way this animates as time passes. Cups of tea appear, are drained, and then vanish. Ashtrays fill up with cigarette butts and are then emptied and replaced, all while a slightly tinny radio bangs out music with interruptions from a very 60s-ish DJ. It’s a tiny thing, but it evokes the period incredibly well.And… this is pretty much where I run out of good things to say about Company of Crime. The melee combat? Actually has some good, clever design elements. The style? Smashing and evocative. The gameplay? Er. Well. Um. It’s not bad, but it’s hard to call it anything more than mediocre.I can’t get no satisfactionThe first and arguably biggest problem is the AI. It is, to put it mildly, unbelievably thick. In tactical combat, it will routinely make incredibly poor decisions that give you an advantage that you simply should not have.The AI won’t think twice about spending one action running through your zone of control (taking four hits in the process) and then its next action running back to where it was, taking twice as much damage. It’ll grapple — which does no damage and just disables a unit — when it’s the only unit around, and adjacent to three of yours that can retaliate. When it’s in a defensive position where only one of your units can reach it, it’ll Bull Rush into the center of the fray, opening itself up to immediate destruction.Putting it bluntly, Company of Crime‘s AI makes a lot of questionable decisions. There’s no real feeling of outsmarting a cunning opponent. Half the time, it’s more like extending your arm and waiting for the game to merrily charge into your fist.Worse, this means most of those abilities your units have are pointless. While a well-timed gouge or nut kick can be useful, it’ll almost never make or break a fight because you’re just not in that much danger. Abilities that reposition or lock down a foe can be helpful, but for the most part, you can happily hit “melee attack” over and over again until you win.Frankly criminalThe strategy layer of Company of Crime doesn’t fare much better. You’re following a reasonably strict campaign with more regions of London opening up as you complete story missions, while taking over and extorting businesses along the way. Interestingly, every business also has a unique tactical map: no randomization here. If you pop into the Tiger pub to cause a bit of a ruckus, then it’ll have the same building layout as when you’re defending it from a police raid or performing an all-out robbery.It’s a neat idea and one that doesn’t work in practice because of the amount of repetition involved. See, you have Fear and Respect in each region, and you need these to take control of businesses and raise your profile. To get Fear and Respect, you do missions like robberies. Often three times in a row. On the same map.And then if you want to remove enemy control from that property, you do a Menace mission on that map. And then a Coerce Ownership mission to take it for yourself before someone else does. Resource management of money, influence, and police Heat play a role in the early game (extorting a place gets more resources, but ownership gets other bonuses) but by the middle of the campaign, you’re swimming in resources and can safely ignore any of these decisions.Bad moon risingAnd that’s without going into the bugs. One map has squares that seem to have invisible walls on them. There are maps (and some unit bugs) that impact mission weirdly and occasionally make them impossible to finish. There are ability interactions that don’t actually appear to work as intended.The police campaign avoids some of these issues and has its own neat mechanics in the overworld. You assign sergeants to patrol areas and raise safety, and to keep an eye out for criminal activity, which leads to tactical missions. It’s a more reactionary campaign that has less resource management, but it also feels like a bit of an afterthought and definitely not the focus of the game. Location descriptions are identical, even when it doesn’t make much sense. For instance, one pub is described as being disliked by Allie in both campaigns, even though Allie is one of the criminal campaign protagonists and barely appears in the police campaign.All of this makes Company of Crime feel like less than the sum of its parts. It’s not bad, despite what the last nine paragraphs might indicate. It’s just a game where — after a little while — you can mostly ignore the resources and mash Melee Attack to win. Company of Crime has some genuinely clever ideas and does some genuinely decent things, but they’re overshadowed by AI problems and massive amounts of repetition. If you love the setting or the idea of it, I daresay you’ll get a fair few hours of fun out of it. Just don’t expect the next great turn-based tactical strategy game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted to like this game, but it has some major balance and interface issues.I like the style, music, vibe, and overall idea - and I was hoping for something that would hold me over until a certain "Sin" based game comes out.However, this game has a couple problems. Firstly, in regards to interface, it's very easy to accidentally take the wrong action in combat because the interface tries to "autosuggest" where your character should be moving - often resulting in a character moving into someone's zone of control and giving them "attacks of opportunity" that can throw the fight and aren't needed. Even if you're incredibly careful, that will happen at least once.Secondly, some balance issues need to be fixed. Firstly, if any of your characters are arrested in the opening act, you're screwed. You can't get them out of jail yet, but you've got to continually pay their monthly wages. Next, there's problems with the constant police raids on your businesses. If you want to directly own an area, expect your businesses to be raided by police "all the freakin' time." These raids are particularly frustrating because you get 2 characters versus 6 cops - so it can be extremely difficult not to get them arrested.Lastly, mission objectives are not even at all clear. In the second act, you're supposed to beat up members of a rival gang. But it doesn't track your progress or tell you how many times you need to do it. So I was just left aimlessly attacking them, hoping that it would eventually lead to the next act and goal. However, that never happened, and I gave up before I got there.So, in essence, I feel like this game has a great concept behind it, but was released too soon. If they fix some of the many, many issues, then I think this could gradually become a better (and more playable) game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's definitely not great. It's repetitive, it's clearly underdeveloped (for example, all your recruits of the same class have exactly the same stats). But when someone ends up in a morgue, it draws a lot more attention from the police than when some shmuck gets his teeth kicked in. So you have to keep that balance and take out your gun only when you really need to.2) You have to choose between buying out businesses and racketeering them. Racketeering gives more money, especially if you beat up the owner once in a while, but owned businesses give various bonuses, like more crew members on a mission 3) In melee combat, you don't just exchange punches, you throw opponents over tables, slam them into walls, throw bottles at them, etc. It's fun.Overall, it's not a game I'd play to completion, but it's definitely worth its low price.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit (9/15/20): This is a revision from my original review. The Dev response may feel out of place now, as I've drastically altered the review. At release, I had originally given this game a not recommend, in large part due to its originally very rough nature at launch. The Devs have since gone through and fixed multiple things and appear to be having even more coming down the pipeline. I've updated my review to reflect my new stances. =The Good=* Super fun concept. Using an XCOM style system to run a criminal enterprise is great. The fact that there is a police campaign is cool too.* Enjoyable artistic design - The graphics suit the game and look pretty good for the price point. The music also matches the theme of the game well.* The story, while a bit sparse so far, is enjoyable from what I've seen. Little touches like the various rival gangs sending messages when you intrude on their turf all add a bit to the atmosphere. * The Police Campaign - Despite seeming to be a "secondary" campaign, the police campaign is actually a much tighter overall experience. Nearly all of your skills are useful at some point or another. There is a use to both melee and ranged attacks because weapon use isn't overly punished. The mission goals, while usually fairly similar, vary enough to change things up from time to time. It appears to be in much better overall condition than the criminal campaign. * The AI has seen much better improvements since the launch and are now semi-competent. They will and do use the full suite of skills available to them, although they still are a bit punch heavy. This has gone some of the way towards making debuffs more useful as well as making the arrival of the cops, while still a concern, no longer the mission ender it frequently once was. * Introduction of random loot from various missions gives you more of a chance to experiment with stuff and introduces a fun element of decision making in how greedy you want to attempt to be on a mission. It feels pretty good when you find a nice non-lethal weapon to help kit you crew out and give them a little more oomph than just fist fighting without having to resort to guns. * Finally, and in fact one of the things that most changed my mind is that the Devs are active both in communicating with the playerbase and are making good on their word that they're going to continue to polish the game. These updates have introduced a fair amount of good polish already, especially considering the speed they've gotten them out, and their descriptions of what else is coming down the pipeline gives me a lot more reason to believe the game will end in a good state. =The "Wait and See"=* There are are a decent number of UI hiccups. Tooltips that are wrong, item descriptions that are missing bits of text. None of these are gamebreakers, but it definitely needs a pass. For example, the heat reduction from buildings currently says its per month, but according to devs, it actually triggers per day. That's a pretty major difference in payout. * Formerly in my bad column, the Devs have commented that they now have a number of tweaks to the heat system incoming in updates. I'm waiting to see where that goes. * Movement UI. This is not something I personally have had a problem with, but a lot of people have commented that they've had issues with misclicks and the like. The devs have also commented they're touching up on this in a new patch. * Another issue I had brought up was the problem of the deadliness of weapons in combination with the "Do Not Kill" requirements negating the use of a lot of weapons as well as them overwriting the ability to use your punches for non-deadly finishing attacks. They've also promised a fix for this. =The Bad=* Influence still feels largely like a sort of pointless currency, but with the upcoming heat changes and the ability to pick what journalists do, it may yet come out balanced since you won't be getting forcefed lots of influence you don't have plans for yet. This is a very minor point though and may or may not be made irrelevant with the heat system changes. * Civilians still strike me as either just an annoyance or having some sort of mechanic to them that isn't well explained. I still feel like players should either be given more reason to care about them or for them to be removed. You only need to have your ability to leave a building blocked by a dumb civilian once or twice for it to just feel incredibly annoying, especially considering the already tight maps in many cases.* The UI is still a bit clunky in places or missing ease of information for certain things in game. For example, the ability to see what resources you have available to you now with the implementation of random loot would be nice, but there is no dedicated inventory screen. It can only be checked when equipping a crew. This hasn't become a dealbreaker for me yet in my time in the game, but I could see how it might depending on just how much equipment you end up gathering. All said and done, I'm actually incredibly impressed with how quickly they managed to turn around a game that had a lot of major flaws and change it into a pretty decent one and I'm looking forward to the implementation of the fixes they say they're working on now which should resolve most of my major concerns with the core gameplay loop.

_childDocuments_.review: My final reviewGAMEPLAY: The gameplay is fun for a TBS game, I mean there can't be much in a variety of TBS games, they all feel the same after awhile. You take over businesses, rinse and repeat pretty much. It can get stale quickly.GAME LENGTH: 20-25 hours at least on criminal campaign.PRICE / QUALITY: $30 is a little steep, I'd say $20 would be a more fairer price.DIFFICULTY: Default difficulty settings (easy, normal, hard). Early on you gain too much heat and not enough power to reduce it. You will constantly stress about it until you get to mid-game.MUSIC: There ain't much music variety and it gets stale quick.GRAPHICS: The graphics are on the okay - good side for a indie isometric TBS game.STORY: The story is simple, it's a mixture of sandbox and story mode. You start as a thug stealing from a jewelry store who builds up into an entire criminal empire taking the whole of London, toppling other gangs in your wake.BUGS: Oh boy...(1) Crew bug - sometimes the game won't let you swap between crew members, after you unlock the 6th crew member slot, it's 100% bugged and can be game breaking if you want or NEED to swap your members as the game will auto fill your missions with low levels or unwanted classes and even people that were injuried on previous missions.SUGGESTIONS TO DEVS:(1) Make a sandbox mode(2) Beat up missions and espionage missions are basically useless, redo them. To the general user do I recommend this game? Not really...I only recommend the game if you absolutely love the crime genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Company of Crime:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Every country and indeed, city, in this beautiful world of ours has notorious individuals or gangs. Some are more famous than others. Al Capone and Lucky Luciano were probably the most notorious and known gangsters during the prohibition in America. In the 1960’s, the small and isolated island known as England had its fair share of dangerous criminals, with the Krays Twins and the Richardson brothers, to mention a couple. So, what is the business of crime? How hard is it to establish yourself and, most importantly, to keep yourself at the top of your game? On the opposite side of the coin, there are people who put their lives on the line to dismantle these organisations and arrest their members one by one. Will you become the next big mobster of the 60’s, or will you fight against them as the boss of Scotland Yard’s task force? One thing is for sure, you’ll know all about Company of Crime!Company of Crime is a turn-based strategy game developed by Resistance Games and Published by 1C Entertainment on the 8th of August 2020 on the Steam platform.After selecting whether you want to play the Police or the Criminal campaigns, as well as the level of difficulty, you’ll arrive on the main screen, which is the London map. It doesn’t matter if you decide to play the cops or the criminal, the map will be divided into 11 districts. Regardless of which one you choose, you’ll start playing in the Newham district. As the gangsters, you’ll have to level up your reputation through fear and respect, but you also need to make sure not to increase too much the level of heat (the higher the heat, the more the police will raid your buildings, etc).  The heat is represented as a gauge (1 to 5) on that London map screen; otherwise, you’ll have more and more issues with the cops. Each district will have a certain number of icons, such as a beer glass for a pub, a razor for a barber etc. If none of the gangs owns the location, the icon will be white, and you can decide to launch a mission to extort money, activate a beat-up, commence espionage or take over the business. If the icon is of another colour, it means that another faction owns these specific locations; there are five other gangs in total. You can still activate a beat-up or a robbery mission, but you can’t launch an extortion mission as the location is owned by another faction. You can launch a menace mission to get rid of whoever owns the building, but you’ll have to increase the fear level first in the current district before you can launch this type of mission. Each mission will show you what you are going to gain or lose regarding fear, influence, respect aspect, and money. For the mobsters, you’ll have 4 types of character that you can hire: bouncer, torturer, brain, and smuggler. However, you must own Pubs and unlock other districts to hire a new member.If you decide to play the cops, the difference is that each of the districts will be divided into three, and you’ll have more personnel. Your goals are to find illegal activities and gather evidence against each of the five factions and make as many arrests as you can. However, you need to make sure it is safe enough (safety gauge) before you do so. You’ll use sergeants to patrol the districts to get information and increase safety. As you receive information, locations will pop up on the map, and a pin will be put on the building icon to show illegal activities. Mind you, you’ll still need a certain safety threshold to conduct an operation. You don’t have to rely on the money with the cops, which is a plus. Cops seem only to have three types of character for selection during missions: Forensic, Detective and Interrogator.Regardless of whether you play the criminals or the cops, you’ll have to plan your moves on the map first. Then, if you’re a criminal, it will tell you how many days before the operation takes place. When you are ready, you press on the time icon and the days will start to flow until you’ll get the combat phase. With the cops, it’s all about finding out if there is any illegal activity in that specific location. If there is, you can jump straight to the combat phase, as long as you have enough safety in that district.You can select up to four characters in each of your combat phases. Whatever you are playing, each of your characters can carry a firearm, a melee weapon and a utility item. The main difference is that you have to buy any of these three items at the black market before you can allocate them to your goons if you are the criminals, but if you are the cops, you ‘ll have access to the entire arsenal, which I find a bit odd, to be honest. Each mission has directives; for example, with the cops it is preferrable not to use excessive force, such as firing a round of bullets with a machine gun. This will usually get the character reprimanded for 1 to 2 weeks. As a criminal, using a firearm will alert the cops a lot quicker, and most of the time you’ll bash people up rather of killing them. It will depend on the objectives for that mission. I do like the combat phases, especially when your characters levels up and you can headbutt, smash vases on the table, throw bottles, whack a chair on your enemy, gauge an eye or even grab an enemy from behind while another character gets him with a good punch. I really like all the possibilities during these phases. The combat phases are neither too long nor short, which I liked. After each fight, you’ll receive experience points that go towards leveling up the characters you use. Each character can level up to 8 times, and you can choose another perk each time. It will also tell you if your character is wounded or tired. If one or two are wounded, they’ll have to either receive treatments at the HQ (criminal) or wait several days (cops). If they are fatigued, don’t use them for a couple of days until they are fully rested.  There is plenty more that I’ll leave you the pleasure of discovering. I do think the game needs some polishing in regards to the combat animations; it’s a bit rough at times.  I also had a few bugs after reloading a criminal game where, during the combat phases, especially the police raids, several cops had only a face and no body; just really odd! Pretty quick loading time before and after missions, which is great. And I also do like that there is a story on both campaigns.Decent graphics, and there is plenty of content in this game. It’s translated into 7 languages, and there are autosaves after each mission (you can save manually too).Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Decent graphics+	Cop and Criminal campaign+	Fun story on both campaign+	Good character progressions+	I love the perks in the combat phase+	Fun and addictive gameplay+	AchievementsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	No trading cards as yet-	Issues with graphics (cops with no bodies, just a head) after loading a gameCrooks against cops or vice versa in London in the 60’S. If you enjoy turn-based strategy games, it’s Yeah baby. . . Shaga…. 7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: This is technically a brilliant game. I'm not familiar with the dev team but my impression is that they are a small company and they've succeeded in making something a bit special here in my opinion.Unfortunately the game does feel like it was rushed out the door before it was fully cooked, if I had to guess then maybe the money ran out or the publisher wouldn't wait and a deadline had to be hit. The balance generally isn't quite there yet and another month or two would have really dialled in things and made this a brilliant game. As opposed to one that has basically seemingly been completely forgotten.But my gosh, the foundation is all here for an excellent turn based game and the world building is excellent.Strangely the devs took a totally different direction for their next game. I do hope they return to this genre.I've played turn based games all my life and it's my genre of preference. I'm a hardcore XCom fan for example.Unlike most turn based games, Company of Crime is mostly up close and personal as opposed to using guns over distance. Guns are in this game but I played and won the whole game (35+ hours) and only fired a gun I think twice. So the strategy and tactics come from creating bottlenecks at doors, funnelling enemies towards you and mugging them hard. Choosing the right ability to cause the maximum damage in the shortest period of time and trying to control your opponents with moves such as grapples and eye strikes. Trying not to alert too many enemies to your presence at a time and controlling how and when combat is initiated. It's all really good stuff. Battles can be very tense and your success is often on a knife edge.The AI is fairly simple but if you start to get swarmed by opponents you will get wrecked quickly. There's a variety of holds, throws and debilitating strikes in the game that will wear down your team fast.Loads of original game mechanics in this as well. As you create havoc in a mission, the noise will inevitably cause the police to be called and as such you will often end up having the battle through waves of the police as you try to reach the exit point. You will have heat in the vacinity which will affect how quickly police are called so this must be managed as well.If you are unsuccessful and arrests happen then a mission can be run to get your team mates out of prison.In the off chance the devs are reading this I would say please return to this genre. Constructive feedback would be:1. Remove the swearing. Why ask for a higher game rating and limit the potential audience?2. Choose a more mainstream setting. RPGs, World War 2 or SciFi are the way to go. Your worldbuilding skills are excellent but there's no real demand for games set in the 60s in London.3. More events and basically some sort of one off missions such as mini bosses with special weapons/armour to overcome.There is a huge demand for turn based games and the obivously excellent game code on display here could surely be built upon for a new game that really could fill the massive void left by the demand for X-Com 3.About 5 hours in you will understand the game and see if this is for you or not. As always I'd recommend picking this up on sale. The last half of the game were quite grindy and repetitive, again I felt this was down to a lack of balance and time spent tweaking player progress events.Having won the criminal campaign, I'll now be trying the police campaign :)Thanks devs, I really enjoyed your game!

name: Dice Legacy
detailed_description: THE GAME In this roguelike survival city builder, you lead your realm by rolling the dice - literally, because the dice rolls determining your fate aren't happening in the background but are one of the main gameplay elements of Dice Legacy. Discover uncharted lands and guide your loyal subjects. Put your faith in the dice as you gather resources, construct buildings and expand the borders of your realm. Create a strategy that fits your playstyle as you explore the wilderness. Test your luck as you make contact with the enigmatic factions populating the ringworld. But beware: something wicked is lurking in the mists beyond your realm, waiting for its chance to strike. FEATURES Your dice represent the subjects of your realm. Keep them happy and healthy by providing food, ale and medicinal herbs - otherwise they might starve, get sick, be injured in combat or even freeze to death in the unforgiving cold of the winter blizzard. Adapt your playstyle to the procedurally generated ringworld that is waiting for you to explore it. Chart the wilderness, gather ressources and construct new buildings to establish your rule. Recruit new subjects and research new technologies as you build your strategy to survive the winter. Your population starts out as humble peasants, but as you roll your way to a clever strategy, they advance and become citizens, soldiers, priests or merchants. Work with the Council and pass new Policies to keep the various dice classes happy and potentially change the course of the game. Create mighty Constructs by forging dice together and empower faces to unlock unique dice abilities. Create the ultimate dice to ensure your triumph through various playthroughs. Roll. Die. Repeat. Unlock all 6 rulers and find out which fits your playstyle best. Face different starting conditions and get the hang of varied wager abilities. Every playthrough of Dice Legacy is unique and presents you with the chance to discover the secret that is hidden in the mists of the ringworld. Discover mysterious civilizations and reveal the secrets of the ring. Defend your settlement against The Others. Find out who they are, how they got to this uncharted land and what lurks in the mists beyond their city. THE WORLD The enigmatic ring-shaped world of Dice Legacy seamlessly blends medieval and steampunk aesthetics, paying tribute to the steadily growing fascination of tabletop and miniature games. You land on the shores of a new, uncharted continent and raise and evolve your settlement, exploring the wilderness in the meantime. On the other side of the ring, The Others await - unknown and ancient and yet eerily familiar at the same time. The Others pledged themselves to worshipping an ancient being, so powerful it is said to be able to change the very fabric of destiny itself. Will you fall prey to these tempting promises or be able to resist and face the truth?

Roll and use your dice to gather resources, expand and defend your settlement, survive the winter and interact with the strange inhabitants of this eerie world.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm surprised by the negative reception this game is getting. It's a pretty fun puzzle type city builder.It is a bit odd that it is real-time instead of turn-based, as many of the mechanics tend to clash with the real-time gameplay. The controls are also a bit clunky, and hotkeys are not customizable. My biggest issue is that the endgame can be a bit grindy as the enemy sends wave after wave at you and it seems more tedious than challenging. The game also has RPG elements of leveling up your dice. This is fun, but some of the traits are useless past a certain level. You can get knowledge to level 8, but there's not benefit to it above level 3. I'm not sure if this was done with the intention of adding more content at a future date, but again it feels a bit clunky.Overall it's a pretty fun 3ish hour rougelike city builder with RPG elements. You can also carry two dice with you from game to game which is a cool hero sort of mechanic.Editing a few months later to add that the developer has addressed these issues and is continueing to update and improve the game, which I love to see from devs after they release.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely suspect I'm missing a big portion of this game. As in I feel it's there, but I can't find it. It's got to be there, right? A game that sells for £15.99 CANNOT just be two relatively short scenarios AND NOTHING ELSE. Two relatively short scenarios that are designed to force you into playing quickly, due to frustrating limiting mechanics.I beat both without ever using 2/5 kinds of dice in the game. I literally saw no use to them, when I had bigger problems. Maybe they make it much easier, but when you only have 12 dice maximum, and there's already too much RNG in getting the faces you want, why the hell would I change dice in my pool into other kinds that can't do the things I need.Plus, when you add a new dice type to your pool, you get a new class to try and keep happy. That just seems like WAY too much trouble.So yeah. Best as I can tell, there are two levels in this game. DLC adds one more, but screw that. There is no freeplay, no stress-free mode, no larger world to play in. You play in the tiny world, facing the exact same frustrating enemy, with different games differentiated by slightly randomised terrain locations.Granted you unlock modifiers (that all make it harder, I think), and different 'rulers'. Dunno if they'd add enough variation to make it...y'know, fun. I unlocked one other ruler and I doubt he'd make much difference in the long run.The gameplay in this is so cluttered, with so much going on and so little that actually makes it clear, with so many buildings, techs, dice types, and terrains...but there's absolutely sweet FA to do with it all. Peasants and soldiers can beat the first level on their own, just peasants can beat the second.Stunning.

_childDocuments_.review: Really really enjoyed playing this game, was hooked immediately after seeing a game play video.Pro's:-City Management is really strong, and intuitive.-Research and upgrades are rewarding-Everything is visually stunning, and soundtrack is gorgeous, amazing atmosphere, even as the music shifts slightly to match the bad guys. Super clever implementation.-Rolling and Placing dice maintains  the boardgame "Push your luck" feel, and tactile incentive.-Gameplay really pushes on that stressful start transition from having nothing and panicking about everything, to having everything and panicking about nothing, and building everything up and planning it out is really rewarding.-Resource use and balance is really great-User interface is super clean and easy to use.Cons:-Tutorial needs work, too many times I was wondering what just happened.(Natural resources having durability, my leader ability having a cool down and eating my dice durability, hell even being encouraged to use my leader ability during the first winter would've made it much less stressful.)-No idea where my dice just came from on reset, except only the face stays the same, so I'm always wondering if it came from a forest / mine and where it is. (Could be easily fixed by highlighting a site, or having a ping that stays while game is paused)-To do stuff like Ascending a dice you have to have to be way beyond able to win the game, and just waste time doing economy stuff and happiness management to set it up for the next game.-Victories feel really anti-climactic, you pile your 15 dudes into the enemy town and then the game wins, there's no attempts, there's no failures there's no risk, it's just pass fail. The "Pay bribes or lose" game mode is the same, you just farm resources until suddenly you realise you can just pay them all and win.-Being able to take 2 ascended dice into a game means that you have to play TWO whole irrelevant rounds to just set them up. Instead being able to ascend multiple dice in one game would be better, but they get eaten upon ascending.-Would love to see more legacy mechanics beyond bringing a single worker into the next game, like once you win a game, there's a cutscene and a big battle or you sail away or something, and take some of your units, and research or resources with you into a harder stage, or auto difficulty increase.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all: the idea is great, the gameplay is fun but would be so much better in a turn based setting instead of being a real time plate spinning simulator. Still, the game as is could be super fun, but......the user interface is terrible. Like, the worst I have seen in decades levels of bad. 1. Buildings obstruct the vision of points of interests behind them: you cannot see ressources and dice placed there and there is no way to turn the camera to get a better look, because...2. It is basically a 1d board where you can only move up and downwards. No turning the camera, no swiping left or right. Your vision will be obstructed just by the nature of how the game board is presented. Whoever made the decision to present the game board in this manner, without any need to handicap the user, made a bad mistake.3. Important effects are hardly visible. You buildings can, given some circumstances, catch fire. You will be notified of a burning building. But finding it on the map? Terrible. Unnecessarily difficult: the fire is barely visible and oftentimes the view at it is obstructed (see point 1). There could simply be a button that takes you to the burning building. But, as is almost always the case, the developers looked past this quality of life feature, which can only be explained by lack of testing time.4. The toolbar is, again unecessarily, too small. I play on 3440x1440 ultrawide resolution and still, my taskbar covers like an eigth of the screen width and makes you scroll through the buildings by manually clicking arrows to the right and left. No shortcut for that. In general, you cannot customize key bindings - again: quality of life is terrible.All added up, the UI is an abomination and could have been notacibly better without much effort. I have had student projects that developed a more user friendly UI within weeks. The final product DESTINYbit offers, reminds me a lot of a bunch of developer students and hobby coders putting together a fun little game: great idea, good concept, very lackluster execution and terrible quality of life.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: The game has an identity crisis. It evokes board games (worker placement games) and risk management games because of the dice mechanics, but once you play it, you sadly realize this is mostly a RTS-Survival game. Such a disappointment.It's not objectively bad, there's a lot of love and ideas in it, but the core gameplay loop ruins the fun.Rolling dice and placing them is interesting and strategic, but they had put f*cking timers everywhere to make it a convoluted RTS. What was the point of using dice as main mechanic if the rest of the gameplay makes you feel like you're playing Overcooked? Yes, you can pause the game, but that doesn't make it particularly better. At its core, it remains a RTS. And as a RTS, I find it just fiddly and not really convincing. Dice Legacy could have been much more satisfying and rewarding as a real turn-based game. I'm harsh because I see a wasted potential below the poor design decisions, but there is certainly a public that could enjoy the game as it is, so don't take my sole opinion into account.

_childDocuments_.review: So TL;DR of this game for me is that its a roguelike / Citysim (or village sim) and i really dont think that Destinybit managed to mix these elements if they even can be mixed at all.ill try to be balanced and give the positives first.1 - The visuals are good, while its a bit jarring i kind of like the way the sidebar scrolls over the ringworld, they really managed to cut down the size of the world to foster the main experience they want you to have.2 - the music is very uhm, generic, its totally fine and just gives an ambient track but its not grating or bad per say.3 - the key concept of managing rng and assigning dice to jobs sounds really intriguing, i just wish it was done better.4 - on a technical level the game is competent, ive yet to experience or see anyone encountering bugs, crashes or jank in general and i for one think thats atleast worth a pat on the back for a game just out of release. seldom is that the case.5 - i really like that you can exeed the dice limit and create a player driven challange with juggling the dice.so now for some less positive thoughts.1 - not being able to play during pause; so a large, LARGE portion of the game you need to roll your dice for correct jobs or even better numbers but you cant do that while paused which is likely because the devs wanted a more "stressful" kind of feel to the whole game, constantly having to think fast and adjusting to rolls.Its a shame then that you can just roll - pause - think - unpause - roll - etc, especially because you cant even lock dice during pause, this meant for me that i had my eyes completely glued to 10% of my screen for about 75% of the time, and making me feel like im fighting the games system just to do what i want, i can admire the choice they made but it 100% fails here, you can still pause and unpause constantly to get around the lack of inputs during pause and it just makes the game frustrating to play the way most will see as better for making correct choices.2 - the tutorials; every, single, tutorial will without fail pop up to inform you about the mechanic/building you just interacted with after the interaction, essentially making you feel like the game is actually backseating you smuggly if you ever did something dumb on your first run which you no doubt will because nothing is explained to you otherwise.I honestly dont understand why they dident make a small scale tutorial level because a run can take 3-5 hours before you know what youre doing.3 - the "nuetral" encampments; so you have 3 options on how to deal with these, you can trade, pray or raid them. exepct you actually have 1 option, first you scout them and unless your brain is that of a 6 year old youl know if you should trade or pray with them, if you choose to raid then you just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ yourself over because that gives you nothing at all compared to the correct option.4 - For a city sim like game i find it confusing why you are only supossed to play 1 way, and thats tall. the best way of playing is to stack effiency and just blow through the tech tree without fail every time.5 - its a shallow game; once you won the first run i dont see why you would play more, every other mode is simply another layer of difficulty which might sound interesting exepct its all really annoying: permanent winter - slower production - bad council meetings - the enemy town is way bigger. i dont want to play any of that, it sounds boring and thats because.6 - very little interesting actually happens in the game, there is no "mechanical" skill unless you count spamming pause and unpause constantly. neither is there any real decision making to be done compared to simular games, there are only 5 unit types to create and they are all identical, you can ofcourse forge them but thats 100% RNG, after winning i dident feel like i did anything important or impactful, i only felt like i played the "correct" way.ill rapid fire a bit now7 - the mercenary dice are pointless.8 - there is way to few perks in the "construct" pool to make other runs feel interesting, for real im getting confused when i roll 7 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ neurotic dice in a row...9 - you can get (somewhat) resource locked depending on seed RNG, yes i know you can trade but its painfully slow and comes off as a flaw in the coding that this can happen + your trader might be the second encampment so..10 - idk why the city district building is also the scouting and the border expansion building and its just odd.11 - class happiness is a tedius underdeveloped mechanic that most of the time you can actually just ignore and making them happy does almost nothing.12 - winter and freezing dice serves no purpose other than to slow you down and frustrate you. (funny side point i like how *seemingly* blatant the frostpunk "ripoff/refference is).13 - im dead certain there must be a *Hidden* timer that ramps up the assaults on your village, just incase you where goofing around having fun or something. so just to reiterate that you should 100% play as effective as possible even if the game refuses to teach you how it works so i kind of doubt most players will beat their first run by no fault of their own because.14 - the game is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ easy once you understand what i wants from you, so i understand now why there are so many ways to make it more difficult but like i said all those ways are just going to make the game more frustrating not mroe challanging.15 - you cant rebind keys, personally i dont mind the keybindings (assuming you enable pause with spacebar) but why in the hecklestuffed gurglebum ♥♥♥♥ did you guys not make it an option for people? what about left handed people or just physically handicapped? i dont see a good reason for a game in 2021 to not have a keybind option.16 - ascension, essentially you should give in to the glorius eugenics simulator (which i ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loath but maybe thats just me for once) and just roll RNG faces/perks so that other runs can benefit from it and its just weird to add in this game, i cant tell if thats the reason for all other modes just being annoying insted of interesting or if they added it after to make it possible to even beat, either way the game is simply shallow as a result, it doesnt build on any mechanics it has because it has only neat ways of interacting with the ui and gameworld, not actual gameplay mechanics.even as a game dev i dont want to sit and armchair develop the game becuase its insulting to the creators but there are ideas that remain untapped, _childDocuments_.review: After 15 hours, I stand by what I have previously said.I will add that saying this game is based on a "legacy" system (you may have noticed it since it is in the name of the game itself) which strongly influence the game. Most of the negative reviewers I have read have played so little they have never even tried it. I feel like they are reviewing less than half of the game.But if you are wondering "will I enjoy this game?". It depends!You will likely lose your first game. You will also probably lose the second one. Play with the pause for the first games to reduce the stress. The first 4 hours of gameplay will be you being kicked in the butt while you learn. Then, you will know most of the mechanics by heart. You will have a clear strategy. And the legacy mechanic will kick in. And then you will win. Pretty easily I would say. And then you will be ready to try more. Try the other scenarios, the other characters, and the greater difficulties.ORIGINAL REVIEWI am kinda puzzled by most of the other reviews I am reading around.It seems like they want to master the game at tge first try and they get annoyed when they can't do it in an hour or so.It is described as a roguelike, the pleasure of playing it reside in learning how it works, what are the best tactics, and failing many many times in the meanwhile.It probably requires many hours before you are able to master it.Best review I have read so far: "It's not a chill citybuilder with dice"...no, it's a survival roguelike citybuilder, just read the damn description of the game!! I have played only one game (which ended with the rebellion of my peasants and my defeat) but so far it is exactly how it was in the videos and I am totally satisfied!It will take time to underatand when is the proper moment to upgrade the citizens, how to balance the production, whether to jump in the middle of the mist as soon as possible to get more resources, or progress more slowly and endure more winters.I still have plenty to learn, there is still plenty to discover!

_childDocuments_.review: I really really want to like this game. I played for 4 hours even though I knew I was pretty bad at it. Being able to pause and manipulate the dice was a must for me and I found that option incredibly helpful. I will not continue playing, not unless the tutorials and encyclopedia get better. Biggest gripes: No way to search for an existing building/ buildings aren't distinct enough - The visuals are nice and I like the art style but the buildings do not look unique enough. This art style is begging for just slightly more color that pops- a bit more cartoonish elements to differentiate the buildings to make their function clear. It took me ages to realize that stone and iron mines were different resources. I spent 5 minutes looking to see if I guilt a school or not. The style is so close to working but is just a bit too muted. WHAT DO KEYWORDS MEAN: I just literally saved and closed the game because I had the option to "purify" a die. I put the die and the priest die on the spot, waited the time, and.... the only viable option I was presented with was to do nothing. The prompt was to chose a face of the die to purify, but I couldn't select any symbol, I could only select "No Change". _childDocuments_.review: + Original gameplay focused on management+ Nice graphisms and music- Poor use of it's original ring world thing (linear map, that's all)- Frustrating RNG & inconsistencies in gameplay- Poor balance, especially on the new game mode.Dice Legacy offers an original turn to city building/economy management with a huge focus on management. Indeed, you'll spend 95% of your time in game rolling dices, moving, healing and unfreezing them along with ressource stocks. In this game, there are 2 seasons that play a major role : summer and winter. In summer, you farm wheat to craft food and beer. In winter, you have % chances to get your dices frozen when used. You may counter this effect with the Generator that produces heat around it.I got addicted pretty fast, but... There are some mains issues :- . Of course, you can expect some in a game with dices. Alas, there are PLENTY other areas with pure rng : ressource availability, enemy attacks, choice of laws (depending on the scenario and your character, laws can save a run, or be completely useless), laws effects (some have percent chance of triggering), few techs, etc.- . They are super oppressive, constantly attacking you. In my last run, I tried a peasants/soldier mix, but I accumulated wounds pretty fast and had a hard time healing them.- . In EVERY SINGLE GAME, you will have to build Generators on strategic positions and craft beers/weat, because it's the only tool to unfreeze dices and make decent amount of food, animal feeding being kinda bad (because herb collecting is rng based and not wheat :'D). You will recruit citizens because tech is necessary and you can't obtain it by any other mean.- . Short list : you can't unfreeze dices with Generators (not hot enough I guess) ; enemies don't have ressources in their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ country, but they attack you every minute or so, even in winter, and by the way, you don't get loot from destroying their buildings (made of nothing I guess) ; 3/4 of the time, trading will result in you paying to get nothing in return, my favorite :)You get it, plenty of balance issues and lack of critical features that make the game very frustrating, at least to my opinion. Not to mention the new game mode that is insanely hard even in normal mode.Also, the different scenarios don't offer quiet a lot of replayability. They tweak rules only applying to you, the goal and the enemies NEVER EVER CHANGES. Every game seems like walking the same path, but with different legs. Meh. The game is very pretty and I do enjoy the ring world thing despite the fact that it doesn't bring anything to the lore.When it comes to UI, all is fine as well, except the tutorial that sucks. It's relying on your will to explore the game too much. I wish there were more songs, because all of them are very nice ! The Sound Design follows this quality line. I always feel weird about this kind of games. Most of their elements are well crafted, even some the core ideas, but the execution of the game designed is . Perhaps the devs aimed at frustration. If it's the case, well, the mark has been hit...

_childDocuments_.review: The concept is SO good, but the whole experience just isn't much fun, for reasons that I can't really put my finger on. The core conceit is that you are in charge of a colony, and your people are represented by dice. Each die is a person. That person's profession dictates what abilities they'll have on their six faces. You roll them, and deploy them to do tasks that match the face that comes up. And then you can do crazy stuff like levelling up faces on a die, or combine multiple dice to get these hybrid construct dice that are more powerful, and it's just a wonderful idea!But the interface is just a little too clunky, and the rewards structure is lacking, and the guidance about what you should be doing next isn't great. The overall package is a game with a fantastic core idea, and then a surrounding execution that doesn't quite back it up. It's just not satisfying to play. I was on the fence in terms of "thumbs up vs thumbs down," because the main mechanic is really neat and I'm glad I got a chance to try it out. If you're like me and think you might like it just for the novelty, then I *do* actually recommend it! But for the average person, and thinking of it as a whole game, I had to come down on the "thumbs down" side.

_childDocuments_.review: Dice Legacy is a promising game but with a lot of issues.1)  First off, the graphics are gorgeous, but some things don't make sense.  For instance, because of the way the map is built and moves, buildings on the sided can be obscured or be incredibly hard to interact with if you're centered to use buildings in the centre of the map, where everything looks fine.  The excessive need to constantly shift back and forth from your city built at the start of the map and resource gathering farther and farther away, is an issue, as there is currently no way to gather resources without completely depleting the nodes that give them.In terms of gameplay, there are several issues.2)  The tutorial is terrible.  You only get popups to explain something AFTER you're done it.  Want to know what a certain dice type does or a building does before your get it?  Tough.  Build it and hope it didn't mess up your plans.3)  Micromanagement stress is real.  The early game especially encourages you to get more and more dice as you're up against the clock of building your city enough so you have the resources to survive the winter.  This forces you to go over the 12 dice pool limit and play a game of speeding against the seconds to use all your dice and reroll and put out more in order to keep things going or else you just throw out your extras.  This improves in the late game as you're able to afford to improve your dice, which is another issue.  But then there's so many extra clicks that are just not needed.  If I place a worker and the site requires 2 resources, I have to shift+click twice more to set each resource, rather than just once.  And there are no toggles for "automatically assign resource" to save you the extra clicks and time as you're trying to juggle 12+ dice.4)  Dice modification isn't explained clearly.  Even now, I still don't understand the logic behind how two dice merge and which faces are kept.  Only after I accidentally tried to improve my regular dice beyond it's x4 modifier did the game tell me that I couldn't, I had to combine dice to go beyond up to x8.  And ascending dice was entirely unclear if I got to keep the dice to keep playing or lost it for the playthrough until I actually did it.5)  Dice classes hardly matter.  I never never used a single monk dice - there wasn't a purpose to them.  I used one military dice, which didn't actually give me any benefits over my peasant dice.  I used one merchant dice to get me gold - I tried using two but ending up discarding it cause it just wasn't as good as the others.  The citizen dice had only one use - research.  And for everything else - peasant dice did the job.  Especially coupled with the benefits of peasant districts, there was hardly any reason to move forward with the others.6)  The UI is a nightmare.  There is no reason that the build menu couldn't be wide enough to show all tabs and buildings.  There is no reason hitting escape can't close a window.  Spacebar to roll dice instead of pause cost me SO MANY dice at the start until I found there was an option to select "spacebar doesn't reroll" and makes it R.  The ability not to change any of the other keybindings is terrible.  My advancement through the tech tree happened by accident because at no time did it tell me to click the tech tree icon instead of the knowledge icon (why they're two different icons and not the same, who knows?!) and I was stuck at level one because I couldn't figure out why I couldn't select level 2 techs until randomly clicking around and unlocking level 2 by hitting the giant level two icon on the left by accident (it may have been a bug as 3 and 4 were glowing when they were available to unlock, but 2 did not).7)  The 'difficulty' is just stress management, and it's more annoying than difficult, even at the default setting.Things the game needs:- Better tutorial, tool tips, explanation of mechanics- Better method to manage your dice on buildings and resources, expand your dice, expand your pool max- More buildings that interact with resource nodes so you have options to not just deplete them until the map runs out and oops game over cause you need more stone but there's none left- Difficulty based on what you can do with your dice rather than "better have x dice ready every 2 minutes or your city is burned to the ground"

_childDocuments_.review: I'm more of a turn-based and tabletop gamer myself. This game seems to draw heavily on the mechanics of some very good tabletop dice games like Roll for the Galaxy and Dice Forge, but with real-time pacing. If you're like me, the RTS pacing of Dice Legacy might be a bit much for you. In that case, I have some advice for a more laid-back gaming experience:1. Start a new game on pacifist difficulty. It effectively disables the biggest source of real-time pressure, the hostile raiders, and lets you think through your moves at your leisure. The game far, far less stressful as a result, largely becoming self-paced. The economy of the game is still involved enough to get many hours of fun even with the raider threat removed. And you can always bump up the difficulty later if you find yourself mastering the rest of the game, and want more of a real-time challenge.2. If you are playing with raiders on, research the Tower from the military tree. It passively fights raiders in its radius, and can be upgraded to be more effective. Multiple towers can work together to defeat enemies. Using even one of these towers can greatly reduce the pressure created by hostile raids.3. Slow down. Just because you can play fast doesn't mean you need to. Once the raider threat is managed, there are very few other mechanics that will actively punish you for playing slowly. Issues like fire and illness require attention, but these are intermittent and you can deal with them if and when they come up. The rest of the time, feel free to just think through your actions.4. Don't stress about winter so much. This isn't Frostpunk. The snow isn't trying to kill you. You don't need to run those huge furnace things the tutorial tells you to build 24/7. All that happens if your dice freeze is that you can't use them until they thaw. They thaw automatically when winter is over. So the plan for winter is simple: Lock some sword dice so you have them on hand in case of winter raids (if playing with raiders enabled), then grab a cup of tea and play the rest of your dice at your leisure as you wait out the cold. If they freeze, they'll thaw, no big deal. (Also, get the coats upgrade for peasant districts that keeps dice from freezing when played inside them when it's offered, then make sure essential buildings are in peasant districts. Nice and cozy.)5. Finally, don't feel bad about restarting if you think things are going badly. The game difficulty is calibrated to require experimentation and learning on your part, even on lower difficulties. Expect to exhaust some essential resource and realize you should have planned differently in your first game or two. Don't feel an obligation to wallow in a death spiral if that happens. It's okay to just restart and build better the second time.I've had a lot of fun with Dice Legacy. I hope you have a chance to enjoy this game as much as I have.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: if two thirds of your library is building games and the other third are roguelikes/roguelites, you'll probably have a nice timeIf you're anything .like me, you played the game Banished some years ago and enjoyed your playthrough but lost interest around the mid/late game due to a lack of clear goals and never really picked it up again. (This is not my only trait as a person, but it is an obviously important one.) The core idea for Banished was solid - peasant village management, juggling basic resources and jobs, preparing for harsh winters - but it lacked a larger-scale hook and loop to the play experience.This game is, as you might have guessed, not Banished. It uses many of those same core ideas, but with genuinely creative responses to Banished's weak points. The roguelite structure gives temporal boundaries and direction much the same way that the setting on a ringworld structure gives spacial boundaries and direction. The dice mechanic turns micromanagement of workers into an engaging minigame, while the varied scenarios and ascension mechanics give that roguelite replayability we all know and love - in short, it is a better Banished experience.Now it ain't perfect of course, though I do credit the developers for their willingness and ability to adapt to the community as it forms. Notably, the original version of the game severely limited your ability to pause, since the devs seemed to envision it as more of a plate-spinning, putting-out-fires (literally) experience. This is not my style, and since active pause has been added, I've played it like a Paradox game, pausing every 2.3 seconds to agonize about another decision as the good lord intended. There are other weaknesses to the game - the name is boring to the point of making it difficult to tell people about, the True Ending (a la Slay the Spire) is just kinda bad to play, and the mechanics around the different leaders fall rather flat (apart from the Corrupted, who is cool and and an all-around nice dude) - but if you like the styles of game going on here, these issues end up not being a big deal.So yeah, check it out, I guess. I liked it at least.

_childDocuments_.review: Dice Legacy is a survival city-builder. Think about your typical city-builder without workers. You have several different buildings like the main hall, a mill, a school, or even what fields as well as surrounding resources like wood, stone, and iron which you need to collect. There are no little people moving around your little town. The dice are your workers. Every dice is one work that you can use for many different things. Every dice has durability and, instead of numbers, symbols. After rolling a dice, you will get a symbol that tells you what you can do with it (for example, collect resources, build something, attack, etc.). If you don't want to use the dice right now, you can keep it for later or roll again. Every time you roll, one durability is lost. If the durability reaches zero, you will lose the dice. There are ways to recover the durability as well as get new dice. But that's not all. There are a handful of different classes. Each class has different dice with different colors and it's symbols. For example, there are peasants which are good to get resources, citizens which can get you more knowledge, or soldiers who can fight off enemies. There are different ways to discover new buildings and so on. In school, you can get knowledge, a currency used to get new techs. But how do you win? Well, this depends on the missions. As far as I can tell, there are six different missions. In the first, there will be enemies attacking you from time to time and you need to find the source of it. While doing that, you need to survive. The winter will make it harder for you to even get there as well as managing everything while maintaining your dice.    Through I like strategy games, I mostly stay away from city-builders if they don't have something special like Frostpunk. Dice Legacy exactly has that something. It's innovative and something new. It's fun to manage all those dices and resources and build/get new stuff. Honestly speaking, I did not get too far into the game yet and spent like 3 hours just on the first mission while others will probably beat it way sooner, but these 3 hours were way more fun than I had in all those other city-builders (except for Frostpunk).The mechanics surrounding the dices are just fun and addictive. There definitely could be more missions for the asking price through. If you're looking for a new city-builder, you should definitely get Dice Legacy.

_childDocuments_.review: In this review I’ll try to explain to you what you can expect from the Dice Legacy exactly. Would you like to listen to it while the game is on the screen? Then you could check it my 16mins long YT content overview video instead:If not, then keep reading, but some tricks I found already not discussed in this review, only on the video, like how you could have 30+ or even more dice while only 12 allowed by the game or what strategy leads you to have A LOT of resources.Dice Legacy feels like a fusion of a city builder game, a board game and real time strategy. The mixture of all these genres actually works fine. The whole game feels refreshing, it is something new and even veteran games won’t have the feeling, that “I played this game 500 times already” There are 6 scenarios. In my playtime, which is 9hours so far, I still have not managed to beat the first one. I needed to restart it, that is true, around 3 playtime hours, but this restart allowed me to experience that the world is randomized, the map is different every time, so there are no 2 similar games.5 different difficulties let you adjust the game to the challenge you want to beat. Just want to expand and build up a kingdom? You could get your wishes too, there is a pacifist difficulty.There are different leaders with different bonuses. The replayability of the game is there, I can imagine many would spend hundreds of hours into this game.Achievement perfection time: I wish I could know:-) I will update this part of the review if I will ever know this, but after 9 hours only on 2/41. Nope, this is not the easiest game to perfect, that is clear already. Need to finish all scenarios on standard or harder difficulties (with enemies, so non pacifist).In a written review it is very hard to explain all the gameplay content of the game. I don’t even know where to start.First of all there are different dice types. I am not just talking about the side of the dice, they are available in different colors too. Each color represents a class, like peasants, citizens, monks, military and merchants. Each type of dice has different sides, and while most of those sides (abilities) are available for some other classes too, each class has its own unique ability too.For example, when a gathering side of the dice is the one which was rolled, then you can adjust that to a mine/forest/herb plant field, etc, to gather resources. It will take time until this is actually executed, like 20-60seconds, depending on which ability was used and on which building/area. After this, the dice gets exhausted.You can roll again with the dice in your hand, that removes the exhausted tag on the dice and it will be usable again. However, during the roll one durability is lost during a roll. Refilling the durability on a dice is possible, but if it reaches zero, that dice is lost and the class related to that dice loses happiness. You don’t want to make the peasants unhappy, they will start a riot and they will burn down all your buildings:-)Your dice could be out of business by other curses too. Enemies could poison them, if the enemy group is not killed, a dice could be frozen if used during winter, make the dice useless until summer or until the freeze is removed in a related building. As you can see, the game has depth.Enemies come and they always get stronger, as time passes you will require more and more dice, or the dice need to be stronger. Technologies, upgrades, additional buildings, unlocked policies help you during the journey until you can conquer the Ring World and beat your enemies.My problems with the game are usually Quality of Life issues. You can’t adjust dice to buildings/enemies while the game is paused. If this will become a hit, then yes, steam will be flooded with this kind of games:-) 8/10, looks great 10/10, I was sold when the game started and my starter ship sailed on a ring world to land. 6/10, The enemies are just coming and coming. _childDocuments_.review: I've just finished my first full game of Dice Legacy (by which I mean, the first one I've played to the end - I've actually started and re-started about 6 times in order to implement new things I'd learnt along the way!)The game took me a bit of time to get into, but once I did I really enjoyed it. There's lots to juggle at once - gathering resources, improving your dice, fending off attacks, keeping an eye on weather conditions/winter - so there's never a dull moment. Once you've built your way up the ring, it can be hard to remember exactly which of your buildings is where, but I suppose that's part of the challenge! I really enjoyed the differences between the dice classes, and how the game feels set up to match multiple playstyles. I'll certainly be going back through and trying other leaders and scenarios.The only drawback for me was the 12-dice limit, as I thought this wasn't very much if you were trying to have a mix of all 5 classes (since the happiness of a class partly depends on the number of dice it has). Yes, you can make additional dice and then park them in various buildings, but I found that sometimes multiple tasks would finish at the same time, meaning I had too many dice in my draw pool and had to remove some. I wish there was something like a dice-pouch where you could store additional dice, and they could be substituted in once there was a free slot in the 12 (that way, you'd still only be rolling 12 at once, but you wouldn't have to lose any of the dice you'd created)That being said, I'd recommend this game for its originality and versatility. It's not one that I feel I could necessarily relax/unwind with, but it's really gripping once you get into it, and I'm looking forward to trying out more in other playthroughs.

_childDocuments_.review: The core mechanics of this game just don't work. The pace is frantic even on the lowest speed, and there's no active pause to consider your decisions. It becomes a clickfest to keep your dice working, plus a scrollfest since everything you want to do is spread across the map.Dice games generally have mechanics to make bad rolls still useful. Here there's nothing, so you have to spam reroll until you get what you want, while "locking dice" and carefully managing the "durability" of the dice to make sure you don't over-re-roll. Again, want to pause while thinking this through? Nope. Unless you want to pause, think, unpause for a fraction of a second to click, and re-pause.A microcosm of the problems with this game: one of my buildings caught fire. I need a "worker" die to put it out. Oops, I don't have any of those. Reroll. Still none. Reroll. Still none. Reroll. Oh, there we go. Drag it to the building ... and ... nothing happens. Because in the ten seconds it took me to do that, the fire "grew" and now I need two dice to put it out. And yup, the fire spreads and burns down the whole town. Another game mechanic "boosting" faces of the dice. Cool concept. Except it makes you just have to spam re-roll more and more when five of the faces are terrible and one is great. The game tries to balance this by requiring "food" to re-roll but it totally fails - when my town burned down I had 70 food, corresponding to 560 re-rolls.I'll echo other problems mentioned by other review like there being way too many resources to manage. In a turn-based game sure, you need some depth. But in a real-time game I can't remember what I need and what I'm saving for, and if I think about it for a few seconds my town will get razed or burn down in the meantime.The game has potential. But it feels like an EA title that needs tons more work before it's fun.
