_childDocuments_.review: It's games like this that I wish had a "Meh"/neutral option. While writing this I've waffled between Yes and No a couple times, and think I've finally landed on giving it a thumbs down. Why? Read on.Dice Legacy can pretty much be summed up by its title - You use dice to build, enhance, and defend a town using dice. With dice you can imagine that there is a lot of RNG/LUCK involved - which you would be right. Sounds fun right? Well....For me, I felt like the pacing of Dice Legacy was off. The major thing was being attacked. Constantly. "Let's build a....and I'm being attacked. Okay they're dead, now I can.....and I'm being attacked again. Ooooooookay now I can gather.......and oh look, another enemy. I am truly shocked". There were also mechanics of the game that made it feel unnecessarily hard. Your dice can become damaged, and if damaged twice you would lose that die. You only have so many rolls on a die before you would lose that die (unless you "fed" it). Winters can grind your game to a complete halt while enemies destroy what you've worked towards. You are left sitting back saying "Yep, there goes another building, and I can't do crap". The odds felt stacked against you. I went on a handful of encounters in things like ruins, and out of a handful of things I only was successful once. I was also only on "standard" mode (one above easiest mode) so I kept thinking "If this is standard, what do the other difficulties feel like?".I think I get where the developers were going. You make an awesome die, you "ascend" it so that it's available in future games, and each future game gets easier. However the game is constantly kicking you when you're down. "Neat I'm building a town!" - NOPE you're getting attacked. "Neat I'm progressing!" Nope it's winter and your dice are frozen. "Cool I have just enough dice to accomplish this task!" Yes, BUT that one was damaged and now you have to make a new one. If I wanted more of a challenge, I will increase the difficulty. Their logic is probably something like "It gets easier/better though!" Maybe, but the beginning of the game is supposed to be easy, fun, and hook you into playing more. Not hit you with grindy mechanics out of the gate.If I could communicate to the developer I would say - Dial the number of attacks WAY down. Make the game a little more forgiving, rather than failing you on every encounter. Make the chance to have your dice frozen a lot less. Focus more on how to make the game more fun to the player, rather than making it harder. Have a tutorial that explains some of the mechanics better - such as durability of resources. Maybe start with an ascended die to get you started?I think the foundation is there to make the game great/fun. I like the dice aspect. The weird round world is interesting and easy to navigate with a mouse wheel. There are neat things to build and upgrade. With a few tweaks and some more explanation of how the game works it could definitely change me to a thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a great presentation. Really nice visuals and the core idea with dice immediately caught my attention when I saw the launch trailer. I would give it a neutral rating if I could, but right now the game design leads to a game experience that I would not recommend to my friends.System: I played it on Geforce Now. I really appreciate this game being available with Geforce Now on release day.Disclaimer: I did watch gameplay videos before purchasing, so I knew it was going to be an RTS. I have played tons of CnC, AoE, and others but just the first scenario of this game felt like a lot more stress than what I have ever felt in any other RTS (when playing offline)Gameplay: It took me 2 lost matches to figure out the basics about economy/fighting/research/upgrading etc. and most important: dice juggling. Dice juggling seemed mandatory to me to have a fluent and efficient pace. From there onward it was pretty straight forward to win the first scenario, but I can't say it was 100% fun. It felt like a stressful grind. Since dice juggling feels so crazy powerful, it led to the problem that I couldn't take time to make decisions or to discover stuff I had not used yet.There is a pause button, but while in pause mode, you can't interact. So when you are doing something for the first time, it felt like I had to decide: try a new game mechanic but risk losing dice because I would have to interrupt my rotation for a moment and the juggling could (or rather would) go wrong. OR just continue with the stuff that I figured out before and keep going with the rotation I know.On my play-through for the first scenario I decided to just ignore any new mechanic that I didn't need. I used orange/green/blue dice + catapults and that's it. The game has more to offer but I didn't want to risk losing.Also saving the game, then trying out stuff, and then loading your save game is not possible. You can save+exit or not save at all. There is autosave but I think that slot is overwritten when manually saving+exiting (I could be wrong about this). I had the feeling that the creators didn't want you to freely try out things and then just jump back to the save game from moments before. (I can see how it would allow cheesing through more difficult scenarios, so I kind of see why it was designed like this)UX/UI:Also some of the UI could be improved. When picking a saved game, the delete-button is just next to the load-button. I could see that someone accidentally hits 'delete' instead of 'load'. My suggestion would be to give the delete-button a trashcan-icon + give the button itself overall less width than the load-button. Deleting is usually not the main action that most people perform on their saved games, especially in this game where the game itself deletes your savegames once you continue.Another UI/UX improvement that I would like to see is: When I'm in the tech-tree, I can't use the ESC button to exit. I have to click  the Close-button below. Once you know this, it is not a problem, but the first time I was in the tech-tree, I didn't immediately spot that button because it is just next to the Tab-Buttons of the tech-tree. Same issue with the Policies-view.Accessibility: For a mouse-only gameplay, locking dice is a huge pain right now since it requires to click the lock first to enter "lock mode", then click the dice you want to lock, and then click the lock again to exit "lock mode". My suggestion would be to lock a dice just by right-clicking it.Would love to see more done with this game. It has a lot of potential!Have a nice day

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever had to take a timed IQ test? This game is like that but with better graphics and lore. There' not a lot of depth to the game aside from matching the right shapes to the right tiles at the right time. Which makes for a game that's constantly trying to tear itself apart into a billion pieces when its in motion, because it's hard to tell the tiles apart and the game is real time. This pain is doubled by the fact scrolling up and down the ringworld is clunky, and you quickly hit the point where you have to start discarding dice if you don't act fast enough. And to top it all off the game has like a dozen unique, competing resources you have to juggle while you're playing the IQ test. I'm not even joking --- just off the top of my head, there's wood, food, stone, iron, gold, wheat, herbs, knowledge, and ale. And then the 6 dice types --- peasant, citizen, soldier, merchant, monk, construct ---  are resources in their own right, each with limited durability and their own convoluted conversion schemes. Again, this would be bad enough if this was a turn based game. it already puts Sid Meier and Paradox to shame when it comes to the number of moving parts you have to keep track of. But real time? It's not even satisfying to master these mechanics, I don't have the time to enjoy anything or think, unlike every other real time strategy game that has 3-4 resources to juggle *at most.* Also how is a glorified real time euroboard game taxing my RTX 3070 this much? Something's wrong here.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this up on a whim, purely because I am a sucker for these hybrid dice games.  While I do recommend this game, it still is a very flawed game and your appreciation of it will surely come down to your flexibility to cope with said flaws.   A lot of games exist that are imperfect and this is one of them.  The core system of building up a unique dice pool, in real-time, with stamina and special powers is pretty fun.  It feels at odds with itself at first but it definitely caters to it's real-time gameplay mechanics unapologetically which I think is a good thing.   You can tell from others' reviews that others do not like the RTS elements and wanted something slower, methodical, and more tactical).  That isn't this game which I think is going to just be a matter of taste. Dice Legacy's initial design is also fun with a fair amount of exploration and solutions to evergrowing problems.  There are multiple ways to tackle problems while maintaining a certain amount of stress trying to stay ahead of the problems that will arrive. Some of the early difficulty walls have multiple solutions.  Some you can gamble on (hoping a good food or wheat policy comes up early) while others are more akin to build orders from something like Starcraft (rush technology or expand and defend early type of things). There are a lot of promising mechanics that look really fun (and can be) when you get to them.  Constructing your own dice, Unique Character Powers, Ascending Dice, Dice Traits, Specialized Dice, etc.  The Priest, Soldier, and Merchant dice/buildings give a lot of flexibility and at first, make the game feel way deeper than it actually is (but could be!).   Sadly, The game just never finds a really strong way to lean into these systems enough despite it feeling fun when you get there.   Despite that... you can quickly theorize paths you want to take and buildings you will want to explore pretty early and most of the combo potential does pay off.   The game has a few unique and even hidden systems to it that give it legs that I won't spoil.  There is one very neat narrative and metapuzzle that exists that is a very fun surprise when you discover it.  It's also very fun to figure out how to break the game... at least... the first time. The polish does wear off quickly, however.  The main issue I have is that there are too many broken solutions to the game that make it trivial once you discover them.  I only lost one game and then figured out how to win and never lost again, at any difficulty.  Some of the solutions feel like bugs and/or unintended consequences.  The act of discovering them is fun but you can't really stop using them once you realize they exist. The UI really has some issues and takes some getting used to.  It's unclear why certain things take so much effort to figure out - like the aura effects for instance like using a Steam Generator - but it's not unmanageable by means, just could be a lot better. My other MAJOR gripe is that the timer is way too slow once you have mastered the game.  SO much so that I probably lost 5-10 hours of my life waiting for the game to catch up to strategies I've implemented or waited for dice to do their effects.   They need an 8x or instant speed mode.  I think the lack of a Campaign also hurts this game.  I personally didn't care but considering I beat it on my second try... and then there was nothing more but some characters + challenges, it was a bit jarring to say the least.  I understand other's criticism on this issue.Lastly - it's difficulty and mastery is pretty one-dimensional.   The depth is just not quite there and the game needs more layers of challenge... of which I hope is added in future updates.   Many of it's more complex systems you barely use since by the time you unlock them, you are already winning.  It is definitely not as deep as many other Popular Hybrid roguelikes, but I think $19.99 or less is a fair price.  I just think they could do a lot more with the system.Ultimately - as long as they update the game, rework some things, and find some more interesting challenges to dive into, I would gladly come back and replay the game a little bit, so I'll leave a positive review for now.  Otherwise, my 40 hours of the game were well spent, flaws and all.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:Single player strategy game using dice.It plays similar to a Worker Placement board game but in real time.Overall it's a neat and unique game but the audience that might enjoy it is quite narrow.Replayability is relatively low.-------------------------------Complexity:Complexity feels at the right spot. Number of units / technologies / game mechanics is on par with regular RTS games. Different classes / buildings can be used to build your economy and achieve victory.Difficulty:This one is a bit iffy.In some ways this game is probably difficult for people who don't have much experience with strategy games. There is a pacifist difficulty level where you do not get attacked, but overall the game is relatively unforgiving as when things start going bad it can snowball relatively quickly.It also doesn't allow you to reload a save more than once, so if you mess up then you have to start again (each game can last around 1h30-4h depending on your playstyle)On the other hand it is too easy if you are more familiar with this type of game. I completed the map on my first attempt. And after that the access to ascended dice made other scenario / difficulties very easy.The only part where I had to try to beat it more than once was the secret ending.Story:There is no campaign and almost no lore. Roguelike/roguelite:The roguelite concept is with the ascended dice that you can generate thanks to the obelisk.But it is a technology that happens relatively late in the game when you are probably close to winning anyway.A strong ascended dice makes the game very easy (except for the secret ending).Although I guess combined with various builds allowing infinite resource generation this enables players to try fun strategies.Secret ending:There is a final boss in this game and I found that particular fight more interesting / challenging.However it is very easy to not even realize it's there if you're not doing achievement hunting.Also, it's very tedious to play 4 hours that are not very difficult / challenging due to infinite resource generation, infinite time available and unbreakable tower defense just to prepare that 10-15 minutes fight.And if you lose the fight then you have to do that long preparation again to build your base and a lot of dices.Price/Value:16£ for a game that will probably take around 20-30 hours to complete for most players. It is not too bad, but not that great either. There are also a few games both in the strategy and roguelite genre with a similar price tag that I would recommend playing first.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable but lacks replay value.Once you complete the "main scenario" you unlock a bunch of other supposed scenarios but unless I missed something it's really just the main scenario again but with different modifiers.  You can also collect new modifiers as you play but that doesn't interest me.  I was hoping for some new objectives or mechanics once the main scenario was completed but unfortunately the game is rather barebones and linear compared to IRL board games.The only way to win is to defeat the enemy using soldiers.  The other 4 classes of dice ultimately exist to help you create and serve soldier dice.  There is no alternative win condition.  The resource conversions are always the same and while there are a few ways to heal dice some are better than others; my point is strategies are always linear too.The game was enjoyable if overpriced for what it offers.  If you go in knowing there's really only one game mode with one ultimate strategy then you will enjoy the game.  But it has no replay value to me as what's on offer (modifiers to one scenario) is not interesting to me.The most interesting idea is the ability to completely create your own custom dice and max out its stats.  Unfortunately given the importance of soldier dice the only worthwhile use is to create a 3 face raid 3 face sword maxed out die.  The other classes are completely under utilized entirely by the game.IRL board games offer richer experiences than this.  For dice games similar to this I recommend Santa Maria and Dice Forge.  There's plenty more out there too with similar gameplay loops to this but with greatly increased replay value.I also felt the main scenario could of been trimmed back a bit as the decisions you make are routine and it ends up on the grindy side.

_childDocuments_.review: 0.8 hrs Review:I researched this game quite a bit before buying it.  It seems it got a lot of bad reviews when it first came out due to the default game-play not allowing pause.  I avoided it in that state.  But now that I'm playing it (I'm still a 'noob') I find it a very relaxing experience.  I insta-pause as soon as anyone finishes a task, then figure out what I want to do.  None of the frantic insanity the developer seemed to want to torture everyone with when the game first came out.The game is at least fairly worth the sale price just for the content tree alone.  The UI is clunky - but I think that was intentional when the game first came out to make you click everywhere in a frenzy.  So some operations make no sense, such as needing to grab food and drop it into the kitchen, or grab individual 3 wood to fire up the furnace.  This is slightly tedious - but because I'm pausing all the time - I don't care.  I'm still having fun watching the village slow grow and accomplish various tasks, and mapping out what building I want to put down next.Also worth mentioning is the music - the best indication of good music is if I don't even notice I've been happily listening to it for over an hour.  This does make a difference and pushes the game into a higher tier of gaming experience.It's possible I might uncover some other part of the gameplay that changes this review later - but for what the game is, I think it does a fine job and would recommend it for some lazy time frittering.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is particularly ambitious, but it definitely misses it's mark. The gameplay focuses around rolling various "classes" of dice and placing them in buildings and locations to harvest resources or perform actions, with every action having a timer. Build new buildings, expand your territory, gather new dice and upgrade your current ones, and eventually defeat The Other. While the Roll->Place part of the game is a delight, every action is keyed to a timer, and once the timer is done, the die goes back to your pool. But your pool has 12 slots total, and you have significantly more than 12 dice by the end of the game - dice that would return to you if your pool is full get discarded. Dice have limited durability, meaning they can be rolled only a certain amount of times before being discarded (though you can repair them). And if certain "classes" of dice lose too many from your total, you end up taking some pretty hefty penalties till you can raise the class's happiness again.Additionally, a lot of mechanics aren't necessarily well explained; the results from some actions, like sending missionaries or traders, isn't fully explained, and the Freezing mechanic for dice that work in the winter away from a Steam Generator (which constantly consumes precious resources for a fairly paltry timer) causes you to constantly have to micromanage so many things, and you get punished heavily for not being quick enough on the to pause the game and clear out your pool so dice coming back in have somewhere to land in your pool. Additionally, the game's resource management - where you have to send dice to collect wood, stone, gold, iron, ect. - is hampered by the Roguelike element. Every map will be randomly generated, but good luck if you somehow didn't end up with enough Wood locations early. It's one thing to play poorly and get screwed up, but it's another entirely to be stuck unable to progress because the game does't give you enough resources to move forward. It's possible this is the result of bad play, but as I noted earlier, there are mechanics that the game doesn't fully explain, which includes the expansion of territory. The game *definitively* needs a more fleshed out tutorial, or more cohesive explanations in it's help menu. It was fun for a run, but I genuinely didn't get much enjoyment out of the campaign, and with how much of a slog it felt constantly trying to keep up with the timers, I probably won't be going back to any of the new modes I unlocked.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: This is the mashup that I respect and want to love because I enjoy dice and roguelites, but now that I'm in the mid game, I am realizing that certain ways the different genres are being mashed up don't go well together for me, and I don't think they will jive for most gamers either.  So I unfortunately can't recommend this overall.Here is what you need to know related to all that to see if you are still interested in the game:+Dice rolling, locking, and multi-pickup is intuitive+Auto-select resources by just shift clicking whatever needs resources is nice, but...?I don't understand the logic behind auto selecting die for certain buildings?Think of it like a real time strategy game that has the option for pausing when rolling or when placing dice.  I think the game might have been better being entirely turn based or having a turn based option like Rebuild 3 had. But what isn't like RTS is that...-Automatic gathering or actions (like research) are not possible because a die roll is required to let you know what any die is capable of doing, and if you want something different from any die than you keep re-rolling it and any others you want.  Some kind of auto roll rule system might have been possible but complex.?The life/durability system for dice is fine - There's only so many (re)rolls each dice can take before it needs to sit down and eat food. This is another element that prevents auto-actions from being possible though.?It is a relatively basic 4x game (compared to Civs) with a moderate tech tree, and different classes of dice/citizens to keep happy.-It is not made clear how to create districts for different classes.?It seems relatively easy to keep all classes happy by regularly using a town square type area to basically throw a drinking party for the citizen/class of your choice.?If you are like me and want to maximize productivity by religiously pausing for rolling and dice placement, then it is possible to spend tens of hours on a single playthrough.-Without pausing (which is what the game says is the "intended" way to play), I agree with other players that a playthrough could take around 5 hours. IMO, this is too long to go well with the roguelite elements: Permadeath, only able to carry forward (ascend) 2 dice if you unlock a certain line of tech, and unlockable modes when beating the base mode or earlier modes.-This means that you could play for hours on a single run and possibly not ascend any any dice or create any memories.  I don't know what the latter are, but it is something mentioned that are gained on playthoughs that can be enabled as double edged game modifiers.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I don't really feel like updating my whole review. They've enhanced how the pausing works and made it available (optionally) at higher difficulties, and this has fixed my biggest complaints with the game.Original review below------Overall, a really great idea. Fun, original, well-executed, etc. However, it has 2 major flaws (one of which is very subjective).1. This game is intended to be played in real time. It's basically a game of keeping plates spinning. At the lower difficulties, you can pause, but you can't do anything while paused. You can't place or pick up dice, you can't even lock them. This leads to my general play style in this game being to keep the game paused most of the time, briefly unpause to do what I need to do, and then fast-forwarding time when I run out of dice.2. The board is very difficult to read. Tall buildings obscure buildings behind them. Many buildings look similar. Many resources look similar. Especially later in the game, finding a building or resource you need can be very annoying if you don't remember where it was. I can't even imagine trying to do that without being able to pause the game.The pausing issue is subjective. You might very well enjoy the time pressure of managing things in real time. The legibility problem, though, is a big issue. I really wish you could turn on a simplified view with icons, or had some other way to quickly and easily scan the map/find what you need.One final issue, this game is borderline unplayable at very wide resolutions. The map zooms in to fit the width of your monitor, and with a super-ultrawide monitor that means you can only see a 2-3 rows at a time which exacerbates the readability problems. Thankfully, the game works very well in windowed mode.If they just made it easier to see and find things on the map, I'd probably change this to a recommendation. If they added support for queuing things up while paused, or even--dare I dream it--a turn-based mode, I could see this becoming one of my favorite games. As is, I like the game, but I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Dice building, city building, resource gathering, survival, roguelike elements, extremely accessible and easy to play with just a mouse along with some great music and nice visuals; if any of that sounds appealing to you, I think there's a very good chance you'll enjoy this game!A fun and relatively relaxing game that has its tense moments and key decisions. I've been enjoying it "the way it was envisioned" as the settings indicate - on normal difficulty in real-time mode with no pause, though you can speed it up - and can pretty easily recommend this. It's pretty fun to figure out how to maximize the potential of your dice and determine when you can afford to roll a few times for a result you really want while gathering resources and building up your dice while balancing the needs of the different factions (dice types) in your village as you press onward.I recommend playing it real-time because it was envisioned that way and the tension ramps up nicely when raiders are attacking you or your peasants start setting fire to buildings and you work to lock dice that are weakening (running out of rerolls) and reroll to get those faces you really need.This is also among the best games I've played in terms of just using a mouse to control everything very easily on default settings, though I did add my middle mouse button for Roll Dice and right click to also Lock Dice and recommend trying this as it works great!Highly recommended for fans of dice games and city-builders with survival elements (e.g. feeding your dice to refill their rerolls, using steam generators to prevent your dice from getting frozen/locked) or for those looking for a pretty fantastic mouse-only game.

_childDocuments_.review: An odd little game.Playing on the settings advised by the dev (that is, difficulty 3 of 5, and NO PAUSE), it provides a surprisingly challenging resource management / colony builder sim, with individual games lasting ~1-3 hours. The dice mechanic takes some getting used to, but reveals to be a very interesting and clever take: You want to use your dice as they fall, as they already consumed the partial food you constantly produce for them, yet dice placed will take a minute to complete their job. So sometimes you would rather spend the 'extra food' on rerolling dice, particularly if you're under time pressure to quickly generate a specific result (i.e. a sudden bandit attack with your key soldier dice busied up elsewhere). On top of that the game's difficulty increases as time passes, so whilst you *can* sit around with a hand full of dice, not doing anything to conserve food (such as during winter), doing so means you'll fall behind the escalating curve.Tie it all together with a simple, but fitting, audio and video landscape, and an oddly humorous theme of living on a ringdworld, and you got yourself a charming little game with a creative take.Now, I keep saying 'little game', and that's kinda it biggest downside: There are exactly two scenarios. The former being a more lengthy 'campaign' (of about 3-4 hours on a first run when you're figuring out all the basics) and the second being a 'Time Attack' mode in which you have to rush procuring specific resources to meet demands (or be kicked out of office). There are some alternate leaders and modifiers that change aspects of the scenario... but whilst the modifiers can be kind of wacky (such as randomizing all costs), the leaders are remarkably... non-impactful. So I'd argue that the game doesn't have too much replayability value.I mean, I'm at 7 hours, and I may get another round or maybe two out of it before I'll end up bored.But, that shortlivety is reflected appropriately in the price, so it's fair and not a big negative.There's also a DLC (with a 3rd scenario), but since I don't own it, I can't rate it.Is this the next big thing? Far from. Is it a well-executed demonstration of an alternative way to manage colony sims? Absolutely. Is it worth your money? On a sale yes, otherwise maybe.Overall rating: 8/10Short, juicy, and I would absolutely love getting a full-priced, full-content-width sequel to this.

Normal and higher difficulty have Pause option disabled, making you waste a lot of time reading description, leading to brain overloadAfter you figure out how to play the game, the tension drops a LOT, so don't worry about it too much.Overall - the game feels really fresh. _childDocuments_.review: It seems like the game has gotten a few updates since I played it, but I followed the development and was a part of the development server long enough to not give it a fourth/fifth chance. Many testers and early players had the same complaints, they went mostly ignored or answered with "this is how it's supposed to be." So keeping in mind it's been a LONG time since I've played, and the game could have changed since then, here's my late-to-the-party review.-Resources are finite, meaning a single misplaced structure in the early game, or even the tutorial for some reason, can immediately spell doom for the run. Sure it's got rogue-lite themes, but with no way to regenerate most resources it was not fun to play.-Relies too heavily on RNG while limiting the amount of times you can reroll. It's mechanically possible to never get a good outcome, which isn't a problem in games where that's a feature; but here it feels spiteful.-It never feels like you've lost because of your own decisions.-THE INABILITY TO PLACE DICE WHILE PAUSED WAS BROUGHT UP BY DOZENS OF TESTERS.Making an edit because I noticed while looking for updates that the developer/steam marked my review as unable to be counted. So I want to make it very clear;I was not gifted this game, didn't receive it for free, did not activate it by a steam key, did not play it via temporary free license. I paid for this, was unsatisfied by how nothing changed since the beta, and then refunded it. So for however this got flagged as not a countable review, when previously it was, fine. But I'm able to edit so people know.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is like Overcooked, and not in a good way.You send your dice out doing the most mundane tasks on repeat. Oh there's a forest with 40 wood? Hope you enjoy clicking on that forest 40 times.You will question why these kinds of tasks can't be automated, but that's the point. The gameplay loop is that if you need 40 wood, you will click on a forest 40 times. You will wait 30 seconds and a dice roll in between each click. What will you do in the 30 seconds while you wait? Find other things to click on for the other 10+ dice.If you like fast micro, and don't mind that you're just gathering wood just to burn in it winter anyway, you'll probably enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay, originally I did not like that it was real-time, but then I realized that you can pause the game and still control the dice while paused, so that is nice. _childDocuments_.review: Ugh, man this is a tough one. Dice Legacy is a sort of hybrid between RTS (with pause ability) and roguelike utilizing dice mechanic for actions. So you have classes of dice - peasant, citizen, merchant, soldier dice - that each have their own particular face combinations and specialty. This is really interesting, because it allows you to specialize your strategy and how you achieve a victory.The core gameplay is really solid and feels good. There's many paths of building and tech paths you can take which does provide some good variance to the game. However, where it falls apart for me is beyond the core gameplay. It just feels like there is very, very little content in terms of scenarios and campaign. Yes, there are some very basic scenarios but there's no depth or direction to any of it. The tutorial is a perfect example of the lack of depth, it is extremely barebones and feels like an afterthought developed in a few days.I really want to recommend this game because the gameplay is good and the premise is so promising, but it ultimately feels half-baked and lacking in depth/content. I paid $4 and I feel like I got my money's worth as a hardcore roguelike enjoyer, but for the average player I can't give it a hearty seal of approval. I'm sorry because I know the devs worked really hard and I commend them for the good work.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is "Legacy Lite" at best. The "campaign" is you settle a world that is roughly the same every time by harvesting resources, building some stuff, leveling up dice, and then fighting some dudes. The END! This feels like a free mobile game and not something I spent $20 on. The Legacy in the name is definitely a cash grab and why I ultimately will rate this down. $5-10 fun lite city builder dice game sure, $20 Legacy city builder.. no way.

_childDocuments_.review: It is nice to see something fresh and new. Unfortunately it is unsurprising that it gets thumbs down from a lot of people because it fails to be what they thought it was. It is amazing that we live in a time where we can make amazing products that are perfect for a smaller audience - and that they can sometimes fail to find that audience because they are reviewed by people who aren't in the audience.I haven't played much but I am impressed by this game, it feels great. My issues:I have to constantly freeze the game because I am not interested in an RTS, though I do want a strategy game. That is annoying - I found it annoying in FTL and the many games that use that - but it is not a game killer for me. I just wish these games would either be turn based or freeze the clock for me at the obvious times rather than make me turn on and off the clock.The clarity of the rules is a bit wanting. The rules are given on a need to know basis and I don't like what they think I need to know.I find the map to be more pretty than useful - though I am getting used to it. I would rather have functionality than eyecandy. I don't like working to see what is behind a building or having to work to find what the distance of something is or recognize by sight a hunting camp, etc. etc. It is a B- in communicating the important information.Those are, for me, real complaints. The quality and originality of the underlying game, though, pays for those complaints easily. I hope the game finds its audience, because it does deserve one.

_childDocuments_.review: If you can get this game for <$5 imo it's a steal. It's basically a worker placement game where your pawns are different types of dice, and there's a surprising amount of depth in resource management, upgrading your dice (you can make the currently rolled face of a die worth its current value + 1, which makes it count as an additional pawn for the purpose of fulfilling a location's requirements), protecting your base, and carrying your best dice over from game to game. After a little bit the "others" start sending waves of enemies that will attack and you repel them with soldier dice or peasants that roll the combat face. My first play through was thoroughly enjoyable.I'm not sure how much replay value there will be here, but at the sale price this is absolutely worth a shout, especially if you enjoy worker placement games.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Dice Legacy is an underrated board game that feels like it was made by people that don't play board games. That means interesting ideas marred by "HOW DID THEY NOT SEE A PROBLEM WITH THIS" design decisions. It's not clear at all if holding dice unused on inactive buildings to go above the dice limit is a core strategy the designers intended or cheating in a way they didn't forsee (but you should totally do it regardless). Enemy waves seem relentless at times, and dice freezing in winter is a frustrating mechanic. Used your dice and got unlucky? Now you can't roll, you know, the entire point of the game. You can speed up game time until summer arrives, but sitting and waiting until you're allowed to play again is an insane player punishment. I've played over a dozen games, and there are entire dice classes I see no value in using (Monks) and large sections of the research tree I see no gameplay reason to unlock.And yet, I kept coming back for more. The scenarios offer variety and force you to change up your strategy in order to survive, my Endless Winter game felt nothing like my other runs (like a mini Frostpunk). Ignore real-time mode and play at your own pace.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: If you fancy Eurostyle boardgames and strategy-heavy gameplay systems, this game is phenomenal to dive into.Dice Legacy offers a unique - and yet simple - approach to all interactions throughout the game: Roll dice, place dice. Yet, this basic functionality expands wildly into a game that can veer off in many different directions to challenge your wits, creativity, and problem-solving.Easy to learn, yet impressively deep and insanely replayable. Be mindful of the clock, as you'll be surprised how quickly time flies when playing this game.EDIT: So as it stands, at the time of this review, there's a lot of different direction you can do ON YOUR FIRST PLAYTHROUGH. Unfortunately, there is a systematic pattern that begins to form, and the game (regardless of scenario or ruler) begins to get rather repetitive through the use of the same strategies over and over. I still recommend the game, but be aware that the game doesn't offer much experimentation as of right now. That said, the developers are active with their title and communicate really well with a couple of their ideas of what's to come, and this exites me.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty split to pick the recommendation. The game has every potential to be great but keeps falling short unfortunately.  Yeah, you can play it, it gives you some thinking, some challenge -- even a fair variety with missions --  but it is simply not fun as it is.It was designed (probably) as dexterity clicker, the main challenge being to juggle with the dice in the limited space and try to see all the places at once.  That's not my bag at all, and seems neither fit for most audience.  So the "not recommended" pause was introduced to at least salvage something. But it becomes boring and repetitive soon, I played a high number of hours to complete a few different games, but it was more work than play.

_childDocuments_.review: I have no idea why winter and real time is a function of this game. _childDocuments_.review: I like boardgame, I really want to play it when it first come out, but once I saw many negative review, it keep my away from this game. Now, after a few updates and a lot of discount, so I try. Turn out it is not bad as I think it will be. I also have some trouble with the real time aspect of the game at first, because I don't have enough time to read all the effect, but after the first game, I think it's fine. The only thing I hate about this game is the dice trait mechanic. Imagine it's late game, you use two yellow dice to create another one, then change that one to another color, then repeat two steps to create another dice, then combine both dice to create construct dice to unlock the max value for 4 to 8. And then you realize that the game give that dice an ignorance trait, now your dice can't be use to power up from whatever  value it had to 8. So, you waste all that time, and have to repeat it again.In the end, it's a fine short game. If you want to spend some time rolling some dice and building something on tile, I would recommend it on discount, since it take around 4-5 hours to finish one run.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate the upvote / downvote system. I don't want to downvote this game. I played it straight for 7 hours, but now I don't want to play it anymore. It clearly has potential, but I have to second what many others have said. It's a bit of a mess of ideas. I personally really enjoy the city-building gameplay and the dice idea adds a lot of fun imo. The class system is not very balance though. Many class die are too situational, and I never feel like the idea of the classes are ever fully brought to its potential due to this.Then there is the exploration idea, which I really feel degrades the game. It pushes you to explore to keep getting resources, but that also means that city-building is kind not really implored. More so hub building. The campaign quests then adds an extra layer of objectives. Having tried just the first one, which basically is a UI asking you for resources all the time (which means you are hindered in building, exploring etc). This again is kind of a detriment to the gameplay. I really feel like there is an identity crisis in the game. It borrows ideas from other games in the genre, even if they don't fit. Ultimately: I don't regret buying the game. It was on a great discount. I however will not get more enjoyment than the 7 hours out of it. Unfortunately the conflicting gameplay mechanics means that I can no longer enjoy the game, as the goal of the game is never city-building, but rather something else. The campaign or quest system being completely decoupled from building a city is what broke it for me.

_childDocuments_.review: As it is right now I cannot really recommend it. Take into account I have played a little but my gosh this game is frustrating. Which feels a bit awkward (I'm also not terrible in this kind of games so I dunno why I suck so much here).Many mechanics seem a bit overlooked. _childDocuments_.review: A deceptively frantic game, gives me something of the feeling of playing a traditional RTS. 100% understand the comments asking for pause and a more readable village, but for me these "abrasive" aspects contribute to an enjoyable challenge. Trying to organise my town so that I can find what I need while under time pressure, constantly juggling dice and trying to plan ahead for the threats of the next season make for a satisfying plate spinning experience.Personally, I don't think this be huge, endless, time-sink style game. The basic scenario isn't changed enormously by the additional starting rulers, but if you want to crank the difficulty there are a bunch of challenge run scenarios. Future patches seems to imply a greater emphasis on replayability, but I'm not sure how interested I am in playing more - I was perfectly happy to play what the game had to offer and then move on, rather than trying to grind out powerful dice to tackle the hardest challenge modes.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Dice Legacy is an interesting and innovative game, which is somewhat held back by a weird difficulty curve. My recommendation would be to play on easy first, which should allow you to get through the game without losing, and to ascend 2 dice. Using those, standard then becomes a lot more doable.I think Dice Legacy is worth playing, because there isn't another game quite like it. The game takes it inspiration from Euro-style worker placement board games, with dice representing your workers, and the whole thing being played in real time. You might want to use the option to remap the space key to pause the game: Although you can only do limited actions while paused, at least it helps with getting an overview of what is going on.Easy difficulty is a tad too easy, because the absence of raider basically removes all time constraints. Standard is already quite difficult, at least for new players. The "rogue-like" part isn't working very well, because you need to progress quite far before you will create more powerful dice and ascend them.The game definitively has a good side, but I do understand the negative reviews: The game is rather complicated, the dice open up the danger of having a bunch of bad rolls, and if things go wrong in real time and you get stuck in a bad situation, you can quickly lose. I would recommend this to fans of worker placement games, but not to casual gamers.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: I took a risk when buying this game because I almost never buy a game that has a score less than positive. However, after looking at the negative reviews and saw that most of them were commenting on difficulty, specifically the difficulty of resource management or the fact that dice eventually get destroyed if you do not use the proper mechanics to maintain them I thought it might still be worth a go as difficulty is something I find enjoyable in a game. Once I started playing though I became a bit confused at the negative reviews. Yes you do need to maintain the dice, but they have far more durability than the reviews seemed to imply and maintaining them is quite easy. Also, yes, if a dice gets wounded it only takes 2 wounds to kill a dice, but, it is pretty easy to avoid putting wounded workers (dice) into situations were they are likely to get wounded and there are fairly easy ways to heal them. The final concern I saw was about the attacks and how they are fairly continuous, this is true, and to be fair I feel the game could be slightly better at notifying you when you are being attacked, but especially since there are workers you can get that are specialized in fighting it doesn't seem like anything to difficult to manage. Simply put, if you like resource management games with the twist of dice and worker placement being key mechanics you will definitely like this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Just want to add because I played more. Playing through a second and third time with different leaders or different scenarios (same map) doesn't have a meaningful impact on gameplay most of the time. It gave you a slightly different early-game, but entirely the same end game. I felt a lack of satisfaction at playing "better" because playing better didn't give me enough meaningful control over how the game progressed. The dice limitations are still too annoying to get any joy out of playing well, and I realized that when you go for their "legacy" mechanic thats in the name, each time you use a legacy piece it gets consumed by that next playthrough. This seems like a needless time sink, if I got it once, I should just be able to keep it and use it in any next scenario that I want. Will this make the next scenarios a lot easier? yeah maybe....but that's fun, and the way the legacy system is set up now is just not. I wasn't sure if I should keep the "not recommended" part of the review for a few days, but after properly putting the game down, i am confident that I wouldnt suggest anyone to check this one out. It's fine. It's a functional game that gives you basically what it promises. It's just not that fun for me after the initial hour of learning how things work.----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Initial Review:I like the game, a little. Enough that I am comfortable with buying it on sale at 75% off.Many comments address the time system. Turn based vs Realtime. The game has a setting when you begin a scenario to choose from three options, one lets you pause whenever you want and assign dice, one lets you pause but you cant assign dice, and one doesn't let you pause. It seems like the game was originally intended to be a no-pause game...I cant believe any real person would actually choose that time system. Without pauses, this game would be zero fun. Let me explain.You have a limited "resting dice" pool of 12. If any worker dice finish their jobs while this pool is full, you have to destroy a dice of your choice. This is a made up "threat" to force you into maintaining high efficiency. Tasks all have differing time to complete from 20s - 90s. While this is somewhat cool to juggle, it also means that you occasionally have 5+ dice finishing jobs all within 2-3s of each other. This game was not designed to be real time. Pausing is the only realistic way to play.Buildings are messy and can cover others up, and there is no was to change camera view. You are never restricted from placing dice even if you cant see the spot, but it just makes the whole settlement seem cluttered. There is no mid-game to speak of, you go from not having enough to having abundance of everything. Quite often you are just waiting for one single thing or another to finish, and there is a limit to how many buildings you need. More will only have a negative effect by cluttering the screen and having potential for burning.The good things about the game:I like rolling dice.I like worker placement.It's an interesting attempt to mix together a whole bunch of different elements. Having it be fully turn based OR no dice pool limit would be better.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Dice Legacy is like playing a solo board game.  Resource management and straightforward strategy with a hint of luck i that each of your "workers" is a dice, and you need to roll the right function in order to perform it. Unlike anything I've played before, exceptionally difficult and frustrating (have not "completed" the first level yet), but landing perfectly in the zone for stimulating the boardgamer cortex and hooking you in.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a lot of potential to be a great game, Graphicly, gameplay wise - The building with dices concept. The keeping different parties happy etc.But there is a HUGE issue with you as a player only able to have 12 dices. And with the growth of your settlement, 12 dices is no way near enough.Other issues are fires just spawning out of nowhere. - Dices getting sick - The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ wounding in battle or raidings of settlement.The constant push from raider and no means to attack back from where they came (Other than raiding and having a settlement close by - But you need to have it so close you can almost look into their backyard. So no far away attacking)So unfortunatly it all just ends in a constant blur of getting civilians - Creating soliders - defending and loosing units because of wounding - until everything is either on fire becuase of unhappy parties or you somehow get close enought to attack their stronghold and then loose every dice you have because of wounding or something like that.. (But attacking their "stronghold" is as close to suicide as possible because of the extreme need for a lot of solider dices and by doing that every other party is on the brink of riot or burning down the city in the meanwhile)
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Fun idea. Well executed. It is really engaging to balance the dice - watching to make sure they don't break, taking chances when a threat arises, holding on to the right powers for the right time. Very engaging.My only drawback is that it takes a very long time to play. At the beginning, every die placement matters - and even later in the game a single face could still matter. So there is a lot of micromanaging. It wouldn't be that bad except that this game ends up being a bit of a marathon. I will play for hours and make minimal progress if things go well - and it is very easy for things to go bad: e.g. getting attacked and spending a majority of your resources surviving and only a tiny amount expanding the powers needed to win. It can be a recipe for battles of attrition or slowly losing resources until failure.I just can't put this much time and attention into scenarios for which there is no benefit. To become more powerful for the next run - by ascending dice - it takes a lot of investment and time. The roguelite loop just takes a very long time. Maybe on the scale of Civ type games, it isn't that bad, but when counting on dice to give you what you need, it really shouldn't be a slog.I love so much about this game. I am enjoying it while I am playing it until I look at a clock.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Dice Legacy is a unique survival citybuilder boardgame style with "you said it" DICE.  Due to the RNGness of Dice rolling, LUCK is defintely in there which might send some away from this game. However, underneath, there really is strategy and fun while trying to create the ultimate die. I failed tons of times before i even knows abit of what i am doing in this game.  I just hope that developers can let me choose what are the items that i can sell in the marketplace.  LOL even the items to sell is RNG. However, be warned that in order to get a great die, an amount of times had to be invested and certainly not in a single run as the resources are limited in the game.  Great fun and its won me with its uniqueness. Give it an 8 / 10.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: This game seemed good in the trailer, but there is just too much gameplay that seems rough and unpolished. The replayability is really low, the customisation of dices is mainly random, some faces do not beneficy from being upgraded (merchant), and there is no variation between two different games.As it stands right now, the game looks more like a demo rather than a released game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly "dice legacy" is very slow and grindy, leaves too many open questions and fails to develop any kind of excitement.The game looks amazing, which is what pulled me in despite the mixed reviews. "Can't be too bad", right? Sadly, I was proven differently. When you first start playing you can only select one single campain, all other options have to be unlocked. This campain starts out very slow and also doen't explain half of what you would want to know. Many tool tips only pop up after you've already half solved certain mysteries. The gameplay is slow, you throw dice, hope to get something useful, put them to use in their respective buildings and then you wait because every building takes a while to perform its action and during this time you can't do much.Eventually winter comes, your dice have a 30% chance of freezing (making them useless until summer, at least for the first year), which will eventually reduce 12 dice to one. Summer comes and yay, the cycle continues...My playtime was filled with frustration and confusion. What is my goal in all this? What exactly is the use of citizen or monk dice? How do I unlock technology? Where am I supposed to get food if my hunting grunds eventually disappear because they've been used up?I was not able to find any valid reason of continuing my journeyin dice legacy sadly and cannot recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: as of 3/7/2022 Freezes have not been rectified. Recommend no purchase until it is.Overall, I love this core gameplay loop. Novel method of framing a city-builder and I do WANT to play more. Two major issues:1. SO. MANY. CRASHES. I lost over two hours on the intro scenario to game crashes. And since this is supposed to be a Legacy style game, you have to exit to main menu in order to Save. But it ALSO doesn't have any form of regular autosave. Both crashes and the auto-save functionality should have been addressed previous to release. Also no Steam Cloud saves, which is annoying if you play on more than one device. 2. One of the most novel systems in the game is the Dice Ascension mechanic, which I LOVE. Until I found out they are one use only.  Why? Why take one of the coolest mechanics in the game and force it into a grind? The game is long enough without this needless waste of time to "farm Ascension dice" since you can only make one per scenario. Hope they make workshop available so someone smarter than me can just remove the Ascension dice destruction mechanic entirely. Needless.I want to play more and I want this to be a positive review for a game that is super fun.  When it works.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Damn, I'm kinda dissapointed, was hyped about this for weeks. Well, the problem is that the game is just too *small*. It has too little content for its price.Pros:* Interesting mechanic on "dice are your main action currency". It is not 100% novel as the steam page would like you to think. I've seen something pretty similar on Dicey Dungeons.* The fact that there are dice "classes" is something genuinely innovative and interesting. I haven't seen this anywhere else and found it overall exciting.* The strategic depth brought by the different dices and the fact that you can only hold a limited amount is very nice. This is only aided further with the "Council mechanic" and faction-related buildings, etc.Cons* No story.* No voice acting.* No memorable music or audio. Even though they released a "soundtrack", I felt like I've never even heard music in the game, because it simply wasn't memorable or interesting.* Only a single map. The map looks very nice, it is this nice "ring repeated ad infinitum". But it's just one map though, even though it would be a simple job to make several map variants.* The game offers several "scenarios", but that's a blatant lie: they are just difficulty modifiers. They are nothing like the different scenarios of e.g. Frostpunk, where you play a genuinely different map with genuinely different goals and thus gameplay orientation. Here all scenarios are "kill the opponent base with the added X difficulty."* Your overall "army" or "pool of characters" is rather limited: the factions of the game have solid distinctions, but the rulers you pick at the start of the game are so unimpactful... I mean, they have some kind of "ability" that is so situational you won't care about it for 99% of the game. Such a lost opportunity to bring flavor and variety with genuinely different and interesting rulers, but completely lost.* If you are not super-hooked into the gameplay loop this game has too little replayability due to the small amount of content.Keep in mind that this is a roguelike game. It has no story because it is supposed to bring replayability through variable gameplay. But, after 3-4 hours I saw everything the game had to offer. There is simply not enough depth to motivate me to play more. I'm honestly surprised by the selling price, given the amount of content. Hope it gets genuinely new and varied content in the future with updates...
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: It's a weird cosmic gumbo of a game. It's supposed to be hard, it's a survival game.  You're supposed to discover the mechanics for yourself, it's a rogue like. I think if this were turn based like many say they want it to be, it would cheapen the whole thing. The frantic rolling of dice trying to get the right symbols before your pool overflows is part of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game I have both returned after playing for a short period and am giving a thumbs up.The design and concept is excellent.Using dice on a city builder roguelike is a wonderful idea; unfortunately the UI I found painful and rendered the game unplayable for me.For others with better hands then mine that is likely not an issue and especially if you can grab it on sale is worth checking out. _childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: An hour in and I like it... I've had this one on my radar for a while and with it being on sale decided to pick it up and yeah, I've found enjoyment in it and decided to grab the expansion as well. Playing it with a very heavy pause button and added it to my "Worker placement board game" folder, not sure how hectic it gets as a pure real time experience (that is one for after the first couple of play through's) but certainly as a think-y RNJeebus it's ticking the right boxes - Think "Tharsis" but a little less dystopian, more medieval fantasy society... Basic premise seems to be your dice have durability, roll the dice to burn the durability to get different faces, buildings require different faces to produce "things", producing "things" reduces the durability of dice that can be healed by "things" or trade those "things" for other "things" and advance in both tech tree / survivability. Game certainly doesn't set the world on fire, not sure how much there is of a story but as a mechanics "game", seems solid enough. Will be putting more time into this one, but happy to have ponied up the dosh for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game despite all of the negative reviews posted. Most of the negativity comes from the fact that this is not a turn-based game; however, I believe that is what makes this game so great and addictive. Playing a strategy game without turn-based mechanics requires quick thinking and composure, which poses a greater challenge than when you have more time to plan out your turns. Personally, I find this very attractive in a gaming setting because it adds a little more realism and activity to the table. For those who do prefer to have more time to think about what they are doing, this game provides an option to play with the ability to pause, which is not exactly turn-based, but it is a compromise between that and real-time.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: The core mechanic of this game is interesting. It's a novel idea and I thought it was going to be quite fun. Immediately it becomes stale. There's not a great deal of depth to "dice-as-workers" the class system is interesting but inherently flawed as certain classes are mostly useless by "late game". The ascension of mutated dice to use in future games is a great idea, sadly the future games hold exactly the same content as the previous ones. Overall the core game loop is pretty stale and doesn't really hold up as a single player video game. This idea could very well work as a simultaneous competitive board game to accrue victory points.As a dice game it's quite peculiar as getting a "bad" role is net negative. There's nothing I can do with certain rolls and simply have to use the re-roll system which lowers my dice durability which requires me to put my dice in a little time out so they don't get too sleepy and die. Watching a timer go down until my very valuable and extremely finite resource is out of "time out" is not fun, or engaging. The game looks like a fun resource management with an element of luck. The game plays like a idle game I can't look away from for very long without everything falling apart and isn't interesting enough to reward me for paying attention to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts interesting, but gets really boring really fast.You are forced to reroll the dices and assign them to the same tasks over and over again.On top of that - the game just ended without me being able to ascend the dices - you are unable to continue the game once you destroy last enemy building.The ascension mechanic is very stupid - you just have to play long enough to build monoliths and powerup the dices to max, then ascend and finally destroy the enemy - an unnecessary hassle.tl;dr: Good design ideas combined with gamebreaking ones.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: First the objectively bad (some may disagree, but largely I think most will find these true)...1. Really poor explanation of the game from mechanics to what certain buildings actually do. Which leads into...2. Hidden mechanics you'll trip upon like the fact that if you bring an ascended die into a game and don't re-ascend it before the end of that game you lose that die.3. Rewarding players by punishing them... generally game design 101 says if a mechanic is meant to help players progress (like forging construct die) it shouldn't be a negative. This happens with dice traits like; Simple Minded, Ascetic, Meek, Gluttonous, and dumb. Nothing worse than constructing multiple buildings and spending multiple rare resources only to have one of your best dice become almost completely worthless.Now for the items of personal preference...1. The game would work much better as a turn based.2. Resource production needs to be boosted slightly with low 'skill' dice. Things like making beer, meant to help un-thaw frozen dice just aren't practical with low level dice. 3. Progression. Either slightly longer games with more progression or shorter games with the same progression. At current pacing a game probably shouldn't be more than 45-60 minutes.4. Policies don't build, i.e. you'll see the same policies at the start of the game as the end, and quite frankly by the end of the game most of these are of little help.5. Dice classes are poorly balanced. There is much more incentive to have Citizens and Soldiers than Monks and Merchants. That is also the order I would place them in if I were ranking them.Suggestions....1. Allow the obelisk to ascend more than one die, but perhaps cap it to a game limit of three. Right now you have to build a separate obelisk for each die you plan to ascend.2. Active notifications of attacks on the town, something that is persistent until either the attack is defeated or otherwise resolved.3.Key rebinding.Final thoughts...1. I will put this away for the next 6-12 months and wait to see if there are any balance changes, if not this is going to get hidden in my steam library like so many other games that fall flat.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game with big hopes. As a big board gamer, with a certain proclivity for dice manipulation games, especially in the context of worker placement such as Troyes. This seemed perfect, unfortunately the game falls quite short of my expectations.The prime issue being the lack of significant strategic or tactical decision making. Essentially, all you do is roll your limited pool of up to 12 dice until you get the symbols that you need. Then plop them down. There are no tricky trade-offs between doing X or Y, you roll until you match the necessary symbol. There is no other option, that is how you progress.Need food? Roll until you get the dice for it. Need to research? Roll until you get the dice for it.Need to build? Roll until you get the dice for it.Need to fight? That's right, keep on rolling!Now this isn't an issue about luck, in fact the luck factor here is pretty minimal. Seeing as you have unlimited rolls, the question isn't "if" you get the dice you want, it's a matter of "when". It feels like any other average survival game, with the added steps of having to roll some 3D dice.Unless you're looking for a somewhat clunky survival game, there isn't much to offer here.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: I saw the reviews of this and still decided to give it a try I got the game for around a dollar and the some change .... I I still feel like I got cheated. The game resolves like a small mindset rpg without the good rpg elements and is so grindy and ill manage that it feel like it just did barely enough not to be a mobile game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting take on a populated genre. If you enjoy city builder/ rogue-likes, then definitely watch some videos to see how it plays in action. It is absolutely a challenging and at times fast paced game, and if you know that going in then you won't be rudely shocked by an barbarian attack and having no dice to fight them, so frantically rolling your dice two, three or four times (each time costing the durability of those dice, where you'll either have to let them die and their durability reach zero, or slowly rotate them into a cookhouse [at the e xpense of food] to restore their durability again) in order to get a peasant dice that lands on the fighting side.Like I said, it's an interesting take. If you enjoy dice games like blood bowl, and you enjoy city builders and rogue-likes, then this is a great game.You will need to restart the game periodically as you learn certain things, because you have built buildings in such a way that they are not efficient. That's ok, it makes the game more replayable, and it increases your chances of success up to that point again and further in the next playthrough.7/10 recommend - If you're on the fence, wait for a sale - if you like city builder/ rogue-like/ dice games , watch some videos to see it in action and get it today.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Some other reviews suggest that it will be difficult to win the first game.Alas, it's also fully capable of failing in the other direction, too, but is a slog. Having won the first game I played on 'legacy' difficulty, it dragged on too long to be fun, but never really put me in danger of losing.Interesting concept, poor execution. The balance and polish just isn't there.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun and the combination of genres makes it interesting to play, but I can't help but feel like I always have to be scrambling over my dice to put them in something to avoid going over the "12 in the bank" limit.It's like if you want to play optimally, it feels as if there is an APM floor you need to reach. As such, I am very happy that the "save run" feature exists
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game, but it is a different game than you might be expecting, go in knowing what it is and you're more likely to enjoy what you find. It's realtime. Session length is a few hours (unless you really wipe out early). It's just as gorgeous to look at in action as it is in the trailer. It has a good savegame system and I highly recommend you use it. Each run is a bit too long for me to comfortably complete in one sitting and it might be for you too. It has satisfying decisions to be made and mostly has a nice arc but I would love a few quality of life features to reduce the amount of needless clicks, particularly when you get into the lategame.It's a challenging and original game and has some satisfying strategy decisions to make in there too. With each run being 3-5 hours long for me (and honestly quite tiring) I'm unlikely to fully fall in love with this game but I've enjoyed these 20 hours. As someone who is interested in game design it's also given me much food for thought!

Strategy game this is not, roguelike game this is not, RTS game this is not, city builder it touches on and survival it touches on but the game feels to be in a really weird place, hopefully it gets better but I am done with this game after 10 hours as it holds zero replayability for me

_childDocuments_.review: I played this for the first time last night, so I didn't try the earlier versions before improvements.I love the look of this game with the ringworld and the way the dice are used. I feel like I have lots left to figure out, and I got to experience the basics and beyond starting with the very good tutorial.I did learn pretty quickly to not run out of food so that I could keep my workers alive with the building near the water's edge.A demo would be a great idea for a game like this so people could get the full idea of it.I'll echo what another reviewer said about this feeling like a very new idea, and hat's off to the developers for bringing this to life so stunningly! _childDocuments_.review: A fun, charming and intricate blend of worker placement board game and light RTS that somehow works. The way you focus mainly on city building with combat happening mostly as a "background" thing, even though it can have important consequences, reminded me a bit of good old Settlers II at times.Note that I started playing after the developers introduced a pause feature that allows you to take your time and consider your next move. Playing without this makes the game a considerably different experience, MUCH more challenging and even stressful at times, even though it's the way the game was designed in the first place. You are expected to fail on your first few attempts but to get better by learning the game's mechanics and strategies over time.Playing with the ability to pause greatly simplifies the game, I was even able to reach the end of the map on my first attempt, but it's still possible to get some challenge by playing harder scenarios or on higher difficulty, which I personally will never attempt in "real time" mode.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but it just feel awkward.Ok they allow you to use spacebar to pause, that is fixed.But just like another reviewer said right to the point:"I have not played this very long so this is just initial thoughts.Its a bad mix of game mechanics."And that is exactly how I felt.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: This game probably could've been good, but it's not. It's definitely bad as a city-builder. Half of the buildings are somewhere between useless and niche, and of the others you rarely need more than one. Getting and providing for workers is trivial. You can easily ignore two of the five types of dice entirely. The "opponent" presents no real choices either strategically or tactically, and is merely a steadily ramping drain on your attention and resources.  The game is pretty enough, but you will have no opportunity to take in the scenery or reflect on what little you have built, since you need to be constantly placing dice anyways.I beat the game, on the recommended level (no pause), on the second attempt, and don't see any reason to play again.tl;dr: The game hopes to keep you too busy to notice that it is bad.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've never played an incremental game before, you're in for a real treat -- This is a fantastic introduction to the genre. Take the time to learn how things work -- the game holds your hand a bit, and then gently lets go.  There's a lot to explore and learn as you progress through the game, and make your way to the ascensions.If you HAVE played incremental games before, this is a good one.  The polish is slick, and the game design is solid.  I have only played for 14 hours, so -- I don't know how deep the rabbit hole goes.  You'll want to make sure to ascend at least 3 dice before you defeat the final building in the first game.  The catapult is enough to destroy the final building, so really, ascend as many as you can, and then fire away.
