_childDocuments_.review: Dice Legacy is a city-builder with a unique twist that incorporates rogue-like gameplay and complexity through new game mechanics not seen before for this genre.Workers are dice. They can do different types of work depending on how you design these dice. As opposed to building a massive sprawling city full of workers like in a more conventional city-builder, you are limited to 12 (and sometimes 6) dice that complete everything you need to do.This game is unique in the sense that it constantly challenges you to complete the game's scenario with many additional layers of scarcity that a game like Frostpunk (which I've played and love) will not have. After you complete your first scenario, you unlock new leaders and scenarios that offer different synergies and challenges to overcome.This is perhaps the most controversial aspect I've seen from other reviewers that is core to the gameplay of Frostpunk. While this may be frustrating, the unending cycle of Summer and Winter within the game forces you as a leader to design your city carefully so that "safe" heated zones exist for your workers lest you want them to become frozen and unusable. As a by-product, this also means that the resource you need (wood) must be stockpiled in advance of every winter season similar to how you might stockpile coal in Frostpunk.There are essentially two tech tree/upgrade systems within this game. One is more traditional city-builder where you unlock economies of scale, powerful buildings, ways to manipulate/upgrade your dice, and religion to mitigate negative affects. The other is much more nuanced where you must decide how to upgrade the 6 sides of all 12 of your dice. Finding a balance between racing up the tech tree and upgrading your dice to complete actions with a higher success rate, fewer combined dice (less rolling required), or less time is another unique decision that must be made as both require significant resources. Where things get more complicated (and less predictable) is the randomness of combining dice and the personality traits these "constructs" emerge with. Some of these make gameplay easier where dice can roll infinitely without repercussions (more on this later) and other personality traits are downright dumb and frustrating. Regardless, this combination process is pivotal part of beating the game as it unlocks the ability to upgrade a dice face level beyond the normal limit of 4.Dice Legacy is encouraged at its harder difficulties to be played in a real-time where you must roll your pool of unused dice and decide where these should be placed. Dice can only do work if the dice face rolled matches that workplace's requirement. After a dice has finished working, it must be rolled again. What makes dice rolling and the decision to lock a dice and not roll a constant evaluation is the durability/food system. A dice can only take roughly a dozen actions before it must be fed food to replenish durability. A dice also loses durability whenever you roll. Once a dice reaches 0 durability, it will perish. This game doesn't allow you to brute force the same predetermined way of playing because there will always be variation in how you roll your dice. At times, I found myself having to make frantic decisions how to lock certain dice to prevent them from rolling while I re-rolled others to find the faces I was looking for to stave off disaster. The variability is low early in the game when your dice traits are homogenous but this grows complex to master as you build more powerful dice. You have influence over this variability based on the different dice factions you choose to be part of your 12 citizens, how you combine their capabilities, and how you upgrade them. In an abstract way, the game operates a bit like a deck-builder where you are constantly trying to influence the likelihood of drawing the card you need at exactly the moment you need it.The game features a core map layout like one would might find with other rogue-likes. It took me 4+ hours in my first playthrough to beat the game on the default difficulty. Across different runs, the locations of resources, events, and encampments will be slightly different. This means you have will have to build the pockets of your sprawling city differently each time. As you progress through the game, your active factions will propose new laws for you to enact each season which may also influence how you build your city within each faction's district. Beyond this, upon completing the base scenario of the game you unlock many challenge scenarios that may completely change how you build your city and complete the game. These range from never-ending winter to wildfire summers.1. Navigating the mini-map can be challenging at first since the map is a gigantic loop. You can snap to your district halls easily but I can't always find my Apothecary, Brewery, or Temple quickly in a pinch.2. The tutorial/objective system is is comprehensive in topics but not thorough. As a new player, the most frustrating moment is when the first winter comes. A timed objective to unlock your first iron mine, steam generator, and stockpiling a certain amount of coal would help ease these frustrations. Frostpunk does a more elegant job of introducing the harshness of winter to a player! The randomness of construct dice is also a double-edged sword for me. I'd like to know more about the possibilities of what I'm getting myself into first!3. Scarce resources lack visual clarity. With how many decisions I am making throughout my city I found myself surprised whenever I ran out of a Meadows to find Herbs or an Iron Mine. The remaining amounts of each resource is viewable if you click on each resource individually, but it's hard to keep track of when there's so much else going on.4. This is more of a QoL issue but the fixed camera can make it hard to see which dice are required for what building. Since everything is viewed at an angle, it wasn't easy at first to recognise each of my buildings. You have to mouse over the building for it to become clear.There is a lot of depth to Dice Legacy accomplished through the combination of new systems unique to this genre of game. As a former Frostpunk enthusiast, this game was immediately intriguing and is worth the price tag. Dice Legacy makes you take hundreds if not thousands of decisions over the course of the run because of the very nature of a dice roll and map that is presented to you. Every building that is placed and every dice you roll can have a consequence and it's this challenge and the various rogue-like elements that makes this game more fun & re-playable than a traditional city-builder.Shout out to my boy Esty8nine on Twitch for introducing and teaching this game to me (as he does for all rogue-likes and indies I play). I was going to buy Dice Legacy anyway, but Ravenscourt was generous enough to give him 10 keys in a community giveaway.Edit:Editing my review now that I've racked up some hours and completed some of the harder difficulties. I haven't lost a single run yet through all difficulties up to Extreme and have completed some of the challenges on Hard difficulty. If a game is "stressful" or too "hard" then it's perfectly fine to play it at a lower difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, this is a game I really had high hopes for and wanted to like. The graphics are good and it has a really interesting theme and premise and I LOVE city builders. But this game is just stress incarnate. It starts out pretty fun, you have a single type of dice that you roll then place on specified icon spaces to take that action, like gathering wood from forests or stone from mines. There is even a neat season mechanic that goes from summer to winter which tosses in another nifty thing, some dice might freeze and be unusable during the winter BUT there is a building you can build to unfreeze them.This continually escalates. Summer-winter-summer-winter and as you progress you unlock new buildings to build, ok nice progression. Then you realize that you are constantly needing SOMETHING and it quickly becoming overwhelming. At a certain point angry peasants just start invading your lands and randomly attacking and setting fire to your buildings. So, you create a couple soldier dice to combat them. Oh no, my dice are injured, *quickly looks through all the buildings to figure out which building heals dice....ok now to buil....OH NO I need 6 wood and 3 stone and 2 iron to build this.....Ok *rolls dice* UGH only got 1 worker roll to help get some wood......*rerolls* UGH one of my dice perished because I rolled it too much and I need to send 2 other dice to the building that adds more rolls to them....OH NOOOO more attackers!!. This is just a small taste of the stress....AND IT'S ALL IN REAL TIME! You can pause the game but cannot do anything while paused. The game has like 3 more speeds that are faster than the slowest. This is the first game I've had where I wish there was a slower speed available. Or, just the ability to make the game turn based would be great. I can feel my anxiety returning while writing this as there is a gameplay video broadcasting in the bottom right of my screen.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Dice RefundedIt's basically Frostpunk, with a different lore, in mediaeval times but worse, so, so much worse….) Bad RNG implementation.) Utterly RNG dependent, which seems to be the only form of real difficulty.) The UI is crap as it looks like it's designed for phones.) The notifications are crap.) The Map does not even fit on the screen properly. To see the last few centimeters of the left/right outer edges you have to scroll a bit, because gAmE dEsIgN, I guess. (FYI: the map is a wheel basically - so.. Yea.. try to explain that design choice).) The buildings hardly look different, which is made even more problematic by the point above.) The graphics are blurry & mediocre even on max settings.) It feels like playing Starcraft 2 on Diamond+ given the amount of micromanagement you have to do. Even if it's just placing & rerolling dice (“workers”) on the buildings they fit in. There is a pause button but if you use that every time you have to re-roll you are basically playing a stop-motion game..) Once you get status effects, different classes and whatnot it gets even more micro-managy, in a bad way, because the RNG also increases exponentially..) You will quickly end up feeling that once you get a bigger part of the map and expand your city, you will be utterly lost in what's going on. Thanks to only being allowed 12 dice (workers) you at least won't be overwhelmed, probably. .) All the games content is locked until you beat the “campaign”, because f* you.Even if there would not be the bad RNG element, Dice Legacy would still be trash given all the other problems. I mean it's literally got Dice in the name, so you’d expect RNG, but not braindead micro management RNG which got slot machine grind written all over it. Battlebrothers uses proper RNG mechanics, so does XCom and even Total War titles to some degree. Dice Legacy is only a perfect example of how not to use RNG mechanics.Ultimately people who recommend Dice Legacy clearly have never played a semi-proper or challenging city building game because otherwise they would not recommend it.It's a unique concept, got to give them that, but in the same instance it's a perfect example of why nobody has done it before: Because it simply does not work. 1  / 10 , not recommended. Dice Legacy has nothing going for it, move along.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely beautiful game, I genuinely enjoy the full experience. I fell in love with it from the start and no matter how hard it gets I always end up coming back. It's a shame it has such a small following, it definitely deserves higher recognition. I don't think I have found a single game that has such a balance in difficulty and progression, most games are either too easy or too hard, at least for me. I will always promote the game to anyone if I get the chance because the devs deserve more recognition.There is a SINGLE thing that I have an issue with, it is a very easy fix and I hope the devs implement it some day, if they are still even updating it, at the start of a season it needs to have a pop up saying "it's time to choose a new policy" or something along those lines, because many times I will be busy with my dice and working away and the screen will pop up as I am clicking and then a policy is chosen that I didn't want, they are an important factor to survival and shouldn't be allowed such a simple accident.Other than that I easily give this game a 20/10, dice style games are fairly niche and the potential for them is far from fully explored and these guys have definitely created something special in the genre

It is also roguelike in that you can "ascend" dice and they become permanent additions to your starting pool, making future campaigns absurdly easy. Then you can smash those dice together in a forge and make constructs made from the remains of other dice like a super mutant dice.

_childDocuments_.review: It's thin, it's repetitive, and it fails to make good on both the "Dice" and "Legacy" things. Every round feels incredibly similar despite the different conditions presented by each scenario. Most of that experience is re-assigning dice to same few tasks over and over again while slowly chipping away at a largely static and annoying enemy threat. The "dice as workers" thing works pretty well in the early game, where there's a pretty good push-pull between trying to reroll for the jobs you need or just taking what you've got and saving food you would spend on rerolls, but once you get past that phase and food is plentiful, the dice just add complexity, not depth. It gets even worse toward the end of a match, where you're encouraged to just upgrade your dice to the point where there's no real trade-off anymore. And as for the "legacy" part, it's just a matter of allowing you to take two dice into your next session, which is otherwise completely siloed off and has no part in a larger web.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write a review but I wanted to add my 2 bits.Pros:  It's a good dice game.  I do not see many so this was big for me.The game is fun to explore and figure out.  After the first round (died) I turned off the tutorial and just had fun throwing myself into the world.  Beyond durability, face types, and face power, I just wanted to learn for myself and enjoy the ambiance.It has a sense of mystery to it.  I just hope it delivers on it over time.The world feels alive.  What I mean is the ground slowly gets covered in snow as winter comes or melts away as summer is approaching.  Your screen has frozen effects at the edges and the environment is punishing with freezing your dice.I like the dice "classes" and they worked together it felt fun and reasonably balancedCons: The game is meant for time crunch and stress.  Strategy must be planned and carried out on the clock and under pressure.  This game is basically meant to be a RTS with dice and in harder levels the pause option is removed and this is described as the intended game play.  I like this twist but I prefer a straight challenge without the added stress.  This game wouldn't work well as turn based and I don't want the game devs to twist their vision on this.  So I'll chalk it up to differences in taste and do my best to play through harder levels.It feels like it will need DLC to be fully fleshed out.  I actually hope something comes out because I want more.  Hence why it's a con XDPacing of enemies.  I get it's meant to be an invisible timer and all I do.  But if I damage the enemy (trying to not spoil anything) I expect them to be weaker. but nothing changed right up until I took out the goal.  All of the other stuff I damaged is just time sinks and walls.  My thoughts on this could all change as I learn the game and some of it's back end but this is a first impression.I like this game a lot and have been enjoying my play throughs of it and just exploring.  It's a fun challenge.  It has good things and bad things but it is still my favorite single player game of this year ( I'm a sucker for dice) and I hope others will enjoy it too.   I *may* update this with new thoughts over time or perhaps corrections depending.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to put this up as a 'maybe' or a 'not quite yet'. This game has a lot of potential, especially if you like Frostpunk. Dice Legacy takes the idea of a survival strategy and adds dice to it. "How?" you might ask. Well, imagine a civ, but instead of people you have dice. Roll your dice too often? Poof. Gone. As far as visual style and actual gameplay goes, it's kinda cool. However....There's a few glaring issues that make this less fun than I'd like. For starters, the game only half-explains itself. When you unlock a new feature, the game provides you with pause-buffered help screens. Nice and all, but when it comes to understanding what each dice face does, you're left to figure it out on your own. Some of them are common sense, but tooltips would alleviate this entirely. There's a minor inconvenience where if you set a die in a cookhouse to restore durability, or in a school to rank them up, you have to manually allocate food (whereas literally every other material is auto-slotted where it needs to be, and no you can't slot more than you need in.)The last major issue is that I feel like this game tries too hard to replicate Frostpunk's core gameplay loop. For Frostpunk, it's unique, fresh, and new, and in Dice Legacy it's... almost shoehorned in. It's a hell of a lot brighter than Frostpunk, so not completely amiss, and the ringworld designs scream "We played Halo and loved the worldbuilding." As for what it can do on its own, it has a way to go before I can happily recommend it to everyone. I don't really wanna spend the first hour of a survival game trying to learn what the base mechanics are, only to learn that I was being an idiot because I didn't know what I was supposed to be doing, and that's what happened here. Hopefully time is taken to make it more accessible to oblivious idiots like myself.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty simple design, works fine with keyboard but should work with controller as well. Takes a little while to unlock all the complexities, the tutorial system works to get you started but you'll probably want to restart several times as you discover new strategies. _childDocuments_.review: This is a very hesitant positive Recommendation, the only thing that saves it from being negative is the price. 20$ is not that bad, I would say there's 12-15 hours of genuine not same-y content which is fine in this day and age for that price. Now to the actual review.First off, this is a game about managing your time and resources, the city building aspect is the smallest part of this game, i'm convinced that genre was slapped on there to possibly increase sales, but it is what it is.The game is very hard to learn initially, lots of things thrown at you and I would argue its almost impossible to win the first time you ever play it on normal 'legacy; mode. Here is my gripe: After maybe my 2nd run I had the game figured out. The AI is predictable and exploitable in its current state to a point where it is not a challenge whatsoever... As long as you get the peasant districts can grow in winter and can't be set on fire this game is a joke, it completely negates any challenge at all, even on the hardest difficulties. And those two options are common, I've been able to get them on all of my runs in the first 2 winters. However, without those options, good lord this game would be unplayable.I do think something super cool they could try to do is implement a PVP mode, where instead of "The Others" its another player on the other side of the ring. All in all, In its current state its barely its barely a positive review, but the polish on the mechanics and relative unique-ness of it pushes it over the edge for me. Its fun, but only for so long.

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly fun euro-like strategy/city builder. I like dice games and mechanics, and the way this game introduces different types of dice, each with unique faces to meet unique mechanics, or abilities to manipulate and enhance dice, or even pass your strongest pieces across games, is all pretty sweet. The gameplay itself feels pretty interesting, balancing the capabilities your dice offer you, the happiness of the classes they represent, and the resources available to you. It all makes for a pretty interesting balancing act.Some criticism I'd like to see addressed in some way or other: Replayability is in a weird state. I could see myself coming back to the game, but beyond starting with some ascendant dice, I don't see much changing. There are other "personas" with abilities, but the abilities trigger at random and at least in my first game I only triggered it about four or five times, and not once did it actually do anything for me. You're already dependent on getting a specific die roll, and then the benefit of that specific die roll has its own conditions that basically make it a non-factor in my games. Resources are finite, which is a bit of a peeve of mine. I actually didn't get to ascend any dice, nor build several buildings, because my map was devoid of stone towards the end. Your merchants can sell a random resource for gold, but can't buy anything with said gold. I think the Merchant Camps might offer a chance for that, but they only seem to sell to you if they like you, and their opinion of you degrades over time, making it unreliable.  This wouldn't be so bad if I could demolish buildings for a partial refund, or if buildings lost to attacks left ruins that could be scavenged for resources.Lastly there seems to be a few limits to the game itself regarding dice faces. A die face can be upgrade up to 4x, and if it's a construct (smooshing two dice together), up to 8x. The only problem I have with this is really the only die that seems to benefit from going anywhere near that many numbers of faces is the combat face, to deal with some very large attacks. Buildings cap out at 3 hammers, workshops only need 3 books, I couldn't see the higher tier religious buildings (again, no stone), and 3 gears only seemed to come up with setting up the fairground, and even then things like theaters make that a nonissue. I could maybe see harvesting if you wanted a Paul Bunyan-esque character that clears out forest/iron mines/ stone quarries in two or three passes, but by and large most dice only need two, maybe three times strength, which loses a lot of the depth/strength in crafting late game "overpowered" dice. All in all it's a really neat game, got some cool gameplay ideas, has a unique feel, and I'd love to see it tweaked and expanded upon.

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting game! I will be honest, I was surprised that the game was fast paced and on the spot management of a city and your workers/dice. Empower when you can.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool little game.  Pretty harshly reviewed.  The core mechanics are very sound, but it could use a little more development time dedicated to quality of life improvements.  Giving a hearty recommendation in hopes others check it out so it will in turn potentially get some of the minor polish it could use to really shine.My main two nitpicks right now would be that the game both tells and expects you to experiment perhaps to a fault.  This means that unless outside of game research is undertaken, a few bonehead mistakes that couldn't have predicted are bound to happen (ie: placing a useless district tower in BFE, or building things in a way that they won't benefit from buffs and/or be exposed to debuffs.)  This isn't the end of the world but may result in wanting to restart the game early on in order to take advantage of new knowledge rather than just rolling with it.  Also, parsing information such as which what locations are usable by which dice and provide which resource can become difficult since when buildings start to get cluttered they occlude the view.  Understanding area boundaries outside of your very obvious territory border is also a bit difficult at times. To end off I'd like to provide some commentary towards points brought up by others.  Pausing and thinking is permitted in the standard difficulty.  One can pause the game and take all the time needed to ask the questions "which dice in my hand do I want to hold on to, which ones do I want to re-roll, and which ones do I want to put to work and where" and then unpause to carry out the plan. The various colors of dice serve a very obvious purpose in that their faces have different probabilities and thus strengths and use cases compared to each other, not to mention their specialties. Dice Legacy very much feels like a digital homage/evolution of a tabletop game called Era: Medieval Age which was designed by someone that knows a thing or two about crafting a cohesive and engaging experience by tinkering with numbers and probabilities.

_childDocuments_.review: So I have mixed feelings about this game.It is a great game but it needs some changes for me to keep playing it.Pro'sThe game looks gorgious.Great Sound track.And an honestly even tho the cons might sound severe, Great RTS experience.Cons. (and i really hope the devs will look in to this)- Game feels rather stressfull. Even for an RTS. But this game is all about dice and stratagy, You have a pause button but you cant do anything during the pause. And at Harder difficulties the pause is removed (which i think makes the game impossible to play btw) The game is already quite stressfull on normal with being able to pause the game. I just get chills down my spine if i cant pause it. A way to solve this and what I would love to see. Make pausing a feature of this game. Where you can still place, roll, and lock dices. Obviously the rest of the game doesnt run. And then allow throughout all difficulty stages to pause and balance the game from that point on. GIves players still that fun feeling of control without the stressfull aftermath. _childDocuments_.review: I can see what the game is trying to be but sadly it's not working. This is a RNG-based micromanagement game which every steps you are allow to do are according to the RNG DICES. You don't think, just use the dice. It's not a strategy-city builder because you can't do anything other than what RNG dices allow you to do. Refusing to do according to the RNG dices will lead to a punishment.In turn-based card games, players can manage their luck by mitigate the loss and work the best with what they have within the RNG cards. Doing so, players have the control over the RNG. This game is not turn-based. It's a RTS. Players are being controlled by the RNG DICES over the long run. RNG elements are accumulated over time. The game is NEITHER about you nor what you what to build nor even when you want to build. RNG DICES never care about you, what you want to do.The game is about DICE and DICES and more DICES and what DICES want to do.The game play is very rigid and does not allow any creativity. There is one and only way to play this game and its not according to you, players but it's according to RNG DICES. Listen to those DICES. Build accordingly. Gather accordingly. Explore accordingly. This is a RNG-based micromanagement game which every single steps you are allow to do in the game are It's a disrespect to all players who can think for themselves. It's a strategy game which you don't need to think and just act according to the RNG. If you lose, It has very little to do with your strategy because the game is ULTRA RNG-based. Some could argue that you're supposed to deal with the RNG like what you do in card games but no that isn't possible here. In card games, It's turn-based and you could manage your luck by selecting the best action within the RNG. However, this game is not turn-based. It's a RTS and the advantage/disadvantage is not decided at the end of the turn but It's a long term RNG.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: Due to recent changes made by the developer - namely allowing the game to be played normally while paused (thank God) and adding the ability to remap the terrible default controls - I have edited this review. It is less critical than previously, the game has definitely been improved; though my rating remains thumbs down.Original Review Starts Here:Were you expecting a city builder game where you can relax and plan your strategy, design your city layout and get your production chains going, expand your territory and grow your population?Forget it.This is no city builder. It is a city builder SKIN wrapped around a dice management puzzle game, which is both played against the clock (you can however pause and make decisions while time is frozen, a new and welcome addition by the devs reacting positively to customer complaints) and somewhat stressful. The theme could have been absolutely anything, but they chose a medieval village city builder, which is probably going to confuse a lot of players and make them regret their purchase as I do.Pushing the game even further from city builder territory is the incredibly frustrating Winter mechanic, where all your dice freeze (become unusable) if you send them to work in unheated areas. This forces you to build all your key buildings clustered tightly round a steam heater. This basically enforces your village layout into being clusters of buildings tightly packed round your heaters, and vast empty space everywhere else on the map. Not only ugly but very frustrating to interact with too (all these tightly packed buildings have work-spaces on them that you need to drop dice and resources onto).And now lets move on to the combat. Play far enough and you encounter an enemy faction on the map. And they will start to spawn raiders who can destroy your stuff. And they will spawn EVERY 30 SECONDS. So not only are you playing a time-based puzzle game, juggling a hundred things already, but the already huge micro-management requirement suddenly goes through the roof as the game wants you to make sure you roll a sufficient number and strength of 'swords' on your dice to kill these guys before your precious building are destroyed. They come far too often and are poorly implemented and drain all the fun there was right out the game. There's a Pacifist mode that turns them off but it suffers from the opposite problem and is too boring to be taken seriously.My final complaint comes from replayability. There is very little. A winning strategy that works on one map will work on them all. And the RNG aspect of map generation is negligible.There's difficulty setting and you can pick different rulers which give you a different set of starting dice (more or less irrelevant) and a different special ability but I suspect that once through the game will be enough for most people. It's one of those games where it's a chore to play and a relief to finish because you can relax and never see the game again. As with all puzzle games, once you've solved the puzzle once there is little point in solving it again.At the end of the day, it comes down to a perfect storm of frustrating mechanics, a game at odds with itself in terms of real-time versus paused, and - perhaps worse of all - a terribly misleading game tag on the Steam store, and I find myself forced to thumbs down this game. Shame, as I had such high hopes. But I am boardgamer/city builder at heart and I was expecting a city builder here, as advertised. But what I got was a real-time puzzle game, requiring quick reflexes and absolutely TONS of constantly frustrating micro-management that just gets more and more intense as the game progresses. It is certainly NOT a city builder. Buyer beware.

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid board gamer but amateur city/civilization builder I really recommend this crossover game even just a couple hours into it. The interface is clean and tooltips were easy to read. _childDocuments_.review: This game has been getting a lot of hate in the reviews, and undeservedly so.VISUALS AND AUDIOBeautiful visuals. Some people complain about buildings blocking the view of those behind, but thanks to building transparency settings this was never an issue for me.The music - which I would describe as atmospheric - does a fine job, however it's not going to win any soundtrack of the year awards. When your camera strays too far into the enemy base, the music changes to sound less like a professional orchestra and more like a child's clarinet recital, which I think is a really cute little touch.GAMEPLAYThe closest relatives for this game are Northgard and, to an extent, Frostpunk. This ain't yo momma's chill city builder. You might be forgiven for thinking the pace of this game to be slow. It is not. It is deliberately fast-paced. Playing optimally means oversubscribing your dice beyond the limit and keeping them churning to avoid fallout. The only time I run into pacing issues is during the first winter when I don't yet have the resources to prevent all my dice from freezing, so I have to wait until winter ends. Could just be a deficiency in my playstyle.A lot of QQing about this in the reviews. Based on what I've read, a lot of people don't take the time to learn the gameplay mechanics, go full Surprised Pikachu when their setup backfires, and then proclaim that the difficulty is too hard and that there's too much plate spinning. After one day of playing I was able to win the Stranded scenario on the hardest difficulty, not once feeling like there's a chance I could lose. Meanwhile, in Frostpunk I still get my ass regularly handed to me on the hardest difficulty level, even after years of playing.In summary: game is not difficult, you just bad.Sorry, no, this isn't a "roguelike". It's roughly about as roguelike as Northgard. There needs to be much more variability to make that claim. There are balance issues between leaders making only a couple viable. There's enough variety in here to keep me going for around 20 hours I reckon, which is still a fairly good value proposition given the game's price point.OVERALLThis game should really be sitting at around 75-80%, so I am doing my part to bring it closer. My target bandwidth could drift higher depending on post-launch support from the developer.It's not a perfect game, but it represents a decent to good value proposition for its price point. If you enjoyed Northgard or Frostpunk, you'll probably end up enjoying this too.

_childDocuments_.review: What a remarkable not-so-little little game. I think the absolutely most important things to state ay the outset is that this is an RNG-heavy game. That doesn't mean it's all down to luck as you can 'freeze' certain die faces that you think you'll need and re-roll the remainder. And you can use any peasant dice you're not using to generate new peasant dice, up to a limit of 12 total. In short, you soon learn to manage your 'hand', which die to freeze and which to re-roll.The second, and also important is that this is a pausable RTS game where you can scroll around and place buildings but you can't place dice while the game is paused. I think this is a good compromise because you can easily pause the game, scroll about and make a plan and then unpause and play your dice. So, if you're okay with both of those, read on.Now, the game. This is a Real Time Strategy game but it's different from any other I've played so far and in a good way. It looks superficially simple but it's not. The tutorial isn't <cough> one of the best I've ever seen but you can easily learn what's best to do like I did, by experimenting and restarting with the knowledge I'd gained in my earlier playthrough. It's not deeply complex or difficult to figure out but if you need more throrough guidance and build queues to get yuou quickly into a new game, you can find all that on the discussion boards.There are five classes of dice, Peasants, Citizens, Soldiers, Merchants and Monks. Each die has six faces with certain skills, build, produce, scout, research, etc, etc. You can enhance a particular die to give a face more power and that now counts as two of that type for whatever skill you're using. You can also change them to a different type of die with a special building.There are a lot of buildings as well and you'll soon suss out what to build and where for the best effects. You place die and resources in buildings for production chains or to produce some in-game effect. You can expand and create special districts by placing district buildings and upgrading them. When you upgrade a District Building, if you upgrade it with a Citizen die, you get a citizen district and iof you use a Mercahnt, you get a Merchant district. It's pretty simple to work out.There's a pretty brutal winter that you'll probably die to in your first attempt but you'll soon figure out the best way to get through it painlessly. In fact, you'll probably welcome the winter because the enemy doesn't seem to raid nearly so frequently during the winter.Yes, there's an enemy that will send raiders to attack your settlements and you can counter them with the sword faces. Soldiers have more of these and as the game progresses, the raids will get stronger meaning you'll need 3 or 4 sword 'faces'. to fight them off.And there's more and more, healing, trading, building defences. I haven't scratched the surface of this game yet but it's a keeper. I'll finish with a really useful tip which the game tells you about but is easy to overlookand that's to use Alt-lef tclick to autofill those building slots. Trust me, once that becomes second nature to you, it'll make the game much easier your clicks more efficient.

_childDocuments_.review: The idea and concept of the game is very original, something I have not see anywhere else. I really like it. One you have played a couple of hours and understand the different dice, mechanics and buildings it becomes easier and easier to juggle more dice. I usually do not write reviews but seeing the resonance on the shop so far, makes me kinda sad. The potential I see in this game and concept is enormous. Yes, there are things that need improvement and the developers certainly did not do themself a favour releasing this as a full version. That is not to say it is not a "full" game but 6-12 months in early access with community feedback could have worked wonders. Not only for the game regarding tutorial, gameplay, mechanics, UI and QoL stuff but also with regards to the reception of the game. As far as I know there were only a few selected people who were able to play the game before release (mainly for marketing purposes). Who knows maybe they ran out of money and had to release it. Nevertheless I like the game and have fun playing it. Price tag is a little on the high side imo, given that you basically play one scenario again and again with different difficulties and restrictions. If your on the fence about the game I suggest keeping an eye out for a discount and give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Really cool city builder game that uses dice as workers.  You start the game with 6 and can earn more by assigning them to various buildings.  You can also combine and upgrade dice to make them more powerful.  Basic premise is that you are constantly rolling your dice pool and using them to power buildings in your empire.  A lot of the negative reviews left for this game feel it needs some sort of "active pause" system, which it really doesn't.  I make liberal use of the pause function when playing in order to figure out the best use of dice after rolling.  Then I just unpause and assign some dice.  You will start getting attacker by various forces, which make you assign a sword face of a die to fend them off.  You have a timer on these enemy units and if you don't kill them by the time it ends they will start setting fire to buildings.  I always keep one or two sword faces locked in my die pool, which means when you re roll they stay locked in place.  If you are fan of board games that use dice as worker placement, you will likely LOVE this game.  Sure it can get hectic at times trying to figure out how to best use your dice, but it's completely manageable using the pause.  It does NOT deserve a mixed review.  I urge you to ignore that and give the game a chance.   Devs are also active in forums and are listening to players feedback.  This means the game will only get better!  My only real criticism is that the tutorial is pretty lacking.  It leaves a fair amount for you to figure out on your own.  Would have liked more of a walk through when first starting out.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been thoroughly enjoying the game so far.  I have yet to feel the need to pause the game as some negative reviews have complained about.  I feel once you understand the mechanics there is more than enough time.  For example once you start getting constant attackers, this can feel a bit overwhelming since you have to deal with them while also managing your other buildings/resources.  But once you build towers in the right spots, those attacks no longer need your attention.  I know some mentioned having to scroll the map which takes to long and is frustrating.  However on the left side there is a line with colored blips.  A red one represent an incoming attack and you can click it and be brought to that location without scrolling.  The others represent your Districts you build to scout ahead and make it easy to click to get to that part of the map.  So you basically have little markers at your choosing to help navigate the map without scrolling back and forth.  Overall I am stilling learning and loving the strategy and depth of it.  Building up constructs (two dice merged together that you've empowered beforehand) and being able to reuse the ones you like in next games.  How each Leader has their own special ability and how to activate it.

_childDocuments_.review: is a nice twist on the city-building genre by introducing a lot of RNG, as the inhabitants of the city will be dice instead of people. You are rolling the dice regularly to determine the next step you will take.The game starts with a good tutorial that explains most of the game. It is also instructive during your playthrough.The goal is to build a city with your subjects represented by dice. You start with 5 dice and you will create more up to 12.There are different colored dice to represent different groups of individuals. For example, orange dice are peasants, while blue ones are militia.You will be placing the dice in the city and they will be acting on those parts. Each area has its own needed actions. Some need a gathering symbol, others will need to build upon, represented by a hammer, etc.You have to reroll your dice if you do not have the indicated necessary symbols for the actions. The dice also have a limited lifespan/durability, and every roll lowers this by 1, until reaching 0, causing the dice to vanish. There are ways to increase the durability, though the dice can also become frozen or suffer illness, etc.Speaking of being frozen, the game features seasons, and the survival in the winter is the most difficult.You will be able to unlock multiple aspects of the game, such as new scenarios, new leaders, etc.The game does have multiple difficulty settings, and I have played only on standard so far. There is a casual mode available that is less stressful, as you will only have to deal with enemies if you provoke them in this mode.The graphics all look fine, especially the dice that look very sharp. This is important as it's the primary focus of the game. Sometimes things are not the easiest to see. I would like to see a patch to allow further zooming out.The music is very calming and it sounds really great in high-stress situations when the music helps to set the tone for the game.The game can be fully played with a mouse. Keyboard is optional but may help out well.I think the price of $/€19.99 is a bit steep, even if you unlock new scenarios and other new things, because the core game stays very much the same. gives a nice twist in the city-building genre. There is a lot of RNG, as expected for any game that involve dice. In my opinion, this can be a bit too much at times. Especially because the sub genre would be RTS without pause. Most games in the city-building genre are relaxing and this game I found to be rather stressful at times, mainly due to the RNG. For example, if you are attacked by an enemy and you need to defend, you will need to roll a sword, but it may take several rolls to accomplish. Fortunately you can either lock dice or play on casual mode that is more relaxing, because the enemies there only attack if provoked. I have only played on standard mode so far.Overall it's a good game and you should check it out if you don't mind the RNG.I would give it a 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Dice Legacy is tough as hell but very interesting and challenging. This level of difficulty is definitely not for everyone. Those who enjoy trickily and brain-tickling strategy games should definitely take a look here.Important note: No city-builder or The SettlersBut the game has nothing at all to do with City Builder games or settlement simulations. Although it looks cutely like The Settlers or Anno on screenshots in some cases, it has almost nothing in common with those games. And whoever is looking for such cozy gameplay is completely wrong here.The controls and the basic concept with the dice are a bit confusing at the beginning. I have to say that I must have spent two or three hours at first working around rather haphazardly and needed several restarts before I had halfway understood the basic principles of the game.Another very positive thing to mention is that the game did not crash once during the entire testing period. And apart from a small inconsistency with the military academy, I didn’t notice a single real bug. So here, great care was taken before the release to bring a really finished game to the market, very commendable.The content of the game is not particularly extensive. So there is only one type of card, which you can then just play more often with different starting requirements and different rule variants. Here I would have liked more variety as well as more content. Dice Legacy builds long-term motivation rather through the level of difficulty and variations than through a larger amount of game content.Overall, as a strategy fan, you get at least 10 hours of gameplay here for less than $20 or €. If the basic principle grabs you or you want to hunt down all the achievements, it’s probably well over 30 hours. And because of the board game-like gameplay, you can play a game every now and then even months or years later without getting bored.Dice Legacy offers a very unusual game system that challenges the mind and wraps this in appealing visuals. The game comes with a price tag of $19.99 or €. For that, you get a minimum of 10 to 20 hours of gameplay, and if you really enjoy the game, you can probably play it almost endlessly.But since the game offers a really hefty difficulty level, it depends a lot on your preferences as to how you should rate it for yourself. If you don’t like big challenges and starting all over again several times is rather annoying for you, this results in a deduction of up to 5%. But if you like that a game challenges you to puzzle and you like to bite through heavy strategy titles, this can mean even up to a 5% upgrade for you.For the very original and unique board game setting, bug-free implementation with snazzy graphics, and nice sound, I would like to give Dice Legacy a base rating of 80%. And since I have nothing else to complain about, this is my final rating. And you should modify the result a bit for yourself, depending on how you classify yourself according to the above-mentioned criteria. Thus, the personal rating can then fluctuate between 75 and 85%.EN DE

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like the game, but now that I'm several hours in I could never recommend it.Dice strategy is not the issue with the RNG. Dice collection is like deck builders with extra sides on each thing — it's entirely possible to plan enough to curtail the randomness of that stuff. It's poor planning as to how RNG will affect the layouts provided.The developer's seemed to be missing a key to the idea of roguelite-strategy RNG: limitations to RNG need to exist.It's entirely possible to start an unwinnable scenario from the get-go.Let's say you pick the character that starts with citizens. They don't start with stone. There is also no stone on the available map. The chances of you managing to expand into the next zone without that stone before your wood runs out is quite slim.Additionally, the unlocks do not make the game easier. They make it harder.This might change when you ascend die, but I haven't been able to figure out what that even refers to. The same character that starts with citizens does not start with any buildings the citizens are useful in. They are actually a liability, and make it harder to make those dice effective. On top of that, the vast majority of their buildings require stone — which doesn't spawn on the map with him (or hasn't in the runs I've done, which seems unlikely to be a coincidence). So now you're starting with *LESS* die that are actively useful.It's got enough unfortunate design decisions to prevent it from feeling enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game, and exactly what I expected. I think the issue some of the negative reviewers are having is that they are not expecting the game to be an RTS colony survival game, fairly similar to They Are Billions or Frostpunk. If you go into this game expecting it to ramp up in intensity and to be "putting out fires" more and more as time goes on, then you should be satisfied. If that kind of game is not your thing, then perhaps it is not for you and that is fine too. The "fires" aren't that bad to put out once you fully understand the game and that's part of the fun. You learn to be more efficient just like every colony sim/colony survival game.EDIT: After looking at more negative reviews, there ARE ways to deal with the endless waves of enemies without freaking out (look at your tech tree omg). There ARE ways to tell which enemies will do what to your buildings (HINT: one of the types has torches, guess what they might do). Lots of the negative reviews want the game to tell them the optimal strategy to deal with everything but that defeats the point of a game like this. You are supposed to learn, adapt, and eventually succeed. These kinds of games are ruined by a guide, for the audience they are meant for anyways. I will admit, maybe they should add in an active pause difficulty BELOW normal for all the people mad that this RTS game is not optionally turn based. Honestly I pause and scroll and then unpause and click and it's a non issue. I'm not frantically clicking or anything, just hit 1 and look and then be like, "okay I need to do these 2 things after I unpause," but I have like 30 seconds to do them... _childDocuments_.review: I love survival city builders and I'm an avid board gamer, so you'd think Dice Legacy would be a perfect match, but even at a steep discount, I can't recommend Dice Legacy.The concept is definitely interesting. I could see this as a great physical board game. However, the pure RNG nature of the dice makes it difficult to plan or recover. Dice have a "durability" that decreases with each roll, and if you employ them at 0 durability, you lose them. Alternatively, you can send them to the cookhouse to eat and recover their durability. If a die doesn't have the face you want or need, you have to keep rolling. I found myself often rolling multiple times in an attempt to get what I needed, but ended up just draining the durability of my dice. In the best dice-rolling board games, there's some way to mitigate the randomness of a roll, but Dice Legacy lacks any way to alleviate a bad roll. At least at the start; there's a broad tech tree and there appear to be some roguelite systems to permanently improve dice between plays, but I'm not really interested in suffering to get to that point.The game is also extremely tedious, with lots of clicking to move dice around and place resources. The first time I placed a die in the cookhouse to restore its durability, I was confused because nothing happened. It turns out I have to click the "food" resource and click on the cookhouse to supply it with food. (I'm not sure why that couldn't have just happened when I dropped the die.)On a positive note, the graphics are lovely and the soundtrack is pleasant. The controls are easy enough to understand even though the interface can be a bit cryptic at times (there's not really any tutorial). There looks to be a good amount of depth as well, for those who want to suffer through the initial hours.

Obvious problems:1. You need to put certain dice to each building, but the buildings in front hide what dice go in the building behind, and all the buildings look the same! It's a resource gathering game, but takes ridiculously long to get almost no resources.4. It's a city builder but you don't get to build anything because you don't have resources, and once you build something, it's kind of like meh....You know it's bad when the only way to win the game is by not playing it how it was designed. I bet the meta is, just make a bunch of farms, huts, and heaters....forever. There is no payoff for anything else.

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely feel that most of the negative reviews for this game are people reeeeeeeally nitpicking.  Is it perfect? Of course not.  Did it succeed in attempting what is essentially a new game genre? Abso-frikkin-lutely.  I'll also wager that many of the negative reviews are from gamers who are used to having their hands held and can't stand having to figure things out on their own.  This is a game of HEAVY strategy, RNG, and more strategy.  If you can't handle it, as we say in my homeland "Take off, you hoser!"  I guess this game is for big boys.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is properly difficult. Don't think for a second that this is just another casual city-sim game... this game is like Frostpunk (in that it's a very punishing and difficult city-sim). If you didn't like Frostpunk or don't like difficult games, then you'll most likely want to avoid this game.Pros: #1. Very fast load times (from main menu, it takes just 7seconds to load into the game)#2. It's a pretty game (obviously, it runs on the unreal engine)#3. It's undeniably unique. I've played every city-sim under the sun, and yet never played one like this. It's quite smart, the way the dice are used for building/gathering/fighting.Cons: #1. There's only 1 'main scenario' (can be completed in less than 3hrs) and then 6 other WAY more difficult versions of that same 'main scenario' (it's literally just modifiers added to the 'main scenario'). So I just really wish that there was more content than this one 'main scenario'. Paying $20 for one 'main scenario' that can be completed in 3hrs is a little steep#2. Can't change your resolution when on 'Borderless Fullscreen'#3. Can't zoom in OR out (which is highly unusual for a city-sim game)#4. The tutorial could be better#5. You can't easily see how many of each dice type you have#6. The game un-pauses itself if you do certain stuff, like look at the help menu, which is irritating.#7. There's no confirmation box when selecting a policy... because of this, one more than one occasion, I've accidentally clicked a policy which I didn't want.Overall, it's a very good (albeit very difficult) city-sim, and fans of city-sim games will love it. If they add more than just the one 'main scenario' to the game eventually, then this game will be a 10/10 city-sim imo. Recommended.Here's 3 hours of raw gameplay: My wishlisted games if you wanna be a bro: For more reviews, visit my curator page:

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a fantastic vibe.  It is beautiful to look at, the ambiance is chill, and the music is very peaceful.  I also really enjoyed the "ring world" mechanic that simplifies controls greatly.  Unfortunately, one of the core mechanics of the game is either very broken or just a bad idea.  The main problem is the dice mechanic itself.  It turns the game into an RNG machine rather than an actual strategy game.  To make matters worse, dice become exhausted so you can easily find yourself in a situation where you lose a good number of dice AND a building because you have no defenders and you reroll a bunch of times, thus exhausting your dice.  This is a game in which you are just not in control.  Worst of all is that I don't think they can "fix it" because the dice and how they behave are a core aspect of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Watch my 9 minute review here (or read below at your own pace): I own a decent board game collection, so when I learned of Dice Legacy, what’s advertised as a roguelike survival city builder with a board game-style twist, I jumped at the chance to check it out.  And when I played, it had me rolling dice faster than an addict at a craps table.  But, I struggle to see how there are any roguelike or lite elements, outside of randomly generated maps, which are common in city builders, and one other exception that I’ll talk about below.Gameplay-You’re given 5 dice at the start of each scenario.  Once you’ve played the tutorial scenario, you’ll unlock all the others, some of which are brutally challenging, as well as unlocking some new leaders with different benefits and play styles that you’ll have to lean into.  Choosing another scenario will spawn you onto a map which looks exactly the same as before, which is kind of a bummer.There isn’t a lot of geographical variety and there really are not new points of interest after the first scenario or two.  Where the variety lies though, is in your colorful dice.  And these are not your typical Yahtzee dice.  They are six-sided, but each side represents a different action that that dice can perform at certain locations on the map, and there are also different dice classes, such as the orange peasants, green citizens, blue soldiers, and so on.  There are several factors you need to keep up with in order to keep your dice happy and healthy.  They do have stamina, which depletes with every roll, so it’s more efficient to use every die on every roll.  However, each action on the map takes time, and you don’t want to wait for those actions to finish, or perhaps you have a more pressing matter, like incoming enemies, which require you to reroll a few times and will quickly deplete your stamina if you’re not paying close attention.  The User Interface is well-designed, and by using a few hotkeys on the keyboard, you can quickly select all dice of the same action, or lock certain dice to prevent them from being rolled until you unlock them or use them.  One part of the interface which is a bit annoying is that when you hover your mouse or cursor over the “roll dice” button next to your dice, helper text pops up and blocks your view of the first couple dice, meaning that if you’re rerolling and looking for something in particular, you need to keep moving your cursor back and forth.  The text just needs to be pushed off the the other side of the cursor, or have an option in the menu to disable helper text for experienced players.  Another crucial piece of the game that is missing is rebindable keys, which to me are essential in a city builder.  In fact, outside of the game’s encyclopedia, where you can read about different actions and effects, there is not a concise place, like a controls panel, where you can view all of the keyboard commands.  In a game which uses almost half of the keyboard for hotkeys, I think you need to have rebindable keys, and at minimum a tab in the settings showing what all the controls are.  Survival-I’m not going to do a deep dive into the different buildings and their uses, although a few of them are key to the game so I’ll mention them briefly as we go.  In each scenario, you’ll have environmental factors like the changing of the seasons, which by the way, looks really cool visually.  Oh, did I mention this world which you’re trying to survive and thrive on is some sort of doomed terrestrial hamster wheel floating in space?  The intergalactic scenery is gorgeous, but it’s no wonder the winters are so chilly out here.  In the winter, your dice can freeze and will need ale to warm their chilled bones.There are also several factions of mysterious enemies which will invade your camp with torches, pitchforks, and plague which will spread if you don’t eradicate it quickly.  Of course, you can meet these mercenaries on their way to your buildings, and strike them down if you have the firepower, but sometimes your dice will be damaged in the process, and they need to be healed or you risk losing them in another battle.  These battle sequences, although very brief, are pretty funny since your dice seemingly open up like trojan horses, and your true soldiers emerge for the fight.  There are fires which can be set to your buildings too, and the longer they burn, the more difficult they are to put out, and sometimes, they are even set by unruly factions within your own classes.  With each new season comes new laws proposed by the council, of which you, as the leader, must choose one to enact.  Each law benefits a different faction, and while uplifting the peasants might make them more resourceful, ignoring them or eliminating too many of their dice will cause unrest, at which point they will begin setting fire to your own buildings.  Each class has similar triggers which will help you prosper or accelerate your demise.  You can also strengthen your dice through buildings like the enhancement chamber, which allows you to upgrade one random face of your die, and the forge where you can sacrifice two different dice to form a disgusting hybrid that will actually enrage both participating classes.  And both of these things will begin to be necessary, since your objectives and enemies later in the game will require strengths and values of your dice that are simply unattainable in their base form.That One Roguelite Element-There is a building which you can unlock later in the tech tree called the Obelisk, which allows you to “ascend” a die of your choice.  In subsequent scenarios, you can choose to replace a starting die with your ascended die, giving you an early advantage as you begin another round.  However, and this is not made clear before you use it, choosing to use an ascended die in a new scenario is a one-time thing.  It will be gone for good unless you manage to ascend it again in your current play.  Roguelikes and lites all tend to have this theme of progressing through randomized dungeons and chambers, finding different enemies of increasing difficulty and chance encounters, and Dice Legacy does not.  While the fog on the map does limit your view of upcoming resources and threats, I never got that feeling of dread or urgency as I progressed further up the wheel.In my opinion, a randomly generated map, and one resource which you can choose to carry over to another scenario, do not constitute a roguelike game.  Even though I’ve spent a couple hours considering the definition, I would be curious to hear from the development team what rogue elements there are in the game that I might be missing.  I could just be dense.  However, even if Dice Legacy isn’t roguelike, it’s still very challenging, and while it eases you into learning all the mechanics, I spent several hours each in a couple different scenarios and always felt like I was fighting from behind, struggling to keep up with incoming enemies and the needs and demands of my citizens.TL;DR-I’ve had a really fun time with Dice Legacy, even though it is missing a true roguelike feel, and I hope that I’ve helped you hone in on what the game is and what it isn’t.  It is a unique take on the city builder genre, with it’s rotating ring world and randomized actions via dice, which require a surprising amount of food and healthcare.  But it’s not really a roguelike, outside of the mechanic of ascended dice that you can only use on one future run.  I can’t really say that the missing rogue elements detracted from my experience, because after I publish this, I’m going to jump back in for a new scenario.

_childDocuments_.review: Changed my review from positive to negative.After completing one round of the game successfully, I have to say I'm very disappointed. The depth that originally presents itself wears thin very quickly. It turns into a repetitive slog by the midgame and I found myself just wanting it to be over. Soldier dice aren't even necessary for the first 3/4 of the game so if you get one, two faces of the dice will be completely useless. Same with the entire military tree, sans maybe the Tower. Once you get to the main enemies at the end, things get a little interesting, but guess what? I ran out of iron. The Catapult is NOT worth using. It consumes iron insanely fast and will burn through your entire maps reserves before you even notice. Once that's gone, you have to exclusively use mercenaries, which you need gold for. This is an ok alternative, but definitely hampers your ability to do much else. I was fortunate to have cleared most of the map by the time I ran out, but on a harder difficulty I'd imagine this would've lost me the game on accident.Really, the problem is none of the stuff you get by the mid-game even matters. Monks are almost totally useless because I get massive amounts of herbs and don't need a special dice roll to heal my units. The repair all is pretty nice but not worth holding monk dice for. I had ungodly amounts of food, so my herbs could exclusively go to repairing. If you save one tree, you have infinite herbs, too. Trading with the encampments is a waste of resources. They provided nothing of note. The only useful mid-game dice is the trader because it can get you gold.Upgrading dice is useless on many dice faces. Gears, build, trading, prayer, and books are useless beyond 3. The only ones that ARE useful are harvest, combat, burn, and survey. More useless than useful. Don't get me started on the laboratory. Consuming 6 dice, one at a time, is painfully tedious and takes forever, all just to get one perfect dice in the late game. You're already dumping SIX dice for this one perfect dice. Why would you make it MORE constricting? It makes no sense. I guess for Ascension dice, but there's no way I'm playing another round of this game.I love Settlers of Catan. It's my absolute favorite board game. I was hoping for some inspiration from that and this fell flat entirely. It could've been a great concept, but the execution is really bad once the gimmick wears off.OH and my fingers got SOOOO cramped playing this because I had to keep my pink finger on shift and left ring finger on 1 as they're the most used hotkeys in the worst places.PRO TIP: Use the pause function liberally to turn this into a turn-based game and maximize your dice usage. I am constantly pausing, seeing where my timers are at, and unpausing. This way I can hold 30+ dice without risking losing them because I can't keep up with putting them back to work.PRO TIP 2: Enemies will path around your towers, so don't think they're too stupid to do that. One max range tower in the center will not protect you.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like being attacked every 20 seconds while frantically going up and down the map, putting your dice in cookhouses, apothecaries, and empowering your dice this game is for you. If you can't keep up putting your dice in the right spot within 5 seconds while constantly being attacked, this game is for you! If you like your population to start burning your buildings because you can't keep up with all above mentioned issues, guess what, you'll love getting stressed out playing this game!Totally unbalanced especially for normal difficulty and first tutorial mission.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR (Original Review):An incredibly unique game. Imagine if you were playing Catan, but it is more of a base builder/survival RPG. The dice are your units that can be upgraded and converted to different classes. Each class specialized in certain tasks. It sounds a bit out there but it is a very fun experience. At a certain point, you can start fusing and upgrading dice to make very unique combinations. The art and music are beautiful and provide great atmosphere. One note, you may want to go into settings and limit the FPS. Mine was set to unlimited by default and made my GPU throw out frames like crazy. Don't want to be burning out your GPU.5/5 dice.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Extended Review With More Details:Now that I have played many hours and read other reviews, I wanted to provide a more in-depth review. I feel this games only real flaw is that it may have been advertised as one kind of game but did not live up to some expectations. If you read negative reviews you get the idea of what the few complaints are. Really, this game just seems to suffer from people's lack of expectations being met. I recommend watching a few game-play videos to see if it is what you are looking for and I have highlighted a few points below to assist.PROS:- A blend of mechanics from many genres: You either love the uniqueness or you hate it doesn't fit in a neat little box. Personally, I find that the game-play is great. This is definitely NOT a cookie cutter game.- Pretty to look at: The visuals do a great job of immersing you in the world. The Ring-World is the right amount of pretty and concerning.- Great sound: The music sets the tone without being a distraction. Audio queues let you know when certain events happen.- Encourages experimentation: The opening scene literally tells you to "experiment". There are 5 classes, but the merge mechanics allows you to make custom dice. If the idea of combining a soldier die with a priest die to create a super cleric die sounds fun to you, give the game a try.- Good Tutorial: The tutorial was just the right amount of hand-holding for me. It told me what I should probably do next and introduces mechanics one at time to get you used to them. After that though, this game is really about figuring things out as you go.Common Complaints:- Not Enough Dice: I disagree. This complaint probably comes from not using the mentioned merge mechanics. So 1, you are missing out on one of the coolest features and 2, you will probably have to upgrade/merge your dice to be successful. For example, it takes 3 books to do research. At the beginning, this will take 3 citizen dice. Yes, that is 1/4 of your population. However, if you upgrade your citizens, you can get to where you only need 1 die to do research. You can merge dice together so your soldiers can also research so they can do something useful when not fighting. Also, 12 is the soft-cap. You can actually have more than that as long as they don't end up in the pool at the same time. I don't recommend it on your first play through but I can see strategies overloading the population.- No custom keybindings: I disagree this is a problem, but your mileage may vary. If you have to remap every key in a game, then maybe wait for the keybindings update.- No pause on harder difficulties: I disagree and feel like it is self-explanatory. The first 3 difficulties allow pausing, including the default. I found that once I had a good idea of what I was doing, I didn't need pause anymore.- Repetitive / Replay: I will give this one half-a-point because you may finally finish a game and feel like "ok, do it again, but harder". That works for me, obviously not for some.- It is an "RTS": I can see how someone might assume that a dice game is turned based. But this has more of an RTS feel. There is pausing for the easier half of difficulties but if you expect that you will be sitting there meticulously planning your next move, this might not be the game for you.- It is not a "Roguelike": I disagree. No save scumming, random maps, custom die can be carried to the next game. Maybe not your ideal example of a roguelike, but it definitely uses a lot of the ideas establish in the genre.- No voice over: I disagree. Yes, I have seen this complaint a few times. Personally, voice acting needs to be perfect or not at all. I feel like the game communicates the information you need to know with colors, symbols, and sounds just fine. Why bog it down with someone talking at you?I just feel like any new and interesting game that comes out gets shot down before it has a chance while I am really not interested in another Overwatch clone. If that is what you like, then great! go play. But leave my little dice adventure alone</rant>
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lites are funCity Builders are also funDice games are meh depending on implementationThis game is a mutated child of all three... not in a good way in my opinion. The dice represent your workforce which is random hence the dice roll. But the side they land on is the type of task they can fulfill. So if you need a sword die to defend from random attacks but RNG is ♥♥♥♥... well you're screwed. If you need to operate a building to make food but can't, then you keep running down the durability of the die. Oh yeah your "dice" can die if their durability gets too low. Which of course keeping the durability up requires... you guessed it... food. So it's a vicious cycle which was tedious and unnecessary in my opinion. Also if your "dice/people" start dying off from low durability the remaining dice become unhappy because their townsfolk are dying.Personally this game is like a domino effect of good or bad at any given time. I didn't find it fun, when a game is too heavily reliant on RNG it ruins it in my opinion. Which makes me wonder is this game fun? Or is the possibility of getting good RNG the real "fun"?When the fun factor is mostly based on good RNG then to me that says the game itself isn't actually good, just has the potential to be good. For $20, I barely "had fun" for an hour before I lost interest. There are just too many little weird mechanics that suck the fun out of what I feel this game could have been. Some people may enjoy it, but I felt it was too much in certain areas and too little in others. Also who combines rogue lites and city builders... Never would I have guessed that would make a good game, based off this game I would say I was right.

_childDocuments_.review: Real time dice-rolling is just a bad core mechanic. If it were a simple engine builder, maybe the chaos of managing dice would be okay, but the first scenario devolved into constant warfare, meaning I had to continually throw soldiers into the mix, who get wounded, who have to heal, which takes herbs you don't have because they're an immensely scarce resource.
