_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr appealing to strategy board game players, but unfortunately balanced around RTS players. A lot of fun on the default difficulty for a run or two if you perma-pause, but is wildly imbalanced and becomes too easy, and the only other difficulty options disable pause and forces you to throw away the fun parts of the game.EDIT: With the upcoming Memories update, will need to update this review, but very satisfied with their response and approach to adjusting the game to suit their fanbase.As a turn-based strategy board game player that's not a fan of RTS:Fun: 9/10Controls: 5/10Visuals: 9/10Sound: 7/10Story: 4/10Difficulty: 4/10 (typical standard game), 7/10 (all content on standard)Replayability: 2/10Value: 2/10Dev Response: 9/10This game has a heapload of potential and honestly I really adore it and want it to succeed. This game is a cute worker placement game that forces you to make decisions and adapt to situations.A lot of strategic depth is in the placement of your buildings; in the beginning you need to plan out how to situate your production buildings such that they can both get efficiency boosts from adjacency, while also planning out where your heat generators will be since everything out of their range will be unusable for 50% of your time in the game (or until you advance further in the tech tree). These early decisions are critical because resources are extremely scarce at the start, and every bit of efficiency you can eke out is important.The resources you balance are literal resources, such as wood, stone, iron, and herbs, in addition to time and dice durability. Every time you place a worker, it takes a certain amount of seconds to complete its job to generate more resource. After usage, a die needs to be rerolled in order to be placed again. Each roll of a die consumes a durability point of the max 16. A die can only be placed on a tile if it matches the tile's requirement, for instance a forest tile requires a "gather" die face. In addition to rerolling after usage, you will often have to decide whether to save a die for later, wasting time not using it, or rerolling it repeatedly right away at the cost of durability to get the face you need right now.Dice also have colors, or classes, and while most classes share some default faces, each class has a unique face too, so you'll need to branch out if you want to adapt to the map you're given and optimize resource usage.Interesting decisions:- Tile placement- Class distribution- Upgrading for late game- Technology tree specializationHowever, the one critical flaw; at higher difficulties you cannot pause. Everything I said above is assuming that you pause the game every time you need to think about a decision. Without the ability to pause, strategy gets thrown out the window, and the game's design instead rewards APM and reflexes, completely avoiding the parts of the game that are most interesting and appealing, and focused instead on how many foolish mistakes you make because you're pressed for time.To add insult to injury, as dice return to your pool as they complete tasks, if they ever exceed the max pool size of 12, you have to choose which will perish. And to throw salt on that wound, the class of dice won't be happy about that, so the game just attempts to punish you for playing the most interesting and strategic way.The game's controls aren't centered around pausing, so most actions can only be taken while unpaused. Because of this, you have to awkwardly pause and unpause almost every second. You also feel guilty for not playing the game how it was designed, but dang is it fun.At least for awhile. While the game is challenging at first, it quickly becomes trivially easy as the game doesn't expect you to have the almost infinite APM you get from pausing, and the end of the game is almost the same difficulty as the beginning, except now you have a lot more resources at your disposal to win.The end of each game is also anticlimactic, as you just throw out all the strategy and class structure you had in the beginning to just get as many sword symbols as you can to end the game.I've played the game for more than 13 hours these last two days but I'm running out of content because the game isn't designed for this mode of gameplay that I find extremely fun.EDIT: After playing for 40 hours, I've cleared all content in the game, including some interesting secret content that hadn't been discovered at the initial time of writing. Was very very cool to figure it out for myself, but soon there will be guides for it everywhere. At this point I'm done with the game, as while it was fun to clear the content, it still felt anticlimactic and did not add any replay value to the game.If I could adjust the design direction of the game, I would recommend a separate turn-based strategy mode that brings out the best and most fun parts of strategic worker placement games, since I have zero interest in the RTS approach. Specifically:- automatically pause whenever dice return to your pool- don't restrict the actions you can take while paused- don't limit the amount of dice you can have in your active pool; perhaps use some other system to limit population cap per class, such as housing or unemployment unhappiness, since you can always just throw dice that you don't want to use into unused buildings anywayThere's also a lot of potential for meta-game advancement other than ascended dice, for instance a meta-game unlock tree that unlocks portions of the in-game tech tree, or increases starting dice, or increases max numbers on ascended dice, while also providing levels of appropriately scaling difficulty and complexity. The new first level could be extremely simple and beatable with 3 peasant swords in minutes without needing any other class, easing you in and letting you feel wonder as you unlock access to civilian dice and tech tree for the first time, while later on the maps would become incredibly challenging as it scales to expect you to have beefy ascended dice.Overall I love the game but can't recommend it in its present state. Due to its lack of replayability (for someone like me anyway) and lack of meta-game progression systems, while polished, I can't say it justifies it's $20 price tag.EDIT: After figuring out the secret content and clearing it and dropping 40 hours into the game, at this point I might say it was worth the $20 if the struggle to clear it was a bit less frustrating. I think most of the fun was in feeling like I was one of the first to figure everything out and clear it, but once there are guides out I expect that the experience would be more frustrating than fun, and I probably would've preferred to just watch a video of someone else clearing it just to see what would happen. 40 hour game for $20 is a bit more palatable though, but I probably still won't recommend it as it still leaves me wanting.If a game designer makes these changes and additions though, I think the game could really be truly amazing, and much more fun, charming, and strategically deep than similar survival city builders.
_childDocuments_.name: Dice Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: A city builder, survival, resource management game has many ways of implementing feedback loops. Cities skylines stagnates the player when the city has problems, waiting the player to improve before advancing the game. Other games outright lead to a lose state, demanding a restart. _childDocuments_.review: Inspired by other city-building games but bringing its own VERY UNIQUE AND ORIGINAL gameplay formula, Dice Legacy, is the perfect game for those who love strategy games, roguelike features, city-building/survival games, and want a game that delivers compelling and authentic gameplay experience—alongside high replay value.My full video review of Dice Legacy:If you love games like Dicey Dungeon, SimCity, Frostpunk, Darkest Dungeon, Timberborn, Civilization, Anno - you'll likely enjoy playing this game.The game feels very original and unique and you feel it immediately when you start playing it. The game relies on RNG using dice-rolls using various dice classes, each one with different (some unique) action facets that can be used with it.The game is designed around resource-gathering and managing your settlement by defending it and trying to expand it, with the goal to destroy the Harbor at the end of the map.The maps are procedurally generated so each playthrough (especially after you unlock different rulers and other campaign playthroughs), feels unique and fresh.The game is VERY CHALLENGING. Especially once you start ramping up the difficulty. You can choose the easiest one if you are a beginner, so enemies won't attack you unless being provoked.What I really like about this game is that it reminded me of the fun of playing Civilization 5. The focus of the game is with much fewer development and progression options, made for much shorter gameplay sessions and it's much less expansive than a civ game. But that's the cool thing about it, less micro-management and something that feels like a board game, not an open-world game.If you are among those who can't really put too many hours on a single playthrough in a game and want to be able to start and finish a playthrough in a relatively shorter time (it sometimes, depends on the difficulty, can be several hours though), this game is for you.Even with a limited amount of options, the game is challenging and super fun. You can approach finish it the way you like and not be forced to any particular playstyle and choices.The game has much more than I can cover in the review. Make sure you turn on the tutorial (or it's active) so you learn all the mechanics as you play. I made a guide on my channel, you might want to check it out as well.The music, sound effect, and visuals are marvelous, and the UI is designed very well to support the unique gameplay mechanics and map browsing style. I haven't encountered any bugs or game-breaking issues whatsoever and it also seems to be balanced very well.what I didn't like: Red numbers on the cube for low durability is hard to read.Overall, my time with the game so far was incredibly fun. Overall, highly recommended - the game is worth your time and money!P.S.On a side note: PvP 1-vs-1 multiplayer could have been amazing but the game doesn't feature any multiplayer game mode. I also wanted to have more of a dice-roll feeling animation, I just like that but that's nothing to be concerned about, just a personal preference (maybe an option for it in the future in the settings).

_childDocuments_.review: An ambitious, if not flawed, genre mashup. This is a downvote that makes me sad because there is a ton of potential here, I just think they tried to do too much at once. There are only two levels in the base game. I heard the DLC adds another, but I do not plan to purchase that. I completed the first level while only tapping into a portion of what the game offers – I only used three of the five dice classes to win and only a handful of available buildings. I was excited to dive in more, but after seeing that the game expected me to play the same level repeatedly in a different way, I wasn’t excited about it, and this is coming from someone who loves roguelike games and has played many of them. What would have been better, I think, is to offer mechanics slowly to the player over time, perhaps adding new dice classes and buildings over a short campaign. I love what they have tried to do here, and I hope to see more of it in the future, but I think there are many things to learn from Dice Legacy. The game gives you just about everything up front. You have access to all the buildings and dice classes straight away, and you only have to build them. There really are no unlocks or a sense of progression that you get in other games from the genre. There are different leaders, but they only start with different dice load-outs that you can get as any leader after spending a short time in the game. The result is that you sort of feel like you have everything available already, so after running through it one time, there is not much reason to return. I will say that the initial run was quite interesting, but it was only a few hours of gameplay.Then there are the dice themselves, which by their very nature are random in their result. As you roll them, they get less and less durable, eventually breaking altogether if not rectified. This is a bittersweet mechanic because it adds both tension and frustration. Unfortunately, I felt as if there were too many occasions in which I was searching for specific faces, therefore rolling constantly, and my dice were becoming damaged quickly as a result. Those faces you end up not needing just have no use, particularly in the early phases of the game. What would be better here is to find a way to offer more player choice for those times when faces may not turn up well. The only solution need not be to simply roll again and again. I applaud the developer for trying something different here. Still, I can’t recommend it unless on a deep sale and with a caveat that unless you are particularly tenacious, you may only play this for a few hours.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a cute experiment if you can catch it on sale. It's like The Settlers games but with dice.Graphics and music are beautiful.That said, at full price is a bit risky because the game takes all the player agency of a regular base-builder and swaps it with RNG, so you may not enjoy that too much.Because of this factor, there's less depth compared to other games in the genre and there's an unnecessary frustration factor that comes inherently with any RNG mechanic.On top of that, resource management also feels untuned compared to a classic base-builder since you do need resources to build stuff (each time you gather a resource is a dice roll by the way) but you don't really "consume" any of them outside of that therefore you can just wait the winter out without using any wood or food as long as you have a few soldier dice ready. And thus, winter just becomes a "fast-forward" period where you just wait.Also, exploration can be a bit linear since you can only advance forward in a narrow lane.All in all, if you want to try out something new, I'd say it's interesting and fun to a degree if you're looking to experiment with the genre a bit. I have respect for the devs for trying to bring something different to the genre and I think the game has nothing but the best intentions behind it. If you adjust your expectations you'll find an entertaining game in Dice Legacy.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, intuitive design. I think this is a good game, but just not for me.The game gets exhausting after a while. The dice system is interesting and unique, but forces an extra layer of micro management over the game that proves taxing, especially as your settlement grows.In a more typical management sim or 4X game, you have units that you put to a task. That task is automated until something of note happens to derail its continuation. In this game, you have to roll the appropriate dice to do the appropriate task and then, a minute or so later, roll to get the same dice to do the same thing again. You end up managing your dice, their different classes, and redeploying works to that mine over there over and over ad nauseam.But, it's something that I'll probably keep plugging away at every now and then, but it just doesn't keep me for very long because I get to a point where I'm like "ok I could expand but why, it just means more work."But if the above doesn't daunt you, well, then maybe this bud is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite enjoyable game with nice aesthetics. Here are some of the most annoying things for me:- Attack notifications... or lack of them. You get some too unremarkable sound when attack starts (which is also used for events and Enhancement Chamber finishing job), some red dot on the right edge of the screen and... thats it. No notification of your building being attacked, destroyed, etc. All buildings that I lost in this game was caused by the fact that I didn't notice the attack! (and there were way to many such situations) Adding more sound notifications and showing attack timer in visible place on the screen would help.- Game is not adapted for widescreen monitors. So option to zoom out or changing FOV would be nice.- Resources - there are ways to generate some of them indefinitely, but others are finite: wood, stone and iron, and I don't know if it's me, but I always run out of stone first (while having 200+ wood). _childDocuments_.review: This game is deceptively simple. It's pretty straightforward on what you need to do, but the challenge comes in how hectic it can get.I see reviews mention the 12 dice maximum, but that's both true and false. You can have 12 IDLE dice maximum. If you place your dice ahead of time, you can have a lot more than 12. This leads to a lot of resource management with your dice themselves. Of course this will be very hard to manage without pausing (which is one of the settings), but that's kind of the point: to set your own difficulty. For your first game at least I'd definitely say to just use the default settings. After you beat your the main scenario, you'll get more options to play: modifiers to collect, variations of the scenario, a new scenario, and new rulers to play as. I haven't delved into it that much, but there does seem to be quite a bit of replayability.Current gripes gameplay-wise: There's no way to know what dice faces are used at a building in-game until you place them. UI and default controls are a little confusing at first. Yes/no are opposite of what you'd expect. Space is to roll rather than pause (although that may be a specifically personal expectation). Small issues though once you get a bit into the game.I would definitely recommend picking this game up if it's on sale (which it is until Nov. 3rd, 2022). Otherwise, up to personal preference if $20 USD is worth it you.

_childDocuments_.review: If I'm going to recommend this game to anyone, it's on the premise of good graphics that can run decently on a mid-range computerIt's a survival game, no problems... it's dice-based, no problems... resources are limited and RNG-based, maybe not so great for beginners... limited labour pool relative to the scenario size/length, maybe not so fun... RNG stacked against the player, might cause some frustration waiting for proper rolls...As a game however, I recommend players who are relative beginners to survival games, to try elsewhere first simply because this game really does limit the player even from the starting block... this game is more like playing Craps with slightly loaded dice at a casino, but without money involved.It's not like the hardest game in the world to get your teeth into, but the choices players can make to just get started are very, very limited in many ways - this means players may end up starting and retiring from games within 5 minute just to ensure a usual starting position (and that's assuming the dice RNG isn't heavily unfavorable to the player)... luckily this isn't an online multiplayer game, so no need to fret about restarting your game often just to find one usual game, just be prepared for that situation...Hint; if you haven't got the basic steam generator placed & built by the time winter comes along, the number of actions you can perform will go down drastically for the winter period (roughly 10 mins of play), which can snowball into making summer into such a mess that restarting from scratch is the better option

_childDocuments_.review: Very intriguing gameplay and esthetically pleasing. The dice manipulation makes the medieval/steampunk themed city building quite fun and ads a layer of complexity to the genre. It has rogue-like elements and you can replay the game with different challenges, objectives and even different rules (ex: the cost of everything being randomized). You can play around with different builds and experiment to create different dice and different gameplay conditions (memories). In this game dice are people… I think. They have roles: peasants, educated citizens, priests, merchants and soldiers; you assign them to temporary jobs; you feed them; you treat them for disease; you send them to the tavern to treat them of the cold (as you would); you kick people out into the void when you run out of UI space and you merge 2 or 6 people together to make a new and better person, just like in real life. But I am a bit iffy on the last two. So maybe dice are… more than people and the game is more than a "medieval" city builder. Give this game a try if you like more action based city builder games. You can make good use of your management skills and your juggling skills as you go over the maximum dice limit.

_childDocuments_.review: Greetings!  Today we’ll be reviewing “Dice Legacy” a City Builder with a toe stuck in the board gaming world.  I’ve been looking at this game for quite some time and decided to finally give it a try; as always the question remains:  Is it worth your time?  Let’s discus!You’re Just a Number:  At the core this game is like any other City Builder in that you gather resources, build structures and help your people along to a better tomorrow.  The change here is that the people aren’t people but dice or at least represented for game sake as dice.  This is a novel idea and something that has been experimented in both the board gaming and video game worlds.  These Citizen Dice have a class (determining their faces), durability (that decreases every time you roll them) and power (a force multiplier).  The 6 faces all represent jobs that the dice will occupy, be that gathering, building, combat and other roles.  The die is then allocated to a role which takes some time to complete (30 – 60 seconds on average) and upon completion will need to be rerolled (decreasing its durability).  It is an elegant system at first glance.  This is the core mechanic and unfortunately also the core issue of the game loop.I’m Just Rolling:  For the first hour or so it is an incredibly ingenious and fun mechanic but… after that not so much.  What originally felt as something new and interesting on the City Building Genre quickly became tedious; gone was the satisfaction of slowly seeing your city link together and begin the process of self sufficiency and replaced was this never ending need to roll, reroll and allocate dice.  The mechanic just isn’t fun and it is such a core concept to the game that it brings the entire game to a halt; similar to the winter mechanic.My Dice are Cold Today:  They say winter is coming but it felt like less of a rush for survival and more of a slog of boredom.  Many winters I could just sit there and do nothing; nothing happened if I didn’t do anything and many times I was left with several minutes of gameplay with nothing to do other than wait for Spring to thaw my dice.  During the cold months there is a chance every time you use a die that it will freeze, being unusable until thawed (either through spring or a building) but there was no urgency to thaw this die.  There are also furnaces you can build to thaw out areas but unlike other city builders this is yet another building you have to micro manage but can be easily ignored.  In the end I’m just not sure that dice have a place in video gaming (outside of the replication of board games) as it is much easier to represent randomness behind the curtain.  I say that as a huge table top and board gamer.  This game has a very interesting core concept in the dice but ends of feeling more like as solution in search of a problem.  Dice Legacy has odd swings of hectic rolling and period of boredom where you are just waiting for winter to end.   With that I can’t say that I’d recommend this over the many better city builders.  I can’t even suggest waiting as the mechanic is a core feature of the game and just isn’t for me; maybe you disagree?  Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Different, fun, good under $20, takes a few full games to get used to game flow, wish it was turn based instead of RTS but RT-pause helps, correct uses of die and dice.Really it's the price that allows me to recommend the game, anything more than $20 and I feel most of the issues I take with the game would bother me more.All and all the game is good, feels very much a standard worker placement board game in the vein of Stefan Feld (See Castles of Burgundy).  Your dice face determine where they can be placed and what action they perform and there are different classes (colors) of dice that have different types of faces for different actions.  Obviously more complex than a traditional board game and in real time rather than turn based. The rogue aspect being in a game you have buildings that can combine dice to make new ones and others that increase face values with the idea that you will "ascend" a die that can be used in other games.  So your first few games is working towards creating better dice to take with you for harder challenges and difficultly levels.The real time aspect is where I struggle and almost feel like the game would be much more strategic if it were turn based.  Early game is not a problem, it's about mid game as you explore more of the map have lots of buildings.  The artwork, though beautiful, makes it hard to tell what buildings are what and often buildings next to each other hide the placement areas from view. You often spend much of the time scrolling up and down the ringlike board trying to find places to put your dice and quickly so you don't lose them. Late game it becomes hectic and problematic as any RTS player can tell you being able to locate your buildings and act quickly is key. I found myself more just frantically placing dice anywhere I could instead of really thinking about what I was trying to accomplish or what needed to be done to win. That said I know that a few more times playing and with more familiarity this won't be as much as an issue.I think people who play lots of worker placement style board games will be more forgiving of it's shortcomings and give it the time it needs to be really enjoyable. Honestly I wasn't sure if I liked it after the first play, but found myself wanting to play again the next day, and the more familiar I got the less bothersome it became.

_childDocuments_.review: I think the game is good anyway, at least 7 out of 10.The graphics are juicy and nice.Narrative - balanced between what the player is given in portions and freedom for fantasy.The mechanics are what makes this game special, original, not without flaws, but generally thought out.Objective cons:Balance problems - this concerns, first of all, resources, and secondly, different social groups and their usefulness.Social groups - merchants lose all their charm due to the inability to change the resource being sold on the market. When a stone has to be sold, the market can be demolished, but you cannot build a new one, because there is no stone. The settlements of the savages are also more annoying than useful and it doesn't matter whether you are engaged in religion or trade with them.Subjective cons:My biggest disappointment is the developers' decision to make this a session strategy game. _childDocuments_.review: EDIT: 1+ Years later: So I came back to this game recently to see what changes might of been made after a year away from it.  While some of my core complaints have been dealt with, there are many that are still there.1) Resolution effect layout: I see that there is now a resolution ui scaling slider, though altering it a little didn't seem to change anything.  My largest complaint with this was that buildings icons were very large and a few categories needed to have scroll or pages (I don't remember which) when it wasn't needed if the image size scaled with the resolution.  This has been fixed and in my recent game I didn't have any category have pages or scoll bar.2) Scroll style view: this is pretty much still the same.  The changes made to the pause and speed options make this more manageable, but it is still pretty annoying late game having to scroll back and forth from where you started and your end of map objective.  The developer apparently commented on my review about this (never noticed) and their response is to use the scroll bar on the right which helps.  Honestly I think the long map is just a core part of the gameplay and even though I find it annoying late game, the pause changes and the scroll bar help mitigate the frustration some.I think that was my core complaints with the game, and so I am changing my non-recommendation to a recommendation (honestly more so if it is on sale then full price), with the caveat that there are still annoyances that users might face with the game, but if you can get past them it is an interesting implementation of the dice games that are on steam.Oh and I haven't purchased the DLC and doubt I would pay full price for it.ORIGINAL REVIEW:I feel like there are already many helpful and insightful reviews of this game telling you all the many good and bad points of this game.  So instead I want to just talk about my experiences.This is an interesting game.  It is an original blend of existing concepts that other games have.  I believe many people have pointed out how it could of blended those concepts better or differently to improve gameplay.  That being said, gameplay is okay.  Does it have issues that are annoying? Yes.  Does it have some good points? Yes.  Does the good points outweigh the annoying issues? In my opinion, they currently do not.  The interesting thing is, that might not always be the case.As of writing this, the game has only been out for 10 days.  This game could easily change over the next year to become better than it's current version.  At the moment I wouldn't recommend buying this game, but if the developers make changes and improve the issues that people have pointed out, then this game might become a great game that I could recommend other people to buy.  The current version of this game that exists feels like it could of used some constructive criticism with beta work before it went live.  Many people have pointed out how the UI feels restrictive.  I think part of that is because the UI doesn't change based on resolution.  I loaded the game up and switched between 1440 and 720 and the UI was the same at both resolutions.  So it feels like they made the UI for the smallest available resolution and then scaled it to higher resolutions without changing it rather than making the UI dynamically change and become more usable at higher resolutions.  There are design choices for the game that when playing for the first 5-30 minutes might not be as annoying, but when reaching the end of a level and constantly having to move from the end of the map to start and back becomes extremely frustrating. The dice limit of 12 is a gameplay choice that is not well implemented.  I actually got the popup for deleting dice during the ending movie three times when I completed the game for the first time.It is my hope, that this game receives further development from the developers in forms of free patches and UI fixes before trying to sell DLC for this game.  Hopefully within a year's time I can update this review and talk about how they fixed all the issues with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A really unique and challenging game that presents a lot of varied strategies and choices to progress as the world gets more complicated around you. This game invokes the "one more turn" aspect that I've come to lovingly appreciate anytime I see as it is not often these days.Juggling multiple different classes of dice, upgrades of dice, and amount of dice is refreshingly complex and can really blow up on you if you're playing risky and way over your capacity. Different random events have me locking and saving a number of dice to avoid having to reroll and waste durability to deal with a time sensitive issue.There's a lot going on in here wrapped up in a deceptively simple tin. Really glad to have gone out on a limb and made the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Changing the recommendation because they've fixed the UI enough to no longer be an impediment to playing. It's not a perfect UI by far and has a number of bugs but it's now quite playable.You can now scale the dice. They've changed how dice look when wounded so it's very obvious. And they have a real pause.The game itself is a fun sort of builder with the unique dice mechanic (unique for solo video games). The dice aren't really a randomizer in the sense of roll well and things become easy. The rolls are more about limiting your options for what you /can/ do so you're forced to make interesting choices based on the options available to you.--------------------The game is fun but it gets ruined by poor UI/UX.Some examples:* The power numbers on dice are too small to read.* It's hard to see if a die is wounded.* It's hard to see buildings behind other building.* It's hard to find your dice so you can tell how soon ones in use will be freed up.* The help pages are hidden till you already unlock something so there's no way to make a strategic decision about new things. Spoilers blah blah spoilers, I don't play this kind of game for story, I want to play a strategy game making decisions with full info, I don't want to play over and over just to learn the rules. * and there's more but that's the list on the top of my head.All of this is exacerbated by not having a real pause where I can assign dice and stuff during pause and I don't see how I can create saves on demand without exiting. I'm tired of having to start games over because of mistakes because the game doesn't give me enough info or the info is hard to see. The sad part is the game seems really fun otherwise. I hope they update the UI some time and then maybe I'll play again and not regret spending money on it.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the gameplay and the fact that it's original. The two layers are perfectly fine with me. Town building and then real time micromanaging via the dice puzzle that continuously regenerates and renew.For sure it's going to be hectic and busy but that's what most of real time games are, like Steel Division. And that, for some people, is fun.It's nonsense to dismiss that as "stress". People find different things stressful, others find the same things fun.Having said that, the mechanic is engaging and addicting. I dropped Frostpunk after 1 run for lack of interest, while this, thanks to the dice mechanic, is keeping my interest fresh.

_childDocuments_.review: This game overall quite good if a bit shallow. The main gripe i have with it is being forced to not pause on the intended difficulty. I am sure i can get better but the slowest speed is too fast for me to keep up, especially once you start getting into the mid and late game and you have more than the max die and you researched efficiency on your districts. Some buildings you place you dice at take seconds to complete and then you throw in constructed and laboratory dice into the mix it gets overwhelming for me. All that being said i enjoy the game at the standard difficulty where i can take my time pause the game and make decisions. So this dice game at the intended difficulty is more like an RTS and not a turn based strategy.If you want a good turn based dice game check out Circadian Dice. Its free, but is not nearly pretty as dice legacy but the mechanics are great.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, I advice to start with normal at most, peaceful might be a good first run to learn all the ropes of this game, as there is a LOT of things to take care of, especially during midgame, and it can be very easy to get overwhelmed.Taken slowly, and once you know what you are doing, the game is much less challenging, especially with the legacy system.  (you can carry over your favorite dices over future game(s))And that's when the higher difficulties come into play. Be warned that the game is designed more like a RTS than a civ-like game, so no pause at higher levels.I find the game system addictive, it flows well, even thought it might be messy at first but you will get used to how dices work together, your main risks of losing dice, etcThe game is also quite beautiful and I like it's atmosphere.I also found out that there is an ending, well hidden in the game, but you will figure it out eventually :)The credits music is pretty neat btw, and you can feel that the dev put out a lot of effort in this game, also they are quite receptives to suggestions on their discord, which is a definite plus !

_childDocuments_.review: I would give a neutral rating currently if it were available.  This game is so close to being a great procedural worker placement/city builder game.  There are too many frustrations as it scales to recommend it though.I can't find what the frantic nature (even with pause) adds to the game.  Lots of losing dice because you can't deploy them fast enough and it feels clunky deploying dice and resource later in the game.  If trying to emulate RTS, I think there need to be more hotkeys.  Lots of the frustration comes not just from the frantic nature, but the feeling that you are fumbling with the clunky click and drag of workers and resources.  I feel like hotkeys would enable players to act quickly and effectively while retaining the frantic aspect of the game.I think I would recommend this game if they find a way to address these issues even if the rest of the game remains largely the same.  It seems like an active pause (where you can place workers while paused) or an option to deploy dice to available spots when your reserve is overfull, would greatly reduce the most frustrating aspects of the game.Really cool game design idea and execution overall though!  I'm going to take a break on it and hope that they eventually provide options to address the frustrating aspects.  Looking forward to see if they build upon the initial release.  I will likely come back and update to a recommendation even without changes, because I feel this game does deserve more than its current "mixed" rating, but it is understanding why it is divisive.

_childDocuments_.review: I left my previous review at the bottom which was negative but with the Memories update I have changed my review to positive.The developers have listened to feedback from the players (in particular the pause) and that has made the game a lot more enjoyable to play. I am not sure as yet if the game would be interesting to play a 2nd time but now I am enjoying my first run through. I would still like to see more information about a lot of things on the map (log of events so that I can go back and check what happened instead of them flashing by in a very quick way, check my dice when they are at a location without having to take them away. More info on buildings and what exactly is happening when I get them. Feels like I have to play the game once to get to know a lot of stuff that I think should be information available to the player at the beginning of the game if he is interested.Previous review at launch :I loved the idea of this game and it looked great for about 20 minutes. This has the potential to be a great game but unfortunately it very quickly got boring and tedious to play. Concept is great but the implementation is just awful (you should be able to manipulate dice when on pause, need a lot more information available about various things happening in the game). _childDocuments_.review: Revised review after further playing the game.Okay, so this game is unique and I enjoyed much of the gameplay. Dice, city builder, exploration, management. All my favorite elements combined into 1 game. Plus, the graphics are beautiful. There are a few things that might hinder the gameplay. However, overall to what the game is offering, I think they are tolerable. All my remarks are from playing the game on Easy & Normal difficulty. Overall GameplayThe purpose of the gameplay is to build your city and expand using dice until you meet the enemy, which is another city. So game play revolves around dice, each dice represents a person in your city. Maxed by 12 dice. However, 12 dice feels like a small number as you move on, Especially since there are 5 types of dice each representing a different class of citizens. (or perhaps I am way under developing my dice). There are 5 different classes of die. Peasant, Citizen, Soldier, Monk. Merchant. Some categories of dice might not be as useful to have as others, especially when you have to give a spot of your 12 slots for it. However, that all depends on how you want to play. There is a wide selection of difficulties and scenarios to pick from, which might ensure at least 50-70 hours of gameplay. (took me around 20 hours just to play 2 scenarios). For the current price, I think it is a good deal. Secondly, game play is time based. Meaning, for some reason I am unable to pause then make my decisions and decide where each die go. Interactions with my dice are locked when I pause, which is weird for this type of game. Perhaps the developer did not want us to take our time and do everything with pressure of putting fires left and right. I feel like the inability to pause and act changes the game from a strategy game into a click fest. Winter/Summer	There are seasons in this game, winter & summer. Like how old human civilizations, you prepare yourself in the summer in the upcoming winter. The arrival of winter hinders your ability to collect resources and even your dice due to the chance of having your die getting a frostbite that freezes them out of gameplay unless you wait for the arrival of summer or curing the freeze through other means. The cycle of seasons in the game is extremely well done, and due to having a few methods of dealing with it, doesn’t feel frustrating at all. TechnologiesThe game has a wide variety of technology trees for you to pick and improve your city/dice. You probably can’t upgrade everything in normal gameplay, due to how slow it could be to acquire technology points. so picking a certain path of upgrades is important.  in which you probably won’t be able to fully complete. RNG	Games with heavy RNG elements could be the most frustrating and fun games. But be ready to be more frustrated than anything else, that's just how the lady of luck works. You will reroll your dice dozens of times to reach a certain face. However frustrating that is, it is still very normal for a dice game. You can develop these dice into soldier dice. The dice can get wounded in battle, sometimes they don't. However, it certainly feels like there is a 90% chance for the dice to get wounded. Even if you upgrade your soldiers to have a lower chance of getting wounded, they most likely will. Doesn't feel very RNG in that aspect. Time based gameEndgame The endgame is tedious and frustrating. Enemy will send wave after wave at you. like every 10 seconds maybe. you barely got time to recover from a wave, then you find another on the way, then another. In the end I got fed up with it, I found it easier to ignore the waves of enemies and just rebuild whatever they destroy. Moreover, the endgame revolves around having most of your dice being soldiers. Because you will mostly have plenty of resources then and other types of die don't matter that much anymore. When an enemy attacks your base/building, you don't know how much beating the building can take. Sometimes it gets destroyed, sometimes it burns, sometimes it survives. why? I don't know. no indications of that. Good game. 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like the game just isn't something that exists right now in other genres. When I first see dice I think board games, thinking over turns, and accepting the dice as they are rolled. None of these really apply (I guess the board part sure). The game feels like Age of Empires overall, gathering resources and expanding. Thinking is definitely important, but just sort of a general couple of goals is all that is needed. You are going to make sub optimal plays constantly, its better to use dice for something rather than just holding onto them for the perfect opportunity. The dice do get rolled, and you should try to find a good use for it, but if you wanted a different face, reroll it! Especially near the end, as you upgrade specific faces, going for one specific face happens, and you just keep re-rolling until you get it, feeding the dice if it ever gets low durability.Overall, don't assume you know what this game is going to be, also don't pause, it's not designed around pausing and you'll just hate that you can't do things while paused. Try it, fail, learn, try again. Make so many mistakes, and you'll be ascending dice in no time!

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so I just finished my first play through of the game on Normal difficulty without having to restart. Feels pretty good because I was expecting no mercy from this game even on Normal difficulty lol. I was a bit iffy on how dice mechanics would work with base building, but it was easy to pick up on the game mechanics by the time the first winter came through so long as you have experience with similar survival type games. I'm hoping Hard difficulty ramps up the intensity because Normal difficulty wasn't that bad at all, it was rather chill once I started slow pushing across the map.Gameplay StuffAs far as game play goes the restriction of 12 dice makes you really think about if you need to diversify your dice pool or risk running a ton of just one class of dice, at least in the beginning. By the end game I could've finished my run a lot faster, but I thought there'd be a massive end boss at the end of the map, so I was just clearing everything with a catapult first and then moving up rather than risking my soldiers in a frontal assault every time. Apparently, there is a pause mechanic in the game too, but I didn't even bother using it cause on Normal difficulty it wasn't needed. The first few winters in the game I can see being brutal because it turns into frostpunk: dice edition with those generators but after the first couple winters I didn't need generators at all so that was a bit disappointing, I'll get to why that is later.Enemies are bland, best description I have for them. One type of enemy demolishes your buildings, one of them sets them on fire, and the other one that looks like a plague doctor poisons your dice, I think. They never got a chance to use their poison or whatever so I’m not sure on that or if there are any other enemy types because that’s all I saw on Normal difficulty. Enemies attack at intervals that can be chaotic at times but so long as you have at least two soldier dice you should easily turn aside all attacks, I had three blue dice so I could dedicate two dice for defence and use the last one to fire the catapult periodically. The enemy also works on a timer when they attack so you have time to respond to the threat, ie: rapidly smashing spacebar to cycle dice to swords if they ever catch you flatfooted lol. Gameplay Tips!Right, so for everybody struggling on Normal difficulty what you need to grab from the council is the perk that keeps your peasants from freezing if they do actions around your district hall, along with the perk that prevents buildings around your district hall from catching on fire and finally the one that lets you use farms throughout the winter. Literally game winning combo right there. Sure, the first winter or so you have generator hell to even get to where you can grab these but once you do the generators become obsolete so you can start stockpiling away. **In addition a side benefit of this is that you no longer have to respond to the Arsonist enemy unit type because they will still attack but because your buildings can’t catch on fire they literally do nothing so that means you also don’t have to fight them, thus saving Herbs and Soldier dice!**As far as I can tell regarding fire, you can demolish buildings to stop fires from spreading, so if your dice aren’t coming up right just blow up the buildings and be content knowing nothing around your district hall can catch on fire so you are now immortal to that RNG so long as you only build around your halls. By the end game I didn’t have a sprawling city but just these hub outposts with all my buildings on top of one another. You don’t need any district other than peasant on Normal. In fact, you don’t need to use a lot of the buildings or the holy dice either on Normal. I only built the holy dice buildings by end game because I wanted to see what they were about, and I was convinced there was an end game boss on Normal Difficulty. *There isn’t, Sad Face* This is a tiny thing here to mention but don’t go chopping down all your forests in the beginning! I made the mistake of doing that before realizing how crucial herbs where which made the beginning more stressful than necessary. Keep at least one forest attached to a herb gathering hut and you should be fine to chop away everything else so long as you keep one forest standing. CATAPULTS PEOPLE. THINK CATAPULTS. Unnecessary fighting is a big drag on resources. I never used the mercenary training center or any watchtowers. The catapult is a guaranteed kill on buildings in one shot and there’s no risk of your soldiers being injured, just frozen since it was one of the only buildings I’d place right up against my territory boundary lol. Destroy it for refund when you obliterate everything and then push up again. Now this might be a thing or not, but I believe that if you destroy the building the AI is targeting the enemy army will also disappear with it. It only happened once when I was still setting up my base, but it looked like I stopped Arsonists from triggering a blaze that would rip through my town because I demolished their target building first. You don’t need more than one farm once you get your base set up!!!! After the initial beginning stages you can get away with one farm + one Mill. Just keep upgrading the number of resources you get from either one and you should be flooding resources in no time. This probably isn’t a solid tip that’s relevant across all games but my dice numbers where: 3 Soldiers, 1 Monk(Didn’t need them), 3 Citizens, 1 Merchant, and the rest peasants. Hope this gives you an idea of what to shoot for in terms of dice diversity at least on Normal. As far as buildings go like I said I didn’t use hardly any of them. Completely skipped the ones involved with the theatre and whatnot except for the market. Didn’t use most of the military ones either. And I only built the enhancement chamber from the modifier buildings. So long as you manage your resources right you can just start enhancing your troops and start snowballing once you get to that point. That about does it for gameplay tips from me! Hope these tips help someone that needs it if they’re struggling with the game. Closing thoughts!The council is an interesting mechanic along with how you can interact with the neutral camps on the map but its rather shallow in terms of what you can do diplomacy wise. Combat isn’t flashy or anything crazy, it’s serviceable. The base building aspect of the game is fun, but I wish there was a need to use a lot more of the buildings in the course of a playthrough on Normal. The map is beautiful, and I love the ring world layout! Wish more games used cool visuals like this one. All in all, DICE LEGACY doesn’t hold your hand which is nice from games nowadays and it also keeps things fresh with the dice mechanics. I’ll definitely be giving the other modes a go to see what else the game has to offer!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like playing Yahtzee while a swinging axe slowly descends down upon you. You might think this game is relaxing, but it is not. It is a game of efficiently using your time and rolling dice constantly to take advantage of the board. Resources are not unlimited, enemies get harder over time. This is not a relaxing game, it is a RTS of calm under pressure.If you are into boardgames, this is basically a worker placement game, with an hourglass. There is one huge flaw with this game though. And it's a biggie. There is only one "mode". You have one type of map, you always go the same way, you repeat the game with resources randomly placed around.Unfortunately, this means I got bored of the game in two sessions. If you are the kind of person who enjoys playing the same game over again with different modifiers, different difficulty conditions etc. you will be satisfied.If you, like me, want to play on different maps, different modes, multiplayer, anything else but this "build north until you find the enemy keep and destroy it", you probably will enjoy this game for a couple sessions and that's it.I really hope they add more to this game. There needs to be variety, and not just various difficulties of the same thing. Otherwise, it's a fantastic game, with a great mechanic, but no depth.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is a fascinating take on realtime dice worker placement.  Dice can be upgraded, altered, fused, and even ascended (?!).  Worker placements are buildings which carry their own proximity and placement games.  As a strategy boardgamer, this scratches so many weird itches that I didn't know I had.  The aesthetic is gorgeous and the worldbuilding brings a real dread that reminds me of Frostpunk.  I would encourage people with a boardgaming bent to really give this game a good shake.  Play on standard mode for sure, check your ego at the door and really give the mechanics of the game a chance to shine.  This is a game that encourages exploration of the mechanics and build tree.  It's like Settlers 7, the dice game.

name: Disc Room
detailed_description: Are you ready to get sliced in half? The year is 2089 and a giant disc has appeared in orbit of Jupiter. Step into the oversized space suit of a brave scientist and explore this sprawling intergalactic slaughterhouse. Explore the expansive orbiting disc ship, moving room to room surviving and completing increasingly complex goals set forth. Use unlocked abilities to outmaneuver dozens of different disc types while solving mysterious puzzles. And remember: what kills you only makes you stronger. Disc Room is a collaboration between Kitty Calis, Jan Willem Nijman, Terri Vellmann and Doseone.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS RECOMMENDATION COMES WITH A FEW CAVEATS. This game is not for everyone.I have 198% completion (out of likely 200%).+ Palatable art style, filled with subtle animations to make the game feel more alive+ Good music--high tempo, designed to keep you in the game+ Controls are tight and responsive--for the most part+ Almost all levels feel fresh and unique--contains a surprising variety of enemies in a game where they're all discs+ Progression is easily tracked- Story feels like an afterthought, told in brief comics with no dialogue- Most abilities are underutilized or only useful for specific levels- Your important abilities can feel bad to use at times- "Mystery" aspect hinted at in the trailer is minimal- Your success is not always in your hands, especially in the game's hardest levelsThis last con about the game's most difficult levels is why I cannot recommend this game for everyone. If you're the kind of gamer who enjoys a short, satisfying experience with a little bit of dabbling in postgame, stop reading this and jump in. You can reach the normal ending in 2-3 hours, and reaching the 20-second/10-second goals can be satisfying--in some levels. But if you're a completionist, you are going to run into some of the most poorly-designed levels I have ever encountered in 25+ years of gaming.Several levels, including the worst offender, Lobotomy, throw so many enemies at you in such egregious numbers that your path to success is often closed to you. Your skill alone will not get you through these levels--you MUST get lucky. We're not talking "purple coin challenge" hard--I spent almost twice as many hours on two levels than I spent on the rest of the levels, normal and hard, COMBINED. My eventual success on Lobotomy was strictly due to the time capsule placements basically coming up one after another in a row for the entire level--there simply isn't enough space to dash or slowly make your way through without the RNG gods blessing you. Maybe these levels (and all levels in general) would have been easier if the movement from the dash and slow abilities did not hurt you so much when used near walls; your dash ends immediately if you dash into a wall and your slow will get you stuck in a wall until you use the speed-up command or wind up with your guts coating the edge of your enemy. It's pathetic--so pathetic that I considered giving this game a negative recommendation as a whole. I noted that I did not fully complete this game because the last level, a boss rush, comes across the same way, and I'm not going to wait another several hours for my skills to be uplifted by the Disc Room gods. Had I known what I was getting into going in, I would've put in about 5-7 hours doing most of the other challenges and left these few gross outliers be, winding up satisfied with my overall experience. Unfortunately, these same outliers have soured my time spent and left me pretty frustrated. If you're a completionist, take note: you WILL get pissed off as your fate is taken repeatedly out of your hands. But if you're looking for a fun, twitchy romp for a few hours, pick this up.

_childDocuments_.review: The year is 2089. A large, mysterious disc is orbiting Jupiter, and it's up to you to investigate it. Entering the disc, you find yourself in an empty room with an ominous open door that catches your gaze. Time to explore the unknown and solve the mystery behind the . is the embodiment of the phrase - . Spending thirty minutes on a single level and then dropping the soap at the very end can be  frustrating. Fortunately, this isn't a problem for , as it only requires you to welcome the sweet embrace of death and let the fun times commence. Your struggles will be . But don't worry if your first time is a bit shorter than that. It's perfectly normal, especially if you are stressed. And with solid disc variety, plenty of rooms, optional secrets, and some clever challenges,  creates a gameplay loop that never ceases to be enjoyable.There are 5 biomes, with plenty of rooms for your pain (or pleasure). Each biome dons a theme: This also trickles down to the design of its discs. While certain discs are consistent throughout your adventure, some are only present in specific areas. And with each room doing a bang-up job of mixing new and "old" discs; From discs that lock onto you like heat-seeking missiles to large discs scattering into multiple smaller discs, the game will punish your complacency. What worked for one room won't, necessarily, work for the next. So channel your inner Batman, and make use of that prep time. With 64 discs and 53 rooms in total, the game does a bang-up job of keeping the rosters fresh and unique. While there are repeats, with some just damaged or smaller versions of the same disc, the amount of visually and ability distinct discs you encounter is still excellent. For my completionists buddies out there, a word of warning - there's a special room of pure , that singlehandedly made me consider a .But to fully explore the game, you need to complete all the objectives each room has. There are two types -  and  The main objectives usually focus on tasking you to reach a specific time or require you seek death. They are the main driving point of the story. If you solely focus on them, Now, the optional ones are what stole the show for me. Firstly, they are used to give more detail about the origin of the giant disc. Secondly, they are fricking fun to do and often throw some weird and wacky challenges at you that require thinking outside the box.While this game may seem like a wet dream for a masochist, the devs thought of people with a sound mind as well. So don't fret, for if a particular room or section is too hard, you can tailor the game to your liking with its state-of-the-art . A surprise, to be sure, but a welcome one.To combat the ever-increasingly challenging discs, you can equip , each unlocked upon dying in a specific room. The first and the best is . One of the more useful ones, as it lets you easily get out of trouble. While dashing, you are invincible, but this is kept in check by keeping the dash distance short. Then there is : You move at regular speed while slowing down pesky discs in range. But, have you ever wanted to see 10 copies of yourself get chopped to pieces? Well, you are in luck, as  lets you do just that. These clones mirror your movement, and as long as there is a single  standing, the timer doesn't stop. , mirror on the wall, why did I teleport myself to the other side of the room full of discs? This ability felt unbalanced, as it was quite easy to sudoku yourself if there were more than 2 discs in the room. Moving on, we have what at first glance appears to be a mighty fart, but it is, in fact, . Especially useful when your buttocks are caressing the wall, as it pushes those naughty discs away from you. It needs a couple of seconds to charge for a greater range and stronger effect, keeping it fair and balanced. And lastly, become the blob you always wanted and  them all. Sadly, your tiny body has a one passenger limit, so be careful about when and what discs you become intimate with.I was pleasantly surprised to see  battles. In a game where surviving as long as possible is the goal, there are indeed boss battles.  – I hear you ask. Well, as you lack any offensive abilities, . The boss battles are similar and use this same gameplay loop, with no differences. They mostly have different disc variations ganging up on you, but the gist is the same -  But there are two that did stand out in both how they attack and the strategy you need to overcome them. The first one is the end boss, and as such, I won't spoil too much, just know, it demands pain. The second boss watches over the best area in the game - . Expect the unexpected here, with darkness completely obscuring your view and brief flashes of light and sound cues acting as your only guides against this otherworldly phantom. The game sports a quirky comic book aesthetic, and it seems fitting, as the story is delivered using comic book panels. Each biome has a different theme: From the seemingly more industrial oriented, abandoned and overgrown, to the weird fleshy rooms that are alive and have the munchies. And the soundtrack was decent.  somewhat successfully gets the juices flowing with its soundtrack. From the synthwave of the mechanical area to the eerie and ominous one in the darkroom area, each brings its own unique flavour to the music score. The sound effects were top-notch. You can almost hear how sharp each blade of the disc is. Whoever made the decapitation sounds, I salute you. Hearing 15 clones get chopped to pieces in a span of 2 seconds is something I never knew I needed in my life.While the story leaves a lot to be desired, even with clearing all optional content, the core gameplay loop is what ultimately kept the game fun at hour 12, like it was at hour 1. With tons of challenges, rooms, entertaining boss battles and some very clever secret puzzles, accompanied by the great custom difficulty slider,  promises a jolly good time for the whole family.

_childDocuments_.review: Disc Room is an experience that's balanced between dying and well, not dying.Each room on your path is locked away behind some minor objectives. Usually this is simply trying to survive for ten or twenty seconds but there are times when the game wants you to die. Part of the Disc Room experience lies in dying to every manner of rotating nightmare you can. There are also various special skills unlocked throughout the game, this includes a dash that turns the player invincible for a brief moment, slowing down time or creating clones of the player. Only one skill can be equipped when entering a room, though. The developers anticipated players of all skill levels wanting to challenge Disc Room and have included a number of sliders that can alter the experience, from overall movement speed of the game to how quickly the enemy discs can move. This is a welcomed addition when certain challenges might seem too difficult or you need a little help to proceed. Disc Room really needs no explanation whether or not you're going to like the motion of dying and retrying. As a fan of self-improvement through trial and error. I loved the sense of finally mastering a room, only to be brought right back down upon failing the next one.In many cases perseverance and a lucky pattern might be all you need to survive for a few extra seconds in Disc Room. But in truth the only limit is your own ability. So if fancy a slice and dice sort of challenge, you’ll definitely want to take Disc Room for a spin.

_childDocuments_.review: A good game, but not a great one.  For most of the main campaign, it executes its novel concept quite well:  you are exploring a mysterious BDO (Big Dumb Object) populated with 50+ varieties of intelligent saw blades that each want to make hamburger of you, and the BDO keeps resurrecting you so it can  and  with you further.  Each blade has its own pattern and tendencies -- but they spawn randomly.  In the later third of the game, these malicious homing bastards appear so thickly that you begin to rely on RNG as much as your own skill -- and in the post-game, which unfortunately contains additional story points, the density of the blade distribution becomes  that you are at the , your only hope being that, in the rare instances you area able to hit a favorable distribution, you will be playing at your very, very best.An interesting arcade game, but a deeply flawed one that I have zero desire to go achievement hunting in.  Buy only on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: provides a relatively short but sweet experience, where your primary objective is to avoid getting killed by spinning discs of death in each room. The game keeps things interesting by introducing new unique mechanics in specific areas as well as a varied amount of discs with different abilities. For such a short game, it has a decent amount of variety to keep you engaged throughout the experience, though it feels too short if you don’t try for 300% completion.• Each new area has a unique gimmick to keep gameplay fresh• A multitude of different discs to ruin your day• A diverse set of 6 abilities to help you survive longer• Multiple difficulty sliders to make the game easier if you're having trouble• Rather short unless you go for 300%• Most of the abilities didn’t seem feasible to use in harder rooms• Some rooms seem way too easy for a game that’s meant to be fairly difficult• Lucks seems to be the determining factor for the much harder rooms rather than skillYou are a scientist who is sent to Jupiter after a giant disc is detected orbiting the planet. Upon entering, you find yourself in a room full of deadly discs (I think they’re saws, but the game refers to them as discs), so what else can you do other than attempt to avoid them before inevitably dying. Each room gets reset upon death, to unlock doors to progress, you must complete challenges in rooms that mostly involve surviving for a certain amount of time. gameplay loop isn’t a complicated one, nor is it overly repetitive either. It managed to keep me engaged for a good eight hours from start to finish and never felt like a chore to play. You’ll go from room to room, surviving for as long as you can as discs spawn with the sole intent of murdering you. The longer you survive, the more discs that spawn. The game doesn’t challenge you to survive for very long even near the end. Most of the time the challenges to unlock rooms are , which made me think the game would get exceptionally difficult, but it never did hit that difficulty threshold I was anticipating. I was up for the challenge but was let down by how easy some of these rooms were.As you progress through rooms, you’ll discover new discs that act differently from one another. Some charge at you every few seconds, some move in odd patterns that are hard to predict, some shoot miniature discs at you, you get the idea. The creativity the developers have with these discs is outstanding, for such a short game there is a lot of variety packed into it. Exploring new areas further increases the amount of variety  has to offer, introducing new gimmicks to keep the timer ticking or make the rooms more challenging. Some areas require you to stand in a specific area to keep the timer going, some require you to step on tiles to increase the time, some require you to pick up golden orbs to increase the time, etc. Needless to say, there’s more than enough varied content to keep the experience entertaining throughout.From the start I was preparing for the game to get challenging quickly, maybe I was expecting too much from the game, but that never really happened. There were a few rooms that had me stumped for a while, but these were far and few between. The difficulty seemed a bit all over the place, even near the end of the game I had a few rooms that I was able to clear on the first couple of attempts. Though my experience with the game might not be like yours, there are sliders that can decrease the difficulty if you find yourself stuck in a room. I can appreciate the fact that the game doesn’t hold you hostage telling you to get good, you are able to make it easier to progress. But I would’ve liked the sliders to have made the game harder, I could’ve made the gameplay at 200% speed, but that just seemed dumb. I would rather have had more discs spawning or made the discs move a little faster. might seem skill-based most of the time, however, when you enter rooms that are a spam fest of discs or limit your vision severely, it feels less skill-based and more luck-based. Since the discs start moving in random directions, you could come up against bad RNG where you're trapped in a corner and there is literally no way of surviving. Combine this with rooms such as Perfect Dark where you literally can’t see anything in the room, unless you use the slow time ability to see temporarily, and you’ve got a recipe for disaster. The skill for that room is practically non-existent since you can’t always predict where discs are going to move. Other rooms that overwhelm you with tons of discs are practically the same, hoping that RNG is in your favour so you can survive for long enough.Progressing through rooms, you’ll uncover abilities that can help you survive longer. You can only equip one ability from the six that you unlock, but I found that most of the abilities were more too situational to be helpful. The only ones I switched between were slow time and dash, whilst others didn’t seem very beneficial in the more challenging rooms.Despite the quality and varied content that  has to offer, I was still somewhat disappointed by the length of the game. My casual playthrough only garnered just over four hours of playtime (including normal and hard mode) which, for someone who compares the price tag to time played, didn’t seem reasonable for the full asking price. This did incentivise me to achieve 300% completion and collect all the achievements (which is extremely rare for me), but admittedly, I only did it to squeeze a couple more hours out of this game. I would’ve liked to see this game be a bit more fleshed out with more rooms, possibly more planets to explore to make the experience a couple of hours longer. is still a great game despite how short and sometimes too easy it can be despite being tagged as ‘difficult. There’s a lot of variety to keep the gameplay fresh, from 60 different types of murderous discs to several areas that change up the gameplay. To get the most out of this game, consider aiming for 300% completion, otherwise expect a relatively short but sweet experience from start to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: Clearly made with love and care, and highly unique.Art-style is adorable, and the core premise is frantic and engaging. _childDocuments_.review: Games that involve dying a lot usually aren’t my thing. It always feels like a sting that just won’t go away even after playing many classics like Super Meat Boy, Celeste, and even another Devolver gem, Katana Zero. Disc Room, for some reason, may be the first game where I didn’t feel it nearly as much. Maybe it was the nature of the progression system or the fact that you could just go to a different room any time, but I rarely found myself too frustrated with all the deaths. That being said, there was no shortage of deaths.Abbreviated Review: The premise of Disc Room is very straightforward. An alien ship shows up around Jupiter and a bunch of scientists goes to check it out. Despite it being an obvious horrible death trap, you head in there anyway and proceed to get chopped up in room after room filled with spinning death blades. That’s essentially the whole story in a nutshell, but of course, some strange things happen in the process. I won’t spoil too much of the story here, but the gist of it is that there’s another scientist on their own little adventure as well. Also, some weird rooms have mysterious contexts as well. Overall though, I don’t necessarily think it’s the allure of the game.The fun of Disc Room is mostly just in the gameplay alone. The bulk of what you’ll be doing in any of the many rooms is dodging the dozens of different types of spinning saw blades that bounce around each. It’s very simple, but the variety of situations lends itself to something that maintains its excitement the whole time. Within this process, your survival time is also directly compared to what your friends and the developers achieved. Since I’m the only one on my friends list to have purchased this game, I’m only competing with the developers, but it’s still a great motivator. It would be nice to have the option to include online players as well, though.Thankfully, you’re not only relegated to just running around to survive. There are special abilities that can be unlocked that allow you to stave off death just a little longer. The first one, dash, is the one I used the most. It simply gives you a small burst of speed and allows you to clip through any discs while it's active. It’s fairly limited, but can be extremely helpful getting out of otherwise unwinnable positions. The others include things like temporarily slowing the environment around you, cloning yourself to have several simultaneous characters at once, and temporarily deflecting any discs nearby. Each has its strengths and weaknesses and works better on some levels than others. It’s up to you to determine which to use on each.One of the more interesting things about progressing through the game is that it’s not all about surviving. A significant part of progression is tied to death. Every level has several discs with unique properties and designs. Altogether these dozens of discs provide most of the variety for the game, and they’re also listed on a checklist marked off each time one kills you. Some of the rooms in the game are locked off until you are killed by enough of these various deadly saw blades.To complete the necessary levels to get to the credits of Disc Room, you don’t need that much time. It probably took me somewhere around 90 minutes. However, the game’s small but odd story isn’t complete. You also have to venture backward through the levels on hard mode to truly finish it. For me, this is probably never going to happen. I’ve tried many times but I am thoroughly stalled. It seems like there’s so much chaos in these “hard mode” levels that you need just as much (or more) luck than skill to succeed.It also seems like Disc Room was designed for speedrunners. The game has a challenge list that features one for completing the game in 15 minutes. It has a built-in speed running timer as well. Other challenges have players trying to die as little as possible and playing the game at 200% speed. This is neat stuff and all, but stuff that will never really appeal to me.So what I ended up with is a game that has an enjoyable 90 minute set of gameplay that doesn’t really offer me much in addition. It does have some accessibility options similar to Celeste where you can slow down the game and make it easy to complete, but it feels like a waste to bother with those. The one I did use was unlocking the rest of the cutscenes so I could see the real final ending – which still wasn’t all that incredible.If you’re not interested in speedrunning or the post-ending extra-difficult gameplay, Disc Room may not be for you. At least not at its base price. I do think the game is worth experiencing if you can get it cheap enough, though. The game just didn’t stick with me as much as some other short indie games. As a fan of short games, one of the things I value in them is making an impact in such a limited time. I think if I was interested in the challenges or could enjoy the speedrunning aspects more, it might have that impact. However, as it stands it seems like it’s only slightly above average.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely fantastic game.Best I can describe it as is a bullet hell, focused entirely on the challenge of dodging varied sawblades.Playing this game none of your time is wasted as you are rewarded for seeking new deaths, encouraged to revisit old challenges for increased mastery and hunt for devious secrets that utterly stump you until you revisit with new tricks you learn through playing.Oh and there's boss fights, those are fun.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game, but 1 hour of story mode and then bonus difficulty in the same levels as an addition is not $15 of value in this case. It's a fun game, but the zone gimmicks honestly are very unbalanced, and most of the time not fun. Sometimes this game doesn't feel like it's fair which in any bullet hell type of game you want balance. For example the zone where the light flicks on and off is absolutely infuriating and really not fun in the slightest. It felt like as you went to each new zone the game became worse.
