_childDocuments_.review: This isn't exactly a negative review, because the time i spent with the game was fun, but it is really bad designed in many ways. Im not gonna bother describing what this game offers as i use to do with other reviews because clearly, im not completely satisfied with my final experience playing it, so i will tell the main problem i found: there is absolutely no balance.The fact that the game asks you to last ONLY 20 seconds on each room, and just 10 seconds on hard mode rooms, shows clearly its faults. Basically, the random patterns of the saws and the RNG involved isn't programmed good enough to make you be able to last more time on the rooms. Sure, you can do it, some dev times make it to 1 minute, and i spent some hours beating many of them, till i realized its mostly because of 80% luck, 20% skill. Many times, after getting 10 seconds on a hard mode room for example, or even 15 because of some of the challenges, i didn't even felt satisfied, because i just knew that my skill was barely involved, i just had more luck with the patterns than the last time, thats all.As i said, i had fun with this title, despite the negative review maybe you should try it if the conecpt interests you, but i felt that i had to clarify why i didn't experienced the amount of fun i was expecting from a game like this, and warn other players so they dont get slightly dissapointed like it happened to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those nearly flawless games that you can hone your skills at. The closest comparison I can make is Super Meat Boy or another challenging platformer. The satisfaction in playing this game comes primarily from becoming better as a player. A few of the levels are more puzzle-like, providing a breather from the intense action.Disc Room is a variation on the bullet hell genre. However, because you are dodging large gears instead of point-like bullets, it becomes an entirely different beast. It has a fresh feel. Gameplay is snappy and tight. (There were a few kinks but the developers ironed these out in the first few patches.) For context, the game expects 10 seconds of survival in a room to establish competency and 20 seconds for mastery. So yes, it's a very hard game, and you will get very good at it.I want to say that the soundtrack and sound design elevates this game from good to great. A game like this would be unbearable without a good soundtrack, and Disc Room has a great one. Also, you'll eventually notice that when you have a near-miss with a gear, the music will warp and become a bit shrill. This tiny feature added a lot for me, and I appreciate the attention to detail.If you are a fan of action/arcade games at all, please do yourself a favor and pick up Disc Room. It's all the open nerve action of Super Hexagon with the satisfying progression of a platformer or metroidvania. The one thing I would wish for is more levels. Any sequel would be an instant-buy for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm conflictedThis game is RNG HELL! In a BAD WAY. Most of the endgame challenges require 25% skill and 75% luck. I died 70 times in one room cause I kept getting 9.5 second time but I needed 10 second to advance. The first 9 seconds are easy and the tenth second is decided by rng. It really makes you ask how long is one second.BUTThis game is so juicy! It's like the developers asked themself "In how many ways can we make the player dodge circles and make it fun?" And then they made a game about that! It's the simpliest idea pushed to it's max potential.Just dodge circles in 100 different ways.You might think that it gets boring, but I played 8 hours of this game in ONE SITTING!The game costs a bit too much, maybe wait for a discount.I enjoyed my time playing this game.Highly recomend for both casuals and hardcore gamers

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved it, even though it destroyed my hands. It blows my mind how many well-executed ideas are in this little game. If you can imagine it, it's a disc! A worthy, brutal challenge for the hardcore gamer.However, a couple levels are unfairly difficult and will probably frustrate most people (myself included). I'm still stuck on one room that just about requires a lucky layout to survive. I've wasted several hours on it and haven't managed it yet.There's also a couple bugs. The slow power can cause you to get stuck in walls, dashes end prematurely if you hit a wall and one of the rooms (the very same unfair room mentioned above) can glitch if you're going to fast. I also experienced a performance issue where the game will stall briefly periodically, causing even more infuriating deaths than necessary.I'd still absolutely recommend it. If you came looking for a mountain to climb, I don't think you'll be disappointed!

_childDocuments_.review: a white-knuckle meditation on the dissolution of selfa frictionless gameplay experience that stretches "don't touch the disc" beyond what you'd think possiblealso includes great accessibility options for people looking to tune the gameplay/difficulty to their likingif you appreciate games that let you respawn to try again instantly after death, this is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid visuals and music, the art is fantastic and the setting is creative enough to support it. The biggest problem though is the gameplay. The bullethell gameplay is fun enough, but becomes a massive slog when you realize just how bad the RNG elements are, with some puzzles and challenges taking me well over 10 minutes because the game screws me over.
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

_childDocuments_.review: Ironically a game that thinks outside the box....by locking you in a box...with copious amounts of sawblades.Not many games like this around, Another Devolver published game that creates new fun experiences.What can best be described as gameplay that derives from the dodging aspect of a bullet hell, Disc Room shoves you in a room and asks that you survive a certain amount of time without getting torn to pieces. You gain new abilities to help you survive such as slowing time and creating clones of yourself, meanwhile the rooms get harder and deadlier. The game has some cool secrets and challenges to conquer as well as the main "campaign" so to speak, no real story here but lots of rooms to beat. Have you got the point yet that there's rooms and sawblades...Yeah that's the game, but if you like it this'll be a fun challenge to work on for 5 or so hours. Cool little game but i am a sucker for mechanical yet simple experiences like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

_childDocuments_.review: A straightforward bullet hell game set in tight rooms where you dodge buzz saws to survive as long as possible. The biggest advantage of this game is how easy it is to pick up and start playing. You can instantly dive in and enjoy dodging saws, and when I first tried it, I ended up playing for 4 hours straight during my first session. I also appreciate how each level only requires you to survive for 10-20 seconds, so dying never feels too frustrating.However, the game has one major flaw for me: a few levels are significantly harder than the rest, not due to complex patterns, but because they require an unreasonable amount of luck. They are so heavily reliant on RNG that I started feeling like a gambling addict, playing them for hours. Admittedly, I am also not the best bullet hell player. Despite these frustrating levels, the game is really fun, especially if you're not aiming for 100% completion. If you are just looking for some quick, enjoyable action, I definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

_childDocuments_.review: Disc Room is a good game but is definitely NOT for everyone. I would go so far as to describe the entire gameplay experience as 'frustrating and punishing.' This is definitely not a game for folks who are easily angered or who have poor dexterity! I really appreciated the visual presentation and minimalist storytelling in Disc World. The artistic design for this game is very stylish and the music perfectly matches the frenetic energy you'll feel while trying to avoid getting sliced to bits! Speaking of getting 'sliced to bits,' you can expect to die a lot....like, 'A LOT' a lot. Thankfully, death in Disc World is a speedy process and you can get yourself back into the action within seconds of dying. The core gameplay is simple enough - proceed from room to room and don't get hit by discs. However, the game ramps up complexity with 'side objectives' required to access neighboring rooms. At times, you may simply need to remain alive for a set duration (easier said than done!). In other instances, you may need to employ your various power-ups creatively and manipulate your environment. Suffice it to say, you will always be met with varying and daunting challenges that keep the otherwise "basic" gameplay loop compelling.
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

_childDocuments_.review: My "short" break between games got extended as I slowly descended into sawblade-obsessed madness.In interviews, I've heard the dev team say they really found the game when they realized it was not a game about surviving but instead a game about dying. This is really the key to seeing how they were able to iterate on the Humble Original, and keep the successor fresh for so long. 8 hours in and well past credits, there's still so much to explore and uncover. And shout out to the indies (and others) trailblazing accessibility options. I didn't use any of them but apparently until the first patch, they are necessary for 100%ing the game due to a bugged achievement. Moreover, they are useful to players of all skills given that they can be used to practice rooms for advanced runs.
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

_childDocuments_.review: Tight movement and a great soundtrack are unfortunately the only positives here. For a highscore-chasing bullet hell, the extreme rng outweighs any options the player has. The only consistency in a level is what saws will spawn and when; their positions and starting directions are almost always completely random. Later levels have even more going on, with orbs to collect and buttons/panels to activate, and some saw ai's being effectively rng dashes; it's too much. To get a best time you need to play extremely well, AND get the optimal spawns, which can add hours of grinding to later levels (and that's just to get the 15-20 seconds required for achievements). Ultimately there are just more rewarding bullet hells to play, where navigating the projectiles is a puzzle to solve. Here, skill can get you half way, but more often than not you'll find yourself praying.
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

_childDocuments_.review: This game explores the extremities of the arena bullet hell as best it can and for such a small team I think that this game is definitely worth the money if you are itching for that kind of experience. I personally have been itching for a bullet hell after playing Undertale a while ago and so this was a perfect pure bullet hell for me to scratch that. It's a relatively small game but it oozes charm, from the combination of simple art style and eclectic music, it was a joy to be able to 100% this game. The controls are tight and the gameplay switch ups are neat. The RNG allows for many moments where you feel absolutely insane at what you just managed to dodge, and though some in the reviews do say that it comes as a detriment to the gameplay, I feel like since there is such a quick restart system, there isn't really much punishment other than a few more minutes of your time. Small-scale RNG I think is okay. To be honest, it feels like a lot of the power-ups were overshadowed by the dash which is a shame, but I think the game did its best at trying to include all of them though I wished there were more level design focused on linearity rather than RNG so that it would be more about puzzle solving. Having a mixture of these generally RNG levels and maybe a section with a more puzzle-focused non-RNG levels utilising power-ups in a unique way would have been cool to see, but I am definitely satisfied with my experience. 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Simple but masterful at what it sets out to be: a unique, challenging, and incredibly satisfying bullet hell. I strongly disagree with many of the negative reviews that cite the game's RNG factor as a flaw; while there's certainly some amount of unavoidable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that does occasionally come up (ok, certain levels  *cough* Lobotomy *cough* are somewhat RNG dependent, but instant restarts mostly alleviates this), the randomness means that you can't rely on memorization. It forces you to become genuinely better at the game as a whole, not just on a level you're trying to beat. Personally, I think the RNG is the game's biggest strength; after so many hours playing games like Enter the Gungeon, static bullet patterns become a breeze.Also, points for replayability. You'll finish the main game in a few hours (and hard mode isn't too long either) but 100%ing and doing the additional challenges will take much longer (in a fun way, not in an artificial length way). Highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Score: 4/5Notes: My initial review of the game was negative and it was because I found the game to be rather repetitive and easy. But I kept hearing other people talk positively about the game occasionally so I decided to give the game another chance. Turns out the reason I found the game initially easy is because the game doesn't support monitor refresh rates above 60hz. And if you try to play the game with a monitor set above 60hz the game will actually run at 75% speed. The games physics are tied to its fps and playing above 60hz will make the game run at 45 fps instead of 60. It's not actually that easy to tell the game is in slow motion but it is obviously quite a bit easier playing this way.And now after having fully completed the base game, hard mode, and 200% challenge. I would say my main gripe with the game now are that it's still a bit repetitive. And while the game isnt easy, the difficulty balancing is really bad IMO. This isn't the worst thing for an initial playthrough, but when going for the challenges post-game it is pretty miserable. Most of the challenges are incredibly backloaded and only 4 or 5 of the rooms are at all challenging. So if you intend to truly complete the game and go for all challenges, be prepared to spend 14 minutes repeating the same rooms over and over again just to die to the same final rooms repeatedly. The 200% challenges is also incredibly obnoxious and only difficult because of a couple rooms, and those couple rooms are horrifically terrible.
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

Ultimately I would recommend, but not at full price. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of these "I wish there was a Neutral rating" situations. The game is solid and has some variety to it, but at the end of the day it's just a very toned-down bullet hell with very heavy RNG dependance. It accomplishes what it intends to, but for my taste there's just not enough to it to keep me hooked for longer than a few short sessions every now and then. That in itself isn't bad, and I *would* rate this game as positive, if it wasn't for the outrageous price tag of 15€. I would never even have touched this thing if a friend hadn't gifted it to me - I would've looked at the store page, gotten mildly interested, noticed the price tag and put the game on ignore. In my view, a game asking for that much money needs to make a really big impact right from the beginning, and Disc Room, for me, didn't deliver on that part. In essence, this is asking for the price of a commercial shmup title, but for a game that people were making in Game Maker 6 for free some 15 years ago.TL;DR: It's not bad, I'll play it more in the future, but it's like double the price it should be.

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun precision, bullet-dodging game.It's well-designed, easy to pick up, and suited for both quick play and long grinding sessions. It is quite hard, but intelligently so, as survival goals aren't insanely high. It's all about being extremely focused (and a bit lucky) for short periods of time.Content-wise, it's both rich and poor. There's a very wide variety of discs with distinct behaviors, a decent amount of boss fights, and you get to discover new patterns pretty much every room you step into. So in that sense, the game never remotely feels boring or bland. On the other hand, it's quite short. You can expect to finish both Normal and Hard mode in 5 to 7 hours, up to 15 if you're really struggling I guess.I don't recommend the game to you if :- you're completely new to the genre. You'll probably find it brutally hard and equally frustrating due to the amount and unpredictable nature of discs.- you have anger issues. Same reasoning here.- you're not the kind of person that likes to set extra goals for themselves. As I said, the game is pretty short, and while it does offer a decent amount of extra challenges, they're all optional and mostly come unrewarded.Basically, this game is about challenge for the sake of it. There's a lot of replay value if you decide to try and beat all the (surprisingly good!) dev times, or decide to compete with  a similarly-minded friend on the leaderboards, or simply to take up on every challenge the game offers you.If that sounds to be up your alley, it probably is.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost I would like to say that at it's asking price and for what you get, I must emphasize that no matter the complaints, this game is 100% worth the purchase.  Overall- 7.5/10Pros -This is the perfect game for those on the go (steam deck especially) -In my experience, although this game is listed as single player it makes a great couch co op game if you take turns passing on deaths or rooms. -Easy to pick up. Controls are so simple that even if this was your first game ever it will be easy to understand.-Longevity. This game has an infinite shelf life in the sense that it's so simple and fun that you can put it down for years and have as much fun picking it back up as you did day 1.Cons-Artificial Difficulty. You will have to progress fairly deep into the game to realize it, but some of the challenges are just outright unfair and will require you to repeat a room and pray that RNG is on your side. The late game takes a tonal shift from not being able to complete a room until you analyze and figure out the method to there's absolutely no method and they're throwing and spawning as many discs as possible and telling you to just last 15 seconds. No pattern rhyme or reason for you to figure out and feel satisfied for being able to complete. The late game gave me a similar feeling to Destiny 2 where you eventually start to feel like the game is dragged on because every enemy is a bullet sponge and there's no real challenge per say other than the time taken to finish.-THE DEVS BEST- Circling back to hard mode. A lot of the challenges are to last 15 seconds in each room. The problem with that is that a lot of the rooms, the devs best times arent even 15 seconds! How do you implement an obstacle to reach 100% that you, the creator, couldn't even overcome? If they didn't feel like sitting there waiting for RNG to be in their favor and accomplish that challenge, why would I, the paying customer, want to do it? PLAY TEST YOUR GAMES PEOPLE.That being said im realizing those complaints years later and still enjoying the game.

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface, Disc Room looks like one of those cheap rage games - the kind of game that's just brutally unfair for the sake of it. But give this one a chance - it's more like a puzzle than anything else... a puzzle spattered with gore and body parts mind you.This game features PLENTY of ways to die. Going into this, I didn't know how many ways a disc could actually evolve to kill you. My death count now looks like a PO box number. You are going to need quick reactions and some precision weaving to overcome this sharp labyrinth - but you can also acquire abilities that will help you conquer rooms. I'm not going to spoil all abilities, but take absorb for example. Struggling to deal with a couple of magnetised discs while dodging all the spawning discs around you? Absorb one and give yourself some breathing room.Many of the rooms in the game can be solved with some quick switching of abilities. And if all else fails, you can throw yourself at the room until you finally work it out. And boy is it satisfying.To accompany you in your quest for total disc domination is an absolutely banging soundtrack. It's almost enough to get you in a hypnotic groove as you duck and dive between the next deadly obstruction.My only one true gripe with the game is I am not the biggest fan of the art style - particularly for the cutscenes. But it's a real small gripe - and doesn't spoil 2020's best disc based game.

_childDocuments_.review: Remarkably consistent with expectations set by its name, Disc Room is a game about trying not to die to discs in rooms.With 64 different disc types (many with unique behaviours) and well over a hundred rooms of varying difficulty, there's plenty to do.There are also bosses, secret rooms, and a few puzzles.If that isn't enough, there are challenges and local leaderboards too.For the most part, the game is slightly less intimidating than it looks, with notable exception of a few levels where there is just Too Much Stuff, at which point your success depends on chance rather than skill alone. A thing to consider if you want to go for 200% completion.If the game  prove too intimidating, there are plenty accessibility options, like game speed, disc speed, level goal multiplier, etc. - this will negatively affect your scoring for leaderboards, but can be adjusted on per-room basis if you just can't handle a room otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: i really would like to recommend this game, as a lot of the design ideas are interesting and fun at first glance. unfortunately, since everything (projectile spawn locations, directions, bounce directions), it really just results in an unfun mess at a higher level (last few areas + hardmode). some levels seem entirely down to rng as you'll be put into unwinnable situation after unwinnable situation. and when you complete these frustrating levels, it's not satisfying as you just beat the grind, not a reasonable challenge. and the game expects you to grind it out, with its 10-30 second (generally) playtimes. you're just supposed to rage retry until it works, and it just stops being fun at some point. again, i really want to like the game, but walking away from it after completing it, i just have a sour taste in my mouth. i could understand if only a few levels were like this and those ones were really for the completionists, but as it is, beating the game and finding out there was a hard mode was disheartening as opposed to exciting. and my expectations were right, it just kept getting worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyable avoidance game.  Doseone's OST's are always total bangers.  9/10!  Definitely a game you can just pick up, play for 5-10 minutes and stop...  Or you can grind it out for 8 hours till 6AM :)As the game revolves (haha) entirely around dodging spinning discs, a lot of what makes this game great is the variety in playstyle and approach needed to beat a level.  Sometimes you've got to just survive for 10, 20 seconds.  Sometimes you've got to pick up some stuff a bunch of times.  The game is  forgiving with its avoidance -- I believe you have a couple frames of invulnerability before dying to a saw blade, but for those who aren't hardcore platformer/avoidance/Wannabe fangamers, this game can still be real challenging.  I think it's got a lot of really enjoyable aspects though, even for non-masochists.  There's a light story in the game, displayed through cute derpy comics as you progress.  And even though the story is very minimalist, I thought it was great.  I also personally love the animation and style of the game.  It's just very aesthetically pleasing of a game!There are 'puzzles' in the game, mostly identifying the optimal strategy to beat a stage, but there are some interesting 'bonus' puzzles. It's really enjoyable seeing if you can beat the dev scores (or anyone else on your friend list).  It gives you a goal beyond simply beating the game.  I would say this is the real 'endgame' for Disc Room.  Note, almost every dev score is pretty tough to reach.  There are a couple stages which are  dependent on luck.  Skill always factors in, but you need both skill and luck to unlock everything.If you'd like hints for what I consider the hardest puzzle in the game (it'll be clear which one I'm referring to), it's provided in sequential spoilers below:AnswerMy stats for a "full complete" (every achievement and unlockable) are...I plan on grinding out some more high scores, so I'm sure I'll rack up another 5-10 hours on the game in the next week or two.  I can see myself coming back weeks/months later too.  It's a fun game!

_childDocuments_.review: Disc Room is a short yet difficult game where you're put into small rooms and have to dodge disc hazards. The goal is to survive in each room for as long as possible. There's a few ability unlocks along the way but the game zeroes in on the single premise and then experiments a lot with it, that's a huge plus in my books.Each room has a mini leaderboard where you can compare your scores to your friends. This simple addition made me spend much longer on levels I already beat to see if I could best my friends score. Next thing I knew a few hours passed, and I was wondering where the time has went.However that feeling didn't last forever. I had fun with the majority of the rooms, but a few of them were infuriating as they seemed to heavily rely on the RNG placement of discs rather than the reaction skills and split second decision making of the player.The game also has a difficulty toggle in options, so despite the game having the difficult tag on Steam I don't think casual players should feel discouraged entirely. It's tough, but not unforgiving, and the option to make levels easier is always there if needed.Outside of a few moments that are frustrating for the wrong reasons, this is an addictive game and is extra worth if you have a few friends that already own it to compare leaderboards to. It ain't perfect but there's plenty of reasons to recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: [Edited on full completion of the base game]At the time of writing I've fully completed Disc Room, racking up 10685 deaths that should have been closer to 7000. I think any let's play of the first twenty minutes or so will tell you whether this game is for you better than any review can.First off: yes, this is a toughie! Disc Room has you evading unstoppable bouncing buzzsaws until they inevitably dismember you. It's just like being trapped in the screensaver of Meat Boy's DVD player. With no way to fight back, survival is the objective. Each chamber has its own leaderboard so you can see how long you fared compared to your peers and the dev team; levels fill with discs so quickly and completely that I suspect there is no room to improve on the top times by now. (If you prefer a lower skill floor, or have motor difficulties, don't stop reading yet!)"Endless" games that always kill you might turn you off - after all, you can have a much longer, more satisfying run in many free mobile games - and a leaderboard isn't much of an incentive to keep playing, but Disc Room has more going for it than that. There's a (at first) comically short minimum survival time for each level for 300% completion: the game seems calibrated to kill you a second before that. Death is woven into progression too: there's a collection aspect to discovering and dying to all 64 disc types, and certain rooms are only unlocked by dying in specific ways. There are also puzzles in certain rooms, where you'll rack up a few deaths experimenting with solutions. These all help take the stigma out of dying - in the Disc Room, you're there for the long run so you might as well get comfortable. Even with all that, I can't help getting hung up on certain levels, where lasting 20 seconds seems to rely on really nice starting RNG, prompting me to sit there dying and restarting in the lowest points of the game. Difficulty is very well pitched for basic completion but these grind the fun out of 300%. However this applies to around 6 of the 101 levels. If you felt 300% wasn't an adequate challenge, you can die to the several additional challenges, which I doubt many players will (or can) complete all of. Level design is really clever, with lots of variety and gameplay twists, giving each chamber its own identity. As well as changing the disc types in each chamber, other gameplay aspects are played with: what you see; how you move; how time works. This and the flavour text give the impression of an unstoppable sentient construct figuring out different ways to torture you. As you progress, even sometimes by dying, you uncover little bits of the general mystery of the story and world. It doesn't seem very complex, but even by 300% completion it doesn't seem to answer that many of the questions it first posed. If story is the main thing you go for in games, you'll probably be intrigued but not fully satisfied. Hopefully the upcoming "Turbo" DLC will address that.If the arcade action's getting too much, Disc Room has plenty of options for blunting the game's teeth. The speed of discs and other hazards can be slowed incrementally, down to just 10% of normal speed. Challenge difficulty can be reduced, and even blocks of levels can be unlocked instantly. It seems there are separate leaderboards for different difficulty settings, and 300% is possible on any setting. Where so many indie developers would insist on challenging the player or worry about compromising the product's value, Disc Room - one of the most imposing die-and-retry games I've played - turns out to be incredibly accessible.So you're not instantly obliterated, the developers hand you some lifelines. Believe it or not, you can spend three frames inside a disc before it tears you apart. When you're near a disc, time actually slows down to give you a brief opportunity to escape. Certain discs confer abilities on you; these are often too situational, but the ol' reliable dodge move usually gets the job done. In the thick of things you'll probably take these for granted, and celebrate each impossible disc dodge, each second over your personal best, as your own hard work. It might be the way that an exciting experience is provided as well as a challenge that has me coming back to it.That experience is made extra vibrant by Disc Room's look, sound and game feel, which all show superb attention to detail. The art is clear even at the game's busiest, easy on the eye and deliciously visceral. The soundtrack has wide range, from metallic existential terror to twitchy, creeping horror to explosive, frenetic chaos, and distorts nervously when you use an ability or get a bit close to danger. A subtle pause of a few frames gives each death a kinetic energy that made me jump sometimes.The story didn't quite do it for me, but in terms of classic 2D arcade magic, Disc Room has the full package, and with its accessibility options, I think a wide range of players will get a big kick out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty neat little game!The name of the game is 'dodge the stuff', and it's setup in a space where those familiar with bullet hell tropes will feel right at home.  The various gameplay trailers end up being an honest representation, outside of some neat puzzle elements that crop up here and there to break up the action.More technically, the implementation of the rules is 'correct'.  The hitboxes are slightly more lenient than they look.  The is no momentum in motion -- these are all good things.  If I had to complain about something, I'd say that the implementation of walking against the wall is pretty weak.  Instead of being able to slide smoothly against the wall, if you run at a slight angle, you tend to get 'caught' by the geometry.  This is a minor complaint in what is otherwise a very competent implementation of hit boxes and movement.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: The game has a ridiculous bug with 120 Hz monitors where the game plays at ~43 fps, which both looks really laggy and actually results in in-game slowdown, which is a very dumb problem to have in a game with leaderboards.The fact that this issue hasn't been fixed more than half a year after release is not a good sign, though I'll rescind the negative review if the devs do eventually fix it.---Neat reflex-based action highscore game. I initially bounced off the game in the first quarter hour, thinking what I saw was indicative of shallow design rather than simply being tutorial levels before the game truly opened up.I really liked the progression system - I usually find highscore games unmotivating, but at any point this game offers you multiple rooms to complete, witch each room in turn having lots of objectives: surviving for X seconds, dying to each disc, beating the dev team's highscore, ...---Now that I've finished the game, however, I do have to mention one huge source of frustration in the game design. The main gameplay room involves having to survive in a small room where a disc spawns every constant time interval (dt), and then you have to survive for X seconds. So the room gets harder the longer you survive, but any particular case of good or bad luck (e.g. disc spawn locations) isn't particularly impactful or frustrating. However, later rooms adjust this gameplay loop so that the survival timer doesn't advance by itself, but you instead have to either collect orbs (which always respawn at a random location once collected), or stand within a small circle or on floor tiles.So when such a level asks you to survive for 10s, it actually wants you to e.g. collect 10 orbs. Unfortunately, the difficulty increase in these levels remains tied to dt, not your actual score! As a result, these rooms are incredibly snowbally, and bad luck has an outsized impact. For instance, the orbs that advance the timer sometimes spawn below slow-moving enemies, thus wasting your precious time. And then you get doubly punished for something that's outside your control: time passes and new discs spawn, which you can't prevent; and you have to try and survive until the orbs are freed again.If the difficulty increases in these rooms were instead tied to your score, rather than the passage of time, you would still have an incentive to complete rooms quickly, but you wouldn't get doubly punished for mere bad luck.

_childDocuments_.review: Had all the achievement requirements, and the last room's timer requirement, been 5 seconds shorter, the game would've been a fun game to 100% and I would've recommended it gladly. As it is now, it's a piece of ♥♥♥♥ without compare.Had they used pre-determined patterns and leaned more into the puzzle aspect of the game for surviving x amount of time in the rooms, the game would've been so much better. Instead they use RNG for which direction each saw should move in.The hardest boss thanks to this RNG is the Armored Gatekeeper, the first boss of the game, followed by Lobotomy, which is an unholy union of 4 bosses (becomes 8 in hard mode).The hardest room by far, just following the game's internal timer requirements is the first room of the game in hard mode. You get an achievement for surviving 10 seconds in all hard mode rooms, and one for surviving 20 seconds in a hard mode room. The time needed to beat the final Hard Mode Room, so you can get to the credits, is 25 seconds. The most annoying room though, is the one that every 1 irl second removes 0.4 seconds from your timer and places it randomly onto the room floor, and you have to manage to clear the floor twice over to get 20s on your timer, and get the room "mastered". Never gonna even ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ try to bother with that, as its so RNG based that the chances of beating it seem to be about as slim as you winning the bloody lottery.Not to mention how the game uses an in-game timer that's disconnected from all other things that's dedicated solely to endlessly spawning more and more saw blades. """FUN""" in combination with powers that either stop your timer, or even decrease your timer, forcing you to engage in these extreme difficulty levels for longer.Almost all the powers in the game are naught but gimmicky:You have your standard invulnerable dash power, which halts the time for as long as you're dashing, has a 0.5s cooldown after using, and sometimes completely ♥♥♥♥♥ you over by either moving in the opposite direction of where you're heading, or doesn't activate when you press down the activate power button.You have a slow down time power, which freezes your timer for as long as it's active, can only be active for a short while, the closer it is to automatically deactivating, the faster everything in the room moves, and recharges really slowly.You have a cloning power, that takes (afaik) 0.4s from your timer and spawns a clone over the next 0.5s where you stood when you activated the power. Dying while the clone is spawning results in the clone insta dying.You have an absorption power that lets you absorb 1 saw blade from a room, and then when you next use the absorb power, the saw spawns where you were when you activated the power, taking about 0.5s before becoming corporeal. Doesn't affect the timer, and is useful in some scant few rooms.You have a blast power, that halts your timer as you charge up the blast, and also slows you down. When you release the blast all saws that are within the blast area get flung straight away from the player circularly, with pretty high velocity.And finally you have a mirror power. If the center of the room is {0,0}, and the bottom left corner is {-1, -1} and the top right corner is {1, 1}, then this power inverts the value of your x and y position. This power almost always teleports you to a spot that is occupied by a saw, as the game is a bullet hell, rendering it completely useless.Related to this is the character movement speed. The character moves like they're competing with Sonic the Hedgehog and the snake from Snake (Nokia 3310). The one hidden level where the character movement is locked to follow the Snake rules, you barely even notice a difference at all. There's no button to slow the character down, instead there are 2 buttons to increase the gameplay speed. Holding one down increases the game speed to 1.5x, and holding both down increases it to 2x. So most of the time you die to the bullet hell because the character moves too fast to perform precision movements.Most rooms are really easy and fun to play in, as you breeze through the goals set for you, both for achievements and unlocking new rooms. Shame the devs didn't bother to make these rooms more of a challenge, and instead compensated by making a scant few floors about as fun to do as placing a nail between your toe and the toenail, then kick a wall full force so the nail is driven into your foot, followed by you pulling it out by wiggling it around as much as possible.♥♥♥♥ this game, and the devs for not caring about the game enough to make it less jarring in difficulty. You could change the speed of the saws to be between 10% and 200% of normal speed, as well as the goal difficulty, making the game a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ joke to 100%, but I'm a person that wants to play hard games the intended way, and holy ♥♥♥♥ am I disappointed in what I got.Could've been great, but is just wasted potential and inane amounts of frustration if you want to get all achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes all you need is a simple concept to make a fun video game. Just a bunch of discs flying around trying to kill you and you’re good to go. That’s the concept behind Disc Room – the latest indie offering from publisher Devolver Digital.So, as I said, the concept behind the game is very simple. You’re dropped into a room with the sole goal of surviving as long as possible against an increasing number of deadly discs flying around. Some rooms you may be able to survive 30 seconds or so and some you may struggle to survive 10 seconds – the difficulty fluctuates wildly depending on the room. This is because the game has a surprising amount of variety both with the different disc types and with the setting for each room.Some rooms may have you simply dodging basic discs, but with very limited light and some may have you dodging a ton of little discs, but only counting time while standing in the center circle. And some may throw out all of that entirely and be a boss fight where your time increases only by picking up little droplets (which also happen to damage the boss). For such a simple concept, there’s a lot of depth packed into each room and it was fun figuring out how each disc worked and how to best handle them.The game also does itself a favor by way of responsive controls. Really, the only buttons you’re going to be pressing are your directional ones, your ability, and the occasional speedup. All are very responsive, and the overall movement feels fluid and intuitive. It makes dodging and weaving in and out of discs much more satisfying, no complaints there.The graphics too, while simple, are very effective for this type of game. The discs are clearly defined against the background and the color choices makes it easy to differentiate between them – all while looking good at the same time. And that is all coupled with some great music, of which there is actually a lot. The soundtrack runs almost an entire two hours, just short of how long it took for me to beat the actual game.My main complaint lies in the abilities. You get some really useful ones, like a dash that allows you to move through discs or a time slowdown, but then you get ones like being able to mirror yourself across a room or being able to consume and hold a single disc. The latter two I found to be very situational and almost useless in most of the rooms, so I pretty much always had either the dash or time slowdown equipped. The rest just simply aren’t that useful, it would have been nice to see the game expand their use maybe through additional objectives or whatnot.I should also mention that the game does have a story, but it’s told in these very small comic book snippets. They’re incredibly basic and don’t really add much, so don’t go into the game expecting much there. This isn’t really the type of game that needs a story anyways.So yeah, I’d recommend Disc Room. It’s got a simple concept, but some solid execution to back it up. Lots of variety, responsive controls, nice graphics and music – there’s not much to complain about here. It’s the type of game that knows what it wants to do and pretty much just does only that. Easy recommendation for fans of these fast-paced indie games or even bullet hell games, as it’s basically a fancy version of one of those.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Let's be real about what you're getting with this game:A grid-based map that you can visit nodes. Each node is a 10 (and 20) second challenge where you essentially dodge bullet-hell waves. Yes, they're thematically discs, but really this is a bullet-hell game.Skill plays a part in success, but in reality, you're going to be victim of RNG again and again and... . Discs are huge and most of the time they converge in a way that is impossible to dodge. Heck, 90% of the time just starting a level is insta-death if you don't guess the right direction to run.I like this game, but it has a deep flaw and that's simply unavoidable. I can't see past the massive amounts of charm and quality the game has, while overlooking the HUGE flaw in the gameplay.It's a game you should get at 75% or or better, because you're not missing a critical game if you skip it. It's just a corny bullet hell with sub-par mechanics and game design.All the floof: the graphics, sounds, theme, etc are awesome. But it doesn't soothe the fact that the underlying gameplay is thin.Sigh.Also don't be fooled by my play time. The game is fully experienced and you can beat it in about 3 hours. The rest I accidentally left it on in the background while I slept which inflated my hours. There's really not much "game" here.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah it's good, definitely one of the easiest bullet hell games out there but that label might not even apply in some peoples opinions because 90% of the time you can very obviously and clearly see the average projectile is bigger than a comparable bullet in other games (look at Isaacs base enemy tears or his base tears as an example) so a lot of this is simpler.Or rather it should be, see the game makes up for being able to dodge and work around the disc patterns easily through the large variety of things it does. Anybody going to 100% will find it difficult if they excel in one area, yeah even if that is dodging or being fast I have to say many rooms are purposely slower and more crammed with enemies all over, you're never going to blitz this game by applying one strategy to all rooms imo.It's criminal that this game doesn't get more love or recognition, you just don't see it pop out on the steam store anywhere unless you've gone far enough on a list of similar games. Many people who look at this will see a lot of discs and death and pass thinking it's really hard BUT on average it isn't, only when you start going to do more challenges or achievements do things start to ramp up.Oh there are also some puzzles that are just so obscure you are almost certainly not going to figure it out through trial and error (okay maybe you will but I didn't) and it isn't one or two rooms that do it, also a couple standout rooms just won't start a timer unless you do something first and I'm not referring to orb ones where you progress it yourself.So what's the verdict here? Simply that Disc Room is difficult but there are certain things you can do (not cheats) that will make it easier IF you need to, it's also pretty generous with achievement requirements because my second to last one was surviving 20 seconds in every room and the game fortunately only counted normal map which was good. Had it also required doing hard mode I would have definitely gave this game a negative review because such extreme difficulty for one achievement vs all the others would really sour the whole package for anybody wanting to complete it.Anyway that's the review and as the games base price is already really low I'm happy to say it is worth it on or off sale, don't let my playtime fool you as I went in with a lot of experience in similar games but you might gel better with it.

_childDocuments_.review: "Disc Room" is a great time-attack bullet-hell adventure where you play an unarmed scientist investigating the appearance of a disc-like structure, ultimatively getting trapped in a death-maze of existential proportions.The stlye of this game is gorgeous: art, animation (mostly spinning discs :D), writing (the bestiary reveals the dreaded thoughts of the protagonist), sound and music all blend well together, making it a trippy and chill, but also cold and exhilarating experience. Gameplaywise you traverse room by room and want to stay alive as long as possible in each of them to unlock further exploration, but some progression is also blocked by puzzles, secrets or unique deaths. Several puzzles were quite elusive (for me at least), but they add a little mystery to the mix.  "Disc Room" has replayability in terms of the many time attacks, but is not that long altogether. After you reach the end of the map, it gets mirrored for the "Hard Mode" (just like in "Symphony of the Night"), which cranks up the difficulty quite a lot.It is a unique title and quite polished, definetly worth checking out!
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty tough game, some few rooms give a lot more trouble than others. The game has really good, satisfyingly responsive controls and gameplay. The thing is that there is a lot of RNG, which can get tedious in some of the harder rooms, but generally you die and go and go again ad infinitum so briskly that along with the times where the sawblades move in your favour it evens out and becomes generally fair.It was interesting how sometimes there was a puzzle element to doing the rooms, as you need to have a good idea of what method to use, or be able to figure out how certain mechanics are working. Some of the puzzley parts of the game can be quite cryptic. There may also come a few times where the room just seems insanely hard and like you know everything there is to it, but turns out there was some thing you hadn't realized or noticed. It is hard to be that observant when it's live-die-repeat all the time. (I ended up looking up some very few things, though I think it might be possible to figure out what you're missing on your own eventually)The game has its own identity, and the music and art style help too.This is more of a 'fun' type of game. There's secrets and mysterious vibes to be sure, but story takes a big backseat to the furthering of the game loop. There are different very distinct areas the rooms are grouped by, which is nice, and you have some flexibility in picking and choosing which challenges you want to tackle next.There are also good accessibility options if the game is too rapid, and if you do use them you're even allowed to still get the achievements (if you care about that sort of thing). Overall I am quite happy with the game and it was a swell pleasant time.
_childDocuments_.name: Disc Room

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games that's so engaging that you forget to blink. There is a great amount of really well designed levels that are a joy to play. Weaving in between discs and trying to last as long as you can is really fun.Not all the levels are good though. There is a dark area that mostly sucks, and a couple of extremely RNG-dependent levels. However, if you're just trying to beat the game and not 100% it, then these won't be a huge issue.You also have abilities in this game, and a few of them are basically puzzle-exclusive, which I feel is really lame. Only 3 of the 6 abilities are widely applicable, and I feel like that's a missed opportunity.Still, this game is extremely fun and definitely worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked it. The concept is really fun and is executed to near perfection. There is also great variety in the different rooms and disc types which prevents the game from ever being boring, further supporting this fact is the absolute killer music that constantly blesses your ears while playing. I do have a few nitpicks with this game. First of all I wish the abilities were more useful. As it is now there are only 2 that are really worth using, which is only one third of the abilities. Another nitpick I have is that some rooms feel like complete bull****, although this is more of a warning than a critique since most of them are completely optional.However these really are just nitpicks and they were not big enough to effect my enjoyment of this game. I would highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: is a frighteningly good top down arcade game where your only aim is to avoid celestial discs moving with a distinctive rhyme and deadly rhythm. It's a polished little experience that's easy to learn and hard to master. A word of warning though, this game is objectively difficult due to it's largely luck based run to run variance. So despite best efforts to do things perfectly, there is always that randomness to each attempt that you have no control over. Anyway, I really did enjoy the style of this game. I tried to play this a year or so ago when it dropped on Xbox Game Pass, but I got all of 20 minutes in before I got annoyed and give up. Maybe I'm just better now but I didn't have as much trouble with it as back then. All of these games are about getting into a frame of mind where dying isn't 'failing' but rather another attempt in which you amount knowledge against said obstacle. It's about getting into a good pattern more than anything else. Oh yeah, another quick word on the technical side. This game doesn't respond well to high refresh monitors so like me you might open the game to a sub-60fps experience that jitters and exhibits slowdown. Go into NCP and set the program max framerate to 60. It will work fine then. I don't think it's possible to go any higher than that. There's an artificial framecap much like say, . Probably to keep all platforms on an even competitive playing field.But yeah, this is good fun. Buy on sale and bash head against wall.

_childDocuments_.review: A incredibly simple concept: dodge sharp pointy circles. That's the game. And boy is it done well.The controls are perfect; moving your joystick ever-so-slightly away from the buzz saws could be what would greatly extend your run. That's not all, but the audio plays a subtle warning of how close you are from death; and detail that just shows that Devolver knows how to create great games. However, while some levels are designed to test the players skills, it's not to say that the inherent design has some flaws.The big death saws are essentially random, which allows endless replay-ability and test of the players quick reflexes and adaptability. But because of that, some levels become incredibly luck based as they grow to levels of chaos hard to control. The level that comes to mind is the final level for the 2nd part after defeating the final boss. There's way too many discs in the room, leaving very few openings unless the randomness is in your favour. With a requirement of surviving 25 seconds, it becomes incredibly stressful as only more chaos is being added to the mixture, and it no longer becomes a test of skill, but rather luck into hoping that you get enough breathing room to survive.All in all, the game is a game I highly recommend. It's an incredibly simple concept and executed perfectly, especially if you enjoy high reaction requirement types of games.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels like for every optimal room designed with perfect symmetry and fairness in mind another three rooms replace it, rooms that are filled with disc types that just simply aren't fun to deal with and have little to no tracking pattern to learn or master. It seems like with Disc Room, the gimmick of a bullet-hell / dodgeball type game in which you encounter a diverse range of killer discs is on paper: a solid foundation for a modern arcade classic. Highscore addictions aplenty. And it can be that in a lot of ways. I just really can't fully recommend this game due to one of the worst end-game content slews I think I've ever experienced in an indie title.Much like The Messenger (which doesn't take long to beat either) once finishing the base levels (within an hour if you're completely uninterested in pushing your high scores) you're plunged into a hard mode where you go backwards through the levels, except now every single one of them are impossibly difficult to even get a pass in. Every disc you ever encountered beforehand now come back in the dozens wielding extra perks. Plenty of space here to just say that it's all completely unbalanced and unfun to partake in, so for what was a really solid 2 hours of perfect disc dodging action get's flipped on it's head and turned into an RNG fest.The charm was spot on and the steady pace of each level felt engaging and really well made but it seems like they had an idea that was spaced out totally wrong after their initial map of content. You can feel it the moment you hit those end-game levels. The fun-factor almost diminishes to nothing because you're suddenly running these rooms yet again but unable to use any of the knowledge and skill you have acquired up to that point. It's a frustrating design choice that ultimately lets Disc Room down.Full of charm and insanely addictive to better yourself on every level through that first run. Yet I can't recommend it due to it's absurdly bad 'cost to playtime' ratio. There is a tiny, fantastic gem of a game in that first stint of levels (which you could happily play over and over again). Therefore I would suggest waiting for a heavy discount

_childDocuments_.review: A game of this style, in my opinion, needs to nail four aspects: be predominantly skill-based, have tight and responsive controls, have fast resetting after every death, and have a kick-ass soundtrack. This game smashes the latter three of those and attempts the fore-most with varying degrees of success and failure.To start with, I most certainly do recommend this game. It is more fun than not and there is a lot of variety in how you’ll approach different challenges depending on the type of saws you are up against in any particular room. One thing that I was hoping would be the case, and I’m thankful it is, is there are multiple rooms open at any one time meaning you can hop between rooms if one is too difficult or becoming annoying (more on that later). The soundtrack is on point and I think it is a truly crucial part of this game because even with some of the aforementioned annoying rooms, the soundtrack is just a great listen and so you can continue to enjoy the game through the soundtrack. On top of that, deaths are a quick interlude between attempts, which is good because you will die a lot; after completing the game 300% I accrued over 3500 deaths. In terms of gameplay and controls the game has a standard mode for you to complete. Each room has a set of connected rooms that can be unlocked by completing certain challenges. Once you’ve completed each room in there you unlock hard mode, which are harder versions of the rooms in the standard mode…in theory. You see, in my opinion, these rooms can actually be far easier than their regular counterpart since you only need to survive half the time to count as being completed. Although they are objectively harder versions with faster saw spawn rates and faster saw movement, only having to survive 10s vs 20s is actually a huge benefit. Part of the gameplay hitches on dying to saw blades; inevitably you will die and to progress you need to die to each different type of saw blades. I heard a lot of people complain that ‘dying to progress’ is a bad game mechanic but having now completed the game, I completely disagree. At first, it seems fairly pointless, but dying to specific saw blades can be really challenging and, in some cases, puzzles in themselves. The controls for this game are very responsive and at no point did I feel like the character moved when it shouldn’t have or lagged behind in anyway, though I would personally recommend a gamepad over a keyboard for the finer movements you can make. There is a story; it’s a bit cryptic, doesn’t make too much sense (to me) and I had to look it up to understand it but it’s there. There are also abilities…all of which pale in comparison to the first ability you get which is the dash ability. To be fair, most of these abilities are fun and interesting and can help unlock extra rooms, but there are far too situational and the dash ability lets you dash through saws, so you can always get out of a cornered situation.However, one thing that I must mention is how much randomness encroaches on the later rooms of the game. It is inevitable that an element of randomness exists in this game; if it weren’t there then you could just memorise the patterns of what would happen and then it is less of a matter of skill and rather a matter of memory. This means that every time you start a room, saws spawn in different orientations. This is fine, except on those occasions were saws spawn in such a way that it becomes impossible to avoid a wall of saws barrelling towards you. For the most part, these are rare occurrences, but the hardest rooms are the ones with pure random nonsense in them. The room lobotomy is the epitome of this where you have to survive 20s with all four of the mini-boss antibody saws (and notice how I say mini-boss, since each of these are considered hard enough to warrant their own room in the game). In order to have a slim hope of surviving the second phase from 10s – 20s, you have to rush through the first phase, because waiting for anytime will let tonnes of saws spawn in to the point where the room is entirely covered. This means that the only way to feasibly win is to deliberately go for manoeuvres that are probably not going to work and die over and over again with no thought-out plan. This isn’t the only offender, but given how the vast majority of the game felt fair and fun, these few rooms really stand out as frustrating. I also did not enjoy the lights-out area, where light is limited or blinking on and off constantly. I get why it is a mechanic but it made that area really painful for hard mode, since saws can spawn and kill you while the light hasn't cycled back on yet.There are also optional challenges, like complete the game with less than so-many deaths or complete the game at 200% game speed, though I can’t imagine the pain of completing the RNG heavy rooms with some of those modifiers.Overall, I recommend this game and I would encourage trying for 300%. You may give up at 299%, which I nearly did with the Lobotomy room, but the main game only takes around 3 hours and some of the hard rooms can be really fun to nail so It's worth going the extra mile. I’m mostly a casual player but even if you’re a casual player or a competitive leaderboard chaser, this game is really fun for a range of audiences.

There are levels you can hit the challenge time easily, but later on find out you need a minimum time in all rooms to progress further. As a lot of people have said it can be very luck based, but overall I felt in enough control of my own destiny that it wasn't an issue.The music is suitable, though not particularly varied. _childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Disc Room is an avoid em up w/ a unique setting and art design.  Devolver Digital is one of my very favorite publishers and is known for high quality, well designed games.  Unfortunately, I found Disc Room to be extremely underwhelming during my 2 hrs playing it.  If you are itching for a well designed avoid em up, I'd highly recommend Just Shapes and Beats, Soundodger+, Hyperdot, or Ellipsis.  What's Good:-Disc Room has a really unique look for a game in this genre.  The environment feels really natural, almost like you are walking from one death room to another in a large, connected world.  I thought this was a cool choice since most games in this genre don't look quite as natural visually.-You can unlock several unique perks which mixes things up.  You can unlock a dash, clone, slowmo, absorb, blast, and a mirror effect.  I unlocked the first 4 during my 2 hrs playing and each one has different advantages and disadvantages.  This can add a layer of strategy when approaching levels.  -This is a very well polished game.  It's extremely easy to learn and movement feels really fluid.  This is something that players can take for granted but is extremely important in making the player feel like he has complete control of his character.-The game runs really smoothly at 60 fps, and I didn't experience a single bug or mechanical issue.  Could Use Some Changes:-The biggest frustration I had w/ this game was the lack of information.  It doesn't provide w/ much information.  In order to learn how the abilities work, you have to experiment w/ them.  Some of the levels expect you to use a specific ability in a specific way, when you probably have never used it like that before.  Several times, I wasn't sure how to progress and I had to go watch a walkthrough to see how to get access to a new level.  -This is an extremely short game w/ a very limited appeal for reaplayability.  I had completed 58% of the game in less than 2 hrs.  To make this even worse, I probably spent almost 30 minutes pausing it while trying to figure out how to move on to the next level.  There isn't a level creator or community made levels.  This seems extremely limited from a $15 game.-Some of the levels feel like pure luck, especially as you are milliseconds away from the goal time.  The patterns in each level never change but the margin for error is so tiny.  It's a fine line between making levels challenging, and making them tediously difficult to the point where you must complete the level perfectly the way the dev intended.  This takes away freedom and creativity from the player.-The Avoid em up genre is an extremely simple genre.  Great games in this genre make sure that the music and aesthetic sink up w/ the moment to moment gameplay.  This is an area where Disc Room falls really short.   Although I like that the environment looks really natural, it's not nearly as visually exciting as better games in this genre.  On top of that, the soundtrack is nothing special imo.  That really limits what this game can offer.  Thoughts:-I was so certain that this would be another solid game for me to enjoy.  I thought that I would have a fun 6-8 hr experience and move on to something else.  Disc Room doesn't really bring anything new to the genre, and it's really tough recommending this when there are some incredible games in this genre for basically the same price.  Just Shapes and Beats is a work of art that is mesmerizing visually and auditorily.  Soundodger+ and it's sequel both offer endless content, tons of variety, and endless replayability.  There are many more that I would recommend before playing this.Consensus:-Bottom Shelf Game (Tier 5 and makes up 10% of my reviews).  If you are a diehard fan of Devolver Digital or the avoid em up genre, I can't fault you for snagging this on a sale.  But I would warn you to lower your expectations.  This game has extremely good reviews, so maybe it just wasn't a good fit for me.  Nonetheless, I can't recommend this game b/c I never found it very fun, engaging, or unique.

_childDocuments_.review: Had a great time with this little game. Very tight and lean gameplay. Basically, you enter a series of rooms with a huge variety of different sawblades to dodge as long as you can. Progress by surviving for a certain amount of time to unlock more rooms. You also unlock a small selection of abilities of which you can use one at a time.This is basically the perfect arcade-y experience for those of us who just want to sit down and play a game, with absolutely no filler. A little short, it took me about 4 hours for me to complete all rooms in normal and hard mode, although I didn't 100% the game. If you do want 100% there's a little more content, but also there is a huge amount of speedrunning support if that's your jam. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: It is what it says in the title, there is a disk room.Or something like 60+ disk rooms. The concept of "stay alive as long as possible in a room full of lethal objects" is nothing new, but what Disk Room pulls off so well is keeping things fresh at almost every turn. Each new room has a high chance of introducing a new hazard to play around, a new combination or even a new gameplay core which makes increasing your score all the more of a challenge.The best bit is this is conveyed most often without a single word of text being needed. No need to spend a bunch of time reading stuff, although you can read little blurbs of text that are unlocked with each new disk that kills you.  Also of note are multiple sliders designed with the sole purpose of making things easier (or harder!) for yourself as you play. There's no shame in using these, and the game will still adjust certain things as needed to keep the experience decent and challenging at the same time.Overall, pick it up. Good pick up and play kind of thing for a quick timesink, or for, in my case, a 2-3 hour binge.
