_childDocuments_.review: This is my first game in the Yakuza franchise, and it's a stand-alone story that makes a perfect entry point for people unfamiliar with the titles.  Before I get to my review though, a warning:If you suffer from motion sickness while playing games, you might think twice about this one.  The combat uses a fixed/isometric camera that only moves when changing targets, or switching between party members after their turn is over.  That might not sound too rough, but once you've got a full party (and you're facing upwards of ~6 enemies at a time) that means the camera will swing pretty wildly from one angle to another, in a way that I found slightly nauseating myself - even though motion sickness is not a usual problem of mine.Carrying on.The story in Like a Dragon is shockingly good, and not something I expected from the goofball trailers.  Expect the first ~5 hours of gameplay to mostly be comprised of you ferrying the main character (Ichiban) from one story point to another, with very little in the way of player agency.  Not necessarily a bad thing, but be prepared for that starting out.As far as the bones of the story go, it's a very good take on the Hero's Journey.  Ichi is a character that is easy to fall in love with, which actually caused me to hate him a bit in the early hours of his story.  He is kind, loveable, an all around Good Guy's Good Guy, but he has zero sense of his own self-worth.  He puts himself in the worst situations imaginable, sacrificing himself again and again, and all for the sake of people who appear to give zero f***s about him.  It's to be forgiven if you begin to get a bit disgusted with a man who willingly acts like a kicked dog, but one without the good sense to just run away.  His story is about finding his own sense of worthiness, finding people who genuinely care about him and are willing to sacrifice for him the way he does for them.  It's a very long story, and Ichi will test your love (and your patience) many times before he finally starts to see the truth himself: That he deserves better.  It's a journey of redemption worth taking, and one I highly recommend.The turn-based combat is good, not great, but the goofy classes and abilities really perk it up.  I don't have a lot to say here, other than that it works, and stays at least somewhat enjoyable throughout the game.  There's not a lot I can tell you that you can't find in the many game guides that exist for LaD.For the rest of the gameplay, there's a lot to do, but the sidequests are really where it's at.  They are quirky, fun, and a great diversion to the unexpected (but not unwarranted), more serious tone of the main narrative.  The minigames are mostly tired examples of the usual open-world minigame fare, and not very well-tuned ones at that.  I recommend skipping any mg's not directly attached to story, stats or achievements - so mostly the business management game.  I should warn you that the games DLC is entirely unnecessary to the gameplay experience.  The additional classes are apparently pretty OP, but I never felt like I needed them, and the business management extras are entirely unneeded.  I was easily able to max out every aspect of that mg using only the employees I found throughout the game, and those earned directly through the mg itself.It's also worth noting that 100% of the game can, and  be done in a single playthrough.  You might be tempted to try NG+ after completing the main story, especially if you're struggling to complete the final tower challenges/achievements, but that is actually a terrible idea.  You can trust me on that, I spent over 125 hours in LaD's endgame trying different paths to see what worked best, and this is the one place the gameplay gets rough.  The reason here is that the only truly important factor of tackling that content is your characters' level/job levels, and leveling those at endgame becomes a true chore.  There is only one method for leveling your characters consistently, hunting/farming Invested Vagabonds in one of the game's dungeons.  The game really provides no other method for farming adequate amounts of EXP, and switching to NG+ makes this problem worse - not better.  All enemies on NG+ (regardless of having the same numerical level as their regular game counterparts) have much more powerful base stats, but the EXP reward is only very slightly higher than fighting them in your first playthrough.  Just stick to the farming guides provided online, and you'll get there fast.Aside from that, my only other disappointment with this game is the ridiculous sexism seemingly inherent in most Eastern games these days.  The game even takes a sloppy stab at mocking "wokeness" without doing anything to address how clearly stilted the game is towards male audiences.  There are no female enemies among the games' regular mobs, there is exactly 1 female enemy in the story, but men handle the fighting for her.  The female characters are all dramatically weaker than the males, and there is nothing the women can do that the men can't do better.  Men get twice as many classes, including things like Hero, Hitman, Gangster, etc.  Meanwhile, the female characters have their own set of jobs, and they are all deeply subservient ones, such as Hostess, Clerk and Barmaid.  The only two that 'break that mold' don't do it well, since they are Idol and Night Queen (Dominatrix), and are essentially just objects of desire, so still servants of male needs.  Literally all of the female characters (save one) can be "romanced" by Ichi, no matter how gross and inappropriate the relationship;  you romance one by saving her from her own ineptitude, taking over her family business in the business management minigame, and steering it towards greatness with the obvious ease that apparently only a man could bring to the table.  Another you romance by again saving the family business she is ineptly running in to the ground, this time by just giving her a bunch of money, and then beating up her deadbeat dad.  The romance scenes themselves are additionally problematic, with two of the female characters having an identical cut-and-paste scene where they wait on Ichi to be passed out drunk before kissing him.  Choosing to pursue all of the romance options is very doable, with the only penalty being a scene where the girls beat Ichi up... but the whole thing gets played off as a misunderstanding, and Ichi is otherwise free from any actual consequences of effectively cheating on all of them with each other.What's sad is that these things could have easily been avoided, by giving women access to the same jobs as men, and by just not including the romance crap at all.  It's all very superfluous and unnecessary.  The conversation or two that take a stab at "woke culture" make it apparent that the developers understand that many players will find this crap distasteful, but decide to go in that direction anyway out of stubborn dedication to the dated sensibilities of the patriarchy.  It's actually a little gross, and the only true stain on an otherwise perfect game.Still, LaD is a B+ experience overall... provided you're not a female player who expects to be in any way respected as something other than a servant of men, or an object of male desire.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely amazing. First of all, there's so many things to do that you'll easily get distracted from the main game. From sub-stories, to running a business, to even hitting baseballs, this game is jam-packed with things to keep you busy. And even if you're not a fan of turn-based RPGs, this game manages to make the battle system fun and thrilling. You'll constantly be doing action commands, getting perfect guards, and making sure you and your opponents are in the right position for your attack. This game has a lot of talking and cutscenes, but they're all interesting and enthralling so you'll never get bored watching them. This game manages to find a perfect balance between serious and hilarious. One minute you'll be trying to expose a fraudulent retirement home, and the next minute you'll be trying to catch a guy who's been pissing in the lake. In conclusion, this game is tons of fun. With tons of things to do, a fun battle system, and great writing, this game gets my full recommendation.(To clarify, the reason it says I got 18 minutes was because the game ran like trash on my computer, so I refunded it and bought on another platform.)

_childDocuments_.review: I don't even really know what to say about Yakuza: Like a Dragon. It's simply transcendent - an incredible advancement and reinvention of a series that already has no misses, seamlessly handling shifts in protagonist, tone, and gameplay style, and setting up the franchise for an even brighter future than before. Yakuza 0 remains the gold standard, but Like a Dragon sits juuuuuust below it.Following Yakuza 6 and the supposed departure of Kiryu as the central protagonist, Like a Dragon introduces Ichiban Kasuga as the franchise flag-bearer going forward, and let me tell you, this is a great move. I love Kiryu, he's an icon, but it was extremely refreshing to play through a Yakuza narrative with a protagonist that's actually able to react to things with more than restrained annoyance. Ichiban is exuberant, expressive, relentlessly positive even after he's handed heaping mounds of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at every turn by the narrative. Kiryu is in some sense a product of the time in which the franchise began - beyond him being an ex-yakuza, the stoic, calm exterior simply was easier to manage with PS2 level 3D models, and once the baseline of his personality was set, there was no way or reason to change him. Ichiban, by contrast, can be more expressive thanks to the leaps and bounds of 3D gaming in the fifteen years between Yakuza 1 and Like a Dragon, and RGG Studio makes the most of that freedom with a protagonist that contrasts quite a bit with Kiryu. The two of them, though, share a strong, caring heart at their core, putting the people they love above all else in the face of impossible odds.Even more impactful than the change in protagonist, though, is the change in gameplay style. Rather than being a beat-em-up, Like a Dragon is a full-on turn-based RPG, with magic, skills, a full set of party members to manage, dungeons...it's a complete change-over in tandem with the shift to Ichiban as the protagonist, and I think RGG Studio did an amazing job considering they'd never made a turn-based RPG before. The battle system is fun and has some intriguing, unusual ideas, containing mechanics that feel specifically referential to the beat-em-up style - character positioning matters in terms of who gets hit by multi-target attacks and whether attacks even land, though positioning can't be controlled by the player, adding an element of randomness to the combat. Ichiban can also pick up weapons in the overworld during battle to use in place of his standard attack, though this doesn't really have much of an impact on battle when it happens. The justification for the shift in battle style comes from Ichiban, explained in-game as a manifestation of his overactive imagination, which allows RGG Studio to throw in a bunch of crazy fantasy elements to the combat, where the enemies who are, in reality, just thugs or hoodlums, turn into more fantastical demon-like characters in battle. Even the major bosses, who mostly retain their own appearances, feature crazy moves with tons of special effects. It's particularly funny to contrast this with the way the job system is implemented, where every job class is literally a kind of profession - barmaid, detective, chef, etc. The battle system is deep and engaging, though I found that the overabundance of skills in the skill list once you've mastered a job to be a bit annoying to scroll through when a lot of them are just stronger versions of earlier skills. And, despite the depth and fun of the combat, there are times during the story when it can get quite monotonous, mashing the standard attack button just to get through the eight millionth annoying random overworld encounter where the enemies are clearly ten levels lower than you and therefore a waste of your time. Couple that with the dearth of EXP you get from non-story fights, and sometimes the combat wears on you more than excites you, but on balance, the gameplay is great and well-considered, and I greatly enjoyed my time with it.The story, simply put, is absolutely incredible. Naturally, given that this is a party-based RPG, themes of friendship and connections are threaded throughout the narrative. It's done incredibly well, though - Ichiban has a natural magnetism to him that manifests constantly throughout the story, pulling together disparate groups of people to unite against a common threat. Family is another major theme running throughout, exploring the idea of what constitutes a person's family, and the things one would do to support the ones they love. This is not a story that could be told with Kiryu, simply because of his stature within the Tojo Clan as early as Yakuza 2 - Ichiban, by contrast, is basically a random thug at the bottom of the clan, and his story importance is derived entirely from the familial connections he's formed within the clan, finding himself wrapped up in a sinister, wide-ranging plot that gripped me and never let me go. I was constantly fighting the urge to blitz through the main story, prying myself away to give the side content the focus it deserved, but if I could have had my way, I would have marathoned the thing. It's a level of engaging, affecting storytelling that the series doesn't always reach, and it results in an all-time narrative, easily top 3 in the franchise to this point.Speaking of side-content, man did I spend a lot of time on it. The major side-game this time is a business management simulator where you buy up properties and have to staff them effectively to maximize revenue generation, fighting through a shareholder meeting every few runs in order to advance the story within the minigame. Once you're really rolling in this mode, it becomes an extremely valuable method of generating money for Ichiban, which is extremely important for ensuring your gear is sufficient as the game grows in difficulty, among other things. The rest of the side-content is what you'd expect - a lot of substories, common minigames like the batting cages, karaoke (particularly satisfying in this game given that every party member EXCEPT FOR ONE has their own song), hostess chats, and new minigames like a Mario Kart clone and keeping Ichiban awake while watching a movie. Side content in this game consumed a huge amount of my play time, and really helps to make this game feel absolutely massive - the new region of Ijincho has a map that's ridiculous large, far larger than any previous region map, dwarfing Kamurocho in particular, and it is packed to the brim with things to do.I could go on forever about Yakuza: Like a Dragon. I had such a wonderful time with this game, and I both never wanted it to end and desperately needed to see how the story wrapped up. The combat is just as fun as the beat-em-up style, Ichiban is an EXTREMELY worthy protagonist going forward, I love every party member, the core story is both uplifting and heartbreaking, with fascinating implications for the future of the series, the side content is seemingly endless...this is a triumph of a game, and RGG Studio should be extremely proud of the end result. Huge, huge, huge recommend.don't buy the DLC though

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the fence when going into this game as it's the first Yakuza/Like a Dragon game to be a turn-based JRPG rather than using the brawler style combat from previous entries. I'm not really a fan of JRPGs typically however there are a few exceptions (such as Persona 3 and 4) but they're few and far between. When I originally started this game back in March 2022, I thought it was alright but in addition to not being a massive fan of the combat to begin with, I was suffering from a huge burnout on the Yakuza series having played through 0-6 in the span of about 3 months (and considering the length of these games, it's very easy to understand why). I ended up stopping midway through Chapter 4 and left it for almost a year. After beating Judgment a few weeks ago I decided to jump back into this game and I am so glad that I did. The combat itself isn't anything particularly special however it manages to keep being engaging through the whole game and for the most part, doesn't require any grinding which is the main reason I'm not a huge fan of turn-based JRPGs. But the story. The story in this game is genuinely one of the best this series has to offer, alongside Judgment. It manages to be a great entry-point for newcomers, while still offering moments for series veterans. The cast is great and has so much depth, especially when you choose to bond with them at Survive Bar. Overall, I may have initially been disappointed about the turn-based combat and a new main character instead of Kiryu, however I can safely say now that this game does almost everything right.

_childDocuments_.review: After 7 games of beat 'em up action, Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio launched a joke video on April Fools Day of Yakuza doing a turn-based JRPG angle. This got so much positive reactions that the devs actually made that joke a reality. So how good did the joke land?Yakuza: Like A Dragon is such a blast to play. It emulates that 0 feeling by having a well structured and engaging story, and effectively serves as an origin story to new series mainstay, Ichiban Kasuga. A lowly grunt working for the Arakawa Family in early 2001, he has to take the fall for a kill gone wrong. 18 years later, he is released from prison to find an unfamiliar world, in an unfamiliar setting. This introduction is ripe for a beginner to the series to indulge in, but certain story events and past characters showing up hit so much harder if you started from 0 and played all the way up until 6 especially. The passing of the torch to Ichiban is a well done one, while Kiryu was certainly a great protagonist in his own right, it is refreshing seeing a protagonist who really goes all out on his emotions and really, you can't help but root for a guy like him. His party members are also a joy to have around, especially as Ichiban relies on his friends much more than Kiryu ever did. The story is also phenomenal, probably the second best behind 0's.But story aside, what about the shift to a turn-based JRPG format? Honestly, Yakuza contextualised in this format works surprisingly well. It doesn't really innovate, but more just evokes that old timey JRPG feel. It probably helps if you're a fan of Dragon Quest, as they actively mention that Ichiban grew up playing them and basically imagines his encounters much like those games would be. A very conventional take on an unconventional setting of modern day Yokohama Japan. Active button presses for skills and guarding give some agency to keeping interest in fights, and being able to skip lengthy skill animations are a good step. It's rather humorous seeing the tropes and hallmarks of those being done in a watered down, down to earth setting (well, as much as Yakuza can get anyways). Having characters being able to switch jobs helps too, but it's obvious which jobs are good for which characters most of the times, having retainable skills from each job helps in encouraging diversity though. It's the Alien: Isolation of JRPGs in that for a first attempt at a different genre shift, it's a damn good first impression. A little bit more tweaking and this would have been perfect.While the main method of going through the games may have changed, one thing that hasn't, the abundance of minigames. Karaoke is pretty well done with the new cast of characters singing, with Adachi's take on Machine Gun Kiss being a noteworthy one. There's a Mario Kart type minigame, a can collecting minigame set against hobos, personality tests that actually improve your personality, fighting sheep men in a movie theatre to avoid falling asleep, and even a capitalist simulator thrown into the mix. However, if you ever decide to do mahjong, they made the AI insanely tough, so don't expect an easy time if you liked doing it in the past. There's no real incentive to do the Completion List (or the Challenges section) this time around as all they give you are Personality boosts, and you'll max them all long before you finish everything on that list anyways.Substories are very charming as usual, and even have some callbacks to older games, a real treat for fans that have been around before this game. Ichiban's take on things helps make these substories stand out. You can even raise your bonds with your teammates by having a drink with them, unravelling their personal stories and problems. Not only does this offer backstory on your crew, it also helps in combat too, so it always helps to be a friend. Soundtrack is a banger, as usual, with many new, and recurring tracks being used to great effect.I see a lot of potential in the future of the Yakuza series as a JRPG series. Was it weird to do a genre shift in the mainline titles, and relegating the beat 'em up gameplay to the Judgment spin-off series? Yes, but after 15 years or so of doing beat 'em up gameplay, I can understand why RGG Studios would want to do something new and different. Ichiban's tales clearly work better given that he himself is a Dragon Quest nut. With Nagoshi gone and a sequel in the works, it will be interesting to see how Yakuza progresses in this new world. As the endgame song says, "welcome Ichiban", I hope you're here to stay.

_childDocuments_.review: So I hated the idea of this game existing when it was announced as Shin Ryu Ga Gotoku (New Yakuza) or Ryu Ga Gotoku 7,  a huge part of why I play the Yakuza series is its gameplay and this game decided to throw that aside and change the genre completely and turn it into a turn based RPG.I only bought this game to test out my new graphics card, and now look at me - ~250 hours invested into the game and all achievements.The game has its downsides - later enemies are just damage sponges taking ages to kill, the grind is intense for two bosses in particular at the end, and the game relies on your positioning in the 3D battlefield to determine what enemies you can hit and how many they'll affect but you are unable to control where your characters are.But the good far outweighs the bad. The job system allows really funny and unique gameplay styles, the characters are really really fun and Ichiban is a well made refreshing new protagonist to carry the Yakuza series' torch for the next decade. I could write, and have written essays on how Ichiban is a well made character with a better start to a saga than kiryu got, but I'll save that for you to experience yourself - just consider playing more Yakuza first and seeing just how much you can tell is inspired from the other protagonists.Y:LAD is a game you can experience without ever having touched a Yakuza game before so turn based RPG fans can get into the series, and I'd love them to, they really should get to experience Yakuza as well. Please consider picking this game up, especially if it's on sale. Thank you.

Why did I start with the latest one? No idea, I'm stupid I guess. Anyways, this game has exceeded any of the expectations I had of it just from the first Chapter you play through. You become intertwined with the characters progression, you care about minimal things like levelling up your characters personality, and it's just a whole boat load of fun to play. I'm nearly 30 hours into it, and I feel like I'm just getting started (mainly due to the fact that the mini games are insanely addictive). The fighting sequences are spot on, the special attacks the people you fight as are hilarious, but also well-fitting to the aura of the game. It doesn't take itself too seriously, and that's what makes this game pretty much perfect to me.Also, this game has made me want to explore other games in the JRPG category which I was adamant I would never get on with. GGs, Yakuza - you've won me over.

_childDocuments_.review: I admit, when I first heard that one of my favorite series is changing it's core battle system, I was scared. I was wondering if I should buy it, and I finally did, and let me tell you... it was one of the Yakuza games I have ever played - and I played all of them. Not only the system turned out to be fun and rewarding, it also opened a new path for the series as a whole. It really feels like you're playing D&D, or Dragon Quest, when you're along Ichiban and his crew, facing odds never seen before.Also, regarding other aspects of the game - the story is superb. Ichiban turns out to be such an amazing character, having the kindness of a saint and a heart of pure gold. However, what I appreciate the most is his tenacity, his neverbending will to go forward - it's inspiring. His crew is also one to remember - every single of his party members feels like a person, not a cardboard cutout. The other aspects of the story also also amazing, with each plot twist feeling like another step in a long journey to the top.The only aspect I didn't like was the lack of more content to do outside of the story - while Ijincho feels good, it lacks essence when it comes to spending your free time. Kamurocho and Sotenbori feel even worse, being more akin to additional restaurant and shop locations that fully fledged areas. I think when Yakuza 8 comes along, SEGA will take opinions into account and make it so that those areas feel more full of life. All in all, I truly loved the game, and I hope I'll get to see the rest of the series on Steam soon!

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished this game yesterday, after a good 3 years I've finally caught up with the mainline Yakuza/Like a Dragon storyline. I am so excited for what's next in the coming years, and of course, doing the spinoff games in the meantime. This game was great and I hate the fact that I went and spoiled some of the juicy parts while the game was fresh out of the oven (A terrible habit of mine when it comes to media) and I was still dabbling with the earlier entries, nevertheless I enjoyed the story a lot. Just, don't be like me yanno?For anyone new who's looking to get into the franchise, this one is a great entry point, and a great game to stand in its own right. While I still recommend trying out Yakuza 0 first for example (You'll come to appreciate some things a lot more, and yknow it's also just a lot cheaper in case you're curious about the franchise as a whole), it is by no means absolutely necessary. While this is now a full on JRPG, it's very much a Yakuza game through and through, it's engaging, at times very silly, and at other times very heartwarming, and at other other times very emotional. You got your silly moves, bizarre sidequests, a plethora of minigames and your virtual Japan to walk on through.I'll talk about the combat from my perspective, since I reckon a lot of people are having mixed feelings about it coming into this game from the previous ones. Coming into this one myself, I didn't actually have any doubts at all. All my friends were enjoying this game to bits, and I already knew how much great stuff this studio has brought to me, so I ended up welcoming the change of pace. I think it started out kinda rough, but once I started getting more moves, more party members and having the job system on my hands, I started to enjoy it a lot more. Kind of a standard JRPG feel in that, and I'm sure that's what they were going for, as the same can be seen in a lot of aspects of the game. The combat itself in action is flashy and goofy, you will have a lot of moves at your disposal, and there's a lot of cool and memorable summons as well, you could tell they had a lot of fun making it and put a lot of love into each and every attack.That feel, however includes those negative aspects too, such as difficulty spikes and grinding sessions. Towards the end the game throws quite a bit of grindwalls at you, though if you're the type of guy who feasts on most if not all of the side activities and tidbits and that, it might not be a problem. Personally, I don't like to spend too much of my time with them as I'm going through the main story so when enemies suddenly started to be like 15 levels above me, and some bosses had some insane difficulty spikes, I started to really hate my time with the combat, finding it more of a nuisance than anything. There's also some balance issues with your own moves, like with one character a move that costs you around 6 MP would be stronger than any other move they have, and I didn't really get it until the very last stages of the game, going off busting moves that cost me 35-50 MP and burning my small meter away prior. The random encounter rates were also a huge pain in the ass lmao, in Yakuza games I really like to just take my time exploring the city, but in this one I felt like I had to be running around at all times since I would encounter a pack of goons at every damn block. During the late game stages this was especially annoying, since the amount of exp and money the encounters give you is next to nothing. Luckily you can obtain an accessory that disables the random encounters later on, but I seriously hope they tone it down on the next entry, and make it feel more rewarding. In the previous entries I didn't mind them at all (except for maybe Yakuza 5), since you could just beat them up in a matter of 15 seconds and they weren't even nearly as disruptive. Overall, I think they did a nice job for a first time, and while in retrospect these JRPG tropes among a lot of other tropes I haven't mentioned are funny and neat to think about in context, I found them to be more frustrating as I was playing. I hope that LAD8 handles these things in a much better way, so that the game would feel fun through and throughout, for a guy who just wants to see what's gonna go down story wise first and foremost.The story itself was fantastic. Lots of twists and turns, each making you want to see what's next, with a lot of emotional weight at different stages. The characters, your party members, your in game buds were so well written too, each feeling so very human and the story handled different subjects revolving around them very well. But man, Ichiban. I wasn't sure of how to take this guy having been watching Kiryu for a couple of years, but all my worries have been washed away. His actor (I played with the japanese audio) did a tremendous job, whatever the guy did or felt, felt so real to me, SO many kudos to him. As a lot of other reviews say, we all need a Ichiban Kasuga in our lives. The guy's a goofball, a ray of optimism and positiveness, and a trooper. Everytime I saw his dumb smile on his face on screen whenever he's goofing off or referencing Dragon Quest, I'd have the biggest smile on my face too. That's not to say that he's always just goofing off, ♥♥♥♥ gets real at times and boy does it feel real. Always fun to follow his adventures and misadventures, he absolutely dominates the screen everytime he's at it. He's a great friend to everyone around him, he's precious, and boy I can't wait to see more of him in the future.Gonna end my wall of text here, after being obsessed with this game for the past few weeks I felt like I had to gush about it in some way or another. Very much recommend to anyone, and for a series fan who's about to take this entry on, kick back and enjoy. Though if you absolutely despise turn-based combat then you might wanna reconsider, but I think the characters and the story carries it a lot. Just... know that you're gonna be in for some classic JRPG bs, mostly the grindwalls that I mentioned later on in the game. You got this though, keep being awesome and I hope you're having a great day, I shall now proceed on to shutting my mouth and ending this ""review"" here lmao

_childDocuments_.review: Whether you're fan of the series or not, this is simply a great game, maybe one of the best I've played in years. I have to admit that JRPG style turn based combat isn't everybody's thing, though everything including classes (literally jobs in the game) are top notch regarding humor. Here's a brief overlook on the game's aspects:- Graphics (9/10)To me, the graphics might not be the most realistic ones but I still find the game itself beautiful, whether it's day or night within the game. I substracted 1 point for facial graphics as they might be slightly better. Overall great though.- Story (10/10)Whether the game story or substories (around 50 I think), the overall narrative is great in my opinion. There are lots of plot twists which are not uncommon in the series. I think the whole experience was great and kept me playing. Some might find the cutscenes a bit long but I enjoyed it very much.- Gameplay (10/10)As a player who enjoys turn based JRPG combat and having played several iconic games of the genre, I prefer this combat system over the previous beat'em up style action combat. Minigames are fun except baseball in which I suck apparently. Jobs are really fun, humorous and variable, making the player experiment with them. I'm guessing that there are meta builds etc. but I had never needed to check online to look up for some builds to complete the challenges the game offered. The end game content can be a little bit grindy but I never got bored. Overall gear variety and crafting was really satisfying. The only thing I could complain about was that most enemies were weak against one specific element, which could've been improved by varying enemy weaknesses more, though it isn't really that bad. Overall great gameplay!- Sound (9/10)Generally the sound and music was enjoyable, though the music was not really memorable so I substracted 1 point there. I really enjoyed the random dialogues among party members and the japanese voice overs were really good. Let's be honest though, nobody plays Yakuza games for the music, except Baka Mitai of course!- Gameplay length (10/10)If you're a completionist like myself, the game offers over 130 hours of gameplay until the end. There's a new game plus which I haven't really checked out. To me this was more than enough to get the money's worth. This game is a 3A game, therefore expensive, but I definitely recommend people to buy this one on discount. - Tone and atmosphere (10/10)To be honest I was expecting less to begin with but the atmosphere and general tone of the game are superb. It really is immersive in the sense that I sometimes had a hard time quitting the game. Like I previously mentioned the humor is on top with a lot of references to pop culture. Although absurd, the game never felt out of place and the humor was never forced. Of course the whole game isn't about being funny. There's a lot of emotional moments in there as well. Overall I'd be shocked if people would complain about this aspect.Overall really great game and worth every last penny spent. Some friends to whom I've recommended this game asked me whether they have to had played previous entries of the series to enjoy this one. SImply no. There are references to previous games but they are really scarce and you don't need to know the previous stories to enjoy this one as even the protagonist is new, Ichiban Kasuga! Looking forward to play more games like this.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, this game is easily one of the best games in the series and it's by far my GOTY for 2020. It's endearing, hilarious, and fun in that special way that only Yakuza can really pull off.So with that out of the way, I am BAFFLED by the CD system in this game. Throughout the game, you collect a number of CD's from various minigames and stores. Each one contains a track from a previous Yakuza or a SEGA property like Persona 5. Cool, right? But here's the thing...you can only play those tracks in the bar that serves as your home base. Nowhere else. "Well, okay. I'll play some P5 music while doing business in there."No, you won't. The second you interact with anyone in the bar, the music reverts back to the generic jazz that plays by default (and sounds suspiciously like "My Old Kentucky Home"). That means the only way to use the CDs is to start playing one and then just stand around--something you can literally just do with Spotify any time. Even worse, there's a FIFTEEN UNITED STATES DOLLAR DLC that adds more.Why?

_childDocuments_.review: This is a revised review!As much as I love this game from perspectives of environment, atmosphere, characters, main story and side stories, the very mechanics of the game are highly annoying, and that's what made me switch review from thumbs up to thumbs down.The game doesn't limit you in going from chapter to chapter per se, but it definitely raises walls in front of you in the middle of the story progression that requires sometimes HOURS of dull grind. Wanna beat a specific boss? Start griding levels and money to get better gear. Want better gear? Grind money for workshop upgrades and materials. Need money? Start learning Ichiban Confections (as the only real means of making money at decent pace) that doesn't come with decent tutorials to begin with. I don't want to do all that arbitrary crap just to enjoy the story. This is artifical playtime pandering. Let me enjoy the events without constantly getting stuck on some dumb stuff I have to sink hours to get through. To give you an example, I got to chapter 12 at lvl 36-37, but to beat the finale successfully, I need to be MINIMUM level 45. So, here I am stuck doing menial tasks and Arena fights just to level up. This is not enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good, and difficult to explain. It's like living alternative life with its weird moments and weird people, references to real life, great sense of humor, exploring harsher aspects of life, lots of absurdity, and characters with child-like dreams and naivety. Some of that, however stupid, is somehow touching to the child-like naive part of me. You can get lost in this game world, exploring the city, fighting battles and playing mini games. _childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoys both the Yakuza series and JRPGs, this game was a blast the whole way through. The main character, Ichiban Kasuga, is an instantly likeable hothead with an unwavering loyalty to his loved ones, proving again and again that he will go the distance whenever he makes a promise. The side characters, whom you meet along the way, all have well-developed, fleshed out personalities that gracefully compliment the story the game tells to the player.Where the game derives it's uniqueness from the previous Yakuza titles, and where it garners both my respect and ire, however, is the JRPG system. Aside from the dumb gender lock on every job, or the lack of information on which specific stats do what (full disclosure: I may have missed this), I would say that it succeeds very well on a conceptual level: gear upgrading, job diversity with some skills carrying over, action commands that reward attacks with a slight damage boost, perfect guarding by timing a block against enemy attacks, etc. The icing on the cake when it comes to the battle system is since Ichiban is a die-hard Dragon Quest fan, what you see while playing the game is how he imagines the fights going down in his head, funny costumes and all!I don't want to give anything away about the story, as it is much better playing games like these blind, but it is worth mentioning that despite this game being the seventh Yakuza game, it is just as equally valid of an introduction to the series as Yakuza 0 is, though longtime Yakuza fans will definitely enjoy certain aspects of the game that may very well fly over the heads of newer players.
_childDocuments_.name: Yakuza: Like a Dragon

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderfully nuts medley of balls to the walls silliness and poignant emotional storytelling spliced with insane turn-based combat out of a fantasy JRPG, slathered in the sauce of a bizarre Yakuza crime story. In no universe should this game possibly work tonally or mechanically but hot damn it does. You'll laugh regularly, you'll feel your heart strings tugged occasionally, and you'll fight like a dragon totally. An experience like nothing else I've played in recent memory. The price can seem pretty steep but if it ever goes on sale, GET IT.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, as expected of the Yakuza series.Although the combat…where to even begin…I know many people were getting tired of the old combat and are a fan of the new one, but turn-based combat is the bane of my gaming experience.The combat gets repetitive quicker than the older combat because it's always the same things. And you have little to no control over when you're blocking or dodging and what combos you want to do. I've always been here for the story, but the beat 'em up combat style was also a big part of the games, and it's a shame this change had to be done on my favourite game franchise. Apart from the subjectively god-awful combat, I really love the story. A lot of crazy plot twists to really keep you on the edge of your seat. Also love Ichi as a protagonist, nice change from an always-gloomy guy to a more fun and outgoing one. Though I also love Kiryu of course. <3

_childDocuments_.review: So far I've played for about 4 hours and I have to say that this game is great. Normally I tend to just skip through dialouges in games because they are usually so damn boring. But in this game, I'm just hooked. And it really helps that almost every dialouge is fully voice acted (I recommend Japanese voices as opposed to English) and they are cinematically presented.A big "controversy" behind this game is that they changed from it's iconic beat em up combat to a turn based one. And in my book, this was just another plus. The turn-based combat may not have a lot of depth (but to be fair, neither did the previous beat-em up style combat), but it's still quite enjoyable due to how it's dynamically presented. The characters are still moving about while you're deciding your move. And it also requires some real time inputs at times. For instance you can perfect block enemy attacks if you press the block button just as their attack hits, this will reduce damage taken and also negate any status effects it would've given. Certain skills also have QTE to empower the attack. If an object is nearby, like a trashcan or bike, then the character might pick that object up and hit the enemy with it. Also if you knock the enemy back, they might actually take damage by the enviroment. For instance you can punch someone out on the road and they might get hit by a car. Also if you knock an enemy down, if you're quick enough and attack again on the knocked down enemy either with the same character or another character before the enemy gets up, you will do increased damage. So my point with that entire paragraph above was to explain that while yes, it is TURN-based combat, it is still very lively and dynamic. So it still very much keeps the core of Yakuza combat. The story so far is great. Keeping the traditional Yakuza comedy but also having serious moments.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time Yakuza fan (played 0 to 6) , Yakuza 7 sums up everything I love about the series. The substories (side quests) and mini-games were well spread out throughout the main story, with each of them being thoroughly enjoyable.I was hesitant on the change of the combat system, however I do believe it is a fresh take, and I really enjoyed it as I unlocked more abilities to experiment with. Nothing really comes to mind when I'm thinking of anything I disliked. This game has got to be the best game I've played this year.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game on day one as it came out because - duh - I had to have it being a Yakuza franchise fanatic. However, I didn't start it until this summer and had chosen to replay other Yakuza games instead because I just couldn't fathom how anyone would want to play anyone other than Kiryu as the main character. Having had run out of Yakuza games to play and after completing Ishin I gave this game a chance. And what can I say? Ichiban is a fantastic addition to the Yakuza family. As I said, I couldn't imagine "bonding" in this series with any other character than Kiryu (and to some love-hate extent Majima) but the creators of this game have done a fantastic job in creating a character that is not only different from Kiryu - which is necessary to give him his own place in the franchise; but they have also achieved to create a character that is incredibly lovable and soft (not in a wet-wipe way) but in a 'I'm a human and I have feelings' way which is something you could argue Kiryu had always lagged (that's just what other people say, I love him no matter what).I had to get used to the turn-based combat and this was one of the reasons why, again, it took me so long to give this game a proper go since I had always enjoyed really going for it with Kiryu and throwing bikes around left, right and centre,Once you get used to it, though, the turn-based combat is quite fun with various special moves - depending on the jobs you give your party members, you have different moves, and some were just constantly in my repertoire - pigeon raid *cough*. If you want to do yourself a massive favour, make sure you get to the end in the management game and there's two reasons for that: 1) you get cool moves and 2) Eri can be added to your party and she kicks serious ass and she's always been on my number 1 team in every fight, big or small.I'll be happy to go back to this game and finish everything that I haven't - I'm yet to have a date with the lady from Romance weapons but I sure am looking forward to the next release of this masterpiece franchise.Tendo was by far the hardest to beat (I had to leave it for almost three weeks because I was so infuriated and then beat him (on new first attempt)) , followed by Kiryu (who never attacked the ladies btw - god I love him), then Majima and Saejima.Ichiban you've 100% earned a place in my heart and I cannot wait to see you again <3

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza: Like a Dragon : By Triple F“Yakuza: Like a Dragon” marks a bold reinvention of the long-running Yakuza series, departing from its traditional action-brawler roots to introduce a turn-based RPG combat system. Developed by Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio, this entry centers on a new protagonist, Ichiban Kasuga, a low-ranking yakuza member with an infectious optimism and a knack for seeing the world through a heroic lens. Set in the bustling streets of Yokohama, "Like a Dragon" offers a fresh perspective on the Yakuza universe, balancing a heartfelt story of redemption and camaraderie with a colorful, dynamic RPG system that reinvigorates the series.The narrative of "Like a Dragon" follows Ichiban’s journey from a loyal yakuza foot soldier to a man seeking answers and justice after a betrayal by the Tojo Clan patriarch he once idolized. After spending 18 years in prison for a crime he didn’t commit, Ichiban emerges into a world where the yakuza landscape has changed entirely, and he must rebuild his life from scratch. Along the way, he forms unexpected bonds with a cast of misfit allies, each with their own complex backstory and motivations. Unlike previous Yakuza games, which focused on the lone-wolf struggles of Kazuma Kiryu, "Like a Dragon" places a strong emphasis on friendship and the idea of found family, lending an emotional resonance to the game’s story.The shift to turn-based combat is one of the game’s most notable changes and, remarkably, it works. Inspired by classic JRPGs, "Like a Dragon" introduces a battle system that combines traditional turn-based mechanics with modern twists. Each character in Ichiban’s party has a unique role, such as healer, tank, or damage dealer, and players can assign jobs to each character, allowing for further customization. Jobs like Breaker, Musician, and Host allow characters to access unique skills and attacks, adding variety and humor to battles. The combat system is also dynamic, incorporating environmental interactions where players can use nearby objects as improvised weapons or deal extra damage by positioning characters strategically. This RPG approach brings a sense of strategy and novelty that keeps battles engaging and fresh.The new location of Yokohama is larger and more detailed than any city previously seen in the Yakuza series. Isezaki Ijincho, modeled after Yokohama’s real-life Isezakicho district, is a vibrant neighborhood filled with mini-games, side quests, and colorful NPCs. The game takes full advantage of the new setting, immersing players in Yokohama’s nightlife, bustling markets, and quieter residential areas. The city feels lived-in, with a blend of high-rise buildings, small shops, and scenic spots that invite exploration. This sense of scale and diversity in Yokohama’s layout provides players with an expansive playground that enriches the world and serves as an exciting backdrop for Ichiban’s journey.One of the standout elements in "Like a Dragon" is its extensive selection of side activities and mini-games, which range from the classic Yakuza activities like karaoke and darts to more unique diversions, such as a Mario Kart-inspired go-karting mode called Dragon Kart. There’s even a full-fledged business management mini-game where Ichiban can run a confectionery business, recruit employees, and navigate corporate meetings. These activities not only add depth to the gameplay but also showcase the game’s humor and willingness to embrace eccentricity. The side quests, known as “Substories,” are equally quirky, often blending comedy with moments of surprising poignancy, allowing players to see Ichiban’s compassionate nature as he helps Yokohama’s eccentric residents.The RPG progression system is both detailed and rewarding, allowing players to build their characters through leveling, equipping gear, and assigning jobs. Each job class offers a distinct set of skills and visual style, with some classes granting access to outrageous moves, such as a chef wielding kitchen knives or a breaker who attacks with flashy dance moves. Job leveling feels satisfying, as it unlocks new abilities and improves character stats, giving players ample motivation to experiment with different job combinations. Moreover, Ichiban’s character progression is tied to “Personality” traits, such as Confidence, Kindness, and Charisma, which can be developed through dialogue choices, side activities, and job experience. These traits impact both dialogue options and interactions with NPCs, giving players a sense of growth beyond combat capabilities.The visuals and sound design in "Like a Dragon" are impressive, with Isezaki Ijincho brought to life through vivid detail, dynamic lighting, and authentic soundscapes that capture the energy of Yokohama. Character models are expressive, especially in cutscenes where the actors’ performances shine through, lending emotional weight to the story’s more serious moments. The soundtrack features an eclectic mix of genres, from dramatic orchestral pieces that underscore major plot points to catchy tunes that accompany mini-games and battles. Voice acting is top-notch, with both the Japanese and English dubs delivering strong performances that capture each character’s personality. Ichiban’s voice actor, Kazuhiro Nakaya, deserves special mention for infusing the character with an earnest, hopeful tone that makes him immediately endearing.On the whole, "Yakuza: Like a Dragon" is a bold reinvention of the series, merging the gritty crime drama the franchise is known for with a lighthearted, JRPG-inspired combat system that feels both nostalgic and refreshing. The new protagonist, Ichiban Kasuga, brings an infectious optimism and camaraderie that stand out in contrast to the stoic Kazuma Kiryu, making the story feel both familiar and refreshingly new. The game’s blend of heartfelt storytelling, diverse mini-games, and deep RPG mechanics offers something for every player, whether they’re series veterans or newcomers. With its charming cast, innovative gameplay, and immersive world, "Yakuza: Like a Dragon" sets a new standard for the franchise, proving that even a series as established as Yakuza can continue to evolve in unexpected and exciting ways.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, listen. This was my first JRPG game and I had a lot of doubts before I bought it. I was also a little confused by the turn-based combat, as I'm not a big fan of such games and most of the time I get bored with them quickly.Thank goodness I bought this game and tried it out for myself. It was an incredible experience that confidently paved the beginning of my love for this genre.   This game has absolutely everything - interesting professions for the characters, a good combat system with beautiful special effects, awesome voice acting and music. This game has a HUGE number of other mini-games and various entertainments that are not much related to the story, but all of them are definitely worth a try. There was never a chance for me to get bored or not know what to do in this game. I'm ready to list the benefits of this game endlessly. But yes, you might sometimes feel like you're not playing the game, but rather watching a very long movie, beating everyone around you during the breaks - but I found it very relaxing and enjoyed going through it.    I'd like to share with you my impressions of the story - I've never gotten this range of emotions from games in general. I was both amused, interested, and sad. There's faith, loyalty, love, friendships, cheating, disappointment, betrayal, murder, self-interest, and much more. At some points I wanted to cry and at other points I wanted to rejoice like a child or just laugh at the local humor. I was angry at the antagonists and I empathized with the main character, as if I really knew that person. I've never experienced such twists and such mood swings in a game (lol). I don't want to spoil anything because it's really worth trying for yourself.   I recommend this game to anyone who likes a really deep story. That's the main reason why I fell in love with this game in the first place. I also recommend it to people who like turn-based games, who like JRPGs, Japan in general and especially the Yakuza theme. And anyone who looking for a new gaming experience, because I'm sure Ichiban's story won't leave anyone indifferent.10/10, no options.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first Yakuza game I ever played and I only tried it because I got it on a sale, looked fun and more importantly is turn-based. I didn't expect much, but it was *really* fun. Very creative, story like a blockbuster in my opinion with twists and turns - and of course some minor weaknesses like every story has. It runs perfectly fine and looks good enough. The characters are likeable too. The minigames... There were a lot of them, truly, and many were fun, but there were also quite a few I didn't like or couldn't get behind. Good thing is they're not mandatory I guess unless you aim for NG+ or whatever. Now I only have 52 hours, but that's because I'm impatient and cheated to skip the usual JRPG grind and I also skipped half the substories aka sidequests. Don't get me wrong though, the sidestories are worth it and sometimes might even let you almost shed a tear perhaps. I'd totally recommend the game. It's fun, it's both lighthearted and dramatic at the same time (TF happened with the stabby c-stain tho? Hope he's dead in a ditch lol He's the worst.). For DLCs you'll have to decide for yourself if it's worth it. It's by no means mandatory; just supplemental.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the best Yakuza games, glad 3-6 are finally on PC, well 6 is almost here at least. I only wish we could get Judgment and an English release of Yakuza Ishin (please Sega).My biggest problem is the naming, why not just call it Yakuza 7 like in Japan? I feel bad for anyone who bought this under the impression that it's a spin-off and just had major plot points of Yakuza 3, 4 and 6 spoiled. It's still great for newcomers but if you played 0, Kiwami and Kiwami 2 in that order, please play 3-6 before this one and you will appreciate every little and big detail so much more.There are also a few notable technical issues. There are missing textures (mostly just a couple particle effects here and there and a missing lense flare texture in specific areas), an LOD issue causing the textures of things like ATMs and shop signs to appear low quality even at max settings. And the worst issue of them all: the karaoke is out of sync... Yakuza 7, the Yakuza game with the best karaoke (unless you play in English lmao), and it's completely out of sync on PC, you either press those buttons too late on purpose (compared to the music) to get the highest score or you just have no rhythm and don't notice it, but it's pretty bad and hard to miss otherwise.Overall it's a great game with a greater story, the combat is now turn-based rather than brawler which I think works in its favour here, it's nicer than being knocked to the ground every 2 seconds and have to spam Cross/A to get back up only to go straight back down again. But it does leave something to be desired, the combat in Yakuza 6/Kiwami 2 was so ridiculously fun that it's sad to see it gone, at the same time, the new skill system opens up way more creative options like way over-the-top essence attacks and such and after all there's nothing stopping you from going back to those, well apart from 6 not being on PC until March.TL;DR: Highly recommended, it's great for newcomers and fans alike, but do yourself a favour and play 0-6 before this one, it's still Yakuza 7 regardless of what Sega's marketing team says and adds much more impact to the story if you have played the previous games.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first foray into the Yakuza games and now I am wanting to play the previous installments. I am still playing through the game, but so far it's been fantastic.At first, the game felt a little slow to get into story wise, some of the mechanics needed adjusting to - but somewhere in that 15-20 hour mark magic started to happen.The story - this is a really well done story - it hits you. Compelling dialogue mixed with excellent voice acting work (both JP and EN) really help push the narrative. I've found myself playing up until the early morning hours with work coming up soon because I was so drawn in and wanting to know what will happen next!The protagonist - Ichiban is amazing. The VA's did a phenomenal job, his personality and outlook is relatable - all the supporting characters bring their own strife and issues and it's this that really helps cement them and lay the ground work for the excellent story telling. You are in for a treat - start to finish. Don't give up on the game if you are only a few hours in, it's laying the ground work for one hell of a ride!

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR Overall the game looks absolutely stunning and ran very well, never crashing during my 100+ hours of play. The plot is filled with the same old Yakuza writing and may lose you at points, but it's fun all the way through. The turn based combat was initially a concer, but for a first iteration it seems well done and I look forward to seeing them build upon it. P.S. If you want to 100% this game be ready for a very long grind. The story is the same great Yakuza writing from the previous series, although that also means the flaws from before are still present. The new lead, Ichiban, organically stands out in his own way without the feeling like he is intentionally written to be different from (our best boi) Kiryu. The side characters are also all interesting enough in their own way, but as mentioned by many others, one of them is awkwardly integrated in to the story. I do wish we got some of the party members earlier for gameplay reasons, but it makes sense to add them slowly to match the pacing of the story. The addition of playable female characters is a welcomed change and they () are written well. The side stories are the same wacky sidestories as before with the drastically different tone from the main story, but that's a big plus for me as it relives some tension. If you're not a fan of turn based combat this game probably won't change your mind, but it does feel good for a first attempt in the series. If you physically struggle (arthritis or other hand pain) with action RPGs and were interested in the Yakuza series, this is the perfect iteration to jump in on (they even have options to turn of QTEs during combat). I really do hope they build on and flesh out the system more if there is a sequel. The class system is fun, but some classes are just much stronger/better than the others. It feels like they made the classes and molded the character stats afterwords to fit a specific class in mind, even though you technically can change to others. Some gripes are that some basic enemies are ridiculously tanky for no good reason, some important fights felt very underwhelming and the grinding for this game feels even more grindy than the predecessors potentially caused by the new combat/stat system.Playing on a 2080ti, the game performed exceptionally well, rarely dropping under 90 frames with all setting maxed at 1440p. During my time playing it, it never crashed and had any noticeable frame drops. The audio sounded clear and, surprisingly to me, simulated directional sound very well (Although the footsteps sounded off to me). Walking through the various cities in first person almost feels like you're there and could be a fun virtual tourism during 2020. The voice acting is very well done and don't feel cheesy. Some detractors were that there were some random low res textures on some things and the faces of the characters looked off in some scenes.TL;DRSeong-Hui can crush me.

_childDocuments_.review: Terrific game on so many fronts - packed with a ton of content that rewards you if you take the time to do it.  Mini-games, side dungeons, scavenger hunts, arcade games, etc.  Almost everything has a purpose - even if some of the mini-games are just subpar versions of activities you've played in other games like the Kart Racing or Golfing - their brief enough to not overstay their welcome.  I loved being able to just engage in the world and overpower my party at the same time.This is a long game - around 50 hours if you just follow the critical path.  The story and characters are really delightful and there's some great moments of introspection offered by your party as you talk to them throughout the game.  A mix of the absurd, comedy, and poignancy.  There's bound to be a few moments in the game that will stick with you for a long time.Combat is much-like a traditional turn-based RPG of old - with a job system something out of Final Fantasy.  Lots of jobs for you to give your party members that allow you to interconnect various skills to fulfill multiple roles.  Not a groundbreaking system but it does it a good job of mirroring what has worked well within this genre.My biggest issue is the lack of diversity in the play-space.  You'll mostly be in city environments for most of the game aside from some of the dungeons that take place in the sewers.  Would have liked to visited some more diverse looking areas.  The game does get a lot of of its somewhat limited play-space.Very easy recommendation for anyone who likes turn-based RPGs or anyone wanting to experience a story that throws the kitchen sink at you.
_childDocuments_.name: Yakuza: Like a Dragon

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza: Like a Dragon is a successful genre transition for the Yakuza series, taking the already present RPG elements present within previous titles and expanding it into a proper JRPG while retaining the feel of classic Yakuza games.While it's also called Yakuza 7 by some, it doesn't require playing any prior games to understand what's going on as the game follows a new protagonist who is just as unfamiliar with things as an incoming player.  Veterans of the series can also appreciate it since it's still a Yakuza game, so it comes with everything the series has been known to offer.I will say that if you're not a fan of turn-based JRPGs then this game may not be for you, especially if you were expecting a more beat 'em up kind of game like the previous entries.  If that isn't the case, or if you have an open mind, then I'd highly recommend picking this game up.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's "Yakuza" experience previously had been a demo disk on the PS2 (Yakuza 0 I think? Had Katamari on it too), and then "Fist of the North Star: Lost Paradise" (PS4 - same studio); the game-play made me resent waiting so long to try one of the "core" games.Combat wise - I get that it is different from the others in the series (turn-based vs real-time), and I traditionally have not been too interested in such outside of the Shin Megami games, as I am admittedly at times impatient with the menus (Pokemon for example, I don't bother with items - same with Persona unless it's outside combat or 100% needed to progress). Here however, it drew me in with all of the allies and interesting skills and I ended up only spamming to grind in the few instances you might end up doing so. It also felt pretty fair throughout - I never totally felt underlevelled (albeit I did a LOT of side-stuff constantly and walked  until chapter 8), with a couple of difficulty spikes that kept it interesting. Turn order also didn't seem problematic; as someone who recently played a ton of SMT3:Nocturne, it was very "safe" feeling - with regards to stuff like "can I wait 1 more turn to heal, and buff now?"Skills wise - there are a lot, it's an "RPG" you eventually pick a "Class" (Career) and get XP by doing your "quests" (Jobs)/fighting. You can keep 2 per class, and so there is some good hybrid action to be had, like AOE Damage+Healer if you really wanted. Each of your teammates can also be swapped around as you level them/max your bond with each, so a LOT of stuff to play with there; obviously this means combat can be somewhat fresh across 2 playthroughs.Side-Content; my god there's so much, and a lot is pretty fun. I thought P4:Golden was busy with their days being pretty packed, but then I am over hear participating in Claw Games, Virtua Fighter, Mario Kart-esque racing, that one ancient car arcade game where you drive like a maniac down the freeway, batting practice, being a legit hero, etc.; you can basically double your play-through with the side stuff.Performance wise - I rock an i5-4670K, RTX 2070, and 16GB of RAM; ran on ultra/highest settings like a dream TBH. I only really had some stuttering when spawning in the over-world near mobs of people (though you can control "mob density" I believe, I just didn't want to lol).Lastly - the story was pretty interesting, although I obviously can't gauge it against the others until I play them, and I see it was intentionally a bit over-the-top on purpose, but I think it was interesting enough for the themes and overall ambiance they shot for. RPGs after-all always have a hero, and the heavens themselves would part if the hero asked; it's how they ask that truly defines the stories quality. Kasuga may be too honest a character for the work he does, but he is also the type of guy to trudge through hell to ask, and his bold attitude certainly draws in a crowd.Overall - I would say an 8 out of 10, maybe 9. The game is certainly fun, and kept me invested for about twice it's value (hour/dollar:DLC included). Lots of memorable moments, fun gameplay, and I enjoyed it enough to almost 100% (one achievement away - on a break). Business Minigame was a little "meh" and the Certificate tests are just "take tests and no actual studying", and rarely I thought enemies spawned a bit too often on the streets (defeat a group and you happen to be on their spawn point basically getting re-engaged immediately); but otherwise had so few faults I am excited to try the other games in the series now.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most surprising games I've come across in a while, this is a Yakuza game that goes beyond just a small, zany open-world sandbox to play in.While the characters and story are always strong in Yakuza games, there is often a small-ish world to move in freely and then a bunch of one-off story segments elsewhere. Like a Dragon deviates from that and sets most of the game within the open-world (instead of one-offs) and has a larger sandbox to make this truly effective. The larger open world is a huge improvement. There is a more real sense that tougher enemies spawn over there, that this area is easier, that I may want to actually take the taxi to a destination. In some prior games, the gamespace was so small I never used the taxi and basically just ran through the same enemies easily, over and over. Yet here, different areas of the map spawn different levels of enemies, and like old school RPGs, you may need to farm an area to level up enough to be able to go elsewhere safely.And it's a semi-turn-based RPG this time. I say 'semi' because it does the whole QTE-in-battle-actions that newer Final Fantasy games (like FF XV) have done. However, this does it really well... where I found it poorly implemented in FF XV, which was mostly real-time for combat with those button pushes thrown in, Like a Dragon has these QTE just as part of your attacks or defenses; you do have actual turns in Like a Dragon, allowing you to plan and use abilities, whereas in FF XV you are always rushing to remember what button and what ability to use as you are fighting mostly in real-time.And the four-character party is a good element to this game, too. I like having the party to work with, and would like to see that kept in other Yakuza games. I get that the story may not always work for having a party like this in the other games in the series, but Like a Dragon benefits tremendously from having a 4-person party to build tactics around and travel with. Finally, the world feels more alive in this than ever. There are cars on major roads... there are more locations in the city... many story areas, like I wrote, are in the open-world sandbox and can be visited while roaming and not just in a linear one-off segment of the chapter.This might be the best Yakuza game I've played, though I have not played them all. This isn't just 'more Yakuza but turn-based'. This is an entirely upgraded game IMO, which was a pleasant surprise. My only complaints are that some mini-games could be changed up a bit more (yet more Virtua Fighter... sigh...) and that the game really, really front-loads story this time around. Yakuza games often front-load the story, but the first 3 chapters (which can take 3 hours if you don't skip any cutscenes) are pretty much fetch quests and cutscenes. The frontloading is something I expect, where usually the first hour or so is going to be a bit slower, but this time it's fairly slow for probably at least 2.5 hours of real time if you take in all the cutscenes. Most can be skipped if you want (hit ESC during rendered cutscenes to get the option to skip), but on a first pass, I wanted the story knowledge so taking them all in did take a while.But overall, a good game, though still a tad expensive three years later (could stand to be $50 rather than $60, but worth it at both prices still).

_childDocuments_.review: This game changed my perspective on life and introduced me to an incredible series.From the jump I couldn't stop playing. Ichiban Kasuga hooked me because I could relate on so may levels. I just lost my job and I had to move back in with my dad after living on my own for 8 years. Next thing I know I see a Dunkey video on the game, so I bought it on a whim, and for 100+ hours I'm straight up taught how no matter how old a person is, no matter how hard rock bottom is, you can always restart and keep going. That, and you should always keep your light.Now, does the game have some issues? Sure, across the board. The gameplay is a solid JRPG effort that doubles as a clear first effort, so it can be a little too easy or wonky (minus the True Final Millenium Tower). The grind isn't bad until attempting the last dungeon, but by then you're 50-100 hours in so your goals, unless intent on all achievements, are only the success of the tower and minigame completion. The story can also be an issue for some, as it begins great, then slows WAY down before picking up again. It can definitely be a slow burn.The strangest yet most understood decision was by the end of Chapter 12 certain things kind of just happen or go unanswered. The intentions with the story were to drive toward the release of Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name + Like a Dragon 8, so RGG also deserve applause for the sheer scope of the story they wanted to tell in this new era. Still, this can deter people. (If you like Japanese Cinema or Malazan, you won't stress it)The silver lining: Like a Dragon is a remarkable experience that helps you keep pushing forwards. It's all about the experience and the characters. Everyone is given a great amount of care and detail, and you really understand them as individuals. They're all facing their own monsters. The game is also hilarious. You'll go from being in your feels to explaining to your cousin that a grown band of yakuza are dressed as babies telling you that baby formula is the "nectar of the gods," while teaching a young man about the dynamics of parenting. I'm not making this up.So buy it and enjoy the ride. You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first Yakuza game I finished after bouncing off of Yakuza 0. I'm a huge fan of turn-based combat games, so I immediately gravitated toward this one when I learned about the combat system. As a newcomer to this universe, I had a really fun time diving into all the wacky, absurd elements of it while also being pretty engaged with the more serious main story line. It is very difficult to balance these two tones, and I think the game does a really good job with it. Ichiban Kasuga is the perfect protagonist for this kind of story too, and I love how the game justifies the odd creatures you fight as Kasuaga's "imagination." As much as I like turn-based combat, I was not the biggest fan of this system. It reminds me a lot of Persona, but it is not as deep or as varied as that. It very obviously feels like a first pass at this kind of style, and I've heard the sequel makes a lot of really good improvements. There's also some crazy difficulty spikes in the final fourth of the game. On the one hand, I did feel that the game was a little on the easy side as I casually played, but on the other, these difficulty spikes came out of nowhere.While I like the story, I do think it peaks in the middle. The entire gang war arc in Ijincho with the 3 main gangs was really compelling with fun twists and turns. How that is ultimately parlayed into the greater story is not the most satisfying to me, though I hesitate to say that it was "bad" (barring one late twist involving a train station locker that is TOO ridiculous for me to believe). Overall, if you enjoy JRPGs, I'd definitely recommend this, especially on discount. The game has a lot of charm and personality, and it will absolutely entertain you with its absurdity.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm currently writing this review almost 90 hours into the sequel to this game, Infinite Wealth, and to look back at this game even though it was very recently i decided to platinum it, fills me with some of the most fond memories a game can give you. this game is what JRPGs and RPGs in general strive for in every sense of the word. absolutely amazing, a true spectacle of videogaming in my eyes. There is almost nothing like this game on the market except it's sequel and that originality really shines through. If you like Yakuza, JRPGs, or really just good games in general, this one is an easy 10 out of 10 and deserves your time.prosfantastic, addictive turn based combat, with a plethora of jobs and skills to use and grind out. in some games grinding is a con, but there was never a moment here where this game felt like a chore.great minigames as always from RGG studiosthe best party cast I've seen in a jrpg in years. they're just normal people, and that's interesting in and of itself to anyone who knows how crazy jrpg stories can get.a very fun and engaging story, with great beats, twist, and some real emotion. RGG studios is usually great at this so it's no surprise.a challenging, yet fair and not grindy platinum to go forgreat musicconsthere is no cons. this was the sleeper goty for 2020 and is truly a milestone in how to take a franchise, reinvent it, and (in my opinion), make it more fun and engaging than ever.you won't regret picking this game up, and here's the real kicker. _childDocuments_.review: This game is outstanding.After believing GTA was the be-all and end-all of (modern setting) open world games, I was honestly expecting Y:LaD to be limited experience. How wrong I was!This game is a legit RPG and for me, a throwback to when I discovered games like Grandia. I love the setting, I love the atmosphere, I love the Japanese humour, I love the combat (if you are old school RPG player then the turn-based combat is enjoyable), I love the story and the characters-enemies are great too.There is a lot here to distract you, and I found almost all the side quests and activities fun to participate in. My only complaint is that despite the excellent story, there is an abundance - even for a modern RPG - of cutscenes, exposition and backstory. Your controller may switch itself off from inactivity at times. Sometimes you just want to get into the world and play, but the main missions often scoop you up and make you go through quite a lot in certain chapters before you can freely explore again.My first serious foray into the Yakuza franchise. Couldn’t be happier that I chose to play this one first. 9/10.
