_childDocuments_.review: If you told me when I bought this I would get nearly 180 hours out of a SINGLE play-through, I probably would have doubted you. Though your mileage will likely vary.My only previous exposure to Yakuza was 20 hours in Yakuza 0 that I did enjoy a lot and I loved the serious / zany contradictions in the tone of the game, but I couldn't get past a certain combat (don't let yourself get hit) that frustrated me some and I just couldn't get past it before finding something that interested me more at the time. However, when I saw how "Like a Dragon" was more of an "RPG" style that was party-based with turn-based combat, I had to give it a try. Then I got nearly 180 hours in on a single play-through!The serious nature of the main story contrasted by the absolute zaniness of so much of the side content is just fun. Ichiban Kazuga was a fun guy to hangout with and experiencing his ups and downs while making it through life was a joy. It was easy to relate to at times. As a semi-completionist the game gives a lot of side stuff to do, that while it can be repetitive, is mostly optional short of giving you additional opportunities to level up you and your party. I honestly found myself doing A LOT of the side stuff, though. I don't mind a bit of a grind when I choose to do it and I am not forced by the game to do it.The party based combat is fun, though it can be repetitive at times, but it allows you to mix it up and try different combinations. Only on rare occasions did I feel it was much of a challenge in normal mode, but the large number of options made it enjoyable to me and you didn't have to feel stressed or rushed making sure you got the right button combinations. Combat is played in a fantasy style as Ichiban likes to imagine everything as a Dragon Quest adventure, but it didn't take away from my enjoyment of the game at all, but enhanced it. While the combat wasn't super difficult, you will suddenly find yourself out of your league in a couple of places, though, if you haven't leveled up properly and worked to improve your gear.The story had me very invested, but be prepared for some very long cut scenes (skippable if you absolutely want to) at the beginning and more even at the end. At the beginning the cut scenes might seem so long you will wonder if you are ever going to get to actually play the game, but hang in there. It's worth the wait. By the time you get to the end and then the after credits scenes, you will be invested enough to see it through to the end.A few random takes from my play-through:1. The RPG elements and turn-based combat were a great risk taken by the developers on this one that definitely kept me in the  game, but it was disappointing to me a bit that new pieces of armor and armor enhancements are only in Ichiban's mind, because you won't ever see any of them actually rendered in game, but only their stat improvements. I understand that it was probably a lot more to have to add, but one of the big draws of an RPG is to see your party's cosmetic changes.2. Spend time playing the Business Management mini-game. It is not only the best way of eventually making large amounts of cash, but will provide an additional party member after you reach the main goal. ABSOLUTELY GO ON YOUTUBE to see how to play the Stockholder Meetings portion of this mini-game if you want to have any idea how to play it. It's very difficult to understand how to play it just based on the instructions given in-game.3. As is apparently part of all Yakuza games, enjoy the journey as you will be both laughing and touched at times from the many random encounters and side quests you will have as you explore the world placed before you.4. Though the developers did provide an English language track for this one, play it in Japanese with English (or whatever other language you can read) subtitles. It's just so much more emotional and the English voices, while maybe well spoken, totally take you out of the immersion.After having completed this game and becoming exposed more to the Yakuza world, I am looking forward now to going back to the other Yakuza games to fill in some things that probably would have made more sense if I had played them, but I also know it wasn't necessary to enjoy this game. If SEGA does decide to keep this particular story going or another with a similar "RPG" feel, I'll go for it! I personally can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very special to me. It came out just before my birthday and, as I was a uni student during covid times, I wasn't able to get up to much with friends. Instead, I decided to start this game on my birthday, and I was gripped and spent the majority of the day playing it.Even I had my doubts when they announced Yakuza would be abandoning its traditional gameplay in favour of turn-based combat, but it just makes so much sense. Unlike Kiryu and his (fairly) realistic style of combat, Ichiban and his group work so well with the goofy, exaggerated movesets that this style of gameplay allows them to have. The combat isn't very complex by any means, but it was more than engaging enough, keeping me entertained throughout the whole main story.Combining the incredible cast, enthralling story, entertaining combat and wacky side content (minigames, substories, etc.) makes for a very high-quality experience worth every penny.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's 100%ed 0-6 and Judgment, I was extremely hyped up for this game. Every trailer I saw, every persons' review of the game in Japan, every little detail revealed made me more and more excited. And guess what?This game was even better than I ever expected.The new cast is extremely refreshing and has more charisma than almost every other character from the past games (except maybe Akiyama and Shinada, they'd fit right in). After 7 games of Kiryu and the old guard, shifting focus to this new group is a breath of fresh air. The story is one of the most gripping and intense with insanely bright parts that got me laughing harder than I ever expected and insanely dark parts that the series has never gotten to (don't get fooled by the wacky, goofy gameplay SEGA's been advertising with, the story is extremely grounded in reality and doesn't typically go in that direction). The new city, Yokohama, is as lively as it can be and all the new content in it feels fresh. And the combat, ooooo boy the combat.I wasn't ever against the turn-based combat for this game. From the first teaser of it on April Fools 2019, I thought it'd be a neat extra minigame to add. When I got to playing though, it fights right into the game just as well as the old beat-em-up style did. Fights are fast, sometimes even faster than in the older games. The enemies are wacky and super varied, having you keep on your toes and memorize weaknesses and resistances. Learning new skills as each class is rewarding since it gives you so many options to utilize. After finishing the game, I am excited to see how they'll refine the combat for 8 because I want MORE.If you haven't played the rest of the series, I implore you to do so. Start with 1 on the PS2 (if you can run this, you can emulate that) and go upward. While the Kiwamis are great and 0 is fantastic, 0 is best played after 5 and the Kiwamis are victory laps to go through before and after 6. It's worth playing every game because there's a reference to every single one in this. You can hop in without any prior knowledge and have fun (you might be a little confused at points and some moments won't have nearly as much impact), but if you get into this series, you won't regret it and this game has some of the best payoff I've ever felt from a series. 10/10, GOTY 2020, one of the best games, if not the best, in the series by far.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply one of the best games I've ever played. The characters are nuanced, fleshed out; the tone is absurd, yet serious and dark, but never makes fun of the people it depicts. It gazes a side of society we often shy away from, and forces us to engage with the simple fact that they are human beings too, and not so unlike anyone else. Yakuza 7 is incredibly funny at times; increadibly dark and sad at other times; but most of all, it is a game that sincerely wants to talk about difficult topics and not shy away from it. And the game is ridden with an empathy about all of it.

_childDocuments_.review: You know why you're here, you want to play Yakuza, you want a game where you can fight your way through the complex politics of a Japanese gang in between late night Disco sessions while you amass a collection crane game figurines. This game is a pinnacle of what makes Yakuza so good, the writing here is amazing, along with a really interesting take on old school RPG mechanics. I was intrigued when I first saw the combat in this game, it was made to replicate the feeling of playing an old Dragon Quest game and they really knocked it out of the park by adding cool dynamic elements to the turn based combat which I feel is going to define RPG games to come. All of this I feel is a vast improvement to the old button mashing combat style of the previous titles, which I always felt was the weakest aspect of Yakuza. In my eyes, like a Dragon perfects what Yakuza was lacking previously and asserts itself as a contender for one of the best RPG games ever made.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon is an important game for Yakuza, some would argue that is due to the combat change. This is true, but ultimately a missed opportunity to discuss the finer details of how, while paying homage to the series' extensive history, it begins the next major step in the franchise going forward.First and formally, Like a Dragon is Yakuza. The name change itself is a signal to the change that occurred in the meta and internal world of the game and series. Going forward, the spin off and sequels to this game are "Like a Dragon: _____" For example, the spin off game to wrap up the previous story is "Like a Dragon: The Man Who Erased His Name." This separates the games from Judgement and any other Yakuza related games, although not retroactively.Secondly, this is a new story, first and foremost. The main character of Yakuza 0-6 is not here, this story is the easiest point to jump into. Considering the sequel game, "Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth" stars the same character, its safe to say that KNOWING Yakuza is a benefit, not required.Thirdly, the turn base combat is excellent, and is worthy of praise. It is a large departure from the previous "street brawl" combat system that continues in Judgement, but not at all bad. However, it is with its own depth, function, and proves the series has plenty of room left to grow as it expands on this style going forward.As with all RGG games, the real star of the show is the world and its expansive nature. Expansive? Simply put, Yakuza builds up, not out. Where something akin to Assassin's Creed would have a player travel in game miles for a new anything, Yakuza places a huge part of its structure on smaller, tighter, and more filled worlds. What is traded in spaces, allows for more and more content that matters. A few city blocks never felt so dense.Art, music, all fantastic. The writing is exceptional, the prowess on display is nothing short of fantastic, although if you bounce off mellow dramatic writing and situations, this will be part of the game without question.Like a Dragon deserves your attention without a doubt, and is a worthy continuation of the series in the absence of the previous characters, stories, and combat. However, call backs are extensive, characters pop up constantly, any you'll never know who you'll run into. If even some of this sounds good, or the life simulation of Japan sounds exciting, go back and play the other 7+ games in the mainline alongside the rest of them. You really can't go wrong with this game or anything of the mainline games.Except 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this game has probably become one of my top RPG's, and I would absolutely recommend it to anyone who enjoys staples of the genre like Persona, Dragon Quest (of course), or the classic Final Fantasy games.The story can be a bit over the top, and some of the twists and plot points really stretch suspension of disbelief, but it still strikes a nice balance of serious and lighthearted moments. I was also surprised at how maturely and empathetically the game treated relevant social issues like homelessness, immigration, and prostitution. Despite the game being centered around the struggles of the bottom rungs of society, it retains a pretty positive and hopeful tone. I also came to find out, for better or worse, that I now find it easier to identify with the band of poor, middle-aged burnouts than the band of magical JRPG high schoolers who seemed so relatable 10 years ago. Ah well.The characters do have lots of charm though, and the protagonist being a video-game loving nerd with a wild imagination makes for a clever and fun way to incorporate game mechanics into the story. Something as mundane as calling a friend on your smartphone suddenly becomes an elaborate "Summon" ritual, complete with flashing lights and elaborate hand gestures. Mechanically, the combat system is pretty standard stuff, but is still plenty fun and engaging. Though the over the top abilities, animations, classes, etc, make battles very entertaining regardless.The only real issue I had, and it's a rather minor and subjective one to begin with, was that the difficulty curve was kind of erratic. For at least the first 2/3 of the game, battles are a breeze if you have any experience with turn-based RPG's, to the point where I avoided upgrading my equipment in order to maintain at least some challenge. Although, while the game becomes reasonably difficult during the later parts, the jump is sudden and jarring, likely requiring some grinding to catch up. All in all though, the game has plenty going for it to keep you engaged, and there are TONS of minigames and sidequests too if you need a break from the combat.Overall, the gameplay is solid, and the world, story, and characters are endearing, if at times ridiculous and over the top. Definitely worth the buy!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm hooked. Yakuza: Like a Dragon, follows the story of Ichiban Kasuga, a character who is both endearing and relatable. The game, which is a departure from the previous Yakuza titles in terms of gameplay, centers around Kasuga's journey to uncover a conspiracy within the criminal underworld of Yokohama.One of the things that stands out about Ichiban Kasuga is his unwavering sense of loyalty and honor, even in the face of overwhelming adversity. Despite being cast out by the Tojo Clan, Kasuga remains true to his beliefs and principles, and his determination to do what is right makes him an incredibly likable character.Another notable aspect of Kasuga's character is his sense of humor. He's not afraid to crack a joke or be goofy, which adds a lightheartedness to the game that balances out the more serious moments. His positive outlook and enthusiasm are contagious, and it's hard not to root for him as he takes on the challenges that come his way.In terms of gameplay, Yakuza: Like a Dragon offers a unique blend of traditional RPG mechanics and classic Yakuza brawling action. Kasuga's various jobs and abilities allow for a wide range of playstyles, and the party-based combat system is both engaging and strategic. It's refreshing to see the series take a new approach to its gameplay, and it works well with the story and characters.Overall, Yakuza: Like a Dragon is a great addition to the Yakuza series, and Ichiban Kasuga is a character who stands out for his personality, values, and sense of humor. Whether you're a fan of the previous games or new to the series, this game is definitely worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been 15 years since the Like a Dragon/Yakuza franchise has begun, and for the first time in the franchise's history we have a game that dares to finally step away from the mediocre, but fun beat 'em up action game play, in favor of using classic JRPG turn based game play. With it is also a new protagonist to go along side the new approach to play, Ichiban Kasuga, whom is incredibly charismatic. The explanation as to why the game is turn based is also great, as Ichiban imagines each fight to play out in classic RPG fashion, much like Dragon Quest. Despite it being the 7th mainline game in the series it's still newcomer friendly, considering it having it's own unique story, and new set of characters. This however doesn't exclude veterans who have played the series front to back, because there's much to appreciate, with references to past games/events, and reoccurring franchise staple characters.The story of this game follows Ichiban hitting rock bottom and slowly but surely climbing his way on up with the help of a few good friends. As cliche as it may sound, it does the "power of friendship" trope exceptionally well.  Each supporting character/party member is well fleshed out with their own trials and tribulations. It's sincerely endearing, and you can't help but root for them. Each Yakuza/Like a Dragon game has their fair share of crime drama, and whacky hi-jinks in order to balance the heavy aspects, and it's no different here. You'll probably laugh your ass off while engaging in sub-stories, or pulling off certain team moves, then find yourself glossy eyed from the main story's heavy plot. It's a well balanced roller coaster ride. Whether you're bonding with friends and learning about who they are, or engaging in a fist fight with grown men in diapers, it's bound to be a great time. The acting is superb, in both Japanese and English (though I personally believe you should play it in Japanese first), and there's matching lip-sync for both languages too!Game play wise it's not as in depth as a SMT game, but it's serviceable nonetheless. It's obvious that this is the studio's first time with this type of game, and it's still a lot of fun, without a doubt, but it's also not very challenging. It would've been better if the game had allowed players to start off on Hard Mode, but alas, that isn't the case. Instead Hard Mode and the even tougher Legendary Mode are locked behind New Game+. Perhaps balancing would have been an issue. I do hope that they stick with this style of game though, because it was really enjoyable and a nice change of pace compared to what the series has been doing for as long as it has existed. If you're a fan of more contemporary settings in your RPGS, like MOTHER/EarthBound and Persona, this is an absolute must have! Despite how simple it can be it's fun to change classes with your party, to see what works, and what doesn't, and the hilarious "Pound Mates" which work like the classic Summons in games like Final Fantasy are an absolute blast to watch in action. There's a lot to enjoy here, and the animations are stellar. Positioning also plays a role in how battles play out, which is a unique aspect of this game's battle system. Hopefully it's fleshed out more in a sequel!There's a lot of side content offered here as well. Just like any other Yakuza game in the past. Mini-Golf BINGO, Virtua Fighters 2 & 5, Outrun, Space Harrier, slot machines, Black Jack, Batting Cages, a kart racer, karaoke, darts, crane games, etc. There's a lot of stuff to keep you busy, and I recommend you don't just blaze through this without experiencing it. Whether you're goofing off at the arcades, or going to the movies with your friends, or grabbing a bite at a restaurant/cafe, it's always a joy, and there's always something to do outside of battling goons.The city of Injincho in Yokohama is absolutely lovely as well. Having visited Yokohama in the past, it reminded me of how stunning it was to be there. If you haven't seen it for yourself, this game can give you slight idea of how lovely it truly is, and may even inspire you to visit some day.I plan on going further in with post-game and New Game+, and I can safely say that this is my personal favorite of the year.Hopefully I haven't spoiled much, and have helped convince some of you who may have been on the fence about it to give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I've now officially beaten every single mainline Yakuza release and it was well worth it. This game is amazingly well written in story, side quests, and cast, but there are huge problems with this game. Some are random, and some are by design. Let's discuss the "by design" issues first:The turn-based battle system in this game is fresh. I see what they were going for and it would have been great if it wasn't so unpolished. It almost feels experimental with the kinds of problems it has. When you get into a fight, your characters and the enemies move around. They walk back and forth, side to side, eyeing each other down, moving in to attack and then falling back, but there are obstacles in the world. Fire hydrants, trees, cars, railings, buildings etc, and A.I. path-finding in this game is horrendously unreliable. You'll press to attack and instead of running around an obstacle like a wall, your player can just run into it, keep running like he's brain dead and start attacking the air, missing every hit. I can give a million scenarios in which path-finding has ruined battles. From hitting allies, to not hitting enemies, to being glitched behind railings. Enemies also fly back when hit, and as you keep attacking you can push them BLOCKS down the road while your players stay in their original spot and have to run long distances just to hit the enemy and run all the way back, sometimes pushing the enemy into a corner that your player can't figure out how to get to even though you would easily do it if you were controlling his movements yourself. It's PRETTY bad and to call it flat out stupid would be an understatement. I hope they refine it in Infinite Wealth because at present it is terrible and should NOT be left as is. I'm actually a JRPG player first and foremost so I enjoyed the combat despite its major shortcomings but I CANNOT fault others for hating it. If it's not even done well...I can't defend it.This actually wouldn't be a problem at all if it weren't for some other issues I'll have to get into later, but they try to artificially increase the difficulty of the game by having long, drawn-out, important sections of the game NOT be able to save. You have to go through the entire sequence and succeed to regain access to saving. I don't mind this design approach at all, but if you're gonna remove save functionality, your game is EXPECTED to run flawlessly during these sections. Freezing, glitching, crashing, is completely unacceptable.I don't know why this game still has denuvo more than 3yrs after its steam release, but I have a feeling that a lot of the issues myself and others have been having with this game is partly to denuvo's presence, and partly just bugs.Now let's discuss the random issues the game has. You may or may not be affected by these, as denuvo does not equally play nice with every system. This is also true for standard bugs. If you get a smooth run that's great, but if you get a run like I did, you may not finish this game. Don't let the reviews fool you, and don't let players fool you into thinking this game doesn't have issues. When you complete a chapter, you get an achievement and you can see how many people have earned it. I can tell you that despite these overwhelmingly positive reviews, only about 30% of players have actually beaten this game. About 60% have yet to even play 75% of it. Back to the random issues:I recommend saving a lot, as this game can randomly crash to desktop without warning. It just closes. This game has also caused BSODs. There is no specific trigger. It's almost like a memory leak. After a while it can just crash on you. I've had this happen to me more than once during those long sequences I just mentioned where you're unable to save. Almost 2 hours playing through a dungeon GONE just like that. This actually happened to me shortly after beating the final boss and I had to run to youtube to finish watching the ending cut scenes. It crashed before I could get my achievement and I will NOT be going back to get it.This game has FPS issues. It's unstable and clunky. I played at 1440p max settings locked at 120fps. I had to lock my FPS from going over 120 and turning on vsync to get the game to stabilize. Denuvo might be responsible here again.During certain cut scenes when characters are speaking, the game abruptly ends sentences mid convo and jumps to a brand new set of text like the CPU can't tell that the character wasn't done speaking. It's extremely jarring and catches you off guard. You can miss things because of it.Sometimes I'll boot up and the game is back in windowed mode with the wrong FPS settings and I have to change it back. It's annoying.There are other things but I've rambled on long enough. I love this game and despite how badly it treated me, I enjoyed it to no end. Haven't enjoyed a bad experience this much since Witcher 3. The game is just that good despite its problems, but if you're not a huge Yakuza or JRPG fan, it may overwhelm you if it doesn't run well. I wish there was a middle ground button, because I love this game, but honestly, I can't recommend it. What if someone buys it and has the same problems I did? I don't want to feel responsible for that. So if we're being honest, yeah personally I loved it and stuck it out, but I'll be thumbsing this down. First Yakuza game I've had this level of problems with.

_childDocuments_.review: Zany and crazy, this JRPG is a wild ride that uses conventional industry design while telling a ridiculous saga through the underworld of Japan. The gameplay is straightforward JRPG affair. While mostly good, there is an over reliance on grinding at certain points throughout the story. This is disappointing, as the leveling process should be smooth through a game; having to grind levels to proceed isn't fun, even when the game tries to mask necessary level grinding behind arena-fighting and non-essential dungeon crawling. Further, some of the enemies you encounter, aside from having wildly higher levels than your party is ready for (without grinding), are absurd damage sponges, unnecessarily dragging out fights. This isn't very fun. The story is just ridiculous. You follow Ichiban, the protagonist, from hitting rock-bottom to society saving hero in probably the most convoluted, plot-hole-convenient, eye-rolling contrived story telling ever made in a video game. And you know what, that's part of this game's charm and endearment. The game is just alright; an okay recommendation to fans of JRPGs, but perhaps not to others. A lukewarm recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember buying Persona 4 Golden months ago, when I really wanted to try out the series and was hopeful for a P5R Port to PC, because all the character moments looked great and I really liked how the character dynamics flowed. When I started up P4G I wasn't expecting to waste literally TWO HOURS on Setting Introduction and the gameplay felt god awful after spending so long just reading dialogue... I couldn't have been any more sick of the game, but by the time I put it down, it was already too late to refund. I was devastated...Yakuza: Like a Dragon is  like P4G in that regard, you'll catch on pretty quickly if it's the kind of game for you! I was watching it on a stream (Thank you Arraxis!) and I was really enjoying how cartoony it could be, but it knew when it drop the gags and have a serious moment, or even give off some life advice through a sidestory. I had to try it, even having never played the other games, because I wanted to know what happened. I've been staying up late into the morning to find out what happens next, and I can't recommend the game enough. It knows when to be serious, when to talk to the player, and when it can pull off it's pants and go wild for a bit because hey, that's a part of the Yakuza charm!There are definitely some gripes I have with the game. Namely, the Minigames (especially Management) while not mandatory, are certainly a pain, and the companion that comes along with it is never actually in the story aside from some optional dialogue you get while exploring the city (She's supposed to be an afterthought because you can't know when you actually get her, but ) and it feels like 60% or more of the sidestories are just focused on giving your employees as rewards rather than useful items. Still, it's a game you can love without worrying about the details, and I cannot recommend it enough.Just... Keep the PC specs in mind. The game can get really freaky when you don't meet the requirements (The worst case was when I infiltrated a  base, there was a spotting minigame that, unfortunately, caused my entire screen to turn black bar the interface. Because it was a dungeon, I couldn't quicksave and restart the client, so I had to navigate basically blind until I found another enemy group, afterwhich the graphics finally reset and I could see things again)

_childDocuments_.review: In many ways, this is the best Yakuza game since Yakuza 0. The storyline is chaotic but entertaining and presented in a very cinematic way, the side stories are hilarious and nonsensical, the minigames are simple but complex enough to have you distracted for hours, and the new city offers enough freshness that you feel the way you felt when you first stepped into Kamurocho, with each corner breathing with life and wanting you to explore every alley even if quests do not lead you there. The new lead Ichiban is a standout of the entire game, easily climbing to my top 5 video game protagonists.Yet, at the same time, the game has one issue that brings it down and makes it almost unbearable to play at times - its combat. The turn-based combat is not only worse than the beat-them-up combat of the previous games in the series, but it is also one of the worst iterations of turn-based combat I've ever seen. Here's why in short: 1. The game gives you plenty of job options for each character as well as a plethora of skills, weapons, and armour to choose from. On the outside, it looks like it has everything a decent JRPG needs. But it doesn't because very quickly you will realize that the stats are useless numbers. Except for obvious ones like defence or attack, the game does not explain what each stat does. The best example of it is the initiative order in battle. I found multiple accounts online claiming that Agility is responsible for this, yet it isn't the only factor. I did a test and had multiple battles with the same items and levels and against the same enemies, and the characters would go in different order despite their Agility not changing. And there is no in-game explanation for this. 2. Each job offers mostly useless skills and you will usually want to use only one or two. Items similarly are practically meaningless, with the only stat that matters being defence, and any strategy in combat is unnecessary - all you have to worry about is having a good healer and appropriate level. 3. Each combat is just a check if you can heal enough to outlast the enemy. In other words, it is a numbers check. I am not joking. Give Saeko the Idol job and you can survive each combat using normal punches only as long as you have her heal the entire party every turn. 4. The enemies are bullet sponges and there is no fast-forward system. You will fight the same boring enemies that do two damage to you per hit on the streets until you are bored to death. I had to busy myself by checking in on my idle game in the browser while I clicked the auto-battle option. It is a nice option, but the combat doesn't go faster, it is as slow as if you were clicking the skills yourself. 5. Finally, the bosses. Not only are they spongy, some bosses (I won't say which exactly because of spoilers, but if you played the game I am sure you know exactly which bosses I am referring to) have damage limits. That is, they can only receive a certain amount of damage before their health stops going down until they switch to the next phase. However, the game lies to you and shows that the boss is still taking damage when it isn't. Those are empty numbers. This is awful because you might waste both MP and a chance to guard against more powerful attacks as you try to bring the boss down faster. But what is absolutely worst in all of this is that the damage limits throw any strategy to the trash. Some bosses have AI which forces them to make at least one move before switching a phase on their next turn. That means that you are sometimes LOCKED INTO taking damage even if you prepare for the boss specifically and target only their weakness and use skills and items to paralyze them. Eventually, you will have to give them a turn during which they will attack you if you want to win. I fought against these three particular bosses that feature this multiple times to confirm this and it is absolutely unforgivable to me.Despite all of this, I am still recommending this game as my overall memories with it are fond. However, if you are looking for a gameplay game, or a jrpg with intircate combat system that will test your understanding of the game's mechanics, steer away from this game. If you are looking to buy it, do it for the story and the characters, but not the gameplay. My only hope is that if the studio chooses to continue with turn-based combat in future installments of the series, they will rebuilt the combat system from the ground up. That is what the current system needs.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on a whim wanting to scratch a JRPG itch I have been having for a while. After watching a few reviews online I decided to take the plunge and buy Like a Dragon. To begin with I was frustrated and found myself watching what felt like hours of cutscenes instead of actually playing the game. This frustration stems from only having a few hours after work and weekends to get my gaming done. I like a rich story in my games but the beginning hours of this game felt closer to a slightly interactive Japanese miniseries than an actual game. But seeing as though it was the weekend when I got the game I pressed on with my newly discovered miniseries.Once the game began to open up and give over more control to me it started to become more and more clear that what was on offer here was something special. The amount of care and deliberation that has gone into creating this world, story and characters is not something that can be rushed through. It takes its time to develop and the longer you spend with Kasuga and his delightful little crew the more things start to make sense. It has been a while since I have been able to invest in a story and its characters and I can safely say that after 35+ hours I have become hooked.The story is rich and deep, there is a mystery to uncover in the main quest and tonnes of fun side quests and activities to engage in. The game is both serious and absolutely goofy at times. The mix between the two is spot on. There are some laugh out loud moments and crazy enemies to defeat. The city you play in is filled to the brim with interesting and quirky people. The city actually feels alive and real unlike some other recent releases (looking at you Cyberpunk). The classic JRPG battle system is at play here. A great addition is the movement of the characters on screen while the battles are taking place, it give the fights a sense of realism that can be lacking in the old school Final Fantasy games for example. You have the choice to change the classes of your party and find a mix of abilities that work for you. So far the balance has been great and I haven't felt like I am forced into an 'OP' class because the others are just not viable. You can just do what you want and play your own way, which in a climate of 'metas' and build guides I found to be very refreshing.Overall, if you are able to sink in the hours and enjoy a fresh take on the tried and true JRPG formula you will not be disappointed by this game. Yakuza: Like a Dragon is not a game that should be rushed through, instead, it should approached with a gentle curiosity and allowed to open itself up to you as progress through an interesting and enthralling tale.

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first dive into the Yakuza series, and I’m genuinely impressed by what it had to offer. From an engaging story to quirky side content and a surprisingly refreshing turn-based combat system, the game left a lasting impression. Here’s my take on what worked well, along with a few aspects that could have been better.Positives:1. Story: The story was one of the major highlights for me. Initially, the pacing felt a bit slow, and it took me quite a few days to progress through the first few chapters. However, everything changes around Chapter 5, where the plot really picks up. The emotional stakes climb higher with each chapter, and by the time I reached the climax, I was fully invested. The twists and turns, along with themes of loyalty, betrayal, and redemption, kept me hooked. I have to give credit to the developers for creating such a gripping narrative—one that I genuinely couldn’t put down after a certain point.2. Combat: I was initially skeptical about the turn-based combat, considering it’s a significant departure from the series' classic brawler style. I wasn’t sure how well it would blend with the gritty, street-level feel of Yakuza. But to my surprise, it was extremely well-executed! The combat system is dynamic, adding just enough flair and creativity to make each battle feel strategic rather than repetitive. The special moves and team attacks are a lot of fun to pull off, and the way environmental objects can still be used in fights adds a unique Yakuza touch. Honestly, this type of turn-based combat deserves to be a standard in other games—it’s the perfect balance of strategy and excitement.3. Side Missions and Minigames: The side missions and minigames are an absolute treat. The sheer variety kept things interesting—I found myself getting lost in activities that ranged from managing a business empire to batting cages and karaoke. The humorous, sometimes bizarre nature of these side quests adds a lot of personality to the game and gives a welcome break from the intense main storyline. Though I didn’t complete every side mission, the ones I did play left a lasting impression. They not only flesh out the world but also offer hilarious, heartwarming, and sometimes strange encounters with NPCs, making the game feel more alive.4. Characters and Relationships: The cast of characters in Yakuza is one of its strongest assets. Ichiban, in particular, is one of the most relatable and endearing protagonists I’ve encountered in gaming. His optimism, even in the face of hardship, really shines through, and it’s refreshing to follow someone who isn’t your typical stoic anti-hero. The bond between Ichiban and his friends adds layers of depth to the story. Each character feels well-developed, and you get a strong sense of camaraderie as the story unfolds. The party dynamic, with every character contributing their unique backstories and abilities, makes the journey all the more immersive.5. World-Building: The city of Yokohama is a character in itself. The attention to detail in recreating a vibrant, bustling city is incredible, from neon-lit streets to cozy restaurants and hidden alleys. There’s so much to explore, and it feels like a real, lived-in place. I enjoyed roaming around, discovering new areas, and finding hidden shops and items. Every corner of the city seems to have its own story, and the blend of realism with the game’s eccentric characters and situations creates a uniquely immersive experience.Negatives:1. Slow Start and Uneven Pacing: As much as I loved the story after Chapter 5, getting to that point felt like a bit of a slog. The first few chapters move at a slower pace, and I can see how it might put some players off before they get to the more gripping parts. I think the story could have benefitted from a bit more urgency or intrigue early on. For newcomers like me, the slow start could be a barrier to fully enjoying the game until it gets going.2. Complexity in Combat Mechanics: While I ended up enjoying the turn-based combat, it could feel a bit overwhelming at times due to the number of mechanics, upgrades, and options to manage. I often found myself sifting through menus and trying to keep track of gear, skills, and job changes. For players who prefer a simpler approach, the depth of customization might feel like too much to handle initially. A bit more guidance or a more gradual introduction to these systems could have made this aspect easier to digest.3. Side Missions Can Be Distracting: As much as I enjoyed the quirky side missions, they can sometimes feel like a distraction from the emotional core of the main story. Yakuza’s tone oscillates between high-stakes drama and goofy, lighthearted antics, which can occasionally feel jarring, especially if you’re deeply invested in the primary narrative. For instance, right after an intense, emotional scene, it can feel a bit odd to jump into a whimsical side quest. While these side missions are great fun, a bit more tonal balance could have helped maintain immersion.4. Difficulty Spikes: Another thing I noticed was the occasional difficulty spike, especially in certain boss fights. Some battles required a level of grinding or strategizing that felt disproportionate to the flow of the game. At times, I’d find myself breezing through the story, only to hit a wall where I had to grind for levels or upgrade equipment to proceed. While I’m all for a good challenge, these spikes can be a bit frustrating, particularly if you’re focused more on the story than on combat.5. Repetitive Enemy Encounters: In some areas, enemy encounters can become repetitive, with similar groups of enemies showing up frequently. While combat is enjoyable, this repetition sometimes slows down exploration and interrupts the flow. I found myself wishing for a bit more variety in enemy types or encounter scenarios to keep things fresh as I progressed through the city.6. Limited Freedom in Certain Chapters: While the game offers a rich, open-world experience, there are moments in the story where freedom is restricted for narrative purposes. I understand the reason behind it, but it occasionally felt a bit limiting, especially when I wanted to explore or tackle side missions. There were moments when the game forced me to progress the main story before I could get back to the rest of the city, which felt slightly restrictive.I’d rate this game an 8/10, and I’m definitely looking forward to exploring more in the series, especially with Like a Dragon Gaiden and Infinite Wealth.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played all the Yakuza's on PC so far this may be the first one i won't finish.Yakuza 0 & Yakuza kiwami so far i think are the best, i say that though as i have only played the Yakuza games that are available on PC. A lot of people are defending the combat on here and i don't know why. I've played lots of turned based games but this game just did not do it well.I was willing to play and not let it bother me and focus on the story; but it becomes a slow repetitive slog. i almost tilted and uninstalled at the sewer section in the story, not to give away too much information.... 4 - 5 levels of a maze like sewer where your forced into battles as you progress through it.  It just seemed so repetitive on top of the combat and the sewer rooms literally copy pasted with little no variation.After escaping the sewer the game tells me i can return to the dungeon for unlimited combat with unique enemies for loot and exp, ect. Trust me, i won't be doing that.Choose attack, watch character slowly run to target, watch the attack animation again. Repeat. I don't even have to block,or do anything. I could set it to auto and the battles would win themselves for me, but at that point why am i even playing this? Am i even playing this? Why is auto combat even a feature? I pushed onward trying to ignore it. Now i'm at another boss fight in the story, my enemies are level 27 and i'm 25 / 24. And i  don't care to continue anymore, the damage i was doing was little and it feels like the fight although not difficult, is going to take some time to chip away at their health pool.To top it all off, i'm not really liking the characters except for Ichiban and Adachi, but even then they are pale comparisons to Goro Majima and Kiyru as main protagonists from the earlier series. The story so far has been a wild goose chase, one thing after another, so many twists? Meeting my enemies and then suddenly they are pleading for me to assist them, prior had a gun pointed at my head, now this character was bowing at me pleading for assistance. _childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of every single Yakuza game and I was hoping LAD wouldn't disappoint...and it didn't. I was never a huge fan of the beat em up style of combat in the past games so I was eager to see how they would pull off the turn based combat and I really loved it, a very welcomed change. It could do with some polish but that's only to be expected with a totally new system. I'm sure they will improve it even more. The cast were all great and Ichiban was a great protagonist, the polar opposite of Kiryu in many ways and welcomed change. I loved the OGs but it was time for a change. The English VAs, as like in Judgment, are generally fantastic but it is VERY weird hearing returning cast speaking in English and they all sounded off to me.If you're new to the series this is a good place to start, although I do recommend all previous games because they are just excellent. The story was, as usual, very good and the antagonist is definitely one of my favourites in the whole series. I found him to be an interesting person and always enjoyed when he was on screen.Yakuza 7 ranks third for me out of the whole series - 0 being first and Judgment second (if you count that). LAD is only third because the stories of 0 and Judgment are stronger, in my opinion. Gameplay wise, LAD is one of the strongest, if not the best.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game as both a Yakuza fan and a Dragon Quest fan. The change of gameplay to a turn based RPG may be a turn off for some but I feel the game did it well enough. The game starts off as a movie with cutscenes for a couple hours but it's to set the world with these new set of characters. Kiryu's story is over and Ichiban Kasuga has some big shoes to fill in. The whole cast is quite diverse and I rotated party members quite often--I never stuck to a definite 4 for a party. There are 9 jobs for the male cast (+1 for Kasuga) and 5 for female. Each job has 2 skills that transfer to other jobs, though I wish the jobs had more skills in general.There are references and parallels to the DQ series. A drunk man in an alley gets you a "No response, it's just a drunk," which is to DQ's "There's no response. It's just a corpse." A lot of enemies have puns for names and attacks reminiscent of Dragon Quest ones. You got enemies akin to Metal slimes and Hammerhoods while still having the Yakuza wacky-ness.This game still has Yakuza's great story telling and world while having DQ elements for a fun and enjoyable RPG. This game has an English dub but I played it in Japanese since I'm used to hearing Japanese from the previous games.

_childDocuments_.review: The play style is easy to understand, there's no Final Fantasy style ATB charges or confusing enemy staggering guidelines. The game tries to mimic the simpler straightforward Dragon Quest-like gameplay (which is also referenced frequently throughout the game and a ton of grinding). The item acquisition and upgrade logic is also pretty straightforward (though requires a lot of in-game currency), and there aren't any convoluted side-quests that need to be accomplished. In all honesty, the gameplay is almost too simplistic. But it is addictive because of its ease and simplicity.The characters caught me by surprise, as I didn't think I'd like them so much, particularly the main character Kasuga Ichiban, who is very different than Kiryu. But in general, all the playable characters (as well as a couple of the NPCs) are extremely likeable. The story itself is also much easier to follow than Kiryu's Yakuza series, which oftentimes are littered with betrayals, rival gangs, multiple backstories, and whatnot (basically, soap operas). So newcomers should not have a problem following the content.Most of the minigames are still there, which are always great (I even learned how to play most of them, but I am still very confused by Pachinko and Shogi). And like every Yakuza game, there are side-job type games. One of the biggest differences though is actually the "adult" content, which has been very toned down here. The previous Yakuza games were more apparent in the red-light type of activities (e.g., saunas, videos, dating, etc.). The dating and hostess bar aspects are still here, but they are much more graphically toned-down versions compared to Kiryu's Yakuza. This is neither a complaint nor a praise, but to each their own...Lastly, newcomers should be able to enjoy this game thoroughly, but there are so many easter eggs, cameos, and references to the past series that very much made me embrace this game even more. There are several moments that really pulled on my emotions purely out of nostalgia. Yakuza 4 and 5 are still my favorites in the series, but LAD is easily just beneath them.

I could go on about how this game is literally 50 games bundled into one and that if you need a break from the game itself, go do that. _childDocuments_.review: Play it for the main and substories, because those seem like they're GOAT.The other Yakuza had better gameplay, and that's not because I like beat 'em ups and not JRPGs, because I love both. Yakuza:LAD just has really awkward combat, where it feels like it was meant to be a beat 'em up at one point in development (much like the other Yakuza games) and they took that and forced it to be a turn-based game. You have to worry about positioning and lining enemies up, which is FINE, but you have no direct control of where your dudes go, and you'll occasionally have to wait for the enemies to just... line up for AOEs, because although turn-based, enemies still idle around and shift about while you make your turn. Example: a fight starts because you walked vaguely close to some enemies, people are clustered up for a nice AOE. You immediately scramble through your skill menu (depending on who starts) to find X or Y AOE, then you select a target in the 3D space and execute it, hoping that the enemy AI has stalled enough to stand in a straight line behind each other so that you can hit them all. You only hit one of them when you could've hit 3, because your guy had to run up to the enemy in question to do the attack, but they had snagged on something while you were running around the overworld, leading to them being stuck ridiculously far back. Also, because of how wonky the camera is with bouncing between your party members/enemies on their turns, Perfect Guarding feels REALLY bad, which isn't horrible against lowbie enemies, but when enemies start hitting harder, it's not fun.If this were a normal JRPG where you engage in a fight and you have dudes doing Street Fighter idle poses while waiting for their turns, it'd be a lot more enjoyable. Right now? It's worth slugging through for the good, which is the dumb minigames, the absurdity of the skills/crazy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that happens to Ichi and crew, and the simultaneously ridiculous and endearing story/substories that the game tells.tl;dr Doo doo gameplay (fun for the eyes, though) but good story (at least what I've played, though ultimately, I'm probably gonna drop it because of the wonky gameplay). For me, the poor gameplay is enough to make the game not enjoyable for me to playthrough.tl;dr x2 The game is great on sale, which is it regularly. I got it months ago at ~35% off, now it's 75%. iirc, you can also play it on GamePass for a dollar to ten dollars, which is the ultimate deal if it's not on sale at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: I played yakuza 0 and was blown away by how amazing the plot was. Everything about it -- the dialogue, the delivery, the themes, the twists, and the emotional impact. However, by the end of the game, I was just SO bored by the button-mashy combat.This game's new battle system represents a huge improvement on that front. It's true that it's just a turn-based battle system, but so much love and creativity was put into it that you can't help but enjoy it. There are a ton of interesting options and jobs for each character. They are not really based on game role archetypes (for example there is no 'mage' class), but rather something in the real world, such as a bodyguard, idol, card dealer, or dominatrix. The game has many standard abilities that you'd see in old RPGs, but represented in a modern way that's very charming. For example, in a standard RPG you might cast fearga to put a fear status effect on all enemies. In this game, one character can pretend to call the cops on her phone so that enemies hesitate to fight. As another example, instead of summons, the main character can call someone on his phone to come in and help out.In terms of plot, this game cannot compare to yakuza 0, but it is good nonetheless. It evokes a lot of the same emotions as earlier yakuza games and I found myself hugely invested in the struggles of many of the characters. There were some characters I loved and some I loved to hate. The game has an extremely satisfying ending, a fantastic payoff. Also, I spent like 6 hours learning how to play Riichi Mahjong.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, when I first bought this game, I played it for a while but dropped it. It just wasn't grabbing me in the way I wanted. But luckily I did return to it, and found out that the game opened up a lot more a couple hours past where I left off.Making a turn based Yakuza game seemed like a major but logical change that the games needed to try and refresh things. Do I prefer it to the classic beat 'em up Yakuza games? No. But I came to enjoy the combat here, and there's certainly a lot to mess around with in terms of party, ability and gear combinations. The combat style works and it fits with the rest of the gameplay that Yakuza games have to offer. What I didn't find as compelling was the new location, Isezaki Ijincho. It's large but laid out strangely, leaving a lot to be desired. It's also not the most exciting in terms of how most of it looks. The other locations you're able to go to, Sotenbori and Kamurocho from the previous games, also have some things lacking in terms of shops and things to do, making them feel a bit like afterthoughts.The main question is... does Ichiban Kasuga make for a good Yakuza protagonist? And does his story lead to a good Yakuza story? Yes and yes, but not without some flaws. I think Ichiban could, through future games, expand into a really solid lead for future Yakuza games. They make him much less stoic than Kazuma Kiryu, while still allowing for those tough guy badass moments. The story has some slumps, and can often (especially early on) feel disconnected from the the greater pre-existing world and lore of Yakuza. But the 3rd act cranks things up quite a bit, and it had some of the coolest moments in any Yakuza game, which makes up for a slower start.All in all, I think the game suffers from some of the problems a game like Yakuza 6 suffered from, for similar reasons. Both games were introducing something big and new (that being turn based combat and new protagonist for this game, a brand new engine for Yakuza 6), and because of that, some of the details get lost in favour of focusing on some bigger things at hand that they didn't want to screw up. Even with those flaws, this ends up being a really great Yakuza game. Something different for the franchise, for better or worse. Mostly better.

_childDocuments_.review: Right, where do I start...Yakuza: Like a Dragon (later in this review Yakuza 7) has been my introduction to the Yakuza franchise as a whole. Prior to this, all I knew about was the Bakamitai meme, which I also only knew as the Dame Da Ne song. I was a bit sceptical about getting into it at first, as I knew absolutely nothing about the game and franchise as a whole, and Brawlers weren't really my thing, but then I heard that this game features a different protagonist, and instead of a Brawler, plays as a turn based RPG. I had some money left over from Christmas, and I'm a big fan of the old Final Fantasy games, so I thought I might as well give it a try. Could always refund it if I didn't enjoy it. In Yakuza 7, you play as Ichiban Kasuga, a Yakuza grunt who goes to jail to cover for a higher-ranking member of the Arakawa family, which he belongs to. Thinking that this would make him climb the Yakuza ladder, and that his patriarch will honour and appreciate his cover, he comes back after 18 years of prison time to find out that everybody had abandoned him. Former police officer Koichi Adachi researched about the Tojo Clan and the Arakawa Family, attempts to convince Ichiban to come with him to Yokohama to stay safe, but Ichiban refuses. Ichiban finds his way back to his former patriarch and is then met with an unfortunate fate.Oh boy, I was immediately hooked from the start. "That's a lot of cutscenes for a game, it's like I'm watching a movie" was my first thought. I liked story heavy games, but I felt a little overwhelmed on my first day, as out of the probably 5 or 6 hours that I was playing, 4 of them were just watching cutscenes. Now this might turn some people down, especially if they just want to enjoy the gameplay, but all the introductory scenes got me more invested in finding out about the presented characters and I didn't just want to stop playing until I found a point where I thought "Okay, now the actual game finally begins."The vast majority of this game takes plays in the streets of Yokohama, more specifically, Isezaki Ijincho, Yokohama's red light district. The world is incredibly detailed and you'll be pleasantly surprised to know that there's things hidden in every single corner. I really enjoy exploring in video games, trying to see if there's things hidden in places nobody would think of and-- to my surprise, they really thought of everything here. I try sneaking into a corner that I think might not even be intended to go to, and yet, there's something there for me to pick up. I personally went for the "50% main story, 50% side story" approach, which to me means - I'll do 2 or 3 side quests, of which there are plenty in Yakuza 7, and then I'll do a few story quests so that I can keep up with what is happening. And trust me, there's a lot of content to burn through. All of the sidequests are very well designed, and most of them got at least a little bit of a chuckle from me, so I'd like to think that they are quite humorous. Once done with the sidequests, I grabbed my imaginary bucket of popcorn and started getting immersed in the story. After I arrived in Yokohama, and the game properly begun for me, I thought to myself that this would be a silly little hero adventure. One of a redemption arc where Ichiban becomes the hero of a big and epic tale. Well, it's kinda like that, it starts off slow and adventurous, but the more the story goes on, Ichiban falls deeper into this crime drama rabbit hole. I will not spoil anything for the sake of letting you enjoy it by yourself, but I can say you're in for a treat. A big one. The gameplay itself is, as mentioned earlier, a turn based RPG. I hit you, then I wait, then you hit me, and then you wait. Yakuza 7 adds a nice little twist to that by adding small, simple QTEs to most of your abilities. Sometimes you might have to press a button repeatedly to give it more power, sometimes you might need to press the button at the proper time instead. Sometimes even both! It's a very, very simple thing but it keeps the combat entertaining, which is the main purpose. All attack animations look nice and polished too, some of the names and descriptions are silly and will put a weird look on your face when you first see it, but all skills feels nice to use. You might not have many skills when you first start the game, but the more you progress, the more and more skills will be added to your arsenal.This game works in a job system, which you might be familiar with if you played some Final Fantasy games. While each character has their own primary main job, they can also switch to other jobs, which in this game are gender locked. Male characters can choose from a variety of different jobs, and female characters have their own jobs to choose from, too. Some of these jobs exist for both genders, although slightly altered, such as Host for males and Hostess for females. They essentially do the same thing, yet they slightly differ from one another.Now, apart from the amazing story that this game has to offer, and the ability to throw ridiculous-looking skills at your enemies, there's also plenty of minigames that you can play in this game. Of course, there's Karaoke (also with Bakamitai!), Mahjong, Shogi and Dragon Kart (yes, like actual kart racing) just to name a few. Each of these felt well thought out and they're fun to do, and you can seriously get invested in them if you're dedicated enough. Sometimes I booted this game up just to play a little bit of Mahjong...But there's probably a few negatives about this game, right? Yes there are, but in my personal opinion, these are just minor things that probably won't even bother you unless you think really hard about it. What I disliked during my playthrough is that there's just. so. many. random. encounters. I was told by a friend that this is common in the Yakuza games, and that you'll have to just deal with it, but god there's just so many. Happens a lot that you walk down one street and you get hit with 3 or 4 different encounters that really badly want to murder you. There is an item in this game that completely removes random encounters, but I feel like you'll get access to it way too late. By the time you have it, you're probably able to finish the game for good already. Another issue that I had in this game is that there was one dungeon that just felt way too long to complete. It wasn't even challenging or anything, you just entered a new floor and thought "this is it", only to be hit with a wave of disappointment as you realize this is just another floor with the same enemies as the last one. It was a slog to get through it, but luckily it's only a one time thing.So, what can I say to finalize this review? I think that Yakuza 7 is an amazing game, with a well written and properly thought out story that is guaranteed to keep you glued to your screen, fun and entertaining combat to keep you playing, and a wide variety of different minigames that you grind out, or even just relax with if you feel like. Ichiban and his party makes it feel like you're part of the crew, that his achievements and goals are yours too, and that you too can overcome any obstacle if you just believe in yourself and don't give up. Ichiban Kasuga has been one of the most relateable characters I have ever met and he's found a place in my heart that I will protect. This game has also made me buy all the other main Yakuza games and I'm motivated to play through all of them, at the time of this review I am currently on Yakuza 4 Remastered. As I found out while playing, there are plenty of references to the older Yakuza games that will make you go "Oooh, I know this" when you see them, and they still don't feel out of place when you're new to it. I am very happy that this game introduced me to the series and I have no shame admitting that I cried when it was over.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 7 was a worrying departure from the formula of it's series, one that very easily could have result in a flaccid disappointment of a game. However the nonsensical change of genre is exactly what elevated the series to a new level of quality it's predecessors could only have dreamt of. Obviously there's the same old Yakuza storytelling that every game in the series has, and if you liked previous games you'll like this one. But where Yakuza 7 truly shines is in how it utilises it's new JRPG shell to unify the various separate parts of the Yakuza formula. In previous Yakuza entries, there were many pieces of the game that felt disconnected, entirely unrelated, shoved in just for the sake of variety or neat little minigames which were more often than not unenjoyable and totally pointless in playing. With Yakuza 7 all of these side activities now all directly feed back into the core JRPG mechanics of the game, whether they be providing money to feed into gear, rewards to permanently increase the statistics of your party members or a simple bond increase with whichever party members you choose to partake in an activity with. This successfully takes this disparate segments of the Yakuza series and unifies them into one cohesive whole, something the series has never managed to do before, despite some lackluster attempts at doing so. Now obviously, this would not really matter if those core JRPG mechanics were not refined enough to make an enjoyable experience on their own, and they most certainly are.The new combat system has something to entice fans of traditional JRPGs whilst also creating a system that is potentially enjoyable for people that otherwise have a distaste for the unimpactful, slow and incredibly repetitive combat formulas of most JRPGs. All of the traditional debuff stacking, party building antics are there, but by utilising the Dragon Engine's physics, characters positioning themselves in real time and Paper Mario style button prompts, Yakuza 7 succeeds in making that traditionally incredibly limp, unsatisfying style of combat that JRPGs have and makes it immensely satisfying to play. Whilst those points may sound vague, Yakuza 7 succeeds in having an incredibly unique and incredibly satisfying combat system that directly benefits from you partaking in the game's various side activities.In Short, Yakuza: Like a Dragon is the best game in it's series, the best game that RGG Studios has made thus far and one of the best games ever made.

_childDocuments_.review: A great entry point into the series for beginners, but also a nostalgic trip through the series for veterans - Yakuza: Like a Dragon provides a fresh take on the series with combat that feels like a mixture of Dragon Quest and Persona with the chaos you'd expect from a Yakuza game, a huge plethora of sidestories and world content that makes the game world feel really lived in, and the narrative has a fresh, yet familiar feeling to it with protagonist Ichiban Kasuga being more of a charismatic leader, than Kazuma Kiryu's more stoic nature, with the differences represented through every aspect of the game.The gear and upgrade system is in-depth and paced, though to complete the game's post-story endgame content you will need to max out everything you can, as the encounters are more than willing to leave you on your ass again and again.Overall, yeah, just get it for the Karaoke tbh, if you need any other reason to play this game. Maybe get the middle tier version of the game too, as some of the DLC isn't as worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s time for a brand new adventure! While Yakuza 6: The Song of Life completely wrapped up the story of the Dragon of Dojima properly, Yakuza: Like a Dragon brings around an all-new cast and an all new genre for the series. But can the new saga stack up to the old one?You play as Ichiban Kasuga, an enthusiastic and incredibly loyal member of the yakuza. When asked to step up and take the fall for a crime he didn’t commit, he does so without question. Now, 18 years later, he’s released from prison to a world he’s not familiar with at all. Searching for his patriarch, he discovers that the clan he was a part of has been dissolved, and that the patriarch he idolized is now working for their known enemy, the Omi Alliance. Even worse, when he confronts his former patriarch, Ichiban is shot in the chest and left for dead in Yokohama, miles from home. Now with no purpose or family to speak of, Ichiban has to start his way from the bottom and work his way back, learning the mystery of what happened while was away in the process.One of Ichiban’s main passions is JRPGs, specifically Dragon Quest. If you give him the opportunity, he will talk about Dragon Quest, to an obsessive degree. This is the first time I’ve seen a video game character be a fan of another video game series, and it’s quite refreshing and interesting to see. Because of his obsession, he sees fights that he has to take part in as random encounters, explaining the genre shift.Yes, the long running Yakuza series has changed from an action brawler to a JRPG. And it does so with style and grace. Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio wears its love for the genre on its sleeve, seeing as how a lot of the new mechanics introduced in Like a Dragon are from a lot of other great RPG titles. It has the job system of Dragon Quest, the item synthesis of Final Fantasy, the crazy enemies of the Mother series, the enemy compendium of Pokemon, the personality stats growth of Persona, even the quick 1 button battle menu system of Super Mario RPG (no, it wasn’t just Persona 5 that did that)! And they all fit together perfectly like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle.Thanks to the game being a JRPG, it won’t just be Ichiban on his adventure. He has a total of 6 other party members to aid in battle. From Nanba the homeless pigeon wizard (no really), to an eager ninja office worker named Eri, each character comes packed with personality, and their own story. It can also be easily said that a legacy character like Kiryu gives the next protagonist a lot to live up to, but thanks to Ichiban’s friends, he’s not alone; and each role that every party member offers can help Ichiban rise to the top. While Kiryu Kazuma’s saga was more about upholding the old world values of Yakuza and being a noble man, Ichiban Kasuga’s saga starts off with a heavy emphasis on friendship.While Yakuza Like a Dragon has flipped the series on its head in more than one way, the incredibly immersive and incredibly addictive side activities remain. With Vocational Schooling that helps Ichiban gain personality stats and certificates, to an entire story arc about Ichiban learning the fun of go-kart racing with rocket launchers in Dragon Kart, it’s incredibly simple to find all sorts of things to do that can easily stack up your playtime. You can even collect popular Sega songs. I found myself spending hours at the batting cages just so I could listen to Nights into Dreams, or Phantasy Star Online 2 music.While on the topic of music, I felt that the compositions stood out more in this game then they usually do. Battle themes usually come and go, but that could more be because I’m too focused on not getting punched. Turning the combat to turn based had me thinking more, and appreciating the music around me. I won’t spoil which, but a certain theme that plays during a boss fight really caught my attention. I also won’t deny that having some of the more popular songs from Yakuza 0 really helped as well.I should also say that for the first time since the original Yakuza on PS2, Yakuza: Like a Dragon has a dub cast! And the way this game handled the dub and the way the original handled the dub are like night and day. It’s an excellently directed cast, every voice actor sounding like they were made for their role. I will definitely include Darryl Kulo in that, reprising his role as Kiryu Kazuma from the original PS2 game. He felt awkward and out of place in that game, but thanks to the direction, I can now only hear the Dragon of Dojima with a deep, bass-y voice. For the parts that he’s in, he does an excellent job. If you’re worried about Majima losing his chaotic energy and defining cackle, lemme put those fears to rest. Unfortunately, Sega was not able to secure Mark Hamill to reprise Goro Majima for whatever reason, but Matt Mercer does an excellent job in his stead.And a big first for the series is English lip sync. It must have been quite the undertaking to do, to remodel every mocap model to move their lips in English, but I can say that it was absolutely worth the effort. Matching the lip sync and dub track really pulls you in and dips you on the dance floor, not letting go of you for a second. Between the writing, the acting, and the lip sync, everyone here felt like a real person and pulled me into their story, even the absurd ones.While I don’t have too many negatives, there’s definitely things to be improved on for Yakuza 8. I know I’m in the minority that enjoys the dungeon segments, wandering around in an underground tunnel ready to jump 5 punks or garbage people just minding their own business, but it could be tightened up. Maybe some secrets that aren’t just “go down the corner that’s a dead end”? In dungeon dialogue would be nice as well. When traveling above ground or eating, the party has plenty to say to one another, but things go quiet underground. It would be nice to see more of that banter in the future. There’s also a difficulty spike near the end of the game, so I would advise to grind a bit in these dungeons.I also think that at certain times that Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio relied too much on fan service to help Yakuza Like a Dragon. Not only does Nugget from Yakuza 0 return (in a way), but there’s also Gondawara from Yakuza Kiwami 2 returns, if anything because he was in the most popular substory in Yakuza Kiwami 2. Personally, the more wild characters that are introduced in Like a Dragon substories are more entertaining than the ones that are brought back. They’re minor gripes, but I think that Like a Dragon stands up on its own merits and doesn’t need a crutch like that to be popular.Overall, if you’re a fan of the JRPG genre, the Yakuza series, or compelling, well acted narratives in general, Yakuza Like a Dragon is absolutely right for you. Being the first in a new saga gives it the luxury of being a great jumping on point for the Yakuza series, so it doesn’t need to be necessary to play the previous 7 games. It helps, but it’s not necessary. Regardless, this has my full recommendation, being my Game of the Year for 2020. It pulled me into a warm bear hug and refused to let go, even weeks after finishing the main story.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza is art.Before starting the game I was worried that the changes in combat and protagonist would make me feel distanced to the story and less immersed, but it was a needless worry.Yakuza Like A Dragon (LAD), while changing the core mechanics of the games battle system from being a fighter to a turn-based RPG still somehow makes the fights feel epic and intimate. Each fight still feel epic, with skills and attacks being ridden with animations, as well as cinematics being used to portray the short intimate seconds of dialogue and bonding that occurs mid-fight. Yakuza LAD pays homage to the previous titles style of gameplay, where side-quests feel like a reward rather than a chore, whereby you can play games inside the game, each seemingly small side-quest has the potential for unlocking different abilities, allies and even romances. Some of the most fun hours I spent in Yakuza LAD were done by playing the business managment minigame and the racing side-quest minigames. Even after playing around 30 hours of the game, I feel like I have a lot of content left to explore, as a lot of things ("abilities, allies and even romances") are hidden in the side-quests.The storytelling of the game itself is rife with parodies and jokes, although it does this to be comedic at times, this does not deter its more serious underlying themes nor inhibit its mature storytelling. The cinematics and cutscenes in the story had me hooked since the first chapter and each time I accidentally skipped a custscene, I would immediately go look it up on youtube, as a lot of powerful and emotional moments are contained within the cutscenes. I felt giddy and hyped each time a character would appear or be introduced (old and new). The character design of Yakuza is always a beautiful thing to behold, each character introduced seems animated and alive, the villains and allies all have wear their intentions on their faces; where it seems like you can read their life story and experiences from their face. The rough and rugged facial expressions and designs help to portray the toughness of the character and build up an expectation of strength, even before fighting them or seeing them fight.  My only problem with this game is with the DLCs, with each DLC feeling unnecessary, like extra resources, costumes or characters in the business management minigame. The DLC's to unlock the classes feel a bit underwhelming, since they lack weapons that can be heavily upgraded unlike the non-DLC classes (Highest Damage DLC class weapon I have is 135, whereas the highest non-DLC class weapon I have is around 300). My only justification for this would be that they came up with the classes after the game, but even then I had hoped the DLCs would contain more extra content rather than fluff.I recommend getting the base game, but not the DLC's.
