_childDocuments_.review: I'd been longing for a great adventure with beautiful visuals to immerse myself in, with the feel of an epic journey, but without demanding heavy gameplay or a huge amount of time. That's exactly what A Highland Song gave (and gives) me. The first thing that stands out is the stunning 2.5D art with breathtaking views of mountaineous landscapes. You could screenshot just about everything. There's a photo mode that supports that, but I hardly even used it during my first playthrough because I was too immersed to enter the settings. There's that sense of exploration and adventure, enhanced by your teen character who gets (often comically) annoyed as easily as she gets impressed and enthusiastic about all the new experiences. There's the sound design that does a lot for the atmosphere and immersion, and the same goes for all the bits of stories, myths and secrets. The nightly animations with excellently voice-acted letter passages give a sense of pacing. Overall, this game feels much more refined than Heaven's Vault by the same devs (of which I loved the concept more than the execution). It's not perfect, but its level of polish is unfortunately rare these days. Gameplay-wise, the update from 14th December (Look Further with path highlighting, helpful comments) helped with a lot of frustrations that I surely would have had. I wanted to play this game for the narrative, exploration and beautiful landscapes. I'm absolutely terrible at dexterity-based gameplay and easily stressed by survival stuff, so I checked off ALL the accessibility settings. That made the survival aspects and rhythm sections almost trivial for me, which was awesome. The adjusted rhythm sections don't require any rhythm if you can roughly time pressing spacebar on visual cues, and generally you don't even have to do them at all. The platforming was still a bit annoying in some parts, but it wasn't terrible, which is the best thing I've ever said about platforming in any game. There's little precision and timing involved, just some figuring out how to reach places and when to rest for a few seconds. And in fact, if you're a fan of colourful profanities, you should make sure to fall at least a couple of times :behappy:My biggest remaining source of frustration was the map system. I was terrible at identifying locations from some scribbles I found, even after my character told me I should be able to see them from the current peak and I spent a lot of time looking. Over time I learnt that I could usually just ignore them and find a different path, though, and I did discover more helpful shortcuts gradually. Content and accessibility notes: While you don't experience any violence directly (as far as I can tell), some of the stories you hear are quite grim. I encountered one mention of . Controls are keyboard or controller only and can't be remapped. There's an update in the works that lets you switch from moving with arrow keys to WASD. UPDATE: There's now a beta build with remappable controls (except for some uses of Enter)! My first playthrough took about 5 hours, which felt long enough for deep immersion and a "serious" adventure experience while also providing a clear break rather than derailing my life because I can't stop while I'm in the middle of something. The game is meant to be replayed and can be played a lot of times without running out of new peaks, paths and secrets to discover. I've done two playthroughs so far and was a bit afraid that my second one would feel less exciting and enjoyable, but it was actually even better. (Update: my 4th playthrough was still exciting: new routes, new discoveries, and new dialogue in old settings)TL;DR: A masterpiece and probably my GOTY together with . * * * If you like chill and story-driven games, check out my curator . You're also welcome to join the .

_childDocuments_.review: I have bought everything inkle had ever released on PC and mobile, and that my game of all time is probably Heaven's Vault, but my experience with this game was frustrating. I'll start by saying this game's visual and audio aspects are gorgeous; the map is satisfying to look at and the soundtracks are of good quality as usual. Unfortunately I cannot find much to praise for regarding the gameplay.The weather system demotivated me. On her way to the lighthouse, Moira will face all kinds of bad weather and her health decreases if she pushes through; or she could take a breath in a structure or under an overhung if she can find one in time, scattered across the map, far and few between. And story-wise, these complications don't bring any new elements to the table either, as our protagonist doesn't share anything unique associated with the weather; so to me the weather only managed to dampen my mood.The caves sound good on paper, but I barely have any idea where to go when underground. The novelty of geography  started to wear off when I saw the third tunnel and was completely gone at the entrance of the fifth. On a side note, do you know that Moira could be V E R Y  S L O W when she's crawling?Moira found all kinds of mundane items during her journey, but unlike artifacts in Heaven's Vault, most of these were just featureless items with no history (grand or personal). Same goes for Moira herself, I knew very little about her as an individual: strengths and weaknesses, aspiration and motivation, her important life events. I mean, it probably was because I am not the most observant person, but with how little I've found about Moira, it was just not enough for me to find her three-dimensional.If only the journey was a bit more fun and plot lines a bit more engaging. Sadly I left the game a lot less enthusiastic about Scotland's unique landscape and the distinct weather pattern of the British Isles.Then there're some minor gripes that hopefully can see improvement:I don't think I'll revisit this game anymore, unless there was a new mode that stops punishing me for playing the game and wanting to see new things. But to be honest, I think I just never was part of the target audience, as I don't find searching for objects or reaching points in a huge empty static map (except for time and weather) very fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements in games.Some gameplay spoilers ahead. A Highland Song is a 2.5 D platformer/climbing game from the same developers of 80 Days, where you need to reach the lighthouse where your uncle lives before the Festival of Beltane. In the beginning, most of the hills is unknown and you’ll feel lost and probably won’t arrive on time, but along the way you’ll find maps with locations that you need to find, some will unlock new paths that will save you time, others will have objects that will be important to also unlock new paths or complete sidequests. In the breaks between different zones or when you complete some tasks, the narrator will talk about the story of those highlands, its myths but also about the main character and her family. The lore was interesting as celtic lore isn’t the most trending one nowadays for the general public, and this one in particular seems very specific to Scotland.  The backgrounds are hand painted and very detailed and beautiful and the characters have more simple designs and plain colors but still look good. The weather effects like rain, lightning and fog are also very well done and overall the game looks great.When there are long, plain distances to cover, the game has a rhythm minigame where you need to press keys at the right time while listening to celtic songs. The songs don’t have lyrics but are very catchy and this activity turns something otherwise boring into something that’s entertaining. The narration and voice actors are also very well done and the thick accent only adds authenticity to the game.Regarding gameplay, while the game has a PEGI 3 rating, finding the map's locations and navigating this world can be confusing and frustrating because the path isn’t always linear and the game doesn’t have a world map. Knowing all the secrets will take several runs and dozens of solved maps, but personally, the difficulty is what makes it interesting and you should play without help until you can reach the goal in time and see the ending of the story. Afterwards, if you want, you can try to get the secret ending and get all the achievements, and to do this you’ll probably need a bit of help from a guide once in while, specially for the sidequests and to know the items needed for the blessings to avoid a lot of trial and error. Still, despite the 20 hours spent and a few frustrating moments, it was an enjoyable and challenging experience        36 Achievements. It took me 20+ hours. Arrived in 2 days on my own and solved around 80% of the maps. Needed help for the rest of the achievements Medium, some locations will be hard to find and navigating the world can be confusing, but after a few runs most players should arrive on time. Medium, getting all the achievements requires some extra effort and completing a lot of maps to gain access to the shortcuts needed to finish the voyage in only one day, HINT:  A Highland Song is a great platformer game with a huge world to explore and secret locations to find. The illustrations are beautiful and the songs and narration are also top notch. Despite looking like a casual game, it requires some effort to navigate and locate the map’s locations.

_childDocuments_.review: A few quick notes before purchasing this game:If you enjoy atmospheric, exploration games, and storytelling that is dynamic and relies on your drive to immerse yourself in the story and the world, then you will likely enjoy this game. Navigation and control will get easier with time, and you'll begin to recognize and use trails and landmarks as you become more familiar with the highlands.This game is beautiful. The art, the music, the way you progress through the layers of the highlands... it's beautiful. Each run is a short experience, my first took me about 2-2 1/2 hours, but that's not the point. This game is meant to be played multiple times. You won't get the full story on one journey, you'll need to explore to uncover the little grains of story and history which will provide deeper meaning on what you've found so far. It's taken me three journeys to more completely understand  I was taking the trip and what it meant, and I mean to play more to unearth yet more stories of the people you meet (I met 3 people on my third run that I'd never even seen before!) and the little mysteries I haven't quite figured out. I still haven't found, climbed, and named all the peaks yet, but that's okay - it's about the paths I take to get there as much as it is to try and reach the peak. I still haven't beaten my time of arriving the day before Beltane at 7 am.As you make your ways to the lighthouse, you'll find maps, items, little mysteries, and sometimes people or situations that you won't be able to solve on that journey. You keep your knowledge, items, and maps as you go forward, so you're able to come back to them. Like Moira is drawn to the lighthouse, I feel drawn to keep trying to learn more and explore the paths I haven't taken. If this sounds like something you'd enjoy, I can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Scamper up hills, climb rock walls, yell insults at a giant snow heap. A lovely, lovely trek across some stunningly beautiful vistas, exploring ruins, forests and old folktale, A Highland Song is a personal, meditative journey and an achingly pretty love letter to Scotland and its nature. Being an Inkle game, there's so many little moments, stories, details and secrets to experience as you make your way to Uncle H's lighthouse. And being an Inkle game, you will want to make the trip again, and then again. I'm on my fourth trip now, and I'm just excited what else I will find along the way this time. A few moments of frustration can pop up as you're platforming and exploring. When you make your way to the other end of a difficult ridge, only to find there is no path anywhere and you have to climb all the way back again, OR when you try to jump onto a surface in the background or foreground and the game instead flings you on the wrong "layer" can be pretty annoying and can snap you out of the magic, but overall these are small blemishes in an otherwise enchanting (and challenging) journey. The hand drawn characters, the oilpainted environments, the gorgeous soundtrack and wonderful voice acting (MJ Deans as Moira is a particular triumph), the hundreds of little moments of story and myths and incidental dialogue or thoughts from Moira, just wonderful stuff.Warm and melancholic, it's another delightful piece from an amazing developer.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: A hidden gem of a game that initially looks like it might be a bit underwhelming, but then turns out to be a cracking experience. The game transports you to the wild yet homely environment of the Scottish Highlands. No previous experience required. The story of the Highlands get revealed as you explore the various possible routes in a soothing and comforting way.The game consists of two main objectives of climbing peaks and reaching the protagonist's uncle in time for the local Beltane festival. These objectives are mutually exclusive in that you cannot actually go out of your way to climb peaks, and realistically expect to arrive at your uncle's place in time. This virtually guarantees the game is replayable, just to accomplish more of the objectives. The game still finishes with a positive outcome, even if you arrive at the uncle's place late. The game mechanic is very enjoyable, making climbing ridges, descending slopes and choosing routes quite fun and playable. Running out of puff was also fun and important to the success of the climbs. Subsequently, the weather and time of day are important factors in the success of recharging the protagonist's energy levels. The highland song musically generated 'dances' mini-games were great and get you hoping over the rocks while chasing deer at a moderate speed. The auto-generated journal was also useful in creating memories and clues to routes to your destination.A very recommendable game for those who might like to try moderate exploration in an idyllic and natural environment, or just enjoysuch a soothing game.

_childDocuments_.review: An exploration-focused 2D platformer that can be fun if you have the patience to handle some questionable design choices. Exploring the Scottish Highlands feels satisfying thanks to gorgeous music/scenery and the sheer quantity of secrets to be found, and it's designed with replayability in mind so that every playthrough feels unique. However, an arbitrary timer prevents you from taking each run at your own pace without resulting in a bad ending; and trying to keep pace with the timer makes even the good ending fall flat because you lack context that can only be earned from thorough exploration. Another one of those games where I wish there was a "mixed" option for reviews, but ultimately I did find more to like than dislike during my time with it.  is a 2D platformer where you play a young girl named Moira on a quest to cross the Scottish Highlands to reach her uncle Hamish. He tells her to come to the lighthouse by the sea before Beltane, one week from the start of your journey, so she can see something of great significance to him (though I won't spoil what that is). Along the way, you'll find yourself climbing tall mountains, racing across valleys, spelunking in caves, and learning more about the history of the Highlands, its inhabitants, and Moira herself.The bulk of the gameplay revolves around 2D platforming with some light survival mechanics—no need to manage resources like food or anything, but you have to minimize actions that drain your health (e.g. long falls, traveling in bad weather) and make sure to find places to sleep before night falls. Traveling from valley to valley to reach the lighthouse in the distance demands exploration and a keen eye, because while some paths forward are indicated by a small marker (e.g. a wooden post), most are hidden and can only be found through the game's main collectible: maps. Maps come in all different styles, and deciphering them can lead you to everything from new shortcuts, items you can use elsewhere in the world, or even just other maps. Lastly, traveling across flat plains lets you play a simple rhythm minigame, requiring just one or two buttons as you jump to the beat of one of several Scottish folk tunes.  You're given this huge sweeping shot of the environment at the start of every playthrough, and that's not just for show: much like their real-life counterpart, the Highlands here are . When you see a mountain or a valley in the distance, you can go there if you can find the right path to it, and each one is liable to hold its own secrets for you to find. Given that it's practically impossible to see everything there is in a single playthrough,  encourages you to play multiple times by letting you retain your discovered locations and inventory on subsequent playthroughs while also providing access to new content. All of this ties into the "dynamic storytelling" advertised on the store page: certain actions you take or locations you visit will give little nuggets of information that tie into the main story, and which parts of it you'll get to see changes with every playthrough. This is a cool concept in theory, but the downside is that , and it's hard for a story's conclusion to make an impact when it isn't given the proper buildup first. You might be asking "why don't you just search the map with a fine-toothed comb to get all this information before beating the game?", which is a fair question to ask. The first issue is that you can't backtrack to previous valleys once you've left them, and it's not always clear when a path you take ends in a point of no return. The second issue boils down to what I think is my least favorite part of the game: the timer.Remember when I said that Moira needed to reach the lighthouse in just a week? While it may not stop your playthrough cold if you go past it, doing so does result in a "bad" ending,  The timer doesn't add much if anything to the narrative, and . Plus, in this particular case, it results in a lose-lose situation: you either rush through the game and fail to get proper context for the ending, or take your time to find that context and fail to get a proper ending at all. In all fairness, you're free to ignore that timer after your first successful trip since the "good" ending never changes; but it still results in that initial playthrough being less satisfying than it could be, which is even worse for players who only want or expect to play one time., and I'm torn on where I stand with it. These issues are harder to ignore the more I look back on the game as a whole, but it also didn't stop me from playing half a dozen times either. For every part of the game's design that made the experience fun, there was something else that took just a bit of that fun away; and although I did still enjoy it at the end of the day, I wish I could have enjoyed it a little more.

_childDocuments_.review: I am left speechless over this game. The story, the level design, the ambience and music. It's just *chef's kiss*. I have never played anything like this before. It is definitely a platformer but done in a very unique and interesting way. I thought this was going to be a chill cozy game, and although it is cozy, it is not very chill!You have to decide if you want to be an adventurer, a mountain climber or just get to your Uncle Hamish in time for Belthane. This means this game does have some replayability, since you cannot do all achievements in one playthrough. It doesn't feel like a cheap way to get people to play though, because you do get curious about the map and which way you should go. Still plenty to see that I missed out on after almost 4h playtime at the time of writing this review.I thought I had gotten lost probably 10 times, but somehow managed to reach the goal.Definitely worth full price in my opinion, and the game isn't that expensive anyways!The cons are that the game isn't always intuitive and controls CAN be a bit wonky, there might also still be some bugs in the game. However the game autosaves every couple of minutes so if you get stuck you might have several saves to get you back in without losing too much progress.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the general vibe of this game, the production, art, music, voice acting. There's a lot to like, but I found myself getting frustrated with navigation and trying to parse the often-confusing layers of terrain, regularly falling off and injuring myself. There are just so many mechanics introduced to try and give a little variety from the general relaxed walking-sim feel of this, but they don't really add anything to it. The health bar, exhaustion system, losing your grip while climbing, and the constant awareness of a looming (soft) time limit really took away from my experience.I did finish this, although not in time for the true end goal, but won't be bothering to do a second playthrough just because of how much I found myself saying "I'm not having fun here". And off the back of that, I'd struggle to recommend this to people like myself.

_childDocuments_.review: Inkle's got some of the smartest devs in all of gaming. This was just as clear to me from their tour-de-dorce, Heaven's Vault, as it was from humbler mobile titles like 80 Days. The quality of the ideas, the beauty of the writing, the cleverness of the design--all those signature things about their games are very much here, too. I'm not even particularly passionate about platforming, but this is a game that does it well, all in the dazzlingly beautiful backdrop of the Scottish highlands (very vaguely reminiscent of Ghibli coloring) rendered with some of Inkle's finest art to date. There's something very satisfying about climbing peaks as Moira, who is no(t exactly) superhuman but an average(ish) teenage girl clambering over rocks, potentially losing grip; it's nice being faced with these hills as someone other than Ezio Auditore. And the music--this has got to be one of the best game soundtracks I've heard in years, with Lawrence Chapman composing a stunning score along with some really amazing Scottish folk artists. Some games are like poetry and this is one of them.My only regret is that I bought this for Steam rather than Switch. I feel like this experience would have been twice as satisfying with console controls. Didn't stop me from making it on Beltane on my first try, though! But in any event, thanks, Inkle, for producing yet another wonderful piece of art.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll preface this review by saying that this is the most different and fresh game i've played in a while. It's just a little game with a lot of heart, tells story of a lass named Moira, who can climb mountains, i won't go in more details as you have to play the game itself to experience it.Gameplay is good, could have used some more variety but the one's being offered is enough for this kind of game. _childDocuments_.review: The character drawings and animations are exceptional, although I felt during gameplay you see very little of it. The camera is too far to really notice and appreciate. Occasionally, when you take breaks, or find some things, the camera zooms in and they can shine.The environment visuals are very artistic, detailed, drawn, and varied. They don't reach the excellence of the characters, but for the most part, they do support the atmosphere and gameplay well. Only rarely the pathing possibilities or intentions were not clear to me.There's a lot to explore, beyond the primary route, and with alternative paths. If you enjoy the atmosphere, stories, interactibles, or discoverables this is a game you can play through and explore through multiple playthroughs.The music one- and two-key pressing-matching didn't convince me. It was okay, but to me, it felt somewhat disconnected from the rest of the game and atmosphere. The note-matching felt kinda random to me. It was on notes, but which notes seemed somewhat random. When you enter the sequence quickly, your character matches the deer, which often made it harder for me to distinguish when to hit the buttons, because the two characters were on top of each other.The health and exhaustion system, specifically the exhaustion system felt annoying at times, sometimes repeatedly. But I can see how it adds depth to the game and game mechanics. Having to consider rest and resting places is an interesting addition, and guides the player to another level of exploration as well.Interactions sometimes felt slow, with you having to stand still, for a dialog to finish, and then you can pick it up.Sometimes one dialog got delayed because of another (a narrated story).Sometimes two dialogs intertwined.Overall though, it was fine.It has interesting Scottish tales, a protagonist story you explore alongside the environment/progression exploration, and very good atmospheric sound, music, and character and narration voicing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really lovely, surprisingly moving game. Artistically, it's a treat. Gorgeous visuals and a fantastic soundtrack, both in the original score and the licenced music. I love how the rhythm sections contribute to the feeling of flow as your run through the mountains. Nice accessability options too for these sections, so they never feel punishing.Gameplay: it's about exploration and platforming, with a dash of light survival on the side. This can be a little fiddly at times but it all feels fitting for the setting. Naming the peaks and finding map fragments makes it feel like a puzzle box at times, especially how new shortcuts and secrets are uncovered from run to run.It's not as story heavy as other Inkle titles but it's still touching. Hits the same spot as the Tiffany Aching books from Pratchett for me (which means I love it). Overall, highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but I just struggled the whole way through, not being able to figure out the mapping system because the clues were either too vague or I couldn't make out the terrain I was mapping because it was foggy and raining almost all the time. So I had no idea where I was going the whole game, sometimes even going in circles. I feel like I failed my way to the end of the game and it ended up just being a frustrating, miserable time for me unfortunately.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Despite loving every game Inkle has ever made, I hesitated on this one. I'm not much of a fan of rhythm games so I wasn't sure if this would hit the right buttons for me.When I finally played it I was kicking myself for taking so long to get to it. It's not really a rhythm game, the rhythm aspect is pretty minor and can be turned to only one button for easier playing.Like other Inkle games, this is really a exploration game with a beautiful story. My first run I felt like I knew where the story was going, and my second run confirmed it. However the beauty of the story is in the journey not the destination. I'm thoroughly enjoying each subsequent run and building my own thoughts on the real truth of Moira's journey.My only complaint is that there are certain parts that become repetitive replaying while trying to unlock all the secrets. If you've played 80 days you'll be familiar with this problem. It doesn't ruin the game but it is a problem I wish Inkle would consider for future games.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: You can view my 3D in VR gameplay here (SBS 3D): Yes, you can play A Highland Song in 3D in VR using the FREE Geo 11 3D Mod (search for it). Game looks great out of the box. Keep in mind output is by default SBS 3D and you'll need to tweak convergence and separation according to your 3D preference. I played this in VR using Virtual Desktop to render the 3D SBS to VR. However, you can use any other 3D viewing program for VR like the free Bigscreen Beta. Either way, the game looks great in 3D in VR. For a 2D sidscroller, this game has a lot of 3D depth. If I didn't know any better, I would think that this game was made with VR in mind. It looks absolutely beautiful and whether the devs realize it or not, their game is best experienced in 3D in VR.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: The trailer kind of over-sold the rhythm part. It's only a small part of the game. It's easy to get lost, which I understand is a feature of the game, but it can be a bit frustrating at times. Ran into a semi-bug where I couldn't re-enter a cave and had the option to fall to my death to the left or fall to my death to the right. Managed to super mario myself back into the cave eventually.Great aesthetics and music. I was unsure if I liked it, but I've played 3 runs already. Each run is a bit different as you discover new routes. Downside is that it looks easy to "go to the dam to find the shortcut", but the way you thought led to the dam is a dead end and the closest cave leads to a completely different part of the map, so it's hard to know where to go.Works well on steam deck.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Cozy game ruined by being frustrating. At the beginning, it was chill and nice, but at one point you are unlucky, you get lost, and you waste 3 hours trying to find where to go next, walking around to the same places. I stopped playing at a point when I suddenly got randomly taken away by a bird to a completely unknown place far away from anything, after trying to find a way for 2 hours.Play time is made out of confusion and being lost in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Very satisfying platforming sequences set to gorgeous music- Beautiful illustrated scenery that felt authentically Scottish- A wealth of lore and things to do- One playthrough doesn't take too long, and I've enjoyed replaying and trying different routes.Cons:- Somewhat frustrating to play, initially, as it's easy to go in circles or get stuck in an area. There's a bit of a disconnect between the ease of the platforming sequences and the difficulty of navigating the landscape. I was glad that I stuck with the game, though, as I got the hang of it in the end and I feel that it rewards replaying.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - The journey is the destination.I really love how A Highland Song blends narrative and gameplay. The story is of a girl who runs away to travel over the Scottish Highlands to the sea. She hasn't prepared for the journey. She has no tent, so she needs to find shelter along the way to rest. She doesn't know the way, so she relies on scraps of maps and interactions with strangers to inform her of the paths forward. The hills are full of stories and magic, and when you recognize and interact with the narrative, you are rewarded not just with more story, but with useful items or features to help you on your way.The complaint I've seen most is that it's frustrating having such limited options forward on the first playthrough, but that's what drew me in. I really felt like Moira was exploring the land and travelling faster and more efficiently because of the knowledge she had gained. If you want a game that will paint a line on the ground to show you the fastest way to get from one place to another, skip this one. The point is to be immersed in the environment and explore all the nooks and crannies.The gameplay is simple enough that a child can play it, but deep enough that there are speadsheets to help figure out routing. You can "die", but there are no fail states. You'll never get a "Game Over" screen. There are accessibilty options to simplify the rhythm and climbing sections, so every skill level should be able to play it.Oh, it has beautiful landscapes and music, too, if you're into that sort of thing.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Like stepping into a Bob Ross painting, and just as ambient, atmospheric, and relaxing as that sounds. Though initially the pressure of feeling the need to reach the destination in time reduced my enjoyment. Combined with my increased familiarity with all the systems, I began to feel less confused and overwhelmed about where to go and what to do, and instead eased into it. And you still get a satisfying ending, even if you're late!I can see why the game has a photo mode, it's one of the most beautiful 2D games I've seen. Those hills and skies (especially at night), the weather effects, the gorgeous 2D animation. It's also like stepping into a Studio Ghibli film.It's one part magical-realist coming-of-age story, authentically told through Scottish people, language, and places; one part innovative platforming hiking simulator; and one part folk music rhythm action game (these sections are great, and a welcome change in pace - though I wished they sometimes had a little more to them). In other words I can't think of another game like it, which is fantastic.I thought it had a few rough edges, though nothing that detracted from everything else the game accomplishes. Examples would be: occasional loading stutters, especially at the beginning of my first run; as clever and neat as the 2D climbing is to make you feel like you're exploring 3D hills, occasionally it's unclear where you can and can't reach, sometimes leading to long detours; the narrative can sometimes feel a little staccato and modular, in the way the dialogue engine surfaces things to say.But lets not end on a downer: I think this might be my favourite inkle game! I'm eager to continue my second run, take it slower, explore with more confidence, and arrive in time for Beltane.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: reminds me of another self-discovery climbing game written in Ink, , but where that took you through a vast 3D desert, here you get 2D mountains and lots and lots of rain. Has rain ever been a fun mechanic? Certainly not in  and neither here. I want to jump and run, which is a a great joy in this game (the skipping from small boulder to small boulder!), when you don't get interrupted doing it. Too often you have to sit and wait and listen to your annoying Uncle Hamish drone on about history. Like in many other Inkle games ( for instance), the small moments and encounters are close to perfection, whereas the overarching story is drenched in too much pathos, not helped by the ever dramatic violin soundtrack. Maybe it sounds controversial, but I actually don't play Inkle games for the story, but their interesting takes on game mechanics: Sometimes it seems like these developers are aliens that are studying the human entertainment form "video games" and the results are often as charming as aggravating: "This is what they like, don't they? S-survival mechanics? Not sure why, but let's include them... but death isn't fun to humans, I've heard, so... No dying. O no, that condensed atmospheric water vapor again... Earth is a weird planet!"Anyway, what really caught my interest was the mapping and wayfinding: Making your way to a peak and trying to match landscape details with one of the many implausibly* placed map pieces you find on the way to find a route to the next layer, I liked that. I've only made it to the lighthouse once so far, fourteen days too late, and I'm curious how the next run will play out.I hope , which is certainly Inkle's most commercial (and convential, in a way) attempt so far, will make them some money, because despite my criticisms I want them to continue producing their alien takes on computer games.*Sometimes it's fun to suspend your disbelief, like Moira not wearing a hat in this ♥♥♥♥ weather, but her flying hair obviously is good movement indicator
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Once the initial beauty wears off, it's basically a walking sim with very not that much dialog in it, the game is 2.5D with very poor delineation between forwards and backwards paths, and is very difficult to visually read. This game needed a lot more polish in terms of subtle visual indicators of what is climbable and what isn't.Ultimately, if you're looking for a game, this isn't really one. It's not really a traditional walking sim with a clear narrative, either. This game is really directionless when played, and the rhythm game feels like an afterthought, and not a core mechanic.This game feels like it was built with the sole intention of being put into a montage/trailer, and not actually to be played.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: The music in this game is so soothing. I love the rhythm runs. However, this game is way harder than I was expecting. I was supposed to make it to my uncle by Beltane. I'm already 2 days late and just over halfway there. I keep going the wrong way and back tracking. Still a fun and awesome game. I need to get back into it.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely game about both the wonder and the danger of the wilderness. Orienteering, choosing your routes, and mild time pressure adds an element of player agency and strategy to the simple joy of navigating these 2D environments that do an impressive job of simulating depth. I completed the game twice, one after another, and each was very satisfying and totally unique. Thanks to the different routes I took there was practically zero repeated content between the two, and I know I would find more if I kept playing. Find crumbling ruins, gleaming caves, and highland weirdos as you absorb the myth-soaked history of the hills. I highly recommend this to anyone interested.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks and sounds nice, but the environment is very hard to read and the controls feel unresponsive and floaty. There are glowing points of interest here and there, but seems to be a random if/when you actually get an interaction prompt.I don't really understand the idea behind the mapping system either. Apparently I need to find predetermined spots to make Moira aware of them, and it makes no difference if *I* see the route.This would be fine if the map system was fun to use, but the different layers and constant zooming around just feel disorienting. Maybe that's the point, so as to make the player really experience feeling lost? Hard to say.I gave this a try as I like platformers and exploration, and enjoyed inkle's 80 Days for dozens of hours, but I just don't get this one. It feels bad to play and oddly frustrating from the get-go; the exploration itself feels tempting, but is ruined by the time limit ticking away in the background.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking forward to this game because of the art style and the licensed music. I thought it was going to be a rhythm game based on Irish/Scottish/Celtic folk music with a nice little story. What it actually is, is a "where am I supposed to go" simulator with only a few rhythm sections here and there.The rhythm sections are awesome and feature licensed songs from great folk bands but are  cut short by finishing the section long before the song has had a chance to end, and they are way too rare (my 2h of gameplay probably contained 5 mins of rhythm sections). The actual core gameplay is that you're meant to pick a random direction and just walk generally "towards the sea", at least that's what I understand from 2h of gameplay. The terrain has this beautiful "layered painting" effect which unfortunately shoots itself in the foot because there are sections with so many layers that navigating not only becomes confusing but also where the platforming reaches its limit mechanically. Twice I was in a position where I wasn't sure if I had discovered a softlock or if I was just missing some hardly visible path.I wish this game was a pure rhythm game but alas.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Everyone at inkle is so talented, this game is so gorgeous and it fills my need for exploration so muchhhhI cannot wait to replay this game a lot, theres so many paths you could take, and things that I missed or couldnt back to on the mountains that were on my pathGenuinely cant wait to sink an exorbitant amount of time into this.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Stupendously pretty. An absolute joy to just become lost in. And you will become lost. That's sort of the point. Like a long, meandering walk.Some jank in the movement aside, I quite enjoyed my time with it. I had hoped that it would lean heavier into the rhythm aspect, however, but I'm almost glad that it didn't. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game which I absolutely love, but I also find deeply frustrating. Not knowing where you're going or what the h*ck you're supposed to be doing is part of the point... but it's also something I don't particularly enjoy when games try it. That said, A Highland Song is so compelling I'm going to try and push through the ignorance threshold.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: An experience I'll remember and a game that lingers in my mind. At first I was frustrated with the lack of direction with no set goal, I was wondering around aimlessly and every time I'd cross into a new valley the feeling that I'd left something behind would set in. Much of the game is about exploring and bagging peaks where you find places matching different scraps of maps. But the overarching story is about getting to a lighthouse for Beltane which has a countdown attached. This game-play loop threw me into two different directions not knowing what I should focus on. But there is some magic here, the landscapes are incredible, the climbing mechanics and the traversal are gratifying to finally master. With free flowing Trad-Folk rythm sections to pace out your exploration I love the vision of a rainy, sombre and melodramatic Scotland.  With heart-felt vocal performances and a beautiful story that pieces itself together over time, there is a lot to love in A Highland Song.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A very pretty journey through the Scottish highlands. To be honest, it's exactly what it advertises. But done in such a way that encourages many hours of exploration and repeated playthroughs to see new sights and meet new people you haven't before, all while enjoying the beautiful art style as well as gorgeous folk music and sounds as you discover new things. Seriously, even the "unlocked something" jingle is pretty. Also, let it be know that the accessibility options are pretty generous, so even if you aren't a fan of rhythm games as a format, don't let that discourage this. While it's not a RHYTHM game, it does involve a lot of musical segments to make it easier. All in all, great game, do recommend!!!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful narrative game with an interesting genre mix. Lots of exploration, a bit of survival, some choose-your-own-adventure, and a little bit of rhythm game. The environments are stunning, the hills are literally paintings, and the storytelling bits make the world come alive with folklore and myths.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: in a year without Zelda it would be my favorite game of the year? It might still be? It just nails everything I love about games: evoking a place and a culture, narrative beats that are both incredibly well-written and reactive to your actions, incredible art and music, and an outrageous amount of vibes and fun. I've lost count of how many playthroughs I've completed at this point, I've speedrun it, and I still have stuff to do. Game rules.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write reviews, but I've thoughts and felt as though it may be worth putting them down. I've put it as a recommended, but I'd probably recommend this while warning a friend that they may find themselves frustrated at times - but that it's worth it for the positive aspects. I've been missing my grandfather since he died earlier this last year, he was so proud to be Scottish. I stumbled upon this game, and was immediately taken by it's beautiful art that reminded me both of Ghibli and of one of my favourite films "L'Illusionniste". A nature game, set in the highlands, an exploration platform with a music component couldn't be more up my street. I then saw it had been released on my birthday, and thought, well, kismet. I loved the way the story unfolded, and the gentle, quite real way that the story is told through letters. I felt like the spirit of the hills was captured in the way the game was designed and the limited interface. It is with all these wonderful, lovingly crafted aspects that I felt all the more sad that I found myself repeatedly frustrated with the gameplay itself. It, too many times, felt almost overly punishing for things that felt out of my hands. I'm not sure if the handling of the rhythm aspect is optimal - I'm fine with it having some degree of consequences if you fail notes, but occassionally, for instance, the lightning of the storm made it difficult to tell when the next note was coming or what colour it was. Then, once I'd tripped, I had no option to heal myself or stop running, forcing myself to essentially die and lose time. The backgrounds are gorgeously handpainted, but there are moments where you may attempt to jump to a ledge only for it to actually be in the background. It's easy to get yourself turned around a bit too, especially with some of the maps. I found myself genuinely so frustrated at times that I had to quit - which made me feel quite bad as I hated getting mad at such a beautiful story and game. I do think that with a little mending, the frustrating aspects could be remedied and I'd feel more confident recommending the game to my friends. Story wise - absolutely lovely use of folklore and Scottish identity as a narrative device, and I was keen to keep exploring and learning about the hills. I may give it all another go or two to fill in some of the gaps of the clues I'd not brought to a conclusion. I got through to the end after three tries, and I was left a bit underwhelmed by the "correct" ending. I think it maybe was just a little too quiet for all the magic that comes before it. Certainly, a satisfying and fufilling ending for the narrative, but I found myself wanting just a little more. Right, TLDR.Beautiful, rich platforming game with a folkloric narrative, interesting characters and themes. The game itself can be demoralizing and frustrating at times, but I'm very glad it exists and I'm thankful that I was able to play it.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Such a beautiful game. Climbing can be tricky, as it's not always clear how and where you can move between layers in the environment (sometimes due to bloom lighting, texture resolution, etc.), and the main character's animated sprites occasionally interact with the environment in a jerky fashion. But the devs really came up with overall smart design here. This obviously is no full blown hiking/mountain-climbing sim, yet they've done enough to really convey scale, adventure and adversity. That all excellently complements the more intimate storytelling--fantastic writing, with solid voice acting too. Shame the game isn't fully voiced, and the audio recording quality weirdly varies from professional-sounding to amateur, however it isn't too detrimental to the experience. The music remains great.I'm hoping the game receives updates that polish the camera, as that was one of my biggest negative distractions; could be smoother. I also think the auto-run rhythm sequences could've had more to them. They felt a tad repetitive, and a few times some of the button icons were obscured by either a tutorial message or the environment itself, causing me to stumble.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I feel inadequate to describe just how wonderful this game. Thankfully there are already loads of glowing reviews out there that do that better than I can. I will simply say I absolutely adore this game - every bit of it is a joy. And I haven't actually seen  bit of it, even being over 100 hours in! So come explore the Highlands with me!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I have a massive review backlog but had to write this as it's one of the best games I played in 2023. Lyrical, whimsical, adventurous and with great music and really charming voice work that can make you laugh out loud at times with the stuff Moira comes out with. This reminds me of visiting my family in Scotland as a kid and tramping the hills with my dad, finding waterfalls and seeing deer from afar. I have done 5 runs so far and each time the adventure has had something new and I'm ready for my sixth attempt. Such a lovely vibe.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A Highland Song deserves all of the praise it gets. I can't overstate how much I was stupidly grinning with every rhythm section. They are an absolute joy. The Highlands are beautiful and the overall design of the world offers great replayability. The writing is also excellent, so many wee lines that I've heard growing up in Scotland, and special thanks to Inkle for hiring Scottish voice actors - they did a great job at delivering lines in Scots and Gaidhlig.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the most visually stunning games I’ve ever played. The art style is not only gorgeous, but it also perfectly complements the serene and calming atmosphere. The music enhances the overall experience, making it even more immersive and chill. The gameplay is incredibly fun, making this game a must-play for anyone seeking a relaxing yet engaging gaming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: As was to be expected, I got horribly lost in the mountains. After banging my head against some rocks, both figuratively and literally, I'm starting to get a feel for this game. It feels incredibly vast, I have no idea what to expect in the coming hours in the best way possible.The rhythm bits are a complete treat, even for someone like me who doesn't have the best skills in this particular area.There are some mild annoyances like the stamina system seriously hindering backtracking / exploration in a game that wants you to look twice in every nook and cranny. But overall, the parts I've played yet simply overflow with joy and wonder.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A really nice and atmospheric game with tremendous sense of presence and mood. Exploring the hills of craggy Scotland in search for stories and truths made me forget the time, and the narrative which you get to explore over multiple runs kept me hooked, wanting to hear more about the hills and people who lived there.A Highland Song is a triump of tone and visuals, its a bit rough around the edges but it bursts at the seam with charm and intention. The music lifts it all up and together with gripping words the narrative had me teary eyed when it mattered most.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A Highland Song is a GEM! I couldn't get enough of it!Even though I encountered some bugs (one softlocked me) I am in love with this game. The storytelling is really good, the voice acting is amazing, I loved the animations and the musical running was BEAUTIFUL! I played it 3 times and got 3 different endings and I am still tempted to go back in to the Highlands to find all of my missing shortcuts and trinkets.When it comes to bugs and accessibility: The bugs I encountered were frustrating at times but the game keeps multiple back-up saves for you so it's easy to go back 1, 5, 10, 20, 60+ minutes which is really neat and we should see this is more games!I had some issues with the musical sequences where I failed the 'skillchecks' even though I had calibrated recently, but there are accessibility settings to help you fail less, or not at all. After a while I switched from keyboard to controller and I can definitely recommend using a controller for this game.

_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I struggled with this one.I thought that this game would be a whole trek, but instead it ended up being one of the most frustrating games I've played all year. I also thought that this would be more rhythm based, and while there were fun rhythm sections, that was only a small portion of the game.Overall I am leaning towards recommending, but do plenty of research first. _childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough, and I'm ready for another. In short, this is exactly the type of game I love and which is so perfect for Steam -- it's not AAA; it's a little sidescrolling platformer disguised as a Ghibli-esque coming-of-age adventure in the Scottish Highlands. You play as Moira, a girl who is more than eager to break out of her sheltered life in an isolated cottage and journey to visit her uncle, the lighthouse keeper, further than she's ever traveled in her young life. To get there, she needs to scale mountains, brave the harsh weather, and keep up her strength, all while discovering the secrets and history of her land.I said this was a game in disguise because I normally would not sign up to play a platformer. HS keeps thing exciting with breezy running and jumping mechanics that match Moira's spirited nature. It's joyful assessing and attempting different routes on your way to the peaks, the difficulty compounded by knowing maps and important items lay on lesser-trodden paths and that you can't dally too long without finding proper shelter before nightfall. The controls are simple -- run, run faster, jump, climb -- but the game makes up for this with the depth and complexity of each mountain level. I felt forced to make choices -- follow trail down the side of the mountain or tail a deer at high speed down a long slope? Search for maps and artifacts or immediately take the most obvious and precarious route to the top? Items sometimes grant boons and maps may reveal heretofore undiscovered shortcuts. I wanted to take more time on each level, but Moira's under a time crunch, needing to make it to the lighthouse by Beltane, so I knew I had to press on. In fact, not being able to accomplish everything at once adds intrigue and interest to the game. There are actual branching paths here, and you might miss a bit of the lore the first time through.There's so much to praise about this game. I'll just say I felt immersed in the environment and landscape, and  I liked keeping Moira company as she revealed more about her family life and her longing to see the wider world. The soundtrack is excellent as well, especially during certain minigames, where the music really becomes the focus.If I have anything to say against HS, it's just that I got bogged down a few times early on, unsure of where I was, if I was making progress, or if I was even backtracking. The game kind of forces you to trust Moira's intuition on how to proceed, and she will even comment to let you know if she feels way off the trail or like she's progressing. Luckily, this is a little bit of an "all roads lead to Rome" deal, though the road you take may not be a fast one. Overall, well written, well acted, easy on the eyes, and fun to play,
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I have so many good things to say about this bold experiment, I don't even know where to begin. It's stuffed full of little design choices that, along with great graphics and great music, add up to something really special. For me, its biggest strength is that it's a game focused on exploration. Not exploration gated by combat, not exploration gated by puzzles. Just exploration, and little mechanics and narratives that all feed into that exploration loop, and even a streamlined inventory where sometimes you just need something good enough to do the job, which is a fun twist on the rigidity of adventure game inventory-based puzzles. The main mechanic where you find dozens of maps and, sooner or later, manage to spot the places those flyers and scribbles depicted is so satisfying. The story is no Heaven's Vault (forever in my heart), but it also doesn't want to be. All the echoes in these valleys add up to a rich world where every corner could hide something both wonderful and strange, and that's a beautiful approach too.I have grown to love these hills. I went from a bumbling first run, where I was rushing blindly (and wetly. so much rain.) into the unknown, to spotting the familiar silhouettes of the places where I experienced my fondest memories. And also staring with disdain at that cocky bastard Forest Crown that keeps distracting me with other things to do, can you believe it's been five runs and I STILL haven't climbed the damn peak, it's sitting right there with its bold can't-miss-me swagger AND YET. ...all this to say that there is always so much to explore and it's always a delight. It feels like the peaks are the perfect size, the perfect complexity (really lovely level design!), and involve the perfect amount of buttons to push for a tactile feeling of immersivity in order to very successfully convey that feeling of hiking in the wilderness.Once again Inkle announced something that sounded super cool but also ambitious in weird ways and hard to pull off, and eventually pulled it off with grace. Always impressed.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I've been three times on that damn peak, ran down gain, finally finding a map for a location directly next to me (a code some door at for skiing lift station) but Moire won't get that only this can be the right spot so I would need to climb that stupid peak again to identify the most obvious spot. After this kind of  situation repeating on other peaks I'm done with the game.Also, why put that stupid time limit into the game, which apparently doesn't have any consequence what so ever?This could have been a nice trip, it looks beautiful. But Moira is chasing through the storm, falling from cliffs, not finding the path to the next valley.Loved 80 Days and Heaven's Vault, but this game is not my cup of tea.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Really comfy little game that's part climbing-simulator, part rhythm game, and part (fictional) history lesson. Seems initially like a disparate mix of elements, but it all comes together really nicely: the bits of family/local history come in the small moments where you're looking around or taking a rest between climbs, the rhythm sections serve as pleasant capstones before hitting a milestone, and the climbing ties it all together. This is the first game I've consciously cringed at when the player character makes a leap and doesn't quite land it: you feel the pain afterward. Really thorough, immersive experience, with replayability coming from trying to optimize runs after beating the game the first time.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: In A Highland Song, it focuses on a girl named Moira who runs off on a journey to reach the sea before Beltane to meet her uncle. You traverse through the Scottish highlands: through fields and mountains and caves as well as other terrain to try and make it to the sea. Only thing is that you don’t have any maps aside from some landmarks to go off of, but as you travel you’ll find little clues and notes to help you along your journey! As you travel you learn more facts and details about Moira’s family, the surrounding areas and local myths.At times, the weather and environment can be a bit harsh to traverse but if you push through it is worth the trouble.The game itself has a very beautiful artstyle along with a lovely soundtrack that adds to the atmosphere. The Scottish tunes give the journey such a wonderful vibe as you run through fields and climb peaks. There are sections of the game where there’s a rhythm game to run across stretches of land that are quite enjoyable. It’s not often that you come across a game that’s a blend of an adventure/platformer with some rhythm mechanics. That being said, because the genre is on the more niche side, it may not be enjoyable for everyone. But if this genre seems like something that suits your fancy then I highly recommend checking it out for yourself!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Do you enjoy beautifully crafted environments, a fun well motivated protagonist, exploration, various routes and storylines to follow and Scottish music? And do you love a developer that's on the ball when it comes to listening to community feedback and fixing possible issues? Then have I got the game for you right here.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely beautiful game. The scenery, character art, music, story, everything here is just breathtaking. Special shoutout to all voice actors involved, I really felt the depth of emotion in every single line of this game, and it crucially contributed to the surprisingly poignant ending. I found the little tidbits about Moira's life, and the manner in which she gradually reveals them, to be deeply moving. Moira herself is a great protagonist, at once precocious and grounded; everything from her dialogue to her animation is memorable and bursting with personality.I was a fan of the rhythm and survival elements, and I didn't even mind the time-limit so much. For those stressing about it, know that the game doesn't punish you for taking longer than seven days to complete your journey - you just get an extra reward and different ending if you manage to do so. I missed that goal on my first playthrough, but I got it on my next go around, and felt it was easier and  quicker the second time.I have plenty of quibbles about QoL and control-feel, but they're all pretty minor. Unclear foreground/background layers, and uncertainty regarding Moira's impending loss of stamina while climbing, were recurring pain points. Otherwise, I found the game to be pretty immaculate. The highlands feel appropriately huge and overwhelming compared to our protagonist, and I found myself chewing my way through each new layer of scenery with a powerful mix of exhaustion and elation. In this regard, the team at inkle really hit the nail on the head trying to express the magnitude of Moira's personal odyssey through both gameplay and map design.My overall takeaway here is that A Highland Song is a really, really special game, a rare and gorgeous expression of its creators' love and affections. This title is well worth your money and time, and is best enjoyed on a rainy night with a hot drink.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Day 1-3: oh man this game is so cozy and im just having a good time takin my time hiking these mountain trails and checking out all this dope sceneryDay 9: I'm FREEZING and I have NO HP cause I DIDN'T ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SLEEP IN A HOUSE and I'm TWO DAYS LATE and I have to SIT HERE IN THIS CAVE and be EVEN MORE LATE cause of this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SNOWSTORM AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAGHgood video game/10
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, the last half of this experience is very underwhelming. I was SO excited to try this game out. The art and music are so charming. The voice acting (when it's there) is lovely! And the first 30 minutes are really strong. The way the rhythm elements tie in with everything is very interesting. However... after the firs half of the game, the climbing and constant rain became tedious. I ran into some bugs that forced me to reload several times. And the songs just... disappeared from what I could tell.I really wanted to love this, but in its current state, it's very rough.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Having lived in Scotland and having bagged my fair share of munroes, here are my assorted thoughts.- The scrambles in this game are a bit ridiculous, but the falling flat on your arse and swearing is very much true to life;- The rare colorful characters are precisely the kinds of people you would meet in the hills;- No bogs! Seriously, what the hell;- Replacing the customary long trudges across the flat landscapes with musical numbers is a stroke of genius;- The puzzle element of recognizing the shapes of hills in the distance is exactly what I would do at the summit, every single time;- The game really nails down the feeling of being cold, broken, miserable, and hopelessly late for a safe descent before the sunset.So, not the real thing, but as close as any other game I've played ever came to the real thing. Buy it, it's great.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Kudos to the music...That about the only positive thing i may say. Wish i could get my time and money back. What a frustrating mess.Softlocked out of last area, cant go back. Dont have nor getting the drop with the last clue for the pathway to the lighthouse. SO the game does not let me take the path to the lighthouse even though one can clearly see the marker pole. And wont let me backtrack last mountain/ hill. Needs immediate fix, so one can go back to sight the path and/or find the random drop with paper of last path.The gimmick of the music driven runs are few and often far between. And get repetative fast.Game should have been called "The Moaner"... Ended up turning off voice to avoid the constant out of breath exhaling. Which leads me to the awful pacing of the game.This might have benefitted from a more linear first game run with a better focus on its selling point and gimmick of the music (not songs, its melodies. No singing).Also... Loads of "scenes" are unskippible and excrutiatingly slow and boring.My recommendation is...
