_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic game as you try to keep young Moira safe on her journey through the highlands to meet her Uncle.It's a 2D platformer with exploration and survival elements, and decisions to be made along the way. There's also a musical sequence where you have to jump in time to the music to sprint across the more open landscapes.The art, the music, the landscape design, it's so well put together. The voiceovers and narrative really pull you in.I love the ability to explore everywhere, to discover new routes and and secrets on every playthrough. I gather there's at least two endings, and while it's a fairly short journey, you'll likely want to play it through a few times to discover more.I love the accessibility options they've added, too.I will enjoy playing this again, and I will enjoy watching my friends play it, as well.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure how universal my experience was or even could be, but it was absolutely thrilling to make it to the lighthouse before Belthane on my first run. Everything was down to the wire in the perfect crescendo with me high tailing it to the last stop right before sundown - brilliant!The game really has the perfect amount of resistance; there is enough jank with some of the hidden paths that I almost walked away in the first hour, but I'm beyond glad I didn't. I loved that experience no matter how intended it was.I might be back after I get lost in the rest of the mountains, I might not - but if you like a game that fights back a little in a lot of fun and surprising ways, definitely pick this up.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Tried the game because it looked amazing. Unfortunately, while the visuals and soundtrack are as good as they look, the game play is very lacking. As some other reviewers have said, it's a glorified getting lost simulator with additionally annoying mechanics like being tired 99% of the time and having to sleep in "good places" or else sacrifice maximum health. The narrative is also very lacking. Some of the voice over work sounds like it was recorded on a phone and the game continuously hurls pointless exposition at you about Moira or Scotland, but very rarely has any acting about the game itself. I never really cared about Moira because even though she's on screen all the time, it feels like her character is never actually present in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty, but didn't land for me. It's never obvious where to go next. You'll spend your time going through the following cycle:- stumble on an item that happens to contain a map- climb to the top of a peak to find that spot on the map- walk to that spot on the mapI was given a deadline for a number of days to reach the sea without much context into how quickly (or slowly) I was actually moving to meet that deadline.The ability to jump between foreground and background hills was interesting, but finicky in practice.Unfortunately, what I think was ~3/4 through the game, I was unable to complete the game because I got soft-locked into the background. Since the game auto saves, my only recourse is to restart the game entirely which I don't have any interest in doing. Since I played slightly more than 2 hours, I was unable to get a refund.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, feels like it was made for me. Starts simple enough but gets trickier along the way and exploring the highlands is a treat. Feels like there are many trails and secrets to be found and I've only scratched the surface during the first journey so will definitely jump in again (the game even supports multiple playthroughs).
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this gameee. I loved exploring and i never felt stressed about the time limit. although I was sad I couldn't do much with the items I collected but when i could it was very fun. I almost wish the game was longer. it is hard to recommend it because its nearly 20 hours and only about 3 hours of playtime so I would really wait for a sale but since this company isnt big I will give it a pass. And the game does alot in those 3 hours I played and I def tried to speed through it. There is replay-ability in the game and it makes every minutes fun. I loved the accent and music in the game alot :)))
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeous and compelling hiking adventure across the Scottish Highlands crafted with palpable love for the region's geography and history. The thing I was most surprised by is how unique and satisfying the exploration and platforming mechanics are. A soft deadline of reaching the destination in a week keeps just the right amount of pressure as you decide which of the many paths to take, which places in the distance you want to reach, and what dangerous peaks you'll try to climb to hopefully get a good shortcut, or at least a fantastic view. Thankfully the game doesn't stop if you happen to pass the deadline, and you even keep most of the items and information you collected if you want to play again and try for a better time. I started this last night expecting to play for a bit and go to bed, but I was so grabbed by it I ended up playing the whole thing in one go. Didn't manage to make it before the deadline though, so I think another playthrough is due soon.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first experience with a game by inkle, and I'm SO impressed! I found myself amazed by the artwork over and over again. That, along with the music, is where this game really shines in my opinion. The score in this game is sooo rich with spirit and culture that it felt like a story element all on its own.The gameplay was fun and the rhythm portions really helped shake things up - I just wish they had a bit more complexity to them. Also, I played on mouse & keyboard, and it felt a little strange playing with arrow keys instead of WASD, although that's just my personal annoyance.The game itself took me about 3 hours to beat... although I didn't even realize that I must have REALLY rushed my first playthrough a lot, as I only discovered like 1/7th of the peaks lol. So, needless to say, this game has immense exploration potential that will offer hours and hours of entertainment in the Scottish highlands. With that in mind, the price point is actually pretty fair! I'd highly recommend this game if you enjoy peaceful, exploration-type games and just getting lost in a game's environment. <3
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A really lovely little game in multiple regardsNot terribly long so if you want to do a short little one session run you cancute little story (some of the little side stories a little confusing but that is probably just me lol)PHENOMENAL MUSIC AND THE SPRINTING SECTIONS ARE JUST GREAT-honestly if they ever did a dlc/update that was just "free run" id do it in a heartbeatCute drawn characters and beautifully painted backgroundif you can't stand rhythm games at all or have issues with controls that can be a little jank (im keyboard and mouse idk about controller) then maybe think about it read a few other reviewsBut i really liked it, solid good cozy games that feels like it could go on a shelf with Cartoon Saloons movies
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I got into inkle games for sorcery and stayed for their unbridled creativity and insane ideas that they somehow make work. This game is an exploratory platformer with treasure-hunting and sparse yet important rhythm game elements set in the scottish highlands where you talk to blue men and get sneezed to new areas, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ does it work. 9/10 there are some wonky platforming bits but it's not a big issue and the story, visuals, and music are unmatched. Play this if you drink hot cocoa, like scottish accents, or have enjoyed any other inkle game.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, what a fantastic game! I must have restarted my playthrough six or seven times in pursuit of the sea that Moira seeks before  travelling down a successful path and reaching the destination--albeit within seven days time--but still  on time for Beltane nonetheless. The visuals, the characters, the journey, the soundtrack, and the unexpected challenge that this title offers kept me hooked for several days straight. And it is sure to do the same to you--the reader--if you possess the grit to see Moira's expedition through. 1. There is no correct path. There are many ways to reunite with Uncle Hamish, so feel free to make Moira's hike as long and complicated and lore rich as you want or as short as three days and straight to the point. In other words, don't be afraid to play at a comfortable pace!2. No two item discoveries are the same! Be sure to collect any and every item you come across, no matter how useless it may seem. Many interactable objects conceal maps to hidden pathways or prove useful to solving dilemmas you may encounter later on!3. If you encounter a deer while hiking in the direction you wish to travel, be sure to chase it. Moira will be compelled to sprint! This is the only in-game activity that slows down the passage of time and regenerates her health simultaneously.4. Be weary of tripping while sprinting. Moira cannot grow (that is to say, become stronger for the sake of additional stamina) if her rhythm is flawed. Embrace the music and you won't miss a beat!5. Listen to Moira's breathing patterns carefully and plan each consecutive action accordingly. Hyperventilation is the bane of your journey! 6. Survey your surroundings often! Missing potential pathways, items, and NPC conversations  prove to be a big mistake later on. 7. If you wouldn't comfortably sleep somewhere or feel inclined to take a particularly risky action, Moira won't either. Prioritize and preserve her wellbeing whenever possible! And last but certainly not least ... try not to get upset when Moira trips or falls. Her body--like that of most humans--is fragile, but she is an excellent climber nonetheless and will continue to push forward even after facing major setbacks. Her motivation is undying, and the player should share this quality if they wish to guide her to the sea that she yearns to find while in pursuit of Uncle Hamish.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: On my first playthrough I got quite frustrated by the weather system and a few bugs (mostly ironed out by now) and found the rhythm music sections oddly difficult. I also missed Beltane by a day and so for me the final feeling was one of indignance and a spiteful relief haha, as opposed to triumphant and reflective on further runs. Turns out i had synched the music poorly and the second run blew the game wide open. So many hills to climb, so many maps and things to discover, so many eccentric and confounding highland hijinks to encounter. I cant stop playing!Runs only take an hour or two, when you can give yourself time to settle into Moira's world its very rewarding.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A Highland Song represents a culmination and refinement of a lot of experience from Inkle. It's got the travel on a light deadline of 80 days, it's got the replay the game to experience more of the backstory from the Arthur game and the archaeology game, but does it at a good pace and an entertaining movement system. I've only done two runs but there are plenty of intriguing mysteries and puzzles to solve. My only complaints are that the musical sections feel punitive when you mess up because messing up one note means you receive no increased stamina. It'd be nicer if there was a little 2 or 3 note leeway, people aren't playing this game to have their reflexes tested. Some other notes on the musical sections, please add an accessibility option for less intense lightning flashes during those musical sections, markers for space bar notes (they blend in to the background a little too often unlike the up arrow notes), and make it clear you don't need to hold any buttons after you start them (my first play through I was holding shift and the direction I was running through every musical section).
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: What a lovely tribute to a very underrepresented part of the world in media. I loved the atmosphere, the music, and the proper ending (which I was sadly only able to reach on my second playthrough). It's not without a little bit of jankiness in parts, but overall I was very impressed with how good the mechanics felt for an indie game made on a budget. inkle is definitely a developer I'll be keeping my eye on in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting and worth your time! At its best, it makes you feel something few other games can, and is the closest to "that feeling" I've had since playing Inkle's 80 Days. The core loop reminiscent of Breath of the Wild's traversal is genuinely fun (and most of my criticisms are small things that make that more annoying, or proc gen edge cases). The few issues (as to be expected in a project of this scope) are outweighed by the moments of awe and clarity - I gasped the first time [something] happened. It is, like so many of the best games, filled with love and tiny details.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I like the setting and the concept. And especially the player character + the voiceovers. It's a different kind of exploration and survival game, pretty cozy at times. The narrative is a nice addition. I was able to reach a nice ending in my first playthrough. It was not the "best possible" ending, so I will play it again and see if I can manage to achieve that. The game still has a few bugs. One time I fell down endlessly, not seeing the character - another time my character was stuck behind some landscape layers. I hope the devs will be able to fix such kind of bugs over time to make the game really stable to play. I was able to continue my playthrough anyway after reloading, so it wasn't too bad. During the rhythm running parts, there was always some strange glitch effect on my 4k screen, would be nice if this could be fixed as well somehow.Overall I would recommend the game, but of course, as always, it's not for everyone. I'm not really into jump'n'runs or rhythm games, but those optional parts didn't annoy me. They support the whole setting and atmosphere.My favorite experience in this game so far was flying with the eagle, because it was a nice and funny surprise.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I spent an enchanting afternoon playing this game - I was feeling under the weather, it was pouring rain outside, and I was cuddled up in a blanket with plenty of tea and immersed myself in this game. I had some tension with severe in-game weather hampering my journey, but like, it's *Scotland* lol (you can turn the weather down a notch in the Settings, but I couldn't bring myself to do it).So yeah, I finished my first playthrough and it felt complete, like a pilgrimage. I saw so much on my journey, and so much more is out there waiting for me. I'm looking forward to this weekend, when I have another quiet afternoon to try out a different route.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This game offers the joy of puzzling out a way through wild paths and peaks, and grounds the experience with beautifully understated characters, hidden histories, and the heartfelt drama of a girl who needs to chart her own path to the sea before she runs out of time. The hills are full of music, secrets, and dangers, and you can reach every bit of land you see in front of you (even the peaks far off in the distance) as you and Moira explore, survive, and discover what you're capable of together. This is a game that reminds me how happy I am that I get to live in Scotland.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Yes.The game is beautiful and it takes you on a journey with platform, music, storytelling and scottish accents. It's a bit difficult as a non-native English speaker to properly enjoy the scottish language (it sounds like dwarves from The Witcher games :) but it's not mandatory to understand everything 100% to play the game. If you're curious, it probably means that game is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I suck at this game and I love it. The premise, mechanics, protagonist, characters, and collectables are all endearingly charming, but the presentation and visual flex is astounding. How this game is presented is its main strength. The game is gorgeous, and it is really addictive. You have a time limit to reach the sea. You do this by exploring the land and deciphering geographical puzzles, to find new paths to take you that every bit closer to your goal. You can upgrade your run and climbing ability with rhythm tests, and you can die (quite easily in my experience) from the harsh conditions and by foolishly thinking you can jump more than twenty feet. Maybe I am rubbish at this game but maybe this game is actually quite difficult. Having said that, every time I felt I had made too many mistakes, it was not a chore to think 'right, let's go again'. You improve with every run and that is what keeps me coming back time and time again. Bravo to everyone involved, A Highland Song is refreshing. I look forward to playing this for a long time to come.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This game is *wonderful*. I've finished one playthrough and am almost done with a second one. While a single run lasts about 4-5 hours, the game is designed to be played multiple times with NG+, as are all of Inkle's games. Just looking at the achievements list I can see there are tons of things left to find that I have zero clue how to achieve, so I definitely still have at least a handful of runs ahead of me. The game itself is super moreish and has a wonderful flow both in the way the story progresses and in your movement. The movement mechanics are really good, especially considering this studio hasn't made anything platformed-adjacent before that I'm aware of. There are lots of accessibility features, too, so if you struggle with some form of input, it won't prevent you from playing. My only wish is the ability to remap inputs on PC. The best game Inkle has put out since HV!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Just completed my first run, going to try more soon. This game knows what it is, and really is the sum of some wonderfully executed parts. What's most impressive is how well they've paced the 'levels', whilst capturing a sense of freedom and being lost amid the highlands. Perfect weekend game, from a reliable studio.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A Highland Song is, simply put, a journey. You travel through the hills, get lost, find secrets, but, above all, you're immersed in this beautiful, cosy, rustic world filled to the brim with things to find and experience.The most interesting I found, however, was how the game managed to strike a delicate balance between replayability and the amount of content within each playthrough, which is not an easy thing for a narrative focused game. Even though I did reach the ending on my first playthrough, I haven't even seen most of the beautiful world within the game. There were still more hills to climb, more places to explore, and more stories to find. I'm 10 hours in yet I think I'll need 10 hours more to get to a point where I can say that I've done most of what I wanted to do in the game.The music was also very good and did well to accompany the scenery. With that said, there was a bit less rhythm sections than I expected given how prominent they were in the game's trailers.My only gripes are the minor bugs here and there and how the background/foreground that you have to transition to are a bit hard to distinguish in some places.Overall, it's a nice, relaxing game with an engaging world and story that you could easily get lost in, both literally and figuratively.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Another beautiful game by Inkle. They continue to experiment with different forms of storytelling and this one is again on target.This game is how hiking is for me. A combination between introspective, awe inspiring moments when you can take it all in, and more grounded time management, and preparation for safe trip (like where to sleep). Ok maybe i havent done a musical sprint with a deer, but no-one said its a hiking simulator ;).Good Job Inkle.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: How do you get Geoffrey to play your game? You make it about walking, set it in Scotland, and include Talisk in the soundtrack – I’m a man of simple tastes. Just a really beautiful game that evokes a strong sense of place, that includes rhythm sections, climbing, running, and, in my case, falling off cliffs. Just a reminder that games can be lovely as well as fun.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of Inkle and their games for a few years now and was very pleased to be able to help playtest this one.  From the early trailers, I was expecting to love the rolling hills and atmospheric music, but hadn't quite appreciated just how much of an intricate and engaging story there would be to discover (stupid of me, really - this is Inkle!); nor just how much I'd come to empathise with - and root for - the cheeky wee heroine, Moira.Knowing my folklore quite well, I picked up on some of the clues early on, but didn't know everything - and found the rich narrative was every bit as lovely as the amazing art (hills, skies AND light) - and the music too; I bought the original soundtrack a few Bandcamp Fridays ago.  The game stands up well in comparisons with other rolling open-world adventure games (the Z-word) and also other platformers - but you do have to remember (as one of the other testers put it) she's not Mario - despite the anagrammatically similar protagonists.  There's a level of realism, taking a sleep or a quick break (and a curly wurly!) and an encouragement to not just run and climb but really enjoy the whole experience.  Maybe it transpires that enjoying the journey is the ultimate goal, not just reaching the lighthouse... Steam tells me I've logged nearly 30 hours and I barely feel like I've scratched the surface.I don't feel my words can do this justice:  I can really only express the full intensity of my feelings about this splendid game in the way Moria does - by punching the air and shouting 'YASSS!'.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Inkle are honestly one of my favourite studios, they always put out really interesting games with a great narrative. Loved Heavens Vault (so criminally underrated imo, the world-building is amazingly done), and I feel like I've only just scratched the surface of A Highland Song; deffo one I'm going to be replaying to find all the secrets and story of the land!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A quick and relaxing exploration platformer, designed with replayability in mind. You play as Moira, who is running away from home to meet up with her Uncle at this lighthouse "near the sea", and from then on it's all up to you to chart a course from peak to peak, climbing cliffs and exploring caves, reading maps correctly to unlock more paths and to find shelter for the night to hopefully make it in time. Accompaning your task is, of course, Inkle's fantastic writing wether it's Moira talking to herself about her family situation or her recalling what her uncle told her about the different peaks and ruins you'll come across on your journey. And that's not to mention the soundtrack which has both some soothing ambient themes but also some more energetic tracks (by Scottish folk bands Talisk and Fourth Moon) for the running sectionsA playthrough will last you about 2 - 3 hours but you won't see everything in just one playthrough but the stuff you did find (like items or maps) will carry over between them, so you're encouraged to try again and maybe find a different path to your destination this time.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: There's something special about inkle games.  It's like they have their finger on the pulse of the unconscious mind.  Something about the way they craft puzzles is just so natural.   If you haven't tried an inkle game before, let this be your first, but definitely give this a try.    The thrill of success violins as you climb peaks while taking Moira from her home to the lighthouse is just one of the many gameplay elements that tickle a puzzler's mind in just the right way.   There are rhythm game elements, but the timing before each session helps get ahead of controller delays and makes that portion of the game feel fun, energetic, and a native experience.  The landscapes are flat-out gorgeous.  The voice acting is done well and this game is superb.Just when you think you're about to die, running in circles in the highlands, a deer walks up and you race to a cheerful tune.  Fall into a hole in a cave?  There's mysteries there as well.  All the while, a story is unfolding as you make your journey.   This game is also replayable, where choices matter and can help your next run.  Definitely do not pass this by!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This is an Inkle game, and Inkle means exploring and it means stories, and it means both done very well indeed. The game involves exploring a richly detailed 2D mountain landscape, with some mild platforming elements, finding odd items here and there (and a few odd….people…) and occasionally a form of rhythm game set to a Scottish folk soundtrack, all while voiced characters tell stories. Folk stories and personal stories, myths and histories, evocative and powerful and strange and beautifully voiced. The whole game is richly atmospheric.Along the way you will find maps and sketches of the landscapes hinting at secrets and mysteries, and a part of the game involves you trying to make sense of them – the game rewards you if you do find them with formally ticking them off your ramshackle notebook, and the feeling of achievement when you do is very enjoyable. And you will encounter mountains, with their own histories and secrets and their own names. It is not necessary for the game to progress (I think) to uncover the names of all of the mountains, but you can be absolutely sure you will want to.At the end of it all is your uncle’s lighthouse, and the first time you play the game, you’ll likely be late for the rendezvous that has started this all off, but never fear, you can play again. Progress, discoveries and items are carried over and this time you will find different elements and if you’re like me, dawdle again because you want to find out what that mountain, that one over there, is called and what stories it has to offer. Inkle are very good at replayability and this is a particularly replayable game.*If* you play this as a dash across the Highlands, you’ll probably come to grief, at least the first time. Moria is a wee girl and although determined and bold (and with a pretty sassy line in repartee), is not a highly skilled mountaineer and falls over a lot and hurts herself. The weather is also pretty accurate for the Highlands – ie it rains all the time, apart from when it snows – and shelter to rest and heal up can be hard to find. I guess if you’re trying to get to Uncle Hamish in time, this is very daunting. The rhythm sections I still find appealing but to be honest they’re a bit incongruous and whilst I see there is value, I’d be just as happy tramping through the peaks and finding nooks and secrets and strange objects and odd voices and birds (birds are important) and cairns and stories and more stories. As far as I can tell, though, you don’t even have to do them if you don’t want to and if you do, the music is, like the rest of the soundtrack, lovely.I found the game that this most reminded me of, oddly, was Kentucky Route Zero. Both have, at root, a deeply embedded focus on the stories of their environment and the environment themselves as key characters. Attention to detail, both from developer and player, are paramount. The atmosphere created is the crucial element of the experience, and sound and music play a vital role. Inkle always try something new with their games, and this is no exception. This won’t be for everyone. If you want a rhythm game, this may disappoint you – the elements are there but they’re not the main focus. It’s far from a conventional platformer. The ‘time limit’ and weather elements may seem oppressive or even unfair if you treat it as a game where you must get to the lighthouse on time or you’ve failed. My friend, you will not get to the lighthouse on time the first time, but you will find out why you wanted to and maybe you’ll do it next time, or maybe you’ll chase another peak. I will.

_childDocuments_.review: So delightful! Absolutely beautiful visuals, lovely voice acting and writing, and a really creative kind of platforming that switches between climbing, rhythm game, and slow paced exploration.Have just finished ym first run at 3 hours, but keen to dive into NG+and find more of the secrets hidden in the highlands.If you know Inkle you know the writing is going to be lovely and the score is going to be memorable. Can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A great exploration-adventure game. I found the writing charming and Moira's character wonderful - I have never before been actually worried when a character I'm playing in a game falls over and hurts themselves. The art and music are beautiful and calming.If you want to lose yourself in the Scottish Highlands there is no better game for you - and believe me, you will get lost, be drenched in rainstorms, and fail to scramble up hills. But on and under some of those hills are fascinating mysteries...(disclosure - I playtested this game)
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: The game is incredibly beautiful. Exploring is fun... but only at the begining. I got tired of aimless wandering with scant directions and hints pretty soon. Chasing the deer to the music is exciting and nice... only for the first 2-3 times. The gameplay seemed rather empty, boring and monotonous to me. To be honest, I regret spending money and time on this game, however beautiful it is.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A Highland Song is a charming platformer.  It's also somewhat frustrating on the navigation side of things.  You can't zoom out far enough at times to figure out which side you should be headed to find the path you need to take next.  There are maps you can find that help, but aren't quite necessary in all cases if you find a cairn or similar paths.  There are a lot of side quests you can take that give you more reason to explore as well..Graphically the game looks quite nice, you might even say it's beautiful in its depiction of this particular part of the world.  The character animations are equally nice, with a very distinct style to them.  The music is nice, and overall the game's very chill.The musical rhythm portion of the game is enjoyable, but it often feels as if it is simply a part of the game designed to take you through what might have otherwise been a boring stroll through the hills.  By that I mean the areas this happens are typically through long stretches of fairly even ground that won't have the same jumps and climbs as other locations.I recommend it, especially for anyone looking to play a charming and relaxing platformer.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Lovely art (except for no climbing rope animation), music, interesting history/lore, believable dialogue.Cons: The most consistent way of making progress I uncovered was to intentionally die so that the game teleports you to the next location/day. What the players short term goal is supposed to be, is so very often, very unclear. This is compounded by the "set your goal of the next peak/point of interest system" which I found, after the tutorial example, profoundly unintuitive, and often has too large a space across which a solution is being sought, or didn't trigger when, what seems to be the "intended/correct" solution was being selected. This compounds unpleasantly with the ability to backtrack so very far, so that you can backtrack multiple days worth of space/progress, trying to determine what you are even supposed to be trying to get towards. Waiting for rain to go away is not enjoyable, just tedious.Suggested improvements: A mapping system. Removal of the "set your goal peak/point of interest system" and replacement with automated triggering/marking of the next goal-point. Failing that, some sort of hot-cold/hint system for the "set your goal peak/point of interest system" so that it can guide the player or be bypassed.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A marvellous little gem. Athmospheric, true to the actual feeling of real-life hiking and full of hidden mysteries. I couldn't stop replaying the game and each time still would discover new stuff.All hills have stories, some historical, some mythological for you to discover and characters to meet.I love the climbing mechanics and how the different layers of 2d environments overlap. It very often reminded me of actual experiences while hiking, when from the top or from the bottom your path seems clear, but once you start walking you realise, that there was a wall our a slope you didn't se from your viewpoint. Or you realize there is a gorge between you and the path you were looking at, that you didn't realize was there. In that regard, I liked the game a little better at first, when you couldn't 'look further' and the paths were not highlighted. Sometimes it was a bit frustrating but that's part of the experience. The better you know the hills, the easier it gets, which is also true in real life.Matching the maps you find to the environment is also really fun. My only criticism is, that there are way more maps for the middle section, compared to the last stretch, so that at some point I still had fun replaying it, but had to run through that last bit.There were some bugs at first, I couldn't encounter any after the first update.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Well! What a wonderfully welcome way to wander!A Highland Song may seem a little daunting at first, as it presents an intimidating expanse of hills and mountains for the player, as teenager Moira, to navigate. These are peaks that seem to go on forever, with no obvious route across them, where stepping out into the wilderness feels like an endless ramble into the unknown. Each successive peak conquered reveals a new horizon, and beyond that, another, and reaching your goal - a lighthouse by the sea - initially seems impossible, because you set out with no idea how to get there. Progress is made by pinpointing the locations of maps dotted about the landscape which unlock shortcuts, some of which result in minor reductions to the journey time across the current range of maze-like peaks. In contrast, others - perhaps more usefully - take you further, closer towards the sea.Each peak in the game is initially nameless, one by one their identity will be revealed by confirming the locations of the sometimes pleasingly obscure maps. From the outset, there is no need to set yourself a goal, as your only task is to press onwards, explore, and survive, the latter being crucial, as learning how to work with the game's systems for waiting out the weather brings a satisfying strategic element to the gameplay - do you sit and wait out the rain and regain some extra health in the knowledge that doing so will advance time and reduce your chances of achieving your goal by the deadline?The game features some remarkably intricate level design, with peaks starting as simple crests conjoined by the vast stretches of terrain that comprise the button-tapping musical sections - pacy, upbeat interludes that provide a welcome contrast to the considered climbing and the mapping mechanic. Upon reaching the later hills and mountainous regions there are some punishing climbs through craggy chasms to endure, the camera pulling back not only to aid the player in their traversal of the space but to emphasise the isolation in these inhospitable, treacherous places, showing Moira as a mere speck at times. Within each ‘level’ of the world are individual planes that can be jumped between, adding further depth to the traversal. Some of these transitions within the hills are more subtle than others, designed to be sought out almost as much as the paths opened by the maps.The majority of the playtime is spent crossing hills where the player is often able (weather-dependent) to see miles into the distance, where they can use the peaks as vantage points to attempt to plot a course. In contrast, there are numerous delves deep into the underground during the caving sections, where visibility is often limited to only a few metres ahead. A highlight of these sections is Moira’s belly wriggle crawl through extremely tight tunnels - claustrophobic moments of tension which make you long for the light and hours of Scottish weather (rain) once more.It is fitting that a game so focused on exploration should explore the limits of what can be achieved within a 2D space. Progression never feels limited to left and right and up and down, as the depth of the environment - both on the peaks and across them - is always apparent, helping to emphasise the sense of scale. This is a 2D game that occupies a tangible three-dimensional space, as paths become worn over time and the unfamiliar becomes known, the position of the peaks in relation to one another is slowly plotted, the player memorising the landscape along with Moira as she records the various details of her travels in her journal.Visually, the game never fails to astonish. Moira doesn’t hike across peaks of continual greys and browns, but environments where beautifully inelegant brush strokes blot the landscape with colour. It is, however, the game’s skies that are the standout - magnificent living paintings rolling above the horizon - never has a gloomy rainy day looked so picturesque.The soundtrack is a mix of a delicate, melancholic score - where sustained notes echo through the hills - set against the up-tempo Scottish folk music that is heard during the rhythmic music-run sequences. If the land could sing, this is what we would hear. Special mention must go to the incidental pieces, succinct punctuations that capture the emotion of certain moments, be it the exultation expressed by the violins upon naming a new peak or the panic-inducing motif that accompanies the (thankfully) rare moments when Moira becomes trapped whilst spelunking.Despite its vastness, eventually, there may come a point where every crag, every chasm and every cliff starts to become familiar, so then what? A Highland Song has the potential to become a speed runner’s delight, partly because there is no obvious route to get to the end without sleeping that the game’s most difficult achievement demands. If you find what you believe to be the fastest route, perhaps there’s a better one, and another, and another, and after all that, maybe you’ll reach the sea without the need to rest. This ties into what is perhaps the most appealing aspect of A Highland Song - its looping, non-linear structure, making for a highly replayable experience, as no route to the sea is ever likely to be the same. It might take a little while to settle into the game’s rhythms, but that’s the point. A Highland Song perfectly encapsulates the sense of feeling lost. You might scale a peak, mark a point of interest, survey the terrain and try and map the lie of the land, but once you descend back down into the foothills, that sense of direction, of orientation, begins to seep away, stolen back by the labyrinthine landscape. If you ever feel stuck or like you’ve reached a dead end, remember, it’s not backtracking, it’s the art of getting lost (and finding your way again).Perhaps the game’s greatest pleasure comes not from finally reaching the denouement, but from becoming sidetracked, being gently persuaded into realising that the real joy lies in discovering the hidden stories of the land. It will take more than one play-through to meet the wonderful cast of quirky characters that inhabit the hills, who provide so many satisfyingly whimsical moments. The main story, however, is a touching, charming and moving folktale, with superb writing and excellent vocal performances. This is a story about discovery, about taking the first steps of many on a journey to find out who you are. A Highland Song is also a reminder that when faced with a seemingly insurmountable task and the question “Can you do it?”, saying “No” is never acceptable, as the answer should always be a resounding “YASS!”.Witness a work of wonder. Enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: (mild spoiler review)Meet mentally challanged natural-free climber Mlub, who's mom is so negligent, she lost custody of her other child already and has lots of troubles with Mlub. Enter Uncle H, who has his sisters back. Having drip-fed Mlub fairy tales her entire life, he lures Mlub on a suicidal journey, convincing her to dive head-first off a cliff into shallow water. You play from Mlub's perspective who totally swallows the fairy tales and it is your job to leave junk on hilltops and try to navigate the highlands with scribbles on old paper rather than a proper map.The game is landscape pron and about discovery and navigational puzzles meant to be played in several playthroughs. It's just that, but it is really good at it. Sprinkled in is the occasional bouncing to a rythm, but this isn't the core of the game, just a mini game. What you do most of the time is try to find spots in the landscape. So it has some escape room vibes. And it's great fun, beautiful and has a great soundtrack.That said, the game has a few shortcommings. Opening the game wants forces you into a music calibration and reads you a poem every time you just want to go to the main menu. Controls aren't properly rebindable and the ending, which you'll see a couple of dozen times, drags on and is not skippable. Also, like in any media regarding Scotland, expect a lot of cherry-picked history. Also, if you want a map - get pen & paper ready.But all in all, great game and suprisingly good, considering there are no enemies in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A nice bite-sized little game with beautiful graphics and soundtrack, and a sweet story. Climbing is fun and I liked the rhythm minigame. Orienteering didn't always work as well as I wanted it to and sometimes it was hard to tell where you could get to from where you were at. Near the end I got lost for 3 days because I couldn't figure out how to climb down a hill. The timed aspect was kind of annoying even though you can still finish after the deadline.Overall I had a good time with the game, but I don't feel any need to do a second run right away.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Boring is the first word that comes to mind when thinking about this game. I was expecting a chill adventure in some beautfiful hand-drawn environments while listening to a nice Irish soundtrack, and while the latter is true, don't expect a leisurely walk through the mountains. Navigating the world isn't very fun. You'll constantly be harassed by the rain while getting lost trying to find where to go next (or where the game allows you to go next if you fail to mark a landmark). Once you're finally on the right track, with a twisted ankle and dirt all over you because your character spent her time angrily jumping all around looking for an exit, you'll be welcomed by a deer that will celebrate your performance with a little run and dance in some simplistic rhythmic mini-game. After this well-earned break, you'll restart the whole process. It's also possible to lock yourserlf in an area without any exit where the only way-out is to commit suicide, as you brought shame to the mountains by getting lost. Don't worry, you'll be resurrected on the next day in a random location closer to your goal. Anyway, it seems the game resonates with a lot of people and I'm glad people enjoy getting lost in the highlands, but I wouldn't personally recommend this game unless you realize what you're getting yourself into.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: The narrative of the game revolves around a young lady who is attempting to reach a lighthouse in order to see her Uncle, who instructed her to meet him at the lighthouse for a big surprise. You move across a landscape that is all the same, with only a few minor differences, while occasionally playing an offbeat rhythm game while chasing a deer, possibly for some symbolic purpose. There is no enjoyment to be had in it, the music is, at best, mediocre, the narrative is uninteresting, and the voice actor's incessant groaning and panting, which she does while doing everything she does, is quite distracting. You stroll, climb, jump, and move around the countryside, that's it.

_childDocuments_.review: As a love of all things Scottish, it pains me not to recommend this, but it just wasn't really fun to play. The Art, folklore/history, atmosphere and music are brilliant, but the gameplay gets stale and frustrating very quickly.I had a game ending bug where I fell through the map and got stuck with a couple of layers left to go before reaching the end, so I quit and uninstalled then.If you love arty games and don't mind glacial pacing while racing against a clock, or much much repetition if the same thing, then this game is for you. For everyone else, probably best to avoid. Or just buy the soundtrack.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing game with nice music and beautiful environments. Play it with headphones because it makes the experience a lot better. Nature sounds are magical. Considerind this is a small studio they have done good work on thatis game. Climb on peaks, name them while searching for secrets through maps or not, going towards the end of the game step by step. I like it! No perfoance issues on my 6700xt.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A Highland Song falls into a category I call a mood game. The main draw is the art and atmosphere and the feelings it evokes in the player and the gameplay is secondary to that.In this game, Moira is a 15 year old girl with a troubled home life. When her Uncle Hammish asks her to come to his lighthouse by the sea before Beltane, Moira sets out on an adventure that will see her running and climbing over the hills and dells of Scotland. But don't worry about the seven day time limit. If you don't make it by Beltane, the game proceeds with no penalty. This feature seems to be here solely for people who want to try completing the journey in the fewest days possible.Most of the game is navigating the Highland terrain. Moira will have to find vantage points where she can scout the surrounding area for pathways to the next area marked on maps in her notebooks or ones she finds scattered along the way. The climbs start as finding high hills, but the end she'll be scaling mountains. Some of the maps she finds can take you to hidden shortcuts, but this heading off the beaten path can actually get you into trouble. I had to restart the game because one of the pathways took me into the inlet that leads to the lighthouse before I climbed a mountain where I could mark the path forward. I couldn't find a way to get back to the mountain the game wanted me to climb before I got to this point from there and was unable to proceed. The game is at it's most joyouse during the rhythm sections. In a flat stretches of land, Moira will start to sprint, the Celtic music kicks in, and she has to jump over small gaps and rocks in time to the music. These segments are exhilarating and easily the highlight of the experience. This game is easy to recommend enjoys these arty games that promise a chill journey.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A Highland Song is a really gorgeous game. The voice acting is great, the music is beautiful, the art is spectacular.You will scale cliffs to find shortcuts and study maps as you explore this vibrant world. I did find the rhythm game to be a bit out of place in this game, so while I still enjoyed it, I didn't find that it needed to be there. The gameplay does mostly loop which I admit is unfortunate I would like to have some other things to do then just finding shortcuts, however I don't think that that completely takes away from the game, because despite the gameplay being a bit lacking in areas the game more then makes up for it in other areas. Either way I still recommend the game for you to try. Check out my curator page for more cozy recs!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed A Highland Song, but I don’t know if I would recommend it at full price. Some of the climbing mechanics are buggy,  and the 2.5D art also makes platform of confusing at some places. The rhythm game portions also seem tacked on, and at least on my older computer, it was sometimes hard to figure out what I was jumping in response to.Nonetheless, I really enjoyed the geographical aspect of this game, and piecing together the backstory was a good experience. The game mostly does a good job of not making replays too tedious, which is important when replaying is very much an intended game mechanic, and the relatively short playthroughs help too.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Great game if you have any interest in the beauty of Scottish nature and it's folklore! The game consists of platforming and exploring in a 2D world. Had a lot fun with the rhythmic platform sections chasing the deer. Reminded me a bit of Rayman Legends. I also had fun trying to reach the many mountain peaks of the game. And to find out about their mysteries and little stories. You can probably get to the credits of the game in a couple of hours if you are quick. But I think it's more fun if you take a little bit more time for exploring. Especially if you play the game for the first time. The game has some replayability as well. You can choose different paths and you can get different endings for subsequent playthroughs.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the game twice. I failed to reach the goal on time the first time, but still encountered an ending one could be satisfied with as their true ending. However, I couldn't let it go. I knew there had to be more and did not want to miss out on the truth (I had my theories). I was so pleased to reach the ending on time (technically two days early *pat on back*) and receive the ending I craved. I cried, I won't lie. Happy tears though. As far as the gameplay goes, I enjoyed it thoroughly despite being frustrated a number of times because I'm not so good at platformers, rhythm games or puzzles to be honest. The second time I played, I turned on a few of the accessibility options which greatly helped me out. The music is phenomenal and the art style is beautiful. The voice acting is lovely to listen to and happens frequently enough. The game is not fully voice-acted, our heroine has plenty of quips during the gameplay that you read to yourself instead of listening. I love her sass (try opening doors that you can't open many times). Overall 10/10 would recommend. Will play again.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Not all who wander are lost... except you are. A LOT. And it's ok... it's about the journey, for real this time. And The Scottish Highlands, its myths, history and traditional music. A triumphal tribute to the Scottish outdoors and its formidable culture.Both cozy and nerve-wracking, breathtaking both literally and figuratively, just as I imagine it would be hiking the Highlands in real life.Tidbits of history and folklore to uncover, stone after stone, in a Ghibli-inspired, dreamy and eerie landscape where fore- and background swapping is seamless and fluid.Replayability is not a plus: it's required and expected, and every new trip unique and more fascinating than the former. There is just SO MUCH to discover, so much you and Moira have left to experience.As to little tweaks to improve player's experience, I can only think of an implementation of the gameplay tutorial, or at least a guide to map matching. I figured out the game mechanics on Steam Deck after hours stuck in dead ends, because I couldn't figure out what controls I needed to use and how.The game definitely doesn't hold your hand; it rather lets you soar free like a goshawk (or a boobrie, whatever it may be).***My curator page
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Rather enjoyable tales mixed with historic snippets on the lay of the land.  The music had a beautiful charm and the journey was made better with it.  The only Problems I had were finding map positions and keeping up with the music taps.  The voice acting made up for all the scraped elbows and bad weather.  If you like stories centered around exploring and discovering cute mythological themed tales then this is a good game to get
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: It's a song with some highs and lows, but it's still an experience worth having.The sense of exploration, the sense of being lost and trying to find your way. The joy in finding another person out there, doing their own thing, crossing paths with them. The beauty of the world and song. All fantastic.I reached the end just after a key time passed, and got a satisfying ending with the hint of more story if i replayed it, but I tried, and gave up.The difficulties of trying to work with the map system, the frustration of when you're on the clock and you waste time, and the unsatisfying tension between trying to go off the path to find some bit of new story versus the clock overhead: it just wasn't particularly fun, and a disappointment as someone who has loved the replayability in their previous games.But none of that takes away from a beautiful journey. Sometimes you only need to travel the once.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVE this game.   The problem I ha e with it is ME - I get lost in a closet with GPS and a map.   Seriously, my lack of path-finding skills is legendary among my family and friends.   I found the lighthouse once.,…but I’m on my 5th run and haven’t found it again.  My last play thru I got stuck going back and forth between the same 2 peaks….and my next run couldn’t find either one.  (It’s me, honestly!)The game is beautiful, and the soundtrack is just *chef’s kiss* perfect.  The lore is great - I do love this game!  I’ll just probably never actually reach the lighthouse on time. Lol
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This game is delightful both visually and musically. I fell in love with the handpainted environments that you navigate. It really makes you think about the Scottish highlands, both because of its geography and because of how much it rains (oh my god, it rains SO much in this game)The exploration premise of finding a mountain peak, getting your bearings, and then using maps to find passes into the next section of your journey was pretty fun once I got the hang of it. Also the rhythm game sprint sections were super fun, and the Celtic music was delightful to listen to.With multiple paths and items and discoveries to make, the game is meant to be played through multiple times. The fact that you get to keep previous discoveries and items, and there's also stats to challenge yourself to finish the game quicker all urge you to try at least one or two more runs after your first one. I know I definitely did better on my second run compared to my first one.The story is pretty cool, but a bit basic, and I already knew what was gonna happen by day 1. This might be because I watched Song of the Seas (very similar in its premise) so I kinda got more easily clued in to what the game was gonna be about, but it was still pretty nice. I felt like learning about the folklore and history of the areas you explored was interesting too.As for some of the bad points: the climbing was somewhat frustrating in some sections of the game. The damage you take from falling felt inconsistent, where I'd bang my knee while going as careful as I could, and yet be perfectly fine on drops and jumps that I'd assume would hurt me. Health management became a bit of an issue because I died a few times in my first playthrough and made a nasty discovery that respawning sets you back with even less health than before.On your journeys you collect all sorts of items but I never quite felt like I managed to find a use for any of them, even with the journal notes providing some hints (probably?) Also the fact that when you interact using your collected objects in certain areas, the game chooses to only give you two suggested objects in your inventory to use instead of the entire inventory was a frustrating and unnecessary design choice. I never felt like I knew what I was doing with any of them. "Feed cool gem to lion statue? nope that's not it. What about this cool sword? nope. Lavender? Nope"Summary: the art is good, the music is good, the exploration is engaging enough, the story you can figure out quickly, but it's got some cool lore you find out about. It's just got some frustrating gameplay issues for me personally.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game about getting lost in the scottish highlands, a clear homage for both the place and culture accompanied by a heartwarming tale of self-discovery, some sections are hard but you mustn't take your wonder through the game in any stressful manner, ignore the timer, it's fine you can leave thay for the next beltane, the controls for some things could be sharper but I never felt like it took away from the experience though I would recommend a controller, this is an underrated gem of a game
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A nice cozy experience. The art is beautiful, the voice acting is very fitting, the plot is interesting, everything visual about this game is perfect. However, gameplay-wise, it is a bit clunky, the rhythm parts are repetitive and the exhaustion mechanic is annoying after playing for a while. It's a game conceptually made to be replayed multiple times to get the full experience - figure out the maps, find lore bits, NPC interactions - but I do not enjoy this approach when the gameplay is not particulary very fun, and that's the case here. If it was a fully exploration game, with backtracking possibilities and less encouragement to 'rush' through the game, I'd enjoy it a lot more, maybe it's just a preference of mine. Still, I think this game is way more positive than negative, and if you're looking for a cozy, vacation atmosphere, this is a perfect fit.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I'm from Scotland and the atmosphere in this game is spot on. I played about an hour of it and then turned it off to go and take a drive up north to go for a walk in the hills myself. Came back and finished it the next day. The game play and exploration style might not be for everyone but I found it very satisfying to explore and move around the landscape, despite the game simulating the difficulties of moving through such terrain. You have a 'time limit' but the story still goes on if you miss it. I I was sort of semi committed to trying to make it in time on my first run but fully expected to be late. I ended up getting lost finding a huge shortcut because of it, making it with a day to spare. I think the best way to enjoy the game is to chill and accept that the journey will be special no matter what the outcome. Looking forward to trying out a different run with a heavy exploration focus next time.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game that sets its own mood of the hills.  (Somewhat like a platforming version of Firewatch?) After my first playthrough I understood there were contrasting twinned modes: open exploring where (very mild spoiler)  and a speed run / optimization goal. _childDocuments_.review: - Animation is fluid- Artwork / scenery is fantastic- Narration and voice work is soothing - and with v.clear diction etc (easy to listen to, even with my mild hearing issues)- music is foot-tapping good (albeit all in the classical Celtic style)- Plenty of replayability (just finished 4th run, still finding new paths, new maps, new events)
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful story wrapped in a very weird 2d climbing/platforming game. Guide Moira to the lighthouse in 5 days. My first run made it in time, in 3 hours. I don't know if I will play it more. You explore the landscape and there is a lot to do.+ Fascinating lore and story.+ Lots of replayability, every new run will preserve your progress.+ Beautiful music to run to!+ Controls are easy enough, though the game is not that easy.- It's pretty unforgiving if you go the wrong way and you can lose precious time. _childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I nearly gave up after a few hours but glad I didn't. The platforming was frustrating at first and I kept getting stuck, but once I figured out managing the multiple layers I started loving it. Whether I'm exploring or trying to find a faster path I find it a chill but fun time with beautiful visuals every time.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: "A Highland Song" is a captivating game that immerses players in the enchanting world of Celtic folklore, weaving a melodic tapestry of adventure and mystery. The game takes you on a journey through the picturesque landscapes of the Scottish Highlands, blending rich narrative with unique gameplay elements. "A Highland Song" successfully combines captivating storytelling, stunning visuals, and innovative gameplay mechanics. While some players might find the rhythm-based elements challenging, the overall experience is well worth the effort. The game manages to carve out a unique space in the gaming landscape, offering a melodic journey that resonates with the heart and soul of Celtic mysticism.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous game with great graphics and music. It just didn't keep my interest. It's a cool game and lots of people will really love it! Just not for me. I don't mind walking simulators but I didn't really feel like a story was unfolding and some of the controls felt a little fiddly to me. It did revive my desire to visit the real Scottish Highlands, though!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Very good 2D exploration/climbing and simple rhythm game. The countryside/folk music are wonderful in this game! I wish there was a bit of fast travel if you reach the peak because there were times where I would fall by accident & re-climb it again or take a wrong turn and run around the whole area again... but then again, it would take away the purpose of climbing and exploring the mountains and hills. I feel like the time limit to reach the lighthouse is a bit short in terms of if you want to explore more around.. the time limit kind of pressured me to finish the game in a rush mode to see that ending rather than taking my time exploring. Even though the description does say that you need multiple play through to see all endings and different secrets and stories. but I rather have it in one play through for exploring everything with a chance to get a good ending, rather than rushing for a good ending; I would replay again for achievements later on when I feel like it. :-]
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A Melody of Misty PeaksRating: ⭐⭐⭐ (Three Stars)In "A Highland Song," the haunting melodies weave a tapestry that echoes through the misty peaks of these Highlands. As I've often said, "The world is indeed full of peril, and in it, there are many dark places," and this game captures the mysterious allure of such shadowed realms. The storytelling, like the winding roads of Middle-earth, takes unexpected turns, though it lacks the epic resonance of tales told in the halls of Rivendell. Its story unfolds in a symphony of artistry and light lore, reminiscent of the tall tales told in the Shire. However, much like Frodo on his arduous journey, the pace falters, and the rhythm of the narrative is not always in harmony. In Moira's tale, the pacing lacks the precision of a well-timed spell. While the world and art are enchanting, connecting with Moira, the central figure, proves elusive and fleeting.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: A incredibly pretty game with great music.The construction of the map is very interesting and I really like the layering and the distance fog. The open map coupled with the time limit is incredibly stressing in the first playtrough, expecially because you want to follow the deer (because the music is good and it gives you health) but they just take you out into nowhere and then you are lost again or can’t/won’t go back to a point of interest on the other side of the map. It forces a replay almost a little too hard, but you get to keep the things you find, so that soothes it over.The story is cute and being told through tidbits is quite engaging, but it might not be the twist it is made out to be. ()
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just magical. The combination of the painted landscape, the mystical Gaelic stories, and for once there is a truly enjoyable game without any violence (apart from the self-inflicted, you will know what peak I am talking about). The music is just a cherry on top. This experience has been spellbinding.I do understand that this might not be everyone's barrel of whisky, but I do recommend this to everyone. Not only for the unique esthetics and setting, but it is good to just enjoy good game design different from the usual. And for 99% of us this is unusual.Thank yous
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just beautiful. There's no other way to put it. It's also scottish through and through: Lots of scottish folklore, you just want to dive in, more of it than you can get in a single runthough. It has scottish quips here and there, a beautiful soundtrack with scottish folk music that accompanies the whole experience.I also cannot praise the game's visuals enough. What they pulled off with that 2D-Parallax-Map-Effect feels just great from a narrative, progression and visual standpoint.The controls and wayfinding are somewhat rough, though. Part of it lies in the detailing of the level design. Terrain and climbalble walls are non-recognizable sometimes. The devs at Inkle tried their best to remedy this with some kind of hint system, but it sometimes rips you a bit out of the experience, which feels kind of sad.Anyways:It's one of these games, that cause me to yearn for being inside this thing, being part of it, living in it. This time I also yearned to revisit scotland some time again, but more thoroughly.I'm not sure, how much of these places exist IRL in some form or other, but if they were, I definitely wish to visit some of them.In the meantime I will definitely try another run when I get the time to do it.My Conclusion: VisitScotland now has it's inofficial advertisement game. :PAnother small indie gem that goes on my "Games that made me cry"-Pile. (Small disclaimer: I've posted this review on some other platform in December last year. Just wanted to show it here as well to support this game a bit.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes object interactions can be cumbersome but the world and the map is so rich! Once I figured out that you are supposed to run through multiple times (retaining your maps and some inventory), it became so enjoyable to explore. This game incorporates several different mythologies and lore beautifully.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions of this game struck me in various ways such as art style, game play and in how one navigates.As a content creator I focus mainly on game-play, game dynamics, exploration, and my ultimate feeling of the games that I play. This game has gorgeous visuals, wonderful music, I must say I am impressed by this game as a whole and I am appreciative of what this game offers to those who are looking into playing this game, but I also encountered some bugs in the game once I restarted it. - I had a difficult time navigating on the map as Moriah was on her way to the lighthouse.  Secondly, When i began to jump on platforms the blurred lines on what controls to  press made game play very difficult.  Thirdly, while I found the character to be one dimensional, but still seems likable. I do not discredit this game because I truly believe this game has potential for its gamer and for others who want to play. I hope in time this game improvesI say don't let these minor mishaps discredit you as you look into playing this game, but I am sure it could bring frustration to some who mind these type of things. - I still say give this game a shot and see what it offers to you without bias or prejudice.  - Thanks :)

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and whimsical game but I wish I got more out of the first playthough. This game is cosy and aesthetic with an added bonus of exceptionally charming music. I really enjoyed the gameplay once I got around not using the “WASD” controls that most other games apply. However, as I progressed, I found that the game contradicts the real-life experience of enjoying the hike and taking in the nature around you. The countdown to Beltane meant that I didn’t have time to properly explore the environment and I found myself racing through it in an attempt to get there in time in fear of missing out on a good ending. Despite my effort to reach the end before Beltane, I was unable to do this on the first play-through. I believe this game has a high replay value as you search for missed peaks, items and, of course, get the lighthouse for Beltane. But personally, I find the first playthrough of a game to be the most enjoyable and I didn’t enjoy this game as much as I would have liked to because I felt rushed to get to the end. Added features, such "look further" could be better explained in a tutorial. Also, it’s very rainy in the game (much like the highlands), blocking your view as you search for map locations, and changing the settings to "mild" made little difference.Despite my gripes, this game is beautiful and original, and well worth it for gamers who enjoy replaying their favourite games.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This is a charming game that you can "finish" in a few hours, though it seems ripe for multiple replays. The visuals, music, and voice acting combined wonderfully to pull me into the Highlands.I found some of the mechanics a bit tedious at times (lots of stopping to catch your breath), but that seems like a design decision that forces you to slow down and enjoy the scenery. I imagine that'll feel better on replays where I'm less curious about the destination.This game has some of the same vibe that I loved so much in Heaven's Vault, and at times the music/exploration bits reminded me of Tchia. It's a combination of elements I wouldn't have expected, but Inkle makes it work!

_childDocuments_.review: Delightful!! I do play all of inkle games by principle now as I always know I enjoy them and they never disappointed. _childDocuments_.review: A pretty and poetic experience with the scottish countryside and its folklore as a background. Navigating the landscape can become difficult to figure out when trying to reach a specific place but there's always the opportunity to backtrack and take another itinerary as long as you didn't progress too much. _childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since 80 days I have loved how Inkle tells stories, Heaven's vault being my favorite game in recent memory. They tell stories not through exposition but through the environment, character snippets and short out of context memories. Instead of the story driven games of recent memory who *tell* you the story and keep having characters monologue the plot, Inkle treats you like something with a working brain and let your imagination fill in the blanks as layer upon layer of story is revealed to you.The gameplay is fair and challenging hill climbing exploration platformer with a stamina system, with frenetic breaks of rhythm game when you are charging across the Scottish highlands.A run (with a soft time limited goal) takes about 2ish hours, and you will not be able to see and experience everything in a run through (nor should you, this is a game about hiking from point A to B). This just makes you want to pick up and start another run, maybe this time I'll go around the mountain rather than across it?I can definitely see myself picking this up in a rainy day just to run through the adventure of Moira (who is masterfully voiced).

_childDocuments_.review: An exploration game unlike anything I've played before. The gameplay loop combined with how Moira expressees herself made me care more about her and my decisions. So I accidentally skipped dialogue every time I started sprinting.- I had to restart the game a couple of times because the game stopped letting me interact with things.- The volume balance between different sounds were a little off and could use some adjustment.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall weakly recommended, but recommended. This is something of a scrapbook-game, pulling together as many different elements as it does different tales. You'll go from rhythm-gaming to platforming to trying to work out a mystery one after another. That said, each element is quite shallow because of this. And sometimes the multiple elements get caught in conflict. For example, the gorgeous backgrounds rapidly diminish as you approach the sea - makes sense, but it makes the game feel emptier as you approach what's ostensibly the objective, a strange kind of pseudo-punishment for progress. What the game is best at is capturing the feeling of walking somewhere unfamiliar, trying to get your map and what you see to cohere into an understanding of the landscape. If this is a feeling you know and miss, give it a shot!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Art style like forgotten Anne, with beautiful music that is synced with the free running sections. Gorgeous views, vistas and scenery. The Voice acting of the characters is absolutely lovely. the difficulty is calm enough to just enjoy the game but it does throw a good challenge of making you figure out where you are and naming peaks correctly as well as using that same knowledge to progress. Its one of those games where i would imagine it being told to others as a whimsical story or fairy tail. Id imagine it is not a long game but it is so well done that it is a breathe of fresh air to play. Highly Recommend
