_childDocuments_.review: I'm not great with words so I'll keep it short. The music, artstyle, exploration, and "rhythm game sections" are all great. But the time limit severely negatively impacts the experience. In a game that's all about exploring the countryside, why do I feel like I'm being punished for checking out areas that look interesting? I want to see what's behind every nook and cranny but if I do that then I won't make it to the lighthouse on time. Thankfully this can be easily fixed by putting the option to adjust the time limit into the settings, or the ability to just turn it off.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: What a lovely gem of a game. It's a mixture of pleasant platforming and navigation, accompanied by a beautiful story that was a joy to unveil. I really enjoyed the writing in particular - felt lite it had a clear voice. It also has some replay value - have ran through the game twice now, and found it quite fun to get to care more about the journey rather than the destination the second time around.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This game actually surprised me, it's a quite relaxing game with nice music and beautiful art. It only took me maybe a little over an hour to finish a playthrough of the game, but that was with me not exploring too heavily and just trying to get to the end. With saying that, there are multiple paths you can take which makes it worth playing over and over again. I'm on my second playthrough and I've explored a totally different area and it has lasted longer than my first playthrough so far with me not even getting halfway through yet. It does have a rhythm element to it sometimes where you will have to press a button to the beat of the music, but it's not too difficult and doesn't show up too often. The voice acting is well done, but not everything is voice acted which kind of makes me sad. I would say the major characters have voice acting, which isn't too bad though since this is an indie game made by a small team. With saying all that, here are my complaints about the game, even though I think they are pretty small complaints. Sometimes the camera will get a little mixed up and will be too zoomed in where you can't see where you're going, nothing major though and it usually fixes itself after a little bit. My other complaint is all the rain. I've never been to the Scottish Highlands so I have no idea how much it rains over there, bit it rains so much in this game. It was enough to the point I was slightly aggravated because the rain makes it so hard to see the wonderful art and at times makes it hard to see anything. On my first playthrough I decided to wait out the rain a couple of times until I learned that it wouldn't matter if I waited out the rain or not because it will come back 30 seconds later. Because I decided to wait out the rain a couple of times it ended up having a butterfly effect which caused me to not make it to my destination on time for an event in the game. Not too big of a deal since this game was made to played multiple times, but doesn't make it any less aggravating. It also doesn't help that most of the promotional pictures show screenshots without rain, showing how beautiful the art is in the game when I got the complete opposite result from playing the game itself where it rained all the time.All-in-all (even with my lengthy complaint paragraph) this is a wonderful and relaxing game. This is one of those games where you get yourself a cup of tea, wrap yourself in a blanket, and have fun exploring, running with deer, and scaling mountain peaks to get a wonderful view. This started as a random game I saw and decided to try to possibly one of my favorite games this year, even with the little playtime I have. I'm excited to playthrough it again and again just to see what adventures await me on a different path.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: If you played 2021's Black Book and liked that it engaged a lot with Russian folklore and historical practices, then A Highland Song will give you a similar vibe with its gaming experience except that it will be Scottish folklore and history. I really liked the exploring, there were so many interesting tidbits of lore and getting a lay of the land just makes you feel utterly insignificant, a drop of water in an ocean. The game has great atmosphere. I was pleasantly surprised that the voice acting was quite good and authentic to the topic of the game. I think all the voice actors turned in the best work they could, but I wanted more voice acting for the main character, I understand that isn't always a realistic expectation for an indie game, but I think it would have enhanced the experience to hear item descriptions and location descriptions in Moira's own words rather than text alone. The music and hand drawn art were both beautiful and really helped me engage with the journey I was on, there was a surprising variety of biomes in the game, from caves to snowy mountains, to more swampy environments, it wasn't what I was expecting.The controls needed some more tuning, both for the mantling/climbing and the rhythm sections, this was a source of frustration for me during my first playthrough. I also found the Map location marking mechanic to be pretty confusing at times, sometimes it felt like I had a map for a location but I just couldn't move the reticle far enough to tag it, I think overall what the game wanted you to do with that could have been explained better.The game has more replayability than you might think from just reading the description or watching the trailer. In a roguelite way, you are tasked with navigating from point A to point B within a set time limit. I am not sure if it is possible to "beat" the game on your first run, but you do get to carryover some progression items from run to run to help you "win". Unfortunately this is a double edged sword for a first timer because you don't know that the game wants you to play it multiple times and so I found myself just trying to salvage what I could to finish instead of spending my time thoroughly exploring regardless of how long it took because it makes you feel like you're failing, which kind of goes against the nature of this type of journey, kind of a flavor fail, but that's my subjective opinion ymmv.Overall I think I'd give this game a solid 7/10, it drips with Scottish lore, history and geography, it's immersive, you never know what's coming around the next hill or valley, it has great ambiance. If that sounds appealing to you, you won't regret giving it a try. Anyway, I'm off to start my next run, best of luck on yours.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first run, reaching the lighthouse a couple of days after Beltane.This is another great game by Inkle! Highlights include the beautifully rendered scenery, the atmospheric and ambience, the soundtrack and (divisive?) sprinting sections, and Moira herself. It reminds me a little bit of the game Journey.That said, the main reason I'm going to replay is the fact I'm pretty sure I'm missing important aspects of the story; I want to see what happens when I do make it in time for Beltane, otherwise the end is confusing and a bit anti-climatic.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly pretty world to explore, with lots of little nooks and crannies. It's a little frustrating if you end up going in circles, though -- when that happens, I recommend trying to puzzle out any and all maps you have on you at the time. Also the recent patch let you get the lay of the land a little better, which definitely helps. Highly recommended if you like exploration, picking up little bits of narrative at a time, and the feeling of being a insignificant speck in the midst of nature.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: I finished my first playthrough of A Highland Song tonight and so far I adore it. It's rare to play a game that creates such a genuine sense of adventure, and it will feel very familiar to anyone who's been lost in a beautiful place. In many ways the world welcomes you in — the endless breathtaking landscapes, the countless intriguing paths and peaks to explore, the endearing and genuine characters, the interwoven folk tales and gorgeous folk music — and yet there's a persistent tension underlying everything you do. Do I know where I'm going? Do I know where I am? Can I trust this stranger? Is this journey even possible? Should I move somewhere with better weather? And, as with a real adventure, the only way things can work out is if you keep trudging (leaping/running/plummeting) forward.Mechanically, the climbing is solid. Often it feels great, occasionally it's a bit clunky, but it never detracted from my experience. I did find the map marking a bit difficult. At times it's very unclear whether a landmark is actually visible or if it's hidden behind something or the map is drawn from a previous layer. My other gripe is that I would have loved the rhythm sections to be more prominent and a tad more complex, but I can see how getting too close to Taiko no Tatsujin might somewhat disrupt the feeling of freely rushing across the hills.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This game makes for such a calming, fun experience as it transports you to the highlands peaks. With simple mechanics that the game walks you through at the start, it quickly becomes intuitive what you are trying to do. Exploration is key, and the game is very thematic in that it can be easy to get lost!My favourite mechanic is when running across the highland to the music - having calibrated your sense of beat with the game, you button mash along to Moira as she runs between peaks to immersive Scottish tunes. It's a fun way of removing some of the tedious moments in the game and maintaining the sense of scale of the highlands.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: While I reached the lighthouse in just about 4 hours, I am in no way done with this game. The art style is beautiful and the game just encourages you to get lost. Gracefully running through the hills, valleys, peaks, and caves with the charming music playing creates a wonderful sense of calmness and transports you to the outdoors yourself.I highly recommend that when playing this game, do not just try to get to the lighthouse, get lost, explore, run around, and eventually you will reach the lighthouse.I just reached the lighthouse in time for Beltane, and I have to say, if you haven't reached it in time yet, play again and again until you do.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: Metroid's labyrinthine levels but without foes. Death Stranding's lonely journeys in beautiful, unforgiving wilderness but in hand drawn 2D. 80 days never-twice-the-same adventurous journey, but intimate and surreal. Oh, and yes it's also a rhythm game too. There really is a lot in this unique, impossible blend. And yet, somehow, it's wholesome and peaty and delightful.I also have to salute the outstanding level of polish for an indie: great voice acting, a photo mode, a flurry of accessibility options to help alleviate any pain point, and already a couple of nice updates such as "look further" mode - which definitely helped me.Took me 4 hours to complete a first game (I took my time) but like in inkle's Overboard! the whole point is to replay, leverage what you discovered, and try new paths. Shortcuts and maps also remain and help make the next game shorter (it is a race after all). And there is always another mystery to solve, another stone left unturned.Runs flawlessly on Steam Deck, a perfect game to play by the hearth on winter holiday nights while Moira gets soaked on a beinn.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: im only a little bit into it, but its very good so farits very nice running through these environments and climbing and jumpingand the small sprinting rhythm game sections that you can run into, very greatlove the music in there too, its a jamthe voice acting is great, i love how the game kinda dulls out info, whether its the surrounding land and its history or moira's personal history with members of her familyim excited to play more and familiarize myself with these highlands
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: As I've come to expect from Inkle, this is a one-of-a-kind game. I've seen it called 'a 2D Breath of the Wild' but it has none of the distractions (combat, saving the princess, shrines and dungeons). This game manages both to have an undiluted focus on exploration and to have a crystal clear destination so that your wandering is never aimless. Unlike most Inkle games, which I find push you forward regardless of your failures, in A Highland Song I sometimes found myself running in circles. This, admittedly, was frustrating when it resulted from the map fragments demanding a little too much precision; I learned the hard way to try a few different x coordinates before concluding that I must have found the wrong spot. But every time I broke out of a loop (and I always did) the feeling of relief (punctuated by Moira's charming "Yas!") seemed to me part of the emergent experience of the game. You cannot experience the celebration of finding your way without first getting lost. I associate that experience more with Hollow Knight than with Breath of the Wild.I finished the game in 11 in-game days: just... just a BIT too slow. But Moira and I are a bit wilier now, and I look forward to beginning again with new shortcuts in mind. If I know Inkle, there are sure to be many surprises left in store for me.
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review: This is a charming exploration game. It strikes an excellent balance between the charm and wonder of exploring an incredible landscape, and how that landscape can be brutal if you're not careful, soaking you through and leaving you bruised and cautious. There are multiple routes through the world, which are unlocked via maps you find. This means that, although the landscape itself doesn't change with each playthrough, your passage through it will always be different. I found this really refreshing: the landscape feels like a really big puzzle that you can't understand in full, so those moments where you find a map which points you to a passage onwards, and you realise where the passage is (even though the map is a poor scribble) are exciting "aha!" moments.The best part, though, hands down, is the highland runs: making platforming jumps to wild, energetic gaelic music. These have a mechanical function (if you get through a highland run and you hit all the notes, you get a stamina boost) but these things are just so damn fun. Every single time I encountered one I got a big smile on my face.It's lovely, it's evocative, it's joyful, and it has some excellent actually-genuinely-Scottish voice actors. Heartily recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I play-tested this game before release."A Highland Song" is a game that truly embodies the observation that it's just as much about the journey as it is the destination.I think the game is strongest in its exploration. Light puzzle elements such as nailing down locations marked on makeshift maps Moira finds and helping out the strange inhabitants you come across really makes the player feel that they're growing to understand the land and it's people. Alongside that, the 2.5D world constructed gives a proper sense of scale while also making the paths winding in and around each hill, valley, and loch feel almost maze-like. I feel that puts you in the shoes of a child just winging it and making her way through a largely unfamiliar landscape with nothing but notes left from strangers or her Uncle Hamish's wisdom to guide her way. Lastly, the game is very re-playable through that exploration. Figuring out the names for each peak, finding every secret hidden in various caves, crevices, and buildings, and trying to reach the lighthouse of Moira's aspirations on time will keep you playing several times over.I have played one previous title from inkle: "Heaven's Vault". In both that and "A Highland Song" one thing that sticks out to me is the effort the dev team puts into conveying the themes of each through every aspect of the game the player experiences. You can feel the respect and passion inkle has for the Scottish highland's natural beauty, music, history, and general culture emanating out of every character you meet, every piece of music Moira sprints along to, and every peak you climb. I would like to specifically highlight the music out of that list as I think Laurence Chapman, along with selected tunes from Scottish folk groups Talisk and Fourth Moon, did a fantastic job at creating a rather dynamic soundtrack that covers several different moods. Chapman's work is largely relaxing, reflective pieces that feel as though their sound comes from the breeze, trees, and waters around you. Whereas Talisk and Fourth Moon mostly offer several energetic pieces that fit perfectly for a child excitedly running across valleys and shores to reach the sea.All-in-all, I really enjoy "A Highland Song", I think it's a beautiful title that gives a real sense of childlike wonder in exploration, all in celebration of a land with a long and storied history.

_childDocuments_.review: Somewhere between struggling to top a mountain, and choreographically clambering down to its toes, this game really connected with me. A Highland Song is a one of a kind experience in many respects; it embraces locality like few games do, by *being* a love letter to the Highlands and their many stories. It wonderfully mixes adventure mechanics with action and rhythm gameplay. It quite simply innovates in being a "2.5D" narrative game with a completely seamless world, from the very first moment of its opening. Whether you can tell by the trailers or not, this is a pretty damn ambitious game, executed beautifully. I love games with decisions to make and a truly reactive narrative, that I can enjoy at my own pace. A Highland Song really delivers that. There's different ways to play: If you just want to relax, take in the scenery and do some exploring (and there's a lot to discover), you're free to do that. There'll be *implications*, not *punishment*. Then again, if you wanna challenge yourself, test your climbing skills, navigation and time management, A Highland Song's got you covered. There's so much to uncover, and it's really up to you to decide where you'll dig deep. I'm a big fan of Inkle's games, and it feels like they've been growing towards something like this for a long time. It's "fun", it's meaningful, and it's gorgeous. Give it a shot!
_childDocuments_.name: A Highland Song

_childDocuments_.review:
Moira McKinnon has never seen the sea. For fifteen years she's lived with her mum in a small house on the edge of the Scottish Highlands - then one day she receives a letter from her Uncle Hamish urging her to come to the coast. If she can reach his lighthouse for the solstice, a wonderful surprise will be waiting...

A Highland Song is a narrative adventure game from inkle, the creators of 80 Days, Heaven's Vault, and last year's surprise hit Overboard!

Explore hills crisscrossed by routes - some well-trodden, others hidden away - that are filled with stories, lost things, echoes, and memories.

Climb peaks to orient yourself and plan your next steps. Then hop, slide, and jump through the valleys in time with the music.

And be prepared to make the journey more than once, because a single trip isn't nearly enough to discover the Highlands' deepest secrets.

name: Halo Infinite
detailed_description: Campaign: When all hope is lost and humanity’s fate hangs in the balance, the Master Chief is ready to confront the most ruthless foe he’s ever faced. Step inside the armor of humanity’s greatest hero to experience an epic open-world adventure and explore the massive scale of the Halo ring. With Network Campaign Co-Op and Mission Replay, you can relive your favorite moments, rediscover collectibles and explore the wonders of Zeta Halo on your own or with up to three other fireteam members. To experience the campaign, purchase Halo Infinite (Campaign). Free-to-Play Multiplayer: Experience Halo’s celebrated multiplayer reimagined and free-to-play! With over 70 maps in matchmaking, billions of customization configurations, and countless community Forge creations to experience, Halo Infinite is the franchise’s most expansive multiplayer offering to date. Enjoy an unprecedented variety of gameplay experiences, ranging from fast-paced intense ranked modes to whimsical mayhem in Custom Games, or even co-operative coordination in the wave-based survival mode Firefight: King of the Hill. Assemble your Fireteam and conquer every mode – Halo offers endless opportunities for teamwork, strategy, and unforgettable victories. Forge Beta: Halo’s legendary content creation tool is more powerful than ever with advanced features like a sophisticated visual scripting engine, mode editor, object scaling, lighting and audio tools as well as marked improvements in fidelity and object budget limits. Forge also includes the powerful AI Toolkit, allowing players to add campaign AI to their creations. Whether it’s remaking iconic experiences from previous Halo entries or creating something entirely unique, the possibilities for thrilling custom maps and game modes are infinite. '

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this as someone who has never played a Halo game before :PC performance :The game runs like a dream on all computers,  even a potato cpu like mine from 2014 can keep consistent 70-80 on 1080p.Graphics :The game isn't mind-blowing graphically but it does its job. I have an issue with the colors looking washed out on PC, I had to use Nvidia Digital vibrance to make the colors pop more Lack of resolution settings is also strange.Why is this review negative :The game is good but I want to raise attention to the game breaking sound bug that has been ignored since the test flights months ago : YOU CANT HEAR PEOPLE BEHIND YOU IN THIS GAME many people are struggling with this game breaking bug, good, you willl keep getting punched from behind 24/7 when no sounds are alerting you. 343 said they are aware of the bug but they are adding pineapple grenades for 10 bucks on the shop instead....Gameplay : Lack of choice when it comes to modes is obnoxious, leaving your fun to rng is never a good idea-As a new person who is playing a Halo for a first time, I'm really surprised old Halo fans enjoy the nade spam in these games, each player can carry 4 grenades, most of your deaths per match are gonna be due to grenade spam.....Second most annoying core gameplay feature is the melee and how 70% of your 1v1 fights will devolve into a ''WHOEVER HAS FASTEST INTERNET AND PC AND MONITOR WILL PUNCH YOU AND KILL YOU FIRST'' type of fight.. it's extremely obnoxious and feels like you are getting cheated as your aim and skill isnt' important in a punching fight in this game. There's this aimbot punch thing built in in this game which makes it worse.Battlepass :I got the battlepass and I feel cheated, all items you unlock look the same, the good stuff is only towards the 100 level mark which will take a good 100 hours to reach. conclusion :I will change this review to positive if they add gameplay modes that we can choose to play and if they fix the game breaking No sound from behind bug. I don't think the nade spam and melee spam will be fixed but I do hope they will add some good modes that have those two disabled. Overall 6/10 with a potential to jump to 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Note: I haven't played the campaign, this is purely from a multiplayer perspective.I wanted to like Halo Infinite so badly. I mean just look at the number of hours I already put into it.But I can't recommend it. Instead, let me tell you a story.It starts with myself and 2 friends. Excited to try the newest Halo. Some of us (me) have never played Halo before. Others are waxing lyrical about the Halo lore and weapons and vehicles. It draws me in.The game is sweet. The grapple feels awesome. The skewer has a thumping sound effect that shakes your bones when it tears through an enemy. The announcer croons "Killing Spree" in my ears as I punch that last punk into the ground. We end the map victorious. The battle pass levels, it's some weird leg armor customization. Strange, but cool. I'm a Spartan. Hell yeah.We play more.I don't get that Killing Spree. I die instead of them on that 5th kill. Strange, I could have sworn I hit my melee in time. I guess not. I'll get better. We lose. I check my quests. I've made a little progress. But I've got a new one for a game mode we don't want to play (free for all, cause, you know, we're a team). No matter, I'll spend one of my challenge swaps.It's another mode we don't want to play. Big Team Battle. For some reason that mode doesn't group our crew together so we're essentially all playing solo. I spend another challenge swap. Now it's get a kill with the Heatwave! I can do that.The next map loads. There's no Heatwave spawn. We're against a team that's well coordinated and mowing us down. We fall behind. I manage to grab the hammer. I make it up close and personal and get a swing on 3 of them at once.None of them die. I'm mowed down again by assault rifle fire. My next life I die to the stolen hammer from across a room. I'll get better, right?We play more.One of the group decides to stop. They're not having fun anymore. They were almost always the bottom of the scoreboard and not seeing any improvement.We're 2 now.We play more.I get a quest for a backsmack kill. I try and try. Sometimes when I think it should register, it doesn't. Then. Finally. A backsmack kill. The match ends. It didn't count. The quest is still there. I keep trying.We play more. I am better. I know it. But the crazy kills (or not-kills) keep happening. I'm suspicious. I start to browse the web. It becomes clearer. It's not me. It's the game. It's gas-lighting me. It's telling me I mistimed the swing, or didn't position correctly. It's a fast paced shooter, maybe you just made a mistake. But no. I can see the evidence before my eyes. Ridiculous non trading melees. Nonsensical hammer kills. Death through walls. It's not my imagination. It's real.We play more, but for a shorter amount of time.Swapping to other games after just a few matches. There's not much enjoyment anymore. It's just frustration. There's no way to know when you made a mistake or the game just deciding to mess with my head.Which brings us to now. Today. An update. Finally. I have hopes. My friend has convinced me to keep it installed just to see what the update brings.We play for 2 hours.He crashes twice. I crash once. I need to restart once because the lobby breaks. The annoying speed lines are stuck on no matter what the setting is. We can't play the special event since it requires solo queuing. My melees still don't seem to kill when they should. My sword swings don't track. We rarely play a match without an Afk player on one side or the other. Scoreboards show 12+ players at the end of matches instead of 8.And that's it. That's how my first experience with Halo ends.A complete disappointment.TL;DR Netcode is awful, if you don't believe me, do a little digging online. Game is also generally buggy, unstable, and sluggish.3/7 - Huge Missed Potential

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specifically for the multiplayer. I really like what 343 did to rework the core halo multiplayer. I love the addition of going back to the roots of halo 3, and expanding upon that with, for example, pickup equipment, no abilities, etc.The gameplay is solid, the sound design is solid, but there is something that just feels so off about the game when playing it since launch that I dont know if I can recommend it (even if it is free). The content feels severely lacking. I found myself losing motivation to play this game over time,  and I finally just stopped. Big team battle still hasn't been fixed (since I last played), in the last couple weeks we BARELY got game modes, like slayer, to choose from. and not only that, the game still does not feel optimized on PC at the moment. Something with performance just feels so off, and its very unsettling for some reason. I have a great build that should run most, if not all AAA games no problem, and i seem to have issues with halo crashing,  dropping frames, and just overall inconsistent performance. (Something also feels very off about mouse movement, but it might just be me).  The game does not feel like it rewards players for doing well, like most halo games have in the past which i find strange. The progress and microtransation system is just... an absolute mess as well. I know this is a new game, i know this is a new generation of halo, and free to play games, but I feel as though its missing things that most halo titles have had in the past. Personally for me, that is unacceptable. I dont know if i can recommend this game in its current state. I want it to be the best it can be, and i hope it is at some point, but it isn't at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: As a longtime Halo fan, I was excited to dive into Halo Infinite and see what the latest installment had to offer. However, after spending some time with the game, I have to say that I'm disappointed with some of the issues that have been raised by other players.One of the biggest concerns is the lack of content in the game. While the core gameplay mechanics are solid, there just isn't enough variety to keep things interesting in the long term. The multiplayer modes are limited, and the single-player campaign feels short and underwhelming.Another issue is the graphical quality of the game. While the art direction is great and captures the spirit of the Halo franchise, the technical execution is lacking. The graphics are often muddy and lack detail, and there are frequent pop-in and frame rate issues that can be distracting.Finally, there are some concerns about the monetization model for the game. While it's great that Halo Infinite is free-to-play, the microtransactions and battle pass system feel intrusive and push players towards spending more money to get the most out of the game.Overall, while I appreciate the effort that went into Halo Infinite and the nostalgia that it brings for longtime fans of the franchise, I can't wholeheartedly recommend it at this time. There are too many issues that need to be addressed before the game can truly live up to its potential. I'll be keeping an eye on updates and patches to see if things improve, but for now, I'll be moving on to other games.

_childDocuments_.review: Halo: Infinite is a unique case. What started off as a total nightmare with no free-to-play motivation, is attempting to redeem itself through a regular set of updates. These updates have granted a new set of ideas to the franchise which in my opinion help greatly.Let's just get this out of the way, this isn't exactly a Halo game in the traditional sense, It's not a well developed story about a heroic cypher for the player being led through a rich story by a lovable AI guide. It's a cosmetics grinding simulation with Halo shooting mechanics. But with that being said Infinite currently feels like a team of developers trying to make a reasonable pass at a grindcore game with a suit at Microsoft mandating corporate policy. There's a battle pass, there's a "premium currency store", there's daily challenges and challenge based progression to slow down earning, increasing playtime. All the hallmarks of a corporate "live service" so they don't have to deliver a "product".Contrary to that point, the developers appear to have made logical choices, by making each battlepass replayable, you don't have to complete 100 levels of nonsense within a tiny timeframe, you can start any battlepass from now or the past at any time, even switch between different tracks of rewards without losing progress. Free content is the forefront of each pass, with all free items being given to you first. Meaning you only have to play 25 levels to complete each pass as a free player. Oh and PVE is a part of the regular MP experience. You don't have to fight over players now to earn XP, you can just play HALO now. These are all massively positive changes which in their wisdom, have pushed me BACK INTO INFINITE. Yes, I will be playing this game to reward these developers with my time, money and patience. Playing the games which make good choices to adapt to rules made by those above them, will greatly encourage developers and publishers to make positive choices!Infinite made me ask questions: "Hold on, wait a minute, why can't I complete a battle pass in any other game like I do in Halo Infinite?", "Why can't I play old passes in other games?", "Why don't other games give players access to PVE as part of the free-to-play experience?". Seems someone, probably a gameplay designer, at 343 does indeed know what they are doing, it's just a shame they're working for 343 of all companies. I'd love to see this concept of being able to come back to games, of which I haven't played for months, to find a whole trove of content for me to play through and earn, rather than being shamed for missing it!Now, with that being said, this recommendation is only to be taken if you're the kind of person who can switch your brain off, ignore all reason, story or character and just click on alien heads. You have to be a special kind of person to really just enjoy the "combat" part of Halo over all of the other pieces, but that is indeed the hill that 343 plans to die on. A combat system from 2001 that they didn't invent.

_childDocuments_.review: (mostly) FIXED  (mostly) FIXEDBiggest issue now is the lack of colour customization. You have basic colour options, and you can unlock more through purchases. There is no longer the ability to choose primary/secondary colours, and you cannot customize emblems further than five or so different colour presets for the emblem of your choosing.Big team battle is also a buggy mess to queue into, with constant matchmaking issues. It can be helped slightly by setting your fireteam privacy to open.There's also something causing occasional freeze crashes in any game mode you might choose, its only happened twice to me, but both times were in the last 10 hours, so it could be me changing something, or it could be a bug.Finally there does feel like there's a lack of maps.Now it may seem weird for me to recommend this game, but despite all these issues, the game taken as a whole is fantastic! The gameplay is varied and captivating, the few maps that do exist are all beautiful and play differently. The weapons sandbox could do with a little re-balancing as the Commando feels very superfluous, and the Skewerer is almost always a worse pick than the SPNKR (perhaps a nerf to the splash damage could fix that *hint hint*), but all the weapons play, sound, and feel great. Most even look nice (I really miss the magnum though)! And apart from the Commando most really do have a use that makes them effective and sets them apart. I cant remember ever before successfully winning a duel against a BR with just a plasma pistol!The release of the campaign has been great, and the wide open world feels like a much more complete take on the scope of what Combat Evolved was originally supposed to be. My only complaints here, are the lack of ability to choose what individual level you want to play, and the lack of par time/score. The former is something 343 has said they're actively working on, and the latter is far from a gamebreaker for anyone but the speedrunning community. Its always harder to write the stuff you like, than it is to write the stuff you don't, much like getting a piece of gravel in your new shoes. You wont go around thinking about how comfortable the rest of your foot, nor how comfortable the other foot is. The focus falls entirely on the wee stone. Halo Infinite has a couple of stones, but boy, if it was a shoe it'd be the one I'd wear everywhere. So if you want to play what is (honestly) by far the best interpretation of Halo since 343 took over Bungies mantle of responsibility, give Infinite a shot. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re reading this, you’re probably at least somewhat aware of this game's initial reputation. A rushed product that at first saw a boom in population, only to swiftly decline after the rose tinted glasses were taken off when fans realized the game had barely 20 maps, no new modes, 4 playlists (slayer not included) and abysmal performance on PC. Well fellow stranger, I am happy to tell you those days are 2 years gone and I can finally recommend the game to any longtime Halo fan or new player. Let's start with the campaign as this section will likely be as brief as the experience was for most of us. Truthfully, unless you’ve got some friends with gamepass and are able to play it for free - or you can all score a sick deal on it - the campaign is worth looking past. 343 has made it clear that this part of the game is nowhere near the main focus of the franchise going forward and thus hasn’t received a lot of support, but what is there is a complete package albeit short and sweet. I completed almost every achievement obtainable solo and had a decent time, but after a while the same biome gets pretty boring and the story is sadly just slightly over mid. Personally the co-op campaign completely overshadowed that experience for me. If you’ve got just one friend to play along with, this is legitimately one of the best campaigns in the series (and that’s coming from someone who played all the Halo campaigns alongside my dad and friends over the decades). The added RPG elements with FOBs, spartan upgrades, unlimited equipment tied with a really tight sandbox and fantastic AI is an absolute joy to blast through with a buddy. Lots of room for shenanigans and clownary like any good Halo title and the co-op achievements are a fun challenge to spice things up. I’d only recommend checking this out if you’ve got someone else interested in trying it with you.Now onto the real reason anyone is still here, the free multiplayer. Oh how far we’ve come. Compared to launch, the game now sports:+A healthy amount of rotating playlists every week with classic game modes and new ones sprinkled in there+A revised challenge system that isn’t too hard to complete and gives okay to really good weekly rewards for completion+$5-$10 battle passes that never expire and give you the cash to buy other passes if completed+A new variation of Firefight which I can’t recommend enough for long time fans+Well over 70 maps, many of which are community made and added into matchmaking+A superb sandbox that continues to expand yet stay pretty balanced+A functioning custom games browser with so much content it makes your head spin+Custom games XP+An actual career rank and player progression outside of battlepasses+Much smoother performance and less crashes (though still not totally ironed out)+An actual player base that isn’t dead anymore (mostly thanks to our friends on Xbox)+THE BEST FORGE IN ANY HALO GAMEAs I hope you can see, the game has come a long way and is now, finally, a “feature complete” product. That is to say, the only things it has left to add are bug fixes, cosmetics, and sandbox additions which the developers have made clear is the goal looking forward. While I don’t believe the corporate lie that this will be a “10 year title” I do see a very good case for this game continuing to receive support for many years to come especially under 343’s new leadership (the team responsible for reviving and nearly perfecting MCC is now calling the shots for Infinite). Now more than ever before it's worth being hopeful for Halo again. As an insane person who has played over 4000 matches of this game and has not stopped playing since the absolutely disastrous launch, I can confidently say the entire game has never been better and I fully recommend you at least give it a shot. Since the game is free, it's always there to jump back into as well; so even if you aren’t interested today, Infnite's community isn't going to disappear on you like the other revolving titles from legacy FPS franchises that keep releasing rug pulls with more fomo in em than a casino based around crypto. If nothing else, at least try out custom games with some friends. If you’ve ever had any fun with Halo custom games in the past, Infinite will not only make you reminisce on those childhood memories and tickle your nostalgia but also show you an endless supply of new experiences the beefed up forge is capable of creating. I have had so much fun somehow convincing 8-12 friends on discord to download the game and join me in exploring all of the different wacky game modes this amazing community has managed to make. Like the ancient gaming sessions of old that have had each of us laughing our asses off hours into the night, a hint of that bygone era of gaming is present here in spades and has been something I treasure every time I get the opportunity to host. I can only hope you get to experience some of that too as that form of unbridled joy is hard to replicate. It's not all sunshine and rainbows however, there are still some major downsides to this game. To keep things somewhat brief in this already too long of a review, BUYER BEWARE of the following: -Absolutely atrocious monetization (all armor and colors in the shop are bundled together with no option to buy individual pieces of the collection and are OUTRAGEOUSLY priced)-Bad netcode (this however is being fixed with an entirely rewritten netcode being beta tested in various playlists currently, time will tell if this is ultimately resolved)-Really stupid skill based matchmaking -Long load times-Armor cores don't have full compatibility with other customization options present in separate cores (yet… this is SLOWLY being resolved)-No commendation system like Halo Reach or Spartan Records like Halo 4If only some of these issues are resolved I truly believe this will be one of, if not THE greatest Halo game of all time. I know for some that rings of heresy, believe me, I too never imagined I'd see the day where this opinion had any weight to it, but after how much progress has been made to improving the title I am at least optimistic that we've taken a turn from the road to recovery and on to the path of success. Halo has had it rough the past decade, the fans of the franchise even rougher, but the flame isn't out yet. I know that in the next coming years both the devs and the forge creators will continue to flesh out what is possible in this game, and we as a community will finally be able to finish this fight.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game but I just can't at this stage.I've played through Season 1, hoping, trying to stay positive, but the release of Season 2 has taken that hope, put it through the grinder and then took a dump on it.Tl;dr:Halo Infinite offers a fun and enjoyable campaign experience with decent replay value at your leisure. The foundations of the game are strong, with a great weapon/equipment sandbox and feel to them. The MP is plagued with a poor challenge system, lacking playlists, long search times in lower population areas, and and sometimes horrible connections with high ping, packet loss and massive desynch. The battle pass leaves a lot to be desired and the map variety, especially for BTB is pathetic. Many classic Halo game modes and features are still missing after over six months.The good:The campaign is solid. It's a fun experience, really allowing the sandbox to shine. The story is above average and the personalities of the various named enemies are genuinely entertaining. The grunt propaganda towers are also a true call back to how grunts were in old school Halo campaigns, whacky, funny dialogue through and through. You have near complete freedom in the "Open World" setting, and you can more or less choose what you want to do. Go straight to the next main mission? No problem. Wanna explore and pick up every Spartan Core to beef yourself up before you tackle a boss? Go for it.The weapons all feel great to use, bar a couple of exception. The weapon variants in the campaign give you some more fun to play around with and keep things fresh, should you choose to use them.The MP maps are all at least average, and most are solidly above average when looking at other FPS maps in comparison.The bad:The MP is a joke compared to previous entries. After six months, they add two maps only (one for 4v4, one for BTB), with no announcements for any additional maps any time soon. This wouldn't be such an issue if the game didn't only come with three BTB and six 4v4 maps.There is no dedicated 4v4 objective playlist. The only way to get them is to play Quickplay, which still includes slayer.While the playlists available aren't as sparse as at launch, a plethora of classic modes are still missing.Ranked is a mess. Between long match searching times, the actual skill based matching seems to be a joke.There's also no way to play either objective or Slayer in ranked and you have to rely on the luck of the draw.With season 2 they tried to mix up slayer by giving AR and BR starts, but instead of keeping it casual with the BR starts, and just changing the AR to a BR, they literally just copied the Ranked set up (including the weapon spawn behaviour from what I could tell) which is honestly just lazy. The Halo 3 AR/BR spawn would have been a fantastic way to freshen things up.The Plasma Pistol has been absolutely massacred in this game. While I understand the removal of its vehicle EMP ability given the introduction of 'Shock' damage, I do not understand the piss poor tracking of the charged shot, nor abysmal shield damage of the single shot. Essentially, the weapon went from a very useful utility weapon to something akin to a nerf gun. The Ravisher is another weapon that has been introduced and seems somewhat pitiful. Its primary fire is plasma with a trajectory of a mortar path, relegating the weapon to shorter range combat. That's not necessarily a problem, if the damage and accuracy weren't hideous. The alt fire unfortunately isn't great either. It chews for just shy of a quarter of your total ammo, and all it does is do AOE D.o.T. in a somewhat large area. The problem is that this will not kill an enemy, even if they remain in the affected area until it runs out.The new pseudo battle royal mode, Last Spartan Standing (LSS, aka Free for All Attrition) needs some major tweaks. The first two minutes or so are fairly fun, but as soon as the first few players are out, it becomes a drag. People camp corners, creep around, and things come to a near standstill. The power equipment is also a huge problem. It basically breaks an resemblance of balance. Both the Overshield and Active Camo have next to no counterplay, and at the frequency they drop at, it's easy for a couple of people to dominate them again, and again, while still reaping the previous equipment they've used. For supposedly being the big "bring back the players mode" it is severely lacking. This may get patched and re-balanced by removing/heavily limiting OS and camo and increasing the 'danger zone' closing rate, it currently is not much more than a camping fest.The ugly:Matchmaking can be an absolute grind. If you're outside the US, you'll likely struggle to find games for certain game modes in any reasonable times. There is still no region/server selection, nor a method to limit matchmaking by ping. Initially you could manually exclude areas via some editing of your network connections, but this got patched out and a replacement to deal with the issue was never released. Playing on +200ms ping servers, and/or dealing with constant packet loss really drains any amount of fun. This doesn't even address the desynch problem that seems to affect a ridiculous number of players still. It sometimes gets so bad, that you will lose gun fights you couldn't possible have lost otherwise.Aim assist for people using controllers is still too strong. Playing with M&K can put you on a serious disadvantage. From what I've seen, controller players have around a 10% higher accuracy than M&K players.The lack of BTB maps has genuinely killed the enjoyment one could get playing the bread and butter of casual play. It's the same grind, over and over again. The maps themselves are fine, but the number thereof after SIX months is pathetic. The challenges and Battle Pass are also a huge slap in the face of fans. While the Season 2 battle pass does look a lot better than the Season 1 one, it does not excuse the utter ♥♥♥♥-show the first season pass was. The challenges, which should be fun and engaging exercises to draw people into certain playlists are a bit of a joke. For one, sometimes progress towards challenges is straight up not registered. Any progress is only counted after you complete the match, so if your game freezes or crashes (which still happens semi-regularly on PC), sucks to be you. Additionally, some challenges are straight up stupid. "Overwatch" is probably one of the worst offenders of this, as you can't do much to even set anything up to have a crack at it. Any challenge which relies on your team mates or enemies doing something highly particular is utter non-sense. These kind of challenges are a waste of time, and honestly just frustrating. You literally just have to get lucky to manage to get the Overwatch challenge done. If they've added it in on purpose, the person who made that call really needs to reflect on how such a challenge is supposed to be engaging and getting players into certain playlists.On a similarly frustrating note, challenges that require you to win any objective game mode are a horrible idea too. Getting objective games in 4v4 scenarios is already hard enough as it is, but then having to rely on your team mates to actually win makes the whole thing so much worse. Finally got that game mode you need to win in two or three times? Have a crappy team that doesn't even try to play the objective. Oh, you wanna play another round of this game mode? Tough luck.For a final piece of info: with season 2, 343i decided to remove two "glitches" in the campaign, despite being asked not to. Thanks for not fixing actual problems and removing things that actually increased campaign enjoyment.

_childDocuments_.review: Wait for a real discount. The graphics are a strict downgrade from previous titles, as is the gameplay. It's very hit and miss in this regard, somethings work but too many don't. A lot of the UNSC weapons feel and function nicely, it's the banished weapons that feel like airsoft. This extends to the grenades and vehicles, they feel like cheap plastic and have no impact either visually or audibly. The vehicles have poor control and the campaign map feels like it's designed to quickly encourage you to abandon them in favour of foot travel. Foot travel would be acceptable if you weren't so painfully slow on foot, you have a sprint function which appears to add speed lines to the screen and nothing else. The grapple feels functional enough but also lacks impact, unlike the grapple from Dying light which it appears to be directly lifted from. I've put five hours in, which means I can't even begin to think of a refund, so all I can do is advise you against falling for the same trick. Don't let rabid consoomers trick you, the game clearly needs way more work, the map is ugly and unpleasant to traverse and the enemies appear to be pretty clever and work together but the guns themselves feel bad and unpleasant to use and many of vehicles feel practically unusable. It's not like old CE, it's way to cartoony for that and is very distinctly 343 style story telling. It's strictly a downgrade from 4 and 5, graphically and gameplay wise. It's frustrating because there are clear signs that they tried, I have no idea why they stopped trying but I can only assume they ran out of time. I don't think this gonna be one of those "patch it until finished" things, it feels like there's too much work needed to fix this, we'll probably be stuck with things as is and some minor patches for major issues that can't be ignored.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to try and keep nostalgia out of the picture for my review, like many I played halo games since I could hold a controller, but I will refrain from using past experiences to rate the game. First things first, has probably the most solid gameplay out of any halo game to release. Everything is smooth from the movement to the aiming and every other foundational thing that makes gameplay great, however, this is where literally my positives of the game end. When I log into a game that's not a live service game and it has a battle pass, that's instantly where you'll lose me. Modern games have adapted this idea that every game needs a battle pass. Battle Passes definitely fit into some games, but if we're being honest, Halo didn't fit that criteria. It makes sense for the Master Chief Collection to have the battle pass to obtain the old armor sets, but it doesn't fit here. The map design for most of the maps I have played were mediocre at best, with a couple of very solid maps that were my favorite maps out of all the halos. There's definitely some fun to be had here, but the novelty and nostalgia can not make up for what this game is missing. I mean this with all of my heart, after about two hours you will have experienced everything this game has to offer (at least for the free multiplayer) and no longer "need" to play it. I have only played an hour of Infinite, but I can't help but feel like I'm wasting my time even launching this game. The progression of this game is absolute dogwater with every level and xp gain coming from challenges that give very little xp. Also if you don't like your daily challenges that you were given and you ran out of free challenge changes, prepare to bust out that wallet buddy or prepare to wait for reset. Just everything in this game besides the gameplay is working against the player and it becomes harder to progress. Let's talk microtransactions, surprise, they're dogwater. Some of the cosmetics look cool, but when your asking $20 dollars on one armor set, that's ludicrous. Extra challenge resets cost 2 dollars for some reason, and this game literally took after one of the most scummy gaming publishers there are, Activision. Honestly, you would think that activision just ♥♥♥♥ on this game and released it, but no it's 343. The skins that you have to pay for in some capacity for the weapons are that of a toddler design. Utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ wheat bread, this game couldn't get your ♥♥♥♥ hard again if it was dressed like Megan Fox from 2008's transformers and she offered you fun time.  Most of the time it's hard to even have a good match when people camp with gravity hammer during game modes like oddball. Absolutely busted and unfun to come across players who just exploit the games weak map design, but I can't even blame them because they're not the ones that designed these god awful maps. I really wanted to like this game, but with the push back of forge mode and having to wait even longer for that and the co-op campaign to release, this game unfortunately for me is a fail. For those that love halo multiplayer, despite what I said, I would say that you would still have high amounts of fun with this game. Unfortunately for those who wanted more out of this game, turn the other cheek and pray that god hasn't abandoned us yet.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not Halo 3. This game is not Halo: Reach.This game is also not Halo 4, or Halo 5.This game is Halo: Infinite. It released in 2021. Context matters. Other AAA studios have been releasing garbage releases one after another. Games are hacked together with pushy microtransactions all over the place. Halo: Infinite is not a perfect game. It may not be the best Halo game. It is a good game.Halo Infinite does have microtransactions, but it doesn't push them too hard. You can easily play the game without spending a cent, and not feel like you are missing out too much. The only thing they really push is the battle pass. Even then, there are no intrusive popups telling you to buy it. The sandbox here is amazing. Weapons are well balanced, with every weapon having a use case. Some weapons are generally worse (disruptor, ravager) and some weapons are generally better (skewer, sidekick) but no weapon is useless. BR does not win every battle. Neither does shotgun. Neither does energy sword, or gravity hammer. Only weapon that can theoretically win every battle is Sniper Rifle, and the tradeoff there is high player visibility (giant weapon, lens reflection) and high accuracy requirement. Disruptor is a common weapon that can EMP vehicles. Ravager has high damage + melee bonus at close range, and AOE is good for specific scenarios, like BTB Capture the Flag, where you can AOE 6+ enemies at once.Vehicles are not perfect, but I love the balance of high damage and speed, to big target with low HP. Vehicles generally have enough HP to take out a few targets, before you need to jump out and find a new solution. That said, if you play your cards right, you can stay in a Wasp (flying vehicle) all day in BTB.The frequently rotating playlists keep per-playlist population high. Social playlists are almost always under 1 minute wait time, and more commonly around 20 seconds. Even ranked playlists aren't too bad, with the worst one being Ranked FFA at around 5 minute average search time (For placement matches).Customization system is straight up worse than Halo: Reach (my personal favorite), but not horrible. Armor cores are cool - although the lack of cross-core customization is not. Coatings suck, but certain coatings bring new style to the game - reflective colors and patterns are awesome. I especially love the visor customization. I don't care if candy can stripes are impractical, they look awesome.TLDR; Halo: Infinite improves greatly above all other Halo games in some aspects, and falls way behind in others. _childDocuments_.review: The quality of the original games have been lost.Visually the maps are forgettable, furnished with buildings that don't appear to serve any real purpose, and look clean with huge metal walls and pointless rooms. They're like a horrible mixture of arena and real-world location, failing to feel like one or the other. It lacks scale and immersion, with only a few characters shooting eachother for no apparent reason. It would be redeemable if the theme tied into a campaign that had good weapons, but I'm not paying £50 for a story that's been dragging on for over a decade.I didn't even find the weapons as satisfying as the originals. There's no weight to them, like shooting the dirt shows an impact effect that's gone in less than a second. If they were trying to optimise for decent framerate, they did a horrible job. The default FPS was set to 60, and mine suffered stutters even with the low playercount. The weapons also feel useless when you get so little ammunition, and it's annoyingly difficult to get more. At one point I picked up a fresh weapon, and after firing one shot I heard an announcer state "low ammo spartan."The game doesn't minimise. I couldn't get interactivity with my shadowplay menu while in-game. There's poor intuition for the button controls, like the number keys not relating to weapons. Even the menu has a broken button system, where to find information about a gamemode that should appear when you mouse-over the button, you have to click it which takes you to another menu, then go back. The information refuses to display otherwise.The matches are small, and it's supposed to be competitive but I found the teams unbalanced. It also rarely shows the killcount at the end, which made the whole thing feel pointless. The design of the maps left them claustrophobically lumpy and sparsely populated, like you go looking for someone to shoot, and eventually you see someone, but after shooting them they just go round a corner and disappear. Previous games had a better mixture of small maps where you could actually catch players, and larger ones where you could easily see them. I couldn't find custom games that were a large part of the culture in Halo 2 & 3, where you'd do things like Zombies, Tower Power, Hide & Seek, and Tremors.Trying to start a match can leave you with "Unable to start Dedicated Server." If you do get in, the start and end of matches force you to watch character animations - but if they cared about personalisation then they wouldn't charge you money to change your name. Making the game free might sound good on paper, but if it's not fun then the only people bothering with it might be cheaters that have no barrier to remake an account after being banned. From what I've seen I have no faith in their anti-cheat, so a pricetag would have actually made some sense to serve as a paywall against banned cheaters coming back.It was a bit annoying hearing the announcers constantly throw lines at you for every little thing that happens. I kinda just wanna focus on the game, not have the game focus on me. There's other things that don't make sense on a sensory level, like information boxes that pop up and disappear so quickly that you wouldn't be able to read them, and the bizarre choice of allowing red team players to use blue playermodels and vice versa. There's an aspect to quality that involves keeping the experience intuitive. Games that do this well allow you to turn your brain off and have fun, and remain competitive experiences because they're so instinctive. This pointless mixing of red and blue destroys that and leads to friendly fire.I don't know how merged the XBOX, Microsoft, Hotmail, Games For Windows Live, Outlook, Windows, Xbox Live accounts are, leading to confusion. I bet there was Mixer and Skype in there. I can't stand this system because you end up trying to remember which accounts work for what, and which one you want to use. I had a Windows account that refused to work when I was more or less forced to move from Windows 7 to Windows 10. My original Xbox Live account was locked after they made an unwanted charge. I had an abandoned Games For Windows Live account that wouldn't let me change its name. I've got one account for Outlook and another for a second Windows key. All this stuff is either ridiculously expensive or just has no utility. Why would I recommend my friends go through this (forced) horrible account system that adds a bunch of numbers to your name when we could play something like TF2 or CS:GO where you can freely pick and change your name?This was done under Microsoft, so one thing I'm concerned about is - why is it free compared to the early (expensive) Halo era? Ontop of the expense of their console, they used to charge a lot for the internet service (Xbox Live subscription every year), and you already had to pay for the games. Why would they suddenly make it free? If they really cared about offering value to the users, why would they still charge to change your name (that they added a bunch of numbers to?) All they did by making it free was remove the paywall against banned cheaters.Which instalment are we even on now? Halo 5? Halo 9? Perhaps they called it  because they intend to milk brand loyalty infinitely. If they weren't going to tie it up as a trilogy, they really needed to justify making more games. I didn't feel an ounce of science-fiction. I can't help but compare it to the originals because it used the Halo brand, but it sorely lacks the quality. If you can afford a PC good enough to run it well, you're probably better off just buying a better game. It's another 50 GB shooter where you have to sort out all the little details like mouse sensitivity and bindings and whether the bindings are toggle or hold, just to find that the experience is dry. It's free, but is it worth your time?

_childDocuments_.review: Halo Infinite’s gameplay loop and sandbox is an outstanding achievement in FPS gaming. The king of console shooters has now, finally, claimed a worthy throne on the PC.What makes Infinite special is how fantastic it feels to play. The entire game has a rhythmic flow where each beat is an input by the player: whether you’re jumping, sprinting, sliding, shooting or grappling, it all feels like a choreographed dance with your opponent. Hitting each input at the exact precise time feels so natural, and it’s bolstered by its excellent performance and scalability on PC. I’ve played this on a laptop GTX 1650, and an RTX 3070, and both have managed to achieve at least 60fps on a variety of settings.The sandbox of Halo creates outstanding depth to the combat, perfectly encapsulating the phrase ‘easy to pick-up, difficult to master’. The grapplehook, for instance, begins as a means to reach high vantage points or escape situations as fast as possible. However, by the end of the campaign you’ll be swinging like Spiderman using momentum to slide through levels at breakneck speed. It requires precision and knowledge to know the exact distance the grapplehook can reach, it makes any terrain in the game explorable, and any combat situation escapable.The campaign took me around 28 hours to see and do absolutely everything, including wiping every Covenant structure off the face of Zeta Halo. Alongside this journey is your new AI campaign, curiously called simply ‘Weapon’ for almost the entirety of the game. She is, effectively, Cortana v2 and provides a light-hearted relief to the sobriety of Masterchief. However, rest assured, this is through genuinely witty and well-written dialogue rather than quips of tension breaking jokes.Multiplayer has earned Infinite a mixed reputation among the community. However, it’s important to note the vast majority of player impressions come from the first year of Infinite’s release. Let’s not beat around the bush, Halo Infinite’s multiplayer was severely lacking in content in 2021. It wasn’t strangely until 343 announced mass layoffs that the game started to feature regular content updates. Forge mode, while still technically still in beta (although should have been there on release), has given the community tools to create endless maps and gamemodes. There have also been new official maps, weapons, equipment and more added, as well as a new progression system.These inclusions really should have existed when Halo Infinite was first released, but better late than never. Theatre mode is, sadly, still not functional which is simply unacceptable given how long ago this game came out. For the most part, Halo Infinite is a 9.5/10 campaign with a multiplayer which, while starting very slow, has evolved into a very respectful and competitive PvP experience. The emphasis on movement and creativity reminds me of genre classics like Quake 3: Arena, while a high time to kill ensures that you’re never truly out in the cold if someone gets the drop on you.Halo Infinite is an absolutely outstanding game and one of the best FPS games I’ve had the pleasure to play. For me, it represents the peak of the series alongside Halo 3 and Reach, and has better core gameplay loop than both of them. The price is a bit steep, but get this for £30 or under and you’ve got yourself an incredible game. Or, better yet, try out the multiplayer for free.

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion, The overall experience is by far one of the best in the franchise. Ive been with halo for 11 years now, so my opinion might not stick as well as people who have been here since Halo CE, but here we go regardless! :)The story is fantastic. and there is plenty of opportunities for more via DLC or whatever. and its also the longest a halo games story has been, for me my first run of the game was on heroic on release day, and i complete it just over 12 hours later. in my opinion its probably one of the best, easy top 5 and maybe even top 3 for me. there is never a dull moment in the story missions, it kept me hooked and on the edge of my seat. i finished it and immediately started a Legendary run afterwards.The multiplayer is so much fun, like the good old days of halo 3 and reach back in their prime. Sure its a bit buggy, and there isnt a whole lot of maps right now at 8 or 9 i think? but they are already working on more, and when it released it only had 4 playlists you could queue into, now its at 8 so thats nice. The overall feel of multiplayer is very solid and a lot of fun, and i would gladly take more. each weapon in the sandbox feels unique, with some old ones like the plasma pistol changing a bit, or how atleast in multiplayer the ravager is not the best weapon, but hey, if i can get kills with it, i aint complaining. Each vehicle feels solid to use, now admittedly the driving feels a bit weird or off from older halos', its not bad its just new, like they feel a little too responsive or they feel glued to the ground 1 minute, then never touch the ground the second. i find it fun personally having to learn how they operate now, its a bit of a learning curve instead of just knowing exactly how it operates like it used to, but maybe thats just meThe Visuals are very good, they might not be as high tier as some other games coming out this year, but i am just blown away with how good Zeta Halo looks, and multiplayer too, the lighting and overall look and feel of everything is very good in my opinion, and the art style encapsulates the best of both worlds from Bungie's art style and 343's. like how the forerunner architecture looks like 343's with there more shiny and silvery colored metals and rooms, with that old warm lighting and classic designs from bungie's side. it really captures the true feel of awe and wonder from the older halo games, without alienating 343's designs from there games. and some explosions, like from grenades almost look like they are from a comic or cartoon, but idk that doesnt bother me really, though to some it does. i really dont notice it, like yea i notice the explosion but in the middle of a fight, who cares if the explosion doesnt look super real, id rather finish the fight (pardon the reference).The sound design is very nice as well. the massive deafening THUMP of the metal and mechanisms that power the Skewer as it fires, or the nice 3 tap BAM of the BR-75 and how audibly, it feels as if those shots are hitting hard and true. the sounds of the explosions, guns, equipment, and the environment around you, really helps compliment the great visuals, as you can very easily tell what sounds go to what, and what they meannow obviously it wouldnt be a modern game without quite a few bugs, but most (not all) aren't game breaking unlike most games releasing at this time alot of them are really funny, like the multiplayer intro screens and how sometimes you can find a character so far away from where they're supposed to be in the intro. or how the game has a bit of a latency issue in multiplayer, im fairly often killed though a wall on my screen, though on the other players screen im still out in the open, ive done the same to others, like "man i really just fired a BR, and all of those shots hit him but only after he was behind cover". the game is by no means perfect, but lets be honest, most games coming out these past few years have been filled with bugs, some are really funny, while others just makes it very hard to play or enjoy the game. and the monetization of the game is fairly heavy, like 20 dollars for a pack of armor from halo reach, and sure it comes with a bit more than that, but still that's a bit high seeing as how it was free back in the day, but there are some fun ones in there, like the new cat ear attachment that can go on any helmet, its 10 dollars but you get a different armor coating and a weapon charm with it. the battlepass is pretty alright, and its quite alot easier to obtain XP for it now than at launch, but i think it could still use a bit of fine tuning.all in all, if you are an older player a but hesitant to get back into the franchise, i could not recommend this game more, and to newer players as well i urge you to try it out, after all the multiplayer is free, so come join us! i'd be happy to help any new or returning spartan find their way through the game!All things considered and me being both biased and not, id give this game a 9.7 out of 10, thanks for taking the time to read this, and I hope I helped you make a decision on weather you wanted the game or not.Have a Great Day and Good luck, and I'll see you out there Spartan's!!

_childDocuments_.review: This a review for the $60 campaign, not the multiplayer.SHORT VERSION is this: Infinite isn't terrible, but is mostly filler and isn't worth the $60 price tag. It's a 6/10 at best and lacks the energy and variety that many previous Halo titles bring to the table.It's hard to believe this game was in development for ~6 years. With the exception of vehicles (more on this later) the core mechanics of movement, gunplay, scavenging are all top knotch. The moment-to-moment gameplay is very fun, which means the game must be good, right? Sadly, the 'grand design' lacks any depth. The first 3 or so hours actually play well, and i had high hopes for the rest of the game. Unfortunately, in those 3 hours you will have seen 90% of what Infinite has to offer. Once it opens up to a more 'open world' experience, it becomes very apparent that this template does not work in the halo universe, at least as it's executed here. At its best, past Halo campaigns are a series of well-designed, hand crafted missions that take place in a wide variety of different locales, and introduce new weapons, characters, enemies, and vehicles, while the story unfolds and you learn more about the world's lore.Infinite may have the largest world yet, but the vast majority of it is empty space peppered with copy-paste enemy outposts, or recycled forerunner rooms. Not just rooms are recycled, but it seems as though, to pad its runtime, entire chains of rooms are recycled, as much as 3 or 4 times. Enemies share the same fate. There are a few different types of brute enemies, as you'd expect, but these fill predictable rolls and don't especially feel unique to the Halo universe. There is really only one new enemy in this halo game that doesn't feel like a minor addition, a sort of flying monkey that is only slightly more threatening than a grunt.Vehicles would seem like an obvious place to innovate and make welcome new additions, right? Especially considering the size and space of the new ring and the emphasis on exploration? Well, apparently not, because there is not a single meaningful addition to Halo's vehicle roster. Even the Wasp, which appears in the multiplayer, WHICH CAN FLY is no where to be found in the campaign. In fact, the brute chopper and mongoose are the only vehicles that are not found in the original Halo 1 campaign from TWENTY YEARS AGO. No, i'm not counting the Razorback. And, bizarrely enough, traversal in a vehicle is barely missed in this game, as the vehicle physics lack the weight of previous games and the winding roads and enormous amounts of geometric detail make navigating the game's many cliffs a chore, where it's even possible. The obvious solution to me is to have incorporated a new vehicle that could climb mountains just as the player can, but such creativity is nowhere to be found. Exploration is NOT worth the effort anyways, since the game has nothing to reward you with. In Halo, a weapon is typically a reward for killing an enemy, but Infinite seems to think a single weapon can be a reasonable reward for completing an entire sidequest. This might be true, if the ammo limits of weapons were much higher, and you could hold more than two weapons, or if it was actually a new weapon (no, a red energy sword is not "new"). The open world and linear campaign paradigms simply do not gel here at all. So... ...how is the story? Well, unless you've REALLY done your homework, a lot of it won't make sense, but that's less of a fault towards infinite and more of a strike against the bloated Halo canon. The story isn't altogether terrible, but the way it's told is: the vast, vast majority of the 'story' in this game unfolds with the Chief and (not)Cortana standing in an empty room, talking. An absolutely insane amount of repetitious dialogue makes one thing clear: even the writers were having a hard time coming up with more things for the characters to say. I must note that, on the whole, the voice acting is as great as you would expect from a Halo game. However, the story takes place in a single location yet can't help attempting to be a grand space opera at the same time. The plot is full of contrivances and, without spoiling anything, towards the end even (not)Cortana stops caring about you, or the objectives. Aside from the chief and his A.I., the characters are fairly one-dimensional and not really worth a mention. Like the rest of the game, the story could've been great, but really just... wasn't.What about the weapons and equipment, though? Well, I've saved this for last because I wanted to end on a positive note. Without a doubt, this is an amazing arsenal and doesn't really get old, even after hours and hours of repetitive enemies and level designs. This really demonstrates all the good that can come out of adding to the Halo sandbox. New guns and ammo types abound, and the Grapple Shot is so undeniably fun that I almost want to recommend the game for it alone. But it just doesn't justify the 60$ entry fee when everything above is considered. The visuals are also generally quite good. Not much to say on its looks, it's attractive and definitely 'Halo' but not doesn't break the mold.I've beaten every Halo game on Legendary (save for the two Halo Wars titles), and the series has always been dear to me. I really wanted to love this game, but was mostly disappointed. There's good stuff here and there but it's so sparsely distributed that the moment-to-moment gunplay can't save this game for me.Undoubtedly, more will be added/changed to the campaign over time, but in its current state, it's a thumbs down from me.

_childDocuments_.review: 343 returns to it's award winning franchise ways with this latest release in the Halo series. Halo Infinite provides nostalgic feelings reminiscent of it's predecessor's while incorporating new additions to keep it fresh. The campaign is different from your traditional Halo game but the story is still as rich as ever and equally enjoyable to explore.
