_childDocuments_.review: The Intro: Another new JRPG inspired by the classics, namely Chrono Trigger and Super Mario RPG. Nothing that there's anything wrong with that! Tis my favorite game genre, and this game has been on my radar and tickling my fancy since I saw the first preview!The Good: Everything you like and expect is done very, very well. Beautiful graphics, flowing music, and a very clever twist added to the traditional JRPG combat system. It demands you to think about your actions carefully, lest you be dealt a lot of damage and die (I could explain it, but there's a demo, so you can check it out for free and experience it for yourself!)The Bad: Like many new games in the classic JRPG style, the story starts nice, simple, and appealing. Naturally, it gets more convoluted the further you go, till you don't care about it. Still, you push on because the combat is great (like FF13, which I will always defend).Overall: 8/10.Outstanding graphics, sound, and gameplay.Damn good game, and definitely worth my time and money. Check it out if you want a good ol' JRPG. Just don't expect a coherent story.

_childDocuments_.review: The combat is bad ... let me rephrase that: The combat is amazing, for the first 30 minutes.After that it becomes a miserable chore to slog through battles due to the timing based QTEs that are embedded into each (and every) action. Thankfully, once you get to the Mole Village, you can buy some of the cheat items (relics) that will allow you to turn on auto execute of the base attack and give you a 40% chance to auto block. I am still giving this game a thumbs up and absolutely recommend that fans of OG JRPGs should buy this, but if these "Relics" didn't exist I would be saying "wait till it is $5, and then you will be getting a value of $1 per hour before you quit."The game presents these timing QTEs as a "bonus," but if you don't use them you will end up getting your ass kicked by basic mobs as pulling them off are mandatory to cancel opponent's special moves (some of which are one hit KO). And if this mechanic was restricted to only the special attacks or team combos, 100% it would be a cool mechanic. But since we are talking about needing to time a button presses on every attack (both when attacking and defending), with an activation window that lasts less than a second, it makes battles exhausting ... I LOVE TURN BASED BATTLE SYSTEMS so if you have me trying to avoid battles because they suck so bad: you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up on a fundamental level.That said, the Relics exist (come on: if you know that your system is so un-fun that you have to put bypasses into the item shop, change your system) and as soon as you get your hands on them, the game becomes a joy to play. The music is high quality, the environments and animations are "art," the story is compelling and well paced, crafting your healing items as food you cook at your camp is a better system than just buying potions (though I would like this to be more of a mini game & expanded to include equipment crafting), and over all I am having fun.P.S. I hate the Pirate crew ... those guys can drown at sea and the game would be better for it.

I love the graphical presentation, I love the skills, the Super Mario RPG timed button presses for more damage on your attacks and less damage taken on enemies attacks. The music is good, the story seems interesting.And then there is the combat.Combat is more akin to a  like  where enemies telegraph when they get their turn and what they are going to do as their attack are "locked" which allow you to reduce the damage of that attack or outright cancel it. This feels really fun and engaging but after a couple hours it starts to grate on me. It becomes a chore, tedium and annoying having to do this in Remember old JRPGs where you could run around a dungeon, just  most enemies, and only certain enemies that had more challenging attacks you had to actually pay closer attention? Then the boss came and that was a tactical dance, to out-heal and counter everything he/she threw at you.In Sea of Stars  and if you not try to cancel the attacks of enemies you will run out of MP to heal, heal items or simply die pretty quickly.Then at each level-up you get to choose some bonus, which doesn't seem to add up to anything. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR Review:This game is fantastic- music, artwork, animations, story, characters, combat, puzzles... it has a perfect mix of it all. You can play as easy or as hard as you want, the story is engaging and like great RPGs before it, it starts out innocent enough and then you're thrown into a huge world and world ending plots. This game feels like a triple A game and there is so much love put into it. I could compare it to all kinds of games but it's it's own thing but with a lot nods to previous titles. It's unfair to compare this game with others because it's unique! Easily one of my favorite games! Please at least check out the demo! It's one of those games that lingers in your head when you're not playing it :)Detailed Review:I will start off with the RPGs I grew up with, completed, and adored (in no specific order): Golden Sun, Magical Starsign, Mario & Luigi Superstar, Super Mario RPG, Chrono Trigger, Secret of Mana, Trials of Mana, Sword of Mana, Earthbound, Octopath Traveler, and Illusion of Gaia (I'm sure I'm missing some).Sea of Stars nails all my favorite things from each of these games. Timed hits and blocks, strategic turned based combat that IS NOT grindy, combos and ultimates, enjoyable and interesting characters, solid and super enjoyable storyline, beautiful artwork and animations, satisfying sound effects, eargasm music... There's so much I want to say but can't fully express how much I love this game! But I'll try:Eargasm music like I said- Catchy, toe tapping, somber, relaxing, chilling; so many variations. The Pirate band plays songs but if you interrupt one of them to talk to them, their instrument goes away in the song. They also play/animate ONLY when their instrument is in the track. Very clever and such a great detail to add. SNES songs of the future! There's a whole BTS of the music on their site.Combat can be easy or hard depending on settings. Combat is super satisfying and full of strategy and options. Battle timing is great and different for every move. As someone who hates grinding to level up and continue the story, this game does NOT do that. There are no random battles and the battles you do have are a moderate amount. You can even add some damage to an enemy before triggering the battle. There are settings for more of a light touch of combat (Storytelling) but also settings to make it very challenging (makes enemies stronger, removes certain weaknesses, etc)! Each character has different timing and a balanced set of skills to use. Plus the animations of their moves are so satisfying!Artwork- holy cow. Absolutely superb! Beautifully animated, day and night cycle is gorgeous. The color theory being used is above and beyond. Lighting effects, atmosphere, reflections, refraction, and sprite artwork used in the backgrounds are worthy of stopping and just drinking it in. Animations are snappy, charming, and fluid. There are 2D animated cutscenes throughout the game that really make the world and story feel more connected and solid and keep you invested. The boss enemies are also highly detailed and VERY monstrous!The story is pretty innocent at first but then evolves into a grand scheme that throws you for a loop a few times! Some might think the main characters are bland but honestly they're fighters. One is more relaxed than the other but they're a group of tight friends. Again feels like going back in time with the way stories were done in the SNES and GBA era of RPGs. Super enjoyable for me, I even cried and got shocked!How anyone could NOT think highly of this game... It made me laugh, tear up, get excited, shocked me, and I even got chills! I am in awe of this game. It feels like a AAA title! It is by far one of the most satisfying RPG gaming experiences I've had in a loooong time. I'm near the end of the game but just couldn't wait to express how much I loved this game!Please pick this game up or at least try the demo. It is absolutely going in my favorites pile!For Garl!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favourite RPGs I've ever played. It's going on my list of classics that I'm bound to return to every few years, right up there with Chrono Trigger and Mother 3.Without spoiling anything, I will say I thought the story was a great mix of familiar and unexpected, and the characters you meet are all wonderfully charming. Garl is hands-down my favourite, he's just the sweetest bundle of joy; the kind of person who instantly makes a room brighter just by being in it. Him, and the friendship between him and the rest of the main cast, are the beating heart and soul of the game in my opinion. Said main characters, Zale and Valere, aren't as deep or emotive as the rest of the cast but I think that's intentional to allow the player to project themselves onto them. Chained Echoes is an obvious point of comparison since that's the other big classic RPG throwback that came out this year, but in my opinion this game is better-paced and doesn't suffer from the same editing/translation issues. It's also a lot more of a straightforward story- so if you're coming from that game and expecting the same kind of political intrigue, you'll be disappointed. If you liked the SNES JRPG era, games like Chrono Trigger, though, you'll settle comfortably into this like a conversation with an old friend, and not just because there's a number of direct references to that game. The opening hour or two is a bit slow but things start to pick up soon. I really appreciate when a game like this knows how to keep things moving—compared to, say, Golden Sun, which didn't know when to shut up, this game rarely has a cutscene last more than a couple minutes unless it's something really important.Moving about the world is really fun and more involved than you might expect; you can climb and jump off ledges and get various other abilities that give you more movement options. The environments are all really gorgeous and detailed, and the dungeons each feel unique and have some fun but not too hard puzzley elements, and they're accompanied by one of the best soundtracks I've heard in awhile. There's a few songs in here that are gonna live in my head for a long time, much like the soundtracks to my favourite SNES games. There's even a traveling band that plays bardcore arrangements of various songs from the soundtrack, you can listen to while you relax at the game's various taverns and play this (pretty fun) side quest-minigame thing called Wheels.Combat is fun and quick and mostly focused on tactics rather than long-term character building or strategy- you don't get many options in terms of how to build your characters, you just get to pick one of four random (I think they're random) stats to boost every time they level. Most of the creativity comes from choosing which accessories to equip- each character has two slots for regular ones that do what you'd expect accessories to do in a game like this, but also one slot for a golden accessory that grants party-wide benefits. Characters learn about 3-4 skills each, plus a number of combo attacks that use multiple characters. Every attack you can do (or almost every attack), and every enemy attack, has timed hits associated with it where if you execute a button prompt correctly you can do additional damage or extra hits (kinda like Super Mario RPG on SNES if you ever played that one.) Every attack also has one or more elements associated with it, which is useful for hitting enemy weaknesses but even more useful for interacting with the game's "lock" system - when enemies are casting a spell they'll display several elements over their head, and if you hit them with the corresponding attacks you can make their spells weaker or even interrupt them entirely. So 3-4 skills per character doesn't sound ilke much, but between the timed hits and the lock system I still found battles varied and engaging and sometimes pretty tricky. The enemies are also all really well-animated and the bosses even look more tired as they start to get low on health, which felt so natural I didn't even clock it as a feature until a few hours into the game.It's not too long, not too short- I finished my first lplaythrough in 35 hours and I think I did almost everything- I'm still missing three achievements and two of them idk what they are so it's hard to say how much is left to do. But I appreciate that it's a game that knows when it's time to end. It also does a great job of making its world seem full of potential, and much bigger than what the game itself actually shows you—I read that it's connected with the studio's previous game, The Messenger, but I haven't played that yet (I just bought it after finishing this) so idk how close the ties are. What I do know, though, is that I can't wait to see whatever they do next, and that I hope at some point we'll get to return to another game in this style from them because this was an absolute treat.

_childDocuments_.review: I was one of the original backers for Sea of Stars, and I'm disappointed to admit that I did not particularly enjoy this game. For the most part, the graphics, music/sound, puzzles, fast travel, and UI all worked quite well. I won't go into details here because, unfortunately, I have so much to say about what *didn't work*.The story / characters / dialogue. I'm haunted by something that the creative director said in the Escapist documentary. He admitted that he was a bit concerned about how the world would receive the game's script, because that's the only thing that had yet to be extensively shown off (prior to release). The dialogue and character development, IMO, are by far the weakest parts of the game. I noticed early on that Valare and Zale were indistinguishable in their spoken lines. If not for contextual clues about their respective Solstice Warrior classes, you could probably swap the dialogue without even realizing that anything had changed. They speak as if from the same empty soul. How is it possible that we got more character development from Brugaves and Erlina than our two main protagonists? The game seemed to go out of its way, through flashbacks and other subtle hints, to show us what motivated the elder Solstice Warriors' inexplicable actions at the end of the first Act. When judged against other games, Brugaves and Erlina are *also* quite underdeveloped and only seem to have some complexity when contrasted with their younger counterparts, which might as well be silent. (I do want to be clear that the character portrait artist did a solid job of illustrating the characters expressing various emotions. Indeed, I may have felt more from those static illustrations than the entire corpus of protagonist dialogue.) My guess is that the core problem wasn't just the dialogue, but rather the intricate relationship between the characters' dialogue and how they characters develop (or, actually, don't) within the story. So in order to fix the deficiencies in the dialogue, Sabotage would have needed to give us a more compelling story. (It's possible that the overarching plot was written first and set into stone, with character development and dialogue being an afterthought.) There were only two main characters that I felt any real connection to: .  but for all of his  was unable to carry the entire weight of the game's narrative shortcomings. And  came to life in ways that I didn't expect and that had me smiling/laughing in just about every scene that he had dialogue. He felt like a  which I loved and wished I could have seen more of. Finally, I won't spend much time on the style of dialogue -- what someone else referred to as "modern internet casual" -- or the sub-par grammar, but there were serious problems with each of these, which prevented me from staying immersed in the game. I could probably write many more pages on this sub-topic, but the bottom line is that the story, character development, and dialogue were not just a missed opportunity, but an anchor that weighs down a game that would otherwise shine just by the magnitude of its other noteworthy strengths. Grade: 2/10.Combat system. If I had to summarize my thoughts on the battles, it would be this: Sabotage seems to have taken everything that they liked about combat systems from various other games and combined them into a hybrid system for SoS, but then seemingly forgot to stop and ask if the hybrid actually *worked well*. IMO, it functioned, but did *not* work well. There was too much emphasis placed on timed hits and blocks. The game reassures the player early on that timing should be thought of as icing on the cake, not the cake itself, but you eventually get to boss fights and even some regular enemies that are either difficult or downright annoying without bringing your timed A-game. I also found it bothersome that enemies would chase after you if you got too close. If the goal was to make grinding unnecessary while also making enemies semi-skippable, the developers didn't outright succeed at either goal. The regular field battles also take too long. This is in part because the developers chose to animate every enemy attack, which of course chews up a *lot* of time, and when you have to fight dozens or hundreds of enemies, that time doesn't feel like time well spent. But it's not just about the enemy animations; the playable character attack animations also consume quite a bit of time. This was clearly a conscious design decision by the developers, but I wonder if they made it with the awareness of how it would impact the overall player experience, battle after battle. Grade: 4/10.Leveling / equipment. Leveling by group instead of individually was an interesting choice that definitely simplified thinking about levels, but it also took some of the fun out of managing the party. And I never felt like the equipment made a big difference in my ability to knock out more baddies. It was as if the developers tuned the game in order to make timing hits and blocks more important than your equipment, which makes the game feel less like an RPG and more like a slow-paced action or street-fighting game. I liked being able to customize my players with my choice of bonus stat increases during level-ups, but because there wasn't an easy way of viewing my characters' base stats in between level increases, it was difficult for me to plan out those bonus stat allocations. This makes me feel like the bonus stat allocations were *intended* to be inconsequential. And if there's anything that makes a player feel down about the game they are playing, it's the game giving them a choice but then ultimately treating it as near-meaningless. Grade: 3/10.Side quests / ending. I didn't care much for how the "true" ending required so many side quest errands to be completed. There were multiple times when I almost threw in the towel to instead watch the rest of the game on YouTube. I was also disappointed to learn that the secret dev room was locked behind various optional completionist quests (for which I *did* resort to YouTube). Most of those quests did not strike me as fun; they struck me as actual work that I would only do if someone was paying me to do them. (That's how laborious it felt.) As for the ending itself, , but I appreciate Thierry taking the time to try to explain some important aspects of it on the Sabotage Discord server. My hope is that  will be revisited in future games, so I'm willing to give the studio a pass on that particular narrative element. Still, the fact that  side quests were required in order to get access to valuable content makes them feel like they were never actually side quests to begin with -- they were just disconnected parts of the main quest disguised as side quests. Grade: 3.5/10.This game was clearly made with love and good intention. But too many design decisions were seemingly made in isolation without regard for how each choice would contribute to the whole. I've never before played a game with such a wide gulf between its most polished and disappointing elements. I cannot recommend this game because a recommendation implies *some* degree of enthusiasm or confidence, and even the parts of SoS that I adore are overshadowed by how far short other parts of it fell. I hope the developers take this feedback to heart and consider ways that they can improve their future productions.

_childDocuments_.review: Sea of Stars is a relatively short, straightforward story with charming characters, upbeat music, and fluid gameplay. The devs were also generous enough to give you multiple options to customize the difficulty. I've not played The Messenger (yet), but I don't feel like I missed any large story events / connections, if there were any.I think my biggest gripe on the game is our main three characters. Valere and Zale hardly develop from the start to the end of the story, while Garl has his hit-or-miss moments. It's almost as if the Devs couldn't decide between choosing a male or female protagonist, so they offered both choices, then had them stand behind the true protagonist, Garl, who actively moves the plot forward.That's not to say the three are particularly badly written, but I found the rest of the party (and non-playable characters like Brugaves and Erlina) to be far more interesting, and I wish we could've seen more of them. Still, the main three do still have their charm, culminating in a particularly sweet true ending that feels very much deserved.I'm not exactly sold enough to play a New Game+, but if there is a sequel / expansion to the story, I'd likely still play it-- if only because it feels like the devs have more story to tell for this world.Overall, Sea of Stars is definitely worth playing if you're a (J)RPG fan. If you enjoyed Chained Echoes, then you'll definitely enjoy this one as well.

_childDocuments_.review: is a turn-based RPG inspired by classic JRPGs, and developed by Sabotage Studio. Taking place in a vibrant, beautifully pixelated world, you follow Valere and Zale—two teens with way too much responsibility for their age—on a journey to prevent an ancient evil from returning. You know, the usual “save the world” stuff, except with beautiful islands and a lot of star magic. With satisfying, tactical combat and a heartfelt story, the game feels like a love letter to the RPGs of the SNES era, while introducing fresh, modern mechanics. Rating: ★★★★☆Featuring a mix of strategic turn-based combat and simple puzzle-solving exploration, the gameplay in  is refreshing with every battle or puzzle feeling unique. Additionally, exploration is rewarding with many hidden treasures scattered throughout the game’s various islands. However, combat starts to feel repetitive towards the later stages of the game as new mechanics taper off and battles stretch longer. I also found myself using the same set of overpowered skills and combos despite the variety available. Nevertheless,  offers a simple and seamless gameplay experience as I’ve encountered minimal bugs throughout its entirety.Rating: ★★★★★The game’s pixel art is so visually stunning that your eyeballs will thank you. Every environment is brimming with so much detail that you’ll want to dive into the screen and live there—except for the not-so-pleasant areas where there are creepy monsters chasing you. The day-night cycle adds another layer of visual depth, making each island, cave, temple, and starry sky feel alive.Rating: ★★★★★Then there’s the soundtrack, which is equally breathtaking. Depending on the vibe of the moment, the music makes you want to either fight monsters or nap peacefully by a virtual campfire. Each area has its own musical theme that further enhances the atmosphere while the combat music perfectly captures the urgency and tension of the battle.Rating: ★★★☆☆ weaves a classic but compelling tale about destiny, friendship, and sacrifice. While the story feels predictable even with its few plot twists, its characters give the game heart. Among its diverse supporting cast is everyone’s favourite “Warrior Cook”, a mysterious assassin who can travel through portals, and many other quirky characters that help balance lighthearted moments with some emotional ones that will get to you—even if you swore you wouldn’t cry during an RPG again. Unfortunately, where this game falls short is with its two main protagonists, who sometimes appear to have indistinguishable personalities and lack the character depth that they deserve.Rating: ★★☆☆☆Once you’ve saved the world, you can go back and… save it again? With the main story spanning roughly 25 to 35 hours,  offers a decent amount of side quests, hidden treasures, and some optional but challenging bosses later in the game for those seeking the “true ending”. However, the game is a largely linear experience, making it not something most players would want to replay immediately. Nevertheless, if you’re a completionist like myself, it’ll keep you busy for another 5 to 10 hours. Additionally, when considering both the full price and playtime of , I personally believe it’s only worth it when the game goes on sale—although my opinion might change depending on how its upcoming free DLC goes. is like that one summer vacation you’ll never forget—beautiful, a little emotional, and full of surprises. While its narrative and replayability could be improved, its overall gameplay and presentation more than make up for it, earning  a thumbs up from me. If you’re seeking a modern turn-based RPG with heart, or want to feel like a hero while sitting comfortably on your couch, this game’s for you. Plus, there’s pirates – what more do you need?

If I'm to be honest some of the combat was a bit repetitive and some of the animations such as Serai's ultimate didn't need to be as long as they were, just show the ship and the canons firing, no need for the pirates to come out and pose. _childDocuments_.review: I don't normally taker time to write reviews for games on steam, but i felt this game warranted it. Overall, this game is one of my favorites i have played in quite awhile, but with few caveats. first off, let me say that i played their previous game the messenger and absolutely loved it. i can tell a lot of effort was put into that game in a lot of ways. the music, the game play, the story. all fantastic. sea of stars exhibits most of these same traits. the music is absolutely amazing, the battle system although not super complicated, felt rewarding and concise. another strong point is the art. the gorgeous pixel art, the over world design, especially the lighting in this game, all great. unfortunately i didn't feel the same way about the story in this game. i liked the story almost all the way up until the very end. its not the most groundbreaking story to be fair, but it was well done and a classic jrpg setting and pacing. the end is what i have qualms with. no matter which ending you get, it doesn't feel like anything was really resolved. it felt rushed and without actual closure. there are so many story points they introduced and just didn't mention ever again. overall i really like this game, but i cant give it a 10/10 solely for the lack of real ending in my opinion. i give this game a 7/10. I overall really enjoyed my time spent playing this game and i love a lot of what this game tries to be. i just wish they fleshed out the ending more.

_childDocuments_.review: - AMAZING sprites. If you love sprite-based RPGs, this is a real treat for the eyes for both retro and modern gamers. The art direction is that great!- Good sound effects/music.- Easy mechanics to understand.- Most puzzles and challenges are fair.- Gives you nostalgia for the simpler RPG times.- The story is fairly average for an RPG. Not bad. Not great. I'll give the story some credit for trying to add some twists and turns, but it also doesn't help that the two main leads have the personality of rocks. - Dialogue lacked some polish and punch. Seriously, when you got one of your characters calling the big bad guy a loser, of all things, that's quite laughable. - Repetitive battles! This is normal for turn-based RPGs at times, but this game lacks a lot of variety. Legit, you will be doing the same tactics again and again until the very final bosses of the game. Sure, some boss fights try to spice things up, but you are still going to repeat your main moves no matter what.- Some of the things you have to collect in this game are tedious and annoying to gather. Gosh, some of the side quests were just plain unpleasant to complete. - You get your fast-travel option QUITE late into the game.Overall, this is a pretty game that is a real treat for the eyes if you love sprite-based RPGs. This game is far from perfect, but I think treating this game as a flawed, retro-inspired experience is the ticket.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the first thing you can hear about Sea of Stars is 'a love letter' to the old classic JRPGs, this game is so much more. It rides on nostalgia so well that this game should already be considered a modern JRPG classic (despite being made in Canada). It brings you some slightly more advanced mechanics to the already worn genre - back in the days this would be called a masterpiece. For those who were growing up along PSX/NES/GBA games in the 90's it still will be. Luckily the game follows the old canon of turn-based fights, stepping away from mindless ARPG structure that you can find in nearly every game now. Battles are quick, fun and easy to learn but hard to master, thanks to the lock system. Music is great, graphics are amazing, especially seeing all those sprites in motion. The story is light but good enough to follow.  There are some little bits that could be done better, like sometimes characters would not jump to the next ledge unless you position yourself in a specific angle, but apart from that I see no real flaws. I really DO hope Sabotage Studio will focus on this direction with their games, by doing simply more games like Sea of Stars.  For me, this is my GOTY for 2023. Don't listen to people complains like 'there is no real map', 'this is hard' or 'there is too much backtracking' - that is the new gen of kids that knows nothing, would die without GPS on their mobiles and say that mayonnaise is spicy.

They're not bad, just a bit boring.It has a lot of persionality otherwise, everything in the world feels alive, you know and tought every corner of the game, personally.It is one of the best adventures I've played and I love this game. If you are a classic rpgs lover, you will enjoy this. As a game overall it is great.If I felt a strong theme, maybe? _childDocuments_.review: I discovered this game through an ad on μTorrent. I went in completely blind and expected a pleasant little 90s-jrpg-inspired indie romp with a fairly short campaign and all the typical limitations of similar indie titles. What I got was leagues above that. The sheer amount of polished, well thought out content in this game is astounding. There are a myriad of fun and unique gameplay mechanics, absolutely gorgeous artwork and fluid sprite animations, an awesome and diverse ost, and surprisingly deep and interesting lore. I highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of Chrono Trigger or the Mario rpg games, and even to those who maybe aren't the biggest fan of jrpgs but want to try something new. There are a ton of great ways that Sea of Stars "modernizes" some of the staples of older rpgs in a way that makes it a more accessible experience for casual gamers while still staying true to its roots.Also Garl MVP

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game but it turned out to be very disappointing. The three main characters are boring and one-note, the dialogue is amateurish, and the plot takes too long to get going and is terribly paced. The bosses are fun but the combat overall is undercooked and repetitive due to no real party progression or customisation. The presentation is gorgeous and the soundtrack is mostly excellent but the world isn't interesting to explore outside of that. The progression is too linear, the puzzles exist, and there is close to no decision making required when navigating the world. A lot of the games later abilities needed to be available sooner to flesh out cool interactions between everything. You're mostly just holding forward through areas until you reach a battle to fight enemies with the same skills and strategy from start to finish. The cool moments in the game are undercut by the weak dialogue which makes it hard to get invested in the world you're trying to save. Sea of Stars had a lot of potential to be great but it focuses too much on trying to be streamlined and accessible. This focus results in a bland game without much substance. Sea of Stars needed to hire a writer and editor, cut out the filler, and expand on the systems that worked. It seems like it would be good for those new to JRPGs, because everything here has been done better before.

_childDocuments_.review: Good, light-hearted fun. Really, really refreshing to see this kind of game receive such a level of polish. Frankly gorgeous landscape, and really easily likeable characters, and a TON of extremely thoughtful finishing touches which I'm not used to seeing in modern titles. The introduction is a tad fast-paced, although it is obviously meant to serve as a tutorial, and not as a substantial portion of the game or story, and there's just 1 too many fourth-wall breaks. Do not let the slightly confounding introductory sequence deter you however, these shortcomings are (seemingly) intentional contrivances used to set up certain narrative structures to aid in telling the story in a more succinct and digestible manner.Words do not do justice to the sheer level of quality this game presents, and there is not a single accolade glowing enough to express the joy that this game has brought me. Cannot recommend this game enough - it's going right up alongside the Ori games, Hollow Knight and OneShot as my favourite games of all time.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll list the bad stuff first, because that list is much shorter.Bad:Dialogue portraits and cutscenes could have used a bit more polish.  Compared to many other aspects of the game, these two seem to lack the same quality.  It's a bit jarring given how beautiful the rest of the game is.Music is repetitive.  Tends to repeat and become stagnant.  Could have used more tracks.Stuttering/skipping frames commonly.  Doesn't happen on the overworld or in battles, just in roaming gameplay.  It could be my computer, but I find that hard to believe given other more intensive games run flawlessly.Puzzles are rather easy.  This could be an intentional design choice, but compared to the combat, the puzzles are incredibly simple.  This is not a knock on their game design, just a personal gripe (grain of salt).Timed button presses for a few attacks/moves are not well telegraphed.  They include an item that is supposed to help with this; it only shows if you HIT the timing, which only seems to solve a problem that, by that point, no longer exists.Good:Spritework is beautiful.Undoubtedly the best interactive turn based combat I've experienced.Characters are interesting and have some depth.The story is interesting and keeps you invested.World design is beautiful and varied.Large amount of content.Boss designs are phenomenal.TL;DR Conclusion:9/10Easily one of the best JRPG's I've played.  I cannot stress enough how this might be one of the best games I own.  See above reasons.  However, the minor inconveniences and little details keep it from being a 10/10 in my book.  If you are looking to buy this game:  If you like Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy 1-10, or Golden Sun, I can all but guarantee you will like this.  Buy it.  IF, however, those are not your style, I'd still recommend getting it on sale.  I don't think you will be disappointed. Recommendations to devs for future consideration:-Increase quality of portraits and cutscenes, (really just the portraits will do).  The artstyle is wonderful, but the cutscenes are choppy, and the portraits tend be a bit lopsided and derpy.-Increase amount of tracks, or have variations of the same tracks (same melody, different pitch/instruments, etc.) and spread them out.  Having a few different battle themes would be nice, just to spice up encounters.-Maybe rework the artifact that helps with button timing.  I had to look up how to do a few of the timed presses, because I had no idea when in the animation it expected me to press the button.  Mending light comes to mind.  Could have it blink your character red if too early, or blue if too late.  Then it's a game of hot and cold until you find the timing.

_childDocuments_.review: Sea of Stars takes place in what’s just called “The World”. Within the world you play as the two solstice warriors Zale and Valere who have the power of Eclipse Magic. This magic allows them to fight back the major forces of evil called Dwellers. Dwellers are the minions of the Fleshmancer, an alchemist who has achieved pseudo-godhood. Through the power of Eclipse magic the Solstice Warriors fend off the Fleshmancer’s minions in an attempt to keep balance within the world. This is supposed to be the way it all works. Within the history of the World, the Solstice Warriors are on their backfoot. If they cannot fight back the Dwellers, they transform into a World Eater (self-explanatory). Zale and Valere are a rare case within the world where the Great Eagle has delivered Solstice Warriors twice in a row. Through rigorous training and mentorship, they are prepped to fight off the last surviving Dweller until the unexpected happens. The overall writing and script in Sea of Stars can come off a bit cliché. Although, once it traps you in that thought it breaks free with twist that sometimes I didn’t see coming. This was a strength in Sea of Stars, its’ implementations of successful twists that compel you to want to keep playing. Even though some of the characters didn’t hit for me, what did hit was the in-game historian Teaks. Throughout your journey you find artifacts and trinkets that give you insight into the world. Is this type of mechanic new? No, but in a vibrant setting it continued to make it convincing to continue giving it my time. The history gives you an idea of the grand scheme of all that’s happening around you. It works well as a supplement to the characters you meet and the places that you go. Sabotage does a good job of making Sea of Stars feel tough all the way through. Not once did I feel invincible like you do in some RPGs. What you lack in raw power is made up in one of their gameplay gimmick called locks. When battles start, your enemies have timers. Every so often above these timers are locks which are in the form of various damage types your party is able to cast or deal. The goal is to ‘break’ these locks to prolong your turn (if you break all the locks) or lessen the damage of the next incoming attack of that enemy.  Once you’ve grasped the idea of how this works, it’s pushed to the next level in boss fights. The intricate lock combinations presented by bosses forces you to think about your line up and forces you to utilize all team members. Luckily in Sea of Stars once you push past the initial three-party members, you’re able to swap them within battle without using a turn. This adds some aid to the player when breaking locks. One of the systems Sabotage studios took inspiration from within combat is the use of team-up attacks. The team up attacks can be used once a meter is built up by attacking, or further increased by successful timed attacks to do more damage and timed blocks to prevent a percentage of damage. Once initiated these team up attacks can have added effects on to the massive damage they do. They can even hasten lock breaking. There are toggleable gameplay options as well that can enhance your experience (in the form of aid or restrictions if you desire more of a challenge) called relics. Overall Sea of Stars does enough to make you think about all your battle decisions which in turn keeps you engaged as a player.   Sea of Stars starts off linear, driving you from point to point. You will never get lost on finding your objective and that’s good. This game gives you some freedom eventually, but its main goal is to push you through their story. Along the way there are some minigames that allow you to take your mind off the growing threat and side missions that help give you useful, but not game breaking, items. While that’s all well, the main driving factor in this game is the main quest to save the world. Everything else is just icing but doesn’t do much in developing places and people outside your party. Off the top of my head the only side missions worth meaning were two of the end game side missions. That isn’t a knock though! Sabotage studios achieve their goal in keeping all the important bits in the main quest while also feeding the player any world building and info through the collection of artifacts with story by Teaks. Sabotage studios leans into a beautiful vibrant 16-bit art style to show off their product. Maps and areas do a beautiful job of telling background stories. Whether it’s the magical town Mooncradle where our story begins or the cursed town of Lucent where the Solstice Warriors are tasked with facing their first Dweller. Sabotage further leans into the retro style by having a well composed soundtrack that harkens back the days of old-school SNES RPGs. These tracks enrich the mood of the places your party visit.

_childDocuments_.review: BLUF: It wants to be a hybrid or, at least a chimera but instead it's a Frankenstein's monster. Pieces and ideas from older games are just sewn together with no connecting tissue of understanding why or how those things worked originally between them. And apart from this generous borrowing the game has little to no essence of its own.Sea of Stars might be a good fit as a baby's first JRPG but for me it tastes like stale and fermented memberberry juice.The graphics and music are okay. Many praise them but, really, it's 2024, I kind of expect the presentation to not be complete garbage.The story is not what I would expect or even want. Defeat a big bad while doing all kinds of "teehee, so random and quirky" side stuff is bad writing and the game doesn't really raise above the bare minimum. It's essentially driven by one secondary character who is a complete Gary Stu and succeeds at most of the things because he's cool and positive while failing the rest of the things because he's also stupid and careless, but that's okay, since the protagonists will immediately drop everything and go to rescue him because they're ! And that character is also the one making all the decisions and doing all the talking, while the player can only look helplessly and never get a chance to feel like they themselves had any impact beyond clearing the way for Gary Stu to solve problems with the Power of Positive Thinking.Other side characters typically stick to one shtick and repeat it in every interaction. Like a character that often breaks the 4th wall and openly mocks JRPG tropes while the game dutifully sticks to those tropes.But a game is not just story, there is also gameplay... And gameplay is dull. The puzzles are "just use every usable object in the order they are presented and things will happen" and the combat stops developing after the first couple of hours - no new moves, no weapons with new functionality (they even look the same!), no new mechanics. all the dungeons are wheels with spokes where you enter a hub zone and then visit 3-6 doors around the hub, each leading to a corridor at the end of which you get a piece of the key, then combine the pieces to enter the final door.The one thing that killed the game for me is the approach to combat difficulty. Most of the combat is based on timed button presses and those do not serve any purpose other than making it quicker. There is little to no turn management - you can choose the character to act or substitute a character in the party and you can, occasionally, delay the enemy's turn by performing the timed button presses well, but there is no speed, no debuffs, no turn manipulation on the party's side - nothing.All animations are overly long and the right time to press the button is often not shown at all, so finding out the timings is guesswork. Combined with the fact that several really strong moves just fizzle out if you guess the timing 2-5 times in a row rather than 20+ times in a row, this turns even the most basic fights against basic field enemies into complete slogs where you're watching long (really long!) animations and using the same 1-2-3 attack patterns to spend and recover MP with no variety. There are also relics that can make combat harder or easier, but they're rather basic and the ones supposed to make combat easier all act on the side of defence and survival - more HP, less damage taken, heal after each battle... But there are no relics that would make my party do +100% damage or skip/auto-win combat, so it would go by faster. I levelled my characters up (which is also plain as hell), I got good gear, I found secret techniques, I want enemies to die quickly because 	I am so cool and powerful! "No!", says the game, "the most I can do is let you ignore the button timings if you really want to, but you will still spend minutes fighting each and every garbage slime or diseased boar".This is not a skill issue, it's a deja vu issue. I've seen all of this in other games, done much better and in this very game in every combat encounter for the last 10 hours. I could do the opposite and turn on all the difficulty increasing relics, but I just don't have the time or the desire to prolong the formulaic combat to 2-3x length and also fiddle with cooking and constant trips to a campfire.I can't really praise a coherent story, a good set of characters or an enjoyable combat/exploration loop, so my advice here would be to cross this sea by plane or, preferably, a teleport, rather than by boat.

_childDocuments_.review: A must-have. Best Indie Title this year. Update (20 hours in): If you want to see people who are incredibly out of touch, read the negative reviews of this game. It is so rare for a game to come out of the woodwork that is so objectively great that those who are criticizing it have almost certainly been dropped on their head as a child. I believe the developers looked at every wonderful JRPG from the 80's and 90's and said, how can we incorporate all the best things about all of these games into one game? And yet, despite the world being full of things to do, it doesn't feel like they half-assed any of it. They gave every component of this game the FULL ASS. So, why is it good? Let's get into it. (Original review after 3 hours of gameplay) I have been hyped for this game for two years and it is living up to that hype. These developers understand what we liked about old school RPG's and also understand what didn't age well from those RPG's. I don't think a lot of folks have the patience for ATB systems and pure turn-based combat so they've added a lot of mechanics to keep you engaged and present during combat. Admittedly I am writing this review early, after only three hours of gameplay, but those three hours have been amazing. It is clear this game was made with passion! The pixel art is so dope. The story has me hooked. I have only gone through a couple of dungeons at this point but I love the level design! It feels like exploring without feeling overwhelming. And to top it all off, hats off and Chef's kiss to my OG RPG favorite game composer of all time Yasunori Mitsuda. That alone is reason enough to buy. I am definitely picking up a physical copy from Iam8bit when they are released.

_childDocuments_.review: Sea of Stars tells a beautiful story of personal development, in the form of an RPG, with mechanics that are a mix of Final Fantasy, and Legend of Dragoon, with the ability to time attacks, defence, and abilities for bonuses and extra affects, amongst a couple of extra mechanics to flesh out gameplay, which I shall not spoil.There are some reviews that are upset about the loose ends at the end of the story, but those loose ends are the point. This is a story about life, first and foremost, in a high fantasy setting, *life is like that*, and there is some hidden stuff at the very end of the game that you can spend just a few extra minutes to actually take the time to listen to, which says as much.To be quite frank with you, I hate games that take all of my interpretive agency away from me. They're fun stories, but they're not great stories. Great stories are both fun, and leave you with something to think about at the end. They stick with you and let you ruminate about the deeper meaning behind the whole story, the reasons reasons certain design elements exist, certain decisions were made with the story, why the characters act the ways they did, until you finally figure it all out, and the lessons the story actually taught you ring clear. You don't grow as a person if you're not given the room to think for yourself, and that was most certainly the teams aim here.I applaud the whole development team, for not only making a fun game that had me hooked from start to finish, but for being brave enough to tell the story they set out to tell, without sugar coating the ending - the ending is almost perfect. I hope, with all my heart, that they are willing to lean into their emotions more next time, if they ever decide to produce another game. To have the courage to make a Magnum Opus, instead of a Swan Song. 9 out of 10!, I would change nothing about this story, except to lean a little heavier into the subtext, and each character's emotional drive, so that you don't have to leave an ending 'Easter Egg' that spells it out for people. But I appreciate it all the same, it's perfect in it's own right, it doesn't get too heavy, it says what needs to be said, and it's clarity is motivating.I don't know you, but I love you, you beautiful bastard!

_childDocuments_.review: I was genuinely enjoying the game until I came to understand the role of relics. For me, these relics feel like on-demand in-game cheats, detracting from the genuine challenge I wanted. I was looking and hoping for that great sense of achievement I used to get from SNES games back in the old days, and the presence of these relics is undermining that experience.While many praise relics for allowing players to customize difficulty, I can't help but feel bad about them. The option to effortlessly switch to an "easy mode" without any real trade-off vastly dilutes the sense of accomplishment. Whenever I defeat a challenging enemy, it's made pointless by the fact that the difficulty was self-imposed. Even the simpe knowledge that another player might have used these relics to breeze through the same challenge diminishes any sense of comparitive play. Or feeling like we all managed to overcome the same challenge... because we did not.In my opinion, relics would have been better positioned as balancing tools, requiring trade-offs for their benefits, rather than as a no-strings-attached easy mode. The current design feels like a missed opportunity to craft a more thoughtful challenge for players.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played through the game on game pass, but it was good enough to the point where I also bought it here! While it is absolutely my GOTY, there is criticism that has been posted by others, that can definitely help you decide if this game is for you. Some of these include:The somewhat repetitive combat. While there are many new mechanics introduced, there isn't as much diversity as other RPG's. Overall, the combat's great in my opinion, but I can definitely see where others are coming from.Next, the story is decent. A large amount of reviews completely ♥♥♥♥ on this game's story, but I don't think it's that bad. Sure, it's not an award-winning story, but I've definitely seen better. I haven't seen some parts of the game, but there are interesting twists.Finally, the exploration aspects could have been fleshed out. While there are quite a couple of complaints from others, I specifically thought a lot of the 'puzzles' were pretty meh. For most of them, you don't really have to think, at least in the main story anyways. There is side content, however, that provides more difficult challenges (in the form of puzzles AND combat), which was nice to see.In terms of pros, this game has so many. The soundtrack is fantastic, having around 200 pieces (including the variants). There are day and night songs for most, if not all environments, and some tracks having specific variants. There's also many banger themes. Even the regular boss theme absolutely slaps (it's probably my favourite out of the sound track).The art style is constantly beautiful. Honestly, I could probably take a screenshot anywhere in the game, and ihen use it as a wallpaper (slight exaggeration, but you get the idea). There's also cinematic sometimes, which have a very nice animation to them, fitting well with the rest of the game.While I haven't played the messenger, I can attest to there being many references it. As openly stated, this game is somewhat of a prequel to the messenger, so if you've ever played it, Sea of Stars might just be the game for you.Overall, I absolutely adore Sea of Stars! I can't wait for the DLC, whenever that comes out (it was a goal on the kickstarter). If you're unsure about Sea of Stars, please please please try the demo or get it on game pass at least!

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the game and here is my honest reviewVisual: 10/10Vibrant colors. Pixel style. Perfectly gives that retro RPG feels. No complaints here.Music: 10/10The music is awesome! Even the small details like the tone for selecting a menu is very retro. Battle music is very catchy and the BGM for every are is on the spot!Game play: 9/10Very engaging for a turn base game. The timing mechanics will always keep you on your toes. The pacing of the enemy difficulty is just about right. The puzzles are simple yet very satisfying. The devs also made sure that the game would fit all players skill level (by placing things that would make the game easier or harder). My only suggestion was make it easier to see which enemies is targeted when enemies are clumped close together. I sometimes mistakenly choose the wrong enemy because they are so close together and I couldn't determine which enemy the pointer is showing. One way to improve this is like in Lunar, if an enemy is selected it also have a glow around it (also include the locks if possible). Also, The tabletop mini-game is not very enjoyable because the system is very gacha-reliant.Story: 9/10 (May included spoilers)The characters themselves are very entertaining. The first half of the story is very awesome that it even made me cry. However, the second half of the story went downhill. It feels out of place and very rushed. I know its designed for us to understand that there are different worlds (because it was split into multiple worlds) but it feels disconnected. It didn't give the feeling that this is a parallel world/split universe that came from a single world. Normal Ending is very bad. I was expecting Erlina battle then Fleshmancer battle then a very difficult world eater normal battle but no. It didn't even let us fight the Fleshmancer (which would be apparent why once you get the true ending) and I didn't like the surprise Galaga-type battle with the world eater boss which is very easy for a final battle (which apparently prepares you for the True ending battle which has a mini battle within it). The TRUE ENDING though is such a plot twist!! And yes GARL is the best character in this game HANDS DOWN! (still giving a minus 1 point because that normal ending really leaves a bad impression especially the world eater battle)PS: The "Breaking the 4th wall" secret area is such a nice treat! you guys are geniuses!!

_childDocuments_.review: I had extremely high hopes and expectations for this game. I backed it immediately upon hearing of the kickstarter, I think it might have even been day 1. I loved The Messenger and was excited to explore more of that world. And it was going to be in the style of Chrono Trigger, one of my favorite RPGs of all time. I even made my tombstone in the Crypt a memorial to a friend who passed away from cancer some years back. To say I was hyped up and ready to give this game my all would be an understatement.Not only did the game meet my expectations, it far surpassed them. The story hit beats that I wasn't emotionally prepared for, and the true ending was cathartic in a way that only the most passionately developed and written stories can be. I don't want to spoil anything but this game hit in such a personal way with it's story and character development for me. The beginning of the game is a lot of setup and may not wow you but stick with it and the story GOES places. It is worth the time investment for sure. The bonus easter eggs are worth the extra effort too I think. Every time I saw a connection back to The Messenger I had an excited "AH HA!" moment of realization and I appreciated just how well everything connected back together.I can't wait to see what Sabotage brings in the future but for now Sea of Stars has found itself among my top 10 games of all time. A list that mostly consists of games for the PS1 that I've been playing since childhood. For it to replace stuff with so much nostalgia behind it I think speaks volumes to just how good of a game it really is. At least for me.The music is amazingThe combat mechanics keep things interestingThe boss fights are unique and the designs are awesomeAnd the story is one emotional gutpunch after anotherI loved every minute of my playthrough and I look forward to going back and playing more in the future.Also the mini game wheels, while at first kind of weird, was a blast by the end and I want more of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Sea of Stars: overall score 6/10, The game is artistically stunning thanks to a magnificent and colorful 2D pixel art, excellent character and boss design and cool and cinematic animations with a catchy and well placed soundtrack. Except the artistic results, the game is just not fun to play and lacks most of the typical JRPG elements, making them either useless or frustrating. Most of the game time consists of long, boring and frustrating backtracking to retrieve collectibles or solve puzzles  (too many, too different and too boring).The lack of a minimap (which is an ABSURD FLAW), the impossibility to run from battles or to exit dungeons/areas and the incredible slowness of any fight (due to a very limited pool of skills and mana) makes every movement and phase of the game frustrating, very slow and practically a torture. The plot full is full of classical clichés of the genre, but sometimes the clever humor used for dialogues and names can make you smile. The two main characters are totally anonymous and Garl is unbearable after 5 minutes. Other secondary characters are better and more interesting, even if not explored enough. The difficulty level is VERY LOW, except for the puzzles and the frustrating level design. The idea behind how to unluck the true ending is just terrible: zero communication from the game on what to do and where: all of this just to lead you to an anonymous and predictable true ending that made you waste hours and hours in backtracking useless and frustrating areas.
