_childDocuments_.review: First off, I'm going to split this review into a couple of different sections, so here goes nothing:In April of 2022, I found this game via a Tiktok video of the fishing mini-game. As an aspiring game dev myself, I found it bore a very striking resemblance to a fishing mini-game akin to one I'd had in my mind a few months earlier, so I decided to look into it more and learned about the 'overworld' exploration (e.g. a 'small' version of the character walking between locations), another idea I'd had floating around! I laughed about it, because what  an original thought anyway, but I kept the game in the back of my mind, checking their Tiktok every now and again to see if there was anything more to the game. In the lead up to the games release the advertising felt a bit.. weak? It focused heavily on the visuals of the game or talking about Moonerang and it made me worry there might not be any substance to the game other than the, admittedly, beautiful art style. As such, I kinda put the game on the back-burner to see what the reviews were like then kinda forgot for a while.Recently I lost my closest friend very suddenly at 25. He was a 6"7 gentle giant who cared more about helping his friends than looking after himself with a passion for food, cooking and especially cooking for others. As such, I decided I wanted to buy a game to cheer myself up. I was in the mood for an RPG, started browsing steam, couldn't find anything. Went through recommendations, still nothing... Then I remembered my wishlist; more specifically Sea of Stars. I figured, what the hell, why not.Oh boy. I started the game and met Garl. It was like my friend had come back to life and been put into a video game. The intro to the game was.. rather slow if I'm entirely honest, but I stuck with it because I wanted to see where it goes. Boy am I glad I did.As soon as combat became involved I immediately fell in love with the game. I didn't expect much but early game, every fight felt , like if I ignored locks or didn't strategise there was a very real chance I could wipe. I liked that a lot and despite the absence of any real story, I was enjoying myself a lot.Now, as the game progressed, the combat felt less and less appealing to me, but still not boring. It found new ways to reinvent itself with new characters, combos and eventually ultimates; for me personally it never got stale but the threat felt lower as the game progressed. Still, nonetheless, very very good combat system and pacing of mechanic reveals. However, as the combat lost its initial lustre to me, the story began to pick up. Several different locations, plot hooks and story notes get revealed to you in a very, very good slow burn style. I can say now after finishing the game that every piece of information given to you, except  is relevant in some way or another. Those very well written stories you hear about through Teaks? All plot relevant in some way or another. The pacing of the game feels just like, well, a Moonerang. Slow to start, but once it gets rolling it's all about the timing, and boy does the story hit them Bouncy achievements. Expertly written story, incredible pacing all wrapped up nicely with some very unique characters, both villains and allies alike. , the only reason it's not a 10 is due to the pacing of the 'ending', even if the true ending made up for it tenfold.Characters. Well. Major spoilers follow for this section but I'll do my best to write a non-spoiler part after.  and now.. for the non spoiler version! As I briefly said in the story part, the characterisation of both allies and villains alike is pretty darn good. The MCs are very typical, being that they don't necessarily have a super strong personality other than "I am justice, I will do good" but it makes a hell of a lot of sense considering their background. Throughout the story, you get to see the flip side of how such an upbringing can affect people, both through  and through some side stories that are told through various NPCs. For a story about fate, the characters don't feel wooden or "rail-roaded" at all. Even the major story NPCs who are canonically incredibly powerful and world-altering level strength don't feel out of place at any time during the story, as they too are as much victims of fate as the rest of the cast is. Each and every character has its place. Expertly written. Now for the one that I think most people are aware of when it comes to Sea of Stars. The graphics. I'd like to say it speaks for itself, but there's more than just the surface level beauty to this game imo. There's a lot of small details that could very easily go unnoticed, from the beautiful distortion effects as you look at yourself through crystals, to , to the way the shadows flicker and move as you cast fire magic at your enemies, there's a whole lot of love gone into the art of this game. However, I do feel that a lot of the cutscenes were very jarring and out of place compared to the rest of the games style. There is however the [spoilers]Sea of Stars entrance cutscene[/spoiler] that is absolutely breathtaking and plays on the changing style immaculately. Last but absolutely not least, the sound design. The music captured me very quickly, despite often being simple it never feels repetitive or in your face, and that's something that gets to me a lot; even in some of my favourite games. The thing that really got me, though, was the incredible idea that is the band. Playing their own version of the games songs, and how it changes when you talk to the instrument player to no longer include that instrument, what a simple but beautiful idea. The taverns in this game feel something more, and that's not even including how great Wheels is (I won't go into insane depth about it, just know it's a very well designed mini-game that I wish I could play against my friends). I will say, however, that at some points in the game the sound design is a bit on the buggy side. From jarring switches, to the fact the second moon ball in Valeres ultimate is incredibly quiet and the others are deafening loud, it can, unfortunately, quite often take you out of the moment. SO. Overall:I've never wrote a review for any game before, but this just hit differently for me. The design contains a lot of my favourite things; flesh shaping, wind mages, fishing and even some familiar soundfonts. It plays perfectly on everything I love, to the point I'd call it one of the best games I've played; and while that might be because of my own preferences, don't let that subtract from how insanely talented the team behind this game is.

_childDocuments_.review: was a game that I had my eyes on for a long time, and it delivers the classic JRPG experience that I’ve been chasing for years. It features highly interactive gameplay, something that turn-based games tend to lack, and rich interwoven story arcs which make it all the more compelling. However,  does drop the ball in a lot of important ways which ultimately makes it less of a standout than it could have been.Characters (5/10):The protagonist of  is Garl, and no-one will be able to convince me otherwise. He has the most character growth, the most compelling motives, and simply has the most charm in the game, period. In his supporting cast are the two (supposedly) real protagonists who have no noteworthy personality to them whatsoever aside from “heroic”. They do exactly as they were told when they were children, and have no deeper reason for existence other than to be Mary Sues. It’s a tragedy that the game centers around them just gaining more power and going around fighting stronger enemies to save the multiverse.Regarding the other playable characters, they are generally written well, with self-consistent motives and some traits and abilities that give them some form of unique identity. There is one exception, however: the overarching antagonist. He is another villain who seems to be evil just for the sake of being evil, which would have been fine had the game not tried to come up with some nonsensical justifications for his actions. Inconsistent characterization makes him constantly seem like he’s out of character. Overall, there’s a roughly even number of perfect characters and awful characters, so it averages out.Gameplay (4.5/10):The gameplay of  was overthought. It features many puzzles and parkour elements that the player is required to solve in order to progress along the main storyline, as opposed to saving these for optional treasures and side quests. When kept in moderation, it adds some intrigue to an otherwise boring gaming experience. However,  was far too heavy-handed in this regard, and overstuffed the main game with these puzzles which makes traveling around incredibly frustrating sometimes.Each character’s skillset is also incredibly simple with only 4 abilities, which also detracts from the strategic element that all the best JRPGs exhibit. On the flip side, the lock system, the combo system and the interactivity of attack and defense in this game do force you to concentrate and have good reflexes instead of just using a skill and dozing off, making the game require some skill. However, this isn’t to say that the gameplay in  is wholly bad. Having puzzle elements does work in its favor when it comes to the side content, and the world exploration makes the game more immersive. Art (9/10):The art and music in  are phenomenal. Visually, the world design is very aesthetically pleasing in the nostalgic 16-bit style. Not to mention the skill animations, particularly the ultimate attacks, which are great.  also features awesome music which is always enjoyable to listen to. There really isn’t much to say; the artistic elements are self-evidently excellent.Story (9/10):Despite its weak protagonists,  manages to spin a compelling, complex, interwoven story of multiple characters, most of whom are actually interesting. It also brings in the concept of multiple timelines and universes, which it executes very well. The story begins as a simple tale of three adventurers setting off to find a way to help their mentors, before learning that not everything is as they once believed and that they would have to search outside of themselves. The arc of Aephorul and Resh’an in particular stands out as a tale of the things we sacrifice to chase our dreams, and of the principles that we hold onto no matter how seemingly irrational. I personally liked that the True Ending gave purpose to a seemingly useless key item given at the start of the game; it’s incredibly poetic.As a side note, though, the phrase “use magic without using magic” is incredibly awkward and stupid sounding.Overall,  is a unique game in the JRPG genre with a fascinating universe and lore which is certainly worth looking at, even though it has some elements that disappointed or annoyed me.Final Score: 27.5/40 (Good)

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the game, it was really fun to play.After the initial part, the game gives you an "open" world, you can technically go anywhere you want but most of those locations are locked.Literally there is no point to exploring the locations you weren't pointed to because they are either locked or unaccessable. _childDocuments_.review: I have given this game 10.8 hours (not sure why Steam says 8) of my time and in those hours my full attention. There is plenty good in this game: fantastic pixel art, fun (enough) combat and a really entertaining minigame.I think my favourite part of my 10 hour journey has been sitting down and listening to the fantastically written short stories told at camp. These were maybe a few paragraphs worth, of sometimes harrowing and tragic tales. They built the world up and added some context to certain characters and events - to the point where I'd often think about the story throughout that day.I didn't get this feeling at outside of camp though, which is a massive shame. The story felt flat, the characters one dimensional, and their motivations... just not very interesting. Its monotonous; the puzzles feel like simple chores that just take time, instead of anything you have to really think about. The levelling system is fine but it doesn't really feel like it would be any different if it wasn't there; you always seem just about as strong as you need to be for that areas boss.This is maybe my second DNF of 2023, of about 30-35 games in total, maybe in time I'll come back to it but right now I'm going to move onto something that hopefully hooks me in a way Sea of Stars hasn't been able to doThis is 'not bad, but more bad than good' sort of review and since Steam has no option for 'OK', I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start off by saying that I normally don't bother reviewing games, but this game truly stands out. This is probably one of the best games I have played in the last 5 years. I don't remember the last time I 100% completed a game, probably over a decade ago. Sea of Stars kept me coming back for more. The visuals are amazing, the story is great, the characters are very well developed and the game play is nostalgic and extreme fun. I absolutely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is visually appealing and looks good in short segments, especially when paying homage to other games -- mountains *are* nice.  Dungeons tend to have a convenient design so there's not much by way of 'wasted' backtracking to heal or save or check deadends for minor secrets, but the game does not allow nuisance and immersion in the experience: character interactions are minimal, and painfully lacking.The "framing device" for the game is problematic.  It uses an outside narrator to tell you the story as you're playing the game.  "Oh hello, I'm reading some books here how about I tell you one?" And any progression in the game is then interrupted by the narrator to tell you the thing that you just did.  Instead of having an introduction that *shows* the audience the delivery of the protagonists to introductory island, we're told that they are significant because they were brought to the island instead.  They have a long 'training montage' flashback (flashback in a flashback at that) but the game doesn't actually use that as an opportunity to teach you how to play the game despite that being a very good time for the characters to learn at the same time the player does. Moments like those -- connecting player experience with character experience -- are what sets this medium apart from other ways to create stories.  Of the chapters of the game I have been though so far, it is very consistent that that game *tells* interesting things instead of *showing* them to suit the game experience.  That isn't a make/break for the game as is -- several games have genre/play issues -- but it does feel doubly worse because the game feels even less like it matters because the character of focus isn't the one you are playing, but their childhood friend instead.I'm still hoping there's going to be a twist yet-to-come that makes the framing device pay off, but as it is right now, the game constantly reminds you of other games and takes you out of the experience to remind you that you are playing a game to the point I'd rather just play those other things it references instead.

The story has a few twists and turns you wouldnt expect, which i really liked.- The characters are great! But i read through some reviews and i have to agree, that the characters feel a bit... dull? SO MUCH MUSIC! If you played the game you know what i mean.

_childDocuments_.review:
Sea of Stars is a turn-based RPG inspired by the classics. A prequel story set in The Messenger's universe, it tells the story of two Children of the Solstice who will combine the powers of the sun and moon to perform Eclipse Magic, the only force capable of fending off the monstrous creations of the evil alchemist known as The Fleshmancer. 

Promising the Sabotage touch in every system, Sea of Stars aims to modernize the classic RPG in terms of turn-based combat, storytelling, exploration and interactions with the environment, while still offering a hearty slice of nostalgia and good old, simple fun.

 Key ingredients :

* Engaging turn-based combat. Combat gameplay includes active player input during attack animations (timed hits), multi-character combo attacks, boosting, and strategic defense options to hinder enemies while they are channeling powerful attacks or spells. For a more immersive experience, there are no random encounters or transitions to separate battlefields, and no grinding. Both navigation and combat happen in the same environment.
* Unshackled traversal. Swim, climb, vault, jump off or hoist up ledges as you run through the world with a navigation system based on platformer expertise that breaks free from the classic bound-to-the-grid tile-based movement.
* Prequel story set in The Messenger's universe. Dozens of original characters and story arcs will take you on a captivating journey. Sometimes epic, sometimes silly, and other times emotional, Sea of Stars does its RPG duty of exploring classic themes of adventure and friendship, while also being chock-full of the unexpected twists and events you've come to expect from a Sabotage production.
* Full-on dynamic lighting our custom-made render pipeline allows the creation of a breathtaking world coming to life by pushing the limits of 2D pixel-art games.
* The Sabotage treatment on the turn-based RPG genre. Every system has been deeply analyzed to create an experience that pays respect to retro classics, while reworking some elements in order to offer a modernized experience free of irritants and overly lengthy sequences.

name: Jurassic World Evolution 2
detailed_description: Deluxe Edition Jurassic World Evolution 2: Deluxe Edition features five spectacular prehistoric animals, including all-new marine and flying reptiles,  as well as six unique building signs,  and three exciting vehicle skins inspired by the Dinosaur Protection Group to use across your Ranger Team, Capture Team, and Mobile Vet Unit  teams in Challenge and Sandbox modes. Purchase the Deluxe Edition for the following species: -          Geosternbergia -          Attenborosaurus -          Pachyrhinosaurus -          Huayangosaurus  -          Megalosaurus About the Game Jurassic World Evolution 2 is the much-anticipated sequel to Frontier’s ground-breaking 2018 management simulation, Jurassic World Evolution, offering an all new narrative campaign voiced by cast members from across the Jurassic World film franchise, exciting new features, four engaging game modes, and an expanded roster of awe-inspiring dinosaurs.    Learn what it takes to be a park management master in Campaign mode, a compelling, original narrative that puts you at the heart of the action following the earth-shattering events of Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom. Work alongside iconic characters from the films, including Dr. Ian Malcolm (voiced by Jeff Goldblum) and Claire Dearing (voiced by Bryce Dallas Howard), and lead the efforts to control, conserve, and contain wild dinosaurs now rampaging across the USA. Take control with deeper management tools and creative options. Construct a range of customisable new buildings and hire new Scientists, and shape your park to meet the needs of both your guests and dinosaurs. Unleash your creativity in Sandbox mode, or test your skills in Challenge mode as you deal with diverse locations and environmental calamities. Play through key moments of your favourite films - with a twist. Experience ‘what-if’ scenarios from iconic Jurassic World and Jurassic Park films, each level set across eras and locations from all five movies. Dive into the Jurassic World franchise and see how events unfold when you take control. Over 75 different prehistoric species come to life in Jurassic World Evolution 2, including highly requested flying and marine reptiles. These animals feel more alive than ever as they preside over territory, fight for dominance, and react intelligently to the world around them. Use bioengineering to customise dinosaurs with bold new colours, and alter their genomes to unlock traits.

_childDocuments_.review: 1. Gameplay MechanicsAt its core, Jurassic World Evolution 2 retains the park-building mechanics of the original, but with significant enhancements that improve the overall experience. Players are tasked with constructing and managing a dinosaur park, balancing the needs of both the dinosaurs and the visitors.The game introduces a more refined construction system, allowing for greater customization of enclosures and facilities. The layout tools are user-friendly, enabling players to create intricate habitats that cater to the specific needs of each dinosaur species. The addition of new building types, such as hotels, gift shops, and research facilities, adds depth to the park management aspect.One of the standout features is the enhanced dinosaur behaviors. Each species exhibits unique needs and social dynamics, which players must consider when designing enclosures. The game does a fantastic job of making players feel the weight of their decisions—creating a comfortable habitat is essential for maintaining the dinosaurs' well-being and, ultimately, the park's success.2. Dinosaur Variety and CustomizationThe range of dinosaurs available in Jurassic World Evolution 2 is impressive. With over 75 species, including fan favorites and lesser-known dinosaurs, players have the opportunity to curate a diverse roster. The addition of flying and aquatic dinosaurs broadens gameplay possibilities, allowing for unique park layouts that incorporate different types of environments.Dinosaur customization has also been significantly improved. Players can now modify the appearance and attributes of their dinosaurs through genetic engineering. This feature not only enhances visual diversity but also allows players to create dinosaurs with specific traits, such as increased resilience or improved appeal to visitors. This genetic manipulation adds a strategic layer, as players must consider how each modification impacts the dinosaurs' social behaviors and compatibility.3. Campaign and Challenge ModesThe single-player campaign offers a compelling narrative that takes place after the events of Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom. Players navigate a series of missions that involve rebuilding dinosaur parks and addressing crises, such as escaping dinosaurs or managing public relations. The storyline is engaging, featuring familiar characters and new faces that enrich the experience.In addition to the campaign, the challenge mode allows players to test their park management skills in a variety of scenarios. These challenges range from achieving specific goals, such as generating a certain amount of revenue or managing a park under adverse conditions. This mode offers replayability and encourages players to experiment with different strategies.4. Visuals and Sound DesignVisually, Jurassic World Evolution 2 is a stunning achievement. The graphics are a significant step up from the original game, with highly detailed dinosaur models and beautifully rendered environments. The lush landscapes, vibrant foliage, and dynamic weather effects create a breathtaking backdrop for players to immerse themselves in.The attention to detail extends to the dinosaurs themselves, which are animated realistically, showcasing their unique behaviors and interactions. Watching a herd of Brachiosaurus graze or observing the predatory instincts of a Velociraptor adds a layer of realism that enhances the gameplay experience.Sound design also plays a crucial role in immersing players in the world. The ambient sounds of the park, the roars of dinosaurs, and the chatter of visitors all contribute to a rich auditory landscape. The voice acting, especially in the campaign mode, is well-executed and helps to bring the narrative to life.5. Management Challenges and StrategiesRunning a successful dinosaur park comes with its challenges. Players must manage various aspects, including visitor satisfaction, dinosaur welfare, and financial stability. Balancing these elements requires strategic thinking and adaptability, as unexpected events—like dinosaur escapes or natural disasters—can disrupt operations.The game emphasizes the importance of research and development. Players can unlock new technologies and improvements that enhance their park’s efficiency, allowing for better dinosaur care and increased visitor attraction. This progression system keeps players engaged, as they strive to unlock all available upgrades.6. Community and Mod SupportJurassic World Evolution 2 has fostered a vibrant community since its release. Players frequently share their park designs, custom dinosaur creations, and management strategies through various platforms. The game’s developer, Frontier Developments, has actively engaged with the community, providing updates and addressing feedback to enhance the player experience.Additionally, mod support has emerged as a significant aspect of the game, allowing players to customize their experience further. With the ability to create and share mods, the community has expanded the game’s content, adding new dinosaurs, buildings, and gameplay mechanics that enrich the overall experience.7. Room for ImprovementWhile Jurassic World Evolution 2 delivers a robust experience, there are areas where it could improve. Some players have noted that the campaign's pacing can feel uneven, with certain missions feeling too drawn out. Additionally, while the AI for dinosaurs and visitors is generally solid, there are occasional bugs that can lead to frustrating moments, such as dinosaurs getting stuck in enclosures or visitors behaving unpredictably.The economic system, while engaging, could benefit from more depth. Players may find that once they establish a successful park, the challenge diminishes, leading to a sense of monotony. Introducing more complex economic dynamics or additional disasters could enhance long-term engagement.8. ConclusionJurassic World Evolution 2 successfully builds on the foundation of its predecessor, offering an expansive and immersive experience that captures the magic of the Jurassic franchise. With its enhanced gameplay mechanics, diverse dinosaur roster, and engaging narrative, the game invites players to unleash their creativity while tackling the challenges of park management.The stunning visuals and sound design further elevate the experience, immersing players in a world where they can bring dinosaurs to life. While there are areas for improvement, the overall package is impressive and provides a satisfying experience for fans of the franchise and newcomers alike.In summary, Jurassic World Evolution 2 is more than just a park management simulator; it’s an invitation to explore the wonder and complexity of the prehistoric world. Whether you’re building the ultimate dinosaur sanctuary or navigating the intricacies of genetic engineering, the game offers a thrilling adventure that will resonate with players long after they’ve put down the controller.

_childDocuments_.review: The main campaign starts off pretty well. The wilderness mechanic seems fun, however it is not utilized as much as it should be. The first map is fairly small, and one would be forgiven to assume you can expand into the wilderness zone. The new fuel mechanic is interesting, however can be confusing and tedious to keep refueling. In addition, some of the buildings require refueling. This system is more tedious than it needs to be, and seems like they only added it to pad out gameplay. This raises the main issue with the campaign, it’s small. Very small. Each mission takes maybe an hour at most, and there’s only like 5 of them. It also ends on a note that makes it seem like there is more, but at best seems like DLC bait, at worse they just couldn’t be bothered making more missions.Some more issues I have with overall gameplay though, the first being the outposts. You can assign rangers, choppers, and vets to each one. The main issue with this is that the range can be fairly small, requiring multiple to a single pen. Secondly, if a dinosaur were to harm or damage a ranger, the chopper would be sent out to tranq them. Regardless if the dino is still attacking a ranger vehicle or not, you will be forced to transport them again. The main overall issue I had with the game is how expensive it is to remove the forest. What in JWE would cost 50k, costs 1 million in JWE2. It’s absurd, and as someone who likes making clean pens and having a clear area, it’s seriously annoying and not needed. But the good from the game. The main thing to take away is that the campaign was fun, and from my experience with the first chaos mission, they will also be fun. And they seem like they are going to be much longer than the campaign missions, if not some taking as long as the main campaign.So overall, the game has its issues. It’s short, fun, has some bad prices changes, has some good price changes, has some good new mechanics, has some bad new mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: I never expected this to happen to an already great game like Jurassic World Evolution, but nevertheless I was excited!! Jurassic World Evolution 2 is not only a worthy followup to the first game, but it also offers so much more than it's predecessor while also delivering the same experience I had with the first, but with different reasons. Starting with the campaign mode, it felt more like a tutorial than anything else. Just go through one quick scenario, do the objective, and move on to the next, rinse and repeat. What does make up for it though is the other modes of the game, the Challenge and Chaos Theory modes! Where you can unlock skins, the areas themselves as sandbox modes, and even the dinosaurs and skins you clone and obtain. The Chaos Theory mode is a huge favorite as it also lets you correct many of the events of the films, and go through these events the way you want to intend them to be. Whether it's to open and run both Jurassic Parks on Isla Nublar and San Diego, obtaining the dinosaurs on Sorna for Masrani for his new park on Nublar after the events of Jurassic Park 3, completely building and running the new Jurassic World hopefully without fail, and finally turning the abandoned Jurassic World resort into a wild sanctuary for the dinosaurs to roam free and live out their lives as they were mean't to.............even though eventually a volcano is going to blow up and cause an extinction level event years later. These are definitely a lot of fun, a challenge at first, but definitely a breeze once you know what you're doing!! The areas are much larger to make the dinosaur parks(or preserves) you dream to make, including actual areas around the world, and even areas on both Nublar and Sorna that you have to unlock! But the biggest and best part of all of it, is the dinosaurs!! You can tell that while a huge majority of the dinos came back for the game, others like the Tyrannosaurus, the Indominus, and I think even the Spinosaurus got a bit of a makeover for this one! And it's not just dinosaurs this time around either, since you not only get to make paddocks to accommodate the creatures on land, but also aviaries and lagoons to cater to the ones in the air and the sea, something the first game didn't even accomplish with the JP3 Pteranodons being the lone exception. Not to mention, you can also make the dinos look however you want, make their colors look how they were in the movies, or ones exclusive to this game. The same applies also to the buildings, as you can make them how big, however color, or even any appearance you want. Sure there are some bugs in it like some lagging issues, and the way the dinosaurs move when hunting, or even the way the marine reptiles just float in mid air over water, but thankfully these are not a big issue for me. Now the game is still young, and is able to add so much more. Maybe some more new dinosaurs, or even some new attractions like the Jungle River Cruise in the style of Jurassic Park or World, or even perhaps the hot air balloons from Operation Genesis! We already got aspects from Camp Cretaceous, while no doubts we'll get content from Dominion, and I can just say I'm gonna be looking forward for more! Because of all of this, I am more than happy to give the sequel the first game's rating of a solid 8/10! It's a lot of fun for anyone who has been a Jurassic fan since the beginning, anyone who loves dinosaurs, and those who love tycoon games. Now, all I can say.....is welcome........to Jurassic World!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good iteration on Jurassic World Evolution but is currently plagued with pathfinding issues and dinosaurs phasing through fences, which makes it pretty darn frustrating to play. I'll hopefully get a chance to update this review in the future when these issues are fixed.Once that gets fixed, then I could definitely recommend this game to people interested in a Jurassic World park manager. I think if you own the first game, you will probably want to wait until it's on sale. It does have a lot of nice iterative changes like improved dinosaur behavior and more in-depth customization for things like amenities and aviaries. The only issue I kind of have aside from the bugginess of everything is that the story content is weirdly paced and not very intuitive. The DFW story campaign is sort of a glorified tutorial in a way that ends as soon as you complete all the mission objectives, so you're going to be spending more time in Chaos Theory for the more long-form story-led park building. That would be fine except the pacing on those episodes is very strange and kind of all over the place. I understand that they're trying to keep them appropriately themed and canon-friendly, but I still kind of miss how the original game had a well-paced story that ramped up toward Isla Sorna, with each park being progressively more challenging to manage than the last.

_childDocuments_.review: Wait to buy this game if you are tempted.TLDR this game will be better when they solve gameplay time and money balance issues. There's a lot of cool looking things and features in this game. The Dinosaurs look, sound, and act beautifully with individual unique animations which was something JWE1 lacked. Aviary's are awesome and are fun to design as the pterosaurs will break out and interact with dinosaurs and their environment. New non jungle areas look and feel fantastic with animals in them. Aquatics are in the game by popular demand. You can now release multiple animals into your environments, and they will set up territories! Rangers will now auto take care of wide areas of your park with little to no input needed. Lots of film actors return to do voice lines for the project which is great. This sounds awesome right?Unfortunately there's so many broken untested features and bugs in this game. Assuming they will get the bugs under control over the next few months before Dominion Releases, Frontier has a bigger problem on their hands. A game like JWE2 needs to balance creative park building, consequences to miss managing perhistoric murder machines, and cool prehistoric animal interactions to oogle at as an overal gameplay system to be fun and successful.The game nails the last part I mentioned with plenty of cool things to oogle at and needs way less work than the other two main things needed to make a game like this tick. The biggest problem is that the game is horribly balanced. On paper the new park management system is more complicated than its predecessor which should be good, but what you get in practice is a system that demands so much of your attention because things cost way more than JWE 1, and it's harder to balance the systems that make you $. Combine this with multiple features that both cost lots of money and time. (revamped scientist system, fossil hunting, synthesis, and incubation) and you realize that you spend so much of your time micromanaging your game and so little time chilling out and designing cool paddocks and prehistoric life. Seeing that things cost so much time and money you are tempted to use the new fast forward option when you need 2 million to incubate your Mosasaurus. While its not an actual mistake it will increase the frequency of consequences to miss managing prehistoric murder machines. Usually a triceratops will fight and get injured (you can fix this if you look up online and teach yourself how to manage dominance stats but till you do, the game gives no hints how to solve this) Your dinosaurs can also get sick. Both scenarios lead you to use the dreaded Animal Vet facility. Its cool on paper. It sucks when you are constantly using it because you fast forward your game to afford to do cool things with your park. All of the automation given to the Ranger Team has been stripped for some reason with the Vet. Because you are a shift supervisor in this game, not a park director. If you don’t solve these issues your dinos will die or kill each other and you’ll lose money. All of this is moot because at some point you will get some variant of storm and if you don’t have 2-3 million in the bank get ready to load your last save. Your income will swing wildly after a storm knocks out a part of your power grid and if you don’t solve it you are done. This is because they removed or changed several bounce back strategies that existed in JWE1. You can’t sell fossils if you don’t have $50,000 and your ranger vehicles can’t repair after you fall into the negative (something they would still do if you assigned them the task in JWE1). The game auto saves every 5 min. Which is honestly about how long it takes to realize your hozed. So do yourself a favor and change it to 20 min so a random tornado doesn’t erase 4 hours of work.  If things cost less and were completed in faster times you would avoid a lot of the unintentionally frustrating aspects to the gameplay loops of this game. Somewhere in this mess there are really cool things and opportunity for a great game, but a lot of work is needed to get there. There are a lot of other minor gripes like missing film exhibits, lagoons needing more interaction and love, and sandbox not letting you play without some of the new management mechanics so you actually can’t escape the new management system at all, but I really think the standard gameplay needs work before I would consider recommending this game. Thanks for coming to my ted talk.

_childDocuments_.review: I can only review this game from the standpoint of NOT having played the first game.  I am enjoying it immensely, although I confess it's not quite what I expected.  I play and love Planet Zoo and thought this was going to be more of a park builder game.  It's not.  This is a game tied into the Jurassic Park franchise and I believe is intended to provide more of a park management aspect, with the intent being to avert the type of disasters encountered time and again in those movies, as well as keeping your parks solvent.  In this respect, Frontier has done a very good job, imo.I've seen some complaints about there being too much micromanagement involved but so far, I haven't found that to be the case for me.  The campaigns are more like tutorials and I, as a new player, appreciate that.  I have also watched some gameplay on YouTube, which I'd recommend doing for new players as it simply gives a confidence boost to starting out.  IMHO, this game doesn't have nearly as steep a learning curve as does Planet Zoo.  I'm just now finishing up the 4th campaign scenario and feel like my grasp of the game mechanics is good for the relatively few hours that I have played.  All things considered so far, I am glad I purchased the game and can recommend it.  There are a few changes I would like to see made and/or improved upon but nothing that has left me with negative feelings.  The game is also running very smoothly on my system with good fps.  I also haven't encountered any of the glitches I've seen others mention to date but perhaps they have been seen in areas that I haven't yet had the time to play.  I look forward to many more hours spent playing and seeing how the game progresses with time and DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game, I haven't played the first version, so everything in the second generation is fresh to me, excellent dinosaur modeling, various dinosaur species and realistic pictures perfectly restore the life and life of dinosaurs. Survival environment, this is a rare work for dinosaur lovers.However, I encountered a bad bug in the process of playing, which prevented me from playing the game. When playing the fourth level of the DWF plot, the task required me to capture the toothless pterosaur. I built the bird cage and hatching room in advance. But when I captured the pterosaur back, the capture team was stuck in the air and couldn't transport the pterosaur to the birdcage. I tried to reload the file and it was still the same. In the end, I had to restart the level and wasted a lot of time, which greatly affected the game. Experience, I hope the production team will pay attention to it and fix this bug as soon as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend the game, with a very big caveat: GET IT WITH THE BIGGEST DISCOUNT POSSIBLE!JWE2 is a good game, don't get me wrong. A great game even, sometimes. It improves and builds upon everything the first game did.The problem here is Frontier's extremely predatory business practices, which is why I'm giving it a negative review.First of all, this sequel, even after a ton of updates and DLCs, still doesn't look nearly as good as the first trailer for the first game did. They literally lied to their customers and never delivered on it.They constantly hold onto extremely basic QoL things that should've been there from the start, so they can then release them as "free updates" whenever a new DLC comes along. There are bugs that have been present since day one that never got fixed. Dinosaurs will constantly, and I do mean CONSTANTLY, clip ridiculously into each other. Yes, you have a hundred "different" dinosaurs, but they all end up behaving exactly the same way. Their communication with the community is basically non-existant, constantly ignoring feedback and what the community actually wants, instead giving us the most basic fixes ever.The game is barely optimized for PCs. Something that has been true since the first game. Slowdows are constant. The fact that they still decided to release this on old-gen consoles is 100% a business move and they clearly didn't care for the playbase or making the best game they possibly could.Most of the DLCs don't actually add anything of value, apart from the big expansions. Just new dinosaurs that, although they look great, end up behaving exactly the same as all the others.JWE2, after several updates and DLCs, is what JWE1 should've been on release day.To this day, Jurassic Park: Operation Genesis, an over-20-year-old game, still has functions and better dinosaur AI that JWE2 lacks.Frontier are nothing more than a money-hungry corporation that gives us the most basic products they can sell. And we gobble them up because... It's Jurassic Park and we love it.So, Frontier, if you're reading this: just because you paid off a couple of youtubers to suck your corporate ♥♥♥♥, and a bunch of reddit mods to silence anyone that speaks up, that doesn't mean us actual fans aren't displeased.Decent game. Don't give them your money, they don't deserve it.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good upgrade from the original game. The very small complaint I have is that it feels the need to stick somewhat closely to what the movies are doing. Maybe I'm alone in this, but I don't really care about the main characters of the movies being worked into the game. It's not quite as awkward as it was in the first but it doesn't add anything to the game to have them in it. There's more stuff to manage, such as supplies, while also giving some quality of life improvements like the stations you can assign staff to. As someone who grew up on Zoo Tycoon, I'm glad I finally got to have a game like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Stunningly inept tutorial and an overly micromanaged design. _childDocuments_.review: (Note: Review Addendum at the bottom)Overall I recommend this game with an asterisk which I will go into a bit. Mechanically, the game is an overall improvement on a base level from the previous game, at least as far as the core functions of the dinosaurs, park building, and pinning down what your guests need to get a five star park is. Makes it a lot more engaging then simply plopping down a hotel, arcade, clothes shop and restuarant near every viewing gallery. Guests wants are communicated slightly better and paths, shelters, etc. make even a bare bones five star challenge park look like a beautiful well done theme park in contrast to previous games where its a mess of buildings and hotels huddled in one place to artificially inflate a rating with a big multisectioned square of fences with nothing but diplos and dilophos in them. The Challenge Modes likewise are more fun than last game, feeling reminescent of the old Zoo Tycoon challenge maps where you were limited to certain animals and challenges.  Even through all the tedium of waiting, at the very least you start off with dinosaurs either with a viable genome already or wild ones about you can tranq and transport to quickly hit the ground running. The cons here come from the sheer amount of waiting you have to do in the core game modes, waiting for scientists to recoop, waiting for expeditions to return, waiting for cash to fill up to allow for anything to happen.  Likewise, bad RNG can really sink a playthrough of even the basic easy sandbox and chaos theory modes. In the first Chaos Theory mission, when the Triceratops got sick (which is an easy cure) at the *same time* my Raptors all got the common cold which developed into pneumonia and I had to painstakingly wait for them to get better before I can proceed and open the park, of which by that point I was already broke due to how long it took for them to get better. In general the "wait" is the biggest gripe I have with the game, however, this is a PC game, and while Frontier does not officially endorse it because daddy Universal said no, Mods especially WeMod makes this game much more accessible and cuts down the busywork expotentionetly making the game considerably more fun to grind through than normal. That said, there is a lot of rough spots that still need to be polished out a bit more, of which I think we can fault both being rushed to release this game ahead of Dominion and secondly the monkey wrench that was Covid. One of the biggest things is the story and VA work is very, very bare bones and characters (beside Cabot) have little personality and the story is just a glorified tutorial. Campaign had a fun aesthetic and premise but super bare bones and undeveloped and Chaos Theory is such a dissapointment due to the aforementioned bare bones character and narrative work. JP Chaos Theory is just a worse Return to Jurassic Park, and the JP3 one is so mean-spirited and tedious, the Lost World and World missions are more fun but in a traditional park builder sort of sense and the Fallen Kingdom mission is narratively the most compelling out of the bunch and seeing an in-game version of the JW was fun. Reminscent of the missions from JPOG.So overall I enjoy the experience and some of the changes made, but I think it could have had more time to simmer and develop. Its in a better state than the original was at launch with almost twice as many dinosaurs , but overall I'd recommend a *wait* to purchase, namely for new content, new patches, as well as for the Modding scene to further crack open the game, which they already have started too in mass. WeMod already has a full trainer ready for JWE2 (which makes the grind so much more enjoyable) and NexusMods already has better terrain tools, no hitbox, and skin replacements available for certain dinosaurs. So while this game is in a mixed state, this game's longevity I can tell already has long, long legs. But if you don't want to invest in mods, then I can see why this game would appear to be such a tedious grind for some other reviewers here. So TL;DR:Recommendation with Asterisk. Story is barebones and the wait in-game can be tedious at times. Use WeMod or other quality of life mods if you can. Wait to buy for more content or patches. Potentially a very long life game with tons of potential replayibility. Core functions and mechanics and dinosaur fun more than makes up for the failings but needs so further ironing out first.Review Addendum:After hundreds more hours and patches, the quality of life of the game, even without mods has improved drastically. The tedium of challenge mode and the campaign maps are now completely optional barring specific skins and the quality of life improvements in game such as species viewer, first person mode, additional scenery items of which most of these have come in *free* updates. New dinosaur species are still DLC locked but thats to be expected for this sort of game's business model.  The game is in a much better state than it was at launch and if your looking for a fun simple sandbox mode experience, you can just start out the gate ready to go with the ability to turn off more divisive features like scientists. The modding scene has slowed slightly but most of the huge quality of life mods still exist even though I'd say they are now fully optional at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: ------------Updated Review---------------When I played this game out of the gate it had a lot of issues, however after several months and dlc's this game became a whole different game. All the original issues I had have beed addressed. One of the best park management games I have ever played!-------------Original Review---------------I really tried to give this game my all. I have over 45 hours invested and it was a true waste of time. This game is so architecturally broken I am shocked it made it past the MVP phase. I am also now a firm believer now that this game is truly un-fixable. There are so many problems with how this game is designed I don't even know where to begin.Pros:1) Graphics- I play on highest settings and it looks great. (We know where they spent there time.)2) Dino Interactions- Really cool with a lot of different animations (Fun to watch, but you won't have the time trust me.)3) Dino variety - Lots of cool new dino's that are exciting to look/learn about.4) Lagoon and Aviary- Cool that they introduced marine dinos and flying dinos (however I don't think this is a real pro as they have a very limited set of animations, needs, and get boring very quick. Building there enclosures is a joke with no real options to customize, and they are not exciting whatsoever.)Cons:1)Micro Management- (Apparently dinos must have needed a physician as they need to visit one every 2 minutes, oh and the storms are a nightmare, not difficult just tedious)2) Dino/Enclosure Management - its just boring, place an enclosure, pop a watering hole in the center, lay down some trees, and your done.3) Scientist/Staff-I thought this was a park management game I don't really know what the hell this is, just another thing to micro manage I guess.4) Campaign- Essentially does not exist, more like a quick tutorial, 1.5-2 hours at most (partly blame this on the fact the new movie isn't out yet)5) Sandbox - What you think would be the crown jewel of the game but its locked behind hours and hours of grinding through all the issues mentioned here.6) Chaos Theory- I want to avoid spoiling everything but this is essentially a mode where you get to re-inact the movies as a park manager. (this is what should have been the campaign but only 3 of the 5 are worth it, and even then you'll find yourself pulling your hair out, as your success truly depends on how lucky you get)7) Bugs- still riddled with them, and yes I have encountered a few that will fully break your playthrough.8) DLC's - just a cash grab (the new dinos are just re-skins with no new animations/needs, etc..)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a straight up cash grab. I'm glad they got rid of some of the stupid stuff from the first game but at the same time they added some really dumb mechanics. Want to transport a dinosaur? Nope, you can't click transport. You have to click around on a random building and find a hidden way to transport them. Makes sense right? I mean, why make the transport button work in all menus... that's... just... silly. Is your scientist unhappy? Well you can't send them on leave from the scientist center... no of course not... you have to build a staff center... and then click the button there because micromanagement. Don't even get me started on the fuel micromanagement. It legitimately adds nothing to the game. Management games are great when there's a purpose behind what you're doing, but adding mechanics without depth is completely senseless.I was itching for a great new JP story was about 3 hours and very repetitive. It was along the lines of a tutorial... just not a good one. Listening to the dumb$$$$ dialogue at the end made me feel like it was an afterthought, limited so they didn't have to pay voice actors additional fees or a salary for a half-decent writer. Apparently there are swimming dinosaurs in this game but they make no appearance in the campaign mode. Sandbox mode sounds great but having to unlock dinosaurs in other modes that are not fun or well fleshed out is not my idea of fun.I can't say that this has nearly the story, gameplay, or UI polish that I'd expect for the price. Not by a long-shot. The exorbitant price coupled with the bad UI and lackluster attention to the campaign are enough for me to give this game a solid 4 out of 10.tldr;Get the game at <$30 and it will probably be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Man this is hard to write. For reference, I aced the first game despite its problems, and was eagerly awaiting this release to see if it would fix my concerns with the series. Since launch, I've completed the campaign, all chaos theory maps, and all challenge maps except the last, with more than 50hrs playtime. So this comes after a pretty thorough review of the entire game besides its creative mode. I wanted to write a huge review but halfway through it I decided to boil it down to bullet points. - New biomes are gorgeous and bring much-needed variety to park builds. - New dinosaur animations are great and add a lot of life to your dinos. - Pack hunting is in the game! (It's completely OP right now but it's still cool). - Paleobotany is now the default way to feed herbivores and the different plant models look great. - New territory system is pretty cool and makes mixed paddocks more interesting. - Avian and sea creatures have been added to the game, plus a few more land dinos. - Large variety of much larger, flat, open maps to build parks on.  - No more feeder refills! Rangers can be set to patrol paddocks: removing most (but not all) of the tedious micromanagement there (now you have to refuel the rangers manually :P). - Terrain modification and building placement are  better(but still not perfect). - There are now time controls allowing you to speed up or pause the game.- Multiple era buildings are baked in for creative mode, for JP and JW buildings (with some weird exceptions, such as JP aviary). There's a nice, unique set of buildings in the campaign that are not usable in other modes for some reason. In general, weird decisions here but at least there's some era support.- Seriously, the game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gorgeous now with the new biomes and plants, making for great screenshot porn. - Campaign is laughably short (2-3hrs), Chaos theory seems to be where the meat of the effort went. - Chaos Theory maps range from really good (TLW: San Diego) to very bad and short (JP3). - Challenge mode maps are really nice, but the actual mode itself is not that interesting (the most unique was building a park with mostly carnivores/herbivores). - Avian and sea paddocks don't really have much in the way of customization and the creatures are hard to see at a distance, which meant that after I'd tried them out once or twice I didn't really feel like using them again in my parks. They also cost a tonne to unlock and construct, meaning you can't really use them until your park is well off the ground anyways. - No new guest attractions. You will be building pretty much the same parks you built in the first game. - Customizable amenities are just OK and are very finicky to modify. - The new skin system adds some more options to dinosaur skins but since incubating dinos is now a longer process, without the ability to preview the new skin I found I rarely interacted with this system.- A new guest system introduces different types of guests to the park (adventure, nature and luxury). A cool idea in theory, but in practice the different guest types really have almost no bearing on gameplay. - Absurd medical system requires controlling several vehicles manually as well as multiple menus to heal a broken toenail. Larger groups of dinosaurs become extremely tedious to manage as a result. It's a cool idea on paper, executed in perhaps the worst possible way I could imagine.  - Timers and costs for  late game that you have to wait or pay for seem to have been adjusted to meet the new speed up mechanics. I am talking 8 minutes to incubate a large dinosaur in some cases, not mentioning the millions of dollars that need to be saved up beforehand. There are ways to reduce these timers, but even then you will wait several minutes for these timers to count down. Is this a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mobile game? , even with a large profit margin. - New scientist system adds another layer of micromanagement as any major park building activity (research, digging up bones, synthesizing and incubating dinosaurs, etc. etc.) now requires an additional step of picking available scientists to work on said task. If they're not available, guess what? You're waiting some more.- Creative mode doesn't disable this annoying scientist system  requires you unlock dinosaurs in challenge mode of all places before you can use them there.- Somehow the writing is even worse than the first game. Ian Malcolm is the only character here who isn't extremely cringe and unlikeable.Despite some nice new features, I have to be honest with myself and recognize that if this game was not themed as a Jurassic Park game, with dinosaurs and beautiful graphics, I would have rated it a 5 at best. As it is, the amazing visuals and our desperate, aching need for a decent JP park builder buy this title (and its predecessor) a lot of love I don't think it has earned. It's heartbreaking because I think there have been some clear attempts to improve the platform they started with in the first game, but the sum total feels like an expansion pack rather than a sequel. For some reason the game design team still thinks that tedium and micromanagement somehow means deep and rewarding gameplay, and have simply shifted that burden from old systems to new, worse systems. This was a very clever sleight of hand that took me a while to see, but now that I've seen it I can no longer enjoy or recommend the game in good conscience.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played around 5 hours of the tutorial campaign, before jumping into a sandbox for 5 hours. Aside from un-skippable cut scenes, the campaign seemed ok. However I bought the game to build Jurassic Park, and I found I became very frustrated with the sandbox mode very quickly, due to poor quality of life features for park management, which are well documented on the internet. My conclusion, this is a pretty park simulator, but in some ways it's behind originals such as Theme Park World. Given the amount of DLC they keep pumping out, I can only assume the developers have no interest in fixing some of these bugs/issues. If you're undecided, buy it on sale, and don't commit to DLCs until you've had a go with the base game. My biggest issue is, If you're looking to optimise the park for efficient operations, there's a number of quality of life bugs that got in the way of my enjoyment of the game and ultimately became very frustrating, and they appear to have been around for years now. Annoying auto-zoom Each time you select a facility, the camera will automatically pan to and zoom into the building in question. For buildings with deploy able staff you then have to re-zoom and scroll back to the dinosaur in question in order to deploy the rangers. There is a hack to get around this by using a hot key, but it only connects to the first ranger/vet building, which is then impacted by my second issue; In Sandbox mode, the game offers you the same type of building, but with different skins applied. What isn't immediately obvious is that despite having the same description and name, they have differing individual abilities, such as starting with two ranger trucks. When using the navigation arrows to jump to different buildings of the same type, it won't jump between themes. i.e; JW Recovery Centre 1 won't then jump to a JW2 Recovery Centre 1. The background code doesn't recognise these as the same type of building but with different skins. Further, the overhead map function gives you very basic information with 4 basic pre-set filters to cover the dinosuars. It doesn't include an option to filter out your power network, or illustrate which buildings have been damaged by a storm. The only way to see damaged buildings is when they either are 100% broken, or if less than that, to manually driver a jeep around and inspect them. Additionally, when tasking your rangers or medics to cover specific dinosaur exhibits, their job list doesn't tell you which exhibits they cover. So one ranger could be driving miles across the park to visit two different places. You can hire multiple scientists, but you can only task them to one of each staff activity. i.e; one expedition at a time, one research project at a time, one genetics project at a time. This limits how quick you can progress in certain areas. There is an option to disable this at the start of the sandbox, but it's in the same area as giving yourself unlimited money. For me, the game ultimately becomes a time sink with running back and forth between micromanaging research activities every 3 mins, and micromanaging your park rangers.

Excited to see what's to come!Pros:✅Chaos Theory✅Expanded Sandbox✅Multiple Biomes to choose✅Tons of Dinos✅Customizable Buildings✅ Rewarding Challenge Modes✅Simplified Quality of Life in some aspects of park managementCons:❌Landscaping isn't as vast as it could be❌No customizable signs or entrance signs❌Limited Habitat editing❌Limited decoration options❌Some awesome decor/attractions limited to certain biomes❌Fauna specific to certain biomes instead of being able to spread across all for decor purposes

It takes the best parts of the original game, adds new ways to play, and changes up mechanics to make them feel more realistic and interesting - making everything more engaging and immersive. _childDocuments_.review: so this game isnt a bad game per say, but its not really like the fist game very much. its very much more of an actual park simulator than a dinosaur park simulator.in the first game once you got some dinosaurs going with a few buildings and you started sending off on expeditions constantly you basically had unlimited money to do whatever you wanted (and with the dr wu genes you could make huge multi-species enclosures)if you go into this game like that (and jump right into chaos theory expecting it to be the same gameplay as before) you'll go bankrupt fast and have to restart.the campaign is basically a tutorial (which is important, because they added a ton of micro-management systems that arent explained outside of it)there are a ton of systems you have to pay attention to now, including amenity distribution, dominance, dinosaur territory, traits, etcyou make batches of dinosaurs all at once instead of one at a time, and power is much harder to come by (you dont unlock small power stations until you do a bunch of research, before that you have to use backup power which needs to be refuelled with gas constantly, by the way, all of the vehicles need to be refuelled now too)and once you do unlock them you have to have backup power set up anyway because you'll run out of power from the power station in like 5 seconds because the limit is super strict, and as soon as a storm hits you'll lose power to it anywaystorms in this game are where you really sink or swim, they're more common and more dangerous than ever before (remember the giant tornados you would get on isla sorna? they're everywhere now) and if you dont open your emergency shelters during a storm your safety rating tanks, but if you do open them you start rapidly hemmoraging money because of ongoing costs, so if you dont have a decent security blanket of money when a storm hits you either have to accept the rating loss or go bankruptand i havent even gone over the dinosaurs yet, they each have individual dominance stats that determine how much they fight, and any dinosaur with the aggressive trait you can basically just not even bother hatching because it will attack and kill anything that even looks at it, the game also gives you a list of types of dinosaurs that each one likes and dislikes, but the dominance system takes priority over this (so, for example, even though velociraptor "likes" compsognathas, if you put them together the raptors will hunt down all of the compys because their base dominance is too high to group them with other dinosaurs)also its kind of buggy right now, like sometimes dinosaurs wont expand their terrain so they cant find water or food and just die, or sometimes their ai breaks so they just stand in place suffering but cant die so you just lose rating if guests see them until you sell themi kind of went on a bit of a rant thereanyway its nice if you like difficult park sims but you might want to wait for patches or mods to fix a few bugs and mechanics because its kinda rough right nowoh btw if you get the deluxe edition or preordered it, you can only change vehicle skins in sandbox and challenge mode, you wont be able to use any of the new skins in any of the story modes, which is something i wish they would have disclosed in the description or something beforehand

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the first one semi-extensively, the real allure of this one for me was the different biomes. Building a dinosaur park is great and all, but... there's only so much you can do with tropical islands. But when I saw the previews showing alpine mountain maps, I was sold, and pre-ordered it the moment I was able. (I like mountains, what can I say.)I have played for about eight hours, and have really only started dipping my toes into it (though not literally, given that we actually have a place for the aquatic beasties!), but I've seen enough to notice a few differences, some of which I go for, others not so much.The pros of what I've seen so far:-As mentioned, the different biomes. I'm a California boy myself - though I live in New England at the moment - and (mild spoiler alert) building in Yosemite is probably the closest I will ever get to going back there. Each of the different biomes have their own challenges - the alpine maps have snowstorms, the desert maps have sandstorms, etc.-Hatches in batches. Breeding new dinos in JWE1, you could only let them out one at a time, even if you incubated a bunch. In JWE2, one slot in the hatchery incubates a whole batch of eggs (you might get one or two, you might get five or six, it all depends), and can release as many as you want. Plus it allows you to airlift the new dinos into the enclosures, so really you only need one hatchery for your entire park, as opposed to one for every enclosure.-Changes to the aviary. The aviary dome in JWE1 was pretty much pre-packaged, all you had to do was build it... and it had only one species, the Pteranodon. Basically a kind of "ooh, ahh". The aviaries in JWE2 actually require a little work to go into them, and you can build multiple connected structures to make one big dome. Plus, you actually have to set up the inside of the thing to make them comfortable. I confess what caught my attention was the Dimorphodon - I thought it was another hybrid like the Indominus, basically taking a raptor and sticking its head on a Pteranodon, but no, it's a real dinosaur.-Customizing the guest amenities. A welcome change from just plopping down the same thing multiple times, you can actually give your amenities buildings a little flair.-Chaos Theory. Although I've only done one so far, there are five to choose from - building Jurassic Park properly (i.e. without Dennis Nedry to screw up the computers), or building it around that amphitheater in San Diego (seen in "The Lost World: Jurassic Park"), etc. Basically expanding on the idea of the "Return to Jurassic Park" DLC in JWE1.The "meh, not so pros":-The campaign. Not great, not terrible. A bit on the short side; I finished it in under three hours. I think (and others have as well) that it was mislabeled - this is the tutorial, not the campaign.-Micromanagement, part one: The ranger teams. On the one hand, getting them to actually be useful outside of personally point-and-clicking them to broken fences and the like (although you STILL have to do that) is an interesting idea, because it makes them actually work for their money. On the other... you basically have to have "ranger stations" inside every enclosure and have a team assigned to them to check on the dinosaurs' status every so often, and given that you have to research having extra teams separately, you'll need to build a bunch of response stations (which combines the ranger station and ACU helicopter) for multiple ranger stations. Seems counterproductive to me, but to each their own...-Micromanagement, part two: The park staff. They decided to make it a little more... I dunno, "interactive", I guess, with the addition of the scientists to your park staff for damn near everything relating to the expeditions recovering DNA for, synthesis of eggs for, and incubation of said eggs for your dinosaurs. And you can't work them too hard, or they'll get disgruntled and THEY'LL pull a Nedry on you and sabotage you. (Thankfully I have not encountered THAT issue. Yet.)-The change to the fossil menu, specifically when dealing with non-DNA items (i.e. the fossilized plant samples, skin impressions, metal, etc.). In JWE1 you could just sell the things. In 2, you have to make your staff sell the things, which ties them up in that when they could be, you know, extracting dino DNA from fossils?It's a case of "let the buyer beware". I personally am happy with most of what I got (and again, I've only scratched the surface, really), but others might not be. YMMV.

_childDocuments_.review: I was so excited to get this game. I loved the first one, and had clocked almost 600 hours in on it, bought all the expansions, and additional dino packs. I'm a huge Jurassic Park fan in general ever since I saw the original when I was 13 years old. (That Brachi scene at the beginning still leaves me in childlike awe, and wonder.) However I digress. This 'sequel' feels more like another $20 expansion pack to me. The updated dino animations were cool, and the fact that they got rid of herbivore feeders was an excellent touch (I hated those senseless things with the passion of a thousand burning suns! There's grass on the ground the dinosaurs have animations that they're eating the grass, but I pay money to refill a box!?), but IMO the Campaign is nothing but an over glorified tutorial. I was 57% through it in a matter of a few hours, and by the time I hit Pennsylvania I was just too underwhelmed especially when I came to find out they replaced herbivore feeders with this new scientist dynamic. Seriously who said "It's a game about wild dinosaurs so let's put in humans that the player has to take care of, and tell them to go to sleep so they can get more wild dinosaurs! They'll love a 2-5 minute wait for that!" I'd like to imagine there is more to this game, but due to Steams refund policies I couldn't play any longer, or else I would be disappointed, and out $55. So in truth this is really just a half review from a long time fan of the earlier game. Please feel free to respectfully comment anything I might be missing out on, and maybe I'll try getting it again sometime once it's more towards the aforementioned $10-$20 dollar price range, but $50+ is just too much for this particular release. Oh, and good try on the holding out on the real new content like flyers, and swimmers until we get past the point of no return on refunds Frontier. Don't think I didn't catch on to that brilliant move. Seriously bravo I imagine they're great additions, but I won't get to see them. Maybe if I had I would be too engulfed in the game myself to care about time limitations. Anyways if you like this game great I'm definitely not here to bash anyone's taste, but to me  a sequel to a game as cool as Jurassic World Evolution needs to offer way more than this.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is graphically very beautiful, but there are a number of flaws, the first of which is the sandbox mode. It's great to build the park of your dreams, but even with research and expeditions, it soon turns into a situation where you cannot lose. The sandbox should come as a reward for completing scenarios or a campaign. And like the first game, you're constantly adjusting the contents of the enclosure to suit the dinosaur. More ground fibre? Oops, too much. A little less water? Too much open space. I really want to like this game, but I became bored very quickly. Yes, you can play the scenarios, the campaign, but then you have endless bad voice acting by actors who were in the film. And Jeff Goldblum's monologues are tedious and annoying.If you enjoyed the first Jurassic Park game, you will also enjoy this. Does it offer lots more? No, I don't think so. Will I play it again? Probably. Can I recommend it? Well, it's teetering on a no, but so close to being a yes. Get it on sale? Yeah, go on.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game, but with some reservations. Like its predecessor, JWE1, it involves a lot of micromanaging and repetitive gameplay, which definitely are not for everyone. The campaign was pretty much just a tutorial to the game. Some of the Chaos Theory Mode campaigns were kind of fun, though. The Challenge Mode is indeed challenging, with it's varying conditions. The sandbox mode is in my opinion the best part of JWE2, with tons of creative possibilities. Have noticed creating dinosaur enclosures and taking care of their environmental needs to be very suitable for a fun activity with my pre-school age kids, too. Furthermore, JWE2 is actually an exceptionally customer-friendly AAA game compared to many of it's contemporaries: New stuff and quality of life -features have been added to the game regularly via free updates, and although I have bought many of the DLCs, the base game itself doesn't really lack anything I would see as essential. _childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Changed to a NO. I had a big review about the game. The Update 1 "fixes" were less than stellar, adding things like landing points to the already existing rocks for flying reptiles (which is nice mechanically as you can now force the assets to land in certain places, but really not very impressive aesthetically). Now the game is on sale for 30% off, barely a month after release. I understand the nature of sales, not complaining about that. What I'm complaining about is 30% is a free Deluxe upgrade or free DLC basically over those of us who were loyal fans and bought the game day 1. Usually a new game doesn't get such a large mark down, if it goes on sale at all that soon after release. A 10%-15% mark down, wouldnt be a big deal imo, it still kinda stings but at least it's not an entire DLC's worth of content. Frontier/Universal (whichever one is responsible) has repeatedly punished fans throughout this franchise's life and this is just the latest of a bunch of fat middle fingers. I REALLY want to like this game. I love everything about it's concept and a lot of the things in it are really cool. _childDocuments_.review: This is what the first JWE should have been. A huge improvement for park management, guests comfort and dinosaurs, including the long-awaited customization for skins and attraction buildings.Even if the story campaign is really short (though we can expect something new when the next movie releases), everything else is mostly focused on Chaos Theory mode, that is good on its own, but reveals some flaws.For example, unless my game is bugged, it is impossible to sell dinosaurs. So if you wish to get rid of one, you must wait for them to die, or get them killed by some others. But the biggest flaw I must mention is the lack of "loan", that can be fatal for your park if you hit massive bankrupt. Getting money isn't hard in this game, just like its predecessor, however if a storm destroys viewing galleries, or electrical poles, or guest buildings, or all three, and you get negative revenues, there is no way to come back from it. No money -> no repairs -> no "visible" dinosaurs -> no money. You can't hope to sell fossils if you don't have cash, as extracting them costs money too, and you can't send your staff to rest, because.. money. Only way to get out of it: Restart. That is something that wasted a whole day on JW era Chaos Theory, but once you know it, it's easy to avoid it.But in overall, I still appreciate JWE2 a lot and enjoy watching dinosaurs with true interactions, and if you're a fan of the genre, or of Jurassic Park/World, you'll have a great time too. Might try to get it on sale though.

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the first game, I was obviously extremely excited for this game to come out. Now that I've experienced mostly everything of what this game has to offer, I can say that it is a big step upLagoons and Aviaries are very fun to play with, even if the lagoons are pretty limited. The new species that were added are also wonderful and I look forwards to any and all new dinosaurs that may come with the DLCChaos Theory is a fun mode, throwing you into a "what-if" scenario themed around each movie. Challenge mode, which is the one thing i never touched in the first game is enjoyable enough in this game, and is the best way to go about unlocking all of your dinosaur genomesMy biggest complaint lies in the dinosaur welfare system. I do like the more in depth treatment of the species, but when my Triceratops are constantly fighting eachother and getting organ trauma, it becomes extremely tedious to tranq them, send them to the medical facility, then back to the enclosure, all while my other dinos are getting sick or injured. it can get very overwhelming and i hope Frontier can add some automation to the system. Another big issue is that your dinos can and will get injuries in sandbox mode, where i would like to avoid this problem.Aside from that one big gripe, I love this game alot, and i look forwards to whatever the devs will do to add on to and improve this game in the future
