_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy this game. If you are a fan of the Jurassic films and building games, you will enjoy this game. It has good building, management and other stuff.The only issues I have with it is the placement sometimes denies you the ability to build because of a rock or another object even if it is clearly not going to be in the way, same with terrain. I had a lake for the dinosaur in my pen and I couldn't add a viewing area because it was too close to the water despite having enough room for a T-Rex to stand between the viewing area and the lake. Also the fact if you want a full sandbox experience, you need to basically complete the entire campaign and chaos theory at minimum if you want everything unlocked. So if you are going in exclusively to build a massive Jurassic world/park in sandbox, you may be disappointed to find out you will need to unlock legit everything in the main game. However this would only be a major issue if you dislike managing money and stuff, otherwise if just might be a slight annoyance to your sandbox.And while we are on the topic of building your massive dream park. Remember how in the films the entire island was used to make a large variety of attractions? Yeah not here, you get like a tiny patch of the island to work with. I barely can fit anything in the tiny patch of land given. I was really hoping for something like Planet Zoo or Coaster where you have more land then you know what to do with, but that is sadly not the case. I also was hoping they would take an page from the old game Jurassic Park Operation Genesis, where you can build anything on the entire island like the films.Overall I do say the pros outweigh the cons, but some things can be a bit eye rolling that it made it past pre-production. But these are just my opinions, you may agree or disagree with me, that's fine. I just hope you have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I want so much to say i recommend this game.  The idea and layout is great. I've invested 132 hours and would love to invest way more time [so many park plans!].  However, be warned.  There is a bug that will cause your dinos to begin freezing in place as your park grows.  They will starve and dehydrate.  Rangers will be unable to find a way to destinations even if its right in front of them also.  Seems to be a pathing issue.  They are aware of this bug and as far as I know, there was even a patch released to fix it.  It has not been fixed.  So unless you want to turn off dino starve/dehydrate, you will eventually run into this issue. (this option really stinks because then they will not graze/hunt, which is part of the game enjoyment). I didn't even get halfway through my planned park when it began, and by the time I rage quit, it was happening constantly.  Obviously I'm hugely disappointed and frustrated at the amount of time already put into the game, only to run in to this.  Honestly if not for this one issue, i would be raving about this game. _childDocuments_.review: As someone who played the hell out of the original JPOG and JWI, I found JWII unnecessarily frustrating. This review will contain gameplay spoilers, but no plot spoilers.What I liked:- No more power lines. Buildings can now receive power from a hub generator with a power radius, which is fairly large.- The maps are larger and less awkward than before, after the first few missions.- Hatcheries aren't the nuisance they used to be, and no longer take up a full city block.What I hated:- The main campaign is long, boring, and dumbed down. I really don't care to hear the characters yap. I'm here for dinosaurs.- Wow! Look at all the new dinosaurs and animations! Oh, wait, you can't, because you're busy micromanaging every other facet of your park. You don't even get to enjoy your actual dinosaurs.- The maps are ugly and same-y, with the exception of the gorgeous deciduous park, which has bright green grass and vibrant red and yellow trees. I was promised variety, but I find most of the maps so displeasing to look at that I'd rather just play in the deciduous park permanently...- Buildings and vehicles now consume fuel. This could have been executed in a much less frustrating way, but you wind up having to babysit your buildings. There are little icons floating over them to indicate fuel is low, and when you run out, you're stopped from using the building, even if it's a generator and you run out of power. Until... you click "Resupply." That's all. An obnoxious roadblock, and simple busywork.- Scientists are annoying. It would be fine if they didn't require you to manually put them at Rest all the time. You put them on three or four jobs, and they get pissed until you Rest them (which costs money). If you don't, they may sabotage you. Just more busywork. It demolishes the pacing of the game when you have to put your objectives on hold because your scientists are crying.- Carnivorous dinosaurs that are compatible to be housed together (according to their info pages) will randomly attack and kill one another despite "100% Perfect" living conditions and plentiful food. So, really, you can't actually house them together. They will just kill each other for no reason.- Every single time you put a dinosaur in your park, even if you've already had the same species in your previous missions, you have to research them all over again to find out what they need in their enclosures. It's a waste of time in a game already wasting your time with monotonous chores.- Figuring out if a new dinosaur is sick is downright exhausting. First, you get three new dinosaurs all at once. Then, you scan them with the Ranger vehicle. Then you find out all three have undiagnosed ailments. So you have to send the medic truck to go find out what's wrong. Then it's either as simple as a vaccine, or as annoying as getting your helicopter to tranq them, then getting your transport team to move them to the medical facility, choosing a scientist (who is hopefully Rested) to heal them, waiting, and then transporting them back. This is while trying to do all the OTHER micromanaging your park requires.- I don't know if it's a glitch, or what, but every time I start the next mission in my campaign, I have to start my research from the VERY BOTTOM again. Used maximum security fences before? Well now you're back down to basic again. This makes absolutely no sense, because you keep your scientists from previous missions, and they're the ones who researched your upgrades in the first place. I can only hope it's a bug, because I hate working my way up, only to start from the bottom over and over again.I don't even want to keep playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I did not think it would be possible for Frontier Development to sink any further down the ♥♥♥♥-ladder, but here we are, with a broken, janky, messy, predatory, and all around bad and completely unnecessary Jurassic World Evolution 2. In the context of what has come before, there is absolutely nothing that is positive about this title. It shows that FD's primary concern is cash grabs, at this point, with extremely predatory DLC practices (you know they would be microtransactioning every single dino and skin if they could get away with it, the cheeky bastards), and an extremely broken base game. It is not wonder that so much of what they make gets shoveled into bundles; gotta try and fleece people on them DLC's, so shovel that base trash into as many accounts as possible. It must be working, because somehow, after years of nothing but horrid, horrible management sims, they are still making dirty money. If there was any dev group out there that I specifically, 100% recommend staying away from, it is Frontier Development. I know after this trash, my wallet is closed to them.Tl;dr - never has such a low-effort, cash-grab product been so poorly conceived or abysmally optimized.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted this to be a positive review. It would be if the game included one thing:  Players being allowed to select a map and have the ability to complete all research and expeditions for all dinos in one playthrough.I’m pretty disappointed in how much it feels like is missing from the game.  It could be a good game if the developers flush it out with DLC, but right now, you’re better off playing JWE1 even without the DLCs.I’m not sure if they rushed the game to match a timetable for the movie release or if the studio tied the hands of the developers to withhold content to hide spoilers that could be dropped as DLC later on.At this point, it feels like just adding this on to JWE1 would have been better instead of releasing it as a new game.  I don’t regret buying the game, but I don’t feel like I got my money’s worth.JWE1 stood on its own at release and felt far more complete.  I played through the campaign as soon as I got it and thought I got my money worth just from that.JWE2 feels hollow at this point like it’s unfinished.  The campaign is a joke, and none of the other modes feel like they measure up to the storytelling of the JWE1 levels.  Maps are bigger, but it feels like there are fewer unique character lines, involvement, and events than in JWE1. Instead, lines are reused from map to map and there’s no progression in the story or what’s available to you.The biggest killer is you can’t just open your own map without doing Challenge Mode or Chaos Theory and be able to complete all the research or do expeditions for all the dinos. There is no research or expeditions on sandbox levels.JWE2 gets rid of some of the frustrations of 1, but it gains its own frustrations. As a result, some things feel corrected while I’m left wondering why they bothered changing other things.-Bigger maps-More social dinos-Simplified guest buildings with size variations-No fixed monorail entrances-Water and air exhibits feel really lacking.  There’s not a lot of terrain requirements inside them, but you can make them your own.-Lost the sense of progression from JWE1. Every new map is a reset which makes it feel like a constant start over and grind.-There’s no true tutorial.  The campaign covers the basics like exhibit building and ranger and capture teams which didn’t change. Unfortunately, they skipped over the new amenities, and it wasn’t until 40 hours in that I finally started to understand how those work.-Characters from JWE1 return, but it feels like they make cameos more than being involved with what’s going on in-game.-Animal needs are vaguer, making it much easier, perhaps too easy, to make dinos happy. It does make it easier to fit more dinos in exhibits, but it’s also difficult to keep track of what vegetation you’ve already dropped that’s required by a specific dino.-Genetics have been downplayed A LOT and I’m not sure it’s a good thing.  There is now a random chance for negative/positive traits to appear and genetics modifies those chances, but making modifications is really limited compared to JWE1. Also, there are traits that will pop in that you won’t be told about before synthesizing the eggs, which does get frustrating at times.-No more factions from JWE1 and it makes the game feel empty.  Your own teams sabotaging you because you played with another division was pretty dumb, and the new staff system is a better system IMO.  Now, staff will sabotage you if you excessively overwork them.The  is a, IMO dumb, short experience where you build a couple of exhibits and are forced off to the next mission as soon as the objectives are met with no option to stay and keep building after completion.There’s no equivalent to jumping between the islands like you could in 1 so there’s no held progression. Instead, every time a new map comes up, you start at square 1 again so you feel like you’re grinding the same things over and over.They could have easily included events from Fallen kingdom as a part of the campaign but chose not to for some reason. So you’re left just “cleaning up” wild dinos in some very short scenarios after the events of Fallen Kingdom.Save one; all  levels are locked behind obtaining a 3-star rating on their challenge mode or Chaos Theory counterparts.  There are many options to set up a sandbox map, but there is no research or expeditions on sandbox maps.All research is already complete and you’re only allowed the dinosaurs you’ve kept in the other game modes.  If you haven’t had a dino in a campaign, chaos theory, or challenge mode then you will not have access to it in sandbox.The options for sandbox can be vague. For example, you have while you can start with "unlimited" or "0" cash, the other options are “Low” “Medium” and “High”… Is it too hard to just give the values? is closer to the JWE1 campaign but still isolated parks with no shared progression. None of them feel like they have access to all the assets, though. Also, the voice acting for Simon Masrani is ear-splitting.  I feel they did his character dirty and made a poor choice of voice actor to try to play him. Not to mention Dr. Grant and Dr. Sattler are nowhere to be seen unless they’re tucked away for the new movie DLC. has unique gameplay that I feel is underutilized.  There are creative restrictions like herbivore and carnivore only parks, as well as wild dinos to capture on the map.  The fact that you don’t have the option to apply these sorts of restrictions or wild dinos to other maps seems like a sorely missed opportunity so you’re stuck with what’s available.

_childDocuments_.review: I found the first Jurassic World Evolution enjoyable because I'm a fan of prehistoric life, and of the wider Jurassic franchise. The videos of EvolutionSquare convinced me to try out the game, despite me not being a park manager gamer. After this experience, I preordered JWE2, which is joyful to play and adds mechanics - like vet services and new feeding techniques - that I find improve on the fun of playing. Quality of live updates make the dinosaurs (and other archosaurs) feel more lifelike in their behavior. I loved the tropical islands from the first game, and the new biomes are gorgeous and give you a new playground that you didn't even know you wanted. I can thoroughly recommend the game. This is for you if youenjoyed JWE1,want to immerse yourself into the world of Jurassic Park/World,or if you'd like to just take care of prehistoric reptiles.

_childDocuments_.review: And yet I beat this game (DLC-Less). It wasn't really fun, it was something to do. A chore, like a clicker game, but somehow worse so than the original.Comparing the original JWE to this one I can say Frontier improved the UI and general handling quite a bit, making things more accessible and steerable with easy pause and speed-up keys as well as UI elements, but then they also went ahead and 'streamlined' any complexity the game had and turned it into mud.The core gameplay cycle still remains. Build a park with dinosaurs, put profit generators (shops, bars, etc.) in places with the attractions and raise profit. Your park is rated in a decimal star system, going up to five full stars. The park's rating is based on the comfort of both your 'attractions' and the guests intent on viewing them.Instead of having each individual comfort stat's percentage (dino comfort, dino variety, guest comfort, guest toilet coverage, etc.) accumulate your milestones are now measured by monthly income. The factors simply create penalties if they aren't met to a decent enough degree (100%). In this iteration the focus is also much more heavily on the guests having fun. JWE 1 had a roughly 50/50 split between dinosaur comfort and guest comfort. JWE2 has dinosaur comfort as an aspect of guest comfort. Ugh, who'd want to see a sick animal?Like the first game, you still get missions from random voiced characters that are from specific divisions. But there is no longer any competition between three factions. Only random chances to earn some extra money. They all offer the same quests from a pool of semi-randomized things. For example, the dino rights advocate Claire may ask you to let a T-Rex eat a Struthiomimus. In this game, however, she explains her idea by telling you 'it's what dinosaurs from different eras meeting would do'. Yes.You now also have to take care of a bunch of toddlers pretending to be scientists. You see, they have a stress meter. The stress meter takes a beating of one point per task you ask them to do. And if you don't pay them to take a lengthy vacation after their bar is full they get angry, possibly resign and / or begin sabotaging your park.You may wonder what you need the scientists for now. The short answer is 'yes'.The longer answer is: Research, Dig-sites, Dino Synthesis, Dino Incubation, Dino Treatment (severe medical issues), random propaganda events, getting sabotaged, losing money.Genetic modification has been overhauled and simplified. There are now stats with a percentage of either 100% or -100%, the positive always being a benefitial trait. You can now add genome specific "mod points" to each stat to improve them. ONLY to improve them. You can't make a purposely xenophobic Parasaurolophus, you can only make it social and tolerant.Do X, achieve Y, but suddenly Z! That's all I can say, really. The campaign (non-DLC) is painfully short, shorter than the original game's campaign, even. It actually serves as more of a tutorial-less tutorial, now that I think about it. But hey, there's Chaos Theory to make up for the lack of campaign.What if Movie 1-5 had a manager like YOU? Prove you could have done better by turning each map into a five star park while vaguely movie related things happen at milestones. Yes, that does mean there's sudden gate fun in the first one. Overall those scenarios are enjoyable.Tie your hands behind your back and play the game with your tongue. It'll be more fun.Old game funner-ish, this game is tedium incarnate. No opinions on the DLC available.

_childDocuments_.review: In spite of its utterly shallow main campaign the game is a decent successor to the original, with better ray traced graphics and dinosaur behavior (incl. more genetic mutations you can research to make dinos less violent and cohabit with other species more). Chaos Theory mode allows you to eg. rebuild the actual Jurassic Park on Isla Nubar - that's pretty fun, you can even operate the OG green and yellow jeep tour and have them drive through cages (like the giant balls did in the 1st game/Jurassic World, but those sucked) The original campaign is basically tutorial mode though - it doesn't even go over aquatic dinos though and there are only like 4 or 5 missions, all very brief, and you don't really get to spend much time at all on any map, planning out a park or enjoying one. It grinds my gears though that the game does only a passing job at explaining to you what a dino's needs are - and there's loads more in this title, gone are the simple herbivore feeding posts etc. you actually have to populate the enclosure with nut producing trees etc. and it's confusingly down to percentages as to whether or not a dinosaur is happy with their 40% of ground nuts or whatever. This makes it quite difficult to plan enclosures or properly size them. Another thing it poorly communicates is dinosaur compatibility - it's all in tables, but you'd be flicking back and forth between dinos trying to figure out 'this one likes that one but this one hates this one' etc. - and unhelpfully, dinos with all sorts of names being lumped together like 'stegasaurids' etc. and you'd be left thinking well is an Axylosaurus a Stegasaurid? Nope, it's an Ankylasaurid or whatever. totally different... Definitely more than a 5/10 and therefore a recommend but not blown away by it and wouldn't spend full price on it or really pay for any DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: Jurassic World Evolution 2

_childDocuments_.review: Jurassic World Evolution 2 is a game developed and published by Frontier Developments and is the sequel to Jurassic World Evolution and I'm gonna point it out, again, Jurassic World Evolution 2 (JWE 2)  another 'reboot' type game of the classic Jurassic Park Operation Genesis (JPOG), only this time, focusing on the boring and mediocre movie reboot Jurassic World which is based off of the Steven Spielberg classic Jurassic ParkI will be comparing a lot, again, of JWE 2 to JPOG, that's because I played JPOG as a young child, it's was absolutely fun and JWE 2, as well as it's predecessor; JWE, follows on the same vein as JPOG did even though they may have separate titlesThe main gist of the game is this; build a park, create dinosaurs and entertain people (if people get that reference, I expect a free game of my choosing, merci). That's it, but what distinguishes this to JPOG is this... JPOG was much more fun to play and JWE 2, yet again, is boring, plain boring... and JPOG came out in 2003What shocks me is that Frontier Developments developed JWE 2, the same developers behind Planet Coaster and Planet Zoo. I love Frontier, they are a great company and have created some of my childhood games and when I heard JWE 2 was being developed by Frontier, I was sceptical, especially with the mediocre JWE, and, yet again, this game was a huge let downThe game is extremely repetitive, but whereas JPOG was fun and yes, indeed repetitive, you  built your  park, in JWE 2 you just follow a set number of missions, fulfill contracts and do the same thingEverything is so tedious, for example, to create a dinosaur, you need to do this, then do that, then after that you have to do this, then that and then- oh no, the incubation failed, you have to do it again and then you need to do this, then do that, then wait and wait and wait and wait and wait and oh no, the incubation failed... do... it... againI must admit, JWE 2 is absolutely beautiful. The graphics are gorgeous and the Cobra engine really brings out the dinosaurs' textures so well and the game is a sure beauty, also having John Williams' beautiful music from the Jurassic Park and Jurassic World movies is an absolute gemBut that's it... that's all JWE 2 does. Everything else is an absolute grind. This game heavily relies on grinding, rinse and repeating, waiting and so onWhat makes JPOG so much better is, although that game came out in 2003, it had more gameplay mechanics and replayability and offered so much fun, that I would play that game anytime over JWE 2The game is... okay to say the least. It's a massive let down, especially from fans like me who were waiting for the next JPOG game, some people may like it, some may not. I enjoyed it but only to a certain extent, I gave the game the benefit of the doubt, but it seems Frontier have moved onto better ventures and have let this game play as it isAll I can say is this, JWE 2 is an okay sequel and at least it's not as bad as other movie licensed games I've played in the past, but it's certainly not the next JPOG game we were all patiently waiting for...

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT - Coming back to change my review now that I'm not as angry about it. Listen, I love Frontier's library of games - I love the original Jurassic World Evolution and Planet Zoo and Planet Coaster. This game is just really bad. Let me break it down into some points.1 - The voice acting and the writing is terrible. It's like listening to an English translation of a Vietnamese game. The voice acting is so stilted I constantly wondered if they had used AI voices to capture the likeness of certain characters. It goes in one ear and out the other - at this point they should have just dropped the storyline entirely for how much it detracts from the game.2 - There waaaay too many steps to do the simplest things in the game. It's so un-intuitive. Even things the original game had and were good now suddenly have three to ten more arduous steps or complexities to completing them. Not every mechanic needs fifteen steps to be completed. It doesn't add life to interactions it just adds noise. Your developers were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn’t stop to think if they should.3 - The time wasting oh my god the time wasting. Why does everything take two to five real life minutes to complete - with how many steps everything takes this issue compounds so damn badly that something as simple as getting a dino takes thirty minutes. Was this originally supposed to be a mobile game with timer micro-transactions?? Runtime padding.4 - The UI is downright hostile to the player. Every menu, asset, and control setting is working against you at every step of the campaign. You'll spend many hours in real life googling things that should be intuitive because things are not where they naturally should be or certain settings and information are lost in the visual noise of "artsy graphic design". Don't get me started on the vanilla controls - whoever decided the scroll wheel should be the back button and the camera movement button at the same time should be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fired.5 - It's super unpolished in the technical department. Sure it looks nice but even on a high end computer there is issues with optimization and the bugs are really really annoying. There is nothing quite like your medic truck deciding to stop driving itself while every dinosaur dies of a disease that came on in seconds.This game makes me so angry.

_childDocuments_.review: Whenever there's a game based on new movies/popular movie franchises I usually expect it to feel like it was made to get more money out of the name, but this is honestly one of the best park management games I've played. A few things immediately stand out:- Interactive, direct game play options. You have lots of opportunities to be hands on with operations. In your park maps there may be a huge area outside of the area you can build in, and it's full of wild dinosaurs (as this has taken place after the most recent movies). You can drive around and get some money by taking photos of dinos, which can give a wide range of money depending on the content and composition of the photo. You can control a helicopter and tranquilize dinos via a fps feature, then transport the dinos back to your park. - Dino behaviors. So far I have only really seen dinos that are the same species interact, and just these interactions feel very dynamic and interesting to watch. You can see them competing to be the dominant pack member, socializing, preening eachother, it feels like packs have their own complex operations going on. Watching them hunt live prey is super interesting. Each species seems to have different social dynamics, I'm excited to mess with sandbox mode to see some interactions between different species.- Attention to detail. So far, I can't find anything it feels like didn't get enough attention, it feels like every little detail has its own details. I went to capture a dino that had one recorded fatality caused. The dino arrived with an ailment, which was diagnosed as a swallowed phone (presumably from eating that person). At one point when I zoomed in, you could hear a phone ringing until it sent the caller to voicemail. Such a little specific detail that I found pretty entertaining. In general all of the relatively small features still feel super fleshed out, the way the cars handle when driving makes them really fun to drive. Photography is rewarded using a very detailed list of criteria, it makes me just want to go take photos to get the best one I can. - It's a complete, fully fleshed game without any DLC. While lots of DLC are offered, the base game by itself still has a TON of dinos and features, it does not feel like the base game is empty. The DLC are what they should be, expansions to the complete base game.Will update as I unlock more stuff

_childDocuments_.review: Back in the mid 2000s, when I was a wee lad with access to a Dell Dimension, I played the ever loving ♥♥♥♥ out of the OG Zoo Tycoon with all the expansion packs. And being a Dinosaur kid, I made my own version of Jurassic Park in ZT. It was hella cool and I genuinely regret losing that disk. But now I have an actual chance to make my very own version with all the bells and whistles? Sign me up baby!Upon reaching the main menu, it advertises a Campaign Mode, Chaos Theory, and Sandbox. I didn't play the previous one so I went with Campaign to learn the ropesCampaign mode feels like a sort of extended tutorial, walking through how the game works and how you manage your park. You get a limited selection of dinosaurs to add, and the reason behind it is that you're like a government agent trying to keep the dinosaurs from eating people. So you only got what you can capture with the containment team. I'm not very far but I imagine it'll expand further as the story progresses.Chaos Theory seems to be a scenario challenge where you build your park around the established story line, like the original 1993 park all the way to Jurassic World. Pretty cool.And sandbox, which I think speaks for itself. It recommends waiting until you finish the campaign.Now, its got some issues. Some of the voice acting work is a little bit stale and cheesy, and it kinda dampens the experience of having a dinosaur safari park.The controls and UI could use some polishing, It kinda feels like Cities Skylines but just different enough that your muscle memory can ♥♥♥♥ up your steez. The UI doesn't have a good flow to it and its easy to forget where you need to go to do important dinosaur things. Or worse, if a Dinosaur breaks out, you gotta send in the containment team, and the process to do that is a bit clunky and easy to foimble requiring up to four menu clicks to subdue one Dino. And it seems like they break out quite frequentlyMaybe my gripes are valid, or maybe I just need to configure some settings and git gud.But it does seem very interesting, and if games like sim city, Cities Ckylines, and Zoo Tycoon were your jam, then maybe give this a try.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're into creating your own dino-filled paradise, Jurassic World Evolution 2 is definitely worth a try. The game offers stunning graphics that make the dinosaurs and the park come alive, with a relaxing atmosphere that's perfect for those who enjoy a more laid-back experience. The gameplay is engaging, allowing you to immerse yourself in decorating and managing your park, from building enclosures to ensuring your guests are having a good time.However, there are a few bugs that can dampen the experience. Vehicles sometimes struggle to find a path into enclosures, despite having multiple gates available, which can be frustrating when you're trying to manage your park smoothly. Dinosaurs, especially smaller ones, occasionally glitch out of their fences and end up outside the park, which not only looks odd but can also cause havoc. The aviary creatures sometimes get stuck in place, leading them to starve or die, which is really disappointing when you're trying to maintain a healthy and thriving park.On top of that, guests sometimes gather in one spot and don't move, creating unrealistic crowds that break the immersion. These issues can be a bit annoying, but they don't overshadow the overall enjoyment of the game. Despite the bugs, I still love Jurassic World Evolution 2  and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys park management games, especially with a dino twist. Just be prepared to encounter some quirks along the way!

_childDocuments_.review: So there's two types of RTS in my experience: fast and slow. This is the slow variety.That said, it's very good - high production value, intricate - I can't imagine how hard it must have been to plan and develop this game, obviously a ton of time went into it. I was very frustrated at first because I didn't understand why my fences were breaking, or why I had no money, or why storms wipe out half my infrastructure, but in the end... it won me over. It's a great game.Here's my advice for anyone about to play this for the first time:1. You won't finish in one session, these are long ordeals, plan accordingly2. There are 4 levels of fencing - ignore them all, they're useless, just use the basic one and keep the dinosaurs happy instead. If you have unhappy dinosaurs, you'll be miserable no matter what fence you have.3. You will run out of money fast, everything is very expensive. Monetize the hell out of every enclosure, stack it with observation and activities.4. Storms will absolutely wreck you if mishandled (random f5 tornado in costa rica lolz) and send you into an unrecoverable state. Open shelters immediately when storms happen (VERY important), go slow-mo and immediately repair all fence damage as it happens, and reopen as soon as the storm is over (and no dinosaurs are loose). Demolish buildings to get emergency cash - but at that point you're probably better just starting over.5. Continuously optimize and check your amenities - this is HALF your income! But bad optimization will actually cost you money and rip apart your finances. I fit's not earning, fix it or delete it. Fortunately, they have excellent tools to help you with this. The gray identity is NOT a symbol for everyone.6. Save religiously. Things can spiral out of control, and it's definitely the easier reset.7. A slightly more advanced tip: you can combine many dinosaurs in the same enclosures, saving you a lot of management headaches and maximizing profits, just check that they don't hate each other and that you can accommodate both with their environmental needs.8. The more dinosaurs, the better your income, make a lot of them. The more diversity, also the better your income. Carnivores are more popular than herbivores.9. One more thing well worth knowing in advance: dinosaurs die eventually. Beware in particular of the T-Rex, it's extremely expensive to replace and when it dies your sales will plummet like a rock, potentially screwing you. If you can't afford to replace it easily, use 3-6 medium carnivores instead of it.10. Pay attention to staff bonus qualities, they're your best tool for maximizing research.That's it, the rest you'll figure out. Good hunting.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR - Could have easily been DLC.I am baffled by this game... You take JWE, adjust the fence sizes to all be equal, remove decorative trees, and add the most infuriating micromanagement systems I have played in a while.Medical system:Initially I had no issue with this, adding different injuries is cool and having to send the medical team to scan a dinosaur is also a good touch. This starts to break down when you put Carnivores and some herbivores together. They fight... CONSTANTLY! This means constant injuries and constant manual assigning the medical teams.  Instead of being fun and engaging this becomes tedious and frustrating at times.Ranger Teams:The need to continually send ranger teams to check the dinosaurs... which takes up the task slots so the bigger the park you have the less likely you have a ranger team available when the storms roll through and wreck your day. The ability to medicate has been taken away from them. They are dedicated scanners and repair drones, and if you are so inclined picture takers.Storms:This system was interesting in JWE, it didn't feel cheap and you were able to stock pile money for the time when this did happen to you. They weren't super constant and depending where you were, wouldn't happen at all. In this game... They feel cheap and are absolutely STUPID! Why the hell is there a hurricane in San Diego?! Have you not paid any attention to the actual frequency of storms there? It rains around 5 days out of the year and the likelihood of a tropical storm is extremely low. Yet it happens form some reason, a lot.Dinosaur unlocksSCREW YOU FOR THIS CHANGE!!! Not only do you have to spend the time unlocking the genome, you have to actually release the dinosaur into your park for it to be unlocked in sandbox. WHY?! Do you remember how to do it in JWE? Hit a 5 star rating in a scenario. That in itself could be challenging but it made you pre-plan your park, especially with the limited space. Scientist Hiring SelectionGarbage system and a financial drain on your park. RNGesus needs to be your friend or you are far past ♥♥♥♥♥♥. You need high logistics, then you need high Genetics, then you need some treatment. Scientists need to be hired in that order so you can start researching things... like the ability to train them to be less useless. You will be firing and hiring a lot so you can research, get fossils, incubate/release dinosaurs. Once the scientists are trained up and you have the +2 attachment on the staff center you will be fine. The more scientists, the bigger financial strain, keep that in mind.Paddock creationExactly the same as JWE minus placeable trees. The lagoon and aviary are the same as each other, I can't complain other than to say, THIS COULD HAVE JUST BEEN DLC FOR JWE!SuggestionsAdd research that keeps a live scan of the area so you don't have to assign ranger teams to it. You could also have the research just have the rangers go to the post and it auto scans everything in the area. As long as you are splitting out responsibilities of teams, why not have a repair teams? Let Rangers focus on the dinosaurs. Add a research item to unlock aerial medical teams to make the medical issues less irritating. Dinosaur unlocks, if you unlock a complete dinosaur genome add it to the sandbox mode!!!!!!!! Getting 100% for every dinosaur is a time consuming chore so reward the player for doing it!SummaryThis is a muddled micromanagement mess that adds additional financial strains and is just a lazy copy paste.

Now the game has some nice dinosaur interactions, the territory system is amazing, and the scientist mechanic adds some nice extra management but those three factors alone aren't enough to save the game.In short, I cannot recommend this game. Jurassic World Evolution 2 has had some nice improvements from the last game, but it also takes steps back and continues to make some of the mistakes the 1st game did. _childDocuments_.review: Alright, just to keep this absolutely clear, it is not going to be an all-positive review, in fact I am going to focus more on the negative aspects of the game.Then why thumbs up you may ask?Well, the game is still enjoyable, one of the major improvements in comparison to the first game would be the dinosaurs themselves. Herbivores now eat plants from the environment instead of relying on feeders, while carnivores can hunt in packs and are overall more dynamic, the comfort and territory system had been completely reworked (for better), and most importantly, the behaviours and interactions between the animals are more plentiful and interesting, which helps to sell the illusion of living and breathing animals.Aviaries and Lagoons are also pretty nice, although not as exciting or refreshing as one might think.Overall, there is much more content than in the previous game, more varied maps, more unique dinosaurs, more building and decoration options, and for the most part, the abundance of content is a good thing, and that is why I still recommend this game, especially to people who enjoyed the first one.However...My biggest criticism are also some of the new inclusions, unfortunately some of them became the foundation of the gameplay loop in this game.Those damn scientists...While the first game already had a considerable amount of micromanagement, this one takes it to the next level by introducing scientists, which have be hired first, then assigned to every major task (incubation, expeditions, research, etc.), then trained, fired, rested, because if not they will sabotage you... If it already sounds like a chore then perhaps it does so because it just is a chore. Honestly in a normal, non-sandbox gameplay i often feel like I am tending more for my scientists than for my dinosaurs. It's stupid, unnecessary, and the only way in which we can not care about scientists much, is if we hire many high-skilled generalists, which is honestly almost impossible, as they are such huge a money drain.The scientists mechanic is honestly my biggest complain, just because of how vital, and how annoying it is. It seems as if they were introduced just to artificially extend the game-time, in the first game in about 5 hours we could have a decent functioning park, in this one (unless on sandbox) there is no way in that time we could have more than 10 species.Another thing would be the campaign itself, which is honestly a joke for multiple reasons, one of them being that it ties to the stupid ending of Fallen Kingdom so much. Another much bigger problem I have with it would be that it is just incredibly short, and is honestly just pointless...Like after finishing it, it's just done, over, all that we have done is lost unless we load a save which we probably don't have, just cuz it was so short.The Biosyn campaign was much better than the original, and I spent about 8 hours in it, but what for if in the end everything I built is just gone. The campaign (at least the major part) ends as soon as we release the Giganotosaurus, and before I even had the chance to properly look at the darn thing, I was transported into a burned down version of the map, with all my progress essentially erased.I mean, I do get what they were going for with all of it, but honestly, what is the point of having a finite campaign in a park builder game? It's just a dumb decision in my opinion, and while the base game campaign kind of only serves as the tutorial, and is so short that loosing progress does not matter that much, the Biosyn campaign is what frustrates me, and that is because it was actually good, I had fun, built a nice big park, and in the end it was all taken away. Biosyn Chaos theory would have been much better.And for those who don't know, chaos theory is the "proper" campaign, in which we can essentially develop our parks forever. It's all good, except...In each scenario, we have to essentially start over. And well, it is kind of cool that each of them has their own story, problems and mechanics, but oh boy, do I just hate researching the same exact things in each maps, STARTING OVER WITH SCIENTISTS, digging up the same fossils, again, and again and again...The previous game had a fantastic, interconnected campaign, and even though we did start over with building a new park on each of the islands, all the research, all the species unlocked, it was all common between all of them, so the most tedious and boring actions, had to be essentially done just once.Well, not here, in JWE2, all the tedium has to be repeated in each scenario, before we can actually have fun developing our parks.Oh and why is there only a possibility of one expedition at a time? If you're making us unlock all the species over and over again, then at least give us an option to speed this process up!Well, all my criticism aside, I still enjoy the game, as I said, because of the dinosaurs. I love them, and for the most part I can tolerate the inaccurate Jurassic Park/World designs, if I want accuracy, there's Prehistoric Kingdom (or mods in the future).Speaking of mods, I was one of the mod creators for the first game, mostly changing up the Spinosaurus, but also adding some new species.The Spino in this game, unfortunately, again looks probably the worst out of all the dinos, and that is not due to the scientific inaccuracy, (because obviously they were going to use the movie design), it just feels... flat.Welp, this review is already too long, so I'll just end it there without proper conclusion.Yep, that's it.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a good game with some unnecessary aspects that make this game annoying at times.- It's a simple game. Not much management involved. There's a lot of new mechanics in this game that make this easier to play compared to the previous title. One single mechanic that comes to mind is putting a ranger post that can cover large areas to automate the activities of the Rangers, which wasn't present in the first game where you had to always assign your rangers to refill feeders. - This game includes all the original and the dlc dinosaurs from previous game, as well as new ones. Also includes underwater and flying dinosaurs.- More maps now.- Sandbox mode has a lot of options to modify your experience.- Dinosaurs not only look a lot better than previous game, but there's actually new dinosaur behavior systems in the game.- Addition of scientists to perform various operations and managing their activities, as well as keeping them stress free to avoid sabotage.- The graphics are amazing.- There's actually game speed control buttons now. The first game didn't have this.- Sandbox mode has a lot of options; however, the sandbox mode isn't really playable because majority of the buildings and dinosaurs are locked if you haven't finished campaign, challenges and chaos theory mode. This honestly makes no sense. We need to finish every mode just to unlock everything in sandbox mode to enjoy it properly? Who thought this was a good idea? I finished the campaign and I just wanted to play a sandbox game with a relaxed mind, and now the game is trying to force me to play other modes so I can unlock everything. Then what is the point of making the sandbox mode available?- Sandbox mode also does not allow you to decide if you want to carry on expeditions and do research to unlock items because of the previously stated feature; unlock everything by finishing every mode.- Dinosaurs can get stuck sometimes, and in cases like this, you need to reload a save. If vehicles get stuck, then you can use a button in the main menu that sends the vehicles to HQ.- Campaign is actually a tutorial. It's really short. If you have played the first game, then you mostly know a lot of things already and can jump right into sanb..... oh nevermind, challenges and chaos theory.Is this a good game? Yes. I'm enjoying it despite the annoyances but at the same time I feel that this isn't something that I would be paying full price to play and fortunately I didn't. I bought the first game when it came out and enjoyed the hell out of it because it was something completely new. Sadly this experience is slightly different than before. Get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the game as a casual player and Jurassic Park fan who just likes looking at the dinosaurs walk around and do things, but there are some gameplay issues at launch that I hope will be tweaked in the future. I would recommend this game if you're a Jurassic Park fan, but if not and you're just looking for a park builder game, maybe wait until its on sale or until more content is added.First off, the good things- The new North American environments are gorgeous! I loved the change of scenery through the main campaign. The trees, bushes, and ground textures blend really well. I also find the water painting tools easier to use than the first game. The dinosaur models are beautiful, and there is more skin customization options than the first game, though I think you can only mix and match two color regions and not actually get different skin patterns. There are so many dino socializing/behavioral animations, its a joy to just watch them interact. There are also different vocalizations. For example I had a lone sucho that was lonely by itself. It would pace around in one spot and sit down for long periods of time and make quiet sad calls, like it was broadcasting hoping for a reply but no answer :( But once it had enough friends its behavior completely changed and the suchos would walk around the enclosure as a group, eat together, and sleep together. It's very cute.You can also pause and fast forward the game now! And clicking C directly brings you into capture mode so you can freely look around and take pictures immediately, instead of having to access the capture mode from the escape menu like the first game. Very convenient, I could spend hours taking pictures of the dinosaurs. However I don't see a function to put the game in slow mo like you are able to in the first game?Unfortunately the main campaign is quite short and feels more like an intro than a whole campaign. I generally enjoy story/campaign content than any timed-challenge-type gameplay. Once you complete the main mission in each campaign level you immediately move on to the next location and cannot stay and continue building. Maybe its short because they couldn't make it longer without spoiling JW: Dominion coming out next June, so its more just some lore context for what happens between the 2nd and 3rd JW movie. There will probably be a DLC with more story content after the next movie comes out, but for now its much shorter than I expected. Chaos Theory mode is more similar to the first game where the goal is the build a 5 star park. The bulk of the game content is unlocked in Chaos Theory mode - I completed the main campaign and only unlocked 21/112 creatures. I like the new mechanic of having to hire and manage a staff team with individual perks, such as reduced cost or time for a task when that staff member is assigned. I like the concept of having a Paleo-Medical team separate from the Capture team. BUT it ends up being more of a hassle than engaging gameplay. There are some dinos that seems to keep fighting among themselves even though I've made sure their needs are all met? There is a new Dominance trait that can be altered through gene modification, I suspect it could be because I bred all the same dinos with the same Dominance stat which is why they won't stop fighting? But only a few species seems to fight and others just accept one individual as alpha with no problems. But it is a  loop of Dinos fight > send medic team to scan for injuries > send capture team to tranq injured dino > transport dino to medic facility and pay hospital bills > return dino to enclosure > dinos fight AGAIN > repeat process and pay mountains of hospital billsI also like how eggs now synthesize in batches so you can release multiples dinos at the same time! This is so nice for dinos who need a high minimum population to be comfortable. However, now the process is split into two steps. You have to spend money and personnel to synthesize the eggs first, and then you have to spend money AGAIN to incubate the eggs, and the price is multiplied per egg you choose to incubate from the batch. I don't know if this whole process is more expensive than the first game where you release one dino at a time, but it sure feels more expensive. I didn't have much problem with money in the first game and had a more relaxing experience, but in this game it feels like I am always running out of money? I don't think I'm THAT bad at the game but maybe I'm doing something wrong cause between paying for the usual upkeep, paying staff, and endless medical bills, everything is so expensive... It's a little frustrating that one wrong purchase at the wrong time could quickly lead to bankruptcy, I have to keep quick saving :')The new building customizations look great, but I haven't had time to look through all of them because my dinos keep injuring themselves and I spend most of my time fixing problems than having the time to play with cosmetics.I preordered the deluxe edition of the game because I know I would play the game regardless of initial reviews, but after trying it, it seems the gameplay is relatively similar to the first game. The graphics are definitely better, but gameplay and customization is more important, and I feel like for now the campaign is too short to justify the full $70 (deluxe edition). The experience is more of a park-micro-management game rather than a park-builder if that makes sense? If you like Planet Zoo then the customization options in this game will probably be disappointing. Frontier made both Planet Zoo and this game, they do amazing work! I can tell a lot of thought and work went into the new dinosaur behaviors such. The models, textures, and animations look great and I love the references to the Jurassic Park movies. If you're not much of a Jurassic Park fan, maybe wait until its on sale or until more content is added.

It takes some time to understand the measurements and do's and don'ts with placing the enclosures (I'm still trying to find my foot hold). Dinosaurs are way more detailed and are very well designed. Back to combat, a lot of time animals of the same species won't stop fighting eachother and is a big hurdle, at some point I stopped caring if they died or didn't. They act like kids of needing to fight eachother. I had triceratops constantly fighting and some others fought once and left it there. My knowledge is lacking to the causes for this conflict. Habitat requirements change when you have multiple species members in one enclosure. Example 1 Rex needs 10% water and 5% sand in its enclosure. While 2 Rexs need 20% water and 10% sand. (Not exact numbers, just an example) I forgot exact numbers for rex. Not sure why some dinos have this hate boner towards eachother sometimes. I usually just choose the eggs with positive traits. _childDocuments_.review: Better than the first part in all aspects. There are more dinosaurs, more flying spieces, more aquatic creatures, more decorations, more buildings, more everything. Dinosaurs are now interacting with each other. It's wonderful to watch. There are new locations, such as the desert of Arizona, the classic jungle or beautiful Canada with a little bit of snow. But the biggest news are scientists. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ scientists. You can hire scientists. They have their own statistics and everyone has their own special ability. That sounds good, doesn't it? But each of the scientists also has their own level of stress. If you give a scientist a lot of tasks, his stress level increases and then sabotage occurs. To prevent this, you have to give scientists a break and it takes time. And you don't have that much time. Why? Do you want to research something? You need a scientist for that. Need to send someone to dig up dinosaur fossils? You need a scientist for that. Do you need to examine those fossils? You need a scientist for that. Do you need to synthesize dinosaur DNA? You need a scientist for that. Do you need to create a dinosaur? You need a scientist for that. Do you need to treat a dinosaur? You need a scientist for that. And so on and so forth. It's annoying and everything takes a long time. There are four modes. Campaign, Chaos Theory, Challenge mode and Sandbox. The campaign was interesting but short and serves as a tutorial. Chaos Theory contains maps based on movies, something like What if ...? Challenge mode contains maps where you have to get 5 stars in a certain time and rewards are skins for dinosaurs. And the sandbox is a classic free game with dinosaurs without restrictions. Overall, this is a big upgrade of the original game with strange management of scientists.

_childDocuments_.review: Is it better than the first? Yes. Is it Planet Zoo with dinosaurs? No. Is it worth $60? Depends on how much you liked the first JWE. If you were able to forgive its faults, you can probably forgive the sequel's. I was able to, so I have quite enjoyed my time with JWE2. When in doubt, wait for a sale or updates.I finished the campaign, in no rush, in about 4 and a half hours. Yeah, it definitely feels like a tutorial from start to finish, without any real feeling of progression that was in the first game's campaign (besides your carried over staff, which will drain your funds if you keep training them). I like the thematic of wildlife reserve and conservation work, but they needed to do more with it than simply a tutorial. It does end up feeling like a cliffhanger for advertising the delayed movie.Anyway, I am mixed on the new tedium work. Some parts make sense, some don't, and some just feel unbalanced. For how necessary scientists are, they're expensive to keep training good ones. It is kind of a bottleneck in a bottleneck that they have to do everything and yet can be prohibitively expensive. Kind of like how multiple jeep teams are a locked upgrade when they have to do so much more compared to the first game. Plus the AI is too stupid to live. My first time assigning a task to one had it driving into a helicopter and stun-locking them both. While I do like the addition of vets, it makes little sense to me that they cannot tranq anything like an actual vet does.I am quite happy with the new environments, weather effects, and cast of dinosaurs to unlock, though. (And I do mean unlock, since sandbox requires unlocking like the first. It doesn't bother me so much even though I prefer sandbox play that they chose to make it more an end game reward.) The new behaviors are pretty nice, too. I am still experimenting, but the old game's rules don't really apply. Which makes them more dynamic, but also fussy. *shrug* I like the dinosaurs, though, and look forward to seeing more of them. If you liked the first JWE, go for it. However, the improvements aren't enough to win back anyone that didn't like the first game in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Jurassic World Evolution 2 takes players on a thrilling journey into the world of dinosaur park management. With its improved graphics, expanded roster of dinosaur species, and enhanced gameplay features, it builds upon the foundation set by its predecessor. The game offers an immersive experience, allowing players to create and customize their own Jurassic World, from building enclosures to researching new dinosaurs. The inclusion of a new narrative-driven campaign adds depth to the gameplay, while the challenge mode tests players' management skills. However, some players have expressed concerns about the game's lack of innovation and limited customization options. Despite these minor shortcomings, Jurassic World Evolution 2 remains a must-play for fans of the franchise and those who enjoy simulation and management games.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people are being very harsh to this game because of a few things that is has that they don't like. But if these people actually played the game they would be able to see that a lot of their issues may not even be bugs or bad things, but instead they could be things that you could solve by playing more. As a huge fan of the original game and a lover of the movies and dinosaurs overall, this game is amazing for almost all people who love dinosaurs. It is true that the campaign is pretty short at around 4-5 hours, but Chaos Theory mode makes up for it by adding a lot more stuff. Frontier has also added Marine Reptiles and pterosaurs who both look amazing. This game is not like planet zoo though in how much managing there is with the guests. This game is more focused on the dinosaurs than the managing. So if you like or love dinosaurs and park building then this will definitely be fun for you. But if you are looking for a game that involves a lot more managing I would get something like Planet Zoo or Planet Coaster. If you want to game to play in sandbox with infinite money then you should know that YOU DO HAVE TO UNLOCK THE DINOSAURS IN OTHER MODES if you want to use them in sandbox. Unlocking them is as simple as having a single one in your park though so if you do like the game this will be pretty easy. All in all this game is amazing for dinosaur lovers but if you don't like dinosaurs this isn't really the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Jurassic World Evolution 2

_childDocuments_.review: First I would like to say I LOVE Jurassic Park. While other kids where playing with light sabers, I was playing with dinosaurs. This is my thing! I was so pumped! But after playing for a couple days I was pretty let down... But we need more dinosaur games so I won't give a thumbs down but I'll list what I've found annoying.The game's graphics are of course, awesome. The ai for NPC's and Dino's is great, nothing has gotten stuck or glitched. Voice clips are great and easy to follow. But, if you want a game where you can decorate your park, have a relaxed progression, or do not wish to micro manage.. Leave now. You do not get everything in sandbox unless you unlock it through challenges and you will have to micro manage most everything. I'll try not to waste time and keep it to complaints I think would be helpful. - It's obvious that the creators tried to lengthen the play time by forcing you to micro manage things, but it's done to an extreme that isn't fun.- I don't mind waiting on things, but the speed up button will become your best friend. I love watching my dino's, but at the same time there's to much to do for me to sit around smelling the roses. So I miss out on watching my creatures and instead just see them all zip around unnaturally fast just so I can collect fossils.- After the first Jurassic World game, we asked for decorations! And this time around we did get... a couple. all the decorations are tiny and look alike, there are only about 20 to choose from (mostly the same flag a different color), their barely worth using unless you want the exact same thing everywhere. Enclosures are kinda the same. You get a brush that adds trees, shrubs, and water.. but you can't actually choose where anything but rocks and water go. The paint brush circle thing is also much to big even on it's smallest setting. Not much wiggle room for creativity, and that's one of my favorite parts.  -  Money is also a HUGE issue in challenge modes. I've never had much trouble in the past amassing money in games like this, but they actively keep you on your toes. It's an interesting thing, I don't hate the idea... But I went from making millions a minute to being so far in the red that, after 8 hours of play, it force quite the challenge telling me I failed. I had near zero time to try and sell, repair, or just process what happened. This happens way way waaaay to much. One storm late game could ruin your entire run through for no real reason. There is no challenge when things are out of your control and it auto fails you quickly. - Scientists... Again, I don't mind the idea behind it and I wouldn't mind fiddling with their skill points more but... it's just not all that fun to deal with them. The starting 3 you get aren't usually all that great. But to get more you must research, which is fine! Till you realize you're forced to waste your new points on your less then good scientists (or fire one and hope for a better replacement). You do not get a lot of ways to increase their skills. If you want anything in the game or need to finish an objective quickly for challenge mode, you better hope they have enough points or you just have to sit there waiting, fail, or start over. Most can also only do a few tasks before they need to take an expensive work free rest too. Not a HUGE problem, as I'm sure it's fun for some people to figure out the best way to use them, but kinda annoying enough to mention.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a huge improvement over the first, although it's still not great. It's good, and the detail and animation on the dinosaurs, underwater and flying creatures, are fantastic. The chaos theory scenarios are a lot of fun, although the main campaign is extremely short. I think this is because it was meant to come out after dominion, but because that movie was delayed they had to cut a large chunk of the missions so as not to spoil that movie. Hopefully when that comes out we'll get a slew of new missions and dinos. The increased control over the park, like amenities and such, is welcome, although parks still look and feel very samey. I wish there were more items to add to enclosures, like there is in planet zoo, and far more items to put around your park.My only real complaints are the lack of missions, the annoying storms and the medical system. I wish it could be automated, or at least some parts of it. When you have a large park you'll be beeped at every couple of minutes because of a disease, usually the common cold that you can't do anything about, or because some dinos have slapped each other and one needs to go to the treatment facility. I'd say this is a 7/10. I'm very much looking forward to future expansions and content. This is a big step up from the previous game, but not quite as big a step as I'd hoped.

_childDocuments_.review: Improves a lot of things compared to the first game. Some of the typical grindy bits to unlock every thing are still around but you can have a fun experience just playing Sandbox mode if you so choose which can now be a little bit more like the traditional 'park builder' that most people probably want to play anyways without all the "Direct control this capture helicopter and go shoot 'X' dinosaur for arbitrary reasons!". Major flaws for me were...-Some of the level requirements during Chaos Theory mode were insufferable. 90% guest comfort on one level made me have to literally bulldoze my entire park just to set it up in a way that could actually get me to 90% because it wasn't possible otherwise.-Some of the environmental needs of the Dinosaurs were almost impossible to meet. At one point I had 3 sauropods in an enclosure and they kept insisting they didn't have enough Forest despite their entire enclosure being nothing but. It wasn't unique to them either. There were several species that are just plain aggravating to please.-The Monorail. You need to have it for the 'Transport' Stat of you park, but makes the park look ridiculous and often blocks off a great deal of usable land just to put it in. -The Lagoon was a little lack lustre. While I love finally having access to aquatic forms of extinct species, there was no Customization available which was a bummer. Would've been nice to landscape the interior of the lagoons like you could with the Aviary. -The Vehicles drive terribly. There are times where you literally end up pivoting vertically while balancing on the corner of your head light. They turn like garbage, spin out, slide, and the slightest bump into anything sends pieces of the vehicle flying off. Feels like driving a bumper car at the county fair only with Dinosaurs and electric fences. It's not nearly as fun as it sounds. Not a perfect game but probably the best Jurassic park builder game out there.

_childDocuments_.review: Had 120 hours on JWE1 on PS4 and this game improves on it in every regard. Even the little things like being able to release multiple dinosaurs of the same species in one hatchery bay, instead of being constrained to one dino:one bay. Adding marine and avian species is amazing too, with more creatures being added with DLC. The different style of buildings from the different eras allows you amazing levels of customisation.Only negatives are:1) The Challenge modes are just tedious. You don't have to get 5 stars under par time, so it's just a pointless goal. Furthermore, the gameplay loop is: wait for money to tick up; spend it; wait for money to tick up; spend; wait for money; spend, repeat ad infinitum. Completely boring and stupid way to slow down the game. Mod menus are your friend here.2) The big DLCs are way too expensive compared to the amount of content they provide. Only buy them when they're 70-80% off. Creature packs are whichever floats your boat. Best imo is the Prehistoric Marine Species pack.If a game can improve on its predecessor to the point where the first is totally obsolete, then it's an instant recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Hire a genetic engineering specialist to research a wider walking path.Grind through endless celebrity cameo missions to piecemeal your way through the same content over and over again.Manually refuel buildings, because you are part park manager and part minimum wage maintenance worker.Suffers from a lack of clear vision in the gameplay loop, preposterous amounts of micromanagement, and the dead weight of the franchise.The game would be fantastic, and I would recommend it, if they cut a bunch of unnecessary content and had all sandbox content unlocked from the start.That being said if you have hours to spend listening to voice actors and being taught the same basic gameplay loop over and over again, and love the idea of being cornered in a dark alley and mercilessly bludgeoned into a fine dead horse pulp with tedious cookie clicker mechanics, there's a great dinosaur park building game floating around in there...  if you can find the time to enjoy it before your scientists demand a $75,000 nap.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite good!In terms of management, it's fairly simple. In terms of being a sandbox game, it comes with a bunch of settings which allow you to alter the way you play the game, leave out certain aspects or make some things easier (or harder!). This offers plenty of levels of difficulty, and is sure to challenge you in just the right way.To me however, what is most impressive about the game, and caught me by surprise. Is the amount of detail in the dinosaurs, the models look amazing! With plenty of options for skin colors and patterns, you can have a varied enclosure in no time. And the interactions the animals have with their surroundings and each other blew me away. I wasn't expecting this level of detail, but I'm really happy the game has this.My only gripe is that some building aspects at times- feel sluggish. Placing fences around a BIG enclosure feels slow, and the game could benefit from more details spacial settings, to help with alligning roads/fences/habitats with each other rather than having to eyeball it all. But that's a minor detail! IF you spend enough time, you can still get it just how you want it.At full price, it might not be for everyone, but if you find it on sale or in a discounted bundle with some DLC; it'll sure keep you going for a while!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm 18 hours into this game, so while I still haven't experienced everything the game has to offer, I feel I've had enough experience to give my thoughts. I've currently beaten the campaign mode and I'm currently going through the Jurassic Park 1 story mission. I haven't unlocked any of the aquatic reptiles yet, however. Here's what I think so far:This game is very addicting. I played a lot of the original game, and in my opinion, this one is just leagues better than the original. The needs of the dinosaurs are more realistic this time. The t-rex, for example, prefers sand over grass. Herbivores now eat directly from the plants placed in their enclosures, rather than from feeders. So a dinosaur that eats nuts will require nut bearing plants to be placed in their enclosures. The downside to this is that this does limit what dinosaurs are compatible, since you may not always be able to balance the needs of multiple species. Some dinosaurs will also fight as a group now. While a t-rex can easily destroy a single raptor, it may have some trouble if a whole pack of raptors start climbing all over it.Buildings are also highly customizeable now. You can change the decorations, the colors, even the orientation of the door. I can see myself spending a lot of time on this later, but right now, I'm just trying to satisfy the mission objectives.The mode most people will be interested in is the sandbox mode, which is where the player is free to create whatever park they want on whatever map they want. Playing other modes will unlock more stuff to work with in the sandbox mode. More dinosaurs, more building types, etc.Unfortunately, some of the weaknesses from the first game carry over. While we do have the legendary Jeff Goldblum reprising his role, many of the other voice actors are stand ins for the original actors, and the quality of the voice acting is...generally pretty bad. And the dialog is very cringy at times. The story itself...well, it exists. It serves its purpose. It's about as good as one might expect for a park simulator.It's a little disappointing that only one month in, the game is getting DLC. That feels a little soon, like they were withholding content from the base game to sell us later. However, while the big wigs in charge just want to make money, that doesn't necessarily reflect the attitudes of the developers who are actually working on the game. I've found that the developers listen very closely to fan feedback, and I get the sense that they care very much about the quality of the game. With the previous game, they've made some pretty big changes to the game via patches, whether overhauling dinosaur behavior, rescaling the sizes of certain dinosaurs, or creating a new need for the spinosaurus so that it would prefer enclosures with a lot of water. If you go to the Frontier forums to report bugs or give feedback, they do actually read it and respond. There was a feature I was going to suggest to them for this game, but i found out they already added it today via a free update.Over my playthrough, I learned a few things that the game doesn't really tell you. Here are some tips to improve your experience:1. Dinosaurs need to be monitored for changes, since this time around, you do not have psychic knowledge of the status of all of your dinosaurs. For this purpose, the game provides a ranger outpost, and will instruct the player to assign a ranger to the outpost. This is useful, as it will remove a lot of micromanaging from the game. However, dinosaurs will frequently attack the rangers when they enter, and replacing a jeep when it is destroyed can be costly. What the game doesn't tell you is that you can also assign a helicopter to the same ranger post. This way, when the ranger is in danger, the helicopter will circle around the enclosure and automatically tranquilize dinosaurs that become aggressive.2. If you've played the previous game, you might have played around with the aviary, which was added late in the game. This sequel's version of that is very different, however. Domes can be attached this time, creating larger structures, and you are going to want to do that. Attach at least two together, and don't try editing the environments inside until after you've built them, or else the terrain might prevent you from building. If the creature living inside eats fish, then you'll need a decently sized watering hole to place a feeding station in. If the game won't let you place one, just make it bigger.3. When playing through story modes, be very careful with your money consumption. I ran out of money in the middle and had to revert to a previous save, because I realized I had no source of income, since the park can't be opened until late in the story. So be conservative, and if you find yourself losing cash too fast, fire some scientists, if you don't need them.4. If a story mission requires you to dig up fossils of a specific dinosaur, and you don't have any dig sites for that dinosaur, you probably have to unlock the location via research. The t-rex is one such case.5. If you find yourself needing to do research, and your current scientists aren't up to the task, you have a few options. First, while having a jack-of-all-trades can be nice for general tasks. it's also a good idea to have specialists, who have high stats in one specific trait. You can hire some specialists, if you can find them. Another option is training. If you have the training points, you can create a specialist out of an otherwise middle-of-the-road scientist. I tend to save a few training points so I can respond to my needs. If you can't train a scientist, you probably need to unlock a higher level of training via research.6. When you first place a dinosaur in an enclosure, you'll want to monitor them to see if you need to make any changes. However, a dinosaur will take a few minutes to walk around their new enclosure and establish their territory. Keep in mind that needs are only met if they are within the dinosaur's territory. So if the game tells you that a dinosaur is "missing forest," and you've placed plenty of forestation in your enclosure, you may just need to give them a moment to find it. You can see the limits of a dinosaur's territory represented in blue when you have them selected and are in the environmental needs tab.7. If you're playing with mouse and keyboard (which I recommend), there are a few shortcuts. R will bring up the menu of the nearest ranger station. T will bring up the menu of the nearest medical facility. P will let you start placing paths. M gives you a different way of viewing the park, highlighting important objects that may be otherwise difficult to find. There are probably other shortcuts I haven't found yet, but these are pretty useful.8. One thing that always confused me in the last game was when it would tell me that guest amenities were in high demand in a certain area of the park, but then I place something there, and no one uses it. It just sits there, draining money. The same was also true in this game, but now I understand it. Guests will only use amenities in crowded areas, and they tend to travel on routes near attractions, such as viewing galleries. This time around, you can also place attractions such as cinemas to redirect guests flow to low crowded areas. This will help to maximize profit, as well as improve ratings.

_childDocuments_.review: While it's true that the game plays very similarly to the previous, I'd say there are more than enough improvements and changes to justify calling this 'Jurassic World Evolution 2' and not just a DLC. With that being said, I will admit that I don't think the $60 entry point is worth it, and $70 for deluxe is very much not worth it. I bought the deluxe edition just so I could determine whether or not it has a $10 value, and honestly you can skip it until it's on sale unless you HAVE to have those 5 extra dinos that it adds plus the skins that are only eye-candy. I'd say this game would be a solid $40 game. I'm not upset at paying full-price though because this is truly a beautiful eye-candy of a game, and is completely worth it if you're obsessed with dinosaurs. I imagine they probably had to price it at $60 and $70 due to the Universal licensing. I've played through the first few campaign missions so far with zero issues or hiccups and everything seems to flow pretty seamlessly together. I do wish they had implemented the ability to choose how far shadows draw out, as it's a bit jarring when you zoom out and see a quarter of your map with shadows and everything else without shadows, but thats about my only complaint.I think the errors and bugs that others are reporting is due to their hardware, which is not the fault of the player as not everyone can afford high-end PCs. This is definitively a graphic-intensive game that appears to have been built with only next-gen hardware in mind, and I can imagine anyone who doesn't have at least a decent RTX 2XXX is going to run into issues. Likewise the DLSS that you can enable in the settings is awesome, and setting it to 'quality' increases FPS exponentially with no visible graphical difference, but graphics cards that are older than RTX 2XXX won't be able to take advantage of it. It's certainly no Planet Zoo type of game, but I also don't believe it was advertised to be one. It does a lot of the heavy lifting for you, and the actual amount of items/buildings/etc that you have is fairly limited, which I think is by design. Playing through the campaign so far, I get the impression this is more-so a game for people who don't care about micro-managing every little detail like tycoon-style games, and who instead want to be more hand-off and just appreciate a park full of beautifully-rendered dinosaurs with really good AI.
