_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: 9/10 - This game is great. Go get it-The combat has been refined, bringing back and upgrading everything from previous games. Free jumping, posture damage, powerstancing, weapon arts being not only fun and useful, but also interchangeable at any time.-The game is just plain beautiful.-The world is MASSIVE. Every time you think you're close to being done, you unlock a new part of the map, be it above or underground.-Cool main bosses-The massive world, while I rated it as positive, is riddled of caves, graves and dungeons that feel copypasted. You'll be fighting the same bosses time and time again (tree spirits and magma wyrms between the most annoying, personally, to fight). This might hurt your opinion of the game if you're doing a "completionist" first playthrough, but it won't matter if you do a second one (or more, obviously), since you'll know what to get and where to get it, and most of the time can just rush to the place it's in. -The open world really does not work with Fromsoft's NPC questlines. Have fun trying to find the next NPC's location without a guide. You'll constantly find yourself breaking/skipping steps in quests because you progressed too far without even realizing.-Speaking of NPC questlines, some of them are unfinished. They don't have an ending, the NPC will just disappear forever.-Optimization so far is horrible, dropping frames (or god forbid, giving short freezes) as early as THE FIRST BOSS YOU FIND IN THE WILD.Something worth mentioning, the OST in this game feels particularly lackluster. Some really good songs here and there, but are few and far between.edit 22/11/2022: game still good just.

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be a long one, go get a cup of coffee if you care enough about it. You know that feeling of being completely hooked to a brand new thematic world? Elden Ring manages to do it just as you start your journey in The Lands Between. Fight your journey through dungeons and catacombs, find treasures, get to know your enemies and discover brand new areas, each containing new lore and development that can be discovered by various meanings, talking to NPCs, reading items descriptions, finding patterns that links the bosses and lords of that area to the creatures there. It's everything we always wanted in a Classic Fantasy Medieval RPG. For the first days If I could I would not have stopped playing this game by any means, I just wanted to discover more and more and unravel it's secrets, so much fun, especially when you have friends to talk about and when you realize, they are in a totally different area that you don't even got to explore yet, but the game gives you that freedom, you are allowed to do what you can in order to progress, by your own pace and your own way. The combat got much better from previous titles in the soul series, being able to jump is amazing and having your horse to battle along side you creates a feeling that the other games simply couldn't give you. The hitboxes are better, the battles are fluid ( When you don't have that FPS drop from nowhere, but I'll get there ) and I truly believe that everyone can enjoy this game, you are the one who defines the actual difficulty of the game, there's a reason people can beat this game without getting hit, and even though of course, many bosses are tough especially if you want to play a certain way, you can and will GIT GUT, take your time. After you are done with that annoying boss the adrenaline rush you will have will be worth it. The soundtrack and the world sounds are just amazing, you can hear the noises inside dungeons, the miners banging their pickaxes against the rocks, the screeches of the creatures, the mad-whispering of the anguished souls, the water flows, the birds chirping, everything feels natural and involving. Everything made so that the world feels alive and true to it's nature. As far as the lore goes, it's a Souls game, it will be cryptic but this one gives you much more to know about, it hints you about it's mysteries and what's happening in a way that feels more natural and approachable. And all the endings and ways to get there will allow you to speculate in your own way if that happened because it had to be this way or you couldn't really do anything else about it, letting a lot for your own mind to imagine and distinguish. You'll have your own theories at the end of the game, wondering what could possibly follow your decisions. What will happen to that world after that lowly tarnished changed it. Well,  not everything is as amazing as it could be, being very straightforward, some recycled bosses felt a bit underwhelming and the optimization could be much better. After the first patch things got better, and it's far from being unplayable, but the game still struggles in some areas, and that it's not dependent on hardware, rather, it's probably related to the way it was programmed. Hopefully the will keep following with the intended patches and keep improving that segment as much as they can.All in all, it truly is an amazing game and I'm happy that it managed to keep up with our expectations, it's certainly a title that Ill keep coming back to play more in the future. It's hard nowadays for games that have an open world to not feel empty and to not make the player feel tired, they sure managed to do it in a much better way than other recent titles could, and that alone is something that I was sure looking forward to.

_childDocuments_.review: I will be revisiting this review later, but 10 hours in and I'm having a great time.  This is one of those few games that I can recommend at full price.EDIT: I have beaten the game, and have played for 75 hours.  Time for a more comprehensive review.This game is a fantastic entry point into Souls for people who bounced off the series before, while still managing to be a top tier entry into the genre for those who were already on board (such as myself).  The open world is expertly done, taking many lessons from Breath of the Wild and improving upon it with a better reward structure for exploration, tense encounters with many different types of adversaries, and a wide possibility of builds for your character to progress through the game with.The sense of discovery found in this game is near unmatched.  Every major area feels unique in both visual aesthetic and gameplay requirements.  Quite a lot of time and love went into making it a joy for players to stumble into areas that were much grander than initially perceived, and those moments just seem to keep coming.  Like all Souls games, Elder Ring has its share of secrets areas and bosses that many people will never see, even after hitting the credits.  While I encourage you to explore actively, I would also advise you to not look up those secrets until after you complete the game, and let your first adventure in the world be truly your own.  Trust me, you will have plenty of resources without having to resort to any walkthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Very well implemented gameplay mechanics on open world, climatic design, well established universe that just sparks detail with lots of places to discover. Elden Ring is an example of how souls like games can be the best. We kill thousands of creatures to find hundreds of places and items waiting to be explored on a huge open world map, and the feeling of freedom and exploration that the game gives you while doing this is incredibly good. I'm actually surprised that without any quest indicators or quest info menu they managed to do an open world game like this and you don't even realise how time flies while you are roaming around and discovering stuff. It accomplishes the RPG elements very well. They have an incredibly wide range of items, detailed character creation, detailed stat management, different outcomes from both side quests and main quests etc.If I want to say briefly the strongest aspects of the game: The range of items, sounds and atmosphere, gameplay mechanics, the feeling of discovery and the feeling of winning are very good.But if you ask me if there are any bad side of this game, I think there are. I think it's definitely not a 10/10 game as most people say. Yes, it does its job as an open world RPG game very well, and it does this in a "souls-like" way. Thats not an easy thing to do but for me to say 10/10, the game has to be flawless. I think the worst part of this game is the online mode. Especially the "invade" mode, there are very frequent situations such as errors in the invade mode, players constantly glitching, not being able to find a match for a long time, and when the opposing player logs out, your pvp item is turn into garbage, waste. I also had lag issues in most of my matches. The second bad feature that caught my eye is that although the variety of weapons is very large, unfortunately the weapon development system does not work very efficiently. Let's say, for example, you made a weapon +10 and you have about 50 weapons in your bag. Your game time has passed 20 hours, now if you want to change weapons after this time, it is not very easy to change. At least, there could be things like transferring the pluses we spent from the weapons we developed to +10 to another weapon. In 70 hours of gameplay, you will usually only using between 5-6 weapons. The rest of the weapons will unfortunately be a waste and never used because of this system. The third feature that I did not like was that the movements of the game were very bland. No animation is used in an AAA game, as if it were an indie game, and this causes scenes that seem strange to your eyes or as if you are playing an outdated game while you are playing. After you've completed half of the way through the game. As whole areas and boss fights end up being copy-pasted and refurbished. The scenery might change a little, the enemies might be differently coloured, but they're same as before. And for the last, the PC port is one of the worst of all time. There is no proper keyboard and mouse support, there are random locked keybindings for menu navigation. It's really so hard and bad to play it with keyboard and mouse.  I am not at all surprised that it was chosen as the game of the year, because apart from the bad features I mentioned above, there is no other bad feature or missing side in the game and this year except playstation exclusive games there were not a strong competitor against Elden Ring. If you are not familiar with souls-like games, it will take some time to get used to the game, but after you get used to it, at least 60 hours of gameplay time with agony and glory awaits you.  8/10 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: performance is a hit or miss, many people are complaining having a good PC and not having good perfomance.I have a RTX 2060 , i7-7700k and 16GB RAM, and the game runs fine on high settings, except for random stutters (which also happens in low settings).Pros:- the size of the world (imo this game is CHEAP for the amount of content and quality it has)- builds- equipment variety and appearance- sightseeing- progression - bosses- combat, maybe like DkS3, but with less R1 spam and more items and weapon skills- lore and quests- feels very familiar compared to Miyazaki's soulsbornes, if you played those, you'll feel at home, while still encountering new challenges and mechanics- respeccing a character is easy and can be redone  18 times per NG/playthrough, you can also rename and remake the appearance of the character for free, so you don't have to create another character if you want to change your build- my first playthrough was 270 hours long :^) I explored every area and missed a few NPC questsCons: (mostly nitpicking)- input lag, input buffer and input decision (when you attack and then buffer a "twohanding", an attack will come out if you let go of Y button)- there's too many actions for a few buttons in the gamepad, sometimes you may be unable to change shield/weapon because there's 2 interactables at your feet- frequent stutters (likely related to multiplayer)- multiplayer connection is rather unstable I guess I got gud... a bit- the world is huge but there's a limit of 10 messages per character ("fixed" in an update)- recycled bosses, enemies, and dungeon structures (I don't see it as a problem personally, given the size of the game) colosseum update lets goooooooooo- there's so much content/quests that you have to note it down so you don't forget what you should do, there should be some kind of note system in the game, or the easier way: quest tracker (yuck).- map needs more and better markers, why is there a limit, and why can't you highlight/search for specific markers? or even name the markers? The npc names update was a step in the right direction- item sorting is a hidden mechanic lol- you can't order your spells, only add and remove them, come on FROM, this is 2022- late game bosses are boring and random, even if you get 60 VIT you can stil get one shot by combos bosses do.  I must try another playthrough to use properly the throwable items and buffs, though they are very boring to use that seems to be the necessary edge to get through hard(er) stuff.- dual wielding jump R2 is OP, it deals more damage, staggers more, and recovers faster and uses less stamina than standing R2, why?

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. I can't believe how easily I've sunk so many hours into the game. I'm close to the ending of my first playthrough, and I think I have a grip on things that are done well and things that irked me.Good:- It's stunning. Every area I visit is beautiful with amazing views.- Very free and broad gameplay. You can play how you want and it will probably work. If you want to switch things up there are a multitude of ways to do so and enjoy different weapons and builds.- Uniqueness. Areas might have some recurring enemies, but it's mostly new, unique, and cool enemies you encounter.- Audio. The music and sounds are just great. Sad to see it's not on Spotify yet.- Story. As a typical FromSoftware game, the story is deep and somewhat obscured. There is a clear narrative, and a multitude of characters that you can meet and help along the way. Going into this game blind is great fun for what you can find and discover.- FREEDOM. The biggest one is that it's open world. In comparison to previous games you can just go somewhere else. In for example Dark Souls: if you're stuck on a boss, you could very well be stuck in the whole game and story. Not in Elden Ring. You can keep bashing your head against the wall hoping it breaks, but just as well you just turn around and go explore somewhere else. This is by far the best thing that keeps you going.Bad:- Bosses and camera. Some bosses are difficult not because of what they can do, but because the camera and targeting screws you over. It's very hard to adjust and if you die to something like this you don't feel bested, but cheated. Luckily this is more an outlier than the norm.- Boss mechanics. Normally it is all about GITTING GUD, but there are a few bosses that feel as if the developers were like ''let's make it hard by increasing the numbers, not by adding to the fight''. It's okay for a boss or two, but it can be aggrevating to see a boss that has unreasonable health, hoping that you fail once so it can kill you instantly. Leveling up helps somewhat, but there are still a few bosses that feel disproportionately beefy and damaging.- Lacking direction. I love how immersive every part of the story is, but there is a caviat to it. Sometimes you talk to an NPC and they tell you where to go, but it's a far off destination and goal or you've never heard of it. A few hours later into the game you have no idea where they said to go, and there is no way of recalling what they said. You're forced to search it up or hope that you stumble upon it by chance. I wouldn't want a journal quest marker thing at all, but for example a journal with one line per character would help keep track of what you've encountered.Overall this game is a near 10/10. Giving it a 9 would be too low, but a 10 would mean nothing could be improved upon so let's give it a 9.5/10! Give it a try if you're unsure, just remember that it is not Skyrim. This is a FromSoftware game, expect to die and fail at every turn and relish in overcoming it.

_childDocuments_.review: Well... I did it. I finished a "Souls"-type game. Am I glad I did it? Yes, I think so. Would I go back and do it again if I could? No, probably not. Not for a very, very long time anyways.Seriously. It's obviously a well-made, high quality game, But MAN, does it have some issues.WARNING: This review is more of a vent than anything. I actually do think it's a decent game, just not worthy of the hype it's garnered. The combat is based almost entirely around timing and learning enemy attack patterns. This isn't a problem in and of itself. The right kind of player would love learning the precise time to press space against each kind of enemy. However, I am not that kind of player. I like to play base-builder type games and occasionally mix in some hack-and-slash rpg and shooter titles when I don't feel like thinking too hard. If I'm going to put in effort to master a game, I like to do it by planning my moves ahead of time and experimenting with the tools I'm given, not by mastering each in-the-moment micro-twitch movement. If you're like me and flip-flop between games like Team Fortress 2 and Factorio, I'd recommend staying away from this one.However, I think that the timing-based combat where one of the game's first huge problems rears its ugly head. For a game so heavily based on timing and careful movement, it has some awfully laggy inputs. Dodge-roll, one of the most important moves in the game, has a delay on it, about a half second, between when you press the button and when your character even starts to move. In the middle of this game's tightly timed fights, that's HUGE. It took me hours upon hours of wondering why dodging felt so bad before I realized what was going one.After looking at some online guides, I learned that this delay is apparently part of every Souls title and that most players simply consider mastering it to be part of the challenge. I suppose they're right, but think about it anyways: A significant portion of this game's challenge finds its source in intentionally poor, laggy controls.I'm also not sure that the developers ever heard the phrase "quality of life" when designing this game. There are all kinds of weird, inconvenient things in this game that simply defy explanation. Why aren't the all-important health and mana potions bound to a unique key? Why can we only use the special effect on our right-hand when we can just briefly unequip it to use our left-hand weapon? Why do equipped-but-unused weapons add to your carry weight? If you're quick with the menus, it's perfectly possible to keep your auxiliary weapons hidden in your inventory and then only equip them when needed. So... Why make us deal with the carry weight issue? Is rapid-clicking through menus supposed to be another combat skill we master?And I think I would be amiss if I didn't point out the poor early gameplay progression of sorcery/intelligence characters.I picked the "Astrologer" starting class, since I felt like playing a spellslinger. I booted into the game and started looking for better gear. But... Nothing. I tried everything I could think of. I followed the path the game sent me down. Nothing. I headed east to the higher level area. No new spells. No new staffs. Still nothing. It was beyond the twenty hour mark that I finally got a new staff as a random drop from an enemy in the high level area. And it was garbage. Literally worse than my starting weapon unless you happened to be using one or two ultra-niche "rock breaker" spells... And I only found them found those hours and hours later still!It was only when a friend clued me in to their location that I was finally able to get my hands on some better spells. Although they were actually pretty close to the starting area, there's nothing directing you there. If you happen to miss the one particular set of ruins where the vendor is hiding, you're screwed. No new spells for ages.Even then, it was probably past the fifty hour mark that I finally found a staff able to replace the starting staff (which by then I had upgraded to be better than most non-unique staffs), and hours more before I hit the minimum level to use it.Let me emphasize something. My friend TOLD me where to get better spells. I started this game determined not to look at the wikis. I tend to be really bad about that, using wikis to look up secrets. However, this was not the game with which I should have made that resolution because, to paraphrase that same friend's words, "This is a game meant to be played with the wiki open on a second monitor."Now, we reach the crux of the game's design flaws. THIS. ENTIRE. GAME. IS. MADE. OF. SECRETS. Like, seriously... I'm not sure that it's possible for a single player to complete a single side quest in this game without looking up instructions on the wiki. At least, not without spending hours upon hours upon hours scouring every last corner of the map for the next arbitrary NPC location and talking with every character second and third times to make sure that some new dialog option hasn't appeared. Even characters who supposedly ACTIVELY WANT YOUR HELP will barely tell you what they want or even why you should help them. e.g. One character, upon first meeting, will ask for your help in her "war against the Erdtree." At this point in the game, I still barely even knew what the Erdtree was other than really tall and glowing. There is no option to ask her why she wants a war against the Erdtree, or how even her cryptic assassinations quests help to combat the Erdtree.That character was nothing but a small contributor to what I consider to be the game's single biggest problem. This game is so cryptic, so utterly and incomprehensibly obtuse and obsessed with secrets, that I don't think I could have told you what the plot was had I not read it on the wiki. Everything else I could have forgiven if the story had just... y'know... Made sense.What's your character's motivation? When you start the game, you are greeted with a cutscene instructing you to "become Elden Lord." Why? Who is my character? Why did they just wake up in this temple? Was the voice in the cutscene something my character experienced? As far as I can tell, this is the story of some psychopath who wakes up and immediately goes on a rampage, killing half the remaining lucid people in this undead wasteland and subjugating the other half. Part of the fun of an open-world game is supposed to be learning about the world, meeting its people and seeing how they live. In Elden Ring though, the world seems to be nothing more than setpiece. A pretty backdrop while you ride between dungeon to boss fight to dungeon. There are people who like this stuff. Lore junkies who will spend hours making crazy theory videos on Youtube. However, if after playing through a whole game I can't identify any motive other than "go kill stuff and get stronger so you can sit on the chair next to the big tree," I think there might be a problem.The game's problem's can be summed up in one fight: Maliketh. Apparently, you fight him to get something called "Destined death." What is that? It's never explained (Cryptic Lore). He moves incredibly fast, and your attack windows are comically slim (Janky timings). Forget Malenia, this is the real hardest boss in the game.  However, there's a secret item that exists specifically to fight him. You'd be lucky to find the item without going to the wiki and looking it up, and even if you did find it you'd be hard-pressed to figure out how to use it (wiki on other screen). He kills you quick. Fights tend to last less than a minute. However, the nearest respawn point is a thirty second walk away. There is no reason it couldn't have been right next to the boss door. It didn't add any challenge, all it did was make the boss take longer (quality of life).TLDR; If you just want to git good at fighting big bosses in a pretty landscape, this game is for you. Otherwise, maybe don't believe the hype.

_childDocuments_.review: Elden Ring is not a flawless game, but it's a game that the more hours you spend on it, the more feels almost unreal for the sheer size, amount of content and average quality.Sure, it has a bit of recycled stuff here and there (but let's get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ real, there's more UNIQUE content here than in few other games combined, so what if some mini-bosses are re-used more than once across the game) and sure, the progression curve applied to the non-linear design cause the difficulty to feel weirdly uneven at times (i.e. You a struggling a bit to make past an area, then you move to the next and you are steamrolling poor suckers and bi-shotting mini-bosses) but when it's at its highest it's almost unbelievably good.And my god, what they did with the landscape design is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ outstanding in some cases (especially moving past the first region, arguably the dullest of the bunch) and interacting with it, finding traversable points, exploring landscape markers etc becomes a significant part of the gameplay on its own.Overall, there are genuinely moments you have to stop for a second and wonder how the hell did they achieve something on this scale and with this level of quality.But sure, you can nitpick and do the usual Souls connoisseur skit with the great classic "ACTUALLY, I liked Dark Souls X better, because...".it's fine, anyone can even preferences and they don't even need to be rationalized strongly. But objectively speaking this one IS their Magnum Opus so far, even people who won't particularly love it will have to admit it after spending enough hours on it.There may be minor things where I rank the previous titles higher (Sekiro is still unmatched for the best boss battles mechanically, for one) but as an overall product it feels like a no-contest. Elden Ring dwarfs From's previous releases in the long run.What's crazy is that I must have something like 70 hours or so of actual gameplay on record so far and my opinion of it keeps improving as the hours go, despise some of the flaws becoming more apparent as well.Just days ago, playing a bit just to kill some time but with no real goal to progress toward, I realized beating a certain boss the day before opened the access to a new area in another part of the world. I dived in to see what kind of easter egg I was setting myself for  ("Will it be an optional arena with a boss?") and it turned out to be an entire new subterranean region, that forked in more than one way, opening access to yet ANOTHER region far away and connecting to previous subterranean areas I visited before.I've never seen anything like this in years of gaming.Do I think it deserves a 10? Not Sure, I don't particularly care for putting it in numbers. But I'm more for the "yes" than for the "no". It's outstanding in far more ways that it is occasionally flawed.And a "10" for me represents nothing less and nothing more than "excellent".P.S. I'll say it upfront: people who love to argue that "a 10 means perfection and no game is perfect, so no game should ever deserve a 10" are mouth-drooling morons.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not really the target audience for Elden Ring given it's a souls-like, but if that is your cup of tea, this game is phenomenal. Despite really, really not being the game for me, it was mechanically engaging with beautiful visuals and audio. Although capped at 60 fps, it runs buttery smooth and never drops frames on my system. The story is complicated, a little too complicated for a game who's target audience is just going to roll and slash through all the bosses without really paying attention to any cut scenes or flavor text. Some are saying its the greatest open world game they have ever played, to those I say stop playing souls-like games and actually branch out. Elden Ring's world is jam packed with content and enemies, but it always felt small to me and too easily traversed to really be compared to any other large open world game. Lets be realistic, if you think this is GOTY or even comparable to other great classic titles like RDR2 or BoTW, then you already think that FromSoftware's next game is GOTY for 2023 or 2024. My only real complaint is that the multiplayer is HORRIBLE. Despite being the most accessible souls-like game for newcomers, no one thought to allow players to opt out of invasions. Definitely a lost opportunity. The game is hard enough without getting sweat on by people who have never seen the outside world. Playing with friends is clunky, unintuitive, and tied to an in-game item that you have to grind for. FromSoftware clearly walked down the street and pulled the multiplayer design from Nintendo who is known ubiquitously for their HORRIBLE multiplayer implementation. Had the multiplayer been more sound, I likely would not have given up on the game at 14 hours in.

_childDocuments_.review: The posibilities how to start this review are numerous. But i think to adress the biggest change to what fromsoft has done before let's talk about...Even though this is Fromsoft's first shot at a real open-world, they did an amazing job with it. The first time I started up the game and came into the open world I just got lost in it. Not like I didn't know where to go because while the game doesn't give you specific directions in form of waypoints, some points of grace (that's what the bonfires/checkpoints are called in this game) have rays of light attatched to them which point in the direction where the story countinues.But no what i meant with getting lost is that i could just ride around in the open-world forgetting about time and just roaming around stumbling from one quest into another, finding dungeons, fighting fieldbosses and before you know it, you rode your trusty horse torrent around for 4 hours. You may not have countinued the story and yet, it's not at all like you didnt do anthing in this time.Elden Ring really does reward exploring of the world. Be it more healing items you can pick up or another area you wouldnt have expected. In one of the first forests I explored I happened to stumble upon a circle shaped building. I didnt think much of it at the time since i was on my way to a castle I spotted on the horizon. After examining the castle I went back to that building I passed in the forest, which i marked on the map so I wouldnt forget about it (I can only recommend to take advantage of the marker tool since you might forget some points of interest with this much to see in the world). Turns out the building was an elevator and brought me far down below the plains I wandered before. On the ride down the wall before me opend up a bit and revealed an underground area with a sky made of sparkling gems resting above it. This is only one of the stunning views you get to see while exploring. Traveling the lands between is not fun and games though. Of course, in these chaotic times the world is littered with enemies. Not just grunts but bosses like giant knights on armored horses or dragons as well. While you encounter most bosses in dungeons you shouldn't go around with a sense of security since although grunts, may just be grunts they are deadly grunts. While we're on the topic let's get into...For those of you who didn't have the pleasure to enjoy any of the dark souls games yet, I'll just give a quick summary of the most used combat strategie: You look how the enemie is winding up their attack, wait for the strike and then dodge through it. After successfully avoiding the attack you either have a short opportunity to deal damage, which consists for most players just spaming the rb button, or have to dodge out of the way of the next attack. If you didn't time your roll right it's retreat and heal. That's basically what combat consisted of in the dark souls games. The third installment of the series introduced also something called weapon arts. Weapon arts are possesed by every weapon in the game and are a unique move of attack that uses up mana. In Dark Souls III I personally rarely used it tho since the risk-reward factor of hitting such an attack to the damage it dealt just wasn't worth it.In Elden Ring some major improvements were made even though Fromsoft might have overdone it in some aspects. The one thing that is responsible for the biggest change in combat is the new poise stat, that was added by the devs. You can imagine poise as another bar besides the health bar. When it runs out the enemy gets staggered and you get to perform a critical strike that deals massive damage (It is simmular to sekiro but differs in that you cant actually see the bar). How does that change the gameplay you might ask yourself now. Well it gets the player to vary their attacks more. As already mentioned combat mostly relied on the rb button or light attack. Light attacks don't do much damage to the poise of an enemy though. So the player has to decide if they solely want to rely on the damage of their light attacks or risk a longer heavy attack to not only deal damage but bring down the enemy's poise as well. Over all you can play Elden Ring combat whise just like the old dark souls games but there is a good new alternative.The Weapon skills are where Fromsoft might have overdone it a little. There are two or three weapons in the game which let you one shot some bosses or just let you cancel enemies attacks, making some passages a bit too easy in my opinion. If you dont want this you can of course just leave your fingers off of 'em.In conclusion, combat whise Elden Ring improved on Dark Souls and Sekiro massively as well.Last but not least there is still one thing left...I'm sad to say, the story is probably not going to be something for everyone. In typical Fromsoft manner, you don't just get the story presented on a silver plate. You have a main story line and yet it might confuse you in some parts. The story is told, not just with cutscenes but with item descriptions, side quests, and dots you have to connect by yourself. The game tells the tales of many dark but also some brighter fates. Be it the swordswoman malenia just trying to desperately protect her brother. Or General Rahdan rotten but Malenia's curse, seeking out one last battle, worthy of a warrior's death and not perish from sickness. All of which, you kinda have to figure out for yourself.To sum it all up: Fromsoft created a masterpiece. They did hell of a job on their open-world and designed their bosses with just as much passion and creativity. The exploring always stays interesting and the combat is very enjoyable. The combination of all this makes up this addicting magnum opus of a game.In my opinion this is a must play title and i can only recommend it to everyone considering getting it just the slightest. Most of all with a dlc on the horizon

_childDocuments_.review: Let’s get a few things straightened out here. You know what Elden Ring is. I don’t have to explain it. I have fully beaten Elden Ring twice. I think it is, overall, a good game. But it is  a masterpiece like you may have heard. It has its amazing upsides, but significant downsides as well. I want you, the reader, to decide if this game is right for you.Let’s get started with the basics. Elden Ring’s core gameplay loop is the Fromsoft Souls classic; you attack the enemy and roll to dodge through attacks. However, it is also sort of an amalgamation of all previous popular Fromsoft games. The stealth from Sekiro returns, as well as the jump button. The speed of combat returns from DS3 and Bloodborne, with enemies faster than ever before. And long forgotten mechanics from the underappreciated Dark Souls 2 return, like powerstancing, the ability to combine two weapons of the same class for a unique dual wield moveset.Frankly, there are too many mechanics to cover in a review that has a character limit. But the CORE of the combat is still the same as before. If you like Dark Souls, Bloodborne, or Sekiro, you’ll most likely like this.However, as you know, Elden Ring is open world, a first for Fromsoft. This means that enemies can come from anywhere, at any time. You have to be on alert constantly or else you can easily find yourself stuck in a massive ambush. On the plus side, this means a lot of player engagement and freedom. But, on the other hand, it means a LOT of content is missable or, frankly, not worth your time. Any dungeon you encounter can either gift you with your new favorite weapon, a core spell for your arsenal, or even a fantastic new talisman. Or, that same dungeon could give you something completely irrelevant to your current build, like a katana for your strength pure, or a faith weapon on your sorcerer. This makes exploring and discovering a treat, but also somewhat tedious, and often kills replayability. What’s the point in going through an open world full of secrets when you know every secret, and know 90% of them aren’t important?Where the game truly shines are in its legacy dungeons, giant sprawling fortresses and cities reminiscent of Sekiro or the levels of the Souls series. The perfectly paced enemies, dense layout, and unlockable shortcuts and checkpoints make them a joy to go through. But on the negative side, the rest of the dungeons range from alright to outright miserable. The vast majority of them follow the same cookie cutter design of cramped tomb tunnels or dug out caves, and they get old pretty fast.That leads to a core criticism of the gameplay as a whole: while the core loop is quite enjoyable, you’ll soon realize a lot of assets get reused throughout the game. Many minibosses are simply late game common enemies with a health bar that give mediocre rewards on defeat. Some enemy types are continuously reskinned to suit the new area. As an example, the basic soldier enemy is reskinned to be a regional soldier for nearly every single area in the game, with little to no change in moveset, regardless of their army or colors. Some minibosses are re-used up to 10+ times, and it gets very tiresome to see the new flavor of the month reskin after reaching the end of another copy and paste dungeon.But the biggest criticism I have for the game is the bosses. With Bloodborne, DS3, and Sekiro, Fromsoft showed they have the true talent for making a memorable and difficult, but balanced boss experience. Sadly, they dropped the ball somewhat for Elden Ring. Many bosses are rather “cheap” in nature, relying on insanely heavily delayed animations to bait and catch rolls, or on input reading, an AI tactic where the enemy reacts the same frame you press a button to give them the perfect response at your detriment and beyond any human’s possible reaction time. Endgame bosses especially feel heavily overtuned, either crammed full of gimmicks, like spraying lingering bleed-inflicting flames on the ground, healing on every hit, and inflicting HP drain, or simply having gargantuan health bars and dealing 900+ damage on every hit, turning even a glancing blow into a sudden life or death situation.I still think the gameplay and bosses as a whole lean more on the positive side. But they distinctly have their flaws, and players NEED to remember to use every tool at their disposal. Even though it plays like a Souls game, it is NOT balanced like one, and will severely punish you for assuming you can approach it like one.As for the story, it is quite excellent. Those familiar with Fromsoft lore can expect the usual vageueness  & bits and pieces of scattered story to be found. Elden Ring definitely has a much denser history compared to the Souls series, but that makes it more satisfying to piece together.And thankfully, Fromsoft provided us with a key NPC, Gideon the All-Knowing, to provide us key information about who we need to be killing and where they are. His addition is invaluable as a player resource.Simply put, the game looks absolutely phenomenal. I do have my distinct issue with the color palette; that it clearly needs to remember colors other than gray exist in some areas, ESPECIALLY in dungeons, but the special effects and enemy designs are 100% on point. The open world especially looks reasonably believable and realistic, with every region having its distinct atmosphere that sets it apart from the others. You can load into the game anywhere and immediately know where you are just based on your surroundings.The “Remembrance” bosses especially hold absolutely nothing back, with strikingly unique designs and insane levels of SFX and color variety. They alone help the game stand out.Thankfully, no criticisms in this category. Weapons feel meaty, attacks have weight, and the music is still up to the historically excellent Fromsoft standard. Not much needs elaborating; look up the OST for Godskin Apostles or Mohg, Lord of Blood. You’ll be hooked in seconds.Elden Ring is VERY demanding in the specs department, and to top it off, its capped at 60 FPS. Even with good specs like mine, I would still suffer frame drops in areas.Most concerningly, the Elden Ring multiplayer servers at the moment are an absolute MESS. At pure random, you can suffer a “connection error” and completely disconnect from your host, whether you be invader or ally. This is thanks to the horrible implementation of Easy Anti-Cheat. I cannot physically count on all my digits how many times I was helping a host beat an endgame boss and got booted out of the session with ZERO warning either a mere minute after joining or significantly into the fight. Solo play using spirit ashes or NPC summons is unaffected, but temper your expectations if you’re a career invader or sunbro.At the end of the day, I had a net positive experience with Elden Ring. The world was very enjoyable to explore, and most of the major story bosses that actually had some thought put into them are very memorable and exciting. However, if you decide to play, you NEED to be prepared for the rotten apples in the basket. Be willing to use every tool at your disposal to win; because Elden Ring certainly will.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like dark souls or any souls like game, play this. If you like breath of the wild or any open world game, play this.Idk, just play this. Give it a chance if you aren't used to this type of gamed.FromSoftware never fails to deliver with the quality of their games. The amount of though that goes into creating the background stories and the environments of this game is unrivalled. This is one of the finest open world games to ever be made. You may be familiar with the classic open world games that studios like ubisoft is making now, go here do this. go there do that. This game is not like that. Exploring is one of the best things about this game and it truly feels rewarding. This game is full of content not just filler. There are so many unique situations that are wonderful. From enemies to friendly npcs and their stories and to weapons there is a huge variety of content. Heck I'm 95 hours in and I havn't finished the game yet but none of it has felt like a chore. I've enjoyed all of it and it 's definitely my favourite game of all time.There are a lot of people getting stuck on this game either saying it's too hard or that it should have a quest log. Some people are seeing the first hard enemy they find and giving up because they can't beat it. You don't have to! It's an important lesson that you can leave that challenge for later and just explore the world. Not having a quest counter makes this game much better. As people have suggested if you really want to you can get a pen and paper to help you remember characters. Don't complain that this is dumb because you aren't in school anymore. I'm sure you can manage. It makes the game so much more natural. You aren't meant to complete quests perfectly and it Isn't really possible to.  If you miss a character or a part of a quest it may change other npcs stories in doing so. This makes them so organic and unique to you. You have to puzzle together their dialogue and this world in your own way. If you find something too challenging there is always something else you can try in this game. A different sword, a ranged weapon, magic, a summon, bring a friend along!TLDR: This is one hell of a game with rich and vibrant environments with deep lore. With a lot of it written by George R R Martin adding to even more of what we've come to love from Miyazaki. At it's core this game is an epic fantasy open world with great solid combat and it goes beyond that and is so much more as it's elements have been refined over years of FromSoftware experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I normally take Gaming Journalism less seriously than I take a child's opinion, but in the case of Elden Ring they got it right. This game is insane. _childDocuments_.review: Easily the best game I've played in many years, and it deserves a longer review than most of you have patience for. I highly recommend it, and here's why:Like many who play this game, this was my first "Soulsborne/Soulslike" game, as it is the most refined and user-friendly version of FromSoftware's game design ethos. I avoided the Dark Souls series for many years. I had a presumptuous view of FromSoftware and their visual aesthetic that made me feel this game was just sad edgelord material.  Like all FromSoftware games, Elden Ring revels in struggle. Only the most basic combat mechanics are explained to the player; the rest is trial and error. It challenges you to tease out its mysteries, not just of the world and lore, but of the combat mechanics and UI. The game asks you to  (you need to be open to that to fully enjoy it), and oh boy, did I struggle...I struggled to simply navigate the user interface, to find the extra info on weapon damage and scaling, armor ratings and status defenses, even item descriptions full of implicit lore that give the player a small understanding of what's happening in the Lands Between. I struggled to accept that not every field boss in the overworld was meant to be defeated when you first encounter them. I struggled to avoid traps and ambushes. Even when I gave up trying to play solo and attempted to use the Co-Op multiplayer system, I struggled to understand the seemingly obtuse system of items that enable it. Even after, I struggled against skilled and relentless Invaders, many of whom have been invading players since Dark Souls 1. I'm ashamed to say I struggled to not uninstall the game and play an easier one with a more forgiving learning curve. Such was my frustration.Most of all, I struggled to get acclimated to the combat mechanics... Until, a whole 40 hours (and many deaths) in, something clicked. I started seeing and feeling a flow to combat, requiring a skillful dance between dodging perfectly  attacks and identifying narrow windows for my own attacks. I started to understand every movement and attack option's purpose and viability in different scenarios. I started understanding how to most efficiently manage my stamina, consumables, and other resources. I started seeing challenges and opportunities where before I only saw difficulties and defeat.This began a shift in my mentality. The developers were not taunting or trolling me, like many players seem to think; they were inviting me to experience a true power fantasy, to feel a tangible sense of actual progression in skill and understanding. The game does not say "git gud, noob"; it says .So many modern AAA games are released with a product mentality first and foremost, and not even as good products; they are often unfinished, rushed, bugged, and bloated with profit-maximizing strategies like microtransactions. Elden Ring is the first game I've played in a decade that felt like a complete game, full of hundreds of hours of content. So many games frontload their "best" content and force you to engage with it to force your interest, but much of Elden Rings best content is hidden or blocked by combat and platforming challenges. I have almost 3k hours logged, and I'm still finding out new things the game has kept hidden from me. This speaks so much to the confidence the developers have in their vision of an adventure fantasy game centered around discovery.The game is not perfect. There are still some bugs and glitches present from launch that have no clearcut development solution. Many bosses, enemy types, and other assets are re-used all over the map to mixed effect. Some lategame and endgame content feels rushed and spread out. Perhaps worst of all, like all games with an active PvP element, the player community is rife with toxic players who seem hellbent on griefing others into making them uninstall the game.Even with these glaring imperfections, this game shines like a diamond in a sea of coal coated with cheap craft glitter. It stands head and shoulders above almost all other modern AAA games in terms of intrigue, combat satisfaction, exploration, and story, and it doesn't even flaunt it. An understated and nuanced gaming experience is such a delight in an era where games are intended to feel more like blockbuster Hollywood movies rather than progressive adventures. Elden Ring is the culmination of FromSoftware’s singular and robust design philosophy, honed over decades of trial and error.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best RPGs of all time by far, but it does have its flaws. Build diversity in PvP has potential to be ridiculous, but you'll find your options a bit lacking for PvE. The "meta" level for PvP in this game will likely be around 150 compared to 120 in Souls 3, meaning you can get multiple stats much higher and have more build options. Faith covering "traditional" faith spells, as well as pyromancies, blood magic, dragon magic, "beast magic", etc. also means that a "faith build" for example isn't the monolith it was in Dark Souls. However, in PvE, to kill endgame bosses you basically need at least one of the following or exceptional skill:-Bleed-Frostbite-Sorceries-Mimic tear-certain incantations such as Rotten BreathI would not advise playing this game with a quality build longsword + shield and no magic or status effects, and especially not with a plain UGS. Indeed, this game marks the end of the reign of the STR Chads. Well, in PvE anyway. Powerstancing colossal weapons typically comes with the asterisk that you use an overpowered weapon art like Hoarfrost Stomp that lets you have a chance against some of the bosses in this game.That leads to the next topic, the bosses of this game. If you're a Souls series veteran, you probably remember bosses like Champion Gundyr that felt very innovative at the time. Wow, a boss that actually tries to stop you from using Estus, that's crazy! Yeah, FROM really liked it too; EVERY boss in this game uses the Champ Gundyr behavior script, complete with all of its quirks and bugs. Ever notice that Margit will first-frame input read you pressing your Use Item keybind? Yeah, he doesn't actually care if you're drinking Estus or not. If you throw a knife, he'll do the same attacks to "punish" you but you have far more frames to react. I don't even mind that this behavior is so easily manipulated, it's more to the point that it's EVERY BOSS. Champion Gundyr was tolerated as a unique challenge, because no other boss behaved the same exact way. This game doesn't really have a "Gael" or "Friede" or "Artorias"-tier memorable fight, because every major boss fight is effectively a Champ Gundyr reskin. The biggest standout is Malenia with her relatively fair telegraphs, unique gimmick, and ability to be staggered.The difficulty is higher than the Souls games on average, but you have a lot of cheap tricks at your disposal if you want to use them. Bosses can die to fall damage if you're crafty enough: most notably Radahn and Fire Giant. If you apply Scarlet Rot once to a boss that doesn't resist it (99% of them), the fight is now on a timer and you can simply avoid death until you win. If you summon a +10 mimic tear, you now have a clone of you with better stats and this game's patented input reader AI. You can get a better version of Dark Souls 3's Prisoner's Chain and 70k souls at SL1. INT builds exist. The list goes on. This game has plenty of "easy mode" options just like every FROM game does, and there's no way your friends will ever find out you cleared the game with a Moonveil or Hoarfrost Stomp.The worldbuilding/lore is much more concrete than the Souls series: you know who did what and you can find out why. You can actually talk to a pretty broad spectrum of NPCs that know what's going on, including characters who were themselves involved in major lore events. This game doesn't feel like a Souls game where everyone is dead or insane and you have to rely on the Item Description God to explain things to you. As an aside, I kind of resent that the fat man was involved in the worldbuilding for this game. Every major character's name starts with a G, R, or M. Just how did he get away with this?Overall, I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone who has ever played an RPG before. I'm focusing a lot on some of the game's negatives because mimic tear-abusing moonveil-toting redditors won't hesitate to tell you that it's a flawless masterpiece. I deleted my previous review that simply stated "it's Skyrim but good", but I absolutely stand by that sentiment. Hopefully Elden Ring helps western devs figure out how to make RPGs again.

Classic mechanics and concepts, nothing revolutionary or downright botched.With Dark Souls being so condensed and Elden Ring so spread out it comes with a territory, thus lots of reused assets and pretty generic and repetitive dungeons. Everything taken into consideration this is still really good especially given the scale they tried to portray.Yeah, strong point here. Most players won't even experience 75% of the content yet their playtime will show over 100h like it's nothing. _childDocuments_.review: I’ve absolutely enjoyed my time with Elden Ring, and while I’d say my expectations were high prior to playing the game, those expectations have certainly been met or even exceeded along my journey. I can’t necessarily say that there’s enough changes here that will appeal to people who have bounced off of Souls games previously, but it’s such a great looking (and playing) game that I think if you enjoy action-RPG’s in the slightest that it’s still worth a shot. To give you further context, my RIG is a 5900X, 3800Mhz 32GB DDR4, 5700XT - Game installed on a Corsair MP510 gen3 NVME. Keep this in mind when reading through the negative points. Let's start with the positives, PvE content wise: + Trademark Fromsoftware attention to detail / world building+ Fenomenal art style / art direction+ The storyline is mysterious, interesting, and 90% of the time you have no f***** idea what is going on. 10/10. + Completly badass enemies and bosses, very fun movesets to learn and counter - I think any souls veteran or newcomer will appreciate them.+ Perhaps the best level design in all of From's titles. + Platforming is actually fun for a change. Changes to gameplay and other observations related with it:+ You can change weapon arts, so in a way you customize your moveset.+ Jumping attacks are viable AND fun AND can be redirected in a 90* arc. + It feels like the movesets have more directional freedom compared to DS3 (feels almost familiar to DS2) + Lock on works like a heat-seeking missile, DS3-esque.+ New mechanic - Sneaking - It's fun to sneak up on groups of enemies or to sneak in bushes in an invasion.+ Powerstancing seems to me more than enough to be considered viable in a PvP setting,- Dualwielding is still dead - unless you powerstance, you have no running/heavy attack for the left handed weapon,+ New mechanic - Block countering - It's useful in PvE, but I have doubts that it'll be of any use in PvP whatsoever, unless they make the counters come out faster than the R1 followup. + The way the netcode has been handled seems to be the best rendition yet when the connection is good. + Inclusion of easy-anti cheat, so, maaaybe goodbye script kiddies? Mules will most likely be still possible, though. + The PvP scaling seems to be doing an alright job of evening out the playing field, so... goodbye twinks? - Nonsensical input chaining, a certain feeling of rigidness or clunkiness - the game will not let you override a que'd R1/R2 attack when you clearly try to dodge. + You don't get three-manned constantly when invading.My initial thoughts are that the PvP is pretty fun in a casual setting - Though I see some things could get out of hand in competitive settings - then again, trying to treat these games in a competitive way is a mistake in my opinion. But whatever floats your boat. The negatives (in order of most to least important in my eyes): - Lack of 21:9 support for a major release in 2022. - Major performance issues that include sporadic stuttering that can basically render the game unplayable for you. They happen at random. So if you're in a sweaty situation, you can die because of it.  - Absolutely terrible input lag / input recognition on the dodge button - You're much better off setting up a macro for dodging than trying to understand how the inputs in the game work. 30ms delay between button press and release is good enough to make it consistent and snappy in my experience - but again - why do you need to set up a macro for dodging when it was not an issue in previous games? This only applies for the dodge button, as attack buttons work as they should. - The UI is a major pain to navigate on M/KB. The funniest part is, DS2 did it right, yet this game (and DS3) fails to properly make the UI usable with M/KB. So, one step forward, two steps back? - UI by default shows controller prompts instead of detecting M/KB. To reiterate once more - this game is everything and more. Just fix the technical issues and it might be the best game of the decade. I was looking for a single word to pinpoint my feelings about this release on PC. And I think I have it. It is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ disgrace. I expected better from Fromsoftware, after years of bad ports, that they would actually give a ♥♥♥♥ about the PC release.

Sometimes the frames drop every now and then which i hope they address this problem soon- Invisible enemies. This doesn't happen often and from what I've seen this happen with people that have low RAM, on the bright side though...It only happens with trash mobs so yay.- Can get addicting.This game is a masterpiece, if i state all the pros then this will be longer than the unabomber's manifesto so i'll post my favorite things:- The art. The moment you open that damn door at the beginning of the game, I was blasted by a magical masterpiece! I wish i was kidding but almost every screenshot you take could easily be a wallpaper.- The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ music. Let's be real here, every From Software game has boss music that will straight up make you shiver and hyped from start to end which makes spending hours on a boss feel like 5 minutes and this game is no different. Hearing the songs of a bunch of secret bosses and the boss before the last felt like i was hit by a trombone.- How big the game truly is.....It took me about 115 hours to completely finish the game from every side quest to every boss it had to offer. At first i was a bit scared that the game wasn't going to be that huge judging from the map at the start but oooooooh boy i was wrong. Everytime i thought i was nearing the end i just kept getting blasted by a new gigantic area with uhm "annoying" enemies and one of my favorite From Software bosses so far. Basically this game is huge, whenever you think you finished an area....you didn't.   A bonus pro that a bunch of people tend to forget, YOU CHOOSE THE DIFFICULTY! You can straight up go to the first boss level 10 or spend a couple of hours to explore and come back just to one shot it, you can use summons or play with friends OR if you like a bit of self torture then you can in like a solo chad gamer with a club.This game is truly a masterpiece, a magical journey. _childDocuments_.review: Are you a contrarian like me who loved Dark Souls 2 the most out of the Dark Souls Trilogy due to its open world aspects and fun, interesting levels at the cost of interesting bosses and strange gameplay quirks? Did you like Dark Souls 3's amazing gameplay but found yourself bored by the gray dead world which, while granted IS the entire theme of the game, but still might not have clicked with you personally? Do you just really need an NPC you can hug after losing 30,000 souls to a boss you choked on at the last second?Sit down, shut up, play Elden Ring. Everything Dark Souls 2 did to make it my personal favorite of the souls games, Elden Ring does better, adds the amazing combat from DS3 AND improves it 10 fold. The world is beautiful and filled with wildlife, the bosses are breathtaking and will make you cry with how hard they can be, there's TONS of replay value because you simply CANNOT experience every single possible combat mechanic with just one build, nor try every weapon you find, and there's a waifu NPC you can hug to make your pain go away for free and as many times as you like who has... Disturbingly detailed panties? I dunno why they added that since you'd never see them unless clipped through her dress, but it sure as hell there and DAMN she got some taste.Only issue I've had?... Eh, multiplayer is kinda lukewarm. No real covenants to keep it spicy, invasions are almost always 1v2's, and this is EXTREMELY petty but it's a bummer there's no "Small White Soapstone" equivalent so you can just help allies with a small part of a map and pimp out with a small paycheck when your time is up. I loved that soapstone in 2, shame it just has not gotten any sort of return yet but it's not really a big deal.That's it really, it's just... It's a beautiful game. 100% worth the wait, no serious bugs that I've seen, if your computer can run it and you're fine with getting your ass kicked a few times going in, go for it! You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Review from someone who has 240 hours in Dark Souls III punching my way through the game, DLCs, and NG+ with only a Caestus using M/KB.Pros:Open world: It isn't linear like previous souls games. The game encourages exploration. Exploration yields hidden gems and treasures. Its a good feeling. Atmosphere: It's dark. Not fluffy, or bright. You get sucked into the dreariness.Graphics: Spells art is incredible. Some of the dragon breath/flame spells art animation is crazy.Combat: Impact to hits and spells. You feel the weight of combat.Story line: is immersive. The characters you meet come to life.Travel system: is immersive unlike skyrim. You have bonfires/waypoints that allow you to travel. In skyrim you can travel anytime anywhere just by access the map. Its little but makes a difference. You also get a horse immediately.Anti-Cheat: If you experienced DS pvp you know what I am talking about. I am so thankful for having anti-cheat.Character customization and theory crafting: ton of builds and options. Game doesn’t differ from DS much. DS build guides apply. Theory crafting options are impressive. Cons:PC performance: There are things you need to do outside game to get it functioning properly. Shouldn't have to do this. I have a RTX3080 and was getting bad screen tearing and stuttering. Had to enable VSYNC in settings and exclude directx 12 from exploit protection in windows 10/11. Whats you tweak it works 98% of the time with minor hiccups.Difficulty: Maybe a CON. for first timers not used to a souls game. There is little tutorial or in game way to prepare newcomers for the frustration, anger and pain to soften the blow. Ramp up in difficulty for new comers might be a bit too quick without the feeling of progression and easing into it as your character develops. However, in my opinion The game isn't difficult per say, People are rushing boss content and then complaining its too hard. People need to slow down and level grind first and collect gear that helps in boss fights. Many People trying to solo Margit at level 13 with no gear and complaining its too hard.M/KB Optimization: I was hoping that this version would be optimized for M/KB. It wasn't. Same janky M/KB problems.COOP: Same issues as other DS games. If you help someone defeat a boss you may not get bossed killed credit. I haven't tested this fully. However, I helped someone recently and it zoned me out before I could get the bonefire for myself. Ended up having to kill Margit myself to get credit.Invasions: In COOP if your someone who doesn't like them. Overall, I give it a 9/10 due to out of the game performance problems. Otherwise 10/10. My advice to new players is dont rush content. Take your time and explore. Level up. Try out weapons, spells, talismans, NPC summons (jelly fish), etc. Find what works for you.AND GIT GOOD!

_childDocuments_.review: Elden Ring is a masterpiece, having mastered the art of showing without telling. From the get-go, Elden Ring doesn't impose any particular playstyle or route on you. You are completely free to do what you want to from the very start of the game. Where in previous titles you followed a general path to success, Elden Ring allows you multiple avenues and tools to navigate. The game hides many secrets, shortcuts, optional quests that develop the story, simultaneously make you rethink of a path you'll take. The game drew not just from the landscape of Soulsborne titles but also from the successful gameplay. The combat is challenging. No surprise there since it's FromSoftware game. The diversity of weapons and unique variety of enemies and bosses is astounding. This allowed it to be incredibly diverse in design. It's hard to choose a specific thing that makes the game so enjoyable, from the combat system and transportation to landscape, lore and storytelling. This game deserves nothing but praise from Soulsborne veterans and new players alike.

_childDocuments_.review: (This review would make a lot more sense if Steam’s review system wasn’t binary. Just please read to see what I mean and ignore the thumbs-up/recommended up there.)I cannot recommend Elden Ring – a game I have been thoroughly enjoying. It feels awkward to say that I cannot recommend a game that I enjoy playing, but it’s also not something that’s new to me. Elden Ring is From Software’s seventh “Souls Game” and the sixth  game that I have played and felt the same way about.I truly enjoy playing these games. I have beat each one and always felt very satisfied to do so. I wouldn’t consider myself a hardcore souls-fan by any means, but I am a fan. I’ve already played Elden Ring for about sixty hours and can see myself spending many more hours happily testing my mettle against more and more ridiculous foes and exploring the vast environment. I could go so far as to say that it’s the best “Souls Game” yet having learned from their previous six games and gradually improving upon a formula that I would consider triumphant. However - although I adore it, I think few people would enjoy the kind of experience that Souls games offer. The fact is that while the games respect the players’ intelligence and skill, one can argue that they disrespect their time. Although, from my personal perspective, the games do not disrespect MY time. I enjoy bettering myself and developing my patience. I enjoy exploring alternative means of stealing victory from seemingly impossible situations. So, as someone who enjoys practice and experimentation, I accept failure and do not see myself as “wasting my time” when I make mistakes within the game. That’s just how practice works.But for everyone else’s perspective? They probably have better things to do with their lives and I totally understand that. You really have to enjoy bettering yourself within Elden Ring’s world and game mechanics. Most people want to play other games as well or prefer a different cadence than what Elden Ring has to offer, or just don’t like the setting. If it doesn’t appeal to you right away, then trying this game is probably a bad idea.I like carpentry, but I can’t expect everyone else to like carpentry too. How can I recommend the art of shaping wood so absolutely? How can I recommend such a beautiful game like Elden Ring when it requires so much time and patience to appreciate the experience? Especially when most people are looking for “just a game?” However, for those who are looking for a challenge in a unique world that demands you take your time with it, I absolutely do recommend the game. If you think you’re one of the few people who can enjoy growing as a player within the world of Elden Ring, then I would say this is the best Souls game yet and urge you to try it.Or you know, if you’re an insanely talented player who likes fantasy games or whatever, and can just casually beat the bosses, then yeah I guess go for it. (Just know that I hate you.)But for everyone else, the game will just end up feeling like it disrespects your time and I don’t recommend you ever put up with having your time disrespected! In an attempt for ME to respect YOUR time, I make this review for you - the player who won’t find satisfaction in beating a boss after having failed thirty times beforeFun Bonus: I just read an article that mentioned fewer than half of Elden Ring players on Steam have beaten the first story-boss, two weeks after release. It's an interesting stat that I think can support my recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Creator Hidetaka Miyazaki called  a ‘natural evolution of Dark Souls’, a statement I wholeheartedly agree with after my 65h long, all bosses beaten playthrough. There’s no denying that  is a Souls-game through and through, from combat design to stat distribution, but with the number of changes introduced, it’s also more than “just another Souls game”.The basics remain the same: Bonfires are now Sites of Grace, Souls became Runes, you got the familiar levelling-up process as well as all the different combat styles – melee, sorcery, ranged and so on. And yes, the Moonlight Sword is of course also making an appearance. What  newly introduces, however, is an open world. Now, this addition might not seem too game-changing at first. After all, the  games already offered a decent degree of exploration, which could even lead to secret areas with their own optional bosses. However, for , this is an actual gamechanger: By opening up an entire world for you to freely explore, you, as the player, now got significantly more power when it comes to game progression.Of course, in order to advance the game, you’ll still need to beat certain boss fights – in a predetermined order as well.  is not , you can’t just challenge the final boss of the game anytime you want. However, and it’s here where the open-world benefits come in, maybe you don’t need to beat a boss just yet. Instead, with the huge number of other activities the Lands Between offer, you might just explore a bit more and come back with better equipment or at a higher level.It can’t be understated how much of a frustration relief this is. Throughout the entirety of , I never felt like I was “stuck” with a certain area or boss. Instead, I always had alternatives in mind: The one castle I came across earlier and marked on my map (honestly, huge thanks to the person responsible for giving us so many markers to work with), those ruins across the valley or maybe a separate area entirely.Still, and this is what strikes me as genius,  never felt like an open-world that adapts the MMO-style of “this zone is for level 1-20, this for 20-40, etc.”. Sure, some areas are intended to be explored with a more developed character – but that doesn’t mean you’re not allowed to try regardless. And indeed, during my journey through the Lands Between, I beat some bosses earlier than probably intended - and others later. Besides a few story-related progress blocks (areas only opening up once you defeat certain bosses), I was completely free to explore – which was more than just refreshing.My favourite story in this regard comes with a very small spoiler, so skip this paragraph if you prefer. As I was exploring the first open-world area, I came across some ruins. After spotting some stairs leading below the surface, I arrived at a treasure chest. Awaiting a new weapon or maybe even armour pieces, I opened it up – and was suddenly enshrouded in mist, teleporting me somewhere else. As I made my way out of the cave I was brought into, I suddenly found myself in an entirely different area of the map, which looked completely different from what I previously saw. And as such, I began exploring …I feel like  is the game that offers all kinds of individual stories like this. Stumbling across bosses, wandering through different areas, solving riddles, doing side quests - this game offers many ways for players to progress. Talking with different people also playing the game already showed me that everyone got their own pace and route through the game. We all got our own moments of victory or defeat, although we all started from the same position.This makes  the most accessible  game yet. That doesn’t mean it’s easy, far from it. But allowing for options lets player choose their challenges as they see fit. And even just exploring the world always nets some benefits: filled with items, you’re almost always getting something out of exploring every nook and cranny. With the addition of Torrent, your mighty spectral steed, you’re not only given the opportunity for horseback battles (sometimes), but you’re also able to travel fast and well. As every Site of Grace also serves as a fast travel option, traversing the huge Lands Between is also remarkably stress-free with only little downtime.If we’re already talking combat, everything you expect is here. It’s simply great – or at least melee is because that’s the playstyle I took up. Still, I don’t expect it to be different for the other playstyles. If you ever played a  game, you know what to expect – greatness. There’s no action RPG combat I enjoy as much as this one and I doubt I’m alone with that opinion.Boss fights are exceptional as well. One fight especially left me overjoyed for quite a few minutes after I narrowly managed to beat an especially tough foe. I almost couldn’t believe I actually did it, I don’t think I ever felt as proud for beating a videogame boss in months. I’m sure others will have their similar story of some of the memorable fights to tell as well. Because of spoilers, I won’t say more, but as with the combat – you’ll know what you get if you played a game before.  Great music, for example.While I already mentioned the music just now, it's also important to mention how wonderfully atmospheric  is. Again, not a surprise to anyone who played a FromSoftware game before, but the cryptic NPCs, beautifully and/or haunting locations, the enemies – they all make for a very special feeling while traversing the world. And while I can proudly say I got basically nothing about the story, I always felt like I was part of something fantastical, melancholic, something special.That said, while  is a near perfect game for me which I could gush about for hours, due to limited review size, I do want to bring up some criticism as well, to not make this one-sided. I feel like a few more explanations in regard to debuffs would’ve been great, considering the symbols alone (red square with a downwards arrow) aren’t really telling much. It’s sometimes hard to determine if a fall will kill or just hurt. Some areas of the world are a little too empty – others are too large for not allowing us to use Torrent. I also wish there would’ve been a little bit more biome variety early on – the really different looking zones only show up later in the game. Lastly, some boss fights are repeated – , for example, happen way too often for me not to wish for some more variety in these extreme cases.There’s one last thing I want to address as well: Who’s this game for? As you now know, I got almost nothing but praise for the game – as do other reviewers (see the MetaCritic/OpenCritic-Score). However, don’t take universal acclaim as  being enjoyable for everyone. While I love it, there’s no denying that  provides little in terms of accessibility beyond the bare minimum, even with open-world allowing you to follow your own path.  got its own identity, a clear design vision - that’s what makes it special for many fans. But the design choices that come with it might prove unenjoyable for others.  is a near perfect game for its target audience – but it also not very interested in extending that audience, however you might feel about that. In short, as with every game: make sure the game looks appealing to you as well, even with glowing reviews like this one.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the few modern AAA games you can buy at full price and get a huge amount of hours per dollar paid.This is Dark Souls ramped up. The world is bigger, the weapons are crazier, the bosses have more BS moves then before and there is just sooooo much to find in the game. Don't go thinking this will be an easier game straight away. It IS easier but not for any mechanical or gameplay reason. It's easier because you can just bypass most roadblocks and go exploring, find more materials and weapons and get levels much easier then previous Souls games. The actual fights will still be challenging and require you to spend time learning boss attack patterns.The game design overall is still "hard but fair" but be aware that by "fair" they now mean you can utilise just as much broken stuff as the enemies can, and not utilising it will often hamstring yourself.Overall it's still not that super tight DS1 design, but it's so, so much larger in scale that it's it's own beast and an absolutely amazing game to play.
