_childDocuments_.review: I had to write a long review, but I respect your time. If you don’t want to read the whole thing, here’s the TLDR: So, the question is, should you invest in Elden Ring? Is it worth the hype? Is this just another soulslike?All the accolades? Well deserved. Believe the hype because you will not be disappointed.What’s not to like? Character creation is fun. This isn't Black Desert, but the sliders can let you make some pretty interesting characters. I've had friends create Giga Chad or horrifying monsters that masquerade as people. I’d say that’s pretty lore accurate so if you want to RP, the game gives you a decent character creator to make things fun. You aren’t as limited as other titles so let your creativity shine!If you've played any of the Dark Souls games, Bloodborne or even Sekiro, you'll see a lot of what FromSoft learned in their past ventures put in this latest iteration (even down the crappy net code). Combat shines in the variety of weapons you can wield, spells and incantations you can invoke, and general openness of fighting. There isn’t one set way of fighting most enemies or bosses. From Daggers, to Katanas, to rock magic, and even using your own blood as a battle art, you have the freedom to fight however you want to fight. The only limitations are your imagination, and your stats.You can build any stats and use any weapon and that build be viable. Want to cheese magic? Want to be a knight who wields heavy weapons and shields? Or an assassin who utilizes their weapon arts to kill effectively? Want to roll around driving people literally insane? That’s an option. Want to Try Finger But Hole? \o/ The game is great in its openness to how you approach combat. By the end of the game I had reinvented how I played. <y weapon and skills were completely different from where I started. You dictate how you want to play and how you take in the story. I wouldn't call this a masterclass in storytelling, but it is a strangely fascinating marriage of a world out of the mind of GRR and Miazaki's game direction. If you’re experienced in any Souls game, you’ll understand. On the surface there are dragons and magic, and Ice people, and warring families. There’s a fingerprint of the typical fantasy tropes told in a very atypical way. It makes learning about the story its own adventure. I love that lore is explained with each new item you uncover or the environmental set pieces you find yourself adventuring into.It’s certainly a ride and you can totally not pay attention and just hit everything that moves. Explore the world to discover answers to questions in the Lands Between. Speaking of….I was lost in Elden Ring for about 100 hours just exploring. I found a town of Jars, a man who sold me shrimp, a wolfman who became best boy. I found churches littered across the world and one church had a dog with a pope hat in it. He was great. I started investigating tombs where spirits of fallen warriors would join me in my quest to something-something Elden Lord. Most of what I mentioned is miss-able and completely optional to pursue.Then I decided to do the main story events and proceeded to get lost even more. There's a wellspring of content in Elden Ring driven by wanderlust. You'll find yourself checking every corner for secrets. Dungeons have layers where you’ll think you’ll find everything, only to go back and see a turn you missed that opens the area to something bigger.The game rewards you for looking around so make it a habit of always exploring.  You'll discover things you never knew you needed. Even if other players flat out lie to you about hidden walls, I always checked… Then downvoted their messages for betraying my naivete. The environments are characters themselves and each new discovery gives you an answer to a question and even more questions. As you can see, I really loved exploring. Does that mean this game is easy? No and yes. Veterans of Souls games will find that bosses aren’t as hard as [INSTERT FAVORITE SOULS GAME HERE]. For a newbie, its still difficult. FromSoft has made it easier for people who causally pick up Elden Ring to not get destroyed too hard. Ashes help you with fights. Without going into detail, they essentially easy mode.Like I mentioned in the title, I’m a casual Souls fan. I played Bloodborned and DS1. So I may not be in that “this game is easy” demographic. I had my fair share of rage quitting. I found myself being destroyed by one of the bosses. I won’t say which one but it beat me so hard I avoided an area for a while. But if you're a veteran of souls games in general you'll find yourself breezing through the game. It may not be for everyone, but it is rewarding. Which leads me to my final point.While I like singing Elden Ring's praises, there are a few things wrong with it. The game stutters pretty heavily. So much so, I'm sure it's frustrated many players (myself included) during tense moments. One minute you're fighting a boss, then the next you're fighting with your machine to not crash or give up during the fight. With each second of precious time lost, it becomes needlessly frustrating to have your PC become the latest boss as you try not to die.I loved this game. What most other game struggle to give a good 100 hour experience, Elden Ring did it effortlessly. Yes, after a while you can make the case that some of the bosses were reused assets or locations became same-y, but honestly I didn’t feel that. I felt genuine joy in going through the experience (for the most part). I loved exploring and seeing the different areas outside of green pastures. I loved the tomb raiding where I’d stumble upon a talisman or an ash and even full sets of armor if I was lucky. The game respected that I was doing things my way and at my pace. Once I discovered what I could and explored every corner of the world, my experience was transformed for the better. When I hit NG + I wasn’t exploring, I was boss rushing, and even then, it was an absolutely blast. Would I recommend this? Yes. I know I didn’t talk about the multiplayer, invasions, EAC, Fall damage, or a slew of other less than stellar experiences, but I would recommend Elden Ring to anyone who wants to get lost for 100 hours. Its worth the hype and I would absolutely Try Finger But Hole.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a diehard Souls fan, and yet after playing this game, I don't think I can go back to Dark Souls 3 ever again, as it'll feel like some of the, how shall we say, grace this game has will be missing.The game gives you the tools to truly break the game wide open, and from that this might be the easiest and most accessible one of Fromsoft's adventures yet - if you use all your tools, that is. And you'll have to find them - if you're looking for a game that hands you everything on a platter, sorry, but you'll have to go elsewhere, as Elden Ring is a game about developing your kit as you explore and learn more. If you want to see a game where you turn from a beginner learning the lays of the land into a mighty death knight that can dual wield flaming scythes and summon a clone of yourself that fires lasers formed from the stars, though, then you might find something here!Probably the only thing to note is that you'll have to contend with hostile player invasions if you plan to play this game through with your friends - if you haven't played a Souls game before, I'd recommend looking up what you're getting into regarding that specifically as that's not necessarily for everyone. However if you're going into it single player that isn't something you'll have to worry about.If your PC can run this game, and you don't own it, you're doing yourself a disservice. It's just that simple. Scroll back up and click the button to add it to cart now.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to begin...I'm a fan of From Software games and soulslike since the first Demon Souls. Elden Ring is a masterpiece in many aspects: beautifully executed in terms of lore, soundtracks, environments, particle effects, cinematics and dialogues. I finished the DLC (I didn't complete everything because no Steam trophies duh) and I couldn't be more disappointed than this. The DLC costs 40 dollars, which is worth the money only for the sheer amount of things that have been implemented and added to the base game. In many aspects, with some more tuning a bit of stuff, you could have released this as a spin-off or sequel of Elden Ring for 60 dollars and nobody would have complained about it. The DLC is even more beautiful than the base game, I sincerely believe that From Software hit its peak in terms of art department. The graphics are simply stunning, the areas rich and vibrant and you could almost forget the obscene amount of unfairness and incompetence that they keep putting into the gameplay...Almost. My personal advice for such a great company: do not produce videogames, switch to graphic novels/movies/books or something that does not include complex gameplay mechanics. You cannot make a decent game gameplay-wise even if your life depends on it, exception made for your only technically well executed game, which is Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. These are the issues of this game:1. Bosses are completely unfair, hitboxes are completely unfair, camera is completely unfair, everything is complete and utter bs in the DLC, 10 times more than the base game. A single swing of a sword passes over you by a mile and you still get hit, you touch the back of the head of a hyppopotamus and get teleported into his mouth, you press R1 in front of the staggered boss and you do not trigger the critical hit, or you hit R1 way further than you should and you get teleported into the critical hit, the particle effects of a boss move prevent you from seeing what's the boss next move, the 5th combo piece of boss triggers randomly, so you cannot plan to trade after the 4th attack;2. Everything has been designed to screw you over without any consideration about the gameplay itself: spending 10 minutes hitting the legs of a giant furnace that oneshots you just to drop a useless item, parkouring yourself on the roofs of the final legacy dungeon just to find a useless item. Why would anyone even care about exploring a map that's 95% empty, 4% filled with garbage and 1% filled with interesting stuff? I explored and got 90% of the useful stuff during the first playthrough just because I'm obsessive about leaving something behind and boy I will never do it again. Do you want to make a compelling open world game? Learn something from Zelda: BoTW, where any single corner of the map has something quick, easy and rewarding to do, instead of filling an entire area of enemies that two-shots you so you can loot an excrement (literally);3. Map expansion was incredibly linear and boring in the base game, very good job implementing a map that dives deep in the "vertical" dimension, just to completely screw any player over because you just couldn't make a map representation that could be remotely intuitive to navigate. Why not adding some vertical layers you could navigate in the map menu? It has already been done with Underground Map (Siofra river for example) and Normal map;4. The damage the enemies deal in the DLC is utter bs and the balance system around the scadutree fragment is the laziest solution you could ever think of: you basically have a chunk of another game stitched to the main one, with zero connection and zero continuity, except for the lore. You talk with Miquella arm and you are projected into Elden Ring 2. Separate map, separate mobs, separate balance system, separate everything: God forbid you could make everything work organically without needing to add external parameters to make things artificially harder;5. Game difficulty. Now, this is a very controversial point. I do not care if a game is complex and difficult, I care how the difficulty has been realised. Chess is an incredibly complex game but the complexity comes from the well thought design: every piece moves in a certain way and the combination of the moves is what increases the difficulty. Elden Ring is artificially inflated with unnecessary, dull defects or shenanigans just to reach a level of difficulty that satifies whoever sadist is in charge of executing the gameplay design. I wonder how the game would be without broken camera, broken hitboxes, more than 0 quality of life features (hey they added the (!) to new items, it took 10 years but they actually did something good QoL wise) and boss patterns that are not completely governed by RNG. There is a difference between a challenge and playing a rigged game, and the latter is exactly how it feels to play Elden Ring SotE, unless you rig it yourself by using Spirit Ashes and many other tools that devoid you from any challenge and allow you to appreciate Elden Ring in the only way you could: without actually playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Review in progress: Elden Ring is the culmination of FromSoftware and Hidetaka Miyazaki's hard work. It goes without saying that if you're a SoulsBorne fan, this is the game for you. If it is your first entry to a FromSoft Souls-like, this is unlike any other game you have ever played and you must go into it with an open mind. You will die and fail but those exact failures will push you to learn from your mistakes and ultimately reward you with a great sense of accomplishment for overcoming tough challenges. We live in an era in which gamers are used to being spoon-fed but Elden Ring is the exact opposite of what the gaming industry has become.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are new to the souls genre, this is as accessible as it should get without killing the essence of the series. This game lets you go at your own pace, but you need to persevere. From's works are all about the struggle and maybe even the unfairness (looking at you, Godskin Duo), so if you can't handle failure maybe you shouldn't bother.The PC port is clearly rushed in some aspects. You might remember the vulnerability issues found on DS3 that happened pretty close to this game's launch, so I reckon that affected stability in some manner.All the previous aside, this game is the culmination of From's work, their magnum opus, if you will. The previous games feel like a build-up to get here, and it does them tremendous justice. A must try, I'd like to say, but I'm aware that this genre may not be everyone's cup of tea.

_childDocuments_.review: First Fromsoft game that I've played, and I'm already 17 hours deep in just a handful of days. I can tell this is going to keep me playing for at least 100 more, if not many more than that.The game is absolutely gorgeous, the combat is tense, and it looks like there are many different builds you can go for replayability. I cannot stress enough how beautiful it is. Every vista looks like a wallpaper. Between the amazing artistic style and the intense, almost equally beautiful soundtrack, it's a delight for the senses to play. For once, I don't regret buying a full price game close to its initial release.Be forewarned: even meeting recommended specs, not minimum, your computer probably WILL stutter and suffer a bit during the course of the game. The performance issues people complain about are very real, and it's possible it could affect your enjoyment of the game if you're particularly put off by those kinds of technical hiccups. That said, it generally runs decent enough, just some rough moments. I can't recall a technical hiccup resulting in my death yet, which is my main fear with stutters. The main cause of my death is the very aggressive buffering in place, guaranteeing that panicked button presses will result in possibly unintended actions.If you have avoided the Souls games until now, this seems like an amazing entry into that universe for you to get your feet wet. Just don't spoil too much for yourself, and don't be afraid to die. A lot.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: This is my first souls-like.Elden Ring is definitly a game for people who don't like to their hands held throughout every little thing.The tutorial area is hard to miss. Pay attention and you will learn the basics of everything you need. Most will die during the tutorial but its designed to be that wayCombat:The combat is incredibly well done, unique and thrilling, incredibly challenging but very satisfying. This isn't your casual RPG like The Witcher, Skyrim or anything else you know where spamming the attack button means you get an easy win. This is not a Hack and Slash either. It's combat is so complex, every movement has to be calculated with a thought in mind of what you're gonna do.It will be hard and you will die alot, but eventually you will get over it and beat whatever gives you a hard time. That feeling of success makes the journey of dying, remembering patterns and studying every enemy so very worth it.Story: (spoiler free)The story itself, is practically nonexistant if you dont know how the Developers approached it. Most of it is told indirectly through exploring, interacting with NPC's, even hidden in Items and Cinematics. While cinematics are incredibly rare, it makes them so much more special and important.Progression:Upon leaving the starter Area you will come across little beams of Light, graces as they are called. Those are basically checkpoints where you can refill your potions, memorize new spells and level up. The golden rays around them, once discovered, lead to the next area you need to go to progress. Though, this is just to lead you to the main story. You are almost required to explore the world and find new gear to help you prepare for whats to come.I haven't finished the game but im very excited to do so. As this is my first souls-like i got a little dragged down as i kept dying alot. But as i kept going i noticed one, very important thing:The enemies dont hinder you on your journey, they are the journey.Don't give up! You will eventually have that rush of dopamine that'll make everything worth it.10/10 will attack the starter npc for calling me maidenless again.

_childDocuments_.review: There's been a lot of talk about size and scale, particularly in open world games. Elden Ring defies the normal (and correct) criticisms that open world games are full of dull tasks and extensively copied content. It's a game full of mechanical choices, systems in play, and rich environmental storytelling. No area of the game feels completely alike and so little feels wasted.Elden Ring is likely to be challenging for most players, it being a From Software game. It has many of the trappings of the other Soulsborne games, but based on my own experience you are given more varied tools to deal with problems you might be having. My favorite thing about the open world nature of the game is if you are having a lot of trouble with a specific spot or boss, just go somewhere else for a bit! There's always something new to find.The final few hours of the game are, in my opinion, weaker overall. The bosses get dirtier, stats are scaled against you MUCH more heavily in comparison to the rest of the game as well. Elden Ring suffers from what I believe is an intentional design choice that has been made since Dark Souls 1, but it's a choice that essentially results in "First half of game ends up feeling better than second half overall."Basically Elden Ring is an extremely impressive achievement in open world game design, and succeeds in being a culmination of all of FromSoft's work up to this point. Whatever that means to you should govern your decision of whether or not to play it. I had a great time, and maybe someday I'll pick it up again for New Game+. Think I'm good for now though!

_childDocuments_.review: My mother has always been a gamer. She played many various series throughout the decades, but her most recent interest was Elden Ring. I've personally never played any of the Souls games for my own reasons, nor did I have much interest, but my mom would tell me about her grand adventures exploring The Lands Between. She was always enthusiastic about it and I would listen, even if I had no idea about anything she was saying.On April 7th, my mom had a stroke and I found her slumped in her chair. She was rushed to the hospital but, after five long days, she passed away. After the funeral and some time to grieve, I was going through her things and found Elden Ring on her computer. It dawned on me that she never finished this game she was so ecstatic about, so I decided I would complete it in her memory.Elden Ring is a fantastic world of exploration and discovery. It allows the player to cheerfully change course as they discover the next distraction every few seconds. There's hardly any required order of activities to perform and you can serpentine across the world at your leisure.The gameplay is challenging, but rewarding and exciting. Hitboxes are tight, animations are fluid, and everything controls well. Melee combat is weighty and the enemies react in a satisfying manner. Magic is powerful and varied in execution to keep things fresh. Just about everything is viable, so have fun with it. There's many small rewards to enhance your gameplay hidden around, so it pays to take your time and comb over areas you think you've completed.Dueling against other players is also exciting. They're capable of everything you are, so you have to stay on your toes. Be ready to counter their actions and punish openings.Difficulty is high, but not impossible. I spent enough time wandering early on that the first real boss fight was no issue at all. You can also level up and grind stats, if you want/need. Some fights are obviously going to be harder than others, but you can learn most of them and overcome anything the boss throws at you if you relax and read their inputs.The story is interesting, but obtuse. Not enough is explained well in-game, and I relied on some abridged lore videos to better understand what's going on. I'll refrain from spoiling anything here though.I played through the first half of the game on my own, offline. Then I decided to try online when a friend was continuously asking if he could join. Both are enjoyable experiences, but I would suggest offline/solo play if you're a slower and more thorough individual.I enjoyed the time I spent in Elden Ring alone, with friends, confused, triumphant, and even despaired. It's an exhilarating experience that invaded my dreams and had me theorycrafting builds during my work hours. I'll enjoy many more hours in the near future when DLC arrives.I hope my mother enjoyed watching me play and was satisfied with the story path and ending I chose. I will never forget the life she gave me and the struggles she faced along the way. There are so many things I never got to say, so many milestones in my life she will never get to see, and locations we never got to visit.To anyone reading this, please do not take for granted the time you have with your loved ones. Life really can surprise anyone at any time, anywhere. Every day you wake up with breath in your lungs on this beautiful planet is a gift. Spend it together.

_childDocuments_.review: My first Souls game and wow.- The lack of hand holding it terms of nearly aspect of the game is so refreshing in an industry where games go out of their way to have everything given to you and told to you.- The difficulty is what it is, but the sense of accomplishment after winning, after beating that boss is absolute ecstasy.- The art style is dark and aesthetic, and the views of the world are absolutely incredible. From endless night to the endless light of the Erdtree, there is so much to see and so much to appreciate.- The dark art style and difficulty of the world contribute to immersing you in the world and how dangerous it really is. Any enemy can kill you, giving you an almost paranoia for every enemy, as you should. Enemies aren't necessarily considered fodder to keep you busy. They are appropriately placed throughout the world and feel as though they have a reason to be there. Also, the range of types of enemies is great too. True, eventually some early game bosses become late game mobs, but it doesn't feel over used, so I'm okay with it.Look, the game was incredible for me and I simply could not stop playing it, even after completing my first playthrough, hell even after completing my second playthrough and 100% the game. I enjoyed it thoroughly and am eagerly anticipating the time when its made its way out of my system and I can have a fresh playthrough again.

_childDocuments_.review: (Just to lay down my bonafides, since every negative review here is instantly spammed with 'git gud' or some cringe 2011-type beat: I've 100%ed every Dark Souls game. I've done speedruns, challenge runs, the whole lot. When I call things in Elden Ring hard, it is NOT for lack of experience.)Elden Ring has a lot of minor flaws (sparse armor early game, some jank w/ teleporting field bosses, boring crafting, boring catacombs, the hundreds of spirits and flowers I will NEVER use), but I can basically forgive all of those, because the game (at the start) is honestly incredible.However... about halfway through, the development budget totally falls out, and every area is now a ten-mile corridor full of enemies that can 2-shot you *alone*. The placement feels almost random at times, and it gets tilting fast. There is an entire lategame subcontinent with *three* graces. That means, if you die to any of the 2-shotting wolves or patrolling archer hordes, you have to cross the entire thing again. The two areas after that are nearly as bad, to the point that sprinting through is the only viable option.Once again, I can totally forgive some bad levels! Every game has some... but the larger bosses feel like pulling teeth.Trying to beat every shardbearer (major boss), you'll find at least two that are literally unplayable. One early game that is easily cheesable, , and one lategame that is entirely unforgiveable, . The latter has an attack that is almost entirely undodgeable, with a half-second tell that only helps if you're 30 feet away, and takes me from 1500 to 0 in a second. After all the shardbearers, you get the semifinal boss, a damage sponge who can 1 or 2-shot with every attack, who has an entire phase where every attack is a room-filling AOE, and who then phases into a grab machine that will instakill you with its comical grab hitboxes and 12-attack combos.If you can beat the AOE/Grab-machine, you get the honor of fighting the final boss... which has a fun-if-unfairish first phase, followed up by a ridiculous final phase full of camera-breaking nonsense and a very childlike idea of "Cool Final Boss", which singlehandedly ruined my belief that the writers had ANY plan for this endgame. Like, Once the comical, humiliating damage sponge is taken care of, you get your pick of ending! There are effectively two, with one obviously bad third choice where  and overall, we leave with very little idea what any of this was about, what our ending choice even means for the world, or what we've really done in the first place. Yay! Game done! After 90 hours, I feel totally numb and ambivalent to this!There are a lot more things to talk about, like how finnicky quests become with an open world, but ♥♥♥♥. I think the worst thing I can say is that I spent all of Elden Ring planning new runs and build ideas, and now that I've beaten it... I just feel tired... and let down. (But the OST does 100% slap, and I do love Torrent, as well as a lot of the NPCs. 100% A+ for them, you can hug a woman, which is more than I can say about my love life)---EDIT: There is actually precisely ONE thing from the comments I'd like to add to this review. If you see anyone saying Elden Ring has 'six' endings, let me break them down for you.There is the basic ending. There is the true-ish ending. There is a bad ending. Then, there are three more endings. These are all the basic ending with a color filter over the cutscene and a single word of dialogue changed. Nothing new is added, and they amount to: Become god, become god but bad (grey), become god but VERY bad (red), and become god but catholic. These feel like extremely late additions, and they only highlight how vapid the difference in non-apocalyptic endings really is. They're meaningless enough that Elden Ring *basically* only has three endings.Also, I only learned after writing this that the game features a field boss who is literally the first shardbearer! The dude from all the trailers just... shows up in the field with a different name, and you fight him again. Elden Ring's copypasting problem is seriously everpresent, and I've not touched on it as much as it deserves, especially considering how mandatory catacombs are to the game. It's fun for one run, but by the second playthrough, I'd really prefer if spirit tuning components were just distributed throughout the fun parts of the game.

detailed_description: Our Next Game About the Game An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs is a first-person open-world comedy adventure game with a very long name. You and your fiancée are the last two human beings left in the universe. Dogs run airports, along with the rest of society. Deal with alien logic, travel issues, and strange stock photo dogs as you attempt to stay in touch with the person you love, when you both live your lives on the go! FEATURING Bribe Dog, the dog who loves bribes. Secrets scattered across a universe of large, simulated airports, complete with timetables and flight cancellations. Awkward conversations with your canine fellow passengers. An alien language you can translate, to discover the bad jokes dogs write when humans aren't around. A cup of coffee larger than your body. A cup of coffee larger than a building. Spray cans you can use to cocoon the building-sized coffee monolith with festive colors before drinking it in a single gulp. A healthy long-distance relationship. An infinite number of hands that you can use to pet any dog, at any time. I'd really like to explain more, but the game is called An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs. Or, Dog Airport Game, if you're tired. It already explains everything. Any further words (and we've used a lot) are meaningless. Pulling these sentences from the void only adds to a debt I cannot pay. Buy my Dog Airport Game. Please.

_childDocuments_.review: "An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs" is an absurdist comedy adventure game with a hell of a lot of heart. There's a quick summary at the bottom if you don't want to read my rambling. On the surface, the game's presentation is extremely silly, in a way that feels cohesive and eye-catching; environments are super stylized low-poly dreamscapes that bring to mind the confusion (& occasionally, the stress) of real airports, movement items let you pull off some very fun Speed And Height Nonsense, characters are (mostly) flat 2D images of dogs that you can chat with, help out & pet with an infinite number of hands, dialogue is a mix of hilarious and heartfelt, & the music is funky and lively, helping to set the mood for the game & also being real good background listening. It would be easy to judge Dog Airport Game as being low-effort at first glance, going by screenshots, but it would also be completely mistaken to do this. The devs have poured an incredible amount of time, effort, and love into this, and it absolutely shows throughout. And at its core, love is, fundamentally, what this game is all about. "An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs" is (on top of being a game about a lot of sapient and silly dogs) a story about, & an exploration of, healthy long-distance relationships; one crafted with an incredible amount of respect, and understanding, and love. A long-distance relationship. like any relationship, is complex, and requires work. It's multifaceted in its own unique ways, with its own challenges; it's not just throwing your lives & wants & needs aside to be together, and it's not just the pining & pangs of longing caused by distance. You're each your own person, living your own lives, with your own dreams and desires and obligations. Sometimes that's because of the distance. Sometimes that *creates* the distance. But you're still in love, and you still make time for each other, As limited as that time together can be sometimes, & as much effort as it takes sometimes to carve out that time, that space for each other, that doesn't devalue or lessen the importance of that time, or the ways you can be together, because you care. Because you care about each other. Because you care about each other's own lives and needs and desires. Because you care about the lives you spend apart *and* the lives you spend together. It's not always going to be easy, or straightforward, and that doesn't change the fact that you *care*. Sure, at any moment you could break things off, and leave, and maybe to some degree things would become easier. But in a healthy, happy, loving relationship, you try to make things work. You learn *how* to make things work. It's in the act of staying, of being there, being together, in the capacity you have, & with the time you have, that you recognise & show your love. You show that it matters. You *care*. And that matters. All of this is tempered in-game by the presentation & atmosphere & mood of it all. The absurdity & alien-ness of the world drives home the feeling of navigating a relationship with as many obstacles and challenges as a long-distance one. The comedy of the game's world & writing also reinforces the point, rather than coming off as flippant or bristly or discordant to the message. You have tender moments together, and you also get to goof off and banter with your fiancee, because that's a facet of love. You have your moments apart, your "what if"s, your "oh no"s, your "I miss you"s, your "I can't wait to tell you about it"s, because that's love, too. The bones of this game, the foundations, are made of love. The game is a conversation about love. It is poignant, it is funny, it is heartfelt and bittersweet, and it is beautiful. An incredible amount of care and understanding and dedication was poured into this game. It shows. TL;DR - The game is a pinprick of light in a dark world. I laughed! I cried! I laughed so hard I cried! I got to pet a lot of dogs! And in the end, after all the getting lost, all the fetching, and being bribed, and getting cursed, all the kidnapping, and being threatened by a dog with a gun asking about the fear in my heart, and existential dread, after all the time being trapped in cages by Cage Dog, the 9 foot tall dog who loves cages - it was worth it. It mattered.

_childDocuments_.review: Can you imagine seeing your pet dog or cat taking the floor in your daily actions? That Cats & Dogs movie where both are spies infiltrating our lives. The aliens we love so much but don't recognize internally and purely. Well, this is the game that if you've ever dreamed about this topic, you'll find a small part of it. When human beings find the processes for an alternative dimension and the construction of their civilizations are more concrete and advanced, perhaps something similar will be found where the planet of our beloved guardians is sheltered in time and space. Until then, you'll find yourself in an airport guarded by dogs and felines traveling with your beloved who, lost in a timeless journey, must find a way to return to your place of origin where humans guard the airports. There are a total of 6 airports and to find your way in this galaxy, you'll have to understand their language and way of thinking. A comical and quaint journey into the alternatives of a universe that, in the eyes of the developer, are the vagaries that are, to a certain extent, all around us too.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright.  is done and dusted. Let's see. What to say about this game?The story is that you and your girlfriend/fiancée are the last two humans alive in the multiverse and are caged by a very large dog who was supposed to be catering your celebratory dinner. And so, you escape said cage and find yourself in an existential airport...for aliens...run by dogs. Your girlfriend asks you to meet her at a different airport, thus giving you a chance to remember more about how and why you both ended up where you are. In the process of doing so, you will meet and befriend a number of dogs and a couple  dogs as well. Eventually, through your initial wanderings, and then meeting up with your girlfriend at various locations, you will unlock the truth as to why you are here and perhaps where you are going.Most of the dogs are presented as cardboard with dog pictures attached, and honestly, it is charming AF. And the dogs are by and large hilarious. They each have a bit of a story to tell (some more than others) and many have fetch quests to give you (because dogs and playing fetch). Which will involve visiting the various airport shops, kiosks, and bathrooms to acquire said items. You will also need to acquire boarding passes to travel to different airports, such as one in Elf lands and one on Uranus. :)The items you acquire are also kind of hilarious in application. Such as delicious toilet water, the forbidden chocolate donuts, a magic wand, scrumptious shoes, etc...And the sounds used in this game also err on the side of completely ridiculous and funny. This dimension is quirky as hell. Visually, it's a bit more of soft tones and pleasant/comfortable artwork. Pretty chill overall.Ultimately, that is the game. It's a very funny romp through various airports interacting with various ridiculous personalities until you eventually reach the end, which in and of itself, actually deviates from the hilarity of the rest of the game and goes with a bit of wistful sadness. Which is a bit of a departure (you know, because airports) from the rest of the game, but makes sense in context.I ran everywhere and it took me about three and a half hours to both reach the ending and get 100% cheevos. I thought that while it had moments of being a little bit boring, going back and forth between various airports while being mindful of the boarding time your boarding passes have listed on them (which is also a gameplay mechanic here), it was still a fun and quirky experience overall. And is fairly unique in both its presentation and mood. I think this is a game best bought on sale but also is one that is worthwhile to check out. It's super casual and I think the laughs will be there for most people throughout the adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay in Airport for Aliens is too repetitive for how long it takes the story between Krista and your character to unfold. I would explore each destination where I was supposed to meet Krista (and/or where I needed to go for an item for a side character/dog) pretty thoroughly on the first visit so once the destinations started repeating there really wasn't much to do other than meet her, read the story, and find out the next destination.Actually getting on the flight is the primary gameplay loop which consists of:1. Getting a boarding pass and deciphering what gate number is printed on it.2. Finding the gate and passing time w/ coffee or rest (sitting or sleeping) until your boarding time.3. Talking to 1 of 2 gate agents to be told what item the dog wanted before letting you on the plane.The first time performing 1, it was a mild challenge but once you understood the symbols it was never a challenge after that.The first time performing 2 was a challenge at each destination until you became familiar with the terminal layouts.The problem with 3--aka the "item hunt"--is that all the shops at every terminal are identical in design, with the same dog picture, and same dialog. This just became a chore--and I learned very early on to have at least 1 of every item in my inventory. I think I carried a cabinet around until the second-to-last flight when one of the boarding gate dogs finally asked for it! Basically, being a hoarder pays off in the game because you don't have to slog through the same tired dialog at a shop over and over.Another example of the story being too long is that I unlocked 100% of the achievements 3 or 4 hops/terminal visits before the story ended so I had even less incentive to explore.I tried to give this game a fair shake. The first time I played it I wasn't enjoying it and put it down but came back to it recently and restarted to see if I felt different--I didn't, but I stuck it out to the end to see if the story would pay off and I don't think it really did.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a 'dog person' so this game looked intriguing. I had it on my wish list and picked it up, on sale. Having spent many hours in airports run by dogs, I have very mixed feelings. It is a silly, somewhat mindless game with the biggest challenge being to find specific characters, objects and gates in each of 6 airports. Woven into this is a love story about a long distance relationship between you and Krista (the last two humans left on the planet). Your busy lives intersect at airports and it is sweet to watch the relationship unfold through many brief encounters.  Although each airport has very different geography, there is a lot of repetition (the same shops, the same vendors, and much of the same dialog).Airports Run by Dogs can be approached for achievements (which are easily earned by performing some basic tasks, visiting all airports, and locating a handful of characters) or for completion (locating all characters of interest and finishing the side-quests associated with each). Or, you could simply travel through the airports, taking in the sights and meeting up with Krista. I will say that the developers did a great job of capturing the insanity of air travel ... delays, cancellations, confusion, lack of direct flights, and bureaucracy. And, of course, the dogs are cute!The game allows free exploration and you can collect/purchase a ridiculous amount of inventory. Cash is unlimited (evidently dogs do not place any value on currency) and one's holdings soon grow very large. Items are cycled through with a key stroke. At times, this becomes a bit cumbersome. Since you never know what items you will need, it is worth it to have a huge stash. I'd encourage you to 'use' everything you acquire as there are a number of objects with interesting properties. There is also a bit of jumping and riding updrafts. When you fall off an edge, the game is quite forgiving and just puts you back on solid ground at the airport entry point.Early on, I had 100% of the achievements, but was missing quite a few characters and side-quests (as evidenced by incomplete entries in my 'Pupperdex' which catalogs such things). Despite my neutral feelings about this game, it is oddly addictive. I keep coming back to it, trying to complete my Pupperdex by finding all dogs and running all errands. Evidently, my immediate future holds quite a bit of air travel!I'd recommend this title to those who want a very light-hearted game with minimal challenge and some interesting areas to explore. And, if you love dogs, that will be a plus! For  those with a heart for discovery and time on their hands, there are many additional 'aha' moments if you gather a host of objects, play with them, and talk to every dog you can find,

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so the game was great for the tutorial zone and the 1st area you go to, you could ♥♥♥♥ around and spend a lot of time there seeing stuff and having fun with the gags and weird boosts and dialogue or whatever. Then you board another plane and realize the rest of the zones are gonna barely offer anything different, but they're all as big or larger. I went from having a great time at the beach zone to slowly getting bored and not wanting to continue, because not only do the other 4 zones not have much different aside from a few unique npc's, but also you are forced to backtrack to every place multiple time either directly by the main quest npc moving to another airport or the fact that the airport you are currently in does not have a direct flight to where she is.This game would have been way better if it was scaled down to smaller areas with no main quest backtracking and the backtracking was optional to complete side quests. Also spreading out certain types of shops to just be in certain airports would have been better with a limit on what secondary gate check dog would spawn so it wouldn't soft lock. If this was 1 1/2 - 2 hours long instead of like 4, it would have been more enjoyable, instead I just kinda trudged through the last half because I thought it'd be over soon and I was wrong many times.

_childDocuments_.review: - Do you like polygons, vaporwave, and JPEGs of dogs? If so, you've come to the right place- To call AAfACRbD—I'm going to get sick of that acronym—an ugly game would be technically accurate but perhaps mistake the intent of the artistic direction. Every single detail from the title, to the concept, to the visuals, is intentionally absurd. As you'll see in the later sections of this review, it's meant to serve as a counterpoint to the surprisingly poignant narrative, excellent soundtrack, and competent writing- Intent or no, it's still a difficult game to look at- The music was a pleasant surprise. The vaporwave visuals bleed into the soundtrack enough that they do often feature open soundscapes with a lot of auditory headspace, but it's such a joy to hear those musical voids fill up with interesting concepts: a malformed chord here, a wrong note there, and unusual syncopation used to disguise the time signature everywhere. The music was stuck in my head for days- In a game with gameplay as ponderous as AAfACRbD's, the soundtrack really helped to increase my engagement. The awkward combination of elements combine to make a lot of strangely beautiful sounds- I suspect that the visuals and music had similar goals in being purposefully "wrong", but the soundtrack manages to create something beautiful in a way that the visuals fail to- To establish AAfACRbD's world, let's explore some of the non-spoilery portions backstory that you'll learn within the first 30 minutes of gameplay. Humanity, sans two people (yourself and your fiancee), is gone. Aliens invaded and decided we were doing a bad job running things, so they've elected to hand over the reigns to the dogs. Tough, but fair. Our canine companions were also left with sentience and the ability to engage in intergalactic travel- It's not really clear where the aliens went after that. It seems that they more or less left the dogs to their own devices. Much of the humor in the game comes from our canine inheritors trying to run things like the humans did, but not quite getting it right- Despite all the overt silliness and absurdity, there's a cohesive and touching story at the core of the game. With your unemployed self and your physicist fiancee being the last two humans, you'd be tempted to think that your planned wedding is simply a matter of convenience. Not so. Instead, we're shown what may be the healthiest relationship I've ever seen depicted in a video game- Of course, the story wouldn't have much point if you were just blissfully hanging out with your beloved at the airport. She's leaving you. Not breaking up with you, mind, but leaving. While the dogs have managed to get a handle on traveling between galaxies, they've only just hashed out how to visit new dimensions. Your fiancee is credited with helping them learn how to use black holes to do this, but she's tabbed to go on the maiden voyage and doesn't know if she'll ever return- The upshot involves some pretty bittersweet vibes. Most of your time in AAfACRbD will be spent milling about airports to accomplish various objectives and having nice conversations with your betrothed, but knowledge that the game will end with no small amount of uncertainty casts a shadow over the vibrant colors and silly jokes- The humor often lands pretty well. Although sometimes eye-roll-worthy (Would you like a boarding pass to... *snrk* URANUS?), those jokes also manage to evolve into funnier callbacks later on (like everyone offhandedly referring to the location as "the butt planet" afterwards)- If you were to avoid all side-content, the general thrust of the gameplay would involve talking to your fiancee to find out where she's headed next, deciphering which gate you need to get to, finding a bribe for Bribe Dog as you're killing time before boarding, and repeating- Side content follows the same rubric for the most part, but a lot of the situational humor can be found off of the beaten path. Helping David Bonie come to grips with his difficult personal history while standing in front of a sign telling me that I should under no circumstances trust him was pretty amusing - Maybe there's some poetic unity in most of the gameplay loop in both main and side content in a dog-centric game involving fetch quests, but those get tiresome quickly regardless of how thematically appropriate they are. You'll spend a lot of time at picking up seemingly random items from various airport shops that you've been asked to acquire- The big obstacle throwing a wrench into what would otherwise be a straightforward series of objectives is the fact that everything is written in an alien language. It's not terribly hard to figure out what all the symbols mean as it's a simple replacement cypher, but I benefited from having a piece of scrap paper nearby to jot down notes- Ultimately, this simulates the experience of international travel pretty well, particularly since I'm a unilingual American who speaks English, a pitiful amount of Spanish, and some incompetent French. Ever tried to navigate an airport in a country that doesn't use the Roman alphabet? AAfACRbD captures that confusion pretty well until you get the hang of the language- Unfortunately, the frustration of getting around large, confusing locations that's endemic to air travel is constant. You'll spend most of your time walking from place to place. There are some QoL features, though. Every moving walkway and jump pad—notably not a real airport feature—can operate as a speed boost. You'll also get a skateboard courtesy of Chad Shakespeare that serves to increase your movement speed- This doesn't seem like the sort of experience that benefits from a replay. I enjoyed the time I had with the game, but a lot of that enjoyment came with being continuously taken off guard by the silliness- Art often plays with your expectations. That's the basic essence of irony, after all: that gulf between what's observed and what's expected. There's so much intentionally "off" about the game (awkward visuals, unusual soundtrack, barebones gameplay, absurd concept) that it often feels like  AAfACRbD wields irony like a club. But in the same way that taking enough lefts eventually results in a right-hand turn, it feels like AAfACRbD has stacked irony on top of itself so many times that the end result is a wholesome, earnest experience- Most media involving romantic relationships seems to focus on the conflict between two flawed people being unfair to each other. It's so refreshing to instead see a healthy, mature relationship between two empathetic people with respect for one another- You shouldn't have any trouble running this game on any device. I won't pretend that this is some sort of hidden masterpiece. I wouldn't even say it's necessarily worth your time unless "fun" and "intriguing" weigh the same on your scales. However, if you have a curious streak and a taste for the absurd, you'll probably find something you'll enjoy in this weird little game

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I really wanted to like this game, and I did.. for like 20 minutes. I don't know if there is more later, but I'm really not inclined to continue, and I regret the hefty price tag. There isn't really a story. I think you and your fiancé are the last humans or something, but there's nothing really beyond that. The gameplay is always the same at each airport:1) Get a ticket (it's always right where you start off)2) Find the departure terminal. This isn't even really a puzzle as the trailer implies, you're just following signs and matching symbols to your ticket3) Obtain both a passport and some random shop item that the gate attendant wants.Here's the problem. All the shops at each airport are identical. Even down to the dialogue and shop keepers’ images. Aside from the music being different, and some slight variation in some characters you interact with, nothing changes between airports. There are a few little easter eggs and secrets to find, but nothing else.The dialogue is occasionally amusing, but often resorts to simple dog related puns. Petting the dogs does nothing from what I can tell. There's also a lot of jank in the controls and how you turn in quest items, inventory management etc. (maybe this has been patched, I'm not sure)This game is not worth the price. Maybe a $5 game at best. I'm not going to refund because I want to support devs. Again, I haven't finished it, but I'm not going to.If you want a meme/surreal walking simulator game, I recommend: Jazzpunk, Broken Reality, Norwood Suite (or any of Cosmo D games), or Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: 'An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs' is an open world comedy adventure set in a series of airports, all run by stock photo dogs. The premise of the game is utterly bizarre, but it works a treat.  In an alternative reality, or future, you play as one of the last humans in the universe and travel through six transit hubs, all with different otherworldly settings, shops, and things to do.  In each hub, your main goal is to get a boarding pass, collect a red passport, check in, and get to the departure gate for the right time. You also bump into your fiancé, Krista, who says ‘hello’, and then tells you to meet her at the next airport.  Along the way, you’ll meet a whole host of wacky canine characters. There’s Photo Dog, who always requires a specific item before letting you collect your passport. Then there’s Security Dog, who will sniff out any dangerous items in your inventory. There’s a dog who has too many cabinets, a book worm dog, Bribe Dog, a dog which sells squeaky meat, and a bartender dog who sells only the finest toilet water!  All of the characters have plenty to say, and many of them offer key items to progress, or help you obtain in-game achievements. Plus, you can pet any of them, at any time, using the dedicated ‘pet’ button!    'An Airport for Aliens Run by Dogs' is a wonderfully surreal adventure. With its simplistic low polygon 3D artstyle and soporific soundtrack, the expansive, but somewhat empty, airport hubs feel dreamlike at times.   It’s, perhaps, not a game for everyone. I can imagine some just won’t get it. But, if you can suspend your disbelief, you’re in for a comical tale of long-distance relationships, alien languages and loveable talking dogs. _childDocuments_.review: This game is quite simply a joyful meditation on the work that goes into a long-distance relationship. In this case, the specifics of that work involve navigating alien airports run by flat photos of dogs, which you can pet with one of your many disembodied hand models (or many of them at once). Don't miss this one, the writing really shines, and the environments and dogs all around you had me chuckling with every new encounter.

_childDocuments_.review: Not for everyone, and I think I would feel differently if I had paid full price for this title, but AAFACRBD is a delightfully nonsensical and absurd art project of a game/walking simulator. There's just enough jank that the whole package works, but there are some issues.The gameplay loop is repetitive. You get a ticket to your destination, you find the gate that matches the symbols on the ticket, you find out what fetch quest you need to complete for the gate NPC dog, you travel to a new "airport", and you repeat. The "airports" are all unique in visual style but all have the same placeholder shops. This is good (mindless fetch quests are easier) and bad (after the third airport it's a bit stale) but even though the sandbox airports are sterile they beg to be explored. There are small secrets/easter eggs in each area. There isn't a lot of a story but what is present is genuine and articulate. Think more Dear Esther than Firewatch or Gone Home. There is a conclusion but not really an ending. That's okay, because Airport is more about the journey than the destination.There's about 4-6 hours of gameplay if you take your time. Asking price is a little high but at the same time I hate using that as a metric. I generally don't buy games at launch/full price because the asking price is never low enough for me, for anything, and games like this deserve to be played.
_childDocuments_.name: An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs

_childDocuments_.review: This game is, on the surface, a simple and cheesy game about a society where you and your fiancee are the only humans left in a universe of dogs. You travel from airport to airport, meeting strange and silly dogs, obtaining strange and unique items. You can find things that make you fast, things that make you jump high, things that pass time faster, and things that just hit you in the face. On the surface, a very cute but simple and shallow game. The game may seem like a basic and fun game thrown together for laughs, but reading into the story contained in the interactions between you and Krista, there is so much more to unpack. The emotional connection between the player character and Krista is one of love, despite being the last two humans. A true bond, not created by , but with true love. Krista herself says that the player character tried to win her over, and that's what made her so in love with him. The conversations you share are filled with friendly banter and jokes and every interaction ends with an exchange of "I love you, weirdo." As the story progresses, Krista gets more involved with her work and gradually more distant from you until reaching a snapping point. This reflects our real lives, how we can be so consumed in our work lives and attempting to change the world that we fail to take care of the small things in live, each other. Krista becomes so consumed with the mission she is embarking upon that she begins to distance from you, and it is shown in your interactions. The banter is toned down or non-existent and the conversations feel heavier. Finally, after she finalizes her plans to go on the mission, you really connect. A heartfelt conversation accompanied by the sunset on Dogdrasil leads to her revealing she's not ready to leave you. On Uranus, you reach her one last time where the game spins that phrase you have been ending every conversation with. Krista can't bring herself to start it, so you have to say it for her. And the last thing she says as she boards the ship heading to a new dimension is  And with that, the credits roll and the game is over.This is an amazing game. The screenshots depict a silly and low quality game made for a bit of fun, but the story within packs a serious punch. It is not what I expected from a game that looks like this, but it was a pleasant surprise. Just buy this game, you won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderfully bizarre, there's a lot of running back and forth, but it's an entire game about traveling around airports, so of course there is. It's weird. Just relax and roll with it. A loose storyline runs through it, but doesn't directly pertain to quests. Surprisingly, it was a bit touching to have to say goodbye at the end. A fun romp for fans of the surreal. B+/A-

_childDocuments_.review: You'll take a lot of flights. You'll pet a lot of dogs. You'll smuggle missiles. You'll beg for illegal bones. You'll have a human heart thrown at you. And you'll pet a lot of dogs.Real talk. This game had some of the funniest, and SOMETIMES HORRIFYING writing I've ever seen. This was the most enjoyment I've gotten out of 20 dollars. Ever. I even teared up a little at one point. If you have a sense of humor, and like the absurdist nature of the visuals you see in the trailer, please play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVED THIS GAME it has everything!!!!- dogs- cats- other pets- it's hilarious, honestly the dialogues are incredible. I was scared the humour would run out fast but you're constantly getting new characters and interactions. I want to replay just for the dialogues- the story: the main character and Krista's chemistry was very sweet. _childDocuments_.review: It was amusing talking to dog images and a random low poly woman for an hour.However the amount of back and forth required doing the same thing/reading the same dialogue just to get to the end of the story made the experience overall boring. I have no clue if there's a faster way to travel between airport levels than doing the ticket and bribe across several levels to get to where you need to go, my brain completely shut off after hour 2.Got it as a filler game from a bundle but it feels like a free to play.
_childDocuments_.name: An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs

_childDocuments_.review: For a game that includes a black hole on Uranus, it's surprisingly deep.Now that I got that pun out of my head.This game is oddly touching for a rather absurd and surreal setting and theme, oddly relaxing, and I swear the visualization of petting so many dog actually does wonders to your mental health.It's simple, easy to understand, and funny.It's largely a walking simulator but the little gameplay there is, is actually engaging.Plus there's a Secret Bear in there that I can pet, so two thumbs up for me.
_childDocuments_.name: An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really funny exploration game set in very condensed & small hubs aka the Airports. You're supposed to travel from airport to airport and along the way you meet a bunch of hilarious, cute & weird dogs that you can talk to (and also pet!).If you're looking for something funny to play, you like dogs & don't mind absurdist humor, then check this game out!
_childDocuments_.name: An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs

_childDocuments_.review: What an odd and wonderful little game this is.  Petting the cute doggos is only the beginning.At its heart, we have a puzzle platformer and lots of stock photos of dogs to interact with in simple but amusing ways.  Underneath that is a pretty dadgum well written narrative which, in the end, is rather heartbreaking.  The writing feels intensely personal and that's not a bad thing.  The graphics and gameplay are crude and basic, but all dogs are good dogs here and there's a real shared experience with the game creator's inner world to be had here.  A thoroughly surreal recommendation for this game, which is oddly spiritual and clearly made with love.
_childDocuments_.name: An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best adventure games I've ever played. Fully captures the spirit of wandering, of exploration, of strangeness and kindness in a universe that's as weird as it is welcoming. There's so much depth to the smallest gameplay features, from messing around with the spraycans to soaring on an umbrella, and the item interactions are packed with such charm. The NPCs are sincere and hilarious and give you all manner of quests, and the main gameplay loop captures the slowness of airports. You'll spend a lot of time wandering from place to place, literally whiling away the hours before your flight, getting together everything you need to get on your plane. You'll also encounter a dog with the largest hat known to dog-kind.
_childDocuments_.name: An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs

_childDocuments_.review: What a treat. What a delight. Zooming around the airports on (or I suppose just holding) my skateboard, utilising umbrella movement and changing the flow of time with coffee. Deciphering alien signs to find the right departure gate on my ticket. Free stuff everywhere. I wish earth airports were like this. Fun fetch quests/trading quests and many wonderful characters. A surprisingly touching story, with jokes that landed for me and many many good animals to meet. A true joy

_childDocuments_.review: An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs, is a long, extended and tedious series of fetch quests (pun intended?), with morsels of comedic stock photos of dogs strewn throughout. The main story is actually really well written in my opinion for such a short game with such an absurd premise, and genuinely made me very sad, even though I think it was aiming to be hopeful.The game has a unique charm but is ultimately very empty. The player could be given a permanent double speed boost and there would still be far to much A --> B --> A travelling. Its environments are large but mainly lifeless, as you spend ages travelling between gates. It has a few different items and various abilities, but none of them are really used for anything other than fetch quest conditions. Overall this game is exceedingly average and NOT worth a $19 USD ($30 AUD) price tag. Maybe pick it up if it's on a considerable sale, and play it whilst yapping with your friends, because the game itself is too boring to be thoroughly enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs

_childDocuments_.review: This is a silly short game that you can have fun with. Is it the best AAA experience of the year? Well it's 3 years old now so probably not. Is it silly and actually requires some thought to figure out? Yes. It's very silly. The puzzle of figuring out which planets connect to which and how to read tickets can be picked up pretty fast. Learning which dog wants what stuff can be picked up pretty quick as well. 100% completion can be done within ~8 hours. The story is pretty interesting and surprisingly solid for such a silly little game.

_childDocuments_.review: I knew it was weird, and I knew it would be funny, thanks to the narrative wonder that is Xalavier Nelson Jr. One thing I didn't know is that it would be a sweet story explaining the depths and difficulties of a [very] long distance relationship. Of course, this is framed in the RIDICULOUS but endearing setting of a universe left solely populated by dogs (*only two humans are left, unseen aliens are said to exist, and some "dogs" are...well, cats).The gameplay here is first-person sandbox-style fun, with mostly clear goals of trying to reach the part of each airport terminal with the right boarding pass and getting past the dog there to verify your journey. Whether you verify via a bribe or you help knock a wistful dog out of its depression, these tasks are fun and make exploring the worlds worth the time. That said, remembering the layout of the worlds without a map can get treacherous, and some of the characterization/fetch quests can be quite repetitive (I suggest grabbing two of every item as you go), but the heartfelt dialogue between the two human characters and the effervescent charisma behind every dog's writing is worth digging into. It's unlikely you've played a game quite like this.If you haven't kept up with Strange Scaffold (I fell in love with Space Warlord Organ Trading Simulator), then I highly suggest you jump on the hype train--their portfolio is wholly unique and full of humor that will help you reflect on what makes us human. Even if that's not what you're looking for, you can at least play this game that lets you pet stock-photo dogs and revels in poop jokes (just know it's a whole lot more than that).

_childDocuments_.review: This game absolutely has the sense of humor and earnest writing I've come to expect from Xalavier Nelson, Jr.!As an added bonus, the way you can stack item effects to do silly movement tricks is a lot of fun. _childDocuments_.review: As heartfelt as it is hilarious. An Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs made me think deeply our current reality and what it would be like it it was all just stock photos of dogs. It also reminded me a lot of my relationship with my fiancee which started out long distance. This game pretty accurately represented some of the challenges we faced and presented it in a charming way. But the stars of this show are the dogs, ALL of which are so quirky and lovable that I could only say that they are all tied for my number one favorite character in the game. Even the cats. The writing alone is well worth the price of admission. The dogs will have you laughing audibly and if you happen to have been in a long distance relationship this is a relatable love story that may make you feel things or cry.

_childDocuments_.review: (Disclosure; key received for free in return for eventually making a review of it. This is that.)See, it's cute at first. The music is jammin, the comedy is solid. But after you've been to the first two areas of the game, you've seen at least 80% of the jokes the game has to offer. Everything else is either repeated, a throwaway line of dialogue that doesn't contribute anything nor make me laugh or a small scene that equally contributes nothing. So what's left after that? Well, mostly just incredibly tedious gameplay broken up by a story that frankly I couldn't care less about because it barely brings much to the table (not helped by the extreme shadow of comedy from, well, literally everything else.) It's possible to see most of the jokes and get all the achievements well before the story ties up and at that point it REALLY starts to show just how little there actually is as it constantly has you randomly jumping from area to area for short cutscenes which take less time to go through than the time it actually takes for you to get to the damn area in the first place. Xalavier Nelson Jr. and Strange Scaffold. I love you lot. You do wonderful stuff. But you spread yourselves far too thin with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a walking simulator with "woah so goofy and wacky!" dialogue, with the main mechanic of the game literally being to wait for in-game time to pass. This would be an acceptable 'quirky' game on itch.io, but as £15 retail game, I absolutely cannot recommend it. I bought this as part of a Humble Bundle, so it was effectively free, and I still feel like my time is being wasted.I imagine this appeals to the "YoWzErS wHaT a WacKY gAmE" twitch streamer crowd who need content to react to, but as someone sitting down alone to play a game, there is no substance here. The fact that you talk to literal PNGs is all you need to know about the entire scope of the game, and just because it's in on the joke doesn't give it value. Again, I don't have anything against the existence of this game, but as paid product, it just isn't worth any amount of money.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most bizarre things I have in my Steam library, and I don't know why it's here. I guess I got it in a bundle somewhere.Is this a Gen Z thing? I don't get it. It comes off as low effort lol so random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at first, but the more you play it, the more you realize this wasn't low effort or shovelware; there was some level of intent and competence put behind it.I don't think I'm the target audience for this, and I really don't think it's worth buying. There seems to be a lot of content, but I personally don't think I would be able to stomach it even if my life depended on it.From what I played it seems to be a text heavy adventure game. You go around talking to stock images of dogs that are sprites that rotate in the world. It's first person, fully 3D, you can jump, and none of these things bring any importance to the game, then you run around abstract airports, supposedly built by aliens. If there's some complex overarching narrative, I don't know. You find items and use them to complete quests for dogs.I don't know if it's an intentional aesthetic or not, but the game's low poly style and crass lighting doesn't do it any favors. PC options are very light, and there's no anti-aliasing, but for all I know, that's intentional too.I think I'd give the game more of a chance if it was more focused and intuitive. I found myself running around aimlessly exploring, talking, and getting items and then figuring out what a dog wanted it. The airports are large and sparse, with no regard for the player's time. There seems to be a complex branching system of choices and possibly the ability to play game multiple times with different paths, but I'll never know. The in-game journal has  of entries for dogs to meet.I'm not going to lie. I installed and played this to drop the Steam trading cards, and then played it out of morbid curiosity. The, again, possibly intentional, garish and basic UI, uninteresting dialog choices, and the overbearing amount of dialog became so off-putting that I couldn't handle it anymore.There's no limit on how many items you can hold, and the game thinks it's cute by letting me pick up hundreds of boarding passes. You can put them in the garbage can, one by one, or throw them off the airport in an endless stream. It was at that point in time I realized, no matter how good the intentions were of the developer, that this was not a well made game, and was no longer worth my time, let alone to write this review.There's no substance here, and there's free to play games on Steam that have more entertainment and respect for a person's time.

_childDocuments_.review: The story takes place in a number of airports, each on a separate planet. These airports are populated by various (canine) characters who will typically have some dialogue and occasionally a quest. While there's really only one 'quest chain' required to finish the game, each of these side quests tells a small story and reveals more about the characters and the world.Unfortunately, the majority of these quests just ask you to fetch one or more items, typically earned via another quest, given by a specific character, and/or found in a specific shop. Compounding this is a mechanic where, in order to fly between the planets, you need to locate the right boarding gate and then complete one of a small number of mini-quests to open it. These mini-quests are almost all fetch quests as well, and one of them requires you to complete  for a different item in order to earn the item you need.While the frustration of these quests can be mitigated somewhat by carrying multiples of each item, the inventory management is incredibly simplistic: you scroll through items one-by-one and there's no way to view a list of them. On top of this, a number of the items are never used and exist purely for flavour or jokes. This means that you have to balance the annoyance of scrolling through a longer list of items with the annoyance of needing to go get items if you don't have them on you. The airports are quite large and so needing to trek from your gate to a specific shop and back can be very tedious.Finally, the graphical style is certainly not going to be to everyone's tastes - as the screenshots show, most 'characters' are simply 2D stock photos. I found this quite fun, and in a few cases it's used to comic effect, but I can understand why some people might consider it a poor or even lazy decision. On top of this, many of the models and effects in the game seem like they could have come from the unity asset store - the low-poly, bright-coloured look is clear and clean but feels a bit bland.From the above criticisms, it would be easy to dismiss the game as not worth playing, but the dialogue is consistently funny and charming, and the 'lore' of the world that's drip-fed through conversations is fascinating (occasionally veering into cosmic horror territory!) The core story, without going into spoilers, concerns the relationship between the player character and their girlfriend and develops into a touching and very believable emotional tale despite the otherwise silly tone.I got just shy of 7 hours playtime out of a single playthrough and, although I did complete all of the quests and met all of the characters, there's still a lot of dialogue I've not seen so I can see myself replaying it sometime in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: A wholesome, chill game with a wacky premise about a couple who find themselves in a universe run by dog.png's. Although it starts quite charming, it unfortunately gets old pretty fast. After the first full airport, you really start to feel how big and spread out the levels are. If you fully explored the first full airport, you already have seen almost all the stores as they are continually copy-pasted throughout the level, with the same stores being in each level. It became a chore to wander until you find the right store to complete the errands the dogs send you on. The experience would improve immensely if the levels were smaller and more densely packed, as well as a better inventory system. I cannot recommend this game, buy it on sale if you are still interested, but I would recommend checking out Pupperazzi instead. It is also a wholesome chill game about exploring a world ruled by dogs but does it MUCH better.

_childDocuments_.review: Delightful dogs abound!Although it does go on longer than I expected, it's an all around charming game, so it's hard to complain and...Hey, it's not like it drew itself out for 20+ hours! The writing throughout this is a joy & absolutely nets grins & giggles, plus the silly secrets scattered about help to break up the main story with fun & peculiar antics.There's a number of said secrets or side quests I never even got around to, but offer something to dig into whenever I might replay this.
